Sensitivity analysis shows that CSI is robust to freemonomer deamination scale and lipid protection, while the 356.96× (~357) fold extrapolated stability ratio (k_U/k_T) is bounded by the activation-energy sweep. The framework is fully stochastic, provenance-tracked, and mass-consistent, providing a rigorous prebiotic pathway from Miller–Orgel monomers to thymine-rich DNA. We further compare our results with the complementary PNAS study of Khosh Abady, Karpourazar & Rentzepis (2026), which demonstrates that UV photodamage pathways act as the dominant evolutionary filter in surface environments. Together, the two mechanisms form a complete two-stage prebiotic model: chemical filtering in the dark (UPDSF) followed by UV selection in the light (PNAS).

papers.title: Assessment of machine-learned vs. classical/quantum atomistic simulations for predicting palladium-hydrogen materials
papers.abstract: Palladium-hydrogen materials are used in a wide range of hydrogen storage, purification, sensing, and catalysis technologies; however, accurately predicting the structural and kinetic behavior of palladium hydrides remains computationally challenging. In this work, we present the first systematic assessment of Meta’s Universal Model for Atoms (UMA), a machine-learned interatomic potential, by benchmarking its predictions against density functional theory (DFT) and two widely used embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials for PdHx systems. All approaches were in close agreement for predicting equilibrium structural and thermodynamic properties, such as lattice constants and cohesive energies. In contrast, simulations of nonequilibrium hydrogen diffusion kinetics revealed substantial differences among the methods. Both EAM potentials predicted qualitatively incorrect hydrogen diffusion kinetics, exhibiting nearly instantaneous diffusion dynamics regardless of temperature and failing to capture the formation of molecular H2. UMA correctly reproduced the temperature dependence of hydrogen diffusion and qualitatively matched the DFT-predicted kinetic behavior, although diffusion timescales remained faster than DFT, particularly at lower temperatures. Overall, UMA provides the best balance between predictive accuracy and computational efficiency for large-scale palladium-hydrogen simulations, with DFT serving as a supporting role to obtain more accurate estimates of kinetic timescales, if needed. Our results show that existing EAM potentials (which were historically the most widely used atomistic methods for large-scale studies of these systems) should be used with caution, particularly for palladium-hydride diffusion kinetics.

papers.title: Connecting Ligand Structure to Reaction Rate and Coordination Behavior in the Undergraduate Laboratory
papers.abstract: A research-oriented laboratory module has been developed for an upper-division undergraduate inorganic chemistry course with the aim to help students connect ligand structure to reaction rate and coordination behavior. The experiments, which have been implemented and refined at the University of Cincinnati since 2021, focus on the synthesis and characterization of twelve nickel(II) salen-type 10 complexes derived from Schiff-base ligands, which differ by backbone linkers and ring substituents. Over four laboratory sessions, students synthesize and isolate the ligands and nickel complexes and characterize them using analytical techniques including NMR and IR spectroscopy, X-ray crystallography, elemental analysis, and mass spectrometry. In addition to learning the synthetic and analytical techniques, students compare experimental observations and data to investigate how ligand 15 structure affects reaction rate, solubility, coordination geometry, and product formation. Several systems provide particularly useful opportunities to examine unexpected outcomes, including incomplete reactions, solubility issues, and formation of a trinuclear nickel complex from a less rigid ligand. A collaborative data-analysis session allows students to compare results across related ligand systems and develop evidence-based explanations for observed trends and anomalies. Overall, this 20 laboratory provides a framework for incorporating authentic research experiences, collaborative analysis, and problem-solving into undergraduate inorganic chemistry education.

papers.title: Catalytic capture of fleeting enamines with palladium electrophiles
papers.abstract: Many reactive intermediates remain chemically inaccessible because they exist only in low equilibrium populations. Although enamines are fundamental nucleophiles in stoichiometric and catalytic reactions, their catalytic use has been largely restricted to systems in which their formation is thermodynamically favoured. Thermodynamically disfavoured enamines exist only transiently and in minute concentrations. Thus, their utilisation requires intermediates with both the stability to capture these fleeting species and the reactivity to drive the subsequent low-barrier bond-forming pathways to completion, thereby preventing the overall reactivity from being governed by the thermodynamics of enamine formation. Here, we demonstrate that low-population enamines can participate efficiently in catalysis through the Lewis-acid-assisted generation of cationic arylpalladium(II) intermediates. This strategy allows a palladium-catalysed α-arylation of acyclic ketones that exhibits broad functional-group tolerance under near-neutral conditions, providing access to transformations that are challenging under conventional conditions. The results of our experimental and theoretical studies support the formation of electrophilically activated cationic palladium intermediates that are responsible for enamine capture and the subsequent formation of carbon–carbon bonds. More broadly, our findings establish a catalytic strategy that involves thermodynamically disfavoured yet chemically valuable intermediates that ordinarily remain latent in equilibrium.

papers.title: Replication Units in Time-Resolved Raman Spectroscopy of Cells and Organoids
papers.abstract: Time-resolved Raman spectra of fixed cells can show reproducible spectral differences without establishing independently replicated biological dynamics. We examined what two public archives can and cannot support. In 450 spectra of LLC-MK2 cells exposed to glucose alone or to glucose plus glutamine at nine nominal times, the glucose-only 15- and 30-min arrays were identical in all 30,000 entries. The fine-scale share of temporal contrasts depended on the processing scale: at 90 min, the residual left after 201-channel Savitzky–Golay smoothing amounted to 0.419 of the full contrast norm for glucose and 0.153 for glucose plus glutamine, and both ratios increased monotonically from 101- to 301-channel windows. The two conditions already differed at 0 min by a distance comparable to that at most later times. An invariance argument shows that, without culture or acquisition identifiers, a time-specific shared offset cannot be separated from a systematic condition–time mean. In a hierarchical null simulation with 2,000 realisations per design, a cell-level test rejected a true null in 52.25% of datasets at intracluster correlation 0.3 with two clusters per condition, compared with 2.30% for a test on cluster means. In a neural organoid archive with three traceable culture batches, day-40 minus day-5 contrasts agreed closely between two batches (cosine similarity 0.755–0.980) but not with the third (−0.716 to 0.502) across nine preprocessing settings. Time-resolved Raman studies should report archive integrity, processing-dependent detectability and independently replicated biological change as distinct levels of evidence.

papers.title: Methylmercury production across an organic carbon gradient in Fe-rich subarctic soils
papers.abstract: Arctic and subarctic soils accumulate anthropogenic inorganic mercury (Hg) transported from lower latitudes. Under reducing conditions, it can be converted to the neurotoxic methylmercury (MeHg). However, the extent and biogeochemical drivers of MeHg production in these soils remain unclear. Here, we investigated MeHg production in various types of Icelandic soils rich in iron (Fe, 40-110 g kg -1 ) and presenting varying organic carbon content (OC, 40-250 g kg -1 ), classified herein as mineral, intermediate or organic soils. Six topsoils (0-25 cm) and three subsoils (70-130 cm) were incubated anoxically for 18 weeks during which MeHg production and release to the aqueous phase were followed together with ancillary parameters (e.g., Fe(III) and sulfate reduction) and microbial community composition. Large MeHg production (up to 11% of total Hg) was observed across topsoils having different characteristics, with topsoils generally exhibiting greater MeHg production than subsoils. A larger release of MeHg to the aqueous phase was observed for mineral soils, indicating a higher potential risk for connected aquatic ecosystems. Total OC content was a poor predictor of MeHg production. In contrast, MeHg concentrations were correlated with (i) the abundance of hgcA , a key gene required for Hg methylation, in a desulfobacterotal group and (ii) geochemical and microbial indicators of both Fe(III) and sulfate reduction. Overall, this study shows that not only organic but also mineral soils are crucial to assess MeHg risks in (sub)arctic environments. Moreover, the extent of MeHg production was better explained by temporal changes in microbial and geochemical processes, including hgcA abundance, Fe(III) and sulfate reduction, than the initial biogeochemical characteristics of the soils.

papers.title: Scaffold hopping from deposited crystal pairs: docking-free contact-conservation benchmark and structure-validated method
papers.abstract: Scaffold hopping—replacing a ligand core while retaining function—is almost always scored by two-dimensional similarity to the reference, by docking to a single pose, or by recovery of one literature ligand, while the trivial baseline of copying the reference decorations is rarely reported. We build a benchmark from the Protein Data Bank: 2,886 ligand pairs that bind the same pocket with different Bemis–Murcko scaffolds, across 27 targets and five families, with scaffold- and target-held-out splits. Superposing the two crystal structures and transferring the experimentally solved hop into the reference pocket gives a docking-free contact-conservation criterion: the true hop recovers 80.6% of reference contacts across 40 crystal pairs, and 97% of pairs exceed 0.6; the criterion tracks pharmacophore overlap (ρ = 0.51, n = 50) but not the potency gap (ρ = −0.13), so it measures pose, not affinity. SV-Hop (structure-validated scaffold hopping)—a 60,069-rule core-replacement lexicon, exact graph swap, property/SA/novelty constraints and a learned contact ranker—returns a novel, property-conserved, synthesizable hop for 62.1% of 298 scaffold-held-out references, against 50.3% (property), 44.3% (2D), 27.0% (random) and 0% (copy). The scaffold split holds out scaffolds rather than pockets, so 97.4% of test pairs share a pocket with training; under target shift the gain falls to +5.3 pp (65.3% vs 60.0%) and the ranker transfers weakly (ρ = 0.13). A 388-rule PDB-only lexicon matches coverage and reaches 81.9% on the same target-held-out split, against 65.3% for the full lexicon, and an equal-diversity control attributes part but not all of that gap to candidate diversity. We release the benchmark, lexicon, model and a 22-compound prospective panel.

papers.title: Sequence order controls silver(I) coordination in aqueous His–Met–Pro tripeptide–nitrate mixtures: an ab initio molecular dynamics study
papers.abstract: Silver–peptide interactions underpin peptide-directed synthesis of silver nanomaterials and the silver-resistance machinery of bacteria, yet the molecular-level speciation of Ag(I) in the presence of short peptides and nitrate remains poorly resolved. Here we report 100-ps ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of three sequence isomers of the tripeptide His–Met–Pro (HMP, HPM and PHM; 220 atoms each) in water, with four Ag(I) ions, four nitrate anions and 32 water molecules at 298 K, using the PBE–PAW description (VASP 6.1.0, 500 eV plane-wave cutoff, Γ-point sampling). In all three systems silver remains mononuclear, with average coordination numbers of 2.6–2.9 and only transient Ag–Ag contacts (present in 2–9% of frames at a 3.2 Å cutoff). The composition of the coordination shell is strongly sequence-dependent: His–Met–Pro is dominated by the His imidazole nitrogen (0.48 contacts per Ag) and nitrate oxygen (0.57), whereas His–Pro–Met is dominated by the Met thioether sulfur (0.73) with nitrate largely excluded (0.16); Pro–His–Met shows an intermediate, mixed N/S/nitrate shell and the largest peptide conformational rearrangement (heavy-atom RMSD 6.1 Å, radius of gyration 5.8 Å). Nitrate and water exchange on ∼0.2–1 ps timescales, while peptide N/S donors remain bound for several to tens of picoseconds. These results demonstrate that, at fixed composition, sequence order controls which donors are presented to Ag(I) and therefore the speciation from which silver nanomaterials nucleate.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
Optical Properties of Different Chemistries of Natural and Synthetic Melanin
papers.abstract: Melanin, a ubiquitous black pigment, consists of at least five chemistries identified by the starting monomers involved in its polymerization. Natural melanin may also contain other components, such as lipids and proteins, that can affect its optical properties. Melanin is known for its high refractive index and broadband absorption. However, most optical-property observations are based on measurements of eumelanin-based chemistry. In this study, we used spectroscopic ellipsometry to measure the complex refractive index over a broad wavelength range (380–1700 nm) for the three main melanin chemistries: eumelanin, allomelanin, and pheomelanin. We compared the complex refractive indices of these materials with values obtained from UV absorption measurements, using an integrating sphere to minimize scattering effects. Our results show that melanin chemistry strongly influences optical properties. Pheomelanin from human red hair has the lowest absorption and refractive index, while poly(L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine) (PDOPA; a polydopamine-based eumelanin chemistry) has the highest refractive index and absorption. We also observed variation in the optical properties of pheomelanin samples extracted from human red hair and rooster feathers. Thus, variations in melanin composition affect both the optical and thermal properties of melanin, highlighting the need to identify its precise chemistry in natural systems to understand melanin's impact on function and performance.

papers.title: False Confidence in Generative Samplers: Exact Physical References Expose Hidden Errors and Diagnostic Blindness
Collision Cross Section Measurement within Time-of-Flight and Multi-Reflection Analyzers
papers.abstract: A proportion of ions travelling through a time-of-flight analyzer inevitably suffer collisions with background gas, resulting in unwanted transmission losses. As collision probability depends upon the ions’ collision cross section, it has been considered that measurement of ion transmission with variation of pressure, or flight path in the case of some multi-reflection analyzers, allows cross section to be determined. A theoretical model is presented, and practical evaluations performed upon a Thermo Scientific Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer.

papers.title: Inhibiting LINE-1 retrotransposons therapeutically in disease
papers.abstract: The LINE-1 retrotransposon is a virus-like genomic element that can activate in diseased cells. It has been implicated in cancer, autoimmunity, developmental disorders, infectious disease and neurodegeneration. LINE-1 can be inhibited by reverse transcriptase inhibitors, small molecules originally developed for HIV. The correlation between HIV and LINE-1 inhibition is ∼0.9 on a log scale, in spite of >450 Mya of evolutionary history since retroviruses diverged from retrotransposons. Suppression of HIV requires prevention of a completed 9.7 kb virus insertion into the genome in immune cells. However, every cell in the body already contains >100 copies of LINE-1 that can potentially activate. Even incomplete LINE-1 mediated insertions can cause damaging mutations and genome instability. Furthermore, partial HIV and LINE-1 products in the cytoplasm of cells can contribute to an inflammatory immune response. Preclinical studies have shown LINE-1 inhibitors slow the progression of otherwise unrelated diseases. LINE-1’s contribution to these diseases can potentially be quantified using single-nucleus whole-genome sequencing on diseased tissue, enabling prioritization of disease selection for therapeutic development. Furthermore, LINE-1’s ORF1p protein can be measured in the blood of individuals with certain cancers. LINE-1 inhibitors could therefore be extended to various diseases. Potentially used both as an anti-inflammatory and prophylactically to help preserve genome integrity. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors are available at low cost for HIV, and higher doses of some could be used to inhibit LINE-1. However, reverse transcriptase inhibitors do not prevent DNA cutting by LINE-1’s endonuclease. Novel inhibitors may therefore be required. This, combined with novel diagnostics opens up possibilities for inhibiting LINE-1 therapeutically in disease

papers.title: Core-to-rim chemical zoning of a Paraíbatype tourmaline from Abulo, Ethiopia: Implications for origin determination
papers.abstract: Copper-bearing tourmaline of Paraíba type is now mined at Abulo in southern Ethiopia. We report the core-to-rim characterisation of one colour-zoned crystal attributed to this locality, obtained in Bangkok in June 2026. A sawn slab about 12 mm across and 5 mm thick was extensively analysed by electron microprobe (113 points), LA-ICP-MS analysis (45 spots on two traverses and 58 isotopes, totaling 2,565 concentration values with silicon as internal standard and GSE and NIST 610 as external standards), LA-ICP-TOFMS imaging (13,500 measuring spots of 24 µm and 55 isotopes, totalling 729,000 concentration values with silicon as internal standard and GSE and NIST 610 as external standard, about 505,000 of them above limits of detection), Raman spectroscopy (24 spectra) and a screening test by ED-XRF. The crystal is an Al–Li tourmaline of the elbaite series, including elbaite, fluor-elbaite, and elbaite with a liddicoatite component. Fluorine at the W site is 0.385 apfu in the core and exceeds the 0.5 apfu boundary to fluor-elbaite in the zones next to the core (0.51–0.53 apfu); 25 of 111 points lie within 1σ of that boundary. Ca/(Ca + Na) increases from core to rim but never exceeds 0.43. Lithium, measured by LA-ICP-MS, increases from about 7,840 µg/g in the core to about 10,000 µg/g in the outer zones. With this lithium taken zone by zone, boron and H 2 O taken from the formula and the unanalysed trace elements added as oxides, the analytical totals of the microprobe are 99.2 ± 0.5 wt.% over 111 points. The trace elements are quantified on this measured matrix, with silicon measured by microprobe as internal standard using GSE and NIST610 as external standards. To our knowledge for the first time, silicon concentrations were measured across a growth profile of this material, in each of the five growth zones of the crystal. The measurements provide 36.3 wt.% SiO 2 in the core, 35.2–35.4 wt.% in the dark-blue zone, 35.5–35.8 wt% in the "neon"-blue zone, 35.9 wt% in the pink zone and 36.0 wt% in the yellow-brown zone. The concentrations of the trace elements are significantly zoned. Copper zone averages decrease from 16,200–25,700 µg/g in the core and the dark-blue zones around it to 1,420–1,820 µg/g in the yellow-brown outer zone. The iron concentration decreases from 4,130–4,150 µg/g to below detection. The bismuth concentration increases from 26–27 to 1,370 µg/g and the lead concentration from 146–160 to 1,650–1,810 µg/g. In contrast , gallium (629–741 µg/g as zone averages) and vanadium (58–158 µg/g at all 45 spots) vary far less. The element ratios used in origin determination therefore change by up to an order of magnitude inside this one crystal. For example, Cu/Ga changes from 2.3 to 41, Pb/Bi from 1.2 to 5.9 and Fe/Mn starts below detection to 1.1 which are calculated as zone averages. The imaging confirms the element ratios of the spot analyses and separates the elements that are present in the tourmaline's composition from those carried by inclusions, which are detected above the matrix composition of the tourmaline. Of the rare earth elements, only the light rare earths, La to Sm, are present in the tourmaline's composition. Yttrium is also present in the tourmaline, at about 0.6–0.9 µg/g outside the core and lower in the core. The other elements found in the tourmaline include Li, Be, Sn, Ga, Nb, Ta and B, all of which are typically found in LCT pegmatites. Compared with our 2009 reference profiles for Brazil, Mozambique and Nigeria, the crystal from Ethopia has higher vanadium and gallium concentrations and evolves toward bismuth rather than manganese. A high vanadium concentration is independently reported for Ethiopian material by other laboratories, and the vanadium test proposed there holds across the growth zones of this crystal, with the core at the limitofdetection. The gallium difference from Mozambique is small, whereas the published Ethiopian gallium concentration extends to 280 µg/g. Because the comparison is based on a very detailed analysis of five growth zones, the reported observations are very significant and represent more information than the analyses of larger sample sets. Therefore, this information is crucial as origin criteria. Individual analyses of samples could represent mixtures of various growth zones and would not easily be identified without knowledge about the growth stage. Any discriminant therefore has to be implemented into the growth-stage concentration profiles of this study as reference. A limited Raman data set, placed on the element maps, shows that the framework bands shift with the copper concentration and that the OH bands follow the fluorine and lithium concentrations; these relations are shown for one crystal.

papers.title: Multi-Criteria Decision-Making Framework for Sustainable Engineering Materials: Integrating Biopolymer Structure, Processing, Properties, Scalability, Techno-Economics, and Life-Cycle Assessment
papers.abstract: Renewable biopolymers are often compared by feedstock origin, biodegradability, or isolated properties, yet an engineering decision concerns a biopolymer processed into a de-fined architecture for a specified application under practical manufacturing constraints. This study develops a multi-criteria decision-making framework for alginate, cellulose, lignin, chitosan, and starch in which the decision unit is a material–processing route–architecture–application system. Each unit is scored on molecular functionality, pro-cessing compatibility, architecture, application-relevant performance, and scalability, with independent evidence-confidence flags, explicit treatment of missing evidence, and bal-anced, performance-led, and manufacturability-led weighting scenarios. Techno-economic and life-cycle evidence is retained as a separate confidence and constraint layer. Fourteen decision units were evaluated from published literature across three contrasting demon-stration cases. Four units were classified as evidence-limited, converting data gaps into explicit research priorities. The framework provides a reproducible, transferable bridge between qualitative renewable-biopolymer reviews and application-specific materi-al-system design.

papers.title: A Unified Theory for Generalized AA+BB Step-Growth Polymerization: From Flory’s Equal‑Reactivity to Kinetic Symmetry‑Breaking
papers.abstract: For nearly nine decades, Flory’s principle of equal reactivity has served as the foundational axiom governing the kinetics and statistics of step-growth polymerization. However, modern monomers with rigid fused-ring architectures or catalytic bond-forming mechanisms routinely deviate from this postulate, defying a unified mechanistic description. Here, I resolve this longstanding discrepancy by establishing an exact analytical framework for AA + BB polycondensation parameterized by a single kinetic asymmetry factor α . Solving the coupled kinetic network in closed form over the entire stoichiometric ratio-reactivity phase space ( r , α ) uncovers three laws. First, a Terminal Dichotomy Law: the A-deficient side undergoes kinetic arrest that permanently retains the α -signature in the end-capped fraction, whereas the A-excess side is strictly α -independent. Second, a Critical-Line Law: at exact equimolarity the terminal dispersity is finite but depends on the direction of approach—non-commuting limits, not a physical divergence; the divergence observed at finite time is a finite-window artefact. Third, a Moving-Target Law: at fixed reaction time the optimal stoichiometry migrates with α , affording strongly asymmetric systems molecular weights nearly an order of magnitude beyond the classical equimolar yield. Within the ( r , α ) plane, the classical Flory-Carothers framework constitutes a measure-zero singular cross-section ( α = 1, r = 1). Rigorous kinetic Monte Carlo simulations (2.28 × 10 9 reaction events over 20,296 replicas) reproduce all analytical predictions and confirm the asymptotic macroscopic absorbing state. As an experimental benchmark, our framework quantitatively predicts, without adjustable parameters, the non-classical behavior of a known extreme system ( α ≈ 384), which achieves a polymer-only number-average degree of polymerization ( Xn ≈153) that exceeds the classical upper bound same-basis ( X n =23) by a factor of 6.6 at an optimal off-stoichiometric feed ( r ≈ 0.91). This work transforms long-standing polycondensation anomalies into deterministic macromolecular design principles and provides an experimentally falsifiable end-group metric to reverse-engineer kinetic landscapes.

papers.title: Rapid, High-Yielding, and Broad-Scope Silicon-Noded Single-Atom Ligation Platform
papers.abstract: The node–module logic underpins DNA, RNA, and metal–organic frameworks. In small-molecule synthesis, SuFEx and PFEx exploit sulfur or phosphorus as single‑atom nodes for 10 modular ligations but are largely confined to amine and phenol modules. Silicon‑based ligation would offer a viable alternative, as both alcohols and phenols can serve as reliable modules, yet it has lacked efficient and controllable platforms. Herein, we report a silicon-noded ligation platform using bis(2,4,6-trimethoxyphenyl)silanes (bis(TMP)silanes) as the ligation hubs, enabling rapid, high-yielding ligation of both alcohol and phenol modules with broad functional-group tolerance.

papers.title: Visible light-driven amide bond formation between carboxylic acids and amines
papers.abstract: The direct formation of amide bonds from carboxylic acids and amines remains challenging due to rapid acid–base neutralisation, which necessitates prior activation of one or both substrates. Here, we report a visible-light-mediated strategy for direct amide coupling using a combination of thiocyanate and Rose Bengal. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions, without the need for anhydrous solvents or an inert atmosphere, and produces amides in moderate yields from a range of aromatic or aliphatic carboxylic acids and α-hydrogen-bearing amines. Control experiments showed that molecular oxygen is required for the reaction, in addition to ammonium thiocyanate. Substrate scope investigation revealed tolerance to both aromatic and aliphatic substituents on both the carboxylic acid and the amine. Notably, substrates bearing stereogenic centres, including amino acids, underwent coupling without detectable racemisation. This work introduces an alternative redox-mediated activation strategy that directly couples carboxylic acids and amines, complementing existing amide bond preparation methods.

papers.title: An addendum to the chemistry of vicinal hexaketones
papers.abstract: This work adds to previous unpublished and inconclusive works on the synthesis of vicinal hexaketone dihydrates. Based on analytical data, chemical reasoning and DFT calculations, we propose that in the conversion of 2,5-bis-diazo-tetrone-1,3,4,6 moieties to vicinal hexaketones highly symmetrical hexaketone hemiketals were formed. Two structures of identical empirical formula (C 14 H 22 O 8 , a dimer and a monomer) are consistent with part of the data and are discussed as plausible hypotheses.

papers.title: Unified Charge-Transfer Diagrams for Teaching Molecule-Surface Interactions
Trans -Spanning Ligands Promote Pd-Catalyzed α -Hydroalkenylation and -Hydroalkynylation of Electron-Deficient Olefins
papers.abstract: The palladium-catalyzed “ anti-Mi chael” α - h ydroalkenylation and -hydroalkynylation of electron-deficient alkenes is reported. The unconventional selectivity of this reaction is achieved through the utilization of trans-spanning bidentate phosphine ligands that stabilize the proposed trans-Pd II L n ( R )(H) (R = alkenyl or alkynyl) intermediate, which is generated through successive reactions of Pd 0 L n w ith an organohalide (or -pseudohalide) and TMA•HCO 2 . The α - h ydrofunctionalization methods tolerate a variety of electron-deficient alkenes including α , β - u nsaturated amides and esters, as well as vinyl pyridines. A range of different alkenyl/alkynyl bromides and enol triflates are demonstrated to be effective coupling partners in the reaction. The method can be performed on decagram scale by implementing DBU•HCO 2 H as a soluble formate source. Stoichiometric studies with CyXantPhos as a model ligand support the proposed trans-geometry of intermediates along the catalytic cycle, and rapid injection nuclear magnetic resonance (RI-NMR) experiments allow detection of the key trans- Pd IIL n ( R )(H) species. DFT calculations reveal that ligand/electrophile steric interplay is the key factor that determines the α - regioselectivity of the reaction.

papers.title: LearnM8: A Simple and Modular Molecular Active Learning Framework for any Oracle
papers.abstract: Make-on-demand chemical spaces contain more than 10 11 compounds, which makes exhaustive virtual screening by docking or another costly scoring method (the oracle) impractical. Active learning reduces this cost by training a surrogate model (learner) on labeled compounds and using an acquisition strategy to select the next batch to evaluate. However, available implementations are built around particular docking programs and need new code for each oracle, learner and acquisition strategy. Here, we present LearnM8 1.0, an open-source Python package for modular active learning in which the oracle is a replaceable function, such that docking, free-energy calculations, precomputed scores or laboratory measurements can drive the same workflow. LearnM8 provides 19 learners, 7 acquisition strategies and 39 featurizers, together with user-defined cycle schedules, removal of compounds from later cycles that scored worst (pruning), per-cycle diversity metrics, saved per-cycle predictions and a persistent feature cache. In retrospective benchmarks on precomputed docking scores, LearnM8 recovered 98% of the best-scoring 0.1% of compounds in AmpC libraries of 1 to 96 million compounds after evaluating 10% of each library. On a 116-million-compound D4 library the same protocol recovered 91%. In the same study, random selection recovered 9.4% of the 1-millioncompound AmpC library. Smaller batch sizes per cycle improved recovery at higher computational cost, and pruning reduced prediction workload while slightly reducing recovery. LearnM8 is released under the MIT license at https://github.com/drugm8/LearnM8.

papers.title: Decoding Ionic Liquid Architecture at the Electrode-Electrolyte Interface in Supercapacitors.
papers.abstract: The increasing demand for efficient energy storage underscores the need to enhance the capacity of electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs), with electrolyte modification being a promising approach to improve their performance. Ionic liquids offer wide electrochemical stability windows, low volatility, thermal stability, and tunable molecular architectures, making them promising electrolytes for EDLCs. To use the molecular tunability of ionic liquids more effectively, it is important to understand how ion architecture shapes interfacial organization of ions near the electrode and controls charge storage. To understand the integrated geometry and electrostatic organization of ions at the molecular level, here we employ atomistic molecular dynamics simulations to compare imidazolium, pyridinium, pyrrolidinium, and piperidinium-based electrolytes at graphene electrodes to understand how five and six membered aromatic planar and saturated non-planar frameworks organize at the electrode-electrolyte interface and affect the device performance. A common tetrafluoroborate anion, electrode geometry, interelectrode separation, and a fixed surface charge density provide a consistent framework for comparison. Molecular orientation, two-dimensional Voronoi tessellation, ion-density distributions, and charge-screening analyses connect adsorption configurations, lateral packing, and countercharge organization at the interface with capacitance behavior of the individual architectural class. Our simulation results show that Imidazolium exhibits the highest capacitance, accompanied by predominantly surface-parallel rings, while pyridinium exhibits the lowest capacitance and is accompanied by mixed orientations. Our simulation results help establish the structure-orientation-capacitance relationship at the molecular scale, which is essential for designing a future ionic liquid-based electrolyte for high-performance EDLCs for applications such as power buffering in renewable energy systems, peak-power delivery in portable electronics, and industrial energy recovery.

papers.title: Stochastic combinatorics with tripeptide dimers: finding the rational outcomes of extended games with structural fluctuations
papers.abstract: While protein- and DNA-based macromolecular systems have previously been used to implement the solutions of certain combinatorial problems, similar progress using small organic molecules has been slow. In this paper, we deploy atomistic simulations to show that the structural fluctuations of the dimers of the tripeptide ProPhePhe (Pro = proline, Phe = phenylalanine) can be used to find the rational outcomes of a special class of extended games. Importantly, the ability of the tripeptides to find rational outcomes is stereochemistry-dependent, with frequencies for finding rational outcomes varying between from around 1 to 17 ns -1 during the course of a trajectory simulation. Overall, ProPhePhe dimer structural fluctuations tend to find the cooperative outcomes of extended games more frequently than self-interested (Nash equilibrium) ones. Our results provide the first example of stochastic combinatorics – the use of stochastic processes to explore the solution spaces of combinatorial problems – using small organic molecules. By demonstrating how complex combinatorial problems can be approached using the structural dynamics of molecular clusters, and suggesting that performance can be tuned through molecular design, this work provides an entirely new direction for research into small-molecule computing.

papers.title: A Multi-Criteria Analytical Framework for the Assignment of Carboxyl-Rich Alicyclic Molecules in Dissolved Organic Matter
papers.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is one of Earth’s major organic carbon reservoirs, with most of this pool persisting as recalcitrant DOM (RDOM) over millennia-long timescales. However, the actual molecular structures within this recalcitrant pool remain poorly defined. Carboxyl-rich alicyclic molecules (CRAM) are widely used as molecular proxies for a portion of RDOM, but their assignment commonly relies only on elemental formula boundaries in direct-infusion mass spectrometry (MS) data, which cannot identify structural features or differentiate between isomers with different reactivities. In this work, we used analytical data beyond molecular formulas to more carefully classify CRAM candidates through two complementary pipelines. The pipelines integrated formula-based classification alongside liquid chromatography retention time, tandem MS neutral-losses, and stability tests based on microbial incubations. These pipelines were applied to a case study where DOM was produced from white-rot fungal incubations using small phenolic substrates to represent an idealized terrestrial production of CRAM. When the fungi had access to phenolic compounds alongside glucose, double the number of CRAM candidate features were produced which summed more than five times the total intensity of phenolic compounds alone. Across the different carbon growth conditions, conventional formula-based assignment classified more than 3000 features as CRAM. However, of the 333 CRAM-like features with available tandem MS data, only 41 candidates met the additional analytical criteria from our pipeline. Dissimilarities between these 41 candidates and DOM led to us further refine the fragmentation pattern rules for CRAM assignment, which reduced the candidate pool to just four features. This drastic reduction highlights the need for analytical techniques that can provide structural information during natural DOM sample analysis and simulated environmental testing.

papers.title: Late-Stage 4-Methylation of [6,5]-Fused Arenes
papers.abstract: Late-stage methylation of [6,5]-fused bicyclic arenes is a transformation of considerable importance in medicinal chemistry, yet the selective C4-methylation of these privileged scaffolds without directing groups has remained elusive. Here we report a relay strategy for the late-stage 4-methylation of [6,5]-fused arenes that couples temporary C3 iodination with a Catellani-type peri-methylation/ipso-H-termination sequence proceeding through an unusual six-membered palladacycle. A rationally designed thio-cycloolefin ligand bearing an N-acetyl pendant accelerates the peri-C–H activation step while suppressing competing C,C reductive-elimination pathways, thereby enabling selective C4-methylation. Inexpensive trimethyl (or trideuteromethyl) phosphate serves as a bifunctional reagent that delivers both the methyl electrophile and the hydrogen nucleophile, providing convenient access to both CH3- and CD3-labelled products. The protocol accommodates indoles, 7-azaindoles, indolizines, benzothiophenes, and benzofurans, and was applied to the late-stage methylation of drug molecules and to 1 mmol-scale synthesis. Mechanistic studies corroborate the six-membered palladacycle intermediate and identify the hydride source of the ipso-H-termination.

papers.title: The liquid-gas equilibrium region for the quantum-volume Bragg-Williams equation of state
papers.abstract: The quantum-volume Bragg-Williams (qv-BW) equation of state, derived from a lattice gas model and a mean-field approximation for the intermolecular interactions, includes a unique temperature dependence theoretically grounded through the connection to the thermal wavelength for particles. Here, the qv-BW equation of state is extended by deriving equations in a semi-analytical approach (one numerical inversion) for the two-phase region describing the liquid-gas equilibrium below the critical temperature. In more detail, equations are derived for the coexistence curve (vapor pressure), the molar volumes of the liquid and gas phases, the vaporization enthalpy, the isochoric heat capacity and the saturation heat capacity. Results are presented for a simple model system with the focus on argon. The results are promising, but limitations in the present model are also revealed. The molar volume of the liquid branch has a minimum contradicting established results, and the result for the vaporization enthalpy is limited by the mean-field approach for interactions. Future prospects are discussed both with respect to method development and applications.

papers.title: A neural surrogate for the natural-gas compressibility factor: reference-equation accuracy from synthetic training data alone, benchmarked on 2426 independent laboratory measurements
papers.abstract: The compressibility factor z of natural gas is obtained either from inexpensive empirical correlations or from reference equations of state that require the full molar composition and an iterative density solve. Machine learning has been proposed as a bridge, but almost all published studies are trained and tested on values digitised from the same 1942 chart, so their gains have never been shown on independent laboratory data. We assemble such a test set: 6726 gas-phase measurements from 40 publishedstudiesintheNISTThermoMLarchive,withabsolutepressure,temperatureand composition, from which z follows exactly. On its natural-gas domain (2426 points, 10 laboratories) we evaluate six established methods and a residual neural surrogate trained only on synthetic states fromareferenceequation.Thesurrogateattainsanaverageabsolutedeviationof0.789%, statisticallyindistinguishablefrom AGA8-DETAIL (0.769%) and ahead ofGERG-2008 (0.917%), while reducing the error of the Dranchuk–Abou-Kassem, Hall–Yarborough and Dranchuk–Purvis–Robinson correlations by about 1.1 percentage points at all ten laboratories. Replacing the teaching equation whileholding states,architecture and seed fixed changes testaccuracy from 0.923% to 0.789%: surrogate accuracy is governed by the reference equation chosen to generate its labels. A search over 31 functional families shows that fitted residual corrections transfer for the empirical correlations but not for the reference equations or the surrogate.We also measure the cost such surrogatesassertratherthandemonstrate:thenetworkisslowerperstatethanthereference equation, and fastest only when batched on a graphics processor.

papers.title: Assessment of honey samples from Nigerian markets using FTIR spectroscopy and machine learning
papers.abstract: Honey adulteration with cheaper sugars is a concern in Nigerian markets, where conventional tests are slow, costly, and not widely accessible. This study assessed whether Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy combined with machine learning can screen honey for added sugar, and whether such a model can be applied to honey sold in Nigerian markets. A Random Forest classifier was trained on a public FTIR dataset of 16 honeys, each measured pure and with 10, 20, and 40% added sugar. It was compared with PLS-DA, logistic regression, and a support vector machine. Models were tested by leave-one-honey-out cross-validation, so each honey was always predicted by a model that had never seen it. ATR-FTIR spectra were also recorded for 11 honeys purchased from Nigerian markets. Random Forest reached balanced accuracy of 0.70–0.71 and AUC of 0.80–0.87 across three pre-processing methods; Random Forest and PLS-DA together ranged from 0.64 to 0.76 (balanced accuracy) and 0.72 to 0.87 (AUC). Most adulterated spectra were detected, even at 10% added sugar, but about half of the pure honeys were also flagged. The amount of added sugar could not be estimated (RMSECV 12.2 percentage points). The most informative bands lay in the carbohydrate fingerprint region (near 1365, 1031, 902, and 818 cm-1, stable across validation rounds). After ATR and baseline correction, the market honeys closely resembled the training honeys (r = 0.965), but they lay outside the range of spectra the model was trained on, so they could not be classified reliably. A leakage-prone test, with augmentation before a random split, gave 0.87 balanced accuracy, against 0.70 when augmentation was kept inside the training data and each honey was held out, showing how test design can inflate reported results. These results support further evaluation of FTIR with machine learning as a rapid screen, but a local calibration set of Nigerian honeys is needed before market samples can be judged.

papers.title: Mixed-Linker Modification of MIL-100(Fe): Structure–Performance Trade-Offs in CO2 Adsorption and Cycling
papers.abstract: Amine groups are often added to metal–organic frameworks to strengthen CO2 binding, usually at a cost in porosity. We examine this trade-off in MIL-100(Fe) prepared by a fluoride-free hydrothermal route, with 5, 10 or 20 mol% of the trimesate linker in the synthesis replaced by the amine-bearing linker 5-aminoisophthalic acid (AIA). Diffraction showed that the MIL-100 framework was retained and spectroscopy detected amine-related groups, although AIA incorporation was not quantified. Increasing AIA content reduced crystallite size from 43 to 18 nm and BET surface area from 1527 to 435 m2 g-1. At 298 K and 1 bar, the modified materials adsorbed 1.3–1.7 mmol g-1 CO2, against 3.1 mmol g-1 for pristine MIL-100(Fe), although the 5 mol% material approached the uptake of pristine MIL-100(Fe) at 14 bar. They also held CO2 less strongly: the isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst), which indicates how strongly CO2 binds, was 16–30 kJ mol-1 at low loading, rising with AIA content, against ~60 kJ mol-1 for pristine MIL-100(Fe). The pristine material also gave the highest predicted CO2/N2 selectivity (~170, against 18–32 for the others, at 298 K and 1 bar). Under flow, however, the ranking changed: in breakthrough tests with 8 vol% CO2 in N2, the 5 mol% material had twice the dynamic CO2 capacity of pristine MIL-100(Fe) (0.20 vs 0.10 mmol g-1), and commercial Basolite F300 the highest (0.46 mmol g-1). Over 40 cycles between 0.15 and 1 bar, uptake reached a steady level and the 5 mol% material kept its crystallinity and surface area (865 vs 861 m2 g-1). No composition was best on every metric: AIA addition reshapes rather than improves CO2 adsorption in MIL-100(Fe), so capacity, binding strength and flow performance must be judged together.

papers.title: Analytical nuclear gradients for the CC2 method using pair-natural orbitals based on localized virtual molecular orbitals for excited states
papers.abstract: Analytical nuclear energy gradients are indispensable for optimizing excited-state structures and exploring excited-state potential energy surfaces. Local correlation methods based on pair-natural orbitals (PNOs) have extended correlated wavefunction calculations to large molecules, and their analytical gradients have been developed for ground states but, to our knowledge, not for excited states. In our previous work [M. Hayashi, S. Nagae, M. Saitow, and T. Yanai, J. Chem. Phys. 165, 164118 (2026)], we established the analytical gradient theory of the PNO-based second-order approximate coupled cluster (CC2) method using localized virtual molecular orbitals (LVMOs), which was limited to the ground state. In this work, we report the development of analytical nuclear gradients for singlet and triplet excited states of the LVMObased PNO-CC2 method. Using the ground-state PNOs for all excited states, we inherit the ground-state Lagrangian, including the PNO-construction constraints, and add only excited-state constraints. To reduce the excitation-energy errors arising from the ground-state PNOs, we introduce a PNO truncation correction and develop the gradients including this correction. The formulation is extended to a projected-atomic-orbital-based variant and to the spin-component-scaled scheme. To verify the implementation, we extended our automated symbolic derivation program to spin-orbital algebra and to the excitation vectors of the excited states, and the analytical gradients were validated against selection-fixed finite differences. Using the present method, we accomplished analytical excited-state gradient calculations for real-life molecules with 80–91 atoms.

papers.title: Guidelines for minimizing contamination from Ag-based reference electrodes in aqueous and non-aqueous solvents
CelluloseForge: Crystallography-first construction of cellulose systems for molecular simulation
papers.abstract: CelluloseForge is an open-source Python package for reproducibly constructing atomistic crystalline cellulose models. It represents experimental unit-cell data separately from molecular-mechanics parameters and generates unit cells, periodic bulk crystals, chain-parallel slabs for four cellulose allomorphs, and literature-defined 36-chain fibrils. Finite and covalently periodic chains can be parameterized with GLYCAM06j-1 or CHARMM36 and exported as matched GROMACS coordinates and topology. Stable identifiers support reproducible heavy-atom position restraints, while PDBx/mmCIF output and machinereadable build reports support large and auditable systems. Automated crystallographic and topology tests, GROMACS preprocessing, minimization, and short NVT workflows define the validated scope and identify exploratory constructions explicitly.

papers.title: Soft-drug design for topical JAK1/TYK2 inhibition in atopic dermatitis
papers.abstract: Topical Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors reduce systemic exposure compared with oral dosing, but they do not eliminate it. Ruxolitinib cream, the current topical benchmark in atopic dermatitis (AD), achieves an Eczema Area and Severity Index 75% improvement (EASI-75) rate of 70.0% at week 8 in TRuE-AD4 and itch relief within 15 minutes, yet its plasma concentrations must still be interpreted against a 281 nM threshold linked in vitro to JAK-mediated myelosuppression. A soft drug — active in skin, designed to be rapidly hydrolysed to an inactive metabolite on entering blood — offers a mechanistically different way to widen that margin, and the approach has been clinically explored with ATI-1777, a topical soft JAK1/3 inhibitor. This study asks what a next candidate would have to look like to be worth making, and how it should be tested before any efficacy claim is entertained. Three analyses were combined. First, a simplified physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) skin–plasma model (1.5% cream, 200 cm2, 12 h, Potts–Guy permeability) compared ruxolitinib, upadacitinib and a hypothetical soft-drug target profile (molecular weight 420, logD 3.2, plasma esterase clearance 300 L/h). Second, 16 known JAK inhibitors with public structures from PubChem were clustered with RDKit using Murcko scaffolds and Morgan fingerprints (Butina clustering, distance cutoff 0.55). Third, five benchmark drugs — ATI-1777, topical brepocitinib, oral soficitinib, tapinarof and ruxolitinib — were compared on published efficacy, plasma exposure and development status, with three commonly repeated figures corrected against primary sources. In the PBPK model the target profile gave a skin partitioning index of 174, about six times that of ruxolitinib (30), and a plasma area under the curve (AUC) of 20 µg·h/L, about one-fourteenth that of ruxolitinib (273 µg·h/L); upadacitinib was intermediate (index 78, AUC 150 µg·h/L). The 16 inhibitors fell into 13 clusters. The pyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidine family was the crowded zone, while deucravacitinib (Tanimoto similarity to ruxolitinib 0.10), filgotinib (0.12), upadacitinib (0.18) and peficitinib (0.22) were the most distant chemotypes. The benchmark analysis shows that novelty can no longer rest on the soft-drug idea alone: it must rest on the combination of soft inactivation, a non-crowded scaffold, JAK1/TYK2 selectivity and measured paraoxonase 1 (PON1) clearance that still holds in low-PON1 donors. A five-step validation chain with a pre-specified PON1 gate is proposed. These are paper-validation and ranking results only; they do not demonstrate that any molecule exists, works, or is safe.

papers.title: A Chiral Photoactive Ligand for Enantioconvergent Nickel-Catalyzed C(sp <sup>2</sup> )–C(sp <sup>3</sup> ) Cross-Coupling
papers.abstract: Integrating photochemical catalyst activation and stereochemical control within a single catalyst architecture offers an attractive strategy for asymmetric synthesis. Herein, we report a chiral photoactive nickel catalyst that enables enantioconvergent light-mediated C(sp 2 )–C(sp 3 ) crosscoupling of an N-Boc-protected pyrrolidine-derived trifluoroborate with (hetero)aryl bromides. The catalyst features a carbazole-decorated biimidazole (biIm) ligand that combines intraligand chargetransfer (ILCT) photoactivity with asymmetric induction, thereby eliminating the need for a separate photocatalyst. The optimized system affords enantioenriched products with high enantioselectivity across a broad range of aryl bromides. Mechanistic investigations provide evidence for stereochemical scrambling through reversible Ni–C bond homolysis, offering a possible pathway for enantioconvergence. These findings establish chiral photoactive ligands as a platform for integrating light-driven catalyst activation and asymmetric cross-coupling catalysis.

papers.title: Support Effects in the Catalytic Transfer Hydrogenolysis of Diphenyl Ether over Ru Catalysts
papers.abstract: The selective cleavage of aryl C–O bonds while avoiding hydrogenation of the aromatic ring is a crucial challenge in the reductive valorisation of lignin. Industrial Ru (5 wt%) catalysts supported on wood-derived activated carbon (RuCw) and δ/θ-Al 2 O 3 (RuAl), prepared by deposition–precipitation using Ru recovered from metal-containing waste streams, were compared in diphenyl ether (DPE) hydrogenolysis under catalytic transfer hydrogenolysis (CTH) with 2-propanol and under molecular H 2 . At 200 °C after 2 h, RuCw gave 92.0% DPE conversion and 63.6% aromatic yield under CTH conditions, compared with 42.8% and 33.4%, respectively, over RuAl. Normalizing apparent rate constants with respect to the Ru accessible by CO chemisorption reduced the activity di]erence to a factor of 1.2-1.4 between 160 and 200 °C, indicating that the accessible Ru population accounts for most of the support-dependent rate di]erence, although uncertainties in CO/Ru adsorption stoichiometry prevent assignment of the residual di]erence to intrinsic kinetics. The corresponding apparent activation energies were found to be 104 ± 7 and 85 ± 5 kJ mol-1. Under CTH conditions, aromatic selectivity followed nearly the same dependence on DPE conversion over both catalysts. At comparable conversion, 2-propanol gave higher aromatic selectivity than molecular H 2 . Under H 2 pressure, dicyclohexyl ether formation was consistent with a greater contribution from DPE ring hydrogenation before C–O cleavage. Under the reaction conditions examined, the support primarily determines the accessible Ru population and hence catalytic activity, whereas the mode of hydrogen supply governs the competition between C–O cleavage and aromatic-ring hydrogenation.

papers.title: Orchestrating literature landscaping in drug discovery by coupling citation expansion with large language models
papers.abstract: Systematic literature reviews guide decisions in drug discovery, yet keyword-based retrieval misses relevant work hidden behind synonyms, compound codes and cross-disciplinary vocabulary. Manual screening of large literature pools is slow and costly. Large language models (LLMs) could relieve this bottleneck, but existing tools address either citation-based retrieval or LLM screening, and rarely validate how well the combination performs. We present CESAR (Citation Expansion for Systematic Academic Reviewing), an open-source workflow that assembles domain corpora by following references and citing works through OpenAlex. It screens titles and abstracts with LLMs calibrated against human-annotated reference sets. We demonstrate CESAR on a broad methodological field, total synthesis, and on a narrow drug target, monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL). For total synthesis, the collected corpus contained 78% of an independently curated reference collection published 2000–2023. The classifier retained 99.3% of those that reached screening, and inexpensive models performed close to the most expensive ones. For MAGL, an open-weight model reduced more than 20,000 records to 893 at no cost, with an estimated 79% of them relevant, while extracting target selectivity, evidence level and compound names in the same step. Run on a single local GPU, the same model matched cloud performance, enabling screening of confidential material without external data transfer. CESAR turns screening of tens of thousands of abstracts into a task of hours to days, at costs from zero to about one US dollar per thousand papers, and keeps expert attention for the decisions that require it.

papers.title: Photovoltaic e-waste for PFAS remediation and H <sub>2</sub> evolution
papers.abstract: End-of-life photovoltaic modules and persistent fluorinated compounds present distinct challenges for waste management and chemical recovery. Here, we report an integrated approach that uses silicon recovered from discarded photovoltaic modules to promote the mechanochemical defluorination of perand polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Subsequent alkaline treatment releases the retained fluorine as fluoride and generates hydrogen through oxidation of the remaining silicon, with SiO 2 as a third recoverable product. The recovered fluoride is used to synthesize a sulfonyl fluoride, while the generated hydrogen is employed in heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenations, including reactions catalyzed by palladium supported on recovered photovoltaic silicon. This approach couples the degradation of persistent fluorinated compounds with the recovery of chemical reagents from photovoltaic waste, enabling their subsequent use in organic synthesis.

papers.title: Enantioselective Cobalt-Catalyzed Enyne Cyclo-1,4-Dienylation: Reaction Development and Mechanism
papers.abstract: Cheap-metal-catalyzed asymmetric enyne cycloisomerizations that directly synthesize 1,4-dienes, named here as enyne cyclo-1,4-dienylation (abbreviated as cyclodienylation), remain scarce. The existing methods are largely limited to racemic transformations and mostly for 1,6-enynes. Here, we report a cobalt-catalyzed asymmetric enyne cyclo-1,4-dienylation using both 1,6-enynes and 1,7-enynes, delivering enantioenriched five- and six-membered rings bearing 1,4-diene moieties. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions with an earth-abundant cobalt catalyst and commercially available chiral phosphine ligands, tolerates a broad range of alkyl-, aryl-, and terminal-alkyne substrates as well as carbon-, nitrogen-, and oxygen-tethered enynes, and remains efficient on gram scale with excellent enantioselectivity. Mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations were performed, indicating that the reaction occurs via a pathway involving oxidative cyclometallation, β-H elimination, and reductive elimination. Distortion–interaction analysis was applied to understand the origin of enantioselectivity of the 1,7-enyne cyclodienylation.

papers.title: A General Strategy for Active Learning When Predicting Reaction Performance in a Target Domain
papers.abstract: Machine learning models can help guide reaction development, but their usefulness is often limited by the scarcity of training data in the chemical spaces where predictions are most needed. Active learning can reduce this burden by selecting a minimal number of maximally informative experiments. However, standard acquisition strategies such as Bayesian active learning by disagreement (BALD) prioritize uncertainty without regard to the specific prediction domain of interest. Here, we approach active learning for reaction outcome prediction using expected predictive information gain (EPIG), a target-aware acquisition function that scores candidate experiments according to the predictive information they are expected to provide about a specified target distribution. In a Wittig olefination transfer learning task, EPIG adapts a model trained on established reactions compiled from a foundational Wittig textbook to a distinct literature-sourced reaction domain using approximately half as many acquired reactions as BALD. Across 118 retrospective active learning tasks spanning four reaction datasets, four split families, and targets including yield, enantioselectivity, and stereoselectivity, EPIG achieves the strongest early learning performance on the majority of tasks, remains statistically competitive on nearly all tasks, and achieves the greatest reduction in required data relative to established acquisition strategies and baseline methods. These results demonstrate how target-aware active learning can improve the data efficiency of reaction outcome prediction across diverse chemical settings.

papers.title: Dual-Microcapsule-Triggered In Situ Polymerization Enables Ultralong Room-Temperature Phosphorescence for Damage Visualization and Dynamic Anti-Counterfeiting
papers.abstract: 2 challenging because efficient triplet emission generally requires a rigid molecular environment that is difficult to establish in situ. Here, we report a dual-microcapsule strategy that activates ultralong RTP through damage-triggered in situ polymerization. Two complementary types of microcapsules, separately encapsulating an epoxy precursor and an amine solution containing organic phosphors, were incorporated into a coating. Mechanical damage ruptured both microcapsules, allowing the released components to undergo localized polymerization and form a rigid cross-linked epoxy network that suppresses nonradiative deactivation of the phosphors and enables persistent RTP at the damaged region. Among the investigated luminogens, the amino-substituted phosphor exhibited the best performance, delivering an RTP lifetime of 1857 ms together with remarkable resistance to water, organic solvents, and extremely acidic and alkaline environments. The localized RTP activation enabled high-contrast visualization of scratches and compressive damage. Furthermore, the time-dependent organic afterglow was exploited to construct dynamic multilevel anti-counterfeiting patterns with programmable temporal information. This work establishes damage-triggered in situ polymerization as a general strategy for on-demand activation of organic RTP, providing a versatile platform for intelligent damage self-reporting, dynamic anti-counterfeiting, and advanced mechanoresponsive photonic materials.

papers.title: A bespoke, token-efficient LLM inference pipeline for extracting polymer diffusion coefficients from scientific literature
papers.abstract: Automated creation of actionable chemical datasets through large language model (LLM) interpretation of chemistry publications has become an engineering challenge rather than a frontier AI problem. We present Chemstractor , a bespoke extraction pipeline designed for use with open‑weight LLMs that can be executed locally on hardware typically available to university research environments. As a test case, the extraction techniques are applied to polymer diffusion coefficients, commonly used for the prediction of polymer molecular weights and for evaluating emerging universal calibration curves. The pipeline combines modern PDF parsing, table focused chunking, structured prompting, and an agent orchestrated calculator tool to handle mathematical transformations and reduce hallucinations. Chemstractor achieves strong performance, including a low hallucination rate, while maintaining extremely low token usage and requiring no paid API access. The methodology provides an accessible and efficient route to generating validated, analysis ready datasets and offers a template for extracting similarly complex scientific parameters in other domains.

papers.title: Chemistry-informed non-covalent graphs and pharmacophore supervision for molecular property prediction
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks describe a molecule by its covalent bonds, however, many molecular properties are shaped by contacts between atoms that are not bonded to each other. Existing models either ignore these non-covalent interactions or approximate them with a distance cutoff that cannot distinguish an interaction from mere proximity. Here we introduce a framework that injects chemical knowledge at two levels. First, intramolecular hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts become graph edges only when they satisfy interaction-specific topological and geometric criteria; these edges form a separate graph whose layer refines the atom states of a covalent encoder, and the two readouts are fused through a task-aware gate. Second, an auxiliary head supervises every atom with its pharmacophoric roles with expanded σ-hole interaction dictionary. We show that the rule-based graph is about twenty times sparser than a 5-Å cutoff graph, that the gated model reduces to a covalent model as its gate closes and adds a generalisation term bounded by a multiple of its maximal gate value, and that its predictions are Lipschitz in the atomic coordinates as long as the edge set is unchanged. On seven MoleculeNet classification benchmarks under scaffold splitting and without pretraining, ChemPrior-GAT achieves the best ROC-AUC on three benchmarks and the lowest average rank, and the same two modules also improve AttentiveFP, demonstrating that the proposed strategy is transferable to other GNN architecture. Pharmacophore-level attributions are consistent with established chemical principles. In prospective experimental validation involving 16 compounds, the model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.50 log units between predicted and experimentally measured logD7.4 values.

papers.title: Development and Evaluation of an Agentic Suite of Tasks Covering a Computational Chemistry Curriculum
papers.abstract: Computational chemistry, increasingly enabled by high-performance computing, accelerates research across many areas of chemistry. However, heterogeneous software packages, input formats, and output conventions create a steep learning curve that also complicates simulation scripting and automation. Large language models (LLMs) can lower this barrier by helping users prepare calculations, execute workflows, and interpret results. We present ASSAY (Agentic Simulation Suite for Automated Chemistry), an open-source agentic toolkit for quantum chemistry designed for undergraduate CC education. To align ASSAY with current curricula, we analyzed syllabi from 17 courses at public and private universities in and outside the United States. ASSAY supports example-driven learning through input generation and output interpretation, while its local and remote workflows can introduce students to distributed computing, batch queues, and file management. In a benchmark spanning 12 skills and 8 LLMs, ASSAY achieved a mean pass rate of 94.04%, with six models achieving at least 98%. These results establish ASSAY as a reproducible, integrity-first foundation for making computational chemistry more accessible to students and reliable for researchers.

papers.title: Assessing the predictive limits of machine learning on cyclic peptides
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) has become a key tool in molecule discovery and optimization. Yet cyclic peptides, which occupy an intermediate chemical space between small molecules and proteins, have received limited attention in ML research, leaving the predictive value of current methods and future research needs unclear. To address this gap, we systematically evaluated ten model families (from classical ML approaches to pretrained deep-learning models) and nine molecular representations (from molecular descriptors to strings and graphs) across twelve prediction tasks spanning three properties and 9,341 peptides. Membrane permeability showed the clearest predictive signal, whereas binding-affinity and half-life prediction remained challenging. Evaluating models against explicit ‘no-skill’ references was central to interpreting these results and contextualizing performance across endpoints and data splits. No single model family performed best across all tasks: tree ensembles were strong in regression, while pretrained chemical language models performed best on average in classification. We further show that data splitting, task formulation, and dataset composition can influence apparent performance. Together, these findings highlight data availability and assay consistency, limited statistical power, and evaluation design as key challenges for cyclic-peptide modeling. To support progress in these areas, we release CycPepNet (https://github.com/molML/CycPepNet), an open framework that brings together curated datasets, evaluation protocols, and full results to enable reproducible comparisons and future method development.

papers.title: Intracellular fate of structurally heterogeneous carbon nitride structures in mammalian cells
papers.abstract: Carbon nitride materials are increasingly investigated for photocatalysis, environmental remediation, and emerging biomedical applications. Although the biological behavior of carbon nitride quantum dots has been studied quite extensively, interactions of larger and structurally heterogeneous carbon nitride structures with cells remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the intracellular fate of two carbon nitride samples possessing markedly different characteristic dimensions, spanning a range from approximately 100 nm to several micrometers. Confocal microscopy and flow cytometry demonstrated pronounced concentration-and time-dependent cellular accumulation of both samples in HeLa cells. Pharmacological inhibition experiments indicated that uptake is largely mediated by actin-dependent phagocytosis. Super-resolution by optical reassignment imaging and transmission electron microscopy confirmed intracellular localization of carbon nitride structures within membranebound organelles. Live-cell imaging showed progressive accumulation of internalized carbon nitride structures within the lysosomal compartment, consistent with trafficking through the endolysosomal pathway. The larger carbon nitride structures exhibited greater intracellular persistence than their smaller counterparts. Despite efficient uptake, vesicular localization, intracellular processing, and prolonged retention, neither cell proliferation nor cellular stress pathways (interrogated through canonical markers for endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and DNA damage) showed substantial alterations after 12 hours under non-illuminated conditions. These findings demonstrate that structurally heterogeneous carbon nitride architectures remain biologically accessible across a broad size range and provide new insight into their intracellular fate and short-term biosafety.

papers.title: MolValenceX: a browser-based, client-side tool for drawing molecules and estimating aromaticity, CIP stereodescriptors, dipole moments and Hansen solubility parameters, with benchmarking against experimental and reference-toolkit data
papers.abstract: MolValenceX is a free, open-source chemical structure editor and analyser that runs entirely in a web browser, with no installation, server or account. A drawn or imported (SMILES) structure is analysed for molecular formula, molar mass and degree of unsaturation, ring aromaticity by Hückel π-electron counting, R/S configuration with optical-activity assessment from Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) priorities, E/Z configuration of acyclic double bonds, an empirical bond-moment estimate of the dipole moment from a generated 3D geometry, and Hansen solubility parameters (HSP) with a ranked solvent-compatibility list. All of this is implemented in dependency-free JavaScript. We benchmarked the five predictive modules. Against 23 experimental gas-phase dipole moments (NIST), the dipole module gave a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.40 D (median 0.17 D; 17 of 23 within 0.5 D), against 0.57 D for a naïve RDKit MMFF/Gasteiger baseline (the difference was not statistically significant, paired Wilcoxon p = 0.057; the bond moments were tuned on small reference molecules, so this is not a strictly held-out comparison). Against 24 handbook HSP sets (23 supported), the mean absolute errors were 0.84 (δD), 2.30 (δP) and 1.61 (δH) MPa½, with a mean Hansen distance Ra of 3.7 MPa½. R/S assignments agreed with the RDKit CIP labeler for 26 of 26 test structures, E/Z for 22 of 24 (the two exceptions are ring double bonds, which the tool does not assess by design), and Hückel ring classification agreed with textbook expectation for 26 of 26 structures. Four large, complex structures are shown as an unvalidated demonstration of scope. The tool is intended for teaching and for quick qualitative screening, not as an analytical reference.

papers.title: Implementation of fully automated continuous serial electron diffraction in Instamatic
papers.abstract: Serial electron diffraction, especially when coupled with precession, utilises transmission electron microscopes to reveal crystal structures of beam-sensitive nanocrystals. Unfortunately, its application remains limited due to a lack of a transferable implementation. To address this issue, we added a new data collection protocol to the popular open-source software Instamatic. Utilising a static beam and continuous stage-sliding strategy, the new approach is well suited for high-throughput acquisition across a wide range of supported hardware. The implementation was tested on a model mineral sample, natrolite, producing crystal structure on par with those obtained using established single-crystal methods.

papers.title: MeCoBi: A fast and accurate transition metal complex builder that generates 3D structures at scale and enables structure-based machine learning
papers.abstract: The three-dimensional arrangement of ligands around a metal centre determines its electronic structure, reactivity, and biological activity, yet generating accurate three-dimensional (3D) structures from a ligand list remains difficult. Existing tools tend to be slow, narrow in coverage, or require manual specification. We present MeCoBi (Metal Complex Builder), an automated pipeline that builds and optimises 3D structures of mononuclear metal complexes from ligand SMILES across 36 d-block and main-group metals and coordination numbers 2–9. On 30,830 experimental structures from the Cambridge Structural Database, MeCoBi generated a structure for 99.6% of complexes with a median error in metal–ligand bond lengths of 0.06 Å. We then used the generated structures as inputs for machine learning. For the cytotoxicity of ruthenium complexes from MetalCytoToxDB, a model trained only on the structures came within 0.02 in ROC-AUC of the best model based on two-dimensional descriptors; for the antibacterial activity of a library of 1,800 iridium complexes prepared in our laboratory, it ranked the new complexes better than the 2D descriptor models (ROC-AUC 0.88 against 0.84). For the dipole moments and HOMO–LUMO gaps of 10,175 complexes from the tmQM dataset, adding the results of a GFN2-xTB calculation on the MeCoBi structures to a two-dimensional model lowered its mean absolute error from 1.68 to 1.24 D and 0.367 to 0.311 eV, and the improvement remained for structures built from the SMILES alone. MeCoBi is open source, with a web interface at mecobi.york.ac.uk.

papers.title: Adsorption fingerprints of proteins at fluid interfaces: a molecular dynamics study of Lysozyme at water/oil and water/air interfaces
papers.abstract: Protein adsorption at fluid interfaces is central to pharmaceutical formulation, food colloids, and bioprocessing technologies, yet its molecular basis remains poorly understood. We investigate lysozyme (LSZ) adsorption at water-air and water-hexadecane interfaces using molecular dynamics simulations with the all-atom CHARMM36m, united-atom GROMOS53A6, and coarse-grained MARTINI 3 force fields. At the waterair interface, only GROMOS53A6 predicts adsorption of native LSZ within the simulated timescales, whereas CHARMM36m and MARTINI 3 show no stable adsorption within 200 ns and 1 µs, respectively. In contrast, all three models predict adsorption at the water-hexadecane interface, consistent with a stronger thermodynamic driving force for adsorption at oil than at vapor interfaces. In the atomistic models, adsorbed

papers.title: Optical Properties of Monocarboxylic and Dicarboxylic Acids in the Atmosphere
papers.abstract: The optical properties of atmospherically relevant molecular clusters remain elusive, as they are difficult to measure using current experimental techniques. Using quantum chemical methods, we here investigate the absorption and scattering properties of selective organic acid clusters. We studied 185 different (acid) 1 (Na + ) 0−2 (Cl – ) 0−1 (w) 0−5 clusters comprised of the monocarboxylic acids: Pyruvic acid (PA), lactic acid (LA), propionic acid (ProA), and 2,2-dihydroxypropionic acid (diol) and the dicarboxylic acids: Fumaric acid (FA) and maleic acid (MA). We calculated the static and dynamic isotropic and anisotropic polarizabilities and the 10 lowest singlet-state excitation energies at the CAM-B3LYP/aug-cc-pVTZ level of theory. We find that the isotropic and anisotropic polarizabilities effectively depend linearly on the cluster size, with all the data residing within the 95% prediction interval for the linear fits. We also find that the Rayleigh scattering activities depend quadratically on the cluster size, with the quadratic fit being very close to the fit obtained for the inorganic acid–base clusters studied previously. This indicates that the scattering properties of organic and inorganic clusters might be very similar in the atmosphere, solely depending on the polarizability. Finally, we find the clusters to absorb in the ultraviolet (UV) region, with an observed redshift in the spectra of the dicarboxylic acids and negatively charged conjugate bases compared to the monocarboxylic acids, and with only a limited blueshifting effect on the organic acid clusters induced by the presence of Na+ and Cl–ions. However, clusters with stronger chromophore units such as several carbonyl groups, extended π-conjugated systems, and aromatic rings are still necessary in the organic constituents for shifting the cluster absorption towards the visible region of the spectrum.

papers.title: Differentiable Search of Compositionally Complex Alloys
papers.abstract: Identifying solid-solution compositions in multicomponent alloys requires exploring a highdimensional design space while accounting for competing phases. We present a differentiable search framework that uses composition gradients of a thermodynamic objective to identify promising alloy regions without exhaustive grid enumeration. In the present implementation, an alchemical machine-learning interatomic potential and ideal configurational entropy provide a differentiable free-energy approximation for random solid solutions. Gradient-based optimization is combined with metadynamics biasing to explore multiple basins, and a tangent-plane criterion screens candidates against precipitation of competing compounds. Applied to the Mg–Al–Sc–Ti–V–Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni system on fcc, bcc, and hcp lattices at 1000 and 1600 K, the search recovers compositionally complex alloy (CCA) families supported by literature.
