Gaussian process (GP) models suit low-data settings, but treat each material separately or need engineered descriptors to learn across materials. Multi-task GPs share information across materials but infer these relationships solely from sparse data, making them unreliable early on. We introduce a chemistry-informed multi-task GP that derives these relationships from a Tanimoto kernel on molecular fingerprints, enabling knowledge transfer without descriptor engineering. In closed-loop, uncertaintydriven exploration of a seven-dimensional synthesis space, comprising one categorical variable (three chiral 2D hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite compositions) and six continuous synthesis parameters, we tested 287 conditions (<0.1% of the discretized synthesis space). Knowledge transfer matched the accuracy of single-task GPs trained on the full target dataset using between 35-60% of the target data. Interaction analysis revealed a three-way coupling among annealing temperature, precursor concentration, and composition. This coupling makes a one-variable-at-a-time optimization challenging. Our framework offers a simple strategy for transferring and interpreting knowledge across related materials.

papers.title: Interaction without an interaction module
papers.abstract: The prevailing way to model a many-body system is to encode every component and then let a module capture interaction. We show that the explicit interaction module is harmful when the number of components increases. We use a simple interaction-carrying encoder that compresses a component’s interaction contribution into its representation, and combine the representations by linear aggregation. This modelling approach is simple in form yet delivers unexpectedly excellent performance: it matches the prevailing explicit route under most conditions and exceeds it when a mixture carries more components than the training set covered. Moreover, an encoder produced this way has a clear advantage over per-component descriptors when it is transferred to a similar task: it greatly reduces the data requirements.

papers.title: OSC700: A GW+BSE Dataset of 700 Organic Semiconductor (OSC) Crystals with an LLM-Assisted Data Extraction Agent
papers.abstract: Key parameters for organic optoelectronic device applications derive from the excited-state properties of molecular crystals. Data scarcity (both experimental and theoretical) limits the ability to train machine learning (ML) models to predict these properties. We present the OSC700 dataset of excited-state properties of 700 crystalline organic semiconductors (OSCs) with up to 1168 atoms in the unit cell, calculated using state-of-the-art many-body perturbation theory within the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW+BSE). OSC700 contains crystals of compounds comprising C,H,N,O,F,S capable of forming a variety of molecular scaffolds and crystal packing motifs. OSC700 is larger and significantly more diverse than the earlier PAH101 dataset [Scientific Data 12, 679 (2025)]. The data records contain the fundamental gap, quasiparticle band structure, static dielectric constant, first singlet exciton energy (optical gap), first triplet exciton energy, full dielectric function, and optical absorption spectra for light polarized along the three lattice vectors. Because absorption experiments on molecular crystals are rare (as opposed to solution or amorphous phases), we developed an LLM-assisted data extraction agent in order to find and retrieve available optical gap data for the materials in OSC700. The agent was able to find experimental data for 16 materials, which we used to validate the results of our calculations. The OSC700 dataset can be used to train ML models to predict the excited-state properties of crystalline organic semiconductors and find promising materials for optoelectronic device applications.

papers.title: High-resolution relaxometry suggests the presence of pervasive nano-second sugar motions in a DNA duplex.
papers.abstract: Nucleic acids are central to many biomolecular processes central to cellular life, yet characterising their molecular motions and fluctuations with atomic resolution remains challenging. We introduce high-resolution relaxometry, combined with high-field nuclear spin relaxation, as a powerful tool to probe motions in nucleic acids. After recording an extensive spin-relaxation dataset from 2 to 23 T, we propose a framework, within the model-free approach, that allowed us to identify motions occurring both on the picosecond and low nanosecond time scales. By integrating these results with molecular dynamics simulations and ensembles, obtained from residual dipolar coupling (RDC) measurements, we propose a time-resolved model that includes fast helical motions and slower pervasive sugar puckering motions. The approach outlined in this study also provides a framework for interrogating molecular dynamics in nucleic acids with spin relaxation experiments and benchmarking molecular dynamics simulations that aim to characterise dynamic processes.

papers.title: FROST III: certified Hartree–Fock limits of diatomic molecules
papers.abstract: We extend FROST (Fock radial orbital shooting with Taylor series) from atoms to diatomic molecules and obtain the Hartree–Fock (HF) energy of H2 at the internuclear distance R = 1.4 bohr to 103 significant figures, that of HeH+ to 101 and that of LiH to 26, each certified by an exact upper bound, where about 11, 9 and 12 figures were known before. In prolate spheroidal coordinates both nuclear cusps are absorbed and the nuclear attraction becomes linear. Expanding the orbitals and their pair potentials in Legendre polynomials of the angular coordinate η then turns the HF equations into ordinary differential equations in ξ that all have the form (ξ2−1)u′′+2ξu′ = g. This is the molecular counterpart of the radial equations of the earlier papers, with a regular singular point on the internuclear axis instead of the nucleus. The expansion of the orbitals is the only truncation besides the wall, and it is variational, while that of the potentials is exact, because Poisson’s equation is diagonal in the Legendre index. The equations are solved by the Taylor-series multiple shooting and homotopy of the atomic code, with no basis-set matrix and no self-consistentfield iteration. What is new is step control that resolves the rapidly growing Legendre modes of the high-order potentials, and a homotopy and wall continuation on a few channels only, after which a single stage on all channels, whose Jacobian is factorised in double precision, reaches the target accuracy. The certificate evaluates the energy of the piecewise-polynomial orbitals exactly: the oneelectron integrals are rational, and Neumann’s expansion of 1/r12 gives the Coulomb and exchange integrals as rationals plus rational multiples of logarithms of the knots, which are rounded outwards. The rate at which the energy converges in the number of Legendre channels is set by the complex singularities of the HF orbitals near each nucleus, found for helium in the first paper. Mapped onto the η interval, they predict the decay of the Legendre channels of H2, HeH+ and LiH to within 6%, with no adjustable parameter, and they show why LiH, and molecules of heavier atoms generally, need many more channels.

papers.title: Applicability Domain of Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials at Solid-State Battery Interfaces
papers.abstract: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are trained predominantly on bulk systems, yet are increasingly applied to solid-solid interfaces. Evaluating six uMLIPs against DFT across 24 Li-metal/solid-electrolyte interfaces, we map their applicability domain (AD) and where they break down. Total energies are predicted reasonably well (MAE < 15 meV/atom), whereas interatomic forces at the interfaces are not. Most models underestimate the interfacial formation energy by 0.32 J/m2 and overestimate the work of adhesion by 0.26 J/m2, and none reproduces the stability ordering of polyanion-containing interfaces. Despite large force errors for the interfaces, Li-ion kinetics agree well across models. The errors concentrate on the interface atoms and are larger for the polyanion chemistries. Descriptor-based analysis traces the higher force errors to interfacial environments that lie outside the pretraining data. Fine-tuning can close the accuracy gap, but only with data that samples the bonding across the interface, whereas slab data alone degrades performance. All models struggle on the same chemistries irrespective of the architecture, indicating the coverage of the pretraining data as the primary limitation. Overall, pretrained uMLIPs are suitable for qualitative screening of interfaces with simple single anion electrolytes, while those containing polyanions require interface-specific data.

papers.title: The Copper(I)-catalyzed Alkyne-azide Cycloaddition “Click” Reaction in Water Requires the Formation of Two Distinct Mononuclear Copper(I) Complexes
papers.abstract: The copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) has seen widespread adoption amongst numerous fields, but mechanistic details remain elusive and controversial. Using a series of experiments involving fluorogenic coumarin derivatives under pseudo-first order conditions, it was determined that the reaction in conditions close to a physiological environment does not proceed according to the accepted mechanism, but rather requires azide chelation to form a mononuclear copper(I)-azide complex as a preliminary step. Stopped flow studies with a copper-chelating azide further enhanced our understanding of the reaction mechanism, emphasizing the importance of copper-alkyne chelation in which a mononuclear copper(I)-alkyne complex is formed. After both copper(I)-azide and copper(I)-alkyne complexes are formed, they come together to yield the triazole product. This mechanistic proposal of CuAAC in conditions close to a physiological environment is distinct from the currently accepted general model, which proposes dual activation of the alkyne by copper(I) followed by azide interaction. Please note that this manuscript was rejected by several leading chemistry journals for publication in 2015 due to its challenging of existing click chemistry mechanisms. The authors decided to release it to ChemRxiv as a reference for others with a purpose of assisting their experimental designs for bioconjugation.

papers.title: Accurate and Rapid Vibrational Spectra of Molecular Crystals from Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Currently, vibrational spectra of molecular crystals often require computational methods to aid in band assignment, especially in the low-frequency region where no functional group specific transitions exist. DFT methods are the gold-standard for computational spectroscopy, but their high computational cost limits simulations to systems characterized by small unit cells. Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer a much cheaper alternative, but their reliability for phonons in molecular crystals has been little explored. In this work, eleven MLIPs from the ANI, MACE or UMA families of models are tested on geometry optimizations, vibrational frequencies and normal mode character with the same computational workflow utilized by DFT. The resulting phonons are then combined with DFT-calculated IR and Raman intensities to obtain vibrational spectra through a hybrid ML/DFT approach. The method is tested on three dispersion-bound molecular crystals, BTBT, naphthalene and anthracene, and three hydrogen-bonded systems, β-glycine and the two polymorphs of the ethosuximide (ETS) drug. MACE-MH omat, UMA omat and UMA omc emerge as the best-performing models and reproduce the experimental spectra with fidelity comparable to DFT.

papers.title: A Doubly Reversible Covalent Adaptable Network for (A)Cellular 3D Manufacturing and Post-Culture Cell Retrieval
papers.abstract: Covalent adaptable networks (CANs) are polymer networks in which bond formation and cleavage occur dynamically and reversibly. They are intensively investigated for 3D cell culture, as they model a more physiologically representative environment than traditional 2D culture. In most 3D matrices, however, cell retrieval for downstream analysis remains limited, and overcoming this limitation would advance in vitro 3D models for biomedical research. Herein, this limitation is addressed by functionalizing a cytocompatible and thermogelling diblock copolymer comprised of poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) and thermoresponsive poly(2-n-propyl-2oxazine) with biogenic, dithiolane-bearing lipoic acid. The resulting copolymer (P-LOx) is designed such that crosslinking forms a disulfide-based CAN, which, combined with the thermogelling behavior of the copolymer backbone, yields doubly reversible hydrogels with three key properties: excellent 3D-printability, long-term shape fidelity, and on-demand degradation under mild conditions. P-LOx-based hydrogels are successfully extruded in 3D bioprinting with NIH-3T3 fibroblasts and interleukin 12 reporter HEK293 cells. After crosslinking, cell-laden hydrogels remain stable in long-term 3D cell culture and support inbound-cytokine / outbound-protein diffusion. The limited cell-adhesive properties of the native P-LOx network are improved in hybrid formulations with bioactive additives. Finally, the established cytocompatible decrosslinking protocol enables non-enzymatic cell retrieval with >95% viability and allows downstream analysis, including flow cytometry.

papers.title: Mass-Constrained Integration of Cryogenic Propellant Management and Carbon–Hydrogen–Oxygen Resource Recovery for Mars Surface Depots: A Monte Carlo Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: A Mars surface propellant depot must make methane and oxygen, liquefy them and keep them cold on a limited launch mass, and each kilogram of added hardware displaces a kilogram of imported feedstock. This study asks which added layers pay for their mass. Seven nested depot configurations are compared at equal launch masses (9 t, a 30 kW array, 3 t of methane and 10.5 t of oxygen storage) by Monte Carlo simulation of 33 uncertain parameters, with paired comparisons and an independent energy audit. In the reference case (medium heat leak, intermittent power), the baseline holds 5,979 kg of usable propellant after one year and the 2 integrated plant 9,005 kg. Almost all of the gain comes from thermal layers: insulation (+1,533 kg), a vapor-cooled shield (+210 kg) and a cryocooler (+1,138 kg). More equipment does not mean better performance: gas and hydrogen buffers change the delivered propellant by only +22 kg, with a sign that depends on the scenario, a titanium-hydride store lowers it by 44 kg against compressed storage; recycled-material buffers change it by −1.3 kg. Coordinated dispatch adds +122 kg, or +4,547 kg, against a strict-priority baseline. With the parameter support widened two- and threefold, the sign of 7 of ten contrasts is unchanged. Only 5 of the 33 parameters are literature anchored, and the thermal model has no pressure-resolved two-phase tank; thus, the results are screening-level simulation outputs, not measurements.

papers.title: Landfill methane recovery and use under deep uncertainty: a satelliteconstrained Monte Carlo decision model for the Norte III landfill, Buenos Aires
papers.abstract: Very large landfills are major methane sources, but site decisions rarely join operator-reported capture, independent emission estimates and the economics of competing gas uses. We built a Latin-hypercube Monte Carlo decision model (300,000 draws, 78 inputs) of landfill-gas generation, collection, surface emission, oxidation, selective covers, biomethane upgrading, additional power generation and photovoltaics, and applied it to the Norte III landfill in Buenos Aires. A bottom-up generation prior is constrained by satellite emission estimates at their own date (2022) and carried to 2025–26. The inferred collection efficiency, 0.13 (0.09 to 0.19) in 2022 and 0.14 (0.10 to 0.21) in 2025–26 (median, 90% interval), follows from the emission, oxidation and reported capture, is conditional on the data and not a measurement, and increases to 0.24 (0.15 to 0.37) with an independent 2025 observation that the model overpredicts by a factor of 3.5. Under no-credit conditions none of eight integrated scenarios has a positive median net present value; wellfield optimization with a selective cover abates methane at a median US$3.6 per tCO2e. Additional engines are profitable in 99% of draws that have surplus gas, but in 69% of all operating states after the planned expansion; biomethane needs US$0.46 per Nm3 (US$14 per MMBtu). A cover helps only if the captured share of blocked gas exceeds an analytic break-even (median 0.14). Conclusions hold under alternative generation histories, satellite scaling and dated Argentine benchmarks.

papers.title: Encapsulation of f-block elements in borocarbide cages: Synthesis of a magnetic NdB3C3 clathrate
papers.abstract: We report the synthesis of a boron–carbon clathrate with neodymium guest ions, which is stabilized under high-pressure conditions and recoverable to ambient pressure. The compound, NdB3C3, crystallizes in the bipartite sodalite structure (space group Pm3̄n), as determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, and exhibits a zero-pressure bulk modulus K0 = 252(12) GPa. The electronic and magnetic properties of NdB3C3 were investigated using density functional theory with PBE, PBEsol, the HSE06 hybrid exchange–correlation functional, and DFT+U . The screened hybrid and DFT+U computations conducted using the experimental 30 GPa lattice constants of 4.73 Å give a band gap of 0.4 eV with spin-orbit origin and a magnetic ground state where the Nd ions each possess a spin moment of about 3 µB . Without spin-orbit we find no gap. The encapsulation of f-block elements within B–C clathrate cages provides a potential platform for realizing isolated, correlated spins with substantial crystal-field effects, expanding the range of tunable properties for this class of diamond-like materials.

papers.title: Active Learning for Fragment-Based Kinase Inhibitor Discovery using Docking
papers.abstract: Drug discovery requires efficient exploration of vast chemical spaces while minimizing computational cost. Fragment-based drug design offers a promising route for generating novel ligands through recombination of fragments, yet the resulting combinatorial search spaces rapidly become too large for exhaustive evaluation. Here, we present an active learning framework for navigating kinase-focused fragment recombination spaces derived from KinFragLib. Our approach combines subpocket-aware fragment recombination, structure-based docking, machine learning surrogate models, and genetic algorithm-inspired exploration through fragment additions, deletions, and substitutions around previously evaluated ligands. Rather than screening a fully enumerated recombination library, the framework iteratively generates and evaluates promising fragment modifications, enabling scalable exploration of large recombination spaces. Using protein kinase A (PKA) as a case study, we evaluate the framework on a recombination space containing approximately 210,000 ligands. Active learning identifies high-scoring candidates while evaluating only about 0.5% of the available ligands with the computationally expensive docking workflow. A greedy acquisition strategy recovers 52% of the global top-50 ligands, substantially outperforming random sampling. In addition, a diversity-aware acquisition strategy increases fragment coverage and exploration of alternative hinge-binding motifs while retaining competitive optimization performance. These results demonstrate that active learning can efficiently navigate fragment recombination spaces and substantially reduce computational screening costs. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a transferable strategy for kinase-focused ligand design and can be extended to other targets when suitable fragment libraries are available.

papers.title: AuditRxn: Auditable Fast-Weight Memories for Multi-Step Chemical Reaction Prefix-Prediction
papers.abstract: Multi-step organic synthesis planning requires tracking dynamic molecular transformations, protecting groups, and reaction conditions across sequential chemical stages. Existing chemical language models treat multi-step reaction sequences as flattened token streams within standard autoregressive Transformers. Under this paradigm, context lengths grow quadratically, low-information solvents and auxiliary reagents dilute attention away from reactive transformation centers, and hidden state transitions remain uninterpretable black boxes that hallucinate physically impossible steps violating valence rules and stoichiometric conservation. In this work, we propose AuditRxn, an auditable fast-weight memory framework for multi-step chemical reaction prefix-prediction and synthetic pathway planning. AuditRxn introduces a Chemical Fast-Weight Memory (CFWM) that dynamically binds reacting functional groups and catalytic states into a recurrent associative matrix state via an online Hebbian update rule, achieving 𝑂 (1) recurrent step complexity. To guarantee physical validity, a Constraint- Audited Recurrent Alignment (CARA) module inspects memory readouts against hard chemical constraints—including atomic valence, stoichiometric mass balance, and solvent-reagent hazard compatibility—projecting unconstrained latent trajectories onto an admissible reaction manifold while issuing step-wise audit certificates. Furthermore, Counterfactual Prefix-Aware Calibration (CPAC) trains the memory dynamics against perturbed reaction prefixes to suppress error cascades in autonomous multi-step rollouts. Comprehensive evaluations across four benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of AuditRxn: on USPTO-50K retrosynthesis, AuditRxn attains a Top-1 accuracy of 51.82% (+1.87% over competitive baselines) with 99.92% chemical validity; on SMolInstruct forward synthesis, it reaches 66.8% Top-1 exact match; on USPTO- Condition, it achieves 0.2985 overall condition accuracy; and on PaRoutes multi-step route planning, it improves Solve@10 route completion to 75.4% while reducing 10-step trajectory inference latency by 62.3%.

papers.title: Sharp Bounds for Raman Band-Area Ratios
papers.abstract: Nonnegative signal and background components, bounded observational error, constraints on background smoothness and band-free anchor measurements define a set of admissible decompositions. Linear-fractional optimization gives the exact minimum and maximum band ratios over this set, while a feasibility problem tests consistency of the imposed constraints. A closed-form bound relates remaining area uncertainty to the anchor spacing, background curvature, noise and band profile. In a study of 320 simulated spectra, the computed intervals contained the known ratios whenever the imposed assumptions were satisfied. Across 3,282 additional simulated configurations, the analytical bound was respected; its finite values were con-servative. Under bounded-noise simulations, restricted central integration windows improved identification for the investigated profiles, particularly for Lorentzian bands; on measured backgrounds, this advantage appeared only at high signal-to-noise ratio. In a semi-synthetic study using 70 measured sulfate-only spectra, leave-one-concentration-out calibration produced intervals containing the known ratios in all 2,520 evaluated window and sensitivity configurations. However, precise identification was often unavailable despite close agreement among six conventional baseline-correction settings. Application to measured nitrate–nitrite mixtures was further complicated by nitrate-band overlap, and the available calibration constraints did not identify the corrected ratios tightly. These results distinguish numerical agreement among baseline estimates from identification supported by explicitly defined spectral assumptions.

papers.title: Sliding Window Attention with Auditable Chemical Sinks for Long-Sequence Molecular Transformation Modeling
papers.abstract: Long molecular transformation sequences require models to track local bond changes and persistent reaction constraints. Conventional Transformers face high context costs, diluted attention, and chemically invalid predictions. We propose ChemSWA, an efficient and auditable framework for multi-step synthesis modeling. Adaptive Chemical Sliding Window Attention combines local windows with persistent attention sinks to retain reaction states at 𝑂 (𝑊 · 𝐿) computational complexity. A constraint-audited attribution mechanism checks chemical conservation and produces step-wise certificates, while counterfactual calibration reduces error accumulation during rollout. On USPTO-50K, ChemSWA achieves 52.14% Top-1 accuracy and 99.95% chemical validity; it reaches 92.85% Top-1 accuracy on USPTO-MIT. On PaRoutes, it achieves 76.10% Solve@10 with 3.85 s average expansion latency, and on USPTO-Condition it reaches 0.3015 multi-slot accuracy.

papers.title: Isocyanide Ligand Tuning of Rhenium Imido N−H BDFE Values for Catalytic Dinitrogen Reduction
papers.abstract: During N 2 reduction cycles that involve transition-metal-mediated N 2 splitting to nitrides, it is often thermodynamically difficult to form the first N–H bond on the way to ammonia. Increasing this N–H bond dissociation free energy (BDFE) is challenging because changes in the pK a and redox potential typically counteract one another. Here, we report that pincer-ligated rhenium complexes containing isocyanide ligands have dramatically higher imido N–H BDFE values than analogous chloride, cyanide, and pyridine complexes. Systematic electronic and steric variation of the isocyanides revealed that the Re V/IV reduction potentials for the nitride complexes can be varied over a range of ca. 2 V with more muted changes in the Re IV N–H pK a values, resulting in large N–H BDFE values that can be tuned over a range of 16 kcal/mol. Using this strategy, several new Re catalysts for N 2 reduction to NH 3 were discovered, including an alkyl isocyanide complex that produced up to 22 equiv of ammonia per Re center at room temperature using SmI 2 as reductant and ethylene glycol as a proton source. The results provide guidance on ligand tuning for forming N–H bonds from nitrides as part of homogeneous catalytic cycles for conversion of N 2 to NH 3 .

papers.title: Copper-Catalyzed Enantioconvergent Synthesis of Sulfoxides from Racemic Sulfinate Esters and Organoboronic Acids
papers.abstract: Chiral sulfoxides are important structural motifs in drug discovery and asymmetric synthesis. Transition-metalcatalyzed approaches to their enantioselective preparation have largely relied on thioether oxidation or coupling reactions involving highly reactive nucleophilic sulfinyl donors, such as sulfenic acids and sulfenate anions. Here, we report a copper-catalyzed enantioconvergent coupling of racemic sulfinate esters with organoboronic acids, in which the sulfinate esters serve as electrophilic sulfinyl donors. This method provides access to highly enantioenriched sulfoxides bearing two minimally differentiated aryl substituents, which are challenging targets for conventional asymmetric oxidation. The reaction also accommodates alkenylboronic acids and exhibits broad functional group tolerance, offering a complementary route for the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of sulfoxides from readily accessible starting materials.

papers.title: Nucleophile-Stabilized Transient o-Quinodimethide Forges a Common Gateway Toward C-1 P/N/O/C-Substituted Tetrahydroisoquinolines
papers.abstract: C-1-substituted tetrahydroisoquinolines (THIQs) represent a highly valuable and biologically privileged class of nitrogen heterocycles, owing to their stereochemically rich, structurally versatile scaffolds and widespread presence in medicinally relevant compounds, natural products, and bioactive molecules. Their remarkable pharmacological diversity and tunable molecular architecture make C-1-functionalized THIQs particularly powerful platforms for the discovery, design, and optimization of therapeutically important molecules. Despite their considerable significance, a general and versatile strategy for accessing structurally diverse C-1-functionalized THIQs remains highly desirable. Herein, we report a unified yet remarkably versatile method for the synthesis of C-1 P/N/O/C-functionalized THIQs, providing direct access to structural motifs reminiscent of the cores of six distinct C-1-substituted pharmaceutically and biologically relevant scaffolds. In particular, we have provided convenient access to the cores of IBR-2 (RAD51 inhibitor) and Eudistomin U (alkaloid), and a precursor of Praziquantel (marketed anthelmintic drug). The transformation proceeds from readily accessible 2-alkenylaldimines and a broad range of nucleophiles, including NH-amides, NH-heterocycles, dialkyl phosphites, and C-nucleophilic indoles, under mildly basic conditions. Notably, the method can be further extended to the selective synthesis of C-1-alkylated and C-1-oxygenated THIQs through the use of primary and secondary nitroalkanes, respectively. The reaction exhibits an exceptionally broad substrate scope, excellent functional-group compatibility, and operational simplicity, while readily enabling synthesis on a multi-gram scale, underscoring its practical potential for the preparation of medicinally relevant THIQ architectures. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the reaction proceeds through the generation of azabicyclo-o-quinodimethide (ABQ) interme-diates via thermal 6π-aza-electrocyclization of 2-alkenylaldimines. Competition experiments involving nucleophiles and Diels-Alder dienophiles, reactivity studies with a discrete iminium intermediate, control experiments, isotopic labelling and kinetic analyses using real-time 31P NMR collectively uncover an intriguing interplay between the nucleophile (NuH) and the ABQ intermediate. These studies support the transient formation of an ABQ•NuH complex, which subsequently undergoes basepromoted nucleophilic 1,4-addition to furnish the corresponding C-1-functionalized THIQ products.

papers.title: Lost in Chemical Space: Local Open-Source Large Language Models Display Model-Dependent Adherence to Reference Data in Molecular Generation
papers.abstract: chemical spaces remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated Gemma-4-31B, GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral-Small-4-119B, and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B at the BF16 (original precision), Q8, Q6, and Q4 quantization levels in two molecular generation tasks. The models were prompted either to generate small molecules without constraints or to generate drug-like molecules conditioned on 69 reference kinase inhibitors provided in-context. Quantization increased inference throughput in a modeldependent manner, with the largest gains, up to 24-fold increase in performance, occurring for Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B. In the task of unconstrained generation, model quantization did not affect molecular validity, uniqueness, drug-likeness, diversity and synthesizability. In the task of reference-guided generation, however, the models displayed markedly different levels of adherence to the provided chemical space. Gemma-4-31B was the only model that consistently generated small molecules similar to the reference compounds at all precision levels. Mistral-Small-4-119B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B failed to generate small molecules according to the reference chemical space. GPT-OSS-120B showed adherence to the reference molecules at BF16, Q8, and Q6, but lost the capacity to generate molecules in the desired chemical space at the Q4 quantization level. These results show that quantization can substantially improve the performance of local LLMs for molecular generation without compromising output quality, although model selection and validation is essential for guided exploration of the chemical space.

papers.title: POLEN: An OpenMM Framework for ML/MM Simulations with Mutually Polarizable AMOEBA Embedding
papers.abstract: Hybrid machine-learning and molecular mechanics formulations have been growing over the years. The attractive cost-effectiveness for big systems (such as protein complexes) has made these methods gain attention in the computational chemistry/biology field. In these theories, one of the most discussed themes is embedding, which can add or remove physics from the system. Here, we present POLEN (POLarizable Embedding for Neural-network potentials), an OpenMM plugin for ML/MM simulations with a mutually polarizable AMOEBA embedding, including a variant whose ML-trained head (MuPE(ML)) predicts multipoles, polarizabilities, and charge penetration at each simulation step. We tested it on three systems: a push-pull chromophore which a strong solvatochromic shift (p-nitroaniline in water); a protease-inhibitor complex with a buried salt bridge (trypsin-benzamidinium); and a kinase-inhibitor complex with a halogen bond (CK2α–TBB−).

papers.title: Crystallographic Continuity Enables Programmable Living Biointerfaces
papers.abstract: Dynamic biological entities are versatile but remain vulnerable to immune clearance, premature chemical exchange, and environmental degradation. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) offer porous matrices for bioencapsulation; however, standard polycrystalline or nanoparticulate shells contain structural defects that compromise protective performance and molecular selectivity. Here, we demonstrate the complete encapsulation of viruses, bacteria, and mammalian erythrocytes within continuous single-crystalline ZIF-90 via biocompatible aqueous routes. Interfacial electrostatics and coordination kinetics shift the nucleation-growth balance to favor particle coalescence and crystallographic fusion at the biological surface. Unlike conventional nanoparticulate ZIF-8 coatings, continuous ZIF-90 single crystals restrict molecular access, shielding host bacteria from ultraviolet radiation and antibiotic stress while preventing premature immunostimulatory signaling. Under acidic conditions mimicking the tumor microenvironment, ZIF-90 degrades, releasing active Escherichia coli and exposing intracellular bacterial triggers. In vivo , these biohybrids induce pyroptotic cell death and suppress pulmonary metastasis. Crystallographic continuity thus provides a structural basis for coupling biological shielding with environment-responsive activation, establishing a physical foundation for programmable biointerfaces.

papers.title: A reactor concept for more sustainable chemical vapor deposition of hard coatings
papers.abstract: Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) is a key technology for producing hard coatings on cutting tools, but its sustainability is challenged by high energy consumption and low precursor utilization. We present a novel reactor concept for hard coating CVD inspired by spatial atomic layer deposition, aiming to reduce environmental impacts through minimized reactor volume, reduced thermal mass, and the possibility for precursor recirculation. The concept is based on a small modular inline reactor in where the substrates are coated with TiN, as a model system, by rotating between areas with TiCl4 and NH3 exposure, allowing separation of the precursors in the different gas outlets. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were used to optimize gas flow management and life cycle assessment (LCA) was used to compare the proposed design with a conventional industrial batch CVD reactor for TiN-coated cutting inserts. The analysis indicates reductions of approximately 40% in global warming potential and 50% in fossil resource scarcity without precursor recycling. Assuming recovery of 50% of TiCl4 and 80% of NH3, the environmental impacts were further reduced to approximately 36% and 23% of those of a conventional process for global warming and fossil resource scarcity, respectively.

papers.title: Structural Analysis of HRF-4467, a Potent Second-Generation HIV-1 Maturation Inhibitor
papers.abstract: HRF-4467 is a betulinic acid-derived HIV-1 maturation inhibitor that targets the canonical CA-SP1 region and blocks the final proteolytic step of viral maturation. Here, we characterize HRF-4467 and its para-fluoro analog using solution and solid-state NMR spectroscopy, supported by quantum-mechanical calculations. Using this approach, we established the molecular connectivity and conformation of HRF-4467 in solution and in the solid state. Introducing a para-fluorine substitution produces localized changes within the aromatic moiety without substantially altering the rest of the molecular scaffold. This work establishes the para-fluoro derivative as a structurally representative analog of HRF-4467 and highlights 19 F NMR spectroscopy as a powerful tool for directly investigating inhibitor conformation and molecular recognition within the HIV-1 capsid maturation intermediate assemblies.

papers.title: Electrosynthesis of Free-Standing Polyoxometalate–PEDOT Hybrid Thin Films at a Polarizable Liquid|Liquid Interface
papers.abstract: Polyoxometalates (POMs) are versatile molecular redox systems, yet their electrochemical behavior at polarizable liquid|liquid interfaces remains unexplored. Here, we investigate Keggin-type phosphomolybdic acid (PMA) and phosphotungstic acid (PTA) at a polarizable aqueous|α,α,α-trifluorotoluene interface and demonstrate their use as molecular oxidants and dopants for the interfacial electrosynthesis of free-standing POM-poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) hybrid thin films. Voltammetry and in situ spectroscopy reveal potential-dependent adsorption and accumulation of POM anions at the interface. Under controlled interfacial polarization, accumulated POMs generate a highly acidic nanoscale reaction environment and catalyze the initial C−C coupling steps of EDOT oligomerization, enabling POM-PEDOT film formation despite thermodynamically unfavorable direct electron transfer between EDOT and the POMs. The resulting PEDOT nuclei evolve into conductive films that sustain growth through a redox cycle in which the POMs act as terminal oxidants and dopant anions. Mixing PMA and PTA markedly enhances growth kinetics, yielding robust, transferable hybrid films with hierarchical three-dimensional morphologies, high POM loadings, and preserved Keggin structures. Ex situ electrochemical characterization reveals the coexistence of PEDOT charging and highly reversible POM-centered redox processes, producing capacitances of up to 48 F g –1 in organic electrolyte and >90% capacitance retention at scan rates up to 1 V s –1 . These findings establish polarizable liquid|liquid interfaces as a powerful platform for synthesizing free-standing electroactive hybrid materials.

papers.title: Chemistry-Informed Transfer and Interaction-Resolved Learning Towards Data-Efficient Materials Exploration
papers.abstract: Optimizing synthesis parameters for new thin-film materials is slow and often relies on intuition and trial and error. Gaussian process (GP) models suit low-data settings, but treat each material separately or need engineered descriptors to learn across materials. Multi-task GPs share information across materials but infer these relationships solely from sparse data, making them unreliable early on. We introduce a chemistry-informed multi-task GP that derives these relationships from a Tanimoto kernel on molecular fingerprints, enabling knowledge transfer without descriptor engineering. In closed-loop, uncertaintydriven exploration of a seven-dimensional synthesis space, comprising one categorical variable (three chiral 2D hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite compositions) and six continuous synthesis parameters, we tested 287 conditions (<0.1% of the discretized synthesis space). Knowledge transfer matched the accuracy of single-task GPs trained on the full target dataset using between 35-60% of the target data. Interaction analysis revealed a three-way coupling among annealing temperature, precursor concentration, and composition. This coupling makes a one-variable-at-a-time optimization challenging. Our framework offers a simple strategy for transferring and interpreting knowledge across related materials.

papers.title: 3D Structure Analysis from XAS using Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: The local three-dimensional (3D) atomic structure of materials and molecules can be interrogated by X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), a powerful analytical technique. Here, we introduce a diffusionmodel-based approach that rapidly infers candidate 3D structures from X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) data. The method is validated on multi-element hard X-ray XAS datasets and generalizes across a broad range of molecular and material systems without imposing restrictions on the number of constituent element types. Compared with multi-round iterative optimization methods for 3D structure determination that use a structure-to-spectrum model as the core spectral calculation engine, our approach substantially improves data analysis efficiency, enabling 3D structure determination within a few reverse diffusion steps. On low-end consumer GPUs, 3D structure analysis takes 0.5–5s. We anticipate that this method will significantly facilitate online data analysis at beamlines and associated real-time experimental planning and optimization, enable batch screening of atomic-level 3D structures, and improve the efficiency of conventional 3D structure fitting.

papers.title: AI Agents as supporting infrastructure for all-solid-state battery development
papers.abstract: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.

papers.title: A Scoping Review of Diffusion-Based De Novo Molecular Generation: Architectures, Evaluation, and Open Challenges for Computational Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Diffusion models form the bulk of generative frameworks used in de novo molecular design, yet the literature remains fragmented across model formulations, molecular representations, and generative tasks, and inadequate systematic accounts exist of how these models are steered towards molecules with desired properties, an aspect of drug discovery that is paramount to acceptance. We present a scoping review of diffusion-based neural networks applied in de novo drug discovery between 2020 and 2026. Following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) protocol, we categorise the literature into non-mutually exclusive themes covering methodological contributions, conditioning mechanisms, molecular representations, symmetries, and multi-modal integrations, and outline the datasets and evaluation metrics used throughout. Three findings emerge. First, diffusion did not displace earlier architectures so much as absorb them: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Autoencoders, and Transformers persist as backbones, and what changed was the training objective. Second, conditioning strategies reduce to structural anchoring, target-aware biochemical conditioning, property-driven steering, and multimodal latent conditioning; within these, the point in the reverse trajectory at which a conditioning signal is applied is a design variable distinct from the signal itself. Third, evaluation remains unstandardised across frameworks, datasets, and definitions. We identify the resulting gaps in controllability and interpretability as the central open challenge for conditioned molecular generation and outline the direction to ease them as this would enable generation of molecules that match the preferred property profiles.

papers.title: Facile Nitrogen Doping of Electrospun Mesoporous Carbon Nanofibers via Urea Addition for Polysulfide-Confining Li-S Cathodes and Interlayers
papers.abstract: Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries offer high theoretical capacity, but polysulfide dissolution and shuttling cause rapid capacity fade. Nitrogen functional groups can anchor polysulfides, yet in our previous work, introducing them through a post-carbonization cyclized-PAN treatment sacrificed much of the carbon nanofiber (CNF) mesoporosity, and Nfunctionalizing both cathode and interlayer performed worst. Here, nitrogen is introduced during fiber formation by adding urea to a PAN/PMMA precursor before gas-assisted electrospinning, followed by stabilization, carbonization, and CO2 activation. This gives N-doped mesoporous CNFs with better control over the balance between nitrogen content and pore structure. Across four cathode/interlayer combinations ,every cell with at least one N-doped component outperformed the undoped cell. The N-doped cathode with N-doped interlayer performed best, delivering 1271 mAh g-1 at 2C with the lowest charge-transfer resistance (8 Ω vs. 11 Ω undoped). Post-mortem XPS revealed Li-N interactions and polysulfide retention, strongest in the interlayers. Precursor-level nitrogen doping is therefore an effective route to Li-S cathodes and interlayers that balance nitrogen and mesoporosity.

papers.title: C2 Homologation of Alkenes with Programmable Substitution
papers.abstract: Alkene homologation represents an efficient strategy for upgrading commodity olefins and expediting the synthesis of their longer homologues. However, current alkene homologation methodologies are limited to the access to terminal alkenes. Herein, we report a radical‑based approach that enables C2 homologation of alkenes with programmable substitution patterns. This transformation features a radical hydro-alkylation of alkenes using bromomethylphosphonium hexafluorophosphate as an electrophilic carbon radical precursor. The resulting phosphonium salt, bearing a C1-extended chain, undergoes Wittig olefination with inexpensive aldehyde/ketone to deliver C2-elongated terminal/1,2-/1,1,2-substituted alkenes (>40 examples, up to 99% yield; Z/E up to >20:1, with photocatalytic access to the E-isomers). This protocol exhibits broad functional group tolerance and is applicable to the late-stage modification of bioactive compounds, pharmaceuticals, and liquid crystals. Furthermore, by iteratively combining this C2 method with our previously established C1 homologation, the olefinic chains of complex molecules can be precisely elongated by three, four, or more carbon atoms. Comprehensive mechanistic studies, including DFT calculations and experimental probes, support a radical pathway and identify hydrogen bonding between HFIP and triethylamine, which raises the competing HAT barrier from 8.5 to 13.1 kcal/mol, as the key element that suppresses reductive debromination and channels the radical toward C–C bond formation.

papers.title: Techno-Economic and Geospatial Assessment of Distributed Fertilizer Production via Wastewater Ammonia Solar Electrochemical Stripping
papers.abstract: Decentralized alternatives to centralized fertilizer production are needed to reduce supply chain risks, minimize transportation costs, and lower environmental impacts. Solar-powered Electrochemical Stripping (ECS) is an emerging technology that can produce ammonium fertilizer in a distributed manner through wastewater nitrogen recovery. We quantify the fraction of fertilizer demand in the United States that can be met by a wastewater feedstock while minimizing transportation distances, finding that 55% (5.54 Mt N per year) of demand is co-located with sufficient supply from domestic, agricultural, or industrial wastewater. A techno-economic assessment of ECS at scales sufficient to meet localized fertilizer demand estimated breakeven prices of US$8.70/kg N for ammonium sulfate, US$9.69/kg N for ammonium nitrate, and US$31.18/kg N for monoammonium phosphate, and US$12.15/kg N for diammonium phosphate. Integration of the techno-economic model with geospatial analysis found ECS-derived fertilizer prices ranged from 2.2x-5.5x local 2016-2026 retail prices, with ECS performing most competitively in the Pacific U.S. region. Sensitivity analysis showed improving current efficiency, increasing current density, lowering capital cost, and increasing equipment lifetime would have the greatest impact on approaching retail cost parity. This work elucidates pathways and barriers to widespread implementation of wastewater-derived fertilizers and advances United Nations Sustainable Development goals for responsible consumption and production, clean water, and zero hunger.

papers.title: Dynamical confinement effects on chromophore photoexcitations in a light-harvesting protein
papers.abstract: Naturally evolved light-harvesting complexes are assembled from highly evolutionarily-conserved sequences of amino acids that form functional chemical pockets for chromophores. The protein environment surrounding the chromophore influences its dynamical structure, which can have consequences for light harvesting efficiency. Here, we explore the impact of the C-phycocyanin protein scaffold on the dynamical structure and photoexcited states of the phycocyanobilin (PCB) chromophore using a combination of molecular dynamics and the ab initio Bethe Salpeter equation approach. We compute low-lying excited states of the PCB chromophore for an ensemble of snapshots from molecular dynamics trajectories, and use a normal mode analysis to understand the nature of thermal displacements of PCB in the confined protein environment. We analyze the excited state energies in terms of one electron and electron-hole contributions, identifying displacement patterns with the strongest exciton-vibrational coupling. Our results provide insight into how thermal motion of the chromophore is altered in protein environments and the resulting impact on photo-excited states, with implications for other natural light harvesting materials.

papers.title: Single-chirality single-walled carbon nanotubes for electrochemical co-detection of serotonin and dopamine
papers.abstract: Dopamine (DA) and serotonin (5-HT) are neurotransmitters whose dysregulation is associated with neurodegenerative diseases. The influence of single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) chirality on sensing remains underexplored. Mixed-chirality SWC- NTs can limit sensor reproducibility and accuracy. Precise control of electrode material structure may promote more specific surface-analyte interactions, enhancing selectivity. Here, screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCE) were modified with four SWCNT types: mixed-chirality metallic/semiconducting (m/s), metallic (m), or semiconducting (s) SWCNT, and single-chirality semiconducting (6,5)-SWCNT isolated by aqueous two-phase extraction. Vacuum filtration produced surfactant-free SWCNT layers. Codetection of 5-HT and DA was evaluated using differential pulse voltammetry (DPV). The (6,5)-SWCNT/SPCE gave the largest potential difference (∆E = Ep(5-HT)− Ep(DA)) of 151 ± 4 mV and a peak current ratio (Ip(DA)/Ip(5-HT)) of 0.99 ± 0.23. Corresponding values for unmodified SPCE, m/s-SWCNT/SPCE, m-SWCNT/SPCE, and s-SWCNT/SPCE were 139±10, 145±3, 143±6, and 147±3 mV, and 0.60±0.23, 0.63±0.12, 0.63±0.11, and 0.69±0.01, respectively. The (6,5)-SWCNT/SPCE detected both analytes even when one analyte was present in excess. Between 0.04 and 1 µM, linear responses were obtained for 5-HT alone, DA in the presence of 1 µM 5-HT, and 5-HT in the presence of 1 µM DA, with sensitivities of 0.024 ± 0.002, 0.011 ± 0.001, and 0.024± 0.001 nA/nM, respectively. These results show that SWCNT chirality control improves the electrochemical co-detection of 5-HT and DA.

papers.title: Integration of Acoustic Ejection Mass Spectrometry Enables Efficient High Throughput Purification Workflow for Peptides in Discovery Space
papers.abstract: 2 ABSTRACT Modern peptide drug discovery combines mRNA display-derived libraries and iterative optimization of hits using solid phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) during hit-to-lead process. Part of this discovery workflow is the need for sufficient amounts of high-quality peptide targets, free from impurities to support the required preclinical assays. In this context, there is a need for streamlined high throughput purification (HTP) workflow coupled with high throughput analytical assays, enabling faster analysis of large volumes of synthetic peptide libraries for purification to accelerate the discovery process. We have developed and validated an ultra-high throughput (uHT) acoustic ejection mass spectrometry (AEMS) based pre-quality control (QC) triage assay for peptide libraries in HTP process, which achieves a sampling rate of ~2 sec/sample with minimal sample requirement (25- 45 µL) and solvent consumption, and fast data analysis, suitable for large sample size in discovery setting. Sample purity profile of the library provided by the newly developed assay is beneficial for HT identification of samples that will or will not advance to purification, enabling a streamlined, faster process, and immediate decisionmaking. Results from the validation and bridging studies are in agreement with the currently employed low-throughput UPLC-UV/MS based HTP pre-QC assay. Integration of the recently developed AEMS-based pre-QC assay in the HTP workflow using a sample purity cut-off of 15% for go/no-go decision renders a minimal false negative, <6% and a false positive results of <12%, making it applicable for the purpose of vetting which samples should be purified to reduce the overall experimental time and cost resource in the HTP process. The recently developed assay demonstrated the first application of AEMS as a pre-QC step in peptide HTP workflow, and its potential application for broad peptide library screening in drug discovery.

papers.title: Recombination-zone position, not charge balance, sets the efficiency ceiling of deep-blue TADF host OLEDs
papers.abstract: Low efficiency in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) is often blamed on charge balance, yet the device models that could test this are rarely converged or constrained by measured inputs. We solve converged drift–diffusion, transfermatrix and dipole models for three deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) phosphine-oxide hosts, S1, S3 and S4, with an open solver verified against a converged commercial reference, and we constrain every hostspecific input by measurement: film optical constants from ellipsometry, film photoluminescence, voltammetric host levels and host transport fitted to quality-gated single-carrier current–voltage data. In every converged model OLED with the fitted transport, and also with a shallow-trap transport alternative and with offsets across their identifiable range, charge balance and host confinement are not the limit. What decides the efficiency is where the recombination zone sits: moving it from the electron-transport interface into the host raises the computed air outcoupling about threefold. The model-conditioned efficiency ceiling is therefore set by zone placement and by the photoluminescence quantum yield, which also fixes the host ranking S1>S4≳S3, and transport engineering becomes an outcoupling lever. Two measurements, thickness-dependent current–voltage and angle-resolved photoluminescence, would pin the remaining model ranges (all device quantities are model outputs).

papers.title: Self-Derived Metal/Oxide Interface Engineering via Active Nitrogen Mediation
papers.abstract: Self-derived phase engineering of metal oxides offers a powerful route to create interfaces without introducing foreign metallic elements, yet achieving systematic control over phase transition remains challenging. Here, active nitrogen-mediated phase engineering was demonstrated across various metal oxides (SnO 2 , ZnO, and TiO 2 ). As a model biphasic material, Sn/SnO 2 was investigated where urea thermolysis enabled the progressive formation of metallic Sn while largely preserving the host structure, allowing the Sn0 fraction to be systematically controlled. Temperature-programmed experiments using mass spectrometry and FT-IR revealed the involvement of nitrogen-containing intermediates during urea decomposition and supported their central role in driving phase engineering of SnO 2 . Density functional theory (DFT) based calculations on a Sn/SnO 2 model constructed using a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) revealed electron transfer from metallic Sn to SnO 2 and the resulting redistribution of surface electron density. The resulting self-derived Sn/SnO 2 biphasic material yields favorable surface chemistry by altered surface oxygen behavior and reactivity translating directly into two applications: enhanced chemoresistive formaldehyde gas sensing under humid conditions with ppb-level detection, as well as improved formate production in electrochemical CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR). Our results identify active nitrogen as a chemical handle for regulating oxide partial reduction and provide a general framework for the systematic engineering of metal/oxide interfaces.

papers.title: Measured Host Optical Constants Shift Deep-Blue OLED Outcoupling by up to 14% (Relative) While Leaving the Stack Design Intact
papers.abstract: Outcoupling designs for organic light-emitting diodes rest on the complex refractive index of every layer, yet host films are often given a constant index without absorption. We show what measured constants change, and what they do not. Variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry of three deep-blue phosphine-oxide host films (S1, S3 and S4), refitted from the raw data with several dispersion models, pins the index of the S1 and S4 films to a model-andspot spread of about ±0.002 (about ±0.004 at 95% once substrate-oxide, incidence-angle and roughness systematics are propagated) and reveals a weak absorption tail in S4 that follows its triphenylamine-centered lowest singlet transition; the S3 film is bracketed. Propagated through a dipole model of a deep-blue stack in which the neat host film is the emitter, the measured constants leave the design itself (best emitter position, optimum electron-transport-layer thickness) unchanged within a few nanometers but shift the predicted outcoupling by up to 14% relative (15.1 against 17.2% at the optimum, about 2 percentage points), with the blue dispersion of the index and, for S4, the absorption tail in the emission band contributing comparably (up to about 7% each). Emitter orientation and the emitter–cathode distance act far more strongly, by factors of 2 to 5. Both films are close to isotropic, yet the calculated transition dipoles of S3 and S4 lie in the molecular plane, so growing these hosts with flat-lying molecules is the clearest route to higher outcoupling, worth about a factor of two in the model.

papers.title: Weak-Form Regression Recovers the Delayed-Fluorescence Rate Law from Flash-Lamp Decays with Near-Optimal Precision
papers.abstract: Delayed-fluorescence rates and their temperature laws are how thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) materials are ranked, yet the rate law is usually fixed before the analysis, and flash-lamp decays mix the emission with the excitation profile. We show that weak-form regression, with photon-counting statistics and the excitation built into its features, identifies the rate law as a sequence of linear problems with calibrated uncertainties. With a known pulse the whole record, including the excitation window, is used; otherwise the emission after the window is tested against first-order, bimolecular and dispersive terms, and temperature laws are ranked by bootstrap selection frequency. On synthetic decays with lifetimes of 1–1000 µs the method approaches the expected-Fisher precision benchmark and, with the full covariance of its weak residuals, matches fullrecord Poisson maximum likelihood on identical data, whereas ignoring the excitation tail biases rates by more than an order of magnitude and creates spurious activation in more than half of temperature-independent series. Applied to two deep-blue phosphine-oxide hosts, it shows that the later-window delayed emission is not purely first order and that its effective rate has no resolved thermal activation between 200 and 300 K. For this effective rate the tested single-gap Marcus law with the computed gaps is ruled out as rate limiting, which points to a temperature-independent or smallbarrier channel. An identifiability map and open code let any laboratory check, before reporting, which rate law its instrument can resolve.

papers.title: Scientific Symbiosis: Bridging Expertise and Fostering Effective Collaborations with Mass Spectrometrists
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS) is increasingly used to answer biological questions, yet effective collaboration between mass spectrometrists and researchers in other fields can be limited by differences in terminology, expectations, and familiarity with analytical workflows. This review provides a practical and accessible guide to incorporating MS into biological and environmental research with an emphasis on improving communication and collaboration. In the review, we walk through the MS workflow including defining the scientific question, selecting an analytical approach, sample collection and preparation, instrumental analysis, data processing, quality assessment, and interpretation. Particular attention is given to concepts that commonly create confusion across fields, including quantitative strategies, analytical controls, sample handling, instrument monitoring, and data reporting expectations. We also discuss the respective roles of both experimentalists and mass spectrometrists throughout the research process and highlight areas where early communication can prevent downstream problems. To support real-world application, the review includes a glossary of commonly used MS terminology and a checklist of key considerations for collaborative studies. Together, these resources are intended to make MS workflows more approachable and to foster the kind of scientific symbiosis between researchers and mass spectrometrists that is needed to generate high-quality, interpretable, and meaningful data.

papers.title: Thermal Formation of a Magenta Merocyanine in Ethanol: A Microsolvated SP→TCC→TTC Pathway in a Nitrospiropyran
papers.abstract: Solutions of 5’-methoxy-1’,3’,3’-trimethyl-6-nitrospiro[chromene-2,2’-indoline] in alcohols are intensely pink in the dark, become colorless under white light and recover their color thermally, with Arrhenius activation energies of 101.1± 0.5, 104.9± 1.6 and 105.3± 1.4 kJ mol−1 in ethanol, methanol and acidified ethanol, respectively. The measured process is therefore the thermal formation of the merocyanine (MC) from the photogenerated spiropyran (SP). The absorbance of the equilibrated ethanol solution, combined with the calculated oscillator strength, indicates that MC constitutes only a small fraction of the compound, of the order of a few per cent. With continuum solvation alone no cis-merocyanine intermediate (TCC) is found, whereas in a complex with five explicit ethanol molecules a fast SP⇌TCC pre-equilibrium precedes a considerably slower isomerization to the trans isomer (TTC). The reversible kinetic model shows that the measured rate constant reflects the position of the

papers.title: Integrating classical similarity and multitask neural representations
papers.abstract: Background. Computational prediction of compound–target associations can help prioritize hypotheses for experimental investigation. While deep learning architectures are increasingly proposed, their apparent superiority often relies on comparisons against untuned classical baselines or evaluation protocols prone to data leakage. Objective. We present a scaffold-disjoint evaluation benchmark derived from ChEMBL 37 to evaluate multitask neural representations against tuned classical similarity search, and we investigate whether combining both paradigms yields improved ranking performance. Methods. The benchmark comprised 100,000 compounds, 1,979 human single-protein targets, and 139,789 positive associations, partitioned by Bemis–Murcko scaffold into train (70%), validation (10%), and test (20%) sets. All hyperparameters were selected on the validation set. We compared a multitask MLP with a tuned K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN-20) baseline, as well as a hybrid model integrating both representations. Results. On the held-out test set, the tuned KNN-20 achieved a Hits@10 of 0.9335, statistically indistinguishable from the 10-seed multitask MLP ensemble (0.9355; Δ = +0.0021, 95% CI [−0.0012,+0.0052]). However, a hybrid model integrating both representations (40% KNN, 60% MLP) achieved a significantly higher Hits@10 of 0.9426, outperforming both KNN-20 (Δ = +0.0091, 95% CI [+0.0066,+0.0116]) and the MLP alone (Δ = +0.0070, 95% CI [+0.0052,+0.0089]). Conclusions. Our results demonstrate that while complex neural models do not inherently outperform well-tuned classical baselines, they capture complementary information. A hybrid approach combining classical chemical similarity and multitask neural representations yields a modest but statistically significant improvement in ranking performance within this benchmark. This study emphasizes the necessity of rigorous baseline tuning and suggests hybrid architectures as a promising direction for compound–target prediction.

papers.title: The Thiolate Shell as a Dynamic Gold Reservoir: Size-Dependent Thermal Restructuring of Gold Nanoclusters from MACE-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Atomically precise thiolate-protected gold nanoclusters are used in catalysis, sensing and nanomedicine, where thermal activation, reaction conditions or local heating can change their atomic structure. Whether the gold–thiolate shell remains a fixed protective layer at elevated temperature, or takes part in the restructuring of the cluster, is still an open question, because first-principles molecular dynamics is limited to small clusters and short times. Here we train MACE-AuSCH, an equivariant machine-learned interatomic potential, on a published density functional theory dataset and validate it against 16 crystallographically characterised clusters (cohesive-energy RMSE of 2.1 meV/atom). We then follow seven Aun(SCH3)m clusters, from Au25 to Au279 and with icosahedral and FCC-derived cores, between 8 and 800 K. In all clusters, the effective stiffness of the Au–S bonds is 3.3 to 7.5 times that of the Au–Au bonds, and the metallic Au–Au network reorganises first while most of the Au–S connectivity is kept. At 500 K, the largest core displacements occur in the FCC-derived Au52 and Au92. At 800 K, Au atoms move in both directions between the metallic core and the staple shell, and the loss of Au–S connectivity generally grows with cluster size, from 3% for Au25 to about 40% for Au144. These results describe the protecting shell as a dynamic reservoir of Au atoms and point to an intracluster route that may precede ligand and metal exchange, fragmentation and sintering.

papers.title: LigandFF: an open-source implementation of rule-based atom typing, charge assignment and parameter assignment by analogy
papers.abstract: The CHARMM General Force Field (CGenFF) covers drug-like molecules through an automated assignment program that types atoms, assigns charges from bond-charge increments, and transfers missing bonded parameters from analogous ones with an associated penalty. The algorithms are published, but the program and its two hand-built rule files are distributed only in binary form. We describe LigandFF, an open-source reimplementation built exclusively from the published algorithms and the public CGenFF 5.0 topology, parameter and charge-increment files. LigandFF implements the published ring, resonance and aromaticity perception, the rule language for atom typing, the bond-charge-increment scheme with peratom charge penalties, the penalty-weighted analogy search, halogen lone pairs, and writes CHARMM stream files, PSF files and OpenMM and GROMACS inputs. Its typing rules were written against the CGenFF training molecules, and its substitution-penalty matrices were fitted to 5,787 analogies that the official program recorded in the parameter file. On held-out test splits, LigandFF types 97.4% and 97.8% of two sets of CGenFF training molecules with every atom correct (99.7% and 99.6% of atoms). Replaying the analogies recorded in the parameter file against the database they were made from, it recovers the official program’s choice of source parameter for 92.1% of 1,447 held-out cases. It reproduces the program-5.0 charges and penalties printed in the CGenFF 5.0 supporting information exactly, and all 2,074 benchmark molecules produce systems that build in OpenMM. All references are CGenFF training molecules or outputs of the official program that are already public; agreement with the official program on new drug-like molecules has not been measured. LigandFF is not the official CGenFF program, and its outputs are labelled accordingly.

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into Ascorbate-Mediated Activation of Pt(IV) Prodrugs: Axial-Ligand Modulation of Dissociative Reduction Pathways and Redox Latency
papers.abstract: Pt(IV) coordination compounds act as anticancer prodrugs that are intracellularly reduced to cytotoxic Pt(II) species, a process whose selectivity and kinetics depend critically on the nature of the axial leaving (L L ) and bridging (L B ) ligands. Using DFT/IEFPCM calculations in water, we examined the ascorbate-mediated reduction of six [PtIV(NH 3 ) 2 Cl 2 (L L )(L B )] complexes bearing different axial-ligand combinations of chloride, bromide, and dichloroacetate (DCA): L L /L B = Br/Cl, Cl/Cl, DCA/Cl, as well as DCA/Br, Cl/Br, and Br/Br. For the full series, the mechanistic analysis was therefore focused on the inner-sphere pathway involving nucleophilic attack of the ascorbate enolate at the C β center (M2), characterized as concerted yet highly asynchronous. Both axial ligands modulate the activation barrier, charge-transfer efficiency, and Pt-L bond dissociation, but the bridging ligand exerts the dominant effect: L B = chloride derivatives display the highest free-energy barriers (Δ[Δ ‡ G298] ≈ 2-4 kcal mol -1 ), high charge-transfer percentages (49%-50%) and later transition states relative to L B = bromide analogs. Additionally, the activation barrier is most strongly associated with the extent of charge transfer and its coupling to C β –L B bond formation, rather than the overall bond-structural event. These results suggest that L B primarily determines the dissociative-reduction behavior, while L L provides secondary control, thereby providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how axial-ligand combinations influence redox latency in Pt(IV) scaffolds.

papers.title: Reconfigurable Nanoscale Material Display
papers.abstract: Dynamic material arrays that combine programmable reconfiguration with direct structural readout could enable materials that both adapt their spatial organization and represent molecular information. DNA nanotechnology offers exceptional control over nanoscale organization, yet most DNA-templated material arrays are static, whereas dynamic DNA circuits typically rely on indirect ensemble readouts. Here, we present a Reconfigurable Material Display, implemented as REMBRANDT (REconfigurable Material-Based Representation of Addressable Nanoscale Display sTates), a DNA-origami platform that decouples structural assembly from programmable organization of nanoscale cargo. A 5 × 5 array of independently addressable DNA pixels organizes DNA-functionalized nanocargo, including gold nanoparticles, quantum dots, and ferritin, and programmably relocates them without reconstructing the underlying scaffold. Pixel encodings define programmable single- and multi-material display states, whereas DNA strand-displacement reactions rewrite cargo-pixel associations to produce sequential and reversible display-state transformations. Each display state is directly resolved by atomic force microscopy and electron microscopy at single-particle and single-display resolution. Programmable cargo relocation further visualizes predefined matrix operations as dynamically reconfigurable material patterns. By integrating programmable reconfiguration with direct structural readout, REMBRANDT establishes a material display in which molecular information is represented, updated, and visualized through nanocargo organization.

papers.title: Sulfur Oxidation State Controls Radical Smiles–Truce Rearrangements through a Switch in Cyclization Selectivity
papers.abstract: The radical Smiles–Truce rearrangement is a powerful strategy for constructing aryl–carbon bonds, although competing ortho addition often limits the utility of conventional S(VI) sulfonamide precursors. Here, we demonstrate that switching to S(IV) sulfinamides enables selective ipso aryl migration while providing a stereochemical handle for asymmetric induction. We report a visible-light-driven nitrogen-centered radical cascade that converts alkene-tethered N-acyl sulfinamides into densely functionalized lactams, fused bicycles, and spirocycles through a desulfinylative Smiles–Truce rearrangement. The transformation accommodates electronically diverse arenes, heteroarenes, and substituted alkenes, affording products in up to 85% yield. Moreover, enantioenriched sulfinamide precursors enable efficient transfer of stereochemical information to the products, with up to 93% enantiospecificity. In contrast to analogous S(VI) sulfonamide reactions, competing ortho dearomatization is not observed. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the S(IV) system disfavors the competing ortho-addition pathway, providing a mechanistic basis for the observed selectivity reversal and establishing sulfinamides as versatile precursors for stereocontrolled radical annulations.

papers.title: Physicochemical Prioritization of Hypothetical Metal–Organic Frameworks for Experimental Synthesis
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of AI-driven and computationally designed metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) raises a fundamental question: which hypothetical structures are most likely to be experimentally realized? Here, we develop a physicochemically informed strategy to prioritize MOFs for synthesis by integrating molecular synthetic accessibility, framework geometry, electronic structure, solvent removal stability, and thermodynamic stability through positive–unlabeled learning. Using 9,033 experimentally reported MOFs as examples of realized structures and hypothetical MOFs as candidates with unknown synthesizability, we identify 5 complementary physicochemical descriptors that enable effective prioritization, achieving a source-averaged normalized positive rank of 0.93 by placing experimentally realized MOFs near the top of candidate rankings across held-out database sources. Further analysis reveals that experimentally realized MOFs are enriched at low linker geometric distortion and low energy above the convex hull of competing phases, highlighting complementary geometric and thermodynamic considerations. Moreover, secondary building unit–linker analyses identify specific chemical combinations enriched among highly ranked hypothetical structures. Together, these findings establish a chemically interpretable approach to prioritizing hypothetical MOFs and help bridge the gap between computational materials design and experimental synthesis.

papers.title: Scalable Density-Based Bootstrap Embedding with Perturbative Triples for Large Molecular Systems
papers.abstract: Extending density-based bootstrap embedding (BE) with perturbative triples to large molecules requires control of both fragment solver cost and tensor storage. We present a restricted and unrestricted BE-CCSD(T) implementation combining density-fitted embedding transformations, fragment parallelism, and streamed contractions of triples density contributions. Explicit one-and two-particle terms and the correction to the coupled-cluster multipliers are retained without assembling a molecular two-particle density matrix or storing a complete triples tensor. Fixed-order fragmentation bounds the local correlated problem under stated locality assumptions, while blockwise evaluation controls temporary storage. Timings for

papers.title: The Evolution of Electronic Structure in Conjugated Molecules Revealed by Mixed-Reference Spin-Flip Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory and Density-Based Analyses: II. Polyacenes
papers.abstract: Large conjugated molecules feature small gaps between occupied and virtual orbital spaces, which results in complex electronic structure patterns in their low-lying states. These orbital near-degeneracies also challenge quantum chemistry methods. Mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT (MRSF-TDDFT) and density-matrix-based analyses provide useful tools to interrogate electronic structure in large conjugated molecules. This paper investigates one such family—polyacenes. Following our recent study of the ground and low-lying excited states of all-trans polyenes, we track this evolution from benzene to dodecacene using MRSF-TDDFT and densitymatrix-based analyses.
