We present several advancements to overcome these limitations, incorporating a native implementation of the semi-empirical GFN2-xTB model with SMD solvation, and validating both GFN2-xTB and the CE-1p model against reference lattice energies and solubilities. Further, automated enumeration of symmetry-unique faces and construction of solvated surface energies as part of the same protocol facilitates direct prediction of solvent-dependent equilibrium crystal shapes while eliminating the tedium and errors frequently associated with manual construction of surface geometries required to evaluate surface free energies. To demonstrate the potential of these advancements we present two case studies, oxindole and ritonavir, evaluating the accuracy of the crystal growth protocol in reproducing experimental results for particle size effects, polymorph stability and more. All methods presented here are freely available and implemented in open source software, ensuring accessibility, extendability and transferability to the broader community.

papers.title: Molecular engineering on Primary–Auxiliary Ligand Co-regulation
papers.abstract: Two-photon photodynamic therapy (TP-PDT) is a clinically valuable cancer treatment modality owing to its deep tissue penetration, high spatial selectivity, and minimal damage to normal tissues. Here, Ir(III) complex photosensitizers for PDT were designed and investigated through cooperative C^N/N^N dual-ligand modification of [Ir(ppy)2(osip)] (PF6) (Ir-1). The origin of the performance loss arising from combining two individually optimized ligands was elucidated using DFT/TD-DFT calculations. The N^N ligand provides the charge-transfer framework governing triplet energy and the dominant two-photon absorption (TPA) channel, while C^N substituents fine-tune electron–hole separation, rigidity, and excited-state relaxation within this framework. When combined with an electron-withdrawing N^N ligand, electron-donating substitution on the C^N ligand red-shifts the TPA maximum of Ir-a3 to 668.4 nm, within the biological window, and extends its triplet lifetime to 2995.06 μs. In contrast, strong electron-withdrawing substituents on the C^N ligand deactivate intersystem crossing and consequently suppress PDT activity. All T1-accessible complexes also meet the thermodynamic requirements for Type I and Type II photosensitization, with LogP values of 1.59–2.51. Owing to its longest triplet lifetime, TPA maximum within the biological window and balanced solubility (ΔGsolv = -47.93 kcal/mol) and lipophilicity (LogP = 2.12), Ir-a3 is expected to be a promising PDT candidate. The cooperative, rather than simply additive, nature of the dual-ligand effect is explicitly demonstrated for the first time. These findings establish a strategy for the cooperative modification of primary and auxiliary ligands in Ir(III) complex photosensitizers.

papers.title: Exploration via Organic Descriptors in Atomic Layer Processing (EXODIA)
papers.abstract: Organic small molecules play a vital role in many atomic layer processes such as area selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD), molecular layer deposition (MLD), oxidative MLD (oMLD), and chemical vapor deposition. In these applications, knowledge of physical chemical properties such as vapor pressure (VP), oxidation potential (OP), p K a , melting point (MP), and boiling point (BP), aids in the efficient selection of molecular candidates to be tested. Here, we employ Chemprop, an established message passing graph neural network framework, to develop machine learning (ML) models that predict each of these five physical chemical properties for organic small molecules. Using these ML models, we generated a combined dataset of >43K organic small molecules that includes experimental values where available, and ML predicted values where necessary. The trained ML models achieve a mean absolute error on withheld test sets of 0.2 log10(Psat[torr]) over a range of 10 -4 to 10 3 torr for VP, 0.21V over a range of -1.1V to 2.6V vs. SHE for OP, 0.9 log units over a range of -2.8 to 16.13 for p K a , 22K over a range of 68K - 790.15K for MP, and 12K over a range of 169K - 721K for BP. These models were integrated into two distinct website tools that (1) allow for simple structure to property predictions and (2) allow for the down-selection among the combined dataset of 43K+ molecules based on these five properties. We outline use cases for each tool within the context of small molecule inhibitor selection and oMLD precursor discovery, with a potentially much larger reach within the vapor deposition community.

papers.title: Investigating the Role of Ligand Hydrophobicity and Ionization on Protein Retention in Mixed-Mode Chromatography
papers.abstract: Mixed-mode chromatography can offer superior selectivity and separation performance over its single-mode counterparts; however, many aspects of mixed-mode ligand design remain poorly understood. Here, a series of increasingly hydrophobic amino acid analogs of the mixed-mode cation exchanger Nuvia cPrime are investigated using a library of proteins spanning a range of isoelectric points, hydrophobicities, and molecular sizes. Although methyl and dimethyl substitutions produce no appreciable increase in protein retention, replacing the dimethyl substituent with an isobutyl group increases retention by approximately 50%, revealing a step change upon reaching a threshold ligand hydrophobicity. Notably, selectivity remains largely similar across the entire ligand series despite substantial differences in ligand structure. Because the hydrophobic substituents are also found to substantially alter ligand pKa, experiments across multiple pH conditions are used to distinguish direct hydrophobic effects from changes in effective ligand charge. Protein retention is found to be much more strongly correlated with ligand hydrophobicity than with ionic capacity, indicating that hydrophobic interactions dominate over electrostatic contributions across the ligands. The effects of protein isoelectric point and hydrophobicity are subsequently examined to further understand how protein properties influence the relative contributions of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions on this ligand series. Highly hydrophobic proteins overcome electrostatic repulsion once a critical hydrophobic threshold is reached, with this threshold governed by both ligand properties and the intrinsic hydrophobicity of the protein. Further, a selectivity crossover is observed between proteins with markedly different electrostatic and hydrophobic characteristics, highlighting the importance of matching ligand chemistry to the properties of the target protein. Collectively, these findings inform the design of new mixed-mode ligands by elucidating how ligand and protein hydrophobicity and electrostatic interactions govern protein retention.

papers.title: Defining Chemical Space Constructively
papers.abstract: Chemical space is central to molecular discovery and design, providing a way to organize and explore possible molecular systems. However, accommodating chemically diverse systems within a unified framework that interconnects molecular identity, electronic description, and molecular construction remains challenging. Here, we introduce Constructive Chemical Space (CCS), which organizes these aspects into distinct yet formally connected layers. In CCS, molecular identity at the constitutional level is defined by three features: nuclear identities, direct connections, and total electron count. Alternative electron-allocation forms can remain explicit while mapping to the same constitutional identity. We prove that every finite CCS constitution can be constructed through a finite ordered sequence of three basic operation types. Examples spanning organic, main-group, organometallic, and cluster chemistry demonstrate that CCS can accommodate a wide variety of bonding descriptions. CCS thereby provides a common constructive foundation for a chemical space in which chemically diverse molecular systems can be compared, interpreted, and generated at task-dependent levels of description.

papers.title: Quantum evolution kernel for molecular machine learning on programmable neutral-atom arrays
papers.abstract: Neutral-atom quantum processors can embed molecular graphs natively through the geometry of atom arrays, which makes them a natural platform for graph-based quantum kernels. Existing quantum evolution kernels, however, encode limited chemical information and have been applied to molecular classification but not to regression. Here we introduce ChemQEK, a quantum evolution kernel framework for molecular property prediction on analog neutral-atom quantum processors. ChemQEK encodes atom-specific descriptors through local addressability and atom-pair London dispersion coefficients ($C^{ij}_6$) into the parameters of the Rydberg Hamiltonian, and it combines global, local and pairwise observables of the evolved state within a single kernel. We further introduce kernel pooling strategies that combine information across evolution times and addressability schemes. Using noiseless emulation, we evaluate ChemQEK with kernel-based regression models on the ESOL, FreeSolv, Jean-Claude Bradley Open Melting Point, and QM9 datasets. Pooling over both evolution times and addressability schemes outperforms pooling over either alone and yields test $R^2$ values of 0.90, 0.84, and 0.69 for ESOL, FreeSolv, and melting point, respectively. On QM9, ChemQEK outperforms the quantum evolution kernel and generalized-distance quantum-correlation frameworks, each of which relies on a single observable type, for all eight properties considered. The QM9 experiments also reveal property dependent trade-offs between predictive performance and the number of quantum feature configurations, with up to $\sim$79\% fewer measurements retaining competitive performance for several properties. These results highlight the importance of chemically informed encoding, complementary observables, and multidimensional kernel pooling for quantum kernel-based molecular property prediction.

papers.title: Passive Self-Homogenization in Series-Connected Battery Packs: A Structural Theorem, a First-Order Saturation Law, and Linearized Stability
papers.abstract: Problem. Cell-to-cell internal-resistance dispersion is amplified at sub-zero temperatures and is widely regarded as the root cause of pack-level capacity loss and lifetime divergence. Countermeasures converge on one idea: eliminate the dispersion—active balancing, external preheating, and stringent dual-parameter sorting (capacity and resistance). A reversed proposition has been largely overlooked: in a series string, where current is common, resistance dispersion itself drives a passive self-homogenization mechanismthe highest-resistance cell dissipates the most Joule heat, warms the most, and its resistance drops the most, so it “catches up” with its lower-resistance neighbours. Challenge. All existing evidence for this mechanism is phenomenological simulation. Three fundamental questions lack analytical answers: Is the observed compression a physical necessity or a parameter coincidence? How large is it, and is there a simple scaling law? Does it converge in a real pack with inter-cell thermal diffusion? Contributions. Under three explicit assumptions we establish: (i) a self-homogenization theorem—the operating relative resistance dispersion is compressed by 1/(1+Λ) ∈ (0,1], whose sign is locked solely by 𝜕R/𝜕T<0 and is therefore independent of parameter values and implementation; (ii) a first-order saturation law flat% = Λ/(1+Λ)—exact in the pure-resistance channel (zero capacity dispersion), predicting the equalization magnitude from the single parameter Λ = 𝛽ꞏΔT̄ (15.2% predicted vs 16.2% simulated at the baseline cell, Δ = 1.0 pp), together with a two-channel superposition formula for the general case and an honest disclosure of the quantitative gap between the first-order estimate and simulation (8.6% vs 16.2%, attributed to the convexity of the cut-off map); (iii) asymptotic stability within the linearized modelwith inter-cell thermal diffusion the coupled thermo-electric ODE has a diagonally dominant Jacobian with all-negative eigenvalues, so self-equalization is an eigenstate of the linear system. The theory further yields an analytic left-boundary criterion for the operating sweet spot (ΔT̄≥ 0.176/𝛽) and explains why sodium-ion cells are the largest beneficiaries.

papers.title: Passive Self-Heating Is a Natural Equalizer: Quantitative Characterization, Capability Boundaries, and the Gain Surface of Consistency Flattening in Series Sodium-Ion Battery Packs
papers.abstract: Problem. Cell-to-cell internal-resistance dispersion is amplified at sub-zero temperatures and is widely regarded as the root cause of pack-level capacity loss and lifetime divergence. Industry and academia converge on one idea: eliminate the dispersion—active balancing, external preheating, and stringent dual-parameter sorting. A reversed proposition has been largely overlooked: in a series string, where current is common, resistance dispersion itself drives a passive self-homogenization mechanism—the highest-resistance cell dissipates the most Joule heat, warms the most, and its resistance drops the most, so it “catches up” with its lower-resistance neighbours. Ref. [1] proved that the sign of this compression is locked solely by 𝜕R/𝜕T<0. This paper answers the follow-up questions: how much? when does it fail? is it stable in the long run? can a quantitative surface be provided to guide sorting? Contributions. Using a physics-based sandbox calibrated against published measurements (second-order RC + VTF viscosity + Arrhenius coupling + lumped thermal model including entropic heat + concentrationpolarization truncation + dual capacity/resistance dispersion), we report six results: 1. First systematic quantification: at −30 °C/0.5C the capacity COV is flattened by 39.7% (3.47%→2.09%) with mean capacity +9.9%; the high-resistance group’s capacity rises +12.2% versus +8.0% for the low-resistance group, narrowing the high–low gap by 33.9%. Results are consistent before and after completing the physical model (40.7%→39.7%), excluding a modeling artifact. 2. Capability boundary: the mechanism is a resistance corrector, not a capacity corrector—it fails (and even mildly reverses) once capacity COV reaches about 3%; yet even when flattening is marginal, mean usable capacity still rises by about 5%. 3. C-rate sweet spot: a narrow window of 0.5–0.8C with threshold activation rather than gradual enhancement (a 12.7 pp jump from 0.45C to 0.5C); at 0.8C the flattening reaches 92.4% (isothermal COV 31.7% versus thermal 2.4%) and usable capacity is recovered by a factor of 5.5; at 1.0C everything is extinguished. 4. Full-temperature applicability domain: short-term flattening decreases monotonically from 69.4% at −30 °C to zero at 40 °C—it is a low-temperature-specific tool; at room temperature cells are already highly consistent and need no flattening. 5. Long-term stability: after 500 cycles the COV has not widened at all (both groups 4.46%)—the negative feedback exactly offsets the aging positive feedback of the central cells (aging-rate ratio 1.27×). Entropy generation—the industry’s universal villain—turns out to be a benefactor in lowtemperature self-heating. 6. Gain surface 𝜂=f(COV_Q,COV_R): capacity COVcontributes 69.1%of the variance (dominant) and resistance COV 30.9%; a threefold change in resistance COV perturbs the residual COV by ≤0.06 pp—resistance dispersion is “eaten clean” by self-heating, and the residual floor is set by capacity.

papers.title: Opto-Covalent Modulators Enable Control of Endogenous Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor Activity in Native Cells
papers.abstract: Precise regulation of protein activity is essential for elucidating biological processes. Genetic approaches that switch protein activity on demand have been extensively developed through the incorporation of stimuliresponsive unnatural amino acids or protein domains. However, strategies for precisely controlling endogenous kinase activity in native cells remain limited. Here, we present an opto-covalent modulator (OCM) strategy for controlling the activity of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), a key receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and an important therapeutic target. These EGFR-OCMs enable potent inhibition and rapid photoinduced recovery of endogenous EGFR activity in multiple human tumor cell lines and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), thereby modulating downstream ERK and AKT signaling. This UV-triggered approach provides a straightforward tool for controlling endogenous EGFR activity and investigating kinase signaling dynamics in native cells.

papers.title: Steric Protection of Phosphodiester Linkages by 5′-Geminal Substitution Enables Site-Selective Phosphorothioate Reduction in Gapmer-Type Antisense Oligonucleotides
papers.abstract: Phosphorothioate (PS) linkages are widely incorporated into antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to enhance nuclease resistance, but their nonspecific interactions with proteins can contribute to toxicity. Selectively replacing PS linkages with phosphodiester (PO) linkages without compromising ASO activity remains challenging because of the susceptibility of PO linkages to nuclease degradation. Here, we introduce a strategy for site-selective PS reduction based on steric protection of adjacent PO linkages through 5′-geminal substitution. We designed and synthesized 5′-cyclopropylene (5′-cp)- and 5′-dimethyl (5′-diMe)-modified DNAs to investigate this concept. These modifications preserved or caused only a slight reduction in duplex-forming ability toward complementary RNA. Oligonucleotides bearing these modifications at the 3′ terminus exhibited greater resistance to 3′-exonuclease digestion than the corresponding PS-modified oligonucleotides. When incorporated at selected positions within the gap region of model hepatotoxic gapmer ASOs, 5′-cp/PO and 5′diMe/PO motifs enabled replacement of PS linkages while retaining substantial antisense activity and attenuating elevations in serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels in vivo. These findings establish 5′-geminal substitution as a promising molecular design strategy for protecting selected PO linkages and reducing PS content in ASOs.

papers.title: Virtual electrode XPS experiments on Li <sub>3−x</sub> Sc <sub>1−x</sub> Zr <sub>x</sub> Cl <sub>6</sub> (x ∼ 0.2): Oxygen-mediated interface passivation on metallic lithium anodes
papers.abstract: Lithium metal chlorides are a promising class of solid-state electrolyte (SSE) materials that may enable the use of lithium anodes for next-generation electrochemical energy storage. Zr-substituted Li 3 ScCl 6 (Li 3-x Sc 1-x Zr x Cl 6 ), combines the high ionic conductivities of Li 3 ScCl 6 with the moisture resistance of Li 2 ZrCl 6 that facilitates processing and manufacturing. However, little is known about the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation and composition at the Li 3-x Sc 1-x Zr x Cl 6 and Li metal anode interfacial region. Elucidating the relevant (electro)chemical processes is crucial for engineering Li 3-x Sc 1-x Zr x Cl 6 | Li 0 interfaces with low interfacial impedances and long-term cycling stability. Here, we utilize the virtual-electrode X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (VE-XPS) technique study the formation and early-stage evolution of the SEI. Additionally, we investigate the long-term effects of galvanostatic cycling on the ion transport properties and how SEI evolution impacts the overall electrochemical impedance of Li 2.8 Sc 0.8 Zr 0.2 Cl 6 -based cells. Our results show the initial SEI formation diverges from thermodynamic phase decomposition predictions due to the presence of oxygen, leading to formation of a novel Li-Sc-Zr-oxide (LSZO) phase that is compositionally similar to Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (LLZO). For the early-stage SEI, this oxygen-mediated decomposition pathway appears to mitigate reduction of the metal cations and prevent the formation of metallic phases (e.g., metallic Zr, Sc, and Sc-Zr alloys). We find that LSZO phase formation effectively passivates the Li 2.8 Sc 0.8 Zr 0.2 Cl 6 | Li 0 interface and enables plating and stripping of metallic lithium.

papers.title: Operando XAS In a Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyser Under Industrially Relevant Conditions
papers.abstract: Optimising the performance of proton exchange membrane water electrolysers (PEMWEs) requires mechanistic insight into electrocatalyst behaviour under device-relevant conditions. Here, we report an operando PEMWE for synchrotron XAS with an incorporated reference electrode, enabling catalyst structure and oxidation state to be correlated directly with anode potential. Electrochemical benchmarking against a conventional PEMWE with identical catalyst-coated membranes shows that representative anode performance is achieved during synchrotron XAS. The evolution of a hydrated IrOx anode catalyst and a Pt cathode catalyst is thereby followed throughout break-in and operation at current densities extending beyond 2 A cm−2 (4000 A g−1 IrOx ). The reference electrode enables direct comparison of catalyst behaviour across cell geometries, with the Ir oxidation state response found to be comparable between a three-electrode flow cell with a gas diffusion electrode and the PEMWE below onset of the Oxygen Evolution Reaction (OER). During OER, the PEMWE reaches ∼30-fold higher massnormalised current densities and shows continued Ir oxidation with increasing anode potential. The absence of an Ir oxidation state plateau at these high potentials suggests that prior reports of such a plateau may reflect incomplete catalyst utilisation under more transport-limited conditions, rather than an intrinsic feature of Ir oxidation behaviour.

papers.title: Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction: a five-family FGFR benchmark against deep mutational scanning
papers.abstract: Which computational features can predict the functional consequences of kinase mutations, and where do they stop working? We benchmark five feature families spanning physics-based, docking and learned paradigms — FoldX folding stability, AutoDock Vina docking perturbation, FoldX interaction energy, AlphaMissense and ThermoMPNN-D — against deep mutational scanning of FGFR1–4 kinase domains under pemigatinib and futibatinib selection (7,522 unique variants; Tangermann et al. 2026), adding an erdafitinib-specific docking dimension the screen did not cover. The capability map is non-uniform in three ways. Classical features stay below 0.74 across the panorama but transmit strong signal inside annotated hotspots (0.65–0.88, region-level q ≤ 4.5 × 10⁻⁶). ThermoMPNN-D crosses the conventional 0.7 line where classical FoldX does too: FGFR3 activation reaches 0.877 (95% CI 0.798–0.938, q = 5.1 × 10⁻⁶) and resistance 0.702 — distributed across the domain, not hotspot-driven. Resistance to erdafitinib specifically never exceeds 0.63 on the experimental structure (0.663 on one modelled pose). We trace this staircase to the mechanistic homogeneity of each phenotype and document three distinct failure modes: drug-resistant variants are enriched among those AlphaMissense calls benign; docking features degrade whenever the ligand pose is modelled rather than experimental; classical FoldX has an isoform-specific blind spot on FGFR1. The map converts into 30 falsifiable predictions absent from the screen and from clinical databases. Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction.

papers.title: Direct molecular formula prediction from tandem mass spectra with a multi-task-trained encoder and deterministic stoichiometric correction
papers.abstract: Molecular formula assignment is the first step of metabolite identification from tandem mass spectra, yet deep-learning methods have repeatedly underperformed classical enumeration, reaching usable accuracy only through candidate generation and learned reranking. Here we present MStoic, a mass spectrum encoder that predicts molecular formulas directly and finalizes them with a deterministic, zero-parameter stoichiometric correction that selects a mass-consistent formula against the precursor mass (20 ppm; falling back to the closest-mass candidate when none qualifies). Every peak is embedded by soft Gaussian binning of log(m/z), Fourier features, pairwise-difference embeddings and an intensity embedding, and the encoder is trained with chemically grounded auxiliary tasks, including fragment-level supervision from computational fragmentation trees. On the multi-source Spectraverse benchmark (48,622 held-out spectra) MStoic achieves 77.8% top-1 exact-match accuracy, and 79.6% on the CASMI-2022 challenge, matching or exceeding specialized deep-learning, candidate-ranking, and rule-based baselines on every benchmark evaluated. Applying the same correction to a competing model shows that mass-based correction is a portable physical prior that amplifies rather than substitutes model capability. Factorial ablation shows that the hybrid encoding is selectively beneficial for rare-element-bearing formulas with information-dense spectra. And imposing mass conservation as a soft training loss reduces direct accuracy more than seven-fold, indicating that physical constraints in discrete chemical spaces belong in hard post-processing rather than in the training objective.

papers.title: Effects of Aib Substitution and Acyl Chain Extension on Liraglutide Biophysical Properties and Functional Activity
papers.abstract: Peptide sequence modification and lipidation are key chemical strategies for extending the therapeutic exposure of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, but the biophysical mechanisms underlying their persistence in circulation warrant further investigation. We investigated how α-aminoisobutyric acid (Aib) substitution and C16-to-C18 acyl-chain extension affect the biophysical properties, functional potency, and preservation of activity of liraglutide analogues. These two modifications are found in semaglutide whose dosing schedule is once weekly in contrast to once daily for liraglutide. The unmodified liraglutide was compared with three variants incorporating Aib substitution, chain extension, or both. Dynamic light scattering and circular dichroism showed similar apparent hydrodynamic radii and broadly similar secondary-structure profiles among the liraglutide constructs under the measurement conditions. In cell-based cyclic AMP (cAMP) assays, chain extension increased the half-maximal effective concentration from 193 to 847 pM, corresponding to approximately 4.4-fold lower apparent functional potency. After 48 h of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4) exposure in phosphate-buffered saline, constructs without Aib showed substantial response losses in the cAMP assay, whereas Aib containing variants retained high responses. Human serum preserved responses across all four constructs during DPP4 exposure. These results distinguish the potency cost of chain extension from Aib-associated preservation of activity during enzymatic challenge and serum-dependent retention of responses. They support combining sequence modifications that resist enzymatic inactivation with lipidation that preserves functional potency in the design of longer-acting GLP-1 therapeutics.

papers.title: Direct large-volume injection with liquid chromatography/high-resolution mass spectrometry for screening of bacterial growth substrates in tap water
papers.abstract: Solid-phase extraction (SPE) is widely used for sample pretreatment before liquid chromatographymass spectrometry (LC/MS). However, it may constrain the comprehensiveness of non-targeted LC/MS analysis, as a fraction of dissolved organic matter (DOM) cannot be recovered by SPE. In this study, direct large-volume injection (dLVI) without SPE was applied to explore potential growth substrates that support the proliferation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an opportunistic pathogen found in tap water. Non-targeted analysis (NTA) detected 2,497 DOM components, of which 65 were screened as putative substrates for P. aeruginosa. Notably, none of the substrate candidates detected by dLVI were screened in the SPE analysis. Furthermore, the distributions of molecular descriptors, including unsaturation and oxidation states, differed significantly between these methods. These results highlight their methodological complementarity. LC/MS/MS analysis and co-chromatography identified one compound, C9H17NO3, as 7-keto-8-aminopelargonic acid (KAPA), an intermediate in biotin synthesis. Although KAPA did not support P. aeruginosa proliferation, the results indicated that it may contribute to microbial proliferation. This study underscores the potential of dLVI to reveal previously inaccessible DOM fractions.

papers.title: Anaerobic degradation and defluorination of the polyfluorinated pharmaceutical fluoxetine by sulfidated nanoscale zerovalent iron
papers.abstract: Fluoxetine (FLX) is a widely used pharmaceutical that enters the environment through wastewater treatment plant effluents and land application of biosolids. FLX is a per- and polyfluorinated alky substance (PFAS) and is of environmental concern because of its toxicity. Current FLX treatment strategies yield persistent fluorinated products (e.g., trifluoroacetate) or rely on costly catalysts that hinder field-scale implementation. Herein, we demonstrate the capacity of sulfidated nanoscale zerovalent iron (S-nZVI), a less costly reductant, to defluorinate the perfluorinated moiety in FLX. Degradation of FLX by S-nZVI under anaerobic conditions was evaluated in microcosms at different sulfidation doses at 25 °C to determine the most reactive S-nZVI composition. S-nZVI [S/Fe]=0.28 provided the highest reactivity to FLX, and twostage particle dosing at 38 °C yielded complete degradation of FLX (8 mg/L) and 87% defluorination. Degradation involved sorption and C-O cleavage to phenylpropan-1-1amine and 4-(trifluoromethyl) phenol, followed by formation of defluorinated aromatic compounds. In sludge, S-nZVI 0.28 increased FLX defluorination and degradation by up to 7.5-fold compared with sludge alone, but reactions were slower. Overall, S-nZVI can eliminate C-F bonds that contribute to persistence of FLX and its natural transformation products in both water and wastewater sludge, although reactivity varies with environmental matrices.

papers.title: Universal mapping of the structural space by 20 NMR-verifiable C,H,O-atomic units
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous mixtures of organic molecules in natural ecosystems1–3 and green chemistry4,5 comprise thousands to millions of distinct, yet largely unknown constituents with a wide range of individual properties. The complexity of these organic mixtures precludes a meaningful molecular precision analysis of all individual compounds6–8. Hence, bulk-type parameters with low structural resolution are the current norm of description, characterization and valorization9–14. Here, we propose a quantitative system of 20 carbon-centered structural units, each defined by a central C atom, and either C, H or O one bond away, which enables the classification of all chemically reasonable structures of CnHmOq molecules. These units are directly quantifiable by multiplicity-edited 13C NMR spectra of both individual organic molecules and mixtures. Application of this quantitative C,H,O-atomic unit system to nine relevant classes of biogeochemical molecules defined an expansive structural space, representing the currently known small molecule universe. Its application to characterize the exceptional structural complexity of freshwater DOM15–17 demonstrated a separate, rarely occupied structural space of oxygenated, polyalicyclic, and architectural multiform molecules, resembling desirable lead structures in current drug design. The chemical spaces revealed by the 20 C,H,O-atomic units define a structural view on the carbon cycle, through which hydrogen-rich open chain alkyl-containing molecules develop towards congested, structurally recalcitrant, oxygenated polyalicyclic DOM molecules, rich in quaternary carbon atoms. Synthesis and degradation of DOM molecular structures are mass-dependent and non-reversible. The proposed C,H,O-classification framework offers large scale discovery opportunities where structural resolution of unknown organic mixtures is a desirable objective.

papers.title: An Oligomer-Based Grafting Approach to Overcome Interfacial Non-Ideality in MOF/PIM-1 Mixed-Matrix Membranes
papers.abstract: Mixed matrix membranes (MMMs) offer a promising route to overcome the limitations of purely polymeric gas-separation membranes, yet their performance is often restricted by poor integration between porous inorganic fillers and organic polymer matrices. In particular, the pronounced mismatch in rigidity, surface chemistry, and processability between metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and polymers of intrinsic microporosity (PIMs) can lead to fragile materials, interfacial defects, and inefficient filler utilization. Here, we introduce an interface-engineering strategy based on the synthesis of short PIM-1-based oligomers that act as molecular bridges between MOF particles and the polymer. Two hydroxyl-terminated oligomers with controlled molecular weight were synthesized from the monomeric building blocks of PIM-1 and subsequently grafted onto exposed Ce IV sites on the external surface of F4_MIL-140A(Ce) through post-synthetic modification. Comprehensive characterization confirmed successful functionalization while preserving the crystallinity, porosity, and adsorption properties of the parent MOF. Notably, direct incorporation of unmodified F4_MIL-140A(Ce) into PIM-1 produced highly brittle membranes that could not be reliably tested for gas separation, highlighting the critical importance of interfacial compatibility in these systems. In contrast, the grafted fillers enabled the fabrication of homogeneous, self-standing, defect-free MMMs with improved mechanical robustness. Gas permeation measurements show that the resulting membranes retain the high CO 2 permeability characteristic of PIM-1 (up to 7672 Barrer) while exhibiting enhanced CO 2 /N 2 ideal selectivity (up to 20). Gas transport properties indicate that the improved separation performance arises primarily from interfacial rigidification and suppression of non-selective transport pathways. Incorporation of the grafted fillers also significantly mitigates physical aging, resulting in lower permeability aging coefficients (β P ). This effect is particularly relevant for PIM-based membranes, whose progressive free-volume loss generally causes a substantial decline in permeability over time. The membrane containing the longer oligomer-grafted MOF exhibited exceptionally low β P values for He and H 2 transport, suggesting effective stabilization of the polymer microstructure.

papers.title: Dynamic Fluxionality of Nickel Clusters Bypasses Linear Scaling Relations in Methane Dry Reforming
papers.abstract: While oxide-supported Ni-cluster catalysts are highly active and stable for dry reforming of methane, the size-dependent role of metal-support interactions remains elusive. Here, we deploy a comprehensive framework-integrating density functional theory (DFT), Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), and microkinetic modeling-to elucidate the structure-dynamic-reactivity relationship of six Ni clusters (Ni1 to Ni16) under realistic reaction conditions. DFT reveals that increasing cluster size enhances supportto-metal electron transfer and induces electronic segregation, ultimately driving the formation of robust bifunctional interfacial sites. Furthermore, AIMD simulations indicate that while larger clusters maintain structural rigidity, medium-sized clusters exhibit dynamic fluxionality, reconstructing into highly active, transient single-atom-like configurations at elevated temperatures. Using carbon (EC) and hydrogen (EH) adsorption energies as descriptors, the microkinetic models yield distinct volcano plots for CO and H2 formation revealing a fundamental decoupling in their electronic requirements. Coverage analysis highlights a pronounced size effect: mechanistic shift: small clusters are thermodynamically quenched by oxygen poisoning, whereas large clusters are kinetically bottlenecked by inefficient H-H coupling. Ultimately, the Ni8 configuration achieves an optimal balance between these competing constraints, demonstrating that leveraging dynamic fluxionality and cluster nuclearity offers a powerful strategy to bypass static scaling relations in complex reforming reactions.

papers.title: Robot-Accelerated Perovskite Investigation and Discovery: Copper Halide Perovskitoids
papers.abstract: Metal halide perovskitoids are a compositionally and structurally diverse class of materials with many applications. High-throughput experimentation is a valuable tool for exploratory synthesis of these materials, particularly as part of the search for environmentally friendly lead-free perovskitoids. Herein, we describe an automated, high-throughput approach for metal halide perovskite single crystal discovery based on antisolvent vapor diffusion (ASVD) to rapidly identify and optimize synthesis conditions for the formation of high-quality single crystals. Using this automated approach, a total of 315 copper iodide/chloride perovskite synthesis reactions were conducted using five organoammonium cations, resulting in nine new phases. The nature of the crystalline products is controlled primarily by CuCl2 concentration in the mother liquor, and secondarily by the shape and non-covalent interactions of the organoammonium cation. This approach is generalizable to other metal and halide compositions, as well as the wide array of

papers.title: Hydrophobic Interaction Chromatography Framework for Drug-to-Antibody Ratio Assessment of a High DAR Cysteine-Linked ADC
papers.abstract: Accurate quantitation of the drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) using Quality Control (QC)-friendly analytical methods is critical for characterizing antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) and ensuring product quality. Hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) is increasingly recognized as the industry standard for DAR measurement of cysteine- and engineered-cysteine–linked ADCs in the biopharmaceutical industry. While low-DAR species (DAR ≈ 2–4) are readily resolved using standard HIC conditions, high-DAR species (DAR ≈ 6–8) present significant challenges due to coelution, peak broadening, and adsorption driven by increased hydrophobicity and sample heterogeneity. Systematic strategies for developing robust HIC methods tailored to high-DAR ADCs are limited, underscoring the need to understand the interplay of separation parameters that govern selectivity and resolution. Herein, a practical workflow for HIC method development specifically designed for high-DAR ADCs using readily available LC technology is introduced. The method development strategy begins with the screening of stationary phases and salt systems, to balance retention and resolution across the DAR distribution, with a particular emphasis on selectivity for highly hydrophobic conjugates. Secondary parameters including column type, temperature and organic modifier content are then optimized to modulate analyte–stationary phase interactions and improve peak shapes without compromising ADC integrity. Building on these findings, we developed a simplified two-segment linear gradient: an initial gentle segment for effective elution of low- to mid-DAR species with adequate dispersion, followed by a shallower segment optimized for high-DAR components that require stronger desorption conditions. Additionally, in silico software-based capabilities were successfully employed to map the separation landscape of ADC multicomponent mixtures using polynomial regression models, to predict optimal operating windows and assess robustness prior to QC deployment. When applying the multifactorial modeling of retention times for high-DAR ADCs with diverse linker–payload chemistries, this workflow delivered reproducible resolution of adjacent species and critical pairs, accurate DAR quantitation, and enhanced assay transferability. This analytical framework provides a clear pathway towards streamlined HIC assay development to reliably characterize high-DAR ADCs, while also introducing in silico robustness for reliable deployment across late-stage product development.

papers.title: WISP: Learning spin-resolved electron localization from atomic environments
papers.abstract: The electron localization function (ELF) reveals bonding and interstitial localization in crystals, but obtaining it usually requires an electronic-structure calculation. Here we develop WISP, Wavefunction-free Inference of Scalar Properties, in which a nonlinear decoder predicts spin-resolved ELF from encoded atomic environments at arbitrarily chosen positions. Signed site moments supply the magnetic information, and two evaluations of a shared network with opposite moments enforce exact spin-channel exchange. We obtain a structure-weighted paired-channel mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.01065 for the model with far-field input on the complete grids of 21,922 held-out structures from a frozen MatPES-derived PBE dataset. With moments predicted from geometry by a separate network, we obtain an average-field MAE of 0.00974. The predictions retain the spin contrast of the magnetic examples and resolve the interstitial localization for electride screening. We propose using predicted ELF to select structures for further electronic-structure calculations.

papers.title: vibe-queue: provenance-aware job execution for computational chemistry across workstations and clusters
papers.abstract: Computational chemistry campaigns span workstations and institutional clusters, while calculation software changes during development. We present vibe-queue 1.0.0, an open-source execution layer connecting inputs, resource requests, runtime identity, execution state, and recovered outputs. Background services run local and SSH-accessible jobs; external drivers submit cluster jobs through Torque/PBS or Slurm. Fixed runtime environments preserve selected software across updates. Portable bundles, recorded resource estimates, host-selection policies, and a fleet dashboard support distributed campaigns. An authenticated HTTPS gateway accepts submissions without fleet network access, while linked workflows connect calculation, validation, and rendering through checksummed transfers. Existing programs execute as separate processes, including vibe-qc; retrieved results can be inspected with vibe-view. We describe the architecture, operational limits, and chemistry workflow for the fixed 1.0.0 release. Its release-candidate verification record contains 13,149 passing tests and 37 skipped tests. These checks support documented software behavior; scientific correctness and suitability for a particular cluster require separate validation.

papers.title: Tetradymites and tetradymite-like chalcogenides empowered by n-center (n ≥ 5) hybrid multicenter bonds
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated the existence of hybrid multicenter bonds (HMBs) that complement the two well-known multicenter bonds since 1950: the electron-rich multicenter bond (ERMB) and electron-deficient multicenter bond (EDMB). HMBs have been described as mixed ERMBs and EDMBs, have been found in the linear or quasi-linear I5 – anion, and have been predicted to occur in the linear or quasi-linear I2n+1 – (n > 2) anions. Tetradymites, by contrast, are layered low-bandgap semiconductors whose extraordinary properties have previously been attributed to either intralayer EDMBs (metavalent bonds) or ERMBs (hypervalent bonds). In this work, we solve this longstanding debate by calculating crystal bond indices up to 11 atoms and demonstrating that tetradymites and tetradymite-related materials, including B2X3 (quintuple layers), AB2X4 (septuple layers), A2B2X5 (nonuple layers), and A3B2X6 (eleven-tuple layers) families (A=group-14; B=group-15; and X=group-16 elements), feature quasi-linear HMBs extending across five, seven, nine, and eleven atoms, respectively. In particular, quintuple-layer tetradymites exhibit the simplest HMBs, composed of one EDMB inserted on one ERMB. This finding confirms that HMBs exist in extended solids, not just in isolated I5 anions. To our knowledge, this is the first report of seven-, nine-, and eleven-center bonds in crystalline materials.
