As a general and extensible approach for spectroscopically driven 3D molecular structure generation, SpecDiffMol opens new avenues for autonomous structure–function discovery and real-time in situ molecular analysis across chemistry, materials science, and molecular biology.

papers.title: Microstructural evolution, phase transformations and magnetic characteristics of Fe@Fe3O4@NaCl core-shell nanocomposites when varying the EB PVD synthesis temperature
papers.abstract: The manuscript is devoted to a comprehensive study of the physicochemical, structural and magnetic properties of Fe-NaCl nanocomposite systems with an iron content of ~30 wt.%, synthesized by the electron beam physical vapor deposition (EB PVD) method at substrate temperatures (Ts) of 50 °C and 410 °C. Using SEM, STEM/HAADF, EDS, XRD, HRTEM, TGA and Raman spectroscopy, it was proven that the thermodynamic conditions of deposition critically determine the phase composition of nanoinclusions. The transition from completely oxidized, highly hydrated agglomerates of magnetite (Fe3O4, coherent scattering region size 17 nm) at 50 °C to the formation of isolated spherical nanoparticles (15.5 - 36 nm) of the "metal core - oxide shell" type at 410 °C was recorded (Fe@Fe3O4). The appearance of a highly crystalline α-Fe core is accompanied by an increase in remanent magnetization from 0.46 to 2.3 emu/g and the saturation magnetization from 16.0 to 24.0 emu/g. The structural perfection and thermal stability of the samples obtained at 410 °C make them promising for use in magnetic devices and ideal objects for studying the spatial distribution of magnetic fields by holographic electron microscopy (Holo-TEM).

papers.title: The efficiency–coverage trade-off of scientific priors in Bayesian search: a registered benchmark on metallic multi-element elasticity data
papers.abstract: Scientific priors speed up Bayesian optimisation in materials discovery, but a prior that steers a small budget toward the materials it favours may miss those it disfavours. We measured this in a benchmark with a registered analysis plan: 7,020 searches (3,000 of them over 3,550 metallic multielement Materials Project structures), for the shear modulus and the specific Young’s modulus, with a historical prior and a composition-only elemental-modulus heuristic, each mixed into expected improvement search with a fixed weight β. Coverage was the recall of the half of the top-5% materials that the prior itself scores lowest. Coverage loss at moderate weight was detected in 4 of 6 prior–objective settings. The elemental heuristic reduced the restricted mean number of acquisitions to a top-1% shear-modulus material by 13.9 at β = 0.25 with no detected loss of coverage, but its shear-modulus form, applied to the specific modulus, lost 44.0% or more of the baseline coverage at every nonzero weight. A weight both beneficial and safe under the registered criterion existed in 3 of 6 settings (2 under a post hoc joint error control), never above β = 0.25, and depended on the safety margin and on curation. At β = 0.5, in 5 of 6 settings the weighted search found more top-5% materials in total but, by its estimates, fewer of those its prior disfavours (a loss detected in 3): the prior redirected the search rather than reducing its yield. Faster discovery alone therefore does not show that a search keeps what its prior disfavours.

papers.title: Site-Selective Fluorination for Decoupling Oxidative Stability and Ionic Transport of Oxychloride Solid Electrolytes
papers.abstract: Fluorination in solid electrolytes is widely used to enhance oxidative stability owing to fluorine's high electronegativity, yet strong Li–F interactions hinder Li-ion transport. Here we show that this anodic stability–ionic conductivity trade-off can be largely decoupled through lattice-level anion design in the highly Li-ion-conductive LiTaOCl4. By distinguishing oxygen's framework-linking role from chloride's transport-defining role, we targeted fluorination at framework-linking O-sites to minimize perturbation of the Li-ion conduction network. The fluorinated oxychlorides retain ~10 mS cm–1-class ionic conductivity while raising the oxidation onset from 4.08 to 4.27 V versus Li+/Li, improving capacity retention as catholytes cycled to 4.5 V. First-principles calculations reveal that fluorination stabilizes oxidation-prone O- and Cl-derived electronic states through an inductive effect, while transport-network topology and correlated lattice dynamics preserve fast Li-ion transport. These results establish site-selective anion occupation as a design principle for decoupling oxidative stabilization from fast ion transport in mixed-anion solid electrolytes.

papers.title: DRAGON: A Versatile Open-Source Software for Diabatization of Multiple Excited States beyond Two Fragments
papers.abstract: The diabatic representation provides a natural framework for describing relevant electronic processes in molecular materials (e.g., optical properties, exciton transport, exciton dissociation, singlet fission, energy transfer between radicals…) using states with a well-defined character (diabatic states) and the electronic couplings between them. This motivates the development of general diabatization methods to generate these diabatic states and couplings. Herein, we present DRAGON, an open-source software for the diabatization of multiple excited states in molecular aggregates beyond two fragments. DRAGON implements the fragment particle–hole density (FPHD) diabatization scheme of Wang and coworkers (J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2021, 12, 1032–1039; J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2023, 19, 3900–3914) and interfaces it with widely used quantum chemistry packages, including Gaussian 16, ORCA, PySCF, Psi4, and xTB. Our implementation provides an extended version of FPHD, validated against reference results, that broadens the application limits in three directions with respect to the original formulation. DRAGON can compute diabatic states of different multiplicity (e.g., singlet and triplet) coupled by spin–orbit coupling (SOC), can tackle unrestricted wavefunctions enabling the diabatization of multiple excited states in molecular aggregates of open-shell systems (e.g., stable organic radicals), and can give an efficient route to obtain massive diabatic states and couplings in large-size molecular aggregates or materials owing to the coupling between FPHD with the Grimme's simplified Tamm–Dancoff approximation (sTDA). We show that the latter extension is interesting to take into account environmental effects beyond the nearest-neighbor approximation during the diabatization process.

papers.title: Highly similar urban and rural air quality in West Bengal, India as revealed by statewide sensor network
papers.abstract: The Indo-Gangetic Plain (IGP) suffers from some of the highest air pollution levels in the world. Compared to the upper and central IGP, air pollution in West Bengal, located in the lower IGP, is relatively understudied. This study presents a comprehensive, statewide assessment of air quality across all 23 districts of West Bengal, using India’s first state-commissioned network of 309 sensor stations. Analyzing this large dataset across a more than four-year period (January 2022- June 2026), we compare pollutant trends, source-linked signatures, and dominant pollutant patterns between rural and urban locations. We find that the differences in pollutant concentrations between urban and rural areas are remarkably narrow, averaging just 3.54 μg m -3 for PM 2.5 and 6.40 μg m -3 for PM 10 . These minor differences are smaller than the baseline variations between nearby stations, that is, rural and urban air quality are not significantly different in West Bengal. Urban and rural ambient air quality profiles across all years differ by less than 10% in 19 of 23 districts. Taken together, these findings suggest that regional-scale pollution rivals local sources in West Bengal, challenging city-centric air quality management strategies, and providing support for an airshed approach.

papers.title: Assessing the Impact of Incorporating Bias-Adjusted Satellite Observations into Global Data Fusion for Ground-level Health-Related Ozone Metrics
papers.abstract: Understanding global ground-level ozone is hindered by significant monitoring gaps. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian Maximum Entropy data fusion framework that includes satellite ozone observations, generating a global 0.1° surface ozone dataset (2005–2022). Satellite observations (IASI+GOME2, OMI/MLS), adjusted to ground-level estimates, were analyzed using Flexible Regionalized Air Quality Model Performance to correct biases and estimate variance. Ground observations (hard data) and satellite-derived estimates (soft data) were then integrated, using a composite of 10 atmospheric chemistry models and 3 reanalyses as the global spatial-temporal trend. Cross-validations demonstrated high overall accuracy (R 2 = 0.83; RMSE = 3.73 ppb). Although integrating satellite-derived soft data yields only marginal performance gains in densely monitored areas, it substantially reduces model uncertainties and improves model accuracy across large spatial gaps. Notably, for the furthest unmonitored gap group at a 20° checkerboard, including satellite data increased R 2 by 25.9% and decreased RMSE by 21.1% after the integration. Applying this optimized data fusion configuration from 2005 to 2022, global population-weighted ozone is estimated to have increased by 0.21 ppb/decade. Consequently, the global population exposed to ozone levels exceeding 50 ppb more than doubled over this 18-year period, rising from 17.2% to 41.0%.

papers.title: Reliability of Short Molecular Dynamics Runs as Screening Labels: Noise Ceilings, Time Dependence and Adaptive Replicate Allocation
papers.abstract: High-throughput molecular dynamics (MD) produces the labels on which electrolyte screening and machine-learning models are built, but each label comes from one short, noisy run whose value still depends on the simulated time. We quantify their reliability, and how to spend a simulation budget given it, on HTP-MD, the largest public set of polymer electrolyte trajectories (6,137 runs of 5 ns and 133 of 50 ns). Lithium motion is diffusive in only 2 short and 5 long runs, the apparent diffusivity at a 5 ns lag is 1.95 times that at 25 ns, and the first 5 ns of a run are 1.63 times faster than its second half, biasing every short label upwards. From 94 systems simulated twice, a single 5 ns end-point label has reliability 0.47 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.63): no model can correlate with such labels much beyond about 0.69, a random forest on monomer fingerprints is indistinguishable from that ceiling (0.71), and roughly half of the run-to-run noise comes from the initial structure. A short run ranks widely different polymers well (Spearman 0.93) but not similar ones (0.68 within the screening set). In simulations with the measured noise, giving further runs only to candidates whose membership of the top set is uncertain matches four uniform replicates with 1.8 runs per candidate for the top 10% and 1.2 for the top 1%; a check on real runs is consistent but underpowered. A decision guide and all code are provided.

papers.title: Fluoroalkynes: The Last Frontier of Organofluorine Chemistry?
papers.abstract: Molecules containing carbon-fluorine bonds are of global importance in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and polymers and are widely studied. However, little is known about fluoroalkynes where a fluorine atom is directly bonded to a carbon atom that forms part of a carbon-carbon triple bond. Pioneering studies in the 20th century established that these compounds are typically unstable, but their chemistry has remained largely unexplored to date. Here, we outline methods to prepare a diverse range of fluoroalkynes for the first time, rationalize the reasons behind their low stability, and demonstrate six different classes of reactions of fluoroalkynes and their difluorocyclobutadiene dimers.

papers.title: Defect Chemistry and Electronic Structure of α-Pu2O3: A Hybrid DFT Study of Charged Vacancies, Interstitials, and Antisites
papers.abstract: Using state-of-the-art hybrid density functional theory, we systematically investigate the formation energetics and electronic structure of native charged point defects in α-Pu2O3, including plutonium and oxygen vacancies, interstitials, and antisite defects. We find that these defects induce significant local structural distortions and modify the magnetic properties of neighboring Pu ions. Furthermore, they lead to a redistribution of electronic states near the band edges and induce in-gap states, resulting in notable variations of the band gap. Defect formation energetics are found to be strongly governed by both the chemical potentials of the constituent elements and the electron chemical potential, resulting in distinct defect stability regimes under different chemical potential conditions. These defects, in general, are found to generate deep electronic levels within the band gap, suggesting their potential role as carrier trapping centers. Overall, this study provides critical insight into the role of point defects in α-

papers.title: Removal of Cu(II) and a PET Glitter Microplastic Surrogate by Alginate, Alginate–Opuntia, and Chitosan-Treated Alginate–Opuntia Beads
papers.abstract: The use of alginate-only beads, alginate–Opuntia (AO) beads, and chitosan-treated AO beads for the removal of Cu(II) and a PET glitter (a microplastic surrogate) from water has been investigated. Each bead type was made from the previous one by the addition of one component. Batch experiments were carried out in water containing glitter, Cu(II), or both, and AO beads soaked in dilute acetic acid without chitosan served as a control for the acid. The removal of Cu(II) in copper-only water was 45.71 ± 1.97%, 59.44 ± 2.28%, and 84.19 ± 2.65% for the alginate-only, AO, and chitosan-treated beads, respectively (mean ± SD, n = 12, 6 h, 140 rpm). Opuntia increased the Cu(II) removal by 13.72 percentage points and chitosan by a further 24.75 points (paired t-test, p < 0.001 for both, and p ≤ 0.0013 for the batch means). In the presence of 2.00 g of glitter, the chitosan-treated beads still removed about 84% of the Cu(II). Meanwhile, the glitter removal increased by about 7 points with Opuntia but changed by less than 0.25 points with chitosan (p = 0.648 and 0.231). No significant difference was found between the acid-soaked and the untreated AO beads. It can be concluded that Opuntia was responsible for the increase in glitter capture and chitosan for most of the increase in Cu(II) removal.

papers.title: Non-catalytic Highly Selective Olefin Production from Complex Hydrocarbons via Pulsed Joule Heating
papers.abstract: Selective catalytic conversion of complex hydrocarbons into light olefins remains challenging because of costly catalyst preparation and catalyst deactivation under severe cracking conditions. Here, we report pulsed Joule heating for highly selective light olefin production from complex hydrocarbon mixtures. By precisely regulating reaction severity, this catalyst-free approach achieves light olefin yields comparable to those reported for catalytic cracking. We systematically characterized the feedstock molecular composition and evaluated olefin yields of diverse hydrocarbon mixtures, including polyolefins, crude oils, Fischer-Tropsch wax, and shale oil. To quantify the effects of pulse parameters on olefin production, we developed a spatiotemporal reactor model based on a quasi-molecular reaction network. The model reveals that pulsed Joule heating regulates high-temperature reactions to match product removal, thereby improving olefin yield and selectivity. Guided by the model, catalyst-free pulsed Joule heating crude oil pyrolysis was optimized and achieved a light olefin yield of approximately 38 wt%. These findings establish a quantitative framework for temporal regulation of complex hydrocarbon pyrolysis and provide a basis for industrial electrified olefin production.

papers.title: The infinitesimal machine surgeon: prospects for upconversion nanoparticles driving molecular motors/nanomachines
papers.abstract: The concept of the “infinitesimal machine surgeon” was envisaged by Feynman in 1959/1983, describing a miniature, human-controllable machine capable of being directed to biological tissue to perform a physical intervention. This perspective explores the potential of combining Feringa-type rotary molecular motors (nanomachines) with upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) to realize the vision of the infinitesimal machine surgeon. In this approach, UCNPs convert near-infrared (NIR) excitation into ultraviolet/visible (UV/Vis) emission to activate molecular nanomachines within biological tissue. The fundamental operating principles are outlined, recent experimental advances in powering molecular motors and UCNPs in organic solvents are reviewed. Simple biophotonic calculations based on the Beer–Lambert law suggest that upconversion from 808 nm to 450–475 nm may offer a promising excitation strategy for activating molecular motors in biological tissues. Key challenges to biological implementation are identified, including permissible tissue light-exposure levels and the effects of tissue absorption and multiple scattering on the photon budget available to drive UCNPs and molecular motors. Finally, experimental strategies for evaluating these systems in biologically relevant environments are proposed, in accordance with the 3Rs principles of biomedical research.

papers.title: Beyond Go/No-Go Decisions: A Regional Selection Framework for Uncertainty-Aware Molecule Screening
papers.abstract: In drug discovery, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models are widely used to guide Go/No-Go decisions within the Design–Make–Test–Analyze (DMTA) cycle. However, conventional decision heuristics typically rely on a single cutoff, leading to a rigid binary select/discard paradigm. This approach is particularly ill-suited for borderline compounds near the decision boundary, where screening decisions are especially sensitive to prediction uncertainty and premature choices may either discard viable leads or advance likely failures, thereby increasing downstream assay costs. To address this limitation, we propose Regional Selection (RS), an uncertainty-aware three-way decision framework that partitions compounds into Predicted Pass, Predicted Fail, and Predicted Indeterminate regions. By explicitly reserving high-uncertainty compounds for targeted follow-up, RS avoids the pitfalls of premature binary classification. We formalize this framework through Regional Selection Inference (RSI), which casts region assignment as a multiple-hypothesis testing problem. We develop two imple- mentations of RSI: an empirical calibration-based method (RSI-EC), which thresholds uncertainty-normalized scores via empirical calibration, and a conformal selectionbased method (RSI-CS), which constructs conformal p-values for region assignment. RSI-EC is supported by large-sample calibration arguments, whereas RSI-CS provides finite-sample, distribution-free guarantees under exchangeability. Extensive evaluations across 15 high-dimensional QSAR benchmarks show that both RSI procedures reliably control the false discovery rate while maintaining high screening power. In limited-data regimes, RSI-CS yields particularly stable FDR control, whereas RSI-EC can be slightly less conservative; both perform strongly as sample sizes increase. We further study a cost-aware extension that incorporates asymmetric downstream costs through the score construction while keeping the nominal FDR target fixed. This extension introduces a tuning parameter that can reduce realized downstream cost, with dataset-dependent trade-offs against screening power. Overall, RSI offers a mathematically grounded and resource-aware alternative to single-threshold screening, allowing discovery teams to better balance decision confidence with assay budgets.

papers.title: Curvature-induced kinetic trapping in chemical reactions
papers.abstract: Crossing an activation energy barrier in a chemical reaction needs time because enough kinetic energy needs to redistribute into the barrier-crossing mode. Kinetic energy redistribution is also needed to get across regions with strong reaction path curvature. This latter fact is frequently overlooked, possibly because barriers and curvature peaks often coincide, and curvature is invisible in the usual, pseudo-one-dimensional reaction energy profiles. For a set of related stepwise Diels-Alder reactions, we examine reaction paths, energy profiles and molecular dynamics trajectories, demonstrating three different cases: (1) one with a traditional IUPAC-conforming potential energy intermediate, in which the surrounding energy barriers coincide with curvature peaks; (2) another case in which the second C-C bond closure is associated with small curvature and no clearly visible energy barrier, accordingly the dynamics towards full ring closure is comparatively fast; and (3) a final case also without an energy barrier for the second C-C bond closure but with a large curvature peak there, leading to exceptionally long kinetic trapping between the two C-C bond formations in the downhill-energy region. Hence, we advocate for calculating reaction path curvature as simple add-on to reaction paths, to identify cases warranting a full molecular dynamics study. Besides reaction path curvature, further features are analyzed that contribute to dynamic delays, opening up unconventional reaction control possibilities.

papers.title: From Electron Density to Ionic Conductivity for the Mechanistic Understanding of a Fast Charging Acetone Electrolyte
Engineering cyanobacterial carbonic anhydrase surface mutations for fast CO2 hydration and capture
papers.abstract: Equilibration between CO 2 and the other forms of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is slow under ambient conditions, bottlenecked by the hydration of dissolved CO 2 to form bicarbonate and a proton. This step is often rate-limiting for aqueous CO 2 capture processes under ambient temperature and pressure, and is precisely the chemistry catalyzed by the family of carbonic anhydrase enzymes. As a result, incorporation of carbonic anhydrases (CAs) into various CO 2 capture schemes may be used to accelerate CO 2 hydration, increasing the rates of downstream processes coupled to this DIC equilibrium. While this potential use for CA has been long-studied, extending these basic chemical principles to real applications have been hampered by practical questions of how to economically source carbonic anhydrase enzymes at mass scale. This work explores the use of modified cyanobacterial expression hosts as a potential resolution to that problem. Successful engineering of carbonic anhydrase surface display in fast-growing, marine cyanobacteria would yield a self-sustaining CO 2 hydration catalyst that requires only sunlight, CO 2 itself, and nutrients freely available in seawater, as inputs for passively generating carbonic anhydrases on the cell envelope during cell growth.

papers.title: Mass-Minimized Lunar Radiation Protection Using In Situ Regolith and Distributed Magnetic Shielding: Physics, Engineering Feasibility, and a Specification for Dose Validation
papers.abstract: We evaluate a distributed superconducting perimeter fence for lunar surface protection against solar energetic particle (SEP) events. A relativistic Boris-pusher simulation shows that a 22-coil, two-channel fence attenuates SEP protons as effectively as a monolithic dipole of equal magnetic moment (94.9% versus 95.1% proton number-fluence removal; 75.4% versus 72.2% energy-fluence removal for a representative soft SEP spectrum), while leaving the protected volume field-free and avoiding a single point of failure. We then address two questions that determine buildability. First, permanent magnets are ruled out as a primary moment source: NdFeB's remanence bounds achievable moment-per-mass roughly four orders of magnitude below the superconducting design, requiring approximately 2.65×105 t of material to match the design moment. Second, propagating previously uncosted engineering margins (current derating, structural/cryostat overhead, thermal cycling, dust mitigation) gives a credible system mass of median 81 t (90% CI 55–116 t); substituting regolith-derived structure for Earth-launched structural mass reduces this to 46.4 t at unchanged attenuation. We add first-order feasibility estimates for launch, cooling, and power, plus a dose-context section situating energy-fluence attenuation against NASA dose limits and published benchmarks (regolith cladding, the AstroRad vest). These fluence-based results establish mass and attenuation feasibility but not dose reduction; we specify the coupled HZETRN2020/Geant4 transport calculation required to close that gap. The central architectural finding is that the optimal lunar SEP-mitigation strategy is asset-dependent: regolith cladding is more mass-efficient for fixed equipment, while the fence's durable role is protecting rovers, EVA crew, and distributed infrastructure that regolith cannot reach. Plain Language Summary A burst of energetic particles from the Sun can be dangerous to astronauts and equipment on the Moon’s surface, where there is no atmosphere or global magnetic field for protection. One proposed defense is a ring of superconducting magnetic coils around a work site — a “magnetic fence” — that deflects incoming particles, similar to how Earth's own magnetic field protects us from the solar wind. An earlier study by the author showed this fence shields about as well as a single large magnet at the habitat, but only roughly estimated how much material it would take to build and launch from Earth and did not connect that shielding to how much radiation a person or a piece of equipment would actually receive. This paper folds earlier physics analysis into a single, complete study and adds three new contributions. First, it checks the mass estimate more carefully and looks for ways to reduce it: ordinary permanent magnets cannot replace the coils' superconducting wire, since they are tens of thousands of times too weak per unit of mass, and building the fence's support structure from lunar soil instead of shipping it from Earth cuts the Earth-launched mass from approximately 81 tonnes to approximately 46 tonnes. Second, it adds a first-order look at the practical engineering problems of actually running such a system on the Moon—how much electrical power the cryogenic cooling would need, how large the radiators would have to be, and how the mass figures compare with what a large future rocket such as Starship could plausibly deliver to the lunar surface. Third, it connects the shielding numbers to what they mean for a person or a piece of electronics by comparing the concept with current approaches such as a few centimeters of soil cover, a water-filled protective vest, or a temporary storm shelter, each of which has published dose-reduction figures from real missions or measurements. The central finding remains that no single technology is best everywhere. For equipment that remains in one place, simply piling on 2 cm of lunar soil blocks more than 90% of the particle energy using almost no Earth-launched material, which is more efficient than the fence. The real value of the fence is to protect things that soil cannot cover, such as rovers and astronauts working outside, and the ISRU-built version of the fence makes that protection less expensive in Earth-launch terms without changing how well it shields.

papers.title: Removal of Lead and Arsenic from Contaminated Water Using a Sugarcane Bagasse Biochar–Metal Organic Framework (BC-MOF) Adsorbent
papers.abstract: The presence of highly toxic metals in aquatic environments is a major environmental concern, affecting both ecosystems and human health. Conventional removal methods are often limited by high costs, low efficiency, and the generation of secondary waste. Biochar produced by the pyrolysis of sugarcane bagasse under oxygen-limited conditions is a sustainable alternative owing to its porous structure, which can retain metal contaminants. In this study, a biochar obtained at 400 °C (BC400) was combined with cobalt ferrite (CoFe2O4) and terephthalic acid to produce a biochar–metal organic framework composite (BC-MOF). The composite was evaluated for the removal of lead (Pb) and arsenic (As) from aqueous solutions (nominal concentration of 2 mg L-1) at initial pH values of 4.5, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.5, using 0.25 g of adsorbent in 250 mL of solution (1 g L-1). Samples were collected at eight contact times between 15 min and 24 h and analyzed by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES). Pb was removed to concentrations reported as zero within 8 h at pH 4.5 and 8.5 and within 24 h at pH 6.0, and the residual concentration at pH 7.0 after 24 h was 0.034 mg L-1. As removal was gradual and incomplete within 24 h, with the best performance at pH 4.5 (residual concentration of 0.696 mg L-1). The composite also showed a marked buffering effect, raising the pH of acidic solutions to near neutrality. These results indicate that BC-MOF is a promising lowcost material for the remediation of water contaminated with Pb and As.

papers.title: Constructive chemical discovery through autonomous reasoning and experiment
papers.abstract: Making a new reaction often requires chemical knowledge that does not yet exist. Self-driving laboratories and language-model agents now plan, run and optimize experiments rapidly1–3, but deciding what to ask next still requires a chemist in the loop4. Here we report AIChemist, a robotic chemist for what we call constructive chemical discovery. It decides what to ask next from its own results, settles each question by calculation or experiment, and builds the next design on the answer. Given a silyl-radical-relay concept, AIChemist developed an asymmetric three-component silylcyanation: it established that the solvent effect depended on the oxidant formulation and built the next formulation on this finding, raising the yield from 20% to 67% at 88% enantiomeric excess. For an intermediate of the insecticide broflanilide, it designed a photoredox/nickel C–N coupling route free of nitro-group transformations, at lower estimated cost than the conventional route. When the base favoured by calculation performed poorly, it withdrew that premise and rebuilt the search around the reaction medium, where non-polar toluene raised the product's HPLC yield from 43% to 86%. In both cases, each conclusion extended what the system knew and became the starting point for the next. These results demonstrate a framework for autonomous chemical discovery in which chemical understanding and experimental design evolve together within a closed loop.

papers.title: Predicted structural models for NaSbBr4 and LiSbBr4 from a prototype-transplant search with machine-learned potentials and DFT
papers.abstract: Many ternary halides studied for solid-state batteries have no reported crystal structure. Their computed stability then depends on whichever structure is assumed, so the 3D crystal structure is the bottleneck. We transplanted 228 prototypes from the Alexandria database into AMX4 chemistries (A = Li, Na; M = Al, Ga, In, Sc, Y, Sb, Bi; X = Cl, Br, I; 9431 transplants) and screened them with the MACE-MPA-0 machine-learned potential. We then compared the best survivors with every database-listed polymorph and competing phase we computed, using PBE-D3. The main result is a proposed C2/c model, TP-NaSbBr4-01, predicted 6.2 meV/atom below NaBr + SbBr3 and 17.0 meV/atom below the lowest computed NaSbBr4 polymorph listed in Alexandria. The sign holds with D3(BJ), with the nonlocal vdW-DF-optB86b functional and without dispersion. Harmonic phonons at 2x2x2 sampling show no imaginary mode, which does not by itself establish dynamical stability. A secondary candidate with less evidence, TP-LiSbBr4-01, lies below its competing phases with D3 zero damping, D3(BJ) and optB86b (7.7, 8.4 and 10.9 meV/atom). With plain PBE, it lies +2.05 meV/atom above them. Its phonons at 2x2x2 sampling also show no imaginary mode. The method's own errors are as large as or larger than these margins. PBE-D3 mis-orders the SbBr3 polymorphs by +15.2 meV/atom, and optB86b mis-orders them by +21.6 meV/atom (with PBE-generated PAW datasets), so the error is not a D3 artifact. The protocol also fails its one false-positive control. It ranks a hypothetical LiAlBr4 model 4.5 meV/atom below a LiAlBr4 cell built on the LiAlCl4 structure type. At this level of theory, both models are candidates for diffraction testing. Their position below the computed binaries does not establish them as phases. No electrolyte suitability is shown. Nothing was synthesized. Machine-learned molecular dynamics found no long-range ion diffusion in the pristine crystals. Sb(III) is expected to be reduced at Li and Na anode potentials. The computed 0 K PBE-D3 windows are narrow (2.47-3.35 V vs Na/Na+, 2.38-3.27 V vs Li/Li+). They lie above the metal potential and below common cathodes, and the oxidation limit is an upper bound. The PBE gaps (2.5 and 2.4 eV) are underestimates. Models in five other screened compositions, including NaBiCl4, also meet all four gates (one machine-learned, three DFT). They did not receive the dispersion, phonon and window checks, so they are reported briefly and not pursued.

papers.title: Hunting the Enhanced Interaction of Donors with Post-Transition and Transition Metal Dichalcogenides: Comparative Study of NO <sub>2</sub> , H <sub>2</sub> S, NH <sub>3</sub> , and Aniline Adsorption on MoS <sub>2</sub> , SnS <sub>2</sub> , and ZrS <sub>2</sub> Monolayers
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional transition and post-transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs and PTMDs) are promising materials for applications in roomtemperature, physisorption-based gas sensing and monitoring. In recent years, the mechanisms behind the adsorption of electron-accepting molecules have been well established, leading to the development of composition-engineering pathways that may be used to enhance the chemiresistive signal, as well as to design and fine-tune selective devices. However, similar trends have yet to be found for the electron-donating species. Consequently, the present study employs density functional theory (DFT) methods to systematically compare the adsorption of three electron donors, hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S), ammonia (NH 3 ), and aniline (C 6 H 5 NH 2 ), and one baseline acceptor, nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), on semiconducting 1H-MoS 2 , 1T-SnS 2 , and 1T-ZrS 2 monolayers. The set was selected to provide direct comparison of different substrate symmetries, d-block versus p-block metal centers, and example acceptor-versus donor-molecule behavior under identical theoretical description. It was found that donor analytes can experience substrate-dependent enhancement in charge transfer only when their HOMO lies sufficiently high in energy. Accordingly, at the vdw-DF-cx level of theory, only aniline shows pronounced differences in adsorption, donating on average −0.049, −0.119, and −0.143 e to MoS 2 , SnS 2 , and ZrS 2 , respectively, whereas NH 3 and H 2 S exhibit no comparable trend. This particular substrate order was correlated with the favorable positions of the conduction band edges as well as the spatial availability of the low-lying acceptor states. These results provide a theoretical basis for the mechanisms governing adsorption of donating species on pristine TMDs and PTDMs, and may aid in selecting a suitable material for physisorption-based devices.

papers.title: Roles of oxygen vacancies and the Ni–support interface in CO2 hydrogenation over Ni/Y-doped BaZrO3 revealed by experimental and computational studies
papers.abstract: Understanding the roles of oxygen vacancies, proton-conducting supports, and metal–support interfaces is essential for the rational design of efficient CO2 hydrogenation catalysts. Herein, we investigate CO2 hydrogenation over Ni-supported Ydoped BaZrO3 (Ni/BZY) by combining powder X-ray diffraction (XRD), surface area measurements, CO2 temperatureprogrammed desorption (CO2-TPD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), catalytic measurements, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. CO2-TPD and DFT calculations consistently show that oxygen vacancies on BZY strongly stabilize CO2 adsorption. Oxygen vacancy enables facile CO2 dissociation and preferential CO formation via the reverse water–gas shift reaction. In contrast, the Ni–BZY interface provides moderate CO2 adsorption together with efficient H2 dissociation, creating favorable sites for the hydrogenation of CO-derived intermediates to CH4. DFT calculations further reveal that proton migration in BZY is energetically favorable, allowing protonic species to accumulate near the catalyst surface and participate in surface reactions. The reaction pathway through CO is identified as the most favorable route for methane formation at the Ni–BZY interface, whereas the carbide and carboxylic pathways are kinetically unfavorable. These results demonstrate the complementary functions of oxygen vacancies, proton conduction, and the Ni–support interface in governing CO2 activation and product selectivity, providing mechanistic insights and design principles for proton-conducting oxide-supported catalysts for thermochemical CO2 conversion.

papers.title: Capturing Transient Growth Windows for Narrow-Emitting Perovskite Nanoplatelets
papers.abstract: Colloidal perovskite nanoplatelets offer thickness-tunable, directional emission, but maintaining narrow ensemble photoluminescence linewidths at greater thicknesses remains challenging. Here, we show that under selected reaction conditions, distinct CsPbBr3 nanoplatelet thickness populations emerge in succession during synthesis, each offering a transient window for isolation before further morphological evolution. By tuning growth kinetics through precursor composition and overall dilution under ambient conditions, we make these windows experimentally accessible. In situ photoluminescence monitoring tracks the successive populations and guides the time-selective isolation of 4- and 5-monolayer nanoplatelets. The resulting ensembles exhibit narrow cyan emission with linewidths down to 70 and 80 meV, respectively. Post-synthetic surface treatment increases the photoluminescence quantum yield to 70 % while preserving narrow emission, and halide exchange extends the approach to red-emitting iodide nanoplatelets. These findings demonstrate that favorable nanoplatelet morphologies can be accessed as transient populations along a growth trajectory, establishing control over growth kinetics and isolation time as a strategy for obtaining narrow-emitting colloidal nanostructures.

papers.title: Co-Titration of Phosphatidylserine Lipids and a Channel Protein Using Constant pH Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: The protonation state of anionic lipids plays a central role in regulating membrane electrostatics, structure, and interactions with membrane proteins. Lipid titration in membranes is inherently collective and strongly influenced by local composition and lateral organization. Experimentally, determining lipid p K ₐ values in heterogeneous and dynamically organized membranes is challenging, making it difficult to disentangle intrinsic lipid properties from collective membrane effects. Moreover, lipid and protein protonation states can be electrostatically coupled, such that changes in the ionization state of one component can influence the titration behavior of the other. Here, we use constant pH molecular dynamics (CpHMD) simulations to investigate the titration behavior of phosphatidylserine (PS) lipids in bilayers with varying PS content, ranging from dilute mixtures with phosphatidylcholine (PC) to fully anionic membranes, as well as the cotitration of proteins and lipids using the OmpF porin embedded in a titratable PS membrane. We show that the apparent pKa of the PS headgroup depends strongly on membrane composition, increasing systematically with PS surface density. We compare the CpHMD-derived pKa values of OmpF acidic residues in various lipid compositions, ranging from fixed-charge PS to mixed PS/PC and fully titratable PS membranes. The resulting pKa shifts demonstrate that the protonation state of the surrounding lipid environment can substantially modulate protein titration, demonstrating coupled lipid–protein ionization. Together, these results highlight the electrostatic coupling between membrane lipids and proteins and establish CpHMD as a framework for capturing composition-dependent protonation behavior in complex membrane environments.

papers.title: Role of water in hydrogen-based iron oxide reduction: effects on pore evolution and gas transport
papers.abstract: Hydrogen-based direct reduction offers a low-emission route to ironmaking. Oxygen removal reduces the mass and volume of the solid, creating pores that provide pathways for hydrogen supply and removal of the water produced. Water accumulation within these evolving pores can inhibit further reduction. Here, we develop a phase-field model coupling water generation, transport, and reaction inhibition to pore evolution during wüstite-to-ferrite reduction. The simulations show that water accumulation slows reduction and allows pores to coarsen. Increasing the pore volume fraction accelerates reduction but does not prevent water accumulation when its removal from the pores is limited. Simulating gas diffusion through the resulting fixed pore structures shows that coarser morphologies have higher directional effective diffusivity even at comparable pore fractions. These findings motivate pellet-scale models that account for how reduction history shapes pore morphology and thereby influences gas transport.

papers.title: Participant-level Raman spectroscopy of circulating EV-enriched fractions reveals distributed spectral differences in ischemic stroke patients
papers.abstract: Raman spectroscopy provides a label-free vibrational profile of extracellularvesicle (EV)-enriched biofluid fractions. Participant-level Raman profiles were obtained from 97 participants with ischemic stroke and 50 controls. After quality control and region-specific normalization, spectra acquired at individual spatial sampling locations were aggregated into a single median spectrum per participant in the fingerprint (734–1788 cm −1 ) and C–H stretching (2451–3197 cm −1 ) regions, so that inference was carried out at the participant rather than the measurement level. The objectives were to characterize participant-level spectral variation, assess exploratory case-control separation, and examine associations with clinical outcomes within the stroke cohort. Participant-level spectra showed 21 reproducible Raman bands and shoulder features associated with lipids, proteins, nucleic acids, and carotenoids. Lipid-associated regions accounted for most of the normalized spectral variance (fingerprint PC1, 75.8%; C–H PC1, 67.1%), a pattern that persisted when PCA was repeated using only spectra from participants with ischemic stroke. All 21 features differed between stroke and control participants after false-discovery-rate correction, with increases and decreases distributed across multiple correlated Raman domains. The primary whole-spectrum partial least-squares discriminant analysis (PLSDA) model gave modest discrimination (balanced accuracy 0.655, 95% CI 0.538–0.771; ROC–AUC 0.711, 95% CI 0.550–0.823; sex-stratified permutation p = 0.005). Within the stroke cohort, no whole-spectrum association survived correction for multiplicity, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores gave negative cross-validated R 2 , so the spectra did not support the prediction of cognitive outcome. Participant-level Raman spectroscopy, therefore, identifies reproducible biochemical differences within compositionally complex EV-enriched fractions and identifies lipid-, protein-, nucleic acid-, and carotenoid-associated regions for molecular follow-up in larger, balanced cohorts.

papers.title: Semisyntheses of Aspercyclicins A and B via Isobenzofuran Cycloaddition
papers.abstract: The recently isolated aspercyclicins A and B from Aspergillus sp. LI2020F001 represent a chimeric scaffold derived from crosstalk of two biosynthetic pathways. These natural products display cytotoxicity against cancer cell lines and potently activate immunogenic cell death (ICD). Herein, we report methodology development for biomimetic [4+2] cycloadditions involving an in situ generated isobenzofuran (IBF) leading to the semisyntheses of aspercyclicins A and B from the fungal-derived natural product (+)-geodin.

papers.title: Methodological Optimization of ATR-IR Spectroelectrochemistry for Powdered and Poorly Conductive Electrocatalysts
papers.abstract: In-situ infrared spectroscopy combined with electrochemistry has become a key tool for studying the processes that govern the activity of electrocatalysts under operating conditions. However, its application has been limited almost exclusively to model electrodes, which are either electronically conductive or specifically designed to maximise the ATR optical signal, thereby limiting its use for a family of emerging heterogenous catalysts typically available in powder form and exhibiting poor electrical conductivity. Extending ATR-IR spectroelectrochemistry to this type of catalyst requires simultaneously reconciling optical, adhesion and electrochemical requirements which, until now, have rarely been addressed systematically. Rather than focusing on the elucidation of electrocatalyst mechanisms, this paper presents a structured and transferable methodology for optimising ATR-IR spectroelectrochemical measurements on emerging classes of electrocatalyst. Three groups of interrelated parameters that mostly affect the feasibility of the technique, namely spectroscopic, interfacial and electrochemical parameters, are discussed proposing a step-by-step workflow that enables their methodological standardization and balance. The proposed workflow is validated by applying this methodology to three different materials (Ni(OH) 2 , ZnO and Zn-Al LDH) showing distinct spectroscopic, electrochemical and interfacial properties. The results demonstrate that, following appropriate optimisation, ATR spectroelectrochemistry can be extended to more challenging powdered catalyst layers, providing a practical and generalisable guide for future robust mechanistic investigations of this broad family of materials and contributing to the rational understanding and development of new electrocatalysts for reactions of energy and chemical interest.

papers.title: Footprint-aware Microkinetics Reveal Spatial Correlations with Catalytic Consequences
papers.abstract: Metal catalysis often involves bulky molecules that cover catalyst surface areas beyond a single exposed metal atom. Common multi-site models account for adsorbate size with simple mean-field correction factors, but neglect how multi-site adsorbates become spatially correlated to avoid overlapping. Here, we combine prior theoretical constructions—the reduction of the Master equation in the fast-diffusion limit and the Widom insertion approach—to develop a footprint-aware microkinetic framework where adsorbates interact through hard exclusion. We use Monte Carlo simulations to construct surrogate models of vacant site clusters and neighboring reactant pairs needed for elementary reaction steps, which introduce missing footprint effects into conventional kinetic models. These models retain explicit kinetic and thermodynamic parameters, support standard mechanistic analyses, and can be reused across temperatures and reaction conditions without repeated configurational sampling. We illustrate the framework using unimolecular and bimolecular reactions of an adsorbate with a seven-site footprint, resembling benzene and phenol. Footprint-induced correlations have two effects relative to mean-field treatments: they (i) enrich the sites surrounding multi-site adsorbates with single-site co-adsorbates or vacancies, and (ii) aggregate empty sites into clusters that accommodate additional multi-site adsorbates. These correlations alter absolute rates, reactant pressure trends, step reversibilities, and degrees of rate control. The correlation effects are most pronounced for bimolecular reactions when surfaces are crowded by multi-site adsorbates and adsorption events at single sites or site pairs are kinetically relevant. For one bimolecular reaction, the mean-field approximation fits footprint-aware rates and elementary-step reversibility across a given range of pressures for a single reactant, but only after reducing the apparent footprint from seven to 3.3 sites and weakening the adsorption free energy by 12 RT. The approximation furthermore predicts different coreactant pressure dependences. Consequently, quantitative model agreement with kinetic trends can conceal physically inaccurate parameters and mechanistic interpretations when accounting for adsorbate size, while neglecting spatial correlations.

papers.title: Rapid One-Step Synthesis of Sodium-Ion Battery Cathodes from Desalination Waste: A Sustainable Approach to High-Performance Energy Storage
papers.abstract: Desalination brine, a hypersaline byproduct of water treatment processes, represents an underutilized sodium feedstock with significant potential for battery material production. In this work, we report a streamlined rapid one-step synthesis (ROSS) method for Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 3 (NVP), a highperformance sodium-ion battery cathode material with demonstrated electrochemical comparability with lithium-based alternatives, directly from desalination brine. Sequential filtration and chemical precipitation were used to selectively isolate sodium ions from brine, effectively removing divalent cations (Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ ), heavy metal impurities and organic contaminants. The purified sodiumion solution was subsequently used to prepare a sodium-vanadium-oxalate precursor, from which phase-pure NVP crystals with carbon coating were obtained via a single-step combustion reaction. Notably, the entire crystallization process was completed within 45 minutes using an open crucible setup under ambient atmosphere, representing a significant reduction in both processing time and operational complexity compared to conventional NVP synthesis routes, which typically require 2–4 hours under inert gas conditions. Our method offers a dual environmental benefit: mitigating the ecological impact of brine discharge while supplying a low-cost, sustainable sodium source for the growing sodium-ion battery industry.

papers.title: Untargeted Lipidomics Reveals Dynamic Changes to the HEK 293T Lipidome During Lentiviral Vector Production Over 72 Hours
papers.abstract: Lentiviral vectors (LV) are biotechnology tools descending from human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) that may be used in cell and gene therapies. HIV transduction efficiency has been shown to be negatively affected when the lipid composition of its envelope is altered, suggesting that targeted lipid envelope composition engineering may serve as a tool to modulate transduction. To investigate this possibility, an untargeted lipidomics experiment was conducted on HEK 293T packaging cells producing LV at three time points: 24, 48 and 72 h. 401 lipids from 23 classes were identified and significant changes to the HEK 293T lipidome from LV production were recorded at each time point. Triacylglycerol (TG) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) species were the most affected lipid classes throughout the time course. Large increases in the abundance of TG species were observed with significant depletion of many PC species, suggesting lipid droplet formation occurs during LV production. Analysis of the fatty acyl chain profiles revealed that LV production significantly increased the average chain length after 24 and 48 h while the double bond index did not change in a statistically significant manner across all time points compared to control cells, possibly serving as a means to maintain homeostasis while large amounts of shorter acyl chains were used for LV envelope formation. 9 of 12 acyl chains had significant trends with increased LV production time, serving as targets for media supplementation or for metabolic pathway manipulation to increase LV titer. Future directions will investigate the effects of media supplementation with phospholipid mixtures on the dynamics of TG species over time with LV production.

papers.title: Sustainable Surface Metallurgy for Public Health: A Review of Barrier Degradation, Structural Heterogeneity, and Aluminum Leaching Dynamics in Low-Income Country Cookware
papers.abstract: Aluminum (Al) consumer cookware remains a cornerstone of global food preparation due to its exceptional thermal efficiency and low cost. However, in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), the widespread reliance on low-purity, informally recycled artisanal alloys creates severe public health risks due to heavy metal migration into dietary pathways. This review explicitly links materials engineering for sustainable development with global safety frameworks by evaluating surface modification technologies designed to mitigate aluminum ion leaching under aggressive thermal and chemical cooking conditions. This review systematically synthesizes the thermodynamic, kinetic, and mechanical performance of three dominant protective systems: electrochemical anodization, sol-gel quasi-ceramic matrices, and fluoropolymer barriers. The chemical stability of these systems is analyzed using mass transport models, chelation-assisted coordination mechanics, and the Arrhenius activation energy framework. Furthermore, a sequential technical characterization workflow is established—linking Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM-EDX), X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS)—to evaluate barrier performance against the strict specific migration limits (SML) enforced by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA). While hard anodization and ceramic coatings offer excellent thermal stability, their long-term barrier performance is often compromised by interfacial shear stresses driven by mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) and mechanical wear. This issue is particularly severe in informal metallurgical sectors. Artisanal castings feature high structural porosity and iron/copper micro-impurities that create localized galvanic micro-cells (Δ E > 1.0 V), accelerating the breakdown of surface oxide barriers and leading to heavy metal migration that routinely exceeds international safety standards by factors of 10 to 50. Critical commercial research gaps are identified, specifically the development of cost-effective, bio-based non-stick barriers (e.g., cross-linked green nanocomposites) and the implementation of decentralized circular economy scrap-sorting upgrades. Resolving these material vulnerabilities is essential for advancing UN Sustainable Development Goals related to good health and well-being (SDG 3), clean manufacturing (SDG 9), and responsible consumption and production (SDG 12). This work provides a clear roadmap for scalable, non-hazardous cookware manufacturing tailored for vulnerable populations.

papers.title: Elucidating thermodynamic infeasibility of the (de)-lithiation process in 5V-class LiNi0.5Ge1.5O4 solid electrolyte
papers.abstract: LiNi0.5Ge1.5O4 (LNGO), a Ge-substituted analogue of high-voltage cobalt-free LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 (LNMO) spinel cathode, has previously been reported to show electrochemical inertness up to 5V vs. Li+/Li. However, thermodynamic and electronic origins of this inert behaviour have remained unexplored. Herein, we investigated the redox mechanism and thermodynamic driving force governing the (de)intercalation behaviour of LNGO using first-principles density functional theory (DFT+U) and verified using experimental findings. Convex hull analysis over the compositional range (0<x<2 in LixNi0.5Ge1.5O4) reveals absence of stable or metastable intermediate phases, supporting electrochemical inert behaviour. This was further reinforced by substantial evolution of structural symmetry, lattice parameters, and electronic band gaps during the process of (de)lithiation, resulting in a high-voltage stability up to 5 V vs. Li+/Li. Moreover, AIMD and CI-NEB calculations predicted Li-ion migration via vacant octahedral sites with a moderately high activation barrier of 0.537 eV. Experimental techniques such as linear sweep voltammetry, electrochemical impedance analysis and chronoamperometry were used to confirm DFT findings. These findings suggests that LNGO can be used as a possible solid electrolyte candidate in high energy density battery applications.

papers.title: Revisiting Percolation and Molecular Diffusion in Disordered Pore Networks
papers.abstract: The relationship between pore network structure and molecular diffusion in disordered nanoporous materials remains unclear. Here, we revisit two methodological choices that may contribute to inconsistent structure–diffusion relationships in the literature: percolation characterization and inclusion of non-percolating pores in diffusivity calculations. Our rigorous benchmarks show consistent results from Zeo++ and Mofography but reveal biased characterization from PoreBlazer due to limitations in its algorithm. Molecular dynamics simulations further consolidate that initializing adsorbates in percolating pore networks is essential for reliable and robust calculations of molecular self-diffusivity. With these issues addressed, we re-examine structure–diffusion relationships for methane across four amorphous material classes. Symbolic regression identifies the percolating backbone fraction as a key, yet largely overlooked, topology-related descriptor that captures a common diffusion trend across classes. Further analysis supports the added predictive value of this new descriptor beyond conventional geometric descriptors in machine learning tasks. Our work provides a consistent methodological foundation and a complementary descriptor for diffusion prediction in disordered nanoporous materials.

papers.title: An Enzyme-DNA Nanostructure with Enhanced Catalysis Accelerates MRSA Wound Healing
papers.abstract: Antibiotic-resistant wound infections are a growing clinical challenge, as bacteria evade singletarget antimicrobials and persist within protective biofilms. Antimicrobial enzymes offer a promising alternative through their catalytic generation of bactericidal species, but their therapeutic utility is limited by instability in protease-rich wound environments. Here, we demonstrate that densely grafting short DNA strands onto lactoperoxidase (LPO), an innate immune enzyme, creates an enzyme-DNA nanostructure (Nano-Lac) with enhanced proteolytic stability and catalytic activity. Whereas polymer conjugation typically compromises enzyme activity, DNA functionalization increased LPO’s catalytic turnover by >10-fold. Mechanistic studies revealed conformational changes consistent with increased active-site accessibility and reduced accumulation of an inactive oxidized intermediate under excess H2O2. These enhancements translated into broad-spectrum activity against multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli (E. coli) and methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Nano-Lac suppressed growth, disrupted biofilms, and compromised membrane integrity, outperforming vancomycin in vitro. In a murine MRSA wound model, daily topical Nano-Lac reduced bacterial burden ~2-fold and accelerated wound closure versus native LPO and vancomycin, without histopathological signs of toxicity. Extending beyond LPO, DNA functionalization also enhanced peroxidase activity across structurally distinct heme proteins, including myoglobin, hemoglobin, and cytochrome c. These findings establish DNA grafting as a general strategy to enhance heme-protein stability, catalysis, and therapeutic function.

papers.title: Anisotropic Electrical Conductivity in Close-Packed Two-Dimensional Polyaramids
papers.abstract: Polyaramids such as Kevlar ® are renowned for their high mechanical strength and chemical resistance; however, their non-conjugated backbones render them electrically insulating. Orbital alignment can allow close-packed stacked molecules to exhibit long range conduction, opening the possibility that insulating nanomaterials may form conducting arrangements. Herein, we report two-dimensional (2D) polyaramids with tailored end-groups that promote tighter molecular packing as their size decreases. Terminal groups with the size of a single methyl result in aligned films that exhibit highly anisotropic electrical conductivity up to 1.39 × 10 –4 S m –1 , comparable to or exceeding many undoped conjugated polymers. Charge transport occurs orthogonally across aligned, stacked polymer platelets while the in-plane direction remains insulating. The anisotropy reverses the behavior typically observed in-plane conduction of stacked 2D nanomaterials. The resulting films are photoconductive under 405 nm illumination with an external quantum efficiency of 0.62%. The mechanical and chemical stability of such conductive 2D polyaramids enables the first single-component, acid-stable polymer electrodes based on non-conjugated frameworks, capable of operating in harsh environments while exhibiting perfectly invariant cyclic capacitance for over 10,000 cycles at pH 2. The stability is enabled in part by the impermeability of such films to moisture and oxygen, underscored by their ability to suppress perovskite degradation with a 150 nm coating. Together, these findings underscore a newly realized mode of electrical conduction in close-packed 2D polymers, enabling ultra-lightweight and chemically stable electrodes for energy storage and sustainability applications.

papers.title: Behaviour of TMT labelled peptides in solid phase extraction, liquid chromatography, electrospray ionisation, and data-dependent acquisition
papers.abstract: In bottom-up proteomics, quantification with isobaric labelling involves derivatising peptides with reagents that are isobaric when intact but upon fragmentation produce reporter ions of different masses. Peptides from different samples are labelled with different reagent isotopomers, and the reporter ion intensities serve as a readout for peptide abundance in different samples, enabling sample multiplexing. Increased chromatographic retention of labelled peptides has been described and considered in models predicting peptide retention. However, how isobaric labelling affects peptide behaviour in other steps of the analytical workflow remains scarcely studied. In this work, we applied isobaric tandem mass tag (TMT) labelling on synthetic peptides to study how TMT labelling affects the peptides’ retention and yield in solid phase extraction, retention in liquid chromatography, and signal intensity. In addition, we monitored how closely reporter ion intensity reflects precursor ion intensity across chromatographic peaks. In solid phase extraction, TMT labelling caused a slight increase in retention without being detrimental to yield. In liquid chromatography, our results confirm those of earlier publications, identifying a retention increase, the magnitude of which is correlated with peptide hydrophilicity. We detected a near-consistent decrease of signal intensity in TMT-labelled peptides that may imply decreased ionisation efficiency but is likely mitigated by increased analyte amount that comes with multiplexing. Finally, we observed that although reporter-to-precursor ion ratios are mostly stable, for some peptides they vary enough to significantly affect quantification. Our results show that while TMT labelling affects peptide behaviour in analytics, changes to the analytical workflow are mostly not required.

papers.title: Consistency Testing of an Integrated SWRO–Brine Valorization Architecture: Alkalinity as the Binding Constraint
papers.abstract: Integrated seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) with brine valorization is widely proposed as a route to lower energy and near-zero liquid discharge, but such architectures are rarely tested against the physical bounds their stages must obey. Here a consistency-testing framework is applied to an architecture combining subsurface intake, isobaric energy recovery, membrane brine concentration, selective Ca/Mg precipitation and mechanical-vapor-compression crystallization. Each subsystem is checked against a thermodynamic or stoichiometric constraint rather than an assumed value. The concentrator duty commonly assumed in this class of study, 0.5–1.0 kWh m−3 of brine, lies at or below the least work of separation for that feed, 0.94 kWh m−3. A bounded estimate from that minimum and a 25–55% second-law efficiency gives 1.7–3.8 kWh m−3, raising the modeled total specific energy consumption to a median of 13.1 kWh m−3. Magnesium recovery is limited by alkalinity rather than by magnesium. The base required carries 10.0 kg CO2 per cubic meter of permeate in embodied carbon, roughly double the plant's grid emissions, or 27 kWh m−3 if generated electrochemically. Lime dosing releases 5.3 times more calcium than the carbonate step removes, so the train does not close. Costing those reagents explicitly is decisive: at $1.70 m−3 they exceed the $1.25 m−3 mineral credit, and Monte Carlo propagation (300,000 samples) gives a net levelized cost of $2.20 m−3 against $0.76 m−3 for conventional SWRO. Closing the calcium balance costs $0.44 m−3; above $0.069 kWh−1 no on-site base can close the loop, because the reversible limit of water dissociation binds.

papers.title: Disrupting Surface Oxo Availability Suppresses Ru Dissolution in RuO <sub>2</sub> Electrocatalysts
papers.abstract: Ru loss from RuO 2 in acidic oxygen evolution requires availability of surface oxo (*O) for eruption of surface Ru to form adsorbed *RuO 4 . Screening 20 dopants on *O-covered RuO 2 (110) (DFT) gave a trend linking *RuO 4 formation to dopant-dependent *O activity. Durability testing (CP, ICP-MS) followed this trend for Mo- and Ta-RuO 2 . Zn- and Hf-RuO 2 retained more Ru than predicted; in situ near-ambient pressure XPS and online ICP-MS reveal that the two do so by different means. Zn inhibits Ru overoxidation while Hf welcomes it, yet both inhibit Ru eruption. Surface-modulated models in which Zn dissolution leaves a cation vacancy and Hf bears a surface *OH both exhibit enhanced Ru retention (DFT): cation vacancies electronically reduce neighboring Ru and lack *O, whereas Hf’s *OH permits Ru overoxidation but inhibits its eruption. Both catalysts retain high activity (LSV) through a Ru-centered oxygen evolution pathway (GC-DFT). These findings reveal how dopants can enhance Ru retention by disrupting *O participation, regardless of Ru oxidation state, all while maintaining high oxygen evolution activity.

papers.title: How thermostats change the thermodynamic, structural and dynamic properties of a Lennard-Jones liquid
papers.abstract: Almost every molecular dynamics simulation is coupled to a thermostat, and every thermostat modifies the equations of motion whose solutions are then interpreted as the physics of the system. The algorithms are well established and their qualitative artefacts are well known, yet a quantitative comparison of the commonly used schemes under one protocol, with the statistical resolution needed to detect their effects, is rarely reported, presumably because such effects are small compared with the run-to-run scatter of a typical simulation. Such a comparison, however, is of practical importance, since it determines which observables a given thermostat can be trusted with. In this work, we compare six temperature-control schemes (windowed velocity rescaling, Berendsen, Nosé–Hoover chains, Langevin, the dissipative-particle-dynamics pair thermostat and canonical sampling through velocity rescaling) at up to four coupling strengths each against an energy-matched microcanonical reference, for the truncated-and-shifted Lennard-Jones liquid, with five independent realizations per case and with finite-size and timestep controls. We find that thermodynamic means and pair structure are the same for all schemes once the mean temperature is matched, whereas the fluctuations differ and the differences propagate into derived quantities such as the heat capacity. For transport, the decisive variable is whether the thermostat acts globally or locally, not how strongly it is coupled: the global schemes leave the self-diffusion coefficient and the viscosity equivalent to those of the microcanonical reference over the whole coupling range, whereas the local stochastic schemes damp diffusion once their friction approaches the intrinsic friction of the liquid. In particular, we show that the Langevin bias at five state points is reproduced to within 16%, with no fitted parameter, by a resistance-addition interpolation whose only input is the cage factor of overdamped Brownian dynamics, and that, once the periodic-box correction is carried over to the screened hydrodynamics of a Langevin liquid, the bath is predicted to remove in the thermodynamic limit a hydrodynamic contribution to diffusion that a finite box conceals. Our results also rationalize two implementation effects in LAMMPS, the kinetic-energy fluctuation deficit of strongly coupled Langevin dynamics and the failure of the stress-autocorrelation viscosity for a strongly coupled pair thermostat, which could otherwise be mistaken for physics. The comparison condenses into simple rules for the choice of a thermostat and its coupling time.

papers.title: Dynamic Disproportionation Shapes Ga Sites in Silica-Supported Propane Dehydrogenation Catalysts
papers.abstract: Ga is a key component of commercial propane dehydrogenation (PDH) catalysts. The regeneration of those catalysts involves oxidation and reduction cycles, the latter typically under H2 at about 550–650 °C. However, the structural evolution of Ga3+ sites under those strongly reducing conditions is underexplored. Here, we monitored the transformations of Ga3+ sites dispersed on a SiO2 support under H2 at 650 °C. The results show that this treatment generates metastable ºSiOGa1+ sites that disproportionate to Ga0 and Ga3+ sites. The formed Ga0 species react with surface silanols, regenerating ºSiOGa1+ sites, and with water formed during the reduction of Ga3+ to Ga1+, ultimately yielding large crystalline particles of k-Ga2O3. In addition, an overall loss of Ga from the catalyst is observed and attributed to the formation of Ga0 and volatile Ga2O. The Lewis acidity of dispersed Ga3+ decreases when it interacts with weakly Lewis-basic ºSiOGa1+ motifs. All of these processes associated with ºSiOGa1+ sites decrease the number of dispersed Ga3+ sites and are therefore detrimental for PDH activity, except that dispersed Ga3+ sites formed from disproportionation of ºSiOGa1+ sites likely have increased strain, beneficial for PDH activity. While H2 treatment alone has a negative impact on the catalyst’s PDH activity and propene selectivity, an oxidative air treatment of the reduced catalyst terminates disproportionation dynamics by oxidizing Ga0 and increases the Ga-based activity relative to both the reduced and fresh catalysts. These findings suggest that the disproportionation of Ga1+ species under an H2 atmosphere appreciably affects gallium speciation, loading, and catalytic performance.

papers.title: Resistance without a detectable bindingenergy penalty: distinct dynamic defects of gatekeeper and molecular-brake mutations in FGFR1–erdafitinib recognition
papers.abstract: The backbone Cα–Cα distance widely used to report kinase molecular-brake status gives a false negative under a clinically relevant FGFR1 resistance mutation: the brake's side-chain contact is destabilized in every replicate, yet the criterion reports it intact. Acquired FGFR1 kinase-domain mutations limit the clinical durability of erdafitinib, the first approved pan-FGFR inhibitor; loss of binding affinity is the assumed mechanism. We tested two questions in a single design: nine all-atom MD trajectories of the erdafitinib-bound kinase domain (wild type, V561M and molecular-brake mutant N546K; three replicates each; 4.491 μs). First, what a fully replicated comparison can resolve: neither MM/GBSA nor MM/PBSA detected a mutation-associated change in binding free energy; the observed mutant-versus-WT ΔΔG values lie below the detection limit of the present replicate set and within the intrinsic uncertainty of the end-point methods (GB ANOVA p = 0.27; PB p = 0.054). A large, E3810-like penalty (≈5 kcal·mol-1) is excluded. Second, the brake itself—N546K destabilizes the persistent engaged state of the residue-546–Glu562 contact: occupancy falls to 16–55% across replicates, entirely below the 95–100% of WT and V561M, at unchanged Cα–Cα geometry, dwell times fall from tens of nanoseconds to sub-nanosecond flickers, and broken periods reach 19 ns. V561M leaves the brake contact intact and instead loosens the gatekeeper-flanking hydrophobic network (Leu484/Val492/Lys514), dispersing its conformational ensemble across replicates. Side-chain proximity occupancy thus emerges as an operational order parameter for the molecular brake; the kinetic corollary, altered rates at unchanged affinity, is testable by SPR/BLI and unbinding calculations.

papers.title: Assessing the Impact of Incorporating Bias-Adjusted
papers.abstract: Understanding global ground-level ozone is hindered by significant monitoring gaps. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian Maximum Entropy data fusion framework that includes satellite ozone observations, generating a global 0.1° surface ozone dataset (2005–2022). Satellite observations (IASI+GOME2, OMI/MLS), adjusted to ground-level estimates, were analyzed using Flexible Regionalized Air Quality Model Performance to correct biases and estimate variance. Ground observations (hard data) and satellite-derived estimates (soft data) were then integrated, 2 using a composite of 10 atmospheric chemistry models and 3 reanalyses as the global spatialtemporal trend. Cross-validations demonstrated high overall accuracy (R2 = 0.83; RMSE = 3.73 ppb). Although integrating satellite-derived soft data yields only marginal performance gains in densely monitored areas, it substantially reduces model uncertainties and improves model accuracy across large spatial gaps. Notably, for the furthest unmonitored gap group at a 20° checkerboard, including satellite data increased R2 by 25.9% and decreased RMSE by 21.1% after the integration. Applying this optimized data fusion configuration from 2005 to 2022, global population-weighted ozone is estimated to have increased by 0.21 ppb/decade. Consequently, the global population exposed to ozone levels exceeding 50 ppb more than doubled over this 18-year period, rising from 17.2% to 41.0%.

papers.title: Peptide nitrile ligation enables thioester-free chemical protein synthesis
papers.abstract: Native chemical ligation has transformed chemical protein synthesis, yet its reliance on C-terminal peptide thioesters suffers from precursor preparation, stability and multisegment assembly. Here we report peptide nitrile ligation (PNL), a thioester-free ligation in which a stable C-terminal peptide nitrile is chemoselectively captured by an N-terminal cysteine and converted through a thiazoline intermediate into a native Xaa-Cys amide bond. Peptide nitriles are generated directly and chemoselectively from the C-terminal amides obtained using conventional Rink-amide Fmoc solid-phase peptide synthesis. PNL proceeds in aqueous buffer at pH 7.5 without an exogenous thiol catalyst, a thioester intermediate or detectable epimerization at the ligation junction. Notably, PNL enables efficient ligation at C-terminal proline junctions, a longstanding challenge in thioester-based ligation, without specialized building blocks or additional synthetic steps. The reaction tolerates internal cysteine thiols and Asn- or Gln-derived side-chain nitriles, with the latter subsequently restored to their native amides. On-demand conversion of C-terminal amide into a new nitrile enables iterative three-segment assembly. PNL therefore establishes C-terminal nitriles as stable, programmable acyl donors for thioester-free multisegment peptide ligation.

papers.title: Computational Interactions between the Endohedral Metallofullerene Gd@C60 and Human Toll-Like Receptor 3: A Molecular Docking and Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: Background: Endohedral metallofullerenes (EMFs), such as the gadolinium fullerene Gd@C60, are being explored as kinetically stable alternatives to gadolinium chelate contrast agents and as platforms for nanomedicine. Their behavior in a biological medium depends strongly on how they interact with proteins. Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3) is an endosomal receptor that senses double-stranded RNA, and it is a relevant partner because nanoparticles are commonly internalized into endosomes. How Gd@C60 might bind to human TLR3 (hTLR3) is not known. Methods: A Gd@C60 model was built by inserting Gd3+ into C60 and optimized with the universal force field. It was docked to the crystal structure of the hTLR3 ectodomain (PDB ID: 1ZIW) using the PatchDock shape-complementarity algorithm. The top-ranked complex was then simulated for 20 ns in explicit solvent (TIP3P water, 0.15 mol/L KCl) with NAMD 2.13 and the CHARMM36 force field. Results: The best-ranked docking solution (geometric complementarity score 3908) placed Gd@C60 in the C-terminal cap region of the horseshoe-shaped receptor. The pose is stabilized by π–π stacking with Trp656, electrostatic interactions with Lys627 and Arg635, and a hydrophobic contact with Ile654, all without covalent bonding. In the simulation, the receptor backbone RMSD fluctuated at about 3–5 Å, whereas the fullerene RMSD fluctuated more widely with intermittent spikes. Conclusions: Aromatic, electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts together define the predicted binding mode of Gd@C60 on hTLR3. The net charge on the cage complicates the identification of a suitable binding pocket. The results provide a starting point for quantum-mechanical and free-energy studies and for the design of nanomaterial-based sensors of nucleic acids.

papers.title: Dielectric Dynamics and Polar Nanoregions in Ferroelectric Nematic Liquid Crystals of the nJK Series
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive investigation of polarization dynamics and phase transitions in a novel homologous series of polar nematics (nJK, n=1-5) using broadband dielectric spectroscopy (DS). The analysis of dielectric spectra in planar and homeotropic cells revealed the evolution of relaxation mechanisms, transitioning from single-particle molecular reorientations in the isotropic phase to complex collective dynamics across the nematic (N), intermediate (N X ), and ferroelectric nematic (N F ) phases.
