Critical soft-mode behavior was observed near the N F transition for both the longitudinal mode (m1, acting as an amplitude mode) and the high-frequency mode (m3, exhibiting phason-like characteristics), indicating strong coupling between molecular dipoles and splay fluctuations. Furthermore, fitting the dielectric permittivity to a modified Curie–Weiss law reveals a broad temperature range of relaxor-like behavior above T c, characterized by diffuseness exponents γ ≈1.6 for ferroelectric members ( 3JK,4JK). This confirms the formation of Polar Nanoregions (PNRs) stabilized by lateral shifted molecular arrangements in the high-temperature nematic liquid, establishing a nematic relaxor ferroelectric (nRFE) state spanning almost the entire N phase window.

papers.title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
papers.abstract: Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

papers.title: Programming Chemoselectivity in Aerobic Oxidation through Zr-MOF/Quinone Multicatalysis for Benzazole Synthesis
papers.abstract: Selectivity control in aerobic oxidation reactions containing several oxidizable functional groups remains challenging. Herein, we show that the chemoselectivity of a Zr-MOF/quinone multicatalytic platform can be controlled through modulation of the organic redox co-catalyst. In contrast to previously reported Zr-MOF-808/(hydro)quinone combinations that promote direct heteroatom oxidation in anilines or thiols to yield the corresponding azoxy or disulfide compounds, Zr-MOF-808/1,8-dichloroanthraquinone unlocks a different reaction pathway to selectively oxidize primary alcohols in the presence of aromatic diamines and aminothiophenols. This pathway enables the one-pot synthesis of 2-substituted benzimidazoles and benzothiazoles under atmospheric air. Mechanistic experiments and post-reaction catalyst characterization support coupled catalytic cycles in which Lewis-acidic Zr sites in the MOF facilitate quinone-mediated alcohol oxidation, while the redox-active MOF/semiquinone interface regenerates the catalytic cycle using atmospheric oxygen as the terminal oxidant. This method furnishes a highly practical and sustainable synthesis of 31 benzimidazoles and benzothiazoles including commercially relevant products such as thiabendazole and fuberidazole, permitting recovery and reuse of both catalytic components.

papers.title: FoldX interface ΔΔG depends on which structure it starts from, and a learned predictor does not: a cautionary analysis on glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase
papers.abstract: FoldX and related methods are widely used to interpret missense variants, and their sensitivity to the input structure is documented: repair of the coordinates is mandatory, averaging over structural ensembles improves agreement with experiment, and the uncertainty of a FoldX folding ΔΔG has been put at roughly ±3 kcal/mol, with binding stability worse. What has not been asked is whether that uncertainty is spread evenly over a protein. We took 258 ClinVar missense variants in glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a homotetramer, verified every reference residue against the 1SIQ structure and computed ΔΔG for the 124 classified pathogenic. Eighteen variants were then recomputed on three molecular dynamics snapshots of the same complex: six interface variants selected on their monomer-to-tetramer difference, six interface variants drawn at random, and six at least 10 Å from any contact. The displacement between the crystal-based value and the relaxed-frame mean had a median of 1.10, 1.38 and 0.20 kcal/mol in the three groups (random interface against distant, Mann-Whitney p = 0.0130), while frame-to-frame scatter was indistinguishable between them (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.385). The variation is therefore positional, and it is not explained by noise in the mean. SAAMBE-3D, a learned interface predictor, run on the same eighteen variants and the same four structures, moved by a median of 0.075 kcal/mol at the interface and by nothing at all away from it, so the instability is largely a property of FoldX. It also depends on magnitude: G171R, scored at +22.53 kcal/mol, moved 2.7%, whereas A421V moved from +0.18 kcal/mol, which reads as tolerated, to +4.37 ± 2.22. Along the way we found that ThermoMPNN given a chain selector on a tetramer returns values identical to the isolated monomer at all 7,800 scanned positions. For variant interpretation the consequence is specific: at a subunit interface, in the range where a classification is actually in doubt, a single starting structure does not support a single number.

papers.title: Fragment-Grounded Neural Simulation of Electron Ionization Mass Spectra at Library Scale
papers.abstract: Electron ionization mass spectrometry (EI-MS) is a sensitive analytical technique, yet compound identification conventionally relies on reference libraries that contain spectra for at most about one million compounds, which is a small subset of chemical space. In silico prediction of EI-MS spectra can extend these libraries, but existing data-driven models generalize poorly beyond their training distribution, and physics-based simulations are too costly for library-scale use. Here, we present a fragment-grounded neural workflow that predicts an EI-MS spectrum by exhaustively enumerating the fragmentation graph of a molecule and then assigning intensities to the resulting substructures with a model trained on experimental spectra. By relating every predicted peak back to a candidate substructure, our model generalizes more reliably to unseen scaffolds and out-of-distribution chemistry than prior fingerprint- and black-box transformer-based predictors. On a scaffold split, it identifies the correct structure among up to fifty same-formula isomers in 43.0% of cases, compared to 32.5% for the strongest baseline. Further, it matches the accuracy of quantum-chemical simulation while being roughly seven orders of magnitude faster. To test the model's capabilities under a harder, formula-agnostic setting, we further evaluate retrieval against a library of 87.3 million compounds from PubChem. There, our model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 3.3%, compared to 1.1% for the strongest baseline, and a peak-mass-window filter further raises its top-1 accuracy to 5.3%. The predicted spectra for 87.3 million compounds serve as an augmented reference library to facilitate database-dependent structure elucidation.

papers.title: IN SITU ASSEMBLY OF ACTIVE THERAPEUTICS THROUGH ALBUMIN-MEDIATED METAL TRANSFER
papers.abstract: Forming active therapeutic agents in situ can be a promising strategy to obtain safer and more effective treatments. However, achieving controlled formation of a drug in complex biological settings requires a detailed understanding of the target environment where the new therapeutic agent will be generated and the use of well-designed activation strategies. Here, we demonstrate that it is possible to form active metal complexes in blood serum and plasma by using ligands that target metal ions transported by albumin after they are bound to the protein. As a proof of concept, we applied this strategy to activate photosensitizers (PS) for photodynamic therapy (PDT). In situ metalation generated photoactivatable complexes with enhanced photochemical properties and anticancer activity, establishing albumin-bound metal ions as an endogenous resource for therapeutic activation.

papers.title: PCAN-PIE: A Machine Learning Tool for Prioritizing Prodrug Candidates by Predicted Bioactivation
papers.abstract: Prodrug design enhances critical drug properties by creating drug derivatives with improved properties while harnessing metabolic activation to regenerate the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) in vivo . However, reliably predicting whether a prodrug converts to the intended API remains challenging, causing project failures and limiting systematic exploration of prodrug design spaces. Here, we developed PCAN-PIE (Prodrug CAndidate Navigator using a Paired-Input Ensemble), a machine learning tool to de-risk prodrug design by distinguishing prodrug candidates likely to release their intended API from those unlikely to activate. PCAN-PIE demonstrates strong performance across different approved prodrug activation chemistries, can identify competing metabolic pathways that may compromise activation, and correctly triages chemically plausible but unreported transformation products. Attribution analysis suggests that PCAN-PIE bases its predictions on chemically meaningful reactive substructures, providing medicinal chemists with an interpretable rationale for candidate prioritization. In a prospective four-candidate prodrug design campaign, PCAN-PIE successfully prioritized the two candidates that ultimately demonstrated measurable API formation and cellular activity, while deprioritizing two candidates that showed negligible conversion and activity. Taken together, this work establishes PCAN-PIE as a focused computational tool for prioritizing prodrug candidates and provides a framework for integrating structure-based prediction into rational prodrug design to support the development of safer and more effective medicines.

papers.title: Molecular Autocatalysis through Interfacial Recruitment of Catalytic Functional Groups
papers.abstract: Autocatalysis enables nonlinear reactivity, self-amplification, and emergent chemical behavior. At the soft interfaces of emulsions and vesicles, autocatalysis has been linked to dynamic behavior such as growth, propagation, and oscillations. Most reported interfacial autocatalytic systems rely on assembly-driven physical effects such as reactant colocalization rather than well-defined catalytic interactions. Whether catalytic function can be molecularly encoded within assemblies, independent of assembly formation itself, remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate molecular autocatalysis through interfacial recruitment of catalytic functional groups. As product accumulates, catalytic groups are concentrated at the interface, creating a positive feedback loop that accelerates further synthesis. The molecular identity of the product, rather than assembly formation, controls autocatalytic behavior. We further show the generality of this mechanism across two distinct reaction classes, oxime condensation and thiol-Michael addition. Autocatalytic lipids self-assemble into growing vesicles, coupling molecular feedback to compartment propagation and establishing a general chemical strategy for self-amplifying soft matter systems.

papers.title: CoOx/Ni foam as catalyst for the electrochemical reforming of a complex ethanosolv-derived carbohydrate stream
papers.abstract: The electrocatalytic reforming of complex carbohydrate mixtures derived from hemicellulose has broad prospects in the green production of hydrogen and high-value chemicals. In this work, a CoOx/Ni foam (NF) electrocatalyst is used to funnel a complex carbohydrate mixture, obtained from a flowthrough mild-ethanosolv fractionation, to simplified valuable organic acid salts at room temperature. The CoOx/NF catalyst was prepared using a Co 9 S 8 /NF precursor and its electrooxidation performance was studied using xylose as a model molecule. At ambient temperature and pressure, the CoOx/NF electrocatalyst is seen to significantly reduce the electrooxidation potential of xylose compared to an activated NF electrode. Moreover, CoOx/NF achieved a formate yield as high as 73% at 1.42 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), while with the activated NF electrode the yield was only 46%. Density functional theory calculations revealed that interfacial electron transfer in the CoOx/NF significantly enhances the adsorption of xylose, thereby effectively improving reactivity and selectivity. When the CoOx/NF catalyst is used in the electrooxidation of crude carbohydrate streams, it reduces the measured potentials compared to the oxygen evolution reaction, and effectively generates formate and oxalate. This work demonstrates an efficient and environmentally friendly strategy for upgrading biorefinery side-streams into value-added chemicals.

papers.title: From Bench to Game Engine: An Instructor-Built Suite of 3D Laboratory Simulations Created with Generative AI
papers.abstract: Virtual chemistry laboratories have historically required either a commercial subscription or a software development team, placing custom simulations out of reach for most instructors. I report the design and construction of a suite of browser-playable 3D laboratory simulations for a non-science-majors chemistry course that has no formal laboratory component — density of an unknown metal, pH of common solutions, double replacement reactions, separations by paper chromatography, and physical and chemical changes — that I built alone in the Unity game engine, with no prior game-development experience, using a large-language-model coding assistant connected directly to the engine. Each lab pairs a 3D fume hood, rendered by a Unity WebGL build, with an HTML worksheet that checks readings, assigns per-student unknowns, and prints a one-page report; the answer data lives in the compiled build rather than in the page, so students cannot read it from the source. The labs serve two purposes: laboratory experience for students who would otherwise have none, and continuity of instruction when hurricane closures disrupt the weekly schedule. I describe the development workflow, the division of labor between instructor and AI, the design decisions that keep the simulations chemically honest, the time and cost involved, and the limitations encountered. All builds, worksheet pages, and prelab reviews are freely available on GitHub. The approach offers a reproducible path for instructors to author their own laboratory simulations: the five described here were built in about one month.

papers.title: Adapting UMA to spin-polarized AQCat25 without catastrophic forgetting with task-gated LoRA
papers.abstract: Universal models for atoms such as UMA rival specialized interatomic potentials across chemistry [2], yet none of their catalysis datasets contains spin-polarized metallic surfaces [4, 9, 10]. On AQCat25 [1], a spin-polarized, higher-fidelity catalysis dataset, UMA loses accuracy where adsorption changes surface magnetization, and fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting [8, 13]. We add a task-specific mode to UMA through low-rank adapters (LoRA) [5] that act only on AQCat25 systems (0.065% of parameters). On unseen adsorbates and materials, the adsorption-energy error falls from 0.193 to 0.119 eV (−38%) and the force error from 0.091 to 0.031 eV/Å, with the largest gains on strongly magnetic systems. All seven original UMA tasks remain numerically unchanged, whereas full fine-tuning raised the OC20 error tenfold. EV2-in+midFiLM [3], the best model in the AQCat25 paper, reaches 0.268 eV on the same systems. Rather than predicting adsorption energies directly, UMA derives them from total energies, as the AQCat25 authors recommend for surfaces that restructure [1]. A foundation potential can thus gain a spin-aware, higher-fidelity mode without forgetting what it already knows.

papers.title: Structural evolution of the P2-Na2/3Ni1/3Mn2/3O2 sodium-ion battery cathode material resolved by 3D electron diffraction
papers.abstract: P2-Na2/3Ni1/3Mn2/3O2 is a promising cathode for sodium-ion batteries, yet its electrochemical behavior is governed by a complex sequence of structural transformations whose microscopic origins remain poorly understood. In particular, Na+/vacancy ordering is expected to play a central role in the phase evolution but is challenging to resolve using powder diffraction alone. Here, we combine continuous-rotation 3D electron diffraction (3D-ED) with operando and ex situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (SXRD) to establish a comprehensive structural picture of NaxNi1/3Mn2/3O2 across the full electrochemical window (1.0 V – 4.5 V). 3D-ED resolves Na+/vacancy ordering in sub-micrometer crystallites, revealing ordered P2 structures at Nax = 2/3, 1/2, and 1/3. In each case, Na+/vacancy ordering lowers the symmetry of the parent P2 framework and produces arrangements that minimize electrostatic repulsion while satisfying Pauling’s second rule. Transient phases at Nax = 3/5 and 2/5 are also observed during charging, while two highly sodiated P2 phases are accessed by discharging to low voltages. At high states of charge, extensive Na+ removal drives the P2→O2 transition and produces pronounced stacking disorder, demonstrating that the layer glide is not fully coherent. Bond-valence analysis further tracks transition-metal charge compensation during Na+ extraction. Together, these results establish Na+/vacancy ordering as a key structural variable governing phase stability, charge compensation, and structural transformations in P2-Na2/3Ni1/3Mn2/3O2, while highlighting 3D-ED as a powerful approach for resolving complex ordering phenomena in battery materials.

papers.title: Tailoring Gas Transport Properties in MOF-Based Mixed Matrix Membranes: The Role of Filler Morphology and Surface Functionalization
papers.abstract: The development of high‑performance mixed‑matrix membranes (MMMs) for gas separations relies on precise control of filler morphology and optimized polymer–filler interactions. In this study, we elucidate how crystal size, morphology, and surface functionalization of the perfluorinated metal-organic framework (MOF) F4_MIL‑140A(Ce) influence the gas transport properties of MMMs based on Pebax® 1657 and Matrimid® 9725 matrices. Through systematic modulation of reaction conditions, we synthesized sub‑micrometric F4_MIL‑140A(Ce) particles with tailored size and aspect ratio, achieving improved dispersion and interfacial contact within the polymer phases. A post‑synthetic grafting strategy using stearic acid further enhanced the compatibility of the MOF without altering crystallinity, pore accessibility, or CO 2 adsorption behavior, as confirmed by powder X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and sorption analyses. MMMs prepared with the surface-functionalized MOF displayed improved polymer–filler adhesion, minimized interfacial voids, and significantly enhanced gas transport properties. In particular, the Pebax® 1657-based MMMs approached the 2008 Robeson upper bound for CO 2 /N 2 separation, driven primarily by increased CO 2 solubility. In contrast, Matrimid® 9725 MMMs exhibited substantial improvements in H 2 /N 2 and O 2 /N 2 selectivity, linked to enhanced diffusivity. The insights presented in this work provide a rational framework for engineering MOF–polymer interfaces and advancing membrane‑based gas separation and CO 2 capture technologies.

papers.title: Controlled Decoration of Electrochemically Exfoliated Graphene with Gold Nanoparticles for Electrocatalysis and Sensing
papers.abstract: The controlled decoration of graphene with metal nanoparticles benefits catalysis and sensing, yet remains challenging. Here, electrochemically exfoliated graphene (EEG) is decorated with surfactant-free gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) through a simple one-pot synthesis that uses only water, sodium hydroxide and glycerol, all inexpensive and green reagents. The AuNPs grow directly on the graphene surface. Base concentration governs particle size, whereas the Au/EEG ratio controls loading with only minor changes in size, allowing the two parameters to be tuned almost independently. The resulting composite reaches an Au loading of 20 wt%, to our knowledge among the highest reported for surfactant-free AuNPs on EEG. In the ethanol oxidation reaction, it outperformed physically mixed, sequentially deposited and ligandstabilized controls, combining the highest mass activity with the lowest Tafel slope and the largest electrochemically active surface area. As a proof-of-concept tryptophan sensor, it oxidized the analyte at 0.57 V, to our knowledge the lowest overpotential reported for this amino acid, with a linear response from 1 to 100 µM, a detection limit of 0.4 µM and good tolerance to common electroactive interferents. This strategy offers a scalable, green platform for printable catalysts and sensors.

papers.title: Elucidating permselectivity mechanisms in polyamide membranes through controlled chlorination and hydrolysis
papers.abstract: Polyamide membranes are widely used in freshwater production because of their high water permeance and water–salt selectivity, but emerging applications require tunable permselectivity. We investigate the structure–property–performance relationships governing membrane behavior by modifying permselectivity through sequential chlorination and alkaline treatment. Chemical, structural, and transport properties are examined using X-ray characterization, free-energy barrier analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations. We find chlorine–alkaline modification more than doubles water permeance through hydrolysis, which enhances swelling, increases water–membrane interactions, and promotes water transport. Despite the resulting looser structure, the hydrolyzed membrane maintains water–salt selectivity because of entropic barriers to salt transport, likely caused by the presence of bulky chlorine groups on the aromatic rings. These findings identify distinct mechanisms by which chemical modification alters water and salt transport, challenge the prevailing view that swelling is detrimental to selectivity, and provide new design insights for tuning polyamide membrane performance.

papers.title: Conformational Dynamics of Cation-Cryptophane Complexes by Ion Mobility Mass Spectrometry
papers.abstract: Cryptophanes can selectively encapsulate small molecules and cations. Tuning host-guest selectivity requires insight into molecular recognition, which is analytically accessible with ion mobility mass spectrometry (IM-MS) via the conformational dynamics of complexation. Using activated IM-MS to differentiate between encapsulated and externally associated species, anti -cryptophanes complexes of the cation H + , Li + , Na + , K + , Rb + , Cs + , Mg 2+ , and Ag + were investigated. The m/z of fragments are characteristic of the binding mode of the host and guest pair. Using the combination of characteristic m/z and changes in ion mobility, IM-MS was sensitive to the host’s binding mode and provided further support to whether encapsulation had taken place. These findings demonstrate that activated IM-MS can sensitively probe cryptophane binding modes and provide new insight into the selectivity of cation encapsulation.

papers.title: Ten-Step Total Synthesis of the Octadride (+)-Zopfiellin via Electrochemical Decarboxylative Cross-Coupling
papers.abstract: We report the first asymmetric total synthesis of the antifungal octadride natural products zopfiellin and deoxyzopfiellin. Our highly convergent synthetic strategy features a bioinspired electrochemical nickel-catalyzed decarboxylative cross-coupling of two readily available fragments to assemble the core skeleton. This key transformation enables a subsequent intramolecular alkylation, forging the eight-membered carbocycle with excellent diastereoselectivity. Notably, the protecting-group-free route is robust and scalable, providing access to (+)-zopfiellin in 10 steps.

papers.title: Explainable Graph Neural Networks Reveal Molecular Features Associated with Umami Taste
papers.abstract: Umami is one of the five basic tastes, and understanding the relationship between molecular structure and umami perception is important for food science. Although machine learning models have been developed to predict umami taste, the molecular features underlying their predictions remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we developed a graph neural network (GNN) model for umami taste prediction and investigated the structural features contributing to its predictions using Integrated Gradients (IG). Three datasets were constructed from ChemTastesDB, comprising 74 umami compounds and different sets of non-umami compounds. Under five-fold Murcko scaffold-disjoint cross-validation, the model achieved mean receiver operating characteristic areas under the curve of 0.935, 0.950, and 0.910 for the strict, full primary, and physicochemically matched datasets, respectively. Atom-level IG analysis revealed that functional-group prevalence did not necessarily correspond to positive attribution toward umami prediction. Notably, carboxylic acids occurred at similar frequencies in umami and non-umami compounds but showed significantly greater positive attribution in umami compounds. Furthermore, analysis of 31 structurally similar umami–nonumami molecular pairs demonstrated that regions specific to umami compounds generally received greater positive attribution than the corresponding regions in non-umami compounds. These findings suggest that the GNN captures molecular features associated with umami taste in a manner that depends on their surrounding structural context. Combining scaffold-disjoint prediction with atom-level attribution analysis provides an approach for investigating structure–taste relationships and identifying molecular features potentially relevant to umami perception.

papers.title: Quantitative Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction from Quantum-Mechanical Scoring
papers.abstract: Quantitative prediction of protein–ligand (P–L) binding affinities is generally thought to require extensive configurational sampling, which is computationally demanding. Here, we examine how closely a fundamentally different approach, a quantum-mechanical (QM) description of P–L binding energetics based on a small set of representative structures, can approach the accuracy of MD-based free-energy calculations. Large-scale validation of the SQM2.20 scoring function is carried out on the Public Free Energy Benchmark data set, comprising 88 P–L series with 1,113 ligands in total. To compare directly with the experimental binding free energies (∆G bind ), a scaling factor derived independently in the PL-REX data set was applied, yielding SQM2.20 sc . With refined receptor structures and an extended pool of ligand poses, SQM2.20 sc achieved a weighted pairwise root-mean-square error (RMSE) in ∆∆G of 1.41 kcal/mol, close to the 1.26 kcal/mol reported for FEP+. n a subset of 58 targets and 872 ligands, SQM2.20 sc (RMSE 1.41 kcal/mol) outperformed OpenFE (1.74 kcal/mol). These results demonstrate the transferability of the approach across a wide range of protein targets and ligand chemistries, further strengthening the case for SQM scoring as a computationally efficient tool for applications in computer-aided drug design.

papers.title: A Readily Scalable Silylated Cyclic Allyl Sulfide Monomer for Degradable Vinyl Polymers
papers.abstract: Introducing degradability into conventional vinyl polymers without sacrificing the versatility of radical polymerization remains a major challenge. Radical Ring-Opening Polymerization (rROP) is currently the most promising technique to impart degradability into vinyl-based polymers through the copolymerization of cyclic monomers with common vinyl monomers. However, among the various families of cyclic monomers reported to date, none simultaneously combines high efficiency, versatility, and compatibility with industrial-scale production. Here, we report a family of silylated cyclic allylic sulfides (CAS) designed to decouple radical ring-opening reactivity from post-polymerization cleavage. The representative monomer LC1 combines a CAS scaffold, which undergoes efficient radical addition–fragmentation, with an independently cleavable silyl ether linkage. LC1 is prepared in two steps from readily available precursors, and a simultaneous dual-feed strategy enables its facile and reproducible scale-up. LC1 displays monomer-dependent reactivity across several vinyl monomer families and introduces cleavable junctions throughout chain growth. Kinetic experiments, Mayo analysis and density functional theory reveal two distinct addition–fragmentation processes: rapid ring-opening incorporation of cyclic LC1 followed by a slower secondary transfer pathway involving the pendant allylic functionality generated after ring opening. The resulting polymers undergo backbone fragmentation under fluoride, acidic, basic and Lewis-acid conditions, with degradation kinetics further tunable through pH and silicon substitution. LC1 also remains compatible with emulsion polymerization and crosslinked networks, enabling chemically and thermally triggered disassembly of 3D-printed materials. Finally, in the context of upcycling, hydroxyl-terminated degradation fragments can be repurposed as polyol precursors for polyurethane network formation. This work establishes silylated CAS monomers as a versatile platform for independently programming radical polymer growth and material lifetime.

papers.title: Structural Basis for Nitrile-Directed Recognition of the Catalytic Lysine in KIT
papers.abstract: KIT and PDGFRA are the major oncogenic drivers in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST). Although clinically approved KIT/PDGFRA-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors (such as imatinib and avapritinib) have improved patient outcomes, long-term efficacy is often limited by additional resistance mutations in these kinases. To explore alternative interaction modes less susceptible to mutational escape, we investigated the catalytic lysine K623 in KIT as an anchoring point for inhibitor design. Starting from avapritinib, we prepared nitrile-containing analogues in which the canonical pyrimidine core was replaced by a nitrile-substituted aromatic scaffold. The compounds were evaluated biochemically against KIT and the closely related GIST driver PDGFRA, including clinically relevant mutant forms, and were further assessed in cellular models of PDGFRA-driven GIST. Co-crystal structures revealed a distinct binding mode in which the nitrile group is directed toward K623, reorienting the ligand within the ATP-binding site while retaining kinase inhibitory activity. Guided by these structural findings, electrophilic analogues bearing squaric ester warheads were developed to probe covalent target engagement. Intact-protein mass spectrometry demonstrated time-, concentration-, and pH-dependent covalent labeling of KIT, with complete mono-labeling of the detectable soluble protein population observed under near-physiological conditions. Pre-occupation of the ATP-binding site with either avapritinib or a covalent ATP-site binder selectively suppressed the earliest and kinetically favored labeling event, supporting an active-site-dependent component of covalent modification. Together, these results establish the catalytic lysine K623 as a structurally accessible interaction site in KIT and show that this binding geometry can provide a basis for proximity-driven covalent kinase targeting.

papers.title: Activity-based Detection of MUTYH using Engineered Dumbbell DNA Switches
papers.abstract: Transitioning from quantitative abundance measurements to functional activity-based assays represents a key opportunity in DNA repair research, particularly for enzymes like MUTYH that currently lack functional assay platforms. Here, we developed a FRET-based DNA switch for real-time monitoring of MUTYH glycosylase activity. The dumbbell-like architecture incorporates an 8-oxoG: A mismatch that leads to structure switching upon MUTYH-mediated adenine excision, resulting in activity-dependent fluorescence signal change. We demonstrate that the rationally designed GC-rich DNA nanoswitch can detect both E. coli MutY and human MUTYH with high specificity, enabling real-time activity monitoring directly in bacterial free cell extracts. In addition, the assay can be easily adapted for inhibitor screening, demonstrating its potential for drug screening applications. The activity-based assay was also implemented in HeLa cells and analyzed by confocal microscopy, confirming preferential localization of the MUTYH activity within the nuclear compartment. Overall, this simple, low-cost DNA-based sensor bridges the need for functional assays by directly monitoring MUTYH glycosylase activity in complex biological environments, offering a scalable platform for future screening applications.

papers.title: Understanding the Relationship Between Synthetic Conditions and H <sub>2</sub> Uptake Capacity in Oxidatively Activated Turbostratic Carbons through Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The relationship between synthesis parameters, porosity, and H 2 uptake in activated carbons is a field of significant investigation and discussion. Conclusions about these relationships are typically drawn from limited datasets of carbons produced for a given publication, and are not able to consider the interplay between various synthesis parameters and properties of the resultant turbostratic carbons. We present the first attempt at understanding the relationship between synthesis parameters and H 2 uptake capacity in turbostratic carbons, using the single point pore volume as a proxy due to the dearth of available high pressure H 2 isotherms. The methods used herein have exploited a dataset of 237 samples to determine the most important synthesis parameters in determining the porosity of the product and thus their suitability for high pressure H 2 storage applications.

papers.title: Random Copolymerization of L-Lactide with Six-membered Cyclic Oxalates Enables Simultaneous Toughening and Tunable Degradation of Poly(L-lactic acid)
papers.abstract: Poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) is one of the most important biobased and biodegradable polyesters, but its intrinsic brittleness and slow degradation in natural environments still hamper its extensive applications. Developing PLLA materials that combine high strength and toughness with tunable degradation behavior remains a significant challenge. In this contribution, we present the bulk ring-opening copolymerization (ROCP) of L-lactide (L-LA) with each of three six-membered cyclic oxalates (sAOx), namely ethylene oxalate (EOx), 1,2-propylene oxalate (POx) and 1,2-hexylene oxalate (HOx), to produce a series of P(LLA-co-sAOx) statistical copolyesters using Sn(Oct)2 as the catalyst. The P(LLA-co-POx) statistical copolyesters exhibited the most favorable strength–toughness balance. At a POx content of 15 mol%, the P(LLA-co-POx) copolyester exhibited an elongation at break of 224% and a toughness of 63.7 MJ m-3 while retaining a high yield strength of 50.3 MPa. This toughness was approximately 33 times that of neat poly(L-lactide) (PLLA). In addition, the P(LLA-co-POx) statistical copolyesters exhibited good barrier performance and showed potential application as packaging materials. More importantly, the incorporation of POx endowed the copolyesters with excellent degradability and composition-dependent degradation behavior under natural environmental conditions. The P(LLA-co-POx) copolyester with a POx content of 50 mol% completely degradation within 80 days in soil. This work provides a chemical modification strategy for designing high-performance and sustainable PLLA-based packaging materials.

papers.title: Side-Chain Structure Reprograms Helical Folding in Isotactic Oligourethanes
papers.abstract: Sequence-defined abiotic polymers could extend the structural organization underlying biological function to new backbones and operating environments, but this requires rules connecting monomer structure to folding. Predictive control over folding is essential for translating molecular information into defined structure and, ultimately, function. Here, we show that side-chain structure reprograms the conformational landscape of isotactic oligourethanes. A systematic series of isotactic tetramers bearing structurally diverse substituents was examined by circular dichroism, two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Side chains that combine effective backbone shielding with steric compatibility favor persistent 2.614-helical states in competitive polar media, whereas less compatible substituents populate broader, dynamically interconverting helical ensembles. Notably, side-chain substitution can reverse the chiroptical bias of an invariant SSSS-configured backbone, reflecting a change in the preferred helical handedness. Experiments and simulations further reveal that helix persistence is associated with the interplay of reduced solvent exposure of the polar backbone, steric compatibility within the folded geometry, and recurrent intramolecular hydrogen bonding. The results establish side-chain selection as a means of directing oligourethane folding without changing backbone stereochemistry and identify complementary molecular criteria for developing scaffold-specific folding rules.

papers.title: Coordination Sphere Control Enables Hydride-Free Tandem Electrocatalytic E-Selective Semi-Hydrogenation
papers.abstract: Hydride-free electrocatalytic semi-hydrogenation offers an alternative to metal-hydride-based platforms, yet controlling alkene stereochemistry through such pathways remains challenging. Herein, we report an E-selective, redox-mediated Co-catalyzed platform enabled by cooperative control of the catalyst coordination sphere via ligand denticity and acid identity. Using a triphosphine ligand and ammonium chloride acid reverses the stereochemical preference of a previously developed Z-selective system, providing access to a range of E-alkenes in high yields and excellent stereoselectivity (up to 92% yield and >20:1 E:Z). Experimental and computational mechanistic studies support a mechanism involving a distinct proton transfer step with a chloride-mediated organization of the ammonium proton donor and Co catalyst. This allows for an initial inner-sphere protonation prior to cobaltocene-mediated reduction of the resultant Co(III)-alkenyl intermediate, followed by subsequent outer-sphere protonation to yield trans alkenes. These findings illustrate that coordination-sphere organization and precise control of proton transfer pathways may serve as complementary design principles in stereoselective electrocatalysis.

papers.title: Self-assembly of DNA-β-sheet peptide conjugates into emergent micrometer-sized rods
papers.abstract: Peptide-oligonucleotide conjugates can unite DNA nanotechnology with peptide self-assembly to create new and unusual nanostructures. We have created the first conjugate of DNA to a Waltz peptide – a class of β-sheet peptides which are important in the study of biological amyloids. Multi-micrometer rods have been identified which are attributable to peptide-dominated assembly. These results could lead to new ways to interface with amyloid, as well as demonstrating the range of self-assembled structures possible with DNA-peptide conjugates.

papers.title: The inhibition mechanism of aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A3 by the antitumor drug DIMATE
papers.abstract: Aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A (ALDH1A) enzymes play central roles in retinoic acid signaling and cancer stem cell biology, yet the molecular determinants governing isoform-selective covalent inhibition remain poorly understood. Here we investigate the binding and reactivity of the activated alkyne inhibitor S-methyl-4-(dimethylamino)-4-methylpent-2-ynethioate (DIMATE), a potent, irreversible inhibitor of ALDH1A currently in phase I clinical trials. Using QM/MM metadynamics simulations based on high-resolution crystal structures, enzyme kinetics and site-directed mutagenesis, we found that active-site cysteine reactivity and cofactor-binding channel occupancy control whether the inhibitor binds reversibly or irreversibly to the ALDH1A3 isoform. We identified two reaction pathways initiated by nucleophilic attack from the catalytic Cys314: transthioesterification at the carbonyl carbon and α-addition to the alkyne. Only the α-addition leads to irreversible inhibition, a process that critically depends on a vicinal cysteine (Cys313) acting as a proton donor. Consistently, experiments show that ALDH1A isoforms lacking this neighboring cysteine, as well as Cys313Ala mutants, display exclusively reversible inhibition. NAD+ binding further modulates reactivity by disfavoring α-addition and promoting hydrolysis of DIMATE to a non-inhibitory carboxylic acid product, establishing NAD+ as a switch between irreversible covalent modification and reversible turnover. Together, these results reveal how vicinal cysteine chemistry and cofactor-dependent activesite dynamics govern covalent reactivity in ALDH1A enzymes, providing a basis for the rational design of isoform-selective covalent inhibitors targeting cancer-associated ALDH enzymes.

papers.title: Growth dynamics and pore trapping in lithium metal electrodes
papers.abstract: Achieving high energy density in lithium metal cells requires minimizing both the electrolyte volume and the excess lithium metal. To ensure acceptable cycle life under these conditions, a dense electrode morphology is a necessity. External stack pressure is a common route to mitigate the development of a porous morphology, however, the electrode porosity still tends to increase during extended cycling. In this work, operando X-ray nano-tomography is used to track the pore evolution with sub-micron spatial resolution and visualize its dependence on stack pressure. A pore formation mechanism is unveiled, based on highly localized initial Li deposition on the uneven electrode surface that develops during cycling. Newly deposited structures grow rapidly and when in contact with the separator, the pressure transmitted induces horizontal growth, coarsening the structures. This type of growth mechanism traps pores between the bulk electrode and a dense layer of columnar lithium. Based on this, a homogeneous initial deposition in each cycle should be targeted to suppress pore trapping, thereby minimizing both the electrode surface area and the required electrolyte volume.

papers.title: Spontaneous defect formation as the origin of superionic transitions in antifluorite-type structures
papers.abstract: Solid-state electrolytes offer the possibility of safer and higher energy density batteries, yet only a limited number of materials achieve ionic conductivities suitable for practical applications. Type-II superionic conductors, which undergo continuous temperature-driven transitions between low and high ionic conductivity regimes are strong candidates for high-performance solid state electrolytes, but the transition mechanism is not sufficiently understood. In this study, we investigate the archetypical superionic conductors Li2O and Li2S with the antifluorite structure using long-time-scale molecular dynamics simulations with an Allegro machine-learning force field (MLFF) trained on density functional theory data selected using an on-the-fly active learning procedure. To this end, superionic transitions are identified around 1450 K for Li2O and around 1100 K for Li2S through continuous peaks in the heat capacity. Diffusion coefficients and concentration of Frenkel defects are found to exhibit strong non-Arrhenius behavior coinciding with the superionic transition where both diffusion activation energy and defect formation energy decrease significantly across the transition. This suggests a self-enhanced spontaneous defect formation mechanism, which drives the superionic transition and promotes increased ionic diffusion. These results identifies the microscopic origin of type-II superionic behavior as a result of correlated defect formation and support the design of improved solid-state electrolytes.

papers.title: Cost-effective nanorough black nickel-based SERS substrates with statistically validated spatial uniformity
papers.abstract: Reliable surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) substrates must combine high enhancement with spatially uniform and reproducible responses. Here, hierarchical rough black nickel (b-Ni) substrates were fabricated by electrodeposition and acid etching and coated with Ag or Au layers (5–50 nm). Their SERS performance was systematically evaluated using 4-mercaptobenzoic acid (4-MBA) and large-area Raman mapping (1.5 × 1.5 mm 2 ; 900 spectra per substrate), supported by statistical analysis of signal intensity, spatial variability, response distribution, and inter-band correlation. Metrics included median signed band areas, relative standard deviation (RSD), the median absolute deviation (MAD)-based coefficient of variation, the contribution of the 10% highest-response positions to the total positive response, and Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. Ag-coated b-Ni substrates exhibited substantially stronger and more spatially uniform enhancement than Au-coated substrates, with performance increasing with Ag thickness. The 50 nm b-Ni/Ag architecture provided the optimal combination of signal strength and spatial reproducibility. Control experiments with bare b-Ni and flat Ag and Au films deposited on polished silicon confirmed that the enhancement arises from the synergistic effect of hierarchical b-Ni micro/nanoroughness and the plasmonic noble-metal coating. These results establish Ag-coated b-Ni as a simple, low-cost, and scalable platform for robust SERS measurements, reducing the need for extensive spatial screening.

papers.title: Binding Mode of the Heterocyclic Amine 2-Amino-9H-pyrido[2,3-b] indole (AαC) to DNA Elucidated by Molecular Docking and Molecular Dynamics Simulation
papers.abstract: Background: 2-Amino-9H-pyrido[2,3-b]indole (AαC) is a mutagenic and carcinogenic heterocyclic aromatic amine formed by pyrolysis of proteins in cooked meat and present in tobacco smoke. After metabolic activation to a reactive nitrenium ion, it modifies DNA covalently, mainly at guanine. How AαC first associates with DNA, before any covalent bond forms, is not well understood. Methods: We docked AαC to three B-DNA dodecamers (PDB IDs 1BNA, 2Z2G and 2HKC) with PatchDock and FireDock, and ran explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the docked complexes in NAMD 2.13 with the CHARMM36 force field (1BNA: 10 ns; 2Z2G: 50 ns; NPT, 300 K, 0.15 M NaCl). Results: AαC bound in the minor groove of all three dodecamers, with global binding energies of -50.08 (1BNA), -53.41 (2Z2G) and -45.22 kcal/mol (2HKC). Atomic van der Waals terms contributed -16.41 to -18.36 kcal/mol, and single hydrogen bonds to thymine, guanine or adenine oxygen atoms were identified (2.2–2.8 Å). In the simulations AαC remained bound with a low, stable backbone RMSD, whereas the DNA backbone fluctuated considerably more. The minor-groove poses were poorly oriented for covalent attack when the base pairs were intact and canonical. Conclusions: Neutral AαC forms stable, groove-bound non-covalent complexes with B-DNA, but these complexes do not by themselves position the amine for C8-guanine adduct formation. Local distortion of the DNA, or the charged nitrenium ion, may be required. The complexes presented here serve as starting structures for ongoing quantum-mechanical studies of nitrenium ion stability and covalent adduct formation.

papers.title: The Disproportionation of Hydrogen Peroxide by Prototype Keggin Polyoxometalates
papers.abstract: Polyoxometalates (POMs) have been widely investigated as enzyme-mimetic compounds because of their ability to activate hydrogen peroxide for its disproportionation into water and oxygen (catalase reactivity), or use it as terminal oxidant for organic transformations (peroxidase reactivity). Here, we report how the prototype Keggin-type POMs H 3 [PW 12 O 40 ] ({PW 12 }) and H 3 [PMo 12 O 40 ] ({PMo 12 }) interact with hydrogen peroxide and lead to H 2 O 2 activation and conversion to water and oxygen. Experimental and computational approaches were combined to elucidate the reaction pathways and intermediates formed, showing that formation of hydroperoxyl radical species is the dominant path, while hydroxyl radicals, if formed, are consumed before they diffuse into the bulk solution. This understanding provides insight into one of the most widely used POM-based oxidation processes and enables knowledge-based control of reactivity.

papers.title: Enhanced Paper-Based DNA Adsorption and Point-of-Care Detection of High-Risk Human Papillomaviruses 16 and 18.
papers.abstract: Cervical cancer screening in low-resource settings requires molecular diagnostics that integrate rapid DNA extraction with sensitive, low-cost DNA amplification and detection. Here, we present a paper-based DNA detection (PDD) platform that introduces two mechanistic advances for decentralized HPV diagnostics. First, we establish a centrifuge-free DNA isolation strategy based on ethanol-assisted capture of DNA onto cellulose paper to provide high-yield DNA. Second, we introduce a coffee-ring-based fluorescence-sensing mechanism that converts the spatial redistribution of PicoGreen-labeled amplified products into a quantitative readout. We report, for the first time, that acid-pretreated cellulose (APC) paper captures DNA efficiently relative to untreated paper, identifying substrate pH as a critical factor in paper-based DNA extraction. FTIR analysis and zeta potential measurements revealed that APC paper retained DNA efficiently primarily through hydrogen-bonding and electrostatic interactions, respectively. Moreover, the mechanism behind the coffee ring-based amplified DNA detection was attributed to the chromatographic and evaporation effects. DNA is quantified using peripheral fluorescence intensity (PFI), enabling robust discrimination between positive and negative reactions. The integrated platform detected HPV16 and HPV18 with a limit of detection of 10 copies μL⁻¹. Clinical evaluation of 52 cervical samples demonstrated 100% specificity for both HPV16 and HPV18, 100% sensitivity for HPV18, and 85.7% sensitivity for HPV16 compared with an IVD-approved real-time PCR assay. By combining mechanistically guided DNA isolation with physics-based spatial DNA detection, this work advances paper-based molecular diagnostics beyond conventional intensity-based assays and provides a simple, inexpensive, and field-deployable strategy for point-of-care detection of HR HPVs.

papers.title: A sustainability-aware self-driving laboratory
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories are transforming experimental science, shifting laboratory operation from human-centric schedules towards continuous robotic execution. Beyond accelerating discovery, this transition creates new flexibility in when scientific research consumes electricity, offering an opportunity to coordinate experimental activity with changing electricity-system conditions. Here, we develop and deploy a dynamic, sustainability-aware laboratory-level scheduling framework that combines reinforcement learning with constraint programming to jointly optimize completion time and electricity cost under scientific constraints. Physical execution of 36 experimental tasks spanning six chemical workflow categories shortened completion time by 39.1% and reduced estimated electricity costs by 28.9% relative to a simulated human-centric scheduling baseline. Across five representative tariff cases, estimated per-workflow savings were equivalent to the cost of 0.83–9.14 kWh of off-peak electricity. Our findings demonstrate how self-driving laboratories can translate operational freedom into electricity-demand flexibility, establishing energy responsiveness as a design consideration for scientific research infrastructure.

papers.title: Raman Spectroscopy–Evolved Gas Analysis–Mass Spectrometry Provides Insight into Thermoset Thermal Degradation
papers.abstract: Raman spectroscopy–evolved gas analysis–mass spectrometry (RS-EGA-MS) was developed to investigate the thermal degradation of a bisphenol A–based thermoset. A new interface was developed that couples a Stokes/anti-Stokes Raman probe to a Frontier microfurnace used for EGA-MS. This new advancement enables collection of Raman spectra from a sample undergoing thermal degradation while simultaneously monitoring evolved gases from degradation. Changes in the Raman spectra were evident at the early stages of thermal degradation and corresponded to loss of bisphenol A monomer units. Later stages of thermal degradation resulted in intense fluorescence that overwhelmed the detector; anti-Stokes RS was used to interrogate these higher-temperature regions. Multiple char-forming regions which corresponded to the formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) were identified at these higher temperatures. The formation of naphthalene and fluoranthene were identified as important PAH products in the overall char formation of the bisphenol A based thermoset. This work demonstrates the successful development of RS-EGA-MS and provides new insight into high-temperature

papers.title: Copper-Catalyzed Borylation of 2-Bromostyrenes via 1,3-Bromine and 1,4-Boryl Group Migrations
papers.abstract: Arylboronates are valuable synthetic intermediates for constructing C–C and C–X bonds. While the coppercatalyzed borylation of aryl halides has been reported, synthesizing 2-borylstyrenes from the corresponding aryl halides remains a challenge because the alkene is incompatible with conventional borylation methods. Herein, we turn this side reaction into the trigger of a productive cascade, enabling the copper-catalyzed borylation of 2-bromostyrenes with diboron reagents. The sequence comprises borylcupration, 1,3-bromine migration to form an arylcopper, intramolecular attack of the arylcopper on boron to give a cyclic borate, and copper-assisted debromination that restores the alkenyl group. Overall, the boryl group undergoes a 1,4-migration from C(sp3) to C(sp2), with the alkene serving as a transient relay. The detailed reaction mechanism for 1,4-boryl group migration was revealed by using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The reaction tolerates chloro substituent and borylates dibromostyrenes site-selectively and is readily scalable to the gram scale.

papers.title: Factorised Cartesian Atomic Cluster Expansion for Low-Cost Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials can reach the accuracy of density functional theory at a fraction of its cost, but the most accurate equivariant models remain expensive, mainly because of the tensor operations they perform for every pair of neighbouring atoms. We present FACE, a factorised Cartesian atomic cluster expansion that removes this bottleneck. Each neighbour contributes only a small set of radial functions and messages, and all mixing of feature channels is done once per atom, so the cost per neighbour no longer grows with the size of the model. Custom GPU kernels evaluate the remaining steps, and long-range electrostatics, dispersion and short-range repulsion attach through a single interface. We show that the training divergences we encountered originate in how the network weights are scaled, and we introduce a distillation scheme in which an ensemble generates additional, uncertainty-checked training data. On five rMD17 molecules, with identical training budgets and hardware, FACE is about as accurate as a 64-channel MACE model (over three seeds: better on one molecule, within the seed spread on two, 7–14% higher force errors on two), while it is 5.7 times faster at inference (4.9 times at the same cutoff) and needs 3.5–3.9 times less GPU memory. Training costs about the same per step. Distillation lowers the energy and force errors of a single aspirin model by 20% at fixed width, to 2.26 meV and 6.74 meV/Å, close to the published MACE values (2.2 and 6.6), and the distilled model runs stably in molecular dynamics.

papers.title: Reassignment of the Near-Infrared Absorption of Dioxidized Rare-Earth Porphyrin Double-Decker Complexes: Identification of a Nearly Dark Lowest Excited State
papers.abstract: The intense near-infrared band (700–1250 nm) of dioxidized porphyrin double-decker complexes, characterized by a metal ion sandwiched between two porphyrinato ligands bearing two holes in total, has been assigned to the HOMO→LUMO transition for three decades. Herein, we demonstrate that this band does not correspond to the lowest excited state. In the spectra of [Y(oep) 2 ] + and [Tb(oep) 2 ] + (oep = octaethylporphyrinato), we observed a weak band near 1430 nm, with 2–3% of the absorbance of the intense band (at 812 nm and 830 nm) and a much smaller dependence on the metal. Time-dependent density functional theory calculations with an optimally tuned functional assigned the weak and intense bands to S 1 and S 3 , respectively, i.e., a configuration-interaction pair of the HOMO→LUMO and HOMO−1→LUMO excitations. As observed in crystal structures reported earlier, the two rings are twisted by 30–36°, which lowers the symmetry from D 4d (45°) to D 4 . The weak band S 1 is symmetry-forbidden in D 4d and owes its low intensity to this twist. The calculated slope of S 3 against the ionic radius was within 3% of the experimental value, whereas S 1 was nearly independent of the metal. Therefore, the lowest excited states of these strongly coupled π dimers are nearly dark.

papers.title: PCl3-Mediated Surface Editing Enables Highly Emissive InP/ZnS Quantum Dots
papers.abstract: Surface chemistry governs the optical performance of InP quantum dots (QDs), but strategies for preparing highly emissive InP/ZnS materials often rely on hazardous fluoride treatments. Here, treatment of carboxylate-capped InP QDs with PCl3 before ZnS shell growth increases the photoluminescence quantum yield from 5.5% to 70% without HF. 31P NMR spectroscopy and time-resolved small angle neutron scattering show that PCl3 removes surface carboxylates through formation of tricarboxyphosphite species. PCl3 treatment alone does not enhance emission, demonstrating that surface modification instead enables more effective passivation during shelling. These results establish controlled ligand stripping as an HF-free strategy for engineering the InP/ZnS interface and reveal how surface coordination can modulate the electronic structure and subsequent passivation of InP nanocrystals.

papers.title: Hydrosilane-Dependent Regiodivergence for Rhodium-Catalyzed Dearomative Hydrosilylation of Quinolines
papers.abstract: Regiodivergent dearomative hydroelementation (E = Si, B) of quinolines represent a powerful, atomeconomic strategy for the synthesis of biologically valuable 1,2- and 1,4-dihydroquinolines (DHQ) scaffolds. However, achieving such regiodivergent H[E] additions at the C2 and C4 positions within a unified catalytic system remains highly challenging. Herein, we report a simple [Rh(cod)Cl]2/PPh3 catalytic system that enables regioselective hydride incorporation dictated solely by the choice of hydrosilane (Ph2SiH2 vs. Me2RSiH, R = Et or Ph). While the Ph2SiH2-mediated 1,2-hydrosilylation protocol proceeds efficiently at 23 oC, the 1,4-hydrosilylation with Me2EtSiH requires a prolonged reaction time or an elevated temperature (23 to 50 oC) to achieve high yields. Preliminary mechanistic studies under the Ph2SiH2 vs. Me2PhSiH systems indicate that (i) chloro-free, phosphine-ligated Rh hydride species in situ generated during the initiation stage serves as the key resting species; (ii) a classic Chalk–Harrod sequence operates to yield the 1,2-DHQ irrespective of the hydrosilane used; (iii) the Me2PhSiH system promotes a facile isomerization of the kinetic 1,2-DHQ product to the 1,4-DHQ via an exclusive 3,4-hydrorhodation process; and (iv) the dearomative 1,2-hydrorhodation is reversible under the Ph2SiH2 system and the liberated 1,2-DHQ is completely resistant to subsequent isomerization.

papers.title: Anomalous Polarization Driven Quantum Confined Stark Effect in Halide Perovskite Polymer Quantum Structures for Single Layer Electroluminescence
papers.abstract: The quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) has emerged as a powerful mechanism for electrically tuning the optical properties of semiconductors. Through QCSE-induced band-structure modulation, we show that the soft-lattice ionic species and electroactive polymer interact in an anomalous polarization field mediating ion conduction, beyond the conventional bias-driven migration. The stability and magnitude of this conduction channel are governed by the spatial distribution of bound charges at the polarized interface, tunable through external poling. Single layer Li+-free light-emitting electrochemical cells (LEECs) with a PAN:PEO:MAPbBr3 composite were fabricated. The resulting anomalous internal electric field not only lowers the turn-on voltage to ~ 3 V by assisting charge injection but also imprints a measurable Quantum Confined Stark Effect (QCSE) on the embedded quantum dots. The results establish polarization-driven ion conduction as a powerful mechanism for designing next-generation solid-state optoelectronics.

papers.title: Photochemical Oxidation of Dilute Methane Using a Filter-Based System for Air-Treatment Applications
papers.abstract: Atmospheric methane (CH4) removal is challenging because of its low concentration and chemical stability under dilute conditions. Here, we demonstrate a filter-based photochemical system for dilute CH4 oxidation designed for potential integration into ventilation and air-treatment applications. A continuous-flow reactor incorporating UV-C irradiation (190–220 nm), a TiO2coated filter and an activated-carbon filter was tested at 10–50 ppm CH4, 25 °C and 1 bar under dry and humid conditions, at light intensities ranging from 4 to 59 W/m2 and flow rates of 100–300 mL/min. The downstream 4 mm activated-carbon filter reduced UV-C generated ozone (O3) to below the detection limit. CH4 conversion increased with light intensity and humidity and decreased with increasing flow rate and, under dry conditions, with increasing CH4 concentration. At 10 ppm and 100 mL/min, conversion reached 96% under humid conditions at 59 W/m2, compared with 73% under dry conditions. Significant conversion was also observed without the TiO2-coated filter, demonstrating that gas-phase photochemistry is the dominant oxidation pathway, while the TiO2-coated filter provided an additional 4–14% CH4 conversion improvement. Water vapour approximately doubled the effective removal rate. Apparent quantum yields (AQYs) for the overall photochemical system ranged from 9.3 × 10−3% at 10 ppm to 0.2% at 50 ppm, exceeding those previously obtained for TiO2-based photocatalytic oxidation under comparable dilute-CH4 conditions [1]. An advection–diffusion–reaction model reproduced the experimental trends across irradiance, humidity, concentration and flow rate. This work establishes filter-based UV-C photochemistry as a potential route for coupling dilute CH4 mitigation with existing airtreatment infrastructure.

papers.title: Strain-Tunable Electron–Phonon Coupling Collapse in Oxide Perovskites: A First-Principles Route to Suppressed Hot-Carrier Thermalization
papers.abstract: Hot-carrier thermalization constitutes the dominant energy loss channel in perovskite photovoltaics, yet the role of epitaxial strain in controlling this process remains largely unexplored from first principles. We present a systematic firstprinciples study of strain-dependent hot-carrier cooling rates in six inorganic perovskiteshalides CsSnI3, CsSnBr3, and CsCaCl3, and oxides BaSnO3, BaZrO3, and KTaO3across a ±2% biaxial strain window. Eliashberg spectral functions ω2F (ε) are computed via density functional perturbation theory and Wannier interpolation, from which hot-carrier energy loss rates →dE/dt↑ are evaluated through the Fröhlich– EPW formalism for carrier temperatures up to 5000 K. Applying +1% tensile strain to BaZrO3 collapses the dominant-mode electron–phonon coupling constant from ϑ = 1.31 to ϑ = 0.011, suppressing the hot-carrier cooling rate by more than 90% relative to the least favorable strain condition and yielding a thermalization time ϖtherm = 1,585 fs and a hot-carrier figure of merit FOMHC = 1,348 fs, surpassing all halide configurations by more than an order of magnitude. Landau polynomial fitting of ε2 min (ϱ) confirms that no strain-induced structural phase transition occurs within ±2% for any compound, establishing a safe phonon engineering window. Orbital-projected densities of states reveal two mechanistically distinct coupling classes: gap-closure-driven coupling in BaSnO3 and CsCaCl3 [Spearman correlation ς(Eg, ϑ) ↓ ↔0.70] and purely phonon-mode-softening-driven coupling in BaZrO3 and KTaO3 (ς ↗ +0.72), the latter being invisible to band structure analysis alone.

papers.title: Characterizing the Hydrophobic Contribution to Adsorption on Ligand-functionalized Surfaces
papers.abstract: The hydrophobicity of functionalized surfaces is critical, as these surfaces are widely used to modulate adsorption, self-assembly, fouling, and molecular recognition by controlling interfacial interactions with surrounding molecules. Despite their importance, characterizing the hydrophobicity of functionalized surfaces and quantifying its contribution to these phenomena remain challenging. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations and enhanced sampling methods to quantify the hydrophobicity of surfaces functionalized with multimodal ligands, which can interact with solutes through multiple interaction modes. Specifically, we study a series of multimodal ligands grafted to these surfaces, including Nuvia cPrime, a commercially available glycine-based chromatography ligand, and its amino acid-derived analogs, which differ from it by additional chemical groups with systematically varied hydrophobicity. We quantify surface hydrophobicity from the free energy of removing interfacial water molecules and compare our results with ligand logP values, the solvent accessible surface areas (SASA) of ligand chemical groups, and protein-induced water displacement observed in molecular simulations. We then validate the relevance of the resulting hydrophobicity ordering using experimental protein binding trends. We find that water removal from small, localized regions centered on ligand clusters better captures adsorption-relevant surface hydrophobicity than removing water from the entire surface because these regions more closely represent proteinbinding sites. Additionally, we show that variations in ligand clustering across the same surface alter chemical group exposure, as indicated by SASA, resulting in spatial heterogeneity in surface hydrophobicity. Overall, this work provides a molecular-level approach for characterizing functionalized surface hydrophobicity and guiding the design of interfaces that control molecular adsorption.

papers.title: Ipso-selective pyridine-to-aniline editing through amine-induced fragmentation
papers.abstract: Skeletal editing enables the remodeling of aromatic frameworks, but pyridine-to-aniline conversions can generate multiple positional isomers, complicating analogue synthesis. Here we report an ipso-selective strategy that separates regiochemical control from diversification of the aniline nitrogen. Pyridines are converted through dearomatization and cycloaddition into stable, isolable bicyclic ketones, which undergo amine-induced condensation–fragmentation to afford anilines with the amino group positioned at the site corresponding to the original pyridine nitrogen. Both primary and secondary amines participate, enabling divergent synthesis from a common intermediate. Notably, regioisomeric intermediates derived from a 3-substituted pyridine converge to a single aniline product. The method also enables preparation of multiple analogues from a tropicamide-derived scaffold, illustrating the potential of this modular approach for medicinal-chemistry scaffold diversification.

papers.title: Image-Charge Barriers, Not Polaron Kinetics, Limit Charge Extraction at Ligand-Passivated CsPbI3 Interfaces
papers.abstract: Charge extraction across inorganic perovskite–organic ligand interfaces represents a critical materials bottleneck in perovskite optoelectronics, yet the defectindependent electrostatic origins of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we present a multiscale framework that combines first-principles density functional theory with macroscopic Scharfetter–Gummel drift-diffusion simulations to isolate and quantify this intrinsic transport barrier on CsPbI3 surfaces passivated by methylammonium (MA), butylammonium (BA), and phenethylammonium (PEA). We demonstrate that effective interfacial dielectric screening is governed by ligand orientational polarizability and adsorption geometry rather than isolated molecular polarizability, producing a counter-intuitive ordering εBA > εMA > εPEA that inverts the conventional molecular polarizability sequence. The resulting imagecharge barriers (Umax im = 202.6–229.8 meV) exceed kBT by nearly an order of magnitude, driving severe thermodynamic carrier depletion (CAF = 1.38 × 10−4–3.95 × 10−4), while all computed polaron reorganization energies (λ < 100 meV) confirm delocalized, large-polaron character—unambiguously establishing that the dominant bottleneck is electrostatic rather than kinetic. Despite its lowest electron reorganization energy (λe = 37.8 meV), PEA’s orientational locking generates the largest image-charge barrier (Umax im = 229.8 meV), whereas the conformationally flexible BA maximizes in-plane screening and reduces steady-state carrier accumulation by an order of magnitude under operational bias. Furthermore, ligand rigidity governs a structural electron–hole reorganization asymmetry (λh/λe = 0.98–1.85), establishing a defect-independent, purely structural mechanism for carrier selectivity. These findings deliver four quantitative design rules for charge-transparent passivation interlayers, replacing empirical ligand screening with a predictive framework anchored in orientational polarizability, adsorption geometry, and carrier-type symmetry. The identified image-charge barrier constitutes a Boltzmann activation energy Uim(T ) that is directly measurable via temperature-dependent photoconductance, providing an unambiguous experimental validation signature.

papers.title: Reactive Machine-Learned Potentials Improve Predictions of Water Diffusion Behaviour in Defective Industrial Zeolite HY
papers.abstract: Dealuminated HY (USY) zeolites are of major industrial catalytic importance, and the defects they contain, such as extraframework aluminum (EFAL) and silanol groups, strongly influence the behaviour of adsorbed species. Here, we show that reactive neural network-based machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) provide a substantial improvement in the simulation of water diffusion in these catalysts. They yield markedly improved agreement with quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) measurements of mobility for models of intact framework regions, refined further once EFAL and silanol defects are included explicitly, capturing the additional hindrance these sites impose on water motion. The ability of MLIPs to generate and stabilise realistic defect structures constitutes a step change in the molecular level and nanoscale modelling of industrial zeolites. This combined capability enables the quantitative investigation of defect-specific effects on nanoscale diffusion and provides a new approach for accurately modelling transport in industrially relevant zeolite catalysts.

papers.title: A Direct-to-Biology Platform for Rapid Covalent Antibiotic Discovery
authors: Richard J. B. H. N. van den Berg
papers.abstract: The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections has created a critical need for new antibiotics. While natural product-based covalent antibiotic classes such as the β-lactams are highly effective, exploration of synthetic covalent antibiotics remains limited. Here, we present a direct-to-biology platform for covalent antibiotic discovery. Using tandem diazo transfer and copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition, we combinatorially synthesized 720 crude chloroacetamides within a matter of days and screened these for activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). By resynthesis and retesting, almost all hits were confirmed to be active, having potency profiles comparable to those of the initial screen. In situ chemoproteomic analyses revealed selective engagement of the essential enzyme HMG-CoA synthase by the most promising hits. We validated this target and obtained a co-crystal structure to better understand the binding mode of the compound. Altogether, this platform generates large libraries of covalently reactive compounds, identifies active compounds, and finds their molecular targets within a single screening campaign.

papers.title: Development of oligo-thioester precursors for native chemical ligation of oligo-protein conjugates.
papers.abstract: Protein-oligo conjugates have emerged as a promising therapeutic modality that unites the target-specificity and favorable pharmacokinetics of a protein carrier with the potency of an oligonucleotide payload. One challenge in the development of these biologics is that conjugation strategies often yield heterogeneous, high drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) products or require non-canonical amino acids and multi-step handling. Native chemical ligation (NCL) is a promising tool for protein-oligo conjugation, as the reaction is single-step and regiospecific to N-terminal cysteines, which can be genetically installed into proteins in a facile manner. However, methods for generating the required oligo-thioesters remain a technical challenge, especially when complex linker groups are desired. Here, we report an efficient protocol to generate four oligo linker-payloads (LPs) incorporating an anti-sense oligonucleotide targeting the MALAT1 gene, bis(2-sulfanylethyl)amine (NSS)- or thioacid-based thioester precursors, and diverse intervening linkers. The LPs were successfully ligated to an affibody and the crystallizable fragment (Fc) of an antibody, key protein carriers for protein-oligo therapeutics. The operationally simple, bespoke nature of this workflow enables the diversification of oligo payloads and linkers required for broad applications.

papers.title: Structural and Spectroscopic Characterization of Californium Polyoxometalate Compounds
papers.abstract: Californium (Cf3+) complexes with several Keggin-type polyoxometalate (POM) ligands have been synthesized and characterized, providing the first serial approach to Cf chemistry and a unique occasion to contrast its coordination properties with that of other felements. Contrary to trivalent lanthanides, americium and curium, californium yields a higher diversity of structures. Using microgram amounts of 249Cf, nine new structures containing Cf3+ have been obtained with the POM ligands [PW11O39]7-, [SiW11O39]8-, [GeW11O39]8-, and [BW11O39]9-, representing the largest series of Cf compounds ever isolated and significantly expanding experimental data on POM compounds with heavy actinides. Cf3+ crystallizes as the typical 8coordinate sandwich complexes with Keggin ions, [Cf(XW11O39)2]n-, but the long-range bond distances and twist angles of the Cf-POM complexes depart from any previous case reported. Comparative compounds obtained with the nearly isometric lanthanides also underline the uniqueness of the Cf3+ compounds beyond the ion size effects. The now extended family of [M(XW11O39)2]n- complexes also revealed previously unobserved topological isomers in such complexes, defined here as iota (ι) and omega (ω), with the Cf complexes’ isomerism often differing from the other f-elements. This first series of isotypic Cf compounds, CsyHz[Cf(XW11O39)2]·nH2O, (X = P5+, Si4+, Ge4+, or B3+), combined with structures previously obtained with Am3+, Cm3+, and lanthanides allows for the determination of bond valence sum (BVS) parameters for Cf3+ as well as the experimental determination of its 8-coordinate ionic radius: 1.066 ± 0.004 Å.

papers.title: Analytical validation in catalytic CO2 conversion: Product identification, carbon accounting, and evidence for process performance
papers.abstract: Reliably evaluating catalytic CO2 conversion requires distinct evidence for product identity, quantity, carbon origin, carbon accounting, and process performance.
