This critical narrative review compares those requirements across electrochemical, photocatalytic, and thermocatalytic conversion, with plasma-assisted hydrogenation as a methodological comparison. A five-step assessment traces the inference, alternative explanation, discriminating evidence, shared measurement dependencies, and remaining conclusion. Published cases distinguish product formation from carbon-source attribution, catalytic selectivity from carbon disposition, and repeatability from transferable performance. For a published plasma-only condition, subtraction and direct analysis differ by approximately 34 percentage points in methanol selectivity; differing collection windows limit attribution to one cause. Constructed calculations show how shared calibration and independent reactor uncertainty affect catalyst rankings differently, and how rankings can reverse when energy is expressed per recovered rather than formed product. The synthesis treats chromatography, quantitative NMR, isotope analysis, sampling recovery, flow measurement, and uncertainty as connected parts of the measurement procedure. The synthesis distinguishes contradictory evidence, insufficient experiments, and restricted source access. Priorities are independent tests of residual allocations, validation of representative collection pathways, matched operating intervals, and staged interlaboratory comparisons. The assessment is an applied interpretive procedure, not a validated scoring instrument.

papers.title: Multifunctional Cellulose via Enzymatic Oxidation of Tripeptides
papers.abstract: Cellulose is a natural, abundant and versatile biopolymer that has long been used in traditional applications such as paper and textiles and has gained interest in advanced applications including energy storage, healthcare, food, cosmetics, and coatings. For these applications, achieving robust functionality in cellulose nanocomposites remains a challenge due to poor control over the uniform distribution of added components. Here, we explore enzyme-activated tripeptides as versatile interfacial modifiers for introducing distinct functions into microbial cellulose. First, we demonstrate peptide-mediated formation of melanin-inspired coating with strong light absorption and potential UV-protective properties. Second, we demonstrate incorporation of graphene to create semi-conducting biocomposites. Microbial cellulose was exposed to the tripeptides KYF or KYW in the presence of tyrosinase, promoting peptide oxidation, assembly, and retention within the cellulose network. Pigmented coatings displayed a clear sequence dependence, with KYW exhibiting substantially greater adsorption and uniformity compared to KYF, which is consistent with additional hydrogen-bonding interactions provided by the tryptophan indole side chain and favorable carbohydrate–aromatic interactions that enhance cellulose affinity. In contrast, graphene incorporation was comparable for both peptides, suggesting that graphene immobilization is governed primarily by the general self-assembly of aromatic peptides rather than sequence-specific cellulose binding. The resulting composites showed uniform graphene dispersion, confirmed by optical and electron microscopy and Raman spectroscopy, together with enhanced mechanical performance and electrical conductivity. These findings establish enzymatic peptide oxidation as a versatile strategy for introducing optical and electrical functionality into cellulose-based materials.

papers.title: ChemConnect: Making chemical identifier relationships and disagreements explicit and actionable
papers.abstract: Chemical identifiers serve as essential links between molecular structures, experimental measurements, biological activities, and regulatory information. Discrepancies can arise when independently curated databases assign different identifiers to the same substance, often due to curation inconsistencies or intentional differences in representing salts, solvates, protonation states, and stereochemistry. Here, we introduce ChemConnect, a provenanceaware graph framework designed to integrate chemical identifiers from NORMAN SusDat, EPA CompTox Chemicals Dashboard, and PubChem without resolving them to a single canonical chemical entity. The ChemConnect graph contains ∼8.5 million chemical identifier nodes and ∼7.5 million connections, of which ∼ 65 thousand are derived structural-parent and stereochemical relationships whose agreement with external references is systematically quantified. ChemConnect preserves the information supplied by each source and stores the derived relationships separately, so that users can see how each relationship was obtained. This allows users to compare sources, identify records whose identifiers contradict each other, and connect related records, such as a salt and its neutral form, that have no identifier in common.

papers.title: Sm-Catalyzed Reductive Transformations of Enones
papers.abstract: We report two Sm-catalyzed reductive transformations of enones. Using catalytic Sm(OTf)3 and Zn0 as the terminal reductant, Wieland–Miescher-type ketones underwent ring contraction to trans-hydrindanes bearing vicinal quaternary stereogenic centers. Under similar conditions but with 2-naphthalenethiol as a hydrogen atom donor, diastereoselective enone reduction outcompeted the ring contraction pathway, furnishing decalin products. The diastereoselectivity of the enone reduction was shown to be controlled primarily by the substrate structure; however, for certain substrates, the thiol structure could be used to improve the diastereoselectivity. Mechanistic investigation by cyclic voltammetry is also reported.

papers.title: Proton-Gated Cobalt Catalysis Redirects Persistent Sulfinyl Radical Coupling toward Enantioselective C–S Bond Formation
papers.abstract: The enantioselective construction of aliphatic C(sp3)–S stereocenters from alkyl radicals remains challenging. Persistent sulfinyl radicals are attractive partners for radical cross-coupling. However, their rapid diffusioncontrolled coupling with transient alkyl radicals provides limited opportunity for stereochemical discrimination. Here, we report a dual photoredox/cobalt catalytic system in which a Brønsted acid acts as a critical mechanistic gate, redirecting persistent sulfinyl radical coupling from a direct PRE-dominated pathway toward cobaltcontrolled enantioselective C–S bond formation. Mechanistic studies support reduction of Co(II) to Co(I) and subsequent formation of a Co(III)–H species in the presence of HX. Hydrogen-atom transfer between Co(III)–H and the sulfinyl radical generates RSOH, which subsequently associates with a chiral cobalt species to organize the sulfur center for stereoselective radical capture. The use of aprotic alkyl radical precursors, including alkyl trifluoroborates and trialkylboranes, decouples radical generation from proton availability and reveals the critical role of the Brønsted acid in stereocontrol. This method accommodates diverse alkyl radical precursors and enables a practical alkene hydroboration–sulfinylation cascade for the synthesis of enantioenriched sulfoxides.

papers.title: Spin-Resolved Reaction-Network Exploration in AutoMeKin with Minimum-Energy-Crossing-Point Localization and an ⟨S2⟩ Single-Reference Check
papers.abstract: Automated exploration of reaction networks typically assumes a single potential-energy surface. However, 3d transition-metal catalysis often involves two-state reactivity, where the rate-determining step may occur on a different spin surface. This work presents an open-source extension of AutoMeKin that incorporates spin considerations throughout. The extension features a GFN2-xTB exploration engine with spin-handling capabilities, identification of closely lying spin states, localization of minimum-energy-crossing-points (MECP) at relevant crossings, integration of MECP nodes connected by nonadiabatic edges within the reaction graph, nonadiabatic transition-state-theory rate calculations, and a multireference diagnostic based on ⟨S2⟩ to disable the single-determinant approach where it is not applicable. The extension is tested on three different iron systems. For H2CO and Fe(CO)5, blind path sampling was utilized, whereas targeted transition-state optimization was applied to the more complex cases. Subsequently, MECPs were localized without manual intervention for Fe(CO)5 and Tp-Fe(II)-ethyl, but not for the Fe(I) alkene-isomerization catalyst.

papers.title: The Nuclear Landscape: A Five-Variable 3D-Printed Representation of the Nuclides
papers.abstract: Traditional charts of the nuclides convey proton number, neutron number, and one other property (e.g. half-life or decay mode). We describe the design and fabrication of a modular three-dimensional model of the nuclides that encodes five nuclear properties. Proton number and neutron number determine planar position, half-life is represented by column height using a quantile-logarithmic transformation, decay mode is represented by colour, and year of discovery is represented by the area of the top of the column. The model provides a tactile and visual representation of >3400 nuclides with the stable nuclides forming the spine of the model. The digital models were made by an iterative human-artificial intelligence (AI) co-design workflow in which generative AI helped translate educational objectives and geometric constraints into 3D printable stereolithography (STL) files. Feedback from visitors to the completed piece was uniformly positive when describing their interaction and learning experience. Complete datasets, STL files, and representative design prompts are provided to facilitate reproduction and adaptation for educational use.

papers.title: Adsorption Free Energy of a Mobile Physisorbed Molecular Catalyst from Well-Tempered Metadynamics and from the Harmonic Approximation
papers.abstract: The adsorption free energy of a molecular catalyst is usually calculated with harmonic frequency analysis of the optimized adsorbed structure, and errors are often blamed on anharmonicity. Here, using fac-Re(bpy)(CO)3Cl on graphene, we show that the main source of error is different. Harmonic analysis treats the complex as vibrating around a single minimum, but at 298 K, the complex can move across the surface, rotate around the surface normal, and rock. In this work, we use multiple-walker well-tempered metadynamics to sample the desorption coordinate and then convert the free-energy profile to a standard-state value, with the gas at 1 bar and the adsorbate at the standard surface concentration as recommended by Campbell et al. The result is ΔG°ads(298 K) = −64.1 ± 2.1 kJ mol−1 at PBE-D3(BJ), while the harmonic approximation gives −26.3 kJ mol−1. Of the 37.8 kJ mol−1 difference, only 1.7 kJ mol−1 comes from the anharmonic shape of the binding well along the surface normal; 36.3 kJ mol−1 is due to the frustrated translations and rotations of the bound complex, which the harmonic model treats as small vibrations around a single minimum. The two exceed the total by the 0.2 kJ mol−1 quantum-to-classical step, which acts in the opposite direction. Insertion-based estimators, which work well for small adsorbates in pores, do not apply here because the ensembles with and without the adsorbate–surface interaction are separated by 34 kBT and do not overlap. The missing entropy cancels out when comparing similar poses of the same adsorbate, but not when referencing the gas phase.

papers.title: “NONO” calix[4]arene zirconium complexes with functionalized side chains
papers.abstract: A series of zirconium (IV) complexes with a bis(N,N-Dimethylethylenediamino)-p-tert-butylcalix[4]arene, (L2H2), and (1S,2S)-N1,N1-Dimethyl-1,2-cyclohexanediamino -p-tert-butylcalix[4]arene, (L3H2), were synthetized and structurally characterized via single crystal X-ray diffraction and NMR. Comparing them with L1 complexes,1 slight increase in the stability towards protic substrates was observed as well as formal HCl elimination and formation of an anilino-anilido complex was observed for L3. Rac-lactide polymerization was attempted as well as intermolecular hydroamination of alkynes. The effect of the coordinating and basic side chains modifies the reactivity of the complexes but still do not show remarkable improvements in the catalytic applications.

papers.title: Taming the 8-Billion Parameter Model on a low-cost GPU card for Retrosynthesis
papers.abstract: We explored the use of post-training quantization (PTQ) to enhance the efficiency of reasoning language models for chemical retrosynthesis in drug discovery. We specifically evaluated the RetroDFM-R model, demonstrating that reducing numerical precision to 4-bit significantly lowered GPU memory requirements while lowering Top-1 accuracy by only about 2 percentage points (3–4% relative) for NormalFloat-4 (nf4) and double-quantized nf4 (nf4dq). The accuracy for 8-bit quantization (int8_ao) was equivalent to the original model but reduced energy consumption by about 17% when only one prediction was required. By testing various quantization methods across different hardware configurations, the study revealed that these techniques allow complex chemical predictions to run on budget-friendly, consumer-grade GPUs. In the augmented setting the 4-bit models returned more distinct candidates, which raised Top-10 accuracy on the full test set by up to 0.8 percentage points; on reactions for which every model filled ten candidate positions, the original model remained the most accurate. In summary this study presents the first evaluation of PTQ applied to RetroDFM-R, a reasoning language model, for chemical retrosynthesis. Ultimately, the research suggests that quantization is a vital tool for making advanced chemoinformatics tools accessible to academic researchers who can run it on cards with smaller GPU memory and can reduce the energy per molecule by about 17 - 30% in the default setting, although it increases it by 30–35% in the augmented setting.

papers.title: Machine-Learning-Guided Prediction and Statistical Analysis of Electronic Bandgaps in Double-Perovskite Oxides for Photovoltaic and Optoelectronic Design
papers.abstract: Double-perovskite oxides (A2BB′O6) are attractive for photovoltaic and optoelectronic applications, but their bandgap depends on a compositional space too large for routine DFT screening. In this study, we build composition-only machine-learning models on 1,306 DFTcomputed (GLLB-SC) double perovskites, using 72 descriptors derived from elemental electronegativity, ionic/atomic radius, group and period position, Mendeleev number, and first ionization energy. Six regression algorithms were compared under 10-fold cross-validation where a tuned XGBoost model gave the best results (test R2 = 0.975, MAE = 0.188 eV, RMSE = 0.245 eV), outperforming all others with statistical confidence (Friedman χ2 = 45.14, p =1.4×10-7; Wilcoxon p < 0.005 throughout). SHAP analysis pointed to A-site group number and B-site electronegativity and radius as the main drivers of bandgap, matching the mechanisms reported in the original DFT study. These results demonstrate that interpretable, composition-only machinelearning models can reproduce DFT-level bandgap trends at negligible computational cost, providing a practical high-throughput screening tool for lead-free double-perovskite discovery.

papers.title: SFEModeling.jl: multi-model, multi-curve fitting of supercritical fluid extraction kinetics with a graphical interface
papers.abstract: SFEModeling.jl is an open-source Julia package for fitting kinetic models of supercritical fluid extraction (SFE) to experimental extraction curves. It implements the Sovóvá broken-and-intact-cells model, solved numerically along the extraction bed, together with a pseudo-steady-state shrinking core model and four empirical models (Esquível, Zeković, parallel kinetics, and a piecewise-linear spline). Several curves, each with any number of replicates, are fitted jointly. In the Sovóvá model the accessible-solute fraction xk/x0 is shared across curves while the mass-transfer coefficients are estimated per curve. Parameters are found by derivative-free global optimization, so no initial guesses are required. Data and operating conditions are entered in laboratory units, and results can be exported to text or Excel files. The same functionality is available from a browser-based graphical interface, distributed with a Windows installer and as a Julia app, so experimentalists can use the software without programming.

papers.title: Selenium Alters the Tissue Distribution of Inorganic but Not Methylmercury in Zebrafish Larvae
papers.abstract: Mercury toxicity is strongly influenced by its chemical speciation, with interactions between mercury and selenium species either mitigating or exacerbating toxic effects. Here, synchrotronbased X-ray fluorescence imaging was used to examine the influence of L-selenomethionine on the tissue distributions of inorganic mercury and methylmercury in zebrafish larvae. Inorganic mercury accumulated predominantly in the pronephric ducts and liver, whereas methylmercury was distributed more uniformly throughout the organism. Administration of L-selenomethionine substantially altered the distribution of inorganic mercury and increased selenium accumulation within the pronephric ducts. Subcellular-resolution imaging revealed strong spatial correlations among mercury, selenium, and sulfur following inorganic mercury exposure, revealing mercury-, selenium-, and sulfur-rich domains within the pronephric ducts. In contrast, L-selenomethionine had comparatively little influence on methylmercury distribution, although combined exposure increased tissue sulfur levels. These findings demonstrate fundamentally different interactions of selenium with inorganic and organometallic mercury species in vivo and emphasize the importance of both chemical form and subsequent metabolism in determining mercury–selenium interactions.

papers.title: Polyoxometalate-controlled oxidative formation of bioinspired polydopamine hydrogels
papers.abstract: Polyoxometalates (POMs) have been extensively explored as enzyme-mimetic catalysts capable of peroxidase-like peroxide-driven reactions. Specifically, transition metal-substituted POMs provide a molecular platform for tunable reactivity and kinetic control. Here, we use a titanium-doped Keggin polyoxomolybdate [(TiOH)PMo11O39]4- {TiOH} to crosslink a dopamine-functionalized alginate hydrogel in the presence of hydrogen peroxide under mild conditions which would otherwise prevent polymer formation. Tuning of the hydrogel rheological properties is possible by molecular-level reaction control. Experimental and theoretical studies are combined for comprehensive insight into the reaction mechanism of the catalytically active species.

papers.title: A Modular Continuous Flow Platform for Safe, On-demand Generation of HCF 2 N 3 from R-22 Gas and Access to N -CF 2 H Triazoles
papers.abstract: The N -CF 2 H motif recently emerges as a promising pharmacophore but modular and general strategy to access this scaffold remains scarce. Although difluoromethyl azide (HCF 2 N 3 ) constitutes an ideal aminodifluoromethyl surrogate in this case, its exceptionally low ratio of C to N atoms (0.33), high volatility (b.p. = 8 o C), and heat/shock sensitivity render it particularly unsafe to handle and use in batch. On the other hand, R-22 (ClCF 2 H gas) is a phased-out refrigerent due to its ozone depletion potential and high global warming potential, and valorization of the reclaimed R-22 is highly desirable. Here, we report a modular continuous flow platform to efficiently enable a safe, on-demand generation of HCF 2 N 3 from R-22 gas and its direct in-line utilization. Two HCF 2 N 3 generation modules are developed to operate under aqueous or organic reaction conditions for accommodating diverse downstream reactions. The freshly generated HCF 2 N 3 is immediately intercepted by downstream base-mediated or copper tube-catalyzed cycloadditions to yield a wide range of valuable N -CF 2 H triazoles using easily available alkynes, aldehydes and β -ketoesters. Our method completely circumvents isolation hazards, mass transfer limitations in batch, and enables previously improbable gas-to-gas transformation and multiphasic conditions.

papers.title: Expanding Antibody-Drug Conjugates Mechanistic Diversity with Verubulin: A Dual Tubulin-Binding and Vascular-Disrupting Payload.
papers.abstract: Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs) have revolutionized targeted cancer therapy, yet their clinical success remains restricted by the limited diversity of cytotoxic payloads. Here we describe the development of verubulin as a novel ADC payload with a dual mechanism of action, combining tubulin inhibition with vascular disruption. Two successive ADC generations were designed and evaluated. First-generation conjugates used amide/carbamate linkage but were hampered by instability and modest efficacy. These limitations were addressed by a quaternarization approach, which delivered stable conjugates with subnanomolar, target-dependent cytotoxicity, and limited bystander activity. In vivo, these ADCs induced tumour regression with excellent tolerability and more durable tumour control than bevacizumab, the clinical reference for vascular disruption, although efficacy remained below benchmark ADCs T-DM1 and T-Dxd. These results support verubulin as a promising payload scaffold for next-generation ADCs.

papers.title: Energy conserving variational dynamics with Gaussian wavepackets in the nonadiabatic regime
papers.abstract: We present a theoretical framework for a “trajectory”-driven nonadiabatic dynamics, that generalizes the variational Gaussian wavepacket approach to dynamics on multiple diabatic states. By applying the time-dependent variational principle to a single Gaussian wavepacket per state, we obtain a set of coupled equations for the Gaussian center and width parameters that include terms arising from the coupling potential. We investigate the role of these terms as they change the Gaussian time-evolution, and of the initial conditions on the wavefunction for several standard benchmarks of nonadiabatic dynamics, including a three-state and a two-dimensional model. The state populations obtained with the fully variational Gaussian dynamics is found in close agreement with exact quantum results. Finally, we demonstrate that the use of Gaussian wavefunction in nonadiabatic dynamics preserves the symplecticity of the variational space, which ensures the energy conservation and minimization of error when solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation.

papers.title: What topology hold-out removes—and what it does not
papers.abstract: Machine-learning screens of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for CO2 capture increasingly report the validation protocol that produced a score, and topology hold-out has become the standard stricter alternative to random splitting. Prior work already reads topology hold-out as a combined structural and chemical distribution shift; this work measures the size of the chemistry that the split withholds. On the hypothetical-MOF library hMOF (324,426 structures), 74.7% of coarse-grained chemical compositions occur in a single topology, accounting for 61.3% of structures, and seven of eleven topologies leave every structure without a chemical counterpart in training. On the one usable chemistry-matched pair (pcu ↔nbo), removing the partner topology raised nbo-side MAE by 70.0% while a size-matched control did not, and removing only the shared-composition partner rows improved pcu-side MAE, so partner coverage is direction-dependent rather than uniformly beneficial. A chemistry-key hold-out produces only 21.1% of the topology hold-out's R2 decrease, so the support loss is real but does not translate proportionally into performance loss. Across five independently redrawn 25,000-sample support sets, the top-1% hit rate fell from 50.4% to 19.3% under topology-grouped validation. A support audit in ARC-MOF, which is partly dependent on hMOF and uses different composition keys, confirms strong coupling under bounded sensitivity rather than as an independent replication. We retain topology hold-out as a stress test while recommending that groupedsplit reports disclose their chemical support, deployment-relevant aggregation and ranking performance.

papers.title: Wigner Momentum Estimation and Sampling with Local Modes: A Second-Moment Approximation to High-Frequency Momentum Marginals
papers.abstract: Instantaneous local Gaussian approximations assign nuclear momentum widths from the curvature of the potential at each sampled configuration. Strongly compressed bonds can consequently acquire large momentum widths even when their positions are drawn from an anharmonic path-integral ensemble. We estimate momentum covariances from pathintegral coordinates and forces in local modes that follow molecular deformations. These covariances define Gaussian approximations to high-frequency Wigner momentum marginals without evaluating a Hessian at each configuration. The resulting sampling recovers the Maxwell momentum distribution in the classical limit. A rotating bond model with harmonic stretching and periodic torsion agrees with an independent quantum reference within statistical uncertainty. For trans-azobenzene at 300 K with 32 beads, the most compressed C–H bond receives a mass-weighted momentum variance of 36.53 kJ mol−1 from LGA and 19.55 kJ mol−1 from the local covariance along the same physical stretch direction. Temporal holdout errors in C–H second moments are 7.2–7.6%, compared with 2.2–5.1% for LGA relative to the finite-bead reference; the demonstrated benefit concerns the suppression of local width spikes. The largest collective C–H width remains sensitive to estimator noise. These results support the method as an approximation to high-frequency momentum widths without a frequency cap. Position-conditioned quantum correlations, non-Gaussian tails, and the continuum-bead molecular limit remain outside the demonstrated accuracy.

papers.title: Calcium Poly(heptazine imide): Reproducible Synthesis for Structural Analysis, Mechanism of CO <sub>2</sub> Uptake, and Evaluation of Photocatalytic CO <sub>2</sub> - to-CO Conversion
papers.abstract: The framework material, calcium poly(heptazine imide) or CaPHI, is reportedly capable for CO 2 absorption, although harsh conditions from literature synthesis method result in low and unpredictable yield that hinders evaluation of its applicability for CO 2 capture and conversion (CCC). This work presents a synthesis procedure for CaPHI with cross-laboratory reproducibility and scalable to 100s mg by employing a CaCl 2 -based eutectic as synthesis medium. Comprehensive characterization confirmed the PHI structure, with Ca 2+ residing in the structural porosity having ionic conductivity of 10 -10 –10 -11 S cm -1 as estimated by electrochemical measurements. In addition to the literature’s physisorption mechanism for dry CO 2 , we demonstrated these Ca 2+ to participate in direct air capture of humid CO 2 , which chemisorbs as CaCO 3 from structural analyses. For photocatalytic CO 2 -to-CO conversion, CaPHI outperforms its K + -bearing counterpart, which we speculatively attributed to strong Ca 2+ –CO 2 interactions that concentrate this reactant near the active sites. In establishing a reliable synthesis and demonstrating its ability for CO 2 capture and photoreduction, further optimization of CaPHI’s structure, morphology and compositing with co-catalyst could reveal its potential for CCC, while incorporation of mobile Ca 2+ may represent a broad design principle warranting future research for material development for improving the efficiency of carbon capture & utilization.

papers.title: Fragment-Grounded Neural Simulation of Electron Ionization Mass Spectra at Library Scale
papers.abstract: Electron ionization mass spectrometry (EI-MS) is a sensitive, reproducible analytical technique, yet compound identification conventionally relies on reference databases that capture only a fraction of accessible chemical space. In silico prediction of EI-MS spectra can extend these libraries, but existing data-driven models generalize poorly beyond their training distribution, and physics-based simulations are too costly for library-scale use. Here, we present a fragment-grounded neural workflow that predicts an EI-MS spectrum by exhaustively enumerating the fragmentation graph of a molecule and then assigning intensities to the resulting substructures. By relating every predicted peak back to a candidate substructure, our model generalizes more reliably to unseen scaffolds and out-of-distribution chemistry than prior fingerprint-and black-box transformer-based predictors. On a scaffold split, it improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from formula-matched compounds by 32% relative to the strongest baseline, and it matches the accuracy of quantum-chemical simulation while being roughly seven orders of magnitude faster. To test the model’s capabilities under a harder, formula-agnostic setting, we further evaluate retrieval against a library of 87.3 million compounds from

papers.title: Photocatalytic Reductive Elimination From A Main Group Centre
papers.abstract: The development of “transition metal-like” reactivity using earth-abundant p-block elements is one of the most prominent and challenging goals of contemporary main group chemistry. This difficulty is exemplified by the key, catalytically relevant bond-forming step of reductive elimination which, while often facile for transition metals, is very difficult to achieve for most main group elements. Efforts to bridge this gap have typically focused on delicate tailoring of electronic structure, supporting ligands, and coordination geometry, a task that is conceptually difficult and synthetically demanding. Herein, we demonstrate an alternative approach. We show that photocatalytic reductive elimination from an already well-known P(V) complex can be achieved rapidly and under mild conditions, via a transient oxidation strategy analogous to “oxidatively induced reductive elimination”. This concept has previously been applied only to transition metal complexes but is now extended to the field of main group chemistry. These results demonstrate a simple, easily accessible, but potentially very powerful new strategy for ‘turbocharging’ transition metal-like reactivity at a main group centre. Thus, it provides a valuable new tool for the ongoing pursuit of transition metal-like catalysis using main group elements.

papers.title: Complete stabilization of surface oxygen vacancies in high-entropy oxides
papers.abstract: High-entropy oxides retain a significantly larger population of oxygen vacancies (OVs) compared to their single-element or binary metal oxide counterparts, highlighting their unique potential as prospective electrocatalytic materials. However, the stabilization of surface oxygen vacancies (S-OVs) is highly challenging due to their inherently dynamic nature generally resulting in defect healing, migration, or initiation of structural collapse under operating conditions. By means of rational high-throughput materials science, we investigate the stability of S-OVs in (Cu-Fe-Ni-Cr-Zn)O x high-entropy oxides covering a compositional search space of at least 5 to 35 %. A methodology based on X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and X-ray absorption spectroscopy is utilized to quantitatively follow the distribution of the OVs across the materials library. For low Zn stoichiometries, (Cu 14 -Fe 13 -Ni 5 -Cr 8 -Zn 4 )O 55 , complete stabilization of S-OVs is achieved even after prolonged exposure to ambient environment. The discovery of S-OV stabilization in our high-entropy oxide system is a prerequisite to exploit the unique properties of this class of materials for electrocatalytic applications and beyond.

papers.title: Ordering-dependent subsurface reconfiguration reshapes the ORR activity ranking of L10 and L12 Pt–Fe nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Nanoparticle catalyst properties are often governed by activation-induced subsurface reconfiguration and ordering-dependent structural responses rather than nominal bulk phases. Static idealized models therefore can miss the kinetic pathways that drive subsurface evolution and active-site redistribution during synthesis and activation. Here, we present an activation-mapped kinetic modeling workflow combining density functional theory (DFT), machine-learning cluster expansion (ML-CE), Metropolis Monte Carlo (MMC), and kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) to trace processing-driven structural evolution in L1 0 and L1 2 Pt–Fe nanoparticles. We define the activation-derived ensemble as the statistically sampled Pt-skin configurations generated by high-temperature ordering, selective Fe leaching, vacancy-mediated restructuring, and room-temperature activation. This ensemble construction links processing history to subsurface composition, surface morphology, and site-resolved catalytic response. Within the modeled activation sequence, phase-dependent Fe leaching produces an inversion in second-layer Fe enrichment relative to the ideal ordered references and changes the dominant active-site families, making L1 0 -derived nanoparticles terrace-controlled, whereas L1 2 -derived nanoparticles become comparatively edge-controlled. When coupled to steady-state *OH coverage kinetics, these activation-derived ensembles recover the experimental oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity ranking and reveal phase-specific size–activity trends missed by ideal models. More broadly, the results show that the activation-derived structures, rather than pristine phases alone, govern catalyst ranking and highlight how ordering-dependent subsurface reconfiguration can reshape static-model predictions.

papers.title: Inhibition of Oxidative Activity by Photo-induced Surface Hydroxyl Groups in Bismuth Titanium Oxide Photocatalyst Detected by Single-Molecule Fluorescence Imaging
papers.abstract: The surface structure of semiconductor photocatalysts plays a critical role in the extraction of charge carriers during photocatalytic reactions. However, the surface structures of many photocatalysts are dynamic under catalytic conditions, which makes identifying photo-induced changes and their effect on photocatalytic activity challenging. Herein we use super-resolution, single-molecule fluorescence imaging to map the spatial distribution of catalytically active regions and quantify the changes in activity of those regions for photocatalytic oxidation in bismuth titanium oxide (Bi 4 Ti 3 O 12 ) nanoplates. Individual nanoplates varied widely in both activity and stability, reflecting significant heterogeneity among a single synthesis batch of photocatalyst particles. We observed that while the nanoplates are more active around the perimeter of the basal facet, those perimeter regions decrease in activity at the same relative rate as the rest of the basal facet, indicating a spatially uniform degradation mechanism. Through ensemble structural characterization of the nanoplates after irradiation, we identified surface hydroxyl groups as the photo-induced feature. Our results indicate that surface hydroxyl groups introduce hole trap states that increase charge recombination at the surface of the nanoplates leading to the observed decrease in activity. Surprisingly, we identified nanoscale features that do not begin with high activity but exhibit a slower rate of activity loss, leading to regions with greater activity relative to the rest of the basal facet at the end of imaging. Our findings highlight the importance of not only understanding how different nanoscale features influence catalytic activity but also how these features evolve over time, which dictates catalyst stability.

papers.title: Alignment and directional ionic transport in liquid-crystalline and related ordered soft electrolytes: a 25-study evidence map with an architecture-aware comparability audit
papers.abstract: Directional ionic transport is widely reported in liquid-crystalline and related ordered soft electrolytes, but a conductivity ratio has no fixed meaning unless the alignment, transport axis, specimen history, and measurement architecture are reported together. This public-source evidence map examined 25 primary studies across ionic liquid crystals, liquid-crystalline polymers, proton-conductive networks, gels, and related ordered soft materials. Each record was assessed for experimental alignment evidence, an explicit axis convention, reporting of both directions, matching of material and measurement conditions, source-located numerical information, and the experimental relationship between the two directional measurements. Nineteen records provided direct alignment evidence, 24 defined a transport axis, 23 reported both directions, 12 met the initial condition-matching rule, and ten retained an exact sourcelocated numerical directional pair for audit. These reporting counts do not constitute a common quantitative dataset. A focused architecture audit of six high-information records applied a conservative rule requiring one specimen, one measurement architecture, matched conditions, and source-located directional values. None met all requirements: four compared separately prepared orientation states and two compared different cell designs. The result does not negate directional transport. It shows that directional evidence, orientation-state sensitivity, and crosscell sensitivity answer distinct experimental questions and should not be merged into a pooled anisotropy. The paper therefore provides a structured map of the field, identifies the reporting links that prevent quantitative synthesis, and proposes a minimum disclosure framework for future directional-transport studies.

papers.title: Aqueous SEC–MALS Characterization of Hydrophilic Azolium-Based Poly(ionic liquid)s in Their Native Halide Form
papers.abstract: The molar-mass characterization of hydrophilic poly(ionic liquid)s (PILs) is challenging due to strong polymer–column interactions and low refractive-index contrast, which limit detector sensitivity. To address these limitations, we analyzed five imidazolium-based PILs using both aqueous and organic (THF/LiTFSI) size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) with polystyrene calibration or multi-angle light-scattering detection (SEC-MALS). In THF/LiTFSI, the low dn/dc values compromised sensitivity, hindering reliable molar-mass determination. We therefore screened various aqueous mobile phases to identify optimal elution conditions. Among those tested, 0.3 M formic acid yielded well-resolved polymer peaks for all five PILs, with significantly higher dn/dc values than THF/LiTFSI. Mass recoveries ranged from 60.5% to 78.5%, enabling accurate molarmass determination. The method was also qualitatively validated for poly(vinylimidazole), partially quaternized poly(vinylimidazole), and a poly(thiazolium). Overall, aqueous SEC with 0.3 M formic acid emerges as a simple, general, and efficient alternative for the SECMALS characterization of hydrophilic azolium-based homo- and co-PILs. Unlike organic SEC, this approach requires no prior counteranion exchange, thus streamlining the analytical workflow.

papers.title: Spectral Identification of Hydrino Compound Fe2O3:H2(1/4) by Five Complementary Spectroscopies R. L. Mills and W.R. Hagen
papers.abstract: Mills solves the hydrogen atom and molecule in exact equations that give the experimental observables of both. Uniquely, Mills predicts that in addition to the reciprocal integer squared excited-state electronic energy states of atomic hydrogen, hydrogen possesses integer squared electronic energy levels corresponding to 1/p replacing n in the Rydberg formula, corresponding so-called hydrino state of hydrogen. Hydrino, H(1/p), is any small form of atomic hydrogen with state energy En = -13.598/n2 eV, in which n = 1/p, and p is limited by the energy in the electric field of the proton to 126 whereafter the proton and electron decay. Electron transitions to a hydrino states involve an initial non-radiative energy transfer to a catalyst that serves as an energy hole or sink of a quantized amount of energy, 2mE1 (m is integer) to be transferred to a catalyst such as HOH, a free or nascent water molecule. Furthermore, hydrino atoms can react to form the corresponding diatomic molecule referred to as molecular hydrino H2(1/p). In contrast to molecular hydrogen (H2), the molecular hydrino (H2(1/p)) is paramagnetic with S = ½, the size is 1/p3 that of H2, the internuclear distance is 1/p that of H2, and the energies such as the rotational, vibrational, and total molecular energies are p2 those of H2. These aspects of H2(1/p) give rise to unique spectral signatures that are characteristic of and identify H2(1/p). The recording of unique gas chromatographic (GC), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, electron beam excitation spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) peaks of H2(1/4) formed by a high energy impact reaction of FeOOH that served as the source of H and HOH catalyst are reported wherein the observed peaks matched those predicted.

papers.title: Examining the Effect of Matrix Composition in Nanocomposite Dielectric Oxides Using Wannier Centers
papers.abstract: Dielectric permittivity is a crucial parameter when designing materials for high energy-density capacitors. Alkaline earth metal oxides are a class of materials with relatively large band gaps and permittivities. Furthermore, introducing metallic nanoparticle inclusions into an oxide matrix provides a reserve of polarizable electrons that in some cases leads to enhancements in permittivity. Herein, we use the displacement of Wannier centers to examine the contributions to permittivity enhancement in four alkaline earth oxide matrices, MgO, CaO, SrO, and BaO, containing molecular-scale Ag8 inclusions. We competing smooth trends in the relative contributions of the inclusion and matrix to the permittivity enhancement as the identity of the matrix cation is changed. In particular, the delocalization of electrons at the interface between matrix and inclusion is found to increase with the matrix lattice constant, resulting in larger electronic polarization of the inclusions. Meanwhile, the dynamic coupling of inclusion and matrix ionic polarization, as measured through changes in the Born effective charges from bulk, decreases as the lattice constant increases. In the end, optimizing permittivity enhancement is seen to be closely tied to the lattice match between the inclusion and host matrix.

papers.title: Terpene Structure Governs Humidity-Enhanced New Particle Formation through an OH-Sensitive Ozonolysis Network
papers.abstract: Relative humidity (RH) impacts new particle formation (NPF) from monoterpene ozonolysis in a non-uniform way. Depending on the precursor, water vapor can either suppress particle formation or increase it, and the chemical origin of that contrast has remained uncertain. Here we use cyclohexane to remove OH and separate the OH-sensitive portion of the particle response from the residual OH-insensitive contribution for α-pinene, β-pinene, and camphene. Experiments were carried out at <0.1% and 60% RH using low monoterpene mixing ratios of 0.5 – 5 ppbv. In the absence of scavenger, the maximum number of particles formed (Nmax) increased strongly with RH for α-pinene and β-pinene (Enhancement Factor, ΔNmax = 1.06 and 0.76, respectively) but not for camphene. Once OH was scavenged, the humid conditions no longer produced higher Nmax compared to the corresponding dry ones. The dry-condition OH-sensitive fractions were 87.5% for α-pinene, 79.9% for β-pinene, and 53.7% for camphene. We then compared these results with literature ozonolysis OH-forming yields for a broader five-terpene set that also includes α-terpinene and γ-terpinene. The comparison shows a useful but limited role for OH yield: compounds with very low OH-forming propensity show little RH enhancement, yet the magnitude of the enhancement is not set by OH yield alone. α-Terpinene, for example, gives the largest ΔNmax response despite an intermediate OH yield, whereas γ-terpinene has a much higher OH yield but a smaller enhancement. We therefore place the RH effect within a structure-dependent OH-sensitive ozonolysis network in which Criegee Intermediate (CI) geometry, radical fate, autoxidation, and precursor concentration all influence whether additional water vapor ultimately produces more new particles.

papers.title: Microscopic Free-Energy Landscaping and Coarse-Grained 3D Dynamics of Scaffolded DNA Computers: Overcoming Kinetic Traps at Scale
papers.abstract: Thermodynamically favoured molecular computing encodes algorithmic solutions into ground-state equilibrium configurations of self-assembling DNA nanostructures, circumventing the dissipation bounds of non-equilibrium kinetic proofreading. However, practical scaling on biologically derived scaffolds (such as single-stranded M13 bacterio- phage DNA) has been severely constrained by heterogeneous base compositions that create energetic traps, kinetic stalls along long carry runs, and uncharacterized steric effects. Here, we present a multi-scale high-performance computational study uniting coarse-grained 3D molecular dynamics (oxDNA2), combinatorial Monte Carlo free- energy flattener algorithms, and continuous-time Gillespie kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations. From 3D trajectories of assembled 4-position complexes, we demonstrate that adjacent bound compute domains remain separated by an average physical distance of 18.43± 5.58 nm with zero direct contact probability, establishing that proofreading proceeds exclusively through solution-phase tile displacement rather than on-scaffold branch migration. By integrating the spatial probability density of the flexible single- stranded arms (RMSF = 10.14 nm), we extract an effective local concentration of Ceff = 63.37 µM, explaining a 63-fold kinetic acceleration that powers the directional assembly ratchet. We resolve the failure of naive global sequence flattening by discovering a hierarchical design window (∆G◦ scaffold ≈ −18.5 kcal/mol), which homogenizes scaffold duplex variances (σ = 0.61 kcal/mol) while preserving a critical 12.7 kcal/mol free-energy gap for error discrimination. Finally, across full 25-bit binary addition problems, we demonstrate that a non-linear dwell annealing schedule enables robust

papers.title: Helium Atom Scattering from Cold Salty Water: Impact of Microscopic and Mesoscopic Surface Structure
papers.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of gas–liquid surface scattering is of fundamental importance to interfacial phenomena ranging from atmospheric chemistry to heterogeneous catalysis. In this work, molecular beam scattering experiments and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are carried out to study collisions of He atoms ( E i = 5.8 kJ mol −1 ; θ i = 45°, 60°, and 75°) from the surface of a cold salty water (8 m LiBr (aq) , 230 K) flat jet. The measured translational energy distributions are collected as a function of the scattering angle in the same plane of the incidence beam and indicate dominant impulsive scattering with little to no trapping–desorption signal. The fractional energy loss values are small and nearly invariant across a wide range of deflection angles. MD simulations with fine-tuned force field parameters reproduce the experimental energy transfer reasonably well, providing insight into the collision dynamics at the microscopic level. However, the highly diffuse experimental angular distributions with significant intensities in the direction parallel to the liquid surface ( θ f = 90°) are in sharp contrast to the narrower and near specular angular distributions in simulations. This theory–experiment discrepancy is attributed to capillary and mechanical waves of the liquid surface and much better agreement between theory and experiment for He scattering is achieved by invoking a mesoscopic washboard model. This model also successfully reproduces previously reported results for Ne at E i = 24.3 kJ mol −1 . Our combined experimental–computational approach establishes that microscopic collision dynamics and mesoscopic surface morphology jointly govern scattering from salty water surfaces, providing a framework for interpreting and predicting interfacial energy transfer in complex liquid environments.

papers.title: An RI-NMR and DFT Study of Boron Homologations: Structures of α-Halo Lithium Carbenoids and the Effect of Boronic Ester Structure on 1,2-Metalate Rearrangement Rates
papers.abstract: Despite the widespread utility of α-halo lithium carbenoids in boron homologations, their solution-state aggregation structures remain unresolved. In this work, a rapid-injection NMR study was undertaken to characterize unstabilized α-halo lithium carbenoids at –105 °C. 13C–6Li scalar coupling established direct carbon–lithium connectivity, and DOSY NMR revealed that the lithium carbenoids exist as monomeric species solvated by THF. Next, the 1,2-metalate rearrangement rates were measured by trapping the α-bromo lithium carbenoid with arylboronic esters and monitoring the conversion of the 8-B-4 complexes generated in situ. The kinetic studies reveal that ring size, backbone substitution, and donor identity strongly influence the rate of the 1,2-metalate rearrangement. Detailed computational studies further confirmed that the lower 1,2-metalate rearrangement barriers of the more reactive boronic esters arise from the combination of the release of steric strain (B-strain), charge redistribution, and more favorable access to the reactive antiperiplanar rotamer of the 8-B-4 complex. Finally, these structure–reactivity relationships were translated into synthetic advances where a faster-migrating 2,4dimethylpentan-2,4-diol boronic ester enabled productive homologation of carbamate-derived carbenoids under mild conditions in which the corresponding BPin boronic ester derivative afforded no detectable homologation product.

papers.title: Benchmarking thermoelectric property extraction from scientific text
papers.abstract: Databases of thermoelectric properties are built largely by extracting values from the literature, and the choice of extraction method determines how many records are recovered and how many are wrong. We compare five methods on the same paragraph-level task: a corpus-informed regular-expression baseline, the published ChemDataExtractor thermoelectric parsers, a MaterialsBERT-based named-entity model with rule-based linking, a single-prompt large language model (LLM) and an LLM agent. The methods were developed on a 100-paragraph development sample (the rules of the regular-expression baseline earlier, on the whole corpus), frozen, and run on a 200-paragraph test sample drawn by stratified sampling from 311 papers (mostly arXiv preprints), with a paper-level split between the two samples. A record counts as correct only if property, value, temperature and material all match the gold standard. On the 160 in-scope test paragraphs (241 core records), the single-prompt LLM reached F1 = 0.79 (95 % CI 0.71–0.87) and the agent 0.73 (0.64–0.83), against 0.22 for the regular-expression baseline and 0.06 for the ChemDataExtractor and NER pipelines. Both LLM methods recover property, value and temperature with F1 above 0.94; most of their remaining losses arise from the material criterion; in most of these cases one material name contains the other. We found no evidence of an accuracy improvement from the tested agent configuration, which differs from the single prompt in several components at once. We release the protocol, code, gold standard and all method outputs in a public repository.

papers.title: Extending the Life of High-Voltage LiCoO2 Phone Cells in Hot Climates: An Evidence-Calibrated Assessment of Electrolyte and Cathode Improvements
papers.abstract: High-voltage lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO 2 ) phone cells age faster in heat, yet public data on their life in hot climates are scarce. This study estimates how much a published electrolyte additive package (nitrile, LiDFOB or LiPO 2 F 2 , TMSPi,low FEC) and further cathode stabilisation (trace Ti–Mg–Al doping, surface coating, single-crystalparticles) could extend the life of an iPhone 17-type cell (3,692 mAh, 4.50 V, rated ≥1,000 cycles to 80%). A Monte Carlo life model (40,000 draws) was calibrated to public measurements: 165 owner battery-health readings, CALCE LiCoO 2 cycling and storage data, and Sandia cycling data at 25 and 35 °C, and was constrained by the EU EPREL rating. Median cycles to 80% were 910 (80% range 733–1,052) for the baseline and 1,239 (915–1,785) for the proposed chemistry at 25 °C, and 674 (533–818) versus 926 (673–1,340) under a defined hot-climate (Indian summer) usage profile. The life ratio was about 1.38x (1.10–1.93), with probabilities of 67%, 36% and 8% of exceeding 1.25x, 1.5x and 2x. A backtest on 20 held-out cells gave a median error of 21%, and the stated ranges are too narrow. The dominant uncertainty is the incremental benefit over additives already present in commercial electrolytes. Measured CALCE data also show severe loss for LiCoO 2 stored fully charged at 50 °C (about 49% in 166 days). A paired electrolyte test is proposed to resolve the main uncertainty.

papers.title: Sulfur-Coordinated Iron Overcomes Stability Limitations in Atomically Dispersed Metal-Nitrogen-Carbon Catalysts for CO <sub>2</sub> Electrolysis
papers.abstract: Metal-nitrogen-carbon (M-N x -C) catalysts are a versatile platform for electrochemical CO 2 reduction catalysis, yet the limited durability of Fe-containing active sites at industrially relevant current densities remains an obstacle. Here we report a synthesis strategy that selectively incorporates sulfur into the coordination environment of atomically dispersed iron centers within a dual-metal Fe-S y /Ni-N x -C catalyst, yielding sulfur rich coordinated Fe active sites, represented by a Fe-S 5 model, alongside predominantly Ni-N x coordinated active sites. Beyond modifying the coordination structure, sulfur incorporation is correlated with higher nitrogen retention and suppressed formation of metal-containing clusters during catalyst synthesis, increasing the abundance of atomically dispersed metal active centers. Operando and ex situ spectroscopic analyses reveal that sulfur coordination stabilizes iron active sites during CO 2 electrolysis in a membrane electrode assembly, mitigating degradation processes that have historically limited durability. The catalyst delivers near-unity CO selectivity and an energy efficiency of 44% at a current density of 500 mA cm -2 , surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art CO 2 to CO catalysts. These findings demonstrate how sulfur coordination can stabilize atomically dispersed iron active sites and establishes a more broadly applicable strategy for designing durable catalysts.

papers.title: Fabrication of a Bimetallic NiFe-Prussian Blue-MoS2 Nano-heterojunction for NIR-Triggered Antibacterial Activity
papers.abstract: Bacterial infections continue to pose a major threat to human health globally, and the rapid emergence of antibiotic-resistant microorganisms has created an urgent need for development of effective non-antibiotic therapeutic strategies for pathogen eradication. In this work, a series of peroxidase-like NiFe-PB@MoS 2 (PB: Prussian Blue) heterostructured nanocomposite (NFPPM) catalysts were successfully synthesised to achieve significantly enhanced antibacterial activity. In the prepared heterostructure, MoS2 nanoflowers were decorated with NiFe-PB nanoparticles through an in situ growth process. The incorporation of NiFe-PB effectively improved the catalytic and photothermal activity of MoS 2 under NIR irradiation. After 10 min of NIR exposure, the NFPPM nanocomposite exhibited remarkable antibacterial efficiency against Staphylococcus aureus Escherichia coli . Peroxidase-like nanozymes have been extensively explored in various biomedical applications because of their excellent catalytic properties. The as-prepared NFPPM demonstrated enhanced peroxidase-like activity, leading to superior antibacterial performance. Furthermore, this work provides a promising strategy based on adhesive nanozymes that can closely interact with bacterial surfaces, offering valuable insight into the design of highly efficient heterojunction-containing photocatalysts with superior antibacterial activity.

papers.title: High-Throughput Combinatorial Screening of Refractory Amorphous Alloys for Fusion Capillary Systems via a Calibrated First-Principles Continuum-Thermodynamic Model
papers.abstract: Liquid metal divertors utilizing Capillary Porous Systems (CPS) represent a critical armor technology for handling extreme heat fluxes (> 10–20 MW/m2) in magnetic confinement fusion. However, conventional crystalline refractory matrices suffer from liquid-metal-induced corrosion along grain boundaries, thermal embrittlement, and grain coarsening. Amorphous metallic alloys eliminate grain boundaries, but identifying high-temperature glass formers remains computationally prohibitive via density functional theory or molecular dynamics. Here, we present a closed-form analytical framework that couples first-principles screened nuclear ion affinities (Ai), Rose Universal Binding Energy Relations (UBER), Voigt–Reuss–Hill (VRH) elastic homogenization, Egami topological size polydispersity (δ), and Miedema macroscopic mixing enthalpy (∆Hmix) with the Johnson–Samwer Cooperative Shear Model (CSM) to predict elastic moduli and glass transition temperatures (Tg) a priori directly from alloy stoichiometry. Nonlinear least-squares calibration against an experimental bulk metallic glass database demonstrates that atomic size strain distortion is intrinsically captured by the elastic shear work (GVRH · Vm, yielding α = 0.000), while core valence charge disparity creates local electrostatic screening perturbations that enhance the shear arrest barrier (β = 0.384), reducing residual root-mean-square error by 18.5% to 41.9 K. Applying this calibrated framework to a combinatorial sweep of the quaternary Zr–Ta–Ni–Ti system evaluates 839 candidate compositions meeting CPS engineering thresholds (Tg ≥ 700 K, GVRH ≥ 45 GPa) in < 1 second. We identify Zr5Ta55Ni35Ti5 as an optimal refractory candidate exhibiting a predicted Tg = 1019.1 K, shear modulus GVRH = 67.0 GPa, bulk modulus KVRH = 178.3 GPa, Poisson’s ratio ν = 0.333, deep exothermic stabilization ∆Hmix = −30.41 kJ/mol, and robust topological frustration δ = 8.23%. This framework establishes a zero-cost computational pipeline for accelerated discovery of extreme-environment amorphous materials.

papers.title: Reliability of Short Molecular Dynamics Runs as Screening Labels: Noise Ceilings, Time Dependence and Adaptive Replicate Allocation
papers.abstract: High-throughput molecular dynamics (MD) produces the labels on which electrolyte screening and machine-learning models are built, but each label comes from one short, noisy run whose value still depends on the simulated time. We quantify their reliability, and how to spend a simulation budget given it, on HTP-MD, the largest public set of polymer electrolyte trajectories (6,137 runs of 5 ns and 133 of 50 ns). Lithium motion is diffusive in only 2 short and 5 long runs, the apparent diffusivity at a 5 ns lag is 1.95 times that at 25 ns, and the first 5 ns of a run are 1.63 times faster than its second half, biasing every short label upwards. From 94 systems simulated twice, a single 5 ns end-point label has reliability 0.47 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.63): no model can correlate with such labels much beyond about 0.69, a random forest on monomer fingerprints is indistinguishable from that ceiling (0.71), and roughly half of the run-to-run noise comes from the initial structure. A short run ranks widely different polymers well (Spearman 0.93) but not similar ones (0.68 within the screening set). In simulations with the measured noise, giving further runs only to candidates whose membership of the top set is uncertain matches four uniform replicates with 1.8 runs per candidate for the top 10% and 1.2 for the top 1%; a check on real runs is consistent but underpowered. A decision guide and all code are provided.

papers.title: Radical Anion of Oxalate Esters: Electrochemical and EPR Investigations
papers.abstract: The oxalic acid/oxalate family is an instrumental C 2 platform for a circular carbon economy strategy. That molecule is the first and simplest of the C‒C bonded products obtained from CO 2 , and production technologies are already available, assisted by renewable electrons or from biomass. Exploiting this family of compounds as C 2 synthons through reductive C‒C couplings into value-added carbon skeletons is a promising opportunity. However, the chemistry of oxalate reduction remains poorly described with the reactivity of these species under reducing conditions or the associated degradation mechanisms still scarcely investigated. Here, we combine electrochemistry, EPR spectroelectrochemistry and computational chemistry to in-depth study the electrogeneration of radical anions from oxalate esters, bringing new perspective on the degradation mechanisms of these reduced species.

papers.title: Ionic router: a shared acidic pivot swaps one salt bridge for another, encoding activation state at non-homologous positions in class B1 and class A GPCRs
papers.abstract: We report the first instance in a class B1 G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) of a charged residue that exchanges one state-specific salt bridge for another, and the first evidence that this arrangement recurs at non-homologous positions in two receptor classes. In the human glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R), E408, generic number 8.49x49, pairs with R348 (6.37x37) in 5 of 5 scorable inactive structures and 0 of 52 active, and with R176 (2.46x46) in 42 of 52 active structures and 0 of 6 inactive. Across all fifteen class B1 receptors, the bond to 6.37x37 is absent from all 131 scorable active structures and the bond to 2.46x46 is present in 97 of 135, so the active-state arrangement holds family-wide; the exchange requires both states, and only GLP-1R carries enough inactive structures to show it. These three positions, together with a fourth at 8.47x47, have been described as a cytoplasmic polar network that holds the receptor inactive and breaks on activation, releasing its residues, a reading carried from homology models and mutagenesis through the first activated structure of the receptor to ligand-free G protein complexes of three class B1 receptors in 2024 and to a clinical report in the parathyroid hormone receptor in 2026 [1-7]. Release predicts that the pivot ends the transition bound to fewer partners. It does not: the number of salt bridges it makes does not change across the transition, only the identity of its partner. The inactive-state bond does break, as reported. The pivot is not released: it takes a second partner that is carried only in the active state. We name this arrangement an ionic router. An ionic router is a charged residue that exchanges salt-bridge partners between two conformational states: in each state it binds at least one oppositely charged partner that it does not bind in the other. Each arm is itself a lock, and the two are mutually exclusive: one is closed in each state, so the pivot is never free. The arrangement was found by an unbiased screen that ranked 2,257 charged positions across 61 receptors, scored only on the separation between partner-identity change and partner-count change. No measure of this form is reported in the literature, and a measure that scores one contact at a time cannot separate an exchange from a loss. The screen places the GLP-1R position first of 48 rankable positions in that receptor. Without reference to that result, it places the equivalent class A arrangement first of 38 rankable charged positions in bovine rhodopsin, recovering the exchange at E247 (6.30x30) between R135 (3.50x50) and K231 (5.66x66), partners that never contact one another in any structure. Prior reports describe the class A exchange from the ligand-free opsin structures, from NMR and from simulation [8-12], and propose an equivalent contact in the adenosine receptors from simulation [13, 14]. Recovering a documented arrangement without being directed at it is the control on the measure, and the measure then finds the class B1 instance at positions already described, where it reverses the direction assigned to them. It is the first such arrangement reported outside class A. The class A pairing could not have been used in GLP-1R: all fifteen class B1 receptors carry a glutamate where class A carries the arginine at 3.50x50, and that position is occupied instead by a histidine contact present in both states. A single side chain that registers activation state by which partner it holds is a candidate site for precision drug design and for understanding the molecular basis of disease.

papers.title: Low-Energy Electron Attachment to Catechin Sulphate
papers.abstract: Low-energy electron (LEE) attachment can initiate molecular fragmentation through temporary negative ion states, with autodetachment competing against nuclear motion toward dissociation. Here, we apply an improved local complex potential time-dependent wavepacket (LCP-TDWP) workflow to catechin sulphate, a metabolically relevant catechin conjugate for which, to our knowledge, a dedicated dissociative electron attachment (DEA) study has not been reported. The present model follows one C–O bond extension coordinate selected for cleavage leading to a C5-centered catechin-derived radical and the stable bisulfate anion, HSO_{4}^{-} . Neutral and anionic potential energy curves were calculated at the CAM-B3LYP/6-311++G(2d,2p) level, and vibrational eigenfunctions were obtained with the Fourier grid Hamiltonian method. A phenomenological coordinate-dependent width was constructed from an exponential envelope centered at the Franck–Condon coordinate, a Wigner-type energy factor based on the local anion–neutral energy difference, and a smooth switch near the curve crossing; its parameters were not benchmarked against an independent stabilization or CAP-EOM-EA width calculation. Propagation used a symmetric split operator with a 0.1000 fs time step for 1.000 ps and a complex absorbing potential (CAP) beginning at 7.250 a0. The neutral Franck–Condon coordinate and first relevant curve crossing are 2.659 and 3.327 a0, respectively, and the modeled width reaches 0.03434 eV. The autocorrelation spectrum has a doorway feature near 0.4512 eV, whereas the calculated DEA cross section peaks at 1.113 eV with a maximum of 4.608 Mb. The cumulative CAP loss from the initial packet at 1.000 ps is 0.003162 (0.3162%); this value is not a branching fraction or an experimentally measured DEA yield. These results provide a methodological basis for analyzing competition between autodetachment and a selected dissociation channel.

papers.title: Ice Deposition of Water Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry at Cryogenic Temperatures
papers.abstract: Water gas cluster ion beams (GCIBs) are increasingly used in cryogenic secondary ion mass spectrometry (cryo-SIMS) to improve the detection of biomolecules while preserving their molecular integrity. However, the effects of water cluster primary ion (PI) beams on cryogenically cooled surfaces are not yet fully understood. Here, we demonstrate that continuous bombardment with (H 2 O) n + GCIBs can induce ice deposition, which competes with sputtering and can ultimately obscure the underlying sample, thus compromising depth profiling and molecular analysis. Using deuterated (D 2 O) n + clusters and subsequent C60 + depth profiling, we confirmed that the deposited ice originates predominantly from water molecules introduced by the primary ion beam. Systematic investigation of cluster size and kinetic energy identified the energy per water molecule (E/n) as the key parameter governing the balance between net sputtering and ice deposition. Significant ice deposition occurred at E/n < 4 eV, whereas the substrate signal remained approximately constant at E/n > 5 eV. Measurements of the deposited ice cross-sections indicated that up to 40% of the incoming water molecules could remain on the surface under deposition-dominated conditions. Substrate temperature also influenced deposition, with ice accumulation observed below approximately 188 K for the investigated beam conditions. Experiments on copper, organic deposits, and mouse brain tissue further demonstrated that this phenomenon is not restricted to metallic substrates and that the deposition rate varies with surface composition. These findings establish beam energy per molecule, substrate temperature, and material-dependent sputtering behaviour as important factors controlling ice accumulation during cryo-SIMS using (H 2 O) n + GCIBs. Careful optimisation of GCIB parameters is therefore essential to minimise deposition artefacts and maintain reliable molecular depth profiling, particularly when cryogenic sample preservation is required. Lastly, the ability to deposit known amounts of ice in localised areas could prove useful for preparing samples with well-defined and controlled characteristics.

papers.title: When Can an Off-Cycle Reservoir Raise a Catalyst’s Turnover Number?
papers.abstract: Off-cycle species are typically considered detrimental to catalytic activity; however, a dormant form can also extend catalyst lifetime. This study shows under which conditions a reversible off-cycle reservoir can increase the turnover number (TON) of a homogeneous catalyst. When both turnover and all deactivation steps are first order in catalyst, branching remains constant over time and the reservoir only holds the catalyst in a dormant state, the distribution of turnovers per catalyst does not change, regardless of the number of reservoirs. The reaction is slowed, and under an external clock, such as a poison that forms independently of the catalyst, the TON decreases. When deactivation is of higher order in catalyst than turnover, a fast reservoir of depth acts as a -fold dilution. This increases the TON up to a ceiling set by the first-order deactivation pathways, and for a given batch time there is an optimal depth. In the published model of (DTBM-SEGPHOS)CuH, the HBpin adduct protects the catalyst from aggregation but is 2.9–5.9 times deeper than optimal. In Hoveyda–Grubbs metathesis, a styrenyl-ether reservoir slows the reaction threefold without reducing the TON. A reservoir can be beneficial only if the catalyst-limited TON decreases as catalyst loading increases, that is, if the slope of log TON against log loading is negative. Dilution experiments and a series with graded amounts of additive then show whether it will be.

papers.title: Patterning Conductive Aluminium onto Temperature Sensitive Polymers and Tattoo Paper at Room Temperature and Pressure
papers.abstract: Currently patterning conductive metal onto thermally fragile substrates remains hindered by the necessary processing conditions required. Aluminium is an attractive conductor for printed electronics, being non-toxic, low cost, having high abundance, while providing excellent electrical conductivity. Here, we report the direct deposition of conductive aluminium lines onto a selection of heat sensitive substrates; namely dissolvable tattoo paper, and a Polyborosiloxane (PBS)/Sylgard blend substrate at room temperature and atmospheric pressure using an atmospheric-pressure plasma jet (APPJ) and an ethereal solution of dimethylethylamine alane (DMEAA) as a metal-organic precursor ink. Unlike conventional metal-organic decomposition methods that require thermal post-treatment, the non-equilibrium plasma drives precursor fragmentation, ligand removal, and metallic film formation in a single step without external substrate heating. Optimised tracks were produced on dissolvable tattoo paper yielding a best sheet resistance of 1.59 ± 0.64 kΩ/sq due to its metallic nature. The tracks were deposited directly onto dissolvable tattoo paper, and sufficiently conductive to complete a functional electrical circuit allowing it to be transferred to skin, demonstrating a viable route to low-temperature aluminium metallisation on porous substrates.

papers.title: Cerium Photoredox-Catalyzed Ring Expansion of Cyclic Allylic Alcohols
papers.abstract: Medium-sized aliphatic rings are underrepresented in drug discovery despite their advantageous balance of rigidity and flexibility. Existing synthetic limitations hinder broader exploration of this valuable chemical space. This work presents a general and efficient method for the one- and two-carbon ring expansion of 5- and 6-membered allylic alcohols to larger cyclic ketones using cerium-based photoredox catalysis. Employing ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) activation, a dual catalytic system featuring Ce(OTf)3 and 9,10-diphenylanthracene (DPA) enables selective generation of alkoxyl radicals under mild conditions. A hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) catalyst, (TRIPS)2, is critical for productive C–C bond formation and radical termination. The method tolerates various nitrogen-protecting groups, vinyl substitutions, and ring systems, including bridged and fused frameworks, affording 7- and 8-membered ketones in moderate to excellent yields (38–98%). Notably, expansion to challenging [5.2.1] bicyclic and fused benzannulated scaffolds is demonstrated. This strategy offers a divergent and synthetically accessible route to sp3-rich, conformationally diverse drug-like scaffolds from simple precursors.

papers.title: Enthalpy-Driven Design Rules for Multi-Shell Multimetallic Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Multimetallic nanoparticles (NPs) offer access to a vast compositional and architectural design space, yet controlled formation of core-shell and multi-shell architectures rapidly becomes unpredictable as compositional complexity increases. As a result, architectural outcomes are often regarded as system-specific and governed primarily by kinetic effects. Here, we identify a unifying thermodynamic principle that governs shell formation in multimetallic NPs based on binary mixing enthalpies and phase behaviour. By systematically establishing enthalpy-driven rules in binary NPs and extending them to higher-order compositions, we show that elemental segregation and the composition and sequence of multiple shells in NPs containing up to five elements are predictable despite their combinatorial complexity, even when synthesised in a simple one-pot wet-chemical reaction. These results demonstrate that thermodynamic interactions maintain predictive power as compositional complexity increases and provide a general framework for rationalising architectural design in multimetallic NPs.

papers.title: Catalytic N -Cbz Deprotection of Amino Acids and Dipeptides over Spherical SiliaCat Pd(0)
papers.abstract: Investigation of hydrogenolytic removal of N -benzyloxycarbonyl ( N -Cbz) protecting groups from amino acid and dipeptide derivatives mediated by spherical SiliaCat Pd(0) under mild conditions using an H 2 -filled balloon allowed to optimize reaction parameters including solvent composition, substrate concentration, Pd loading, temperature, and catalyst particle size. The spherical catalyst enabled efficient N -Cbz deprotection at Pd loadings as low as 0.25–0.50 mol% under selected conditions, with high conversions, isolated yields, and selectivities across a broad range of amino acid derivatives. The methodology was successfully extended to N -Cbz-protected dipeptides, although substrate-specific optimization of solvent composition and Pd loading was required for more challenging substrates. Catalyst particle size primarily influenced reaction kinetics, with smaller particles providing faster deprotection, and larger particles advantageous for packed-bed continuous-flow applications. The catalyst showed useful chemoselectivity in the presence of Boc and tert -butyl ester protecting groups, while selective N -Cbz removal in the presence of benzyl esters could be achieved through appropriate control of reaction conditions. Comparison with commercial heterogeneous Pd catalysts showed that the spherical organosilica catalyst provided a favorable combination of complete conversion, high isolated yields, and consistently low Pd leaching. Overall, these results establish spherical SiliaCat Pd(0) as a practical, non-pyrophoric, and versatile heterogeneous catalyst for N -Cbz deprotection of amino acid and dipeptide derivatives, supporting its application in peptide-oriented synthesis.

papers.title: Artificial Cells with a Cytoskeleton from Synthetic Self-Replicating Molecules
papers.abstract: Living cells couple molecular replication and cytoskeletal assembly to changes in shape and mechanical stability, but reconstructing this relationship in synthetic compartments remains challenging. Here, we confine self-replicating supramolecular fibers within giant polymer lipid hybrid vesicle-based artificial cells. Seeded replicator growth produces luminal fiber networks and deforms the surrounding membrane into spindle-like morphologies, with fiber and membrane interactions controlled by membrane composition and fiber glycation. Covalent crosslinking of the fiber network within the lumen enables the artificial cells to withstand cellular aggregation during prolonged co-culture. The stabilized artificial cells remain incorporated within HepaRG cell-based microtissues for 28 days while the surrounding cells differentiate into hepatocyte- and biliary-like phenotypes. These results establish a chemical route by which assembly-driven replicators within a compartment can generate cytoskeletal

papers.title: Rigor & Reproducibility in Electrocatalysis: Best Practices for Kinetic Studies
papers.abstract: Kinetic measurements can support or falsify mechanistic hypotheses in electrocatalysis, but only when rates reflect intrinsic catalytic behavior and models separate kinetic information from experimental artifacts and interfacial complexity. This perspective presents best practices for acquiring and interpreting electrocatalytic kinetic data, including mitigating artifacts arising from transport, ohmic losses, catalyst restructuring, contamination, and incomplete product accounting. Similarly, we provide guidelines for constructing rate expressions that treat elementary charge transfer, adsorption, and surface coverage, which enable interpretation of kinetic observables like apparent transfer coefficients, rate orders, and apparent activation energies that reflect properties of an interconnected reaction network. Mechanistic conclusions are strongest when competing hypotheses are tested against multiple complementary observables, including spectroscopy, isotopic labeling, and theory, enabling meaningful and reproducible mechanistic comparisons across laboratories.

papers.title: Gold-Mediated Cascade Cyclization on-route to the Total Synthesis of (−)‑Presilphiperfolan-1-ol
papers.abstract: We report a concise and convergent total synthesis of (−)-presilphiperfolan-1-ol, a highly strained tricyclic sesquiterpene bearing five contiguous stereocenters.
