The catechol catalyst exhibits broad functional group tolerance in diverse substrate combinations. Further, the reaction was performed on multigram scale under solvent-free conditions. Combined NMR spectroscopic studies, titrations, kinetic experiments, and DFT calculations suggest a concentration-dependent association of the catechol catalyst into dimers or higher aggregates. Remarkably, 4-bromocatechol outperformed established hydrogen-bond donor catalysts. These results establish catechol as a simple, readily tuneable, and highly effective hydrogen-bond donor motif and provide a fundamental understanding of their high activity.

papers.title: Accelerating Mechanistic Understanding and Prediction of Chemical Selectivity with Foundation Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Selectivity in chemical reactions is often dictated by small energetic differences between competing transition states of less than 2 kcal mol -1 . Computational predictions of selectivity for organic and organometallic reactions must reach these levels of quantitative accuracy, while simultaneously navigating the mechanistic and conformational complexity involved. Here, we assess the suitability of foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for this task. We introduce the SELECT50 dataset, a chemically diverse collection of paired selectivity-determining transition state structures, evaluated at the ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPD//ωB97X-D3(BJ)/def2-TZVP level of theory, spanning representative cases of kinetically-controlled stereo-, chemo- and regioselectivities, along with competing mechanistic pathways. We compare the performance of four MLIPs, alongside semiempirical and low-cost quantum chemical approaches, in determining transition state geometries, energetic discrimination, and pathway ordering. The Universal Model for Atoms MLIPs UMA-M-1.1 and UMA-S-1.2 predict relative transition state energies with sub-kcal mol -1 accuracy and mean absolute errors of 0.36 and 0.44 kcal mol -1 , providing saddle points that closely reproduce triple-ζ DFT geometries. DFT single-point refinement further reduced the mean absolute error (MAE) to 0.25 kcal mol -1 , supporting DFT//MLIP as a practical strategy for selectivity prediction. The major reaction pathway was correctly assigned in up to 98% of cases. Beyond individual transition structures, MLIPs reproduce complete organic and organometallic reaction landscapes and enable full-system treatment of selectivity-determining assemblies containing up to 211 atoms. Finally, MLIP-derived transition state energetics strongly track experimental selectivity across Ni- and Pd catalyzed reaction families (R 2 = 0.87–0.90; ρ = 0.80), and with calibration, yield mean held-out MAEs of 0.12 and 0.63 kcal mol -1 . Our results position foundation MLIPs as practical surrogates for the exploration and screening stages of DFT-based mechanistic analyses, enabling the throughput required for large-scale catalyst, substrate, and reaction screening.

papers.title: Ab-initio Exploration of Structural, Electronic, Optical and Transport Properties of Rb2Te Photocathodes
papers.abstract: Using state-of-the-art first-principles calculations based on hybrid density functional theory, we investigate the key material properties governing photoemission in Rb2Te for photocathode applications. Multiple crystalline phases of Rb2Te are examined, among which the α-and ω-phases are found to be both dynamically and mechanically stable. These phases exhibit exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivities of 0.27 Wm−1K−1 and 1.61 Wm−1K−1 for the α-and ω-phases, respectively. Analysis of phonon transport reveals that low-frequency acoustic and optical modes dominate the lattice thermal conductivity. Furthermore, the calculated intrinsic electron mobilities are 22.11 cm2V−1 s−1 for the α-phase and 20.91 cm2V−1 s−1 for the ω-phase, while the corresponding hole mobilities are significantly lower, at 0.46 cm2V−1 s−1 and 0.14 cm2V−1 s−1, respectively. The limited carrier mobility is primarily attributed to strong scatterings of the carriers by the polar optical phonons. This work provides microscopic insight into the electronic, vibrational, elastic, and transport properties of Rb2Te and its suitability for photocathode applications.

papers.title: Contact-electro-catalytic degradation of 4-hydroxybenzoic acid using PTFE
papers.abstract: This study introduces an ultrasound-powered contact-electro-catalysis (CEC) method for degrading 4-hydroxybenzoic acid (HBA) using polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) microparticles. Under neutral conditions, the system achieved over 99% HBA degradation in aqueous solutions. Mechanistic analysis confirms that hydroxyl radicals act as the primary oxidants. HBA degradation proceeds via primary hydroxylation and secondary decarboxylation pathway. The effects of acidic and alkaline conditions were investigated, demonstrating the non-innocent role of counter ions. Furthermore, recycling tests showed that the PTFE catalyst retains high structural integrity and consistent degradation efficiencies (96%–99%) of HBA across consecutive cycles. These findings demonstrate the potential of ultrasound-driven CEC as a robust technology for wastewater remediation.

papers.title: Spontaneous Curvature and Differential Leaflet Tension Are Additive Drives for Outward Membrane Budding
papers.abstract: Two recent models derive outward plasma-membrane budding from different starting points. Mahapatra, Malingen and Rangamani treat a microparticle as a Helfrich membrane in which phosphatidylserine exposed on the outer leaflet imposes a local spontaneous curvature over a prescribed domain, coupled to cortex linkers modelled as springs. Our own treatment derives an energetic threshold from the differential tension between leaflets generated by a net transbilayer lipid flux, with vesicle size as an output rather than an input. Here we show that the two are not alternatives: they are the two linear terms of one energy functional. Writing the bud energy with both a spontaneous curvature c0 and a differential leaflet tension ∆τ , the expression collapses—once the energy the flat reference state already carries at the same spontaneous curvature is subtracted—to the canonical form ∆E(r) = 8πκ − 4πFr + 4πΣr2, with an additive drive F = 2κc0 + h ∆τ and a resistance Σ = σ + w + KAh2/R2 containing neither drive. Budding requires F 2 > 8κΣ; the bud radius is r∗ = F/2Σ, equal to √ 2κ/Σ on the threshold locus. The additivity is exact. It is the single effective combination already known from area-difference elasticity [5, 7], written here as a force and thereby made comparable between the two treatments. A dimensionless ratio Ξ = 2κc0/(h∆τ) orders the contributions, and we exhibit a case in which each drive alone leaves the membrane below threshold, at 0.25 and 0.49 of it, while together they carry it across at 1.44 and bud at 91 nm. Evaluated with the bending moduli and boundary tensions of the curvature model, r∗ spans 41–414 nm and brackets the 45–63 nm domain sizes that model takes as input, which is a consistency check rather than a discriminating test. Retaining the KAh2/R2 term repairs the tension-free limit: the threshold does not vanish but tends to ∆ac → √ 2κ/KA/h, recovering the O(1) areadifference criterion as a derived result. We then argue that the two drives are not simultaneous—one scramblase generates differential leaflet tension transiently and spontaneous curvature persistently, so Ξ sweeps across a single calcium response, and the departing bud exports the phosphatidylserine that drove it—which makes the discriminating experiment a time course rather than a titration.

papers.title: Formate Electrosynthesis via Selective Ethylene Glycol Oxidation on Ni-Modified CeO2−x/NF
papers.abstract: Ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR) offers a route to replace the anodic oxygen evolution reaction while converting ethylene glycol into value-added products. Here, electrodeposited CeO2−x//NF and Ni-modified CeO2−x/NF were evaluated for EGOR in alkaline electrolyte. Ni modification markedly enhanced the polarization response, enabling a current density of 100 mA cm-2 at 1.61 V vs RHE without iR compensation, approximately 97 mV lower than that of the parent CeO2−x/NF electrode at the same current density. During potentiostatic EGOR at 1.8 V vs RHE in 1 M KOH containing 1 M ethylene glycol, the parent and Ni-modified electrodes sustained average current densities of 192 and 241 mA cm-2, respectively. 1H-NMR analysis identified formate as the dominant detected liquid product, with estimated formate Faradaic efficiencies of 83.2% and 92.9%, respectively. These results show that Ni modification enhances EGOR activity while maintaining efficient formate formation on CeO2−x-based electrodes.

papers.title: Synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation on microplastic and nanoplastic removal from stormwater runoff in bioretention systems
papers.abstract: Microplastics and nanoplastics (MNPs) are emerging contaminants in stormwater runoff, posing potential ecological and human health risks. Bioretention systems offer promising nature-based stormwater treatment, yet their performance remains highly variable. Biochar, particularly post-processed biochar, has demonstrated strong potential for contaminant removal; however, its effects on MNP removal, leachate quality, and plant performance in green infrastructure remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the combined effects of untreated and thermal air-oxidated (hereinafter: treated) biochars and native vegetation ( Rudbeckia hirta ) on the removal of polystyrene MNPs (0.02, 0.2, and 1 μm) from synthetic stormwater runoff, leachate quality and plant performance in bioretention systems. Both biochars effectively removed nanoplastics during the early MNP-spiked storm events. Vegetation substantially reduced MNP leaching during subsequent simulated rainfall events, supported by the detection of microplastics within root tissues, indicating plant uptake. Vegetation also reduced nutrient leaching, with larger plants exhibiting more pronounced effects, highlighting the importance of enhancing plant growth for contaminant removal. Although treated biochar reduced total organic carbon leaching during initial spiking events, both biochars increased P, K, and S leaching. Overall, our findings demonstrate synergistic effects of biochar and vegetation in enhancing contaminant retention in bioretention systems, advancing green infrastructure design and sustainable stormwater management.

papers.title: Disclosing the Effect of Activation on the Micro- and Meso-structure of Activated Carbons with SANS and Gas Sorption
papers.abstract: Tuning the performance of a porous material is a major leap towards more efficient use and reduced production costs. The performance of activated carbons (ACs) in applications such as catalysis, energy storage, and environmental remediation is closely linked to their micro- and meso-structure, side to their surface chemistry. However, their intrinsic disorder and large panel of possible synthetic treatments bring to a complex structure that standard analysis technique only are not capable to depict entirely. To access a complete understanding of such a complex pore architecture, we coupled standard gas physisorption (N 2 at 77 K, Ar at 87 K and CO 2 at 273 K), with Small-Angle Neutron Scattering (SANS) to investigate five ACs obtained from different precursors and activation methods. By integrating gas physisorption and SANS, we obtain a coherent picture of the pore architecture and its dependence on activation strategy, revealing that the activation method governs pore structure more than the precursor type. SANS further reveals structural details beyond the reach of Ar adsorption alone by reconciling the competing models of non-graphitic carbon microstructures (i.e. curved vs flat carbon platelets) – suggesting that the balance in between models contribution depends on the activation strategy. Contrast matching with D 2 O further reveals that water actively modifies the carbon framework, compressing and curving defective layers. These results – relying on previous knowledge of the surface chemistry of the very same samples – provide a multi-scale understanding of structure and properties of ACs, clarifying how activation shapes microstructure, porosity and surface chemistry, with direct implications for their performance in real-world applications.

papers.title: Outpacing H-Phosphonate Oxidation: Enantioconvergent Deborylative Synthesis of α-Stereogenic Alkyl Phosphonates
papers.abstract: The growing biomedical relevance of α-stereogenic alkyl phosphonates, such as their use in enhancing the metabolic stability of oligonucleotide therapeutics, motivates versatile approaches to their asymmetric synthesis. The enantioconvergent coupling of C(sp3) building blocks and H-phosphonates offers a straightforward synthetic disconnection. Herein we report the first asymmetric deborylative C(sp3)–P coupling, harnessing the synthetic modularity of alkylboron reagents to streamline access to structurally diverse, enantioenriched α-stereogenic alkyl phosphonates. Developing an oxidative C(sp3)–P coupling must contend with the susceptibility of H-phosphonates to oxidation, a property underlying their established use as sacrificial reductants in copper catalysis. We propose a twofold strategy to overcome the facile P–H oxidation: (1) kinetically favoring N–H over P–H activation to promote aminyl-radical-mediated C(sp3)–BPin bond scission and (2) incorporating a strong X-type donor into the chiral ligand to suppress Cu(II)–P homolysis. The resulting transformation combines high enantioselectivity with broad tolerance for functional groups and pharmaceutically relevant heterocycles. Cyclic voltammetry supports our proposal that an anionic pincer ligand renders Cu(II) less oxidizing than its neutral counterparts. The stoichiometric reaction of the transient Cu(II)–phosphonate intermediate with a persistent trityl radical establishes its competence for C(sp3)–P bond formation. Hammett analysis revealed accelerated coupling of electron-deficient alkylboron substrates, corroborating the design principle that increasing electron density at Cu, as achieved with the anionic ligand scaffold, promotes the oxidative coupling. Density functional theory calculations identified C(sp3)–P reductive elimination as the enantiodetermining step and attributed stereocontrol to differences in alkyl-fragment distortion energy within the chiral ligand pocket. Together, these findings establish ligand-controlled modulation of Cu redox properties and radical-trapping reactivity as a strategy for reconciling asymmetric oxidative coupling with oxidation-sensitive nucleophiles.

papers.title: Polymorphism, Crystal Habit and Intermolecular Contact Topology in Benzothiazine Derivatives: A Comparative Hirshfeld Surface Analysis of Seven Crystal Structures
papers.abstract: Seven deposited benzothiazine crystal structures (CCDC 1835802, 1835803, 1964377–1964379, and 2102851–2102852) were reanalysed to distinguish differences in periodic crystal structures from crystal habit and positional disorder. Eight independent molecular environments were evaluated with fragment-based Hirshfeld surfaces and element-resolved contact contributions in Multiwfn. Convergence was assessed at grid spacings of 0.20 and 0.15 Bohr and with crystal-environment clusters extending to 4 and 6 Å. In the 2018 polymorph pair, H···C/C···H contributions increase from 10.647% in 2M to 16.932% in 2O (6 Å, 0.15 Bohr), whereas H···H decreases from 40.277% to 36.922%. The 2020 deposits share closely similar major contact contributions, with H···F/F···H ranging from 24.193% to 24.600%. The two independent molecules of monoclinic CCDC 2102852 exhibit distinct H···C/C···H fractions of 19.048% and 22.066%. Alternative orientations of the disordered CF 3 group in CCDC 1964379 preserve the identity of the dominant contact categories but change the F···F contribution from 3.482% (major) to 1.884% (minor at all sites) or 2.871% (minor in the central molecule only). This comparative analysis illustrates the need to distinguish polymorphism, habit, disorder and chemical substitution when interpreting contact-area descriptors; percentage contributions do not measure interaction energies.

papers.title: Vinylene-Linked Covalent Organic Frameworks with Heteropore-Tuned Compact Motifs for Boosting Spin-Spin Interactions
papers.abstract: The rich porosity of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) renders them abundant mass transport channels and easily accessible active sites. However, relatively low compact skeletons of COFs are unfavorable for in-plane and out-of-plane electron spin coupling. Herein, we report a new π-extended polyheterocyclic aromatic derivative by fusing three 2,3-dimethylpyrazine moieties to a triphenylene core, which serves as a D3h-symmetric hexatopic monomer to undergo Knoevenagel condensation smoothly with linear dialdehyde aromatics, forming a novel type of two-dimensional vinylene-linked COFs. Their three pairs of vinylene linkages at the adjacent positions of each disc-like vertex with seven fused aromatic rings tend to geometrically constrain the orientation and alleviate the congestion in the chain growth process, leading to in-plane compact Kagome motifs, alternatively patterned with the pseudohexagonal micropore and triangular ultramicropore. The as-prepared COFs enable efficient uptake of iodine molecules and generate a strong charge transfer complex at the pyridine nitrogen atoms, as revealed by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) signals. The resultant radicals, densely confined in the highly ordered reticular skeletons, allow for unidirectional electron spin alignment, which further induces a typical ferromagnetic phase transition, delivering metal-free magnetism with a tunable intensity through the compacting of the backbones of COFs.

papers.title: Calcium Poly(heptazine imide): Reproducible Synthesis for Structural Analysis, Mechanism of CO <sub>2</sub> Uptake, and Evaluation of Photocatalytic CO <sub>2</sub> - to-CO Conversion
papers.abstract: The framework material, calcium poly(heptazine imide) or CaPHI, is reportedly capable for CO 2 absorption, although harsh conditions from literature synthesis method result in low and unpredictable yield that hinders evaluation of its applicability for CO 2 capture and conversion (CCC). This work presents a synthesis procedure for CaPHI with cross-laboratory reproducibility and scalable to 100s mg by employing a CaCl 2 -based eutectic as synthesis medium. Comprehensive characterization confirmed the PHI structure, with Ca 2+ residing in the structural porosity having ionic conductivity of 10 -10 –10 -11 S cm -1 as estimated by electrochemical measurements. In addition to the literature’s physisorption mechanism for dry CO 2 , we demonstrated these Ca 2+ to participate in direct air capture of humid CO 2 , which chemisorbs as CaCO 3 from structural analyses. For photocatalytic CO 2 -to-CO conversion, CaPHI outperforms its K + -bearing counterpart, which we speculatively attributed to strong Ca 2+ –CO 2 interactions that concentrate this reactant near the active sites. In establishing a reliable synthesis and demonstrating its ability for CO 2 capture and photoreduction, further optimization of CaPHI’s structure, morphology and compositing with co-catalyst could reveal its potential for CCC, while incorporation of mobile Ca 2+ may represent a broad design principle warranting future research for material development for improving the efficiency of carbon capture & utilization.

papers.title: Development of 3D-Printed Photoreactors for Medicinal Chemistry Applications
papers.abstract: 3D-Printing has revolutionised the landscape of life sciences by enabling the rapid and affordable creation of bespoke equipment. The adaptation and design of light, cheap and easy to use photoredox reactors, where temperature control is introduced by compressed air flow, has allowed our laboratories to access a standardised and reproducible setup for all photoredox experiments. This work highlights the favourable comparison between these in-house 3D printed reactors and commercially available equipment across three industry-relevant transformations, decarboxylative sp2-sp3 coupling, cross-electrophile sp2-sp3 coupling and synthesis of aryl ethers. Furthermore, we report and share the design of a 3D-printed High Throughput Experimentation (HTE) box that enables rapid reaction optimisation, scoping and structure-activity relationship (SAR) generation in medicinal chemistry projects.

papers.title: Toward Interpretable Graph-Based Machine Learning for Combustion Kinetic Model Generation
papers.abstract: This work presents an atom-conserving and interpretable graph neural network (GNN) for combustion kinetic model generation, where atoms are represented as nodes, covalent bonds are represented as edges, and reactions are represented as bond-rearrangement operations. Its artificial-intelligence (AI) contribution is a reaction generator that extends a standard Graph Isomorphism Network with Edges (GINE) architecture through reaction-context embeddings, reaction branching & third-body reaction inputs, Arrhenius-rate-parameter prediction, pairwise decoding, and stochastic inference over evolving reactant pools. Trained on the Li–Dryer hydrogen combustion kinetic model (8 species and 21 reactions), the GNN reproduces trained chemistry and generates element-balanced new reactions and intermediate species outside the training dataset, many of which have experimental analogues. When trained on a subset of the Li–Dryer dataset, the model recovered most held-out reactions and revealed relationships between samples (reactions) in the model’s latent space. The results suggest that the model learns transferable local reaction structures and generates valid species and reactions. As with any reaction generators, the generated reaction models require thermochemical and kinetic verification; the intended engineering application is low-cost reaction-pathway exploration for new fuels and prioritization of experiments and first-principles calculations to develop new combustion kinetic models.

papers.title: Electrochemically-driven dynamic surface chemistry breaks the selectivity-conversion tradeoff in the oxidative coupling of methane
papers.abstract: The partial oxidation of methane to C 2 products such as ethylene (C 2 H 4 ) and ethane (C 2 H 6 ) is a notoriously challenging catalytic reaction since the key properties, namely the C 2 selectivity and CH 4 conversion, scale inversely with each other. Despite decades of research on catalyst design, this fundamental C2 selectivity-CH4 conversion tradeoff remains a preeminent challenge. 1 While traditional thermochemical catalyst design approaches seem inadequate to surmount said challenge, the electrochemical oxidative coupling of methane (EOCM) presents an alternative approach to enhance catalytic performance by dynamically altering the working state of the catalyst. In this study, we use (La, Sr) 1-x TiO 3±δ as a model system to demonstrate how electrochemistry enables one to dynamically tune the surface chemistry for enhancing C 2 selectivity. Depending on the bulk composition, we observe either step changes in C 2 selectivity or even a continuously increasing C 2 selectivity trend by using La 0.24 Sr 0.60 TiO 3-δ : this composition, once electrochemically activated, can break the traditional OCM tradeoff. We demonstrate that any C 2 selectivity enhancement effects are determined by the surface La/Ti and Sr/Ti ratios which dynamically evolve under electrocatalytic conditions. The enrichment of La at these surfaces is central to enhanced C 2 selectivity values and is crucially modulated by both the initial surface and bulk composition. The results presented herein highlight the potential of electrochemical materials activation for overcoming traditional challenges in partial methane oxidation and provide guidance on materials design for maximizing the C 2 selectivity of EOCM.

papers.title: A Broadly Deployable Method for Repeated Hyperpolarized <sup>13</sup> C Metabolic Imaging in Living Animals
papers.abstract: Hyperpolarized 13 C-MRI enables real-time imaging of metabolic conversions in vivo, but remains largely restricted to specialized sites with superconducting high-field MRI and polarization infrastructure. Here we present a broadly deployable method for preclinical hyperpolarized 13 C-metabolic imaging, which combines signal amplification by reversible exchange (SABRE), a parahydrogen-based hyperpolarization technique, with detection of [1- 13 C]pyruvate-d 3 in a compact 436 mT permanent-magnet small-animal MRI system. SABRE yields 13 C-pyruvate polarization of 13% at ~30 mM in a purified, biocompatible solution, with a T 1 relaxation time of 140 s. In a transgenic breast cancer mouse model, 13 C-chemical shift imaging after injection resolves pyruvate, pyruvate hydrate and lactate in vivo, maps elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratios in mammary tumors and images three freshly prepared pyruvate doses sequentially in the same animal in less than one hour. This compact SABRE-to-low-field method makes repeated hyperpolarized 13 C-metabolic imaging mobile and accessible in standard preclinical research environments.

papers.title: Galvanic Coupling Links Heterogeneous and Molecular Palladium Catalysis in Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
papers.abstract: Thermochemical catalytic reactions often consist of coupled electrochemical half-reactions, which can even serve to generate the active catalyst itself. Here we show that oxygen reduction on heterogeneous palladium drives corrosion of Pd through galvanic coupling: oxygen reduction consumes the electrons released by oxidation of Pd(0) on the same catalyst, while the soluble Pd(II) forms a homogeneous complex which facilitates benzyl alcohol oxidation. Combining corrosion measurements with quantification of Pd(II) and reaction products, we find that supplying more O 2 raises the catalyst potential and accelerates Pd(II) generation and alcohol oxidation rates. Applying equivalent electrochemical potentials in the absence of O 2 reproduces Pd(II) generation, and alcohol oxidation rates follow a similar dependence on the catalyst potential, which suggests that Pd corrosion is the kinetic link to thermochemical turnover. Diverting the anodic reaction to a sacrificial anode suppresses Pd(II) generation and thus the thermochemical reaction rate. Hence, O 2 has two roles: it sets the potential for forming the molecular catalyst and regenerates Pd(II) after alcohol oxidation. Together, our results show that galvanic coupling provides a framework that links electrochemistry and thermochemical catalysis.

papers.title: The eventful journey of a ligand in and out of the binding site
papers.abstract: The route a ligand follows to reach and leave a protein binding site typically involves complex molecular mechanisms that shape its efficacy as a biologically active compound. These mechanisms are reflected in the binding and unbinding kinetics, which often predict biological activity better than binding affinity alone, yet their calculation remains a bottleneck in ligand characterization. Here, we propose an approach that combines committor-based enhanced sampling with spectral analysis of the infinitesimal generator to characterize in detail how a ligand reaches the binding site of a protein and is eventually expelled. Applied to the paradigmatic benzamidine (BEN)–trypsin complex and the congeneric para-amino benzamidine (PAB), this framework reveals distinct and multifaceted binding pathways for the two ligands, uncovering a previously uncharacterized BEN binding site that competes with the crystallographic site, while identifying a common rotational bottleneck for unbinding. The computed unbinding free energies closely agree with experimental measurements. The spectral decomposition of the infinitesimal generator provides access to the slow dynamical modes of the system. From the slowest mode, we derive residence times and kinetic rate constants that agree with available experimental data and with independent OPES flooding simulations, while requiring substantially less computational effort. This approach offers a privileged perspective to resolve the complexity of protein–ligand binding-unbinding process, with potential applications to ligand screening and the characterization of multiple binding sites.

papers.title: Mapping How Ligands Shape Spin-State Thermodynamics in Fe(II)N6 Complexes: Insights from the SCO ATLAS
Directional Control of Droplet Motion via Geometric Gating
papers.abstract: We explore new methods for inducing the movement of water droplets on elastomeric substrates, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Our approach builds upon the well-known phenomenon that water droplets move easily across these substrates when swelled with silicone oil. While designing shallow open channels and traps on a PDMS film offers a simple way to control a droplet's trajectory by tilting the substrate in two orthogonal directions, this method is poorly suited for manipulating multiple droplets simultaneously. To address this limitation, we introduce two new methods. The first method utilizes a piano-concave PDMS platform with a radius of curvature significantly larger than the size of the droplet and its translation distance. When the system's configuration is altered, this curved substrate consistently guides the droplet along a curved geodesic. The second method incorporates diode-like gates on the PDMS. These gates are created on either flat or piano-concave PDMS films by embedding thin, rigid plates into the elastomer prior to crosslinking, followed by swelling in silicone oil. This process generates sigmoidal steps that restrict droplet motion to a single direction. Finally, we demonstrate how combining these two strategies enables various forms of directed motion for both single and multiple droplets.

papers.title: Flow-Through Capture Reversed-Phase to Hydrophilic Interaction Chromatography HRMS/MS to Expand Chemical Coverage in Environmental Non-Targeted Analysis.
papers.abstract: Chemical coverage remains a major limitation in environmental non-targeted analysis (NTA), as conventional one-dimensional liquid chromatography (1D-LC) provides incomplete retention and separation across the broad physicochemical space of complex samples. To extend NTA coverage, we developed an online two-dimensional liquid chromatography–high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (2DLC–HRMS/MS) approach that combines reversed-phase (RPLC) and hydrophilic interaction (HILIC) separations. Flow-through capture (FTC) modulation collects the unretained RPLC fraction using a dual-trap system combining porous graphitic carbon and trimodal reversed-phase, cation- and anion-exchange sorbents, recovering complementary sample polarity space regions within a single analysis. FTC effective transfer to HILIC was tested on a representative set of polar and mobile contaminants of emerging concern (CECs), with recoveries generally ranging from 35–100%. Feature-based NTA performance of the optimized FTC 2DLC method was compared in real water samples vs the corresponding 1D-HILIC and 1D-RPLC. FTC 2DLC yielded approximately 2.3–2.6-fold more features than individual 1D separations under both acquisition polarities. Beyond feature level coverage, data-independent componentization demonstrated that precursor-associated MS/MS information increased and was successfully distributed across both HILIC and RPLC chromatographic domains. Fragment Ambiguity Score (FAS) analysis further confirmed low-ambiguity, structurally informative fragments within the expanded separation space. Our results show that exposing the unretained fraction from RPLC separation to HILIC-MS expands the measurable chemical space and provides fragmentation information relevant to structural annotation, supporting FTC RPLC→HILIC–HRMS/MS as a promising strategy to increase chemical coverage in environmental NTA.

papers.title: In-column Synthesis and Atomic-resolution Electron Microscopic Analysis of Metastable Reactive Nitrides
papers.abstract: Metastable and air-sensitive compounds are challenging to synthesize and characterize because their formation often requires harsh conditions and their structures can rapidly evolve upon exposure to the environment. Here, we demonstrate that a high-vacuum environment inside a transmission electron microscope (TEM) column can serve simultaneously as a reaction platform and an atomic-scale analytical tool for generating and interrogating such materials. Electron-beam irradiation on sodium azide (NaN3) produces crystalline sodium nitride (Na3N) at room temperature, despite the conventional decomposition of NaN3 into sodium and nitrogen. The formation of Na3N is supported by high-resolution TEM, electron diffraction, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, which reveal correlated structural and compositional changes through irradiation. The resulting Na3N subsequently undergoes oxidation through an amorphous intermediate to form polycrystalline Na2O. The high-vacuum environment sufficiently suppresses this reaction to resolve its otherwise unachievable microscopic mechanisms. Extending this approach to potassium azide (KN3), we observe a transient crystalline phase that is most consistently indexed as K3N, a nitride known to be thermally unstable even under room temperature. Its transient appearance and decay indicate a dynamic balance between electron-beam-induced formation and degradation. These results establish in-column electron-beam chemistry as a route to metastable nitride formation while enabling multimodal characterization of highly reactive products. More broadly, this strategy offers a means of exploring nonequilibrium metastable compounds that are difficult to access using conventional synthesis and characterization workflows.

papers.title: Rate Theory in Chemical Potentials and without Transmission Coefficients: A Proposal
papers.abstract: Most microkinetic models of catalytic, electrochemical, and chemical reactions neither define nor measure the transition-state theory behind their rate constants, and whether a step recrosses, tunnels, or passes non-adiabatically is unknown. This paper proposes to write rate theory for these applications in chemical potentials, so that the configurational count that a rate law assumes is explicit. It proposes, second, to write the rate in its exact form at the thermal reference rate, at which the coupling of every reactant microstate to every product microstate defines the energetic chemical potential of the transition state. This chemical potential is exact but in general not computable, and every established rate theory is a computable model of it. The transmission coefficient of a model is the correction factor from that model to the exact rate, so it belongs to the model and not to the rate law. With the transition state described by its two populations, coupled to the reactant and to the product state, mass action, Langmuir, Butler-Volmer, and the classical two-rate-constant law are special cases of the exact form. Written in chemical potentials, the treatment of the symmetry factor by Marcus and by Agmon and Levine is explicitly limited to the energetic piece of the driving force. Likewise, the Sabatier principle takes a more precise form, because an interior optimum of the overall rate of an unbranched mechanism requires a configurational or energetic excess of the transition state to respond to the binding energy of an intermediate.

papers.title: Antisolvent precipitation of Zinc Porphyrin Hydrogen-Bonded Organic Frameworks Enables J-Aggregation Mediated Electrochemiluminescence for Synthetic Cannabinoid Sensing
papers.abstract: Zinc porphyrin hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (ZnTCPP HOFs) represent attractive electrochemiluminescence (ECL) luminophores; however, their tendency to undergo uncontrolled short-range π–π stacking at solid/liquid interfaces induces aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) and severely limits the ECL efficiency. Existing strategies for suppressing ACQ rely mainly on covalent or coordination-mediated ligand engineering and often require laborious multi-step synthesis. From the perspective of colloid and interface science, we herein report a chitosan (CS)–DMF antisolvent precipitation strategy that reorganizes the interfacial hydrogen-bond network between CS and the carboxyl groups of ZnTCPP HOFs, enabling a controlled transformation of bulk crystals into short-range aggregates with local J-type coupling. Such synergistic colloidal-interface regulation suppresses short-range π–π stacking while enabling J-aggregates to enhance the ECL emission, boosting the peak ECL intensity without the need for an additional co-reaction promoter. On this basis, an aptamer-based ECL sensor was constructed for the ultrasensitive detection of the synthetic cannabinoid 5F-EDMB-PINACA, achieving a limit of detection of 8.61 × 10 ⁻16 g/L together with satisfactory selectivity and reliable determination in e-cigarette liquid samples. These findings demonstrate that colloidal-interface regulation provides an efficient and synthesis-free route toward high-performance ECL sensing.

papers.title: Carbonyl Recycling Limits Productive Ethanol Formation during Syngas Conversion on Rh(211): A First-Principles Microkinetic Analysis
papers.abstract: Higher alcohol synthesis from syngas on Rh involves a highly branched and reversible reaction network in which formation of a C–C bond does not necessarily lead to a higher-alcohol product. Here, a thermodynamically consistent first-principles mean-field microkinetic model is used to determine how carbon is partitioned among methane, methanol, ethanol, and higher-carbon intermediates on Rh(211). Across a 100-point temperature–pressure domain, increasing turnover progressively favors methane and methanol over ethanol. CO insertion provides the dominant entry into the C₂ carbonyl pathway. However, 79–94% of this carbonyl flux is subsequently returned to C₁ species through the C–C bond scission of CH₃CO* to CH₃* + CO*, a process referred to here as carbonyl recycling . Consequently, the principal C–C-forming reactions carry substantial flux but have relatively small degree-of-rate-control coefficients for ethanol production. Instead, hydrogenation of ethoxy to adsorbed ethanol becomes increasingly rate controlling, while methane formation and oxygen-removal chemistry strongly influence ethanol productivity. CHO insertion contributes productively at low activity but carries net reverse flux at high activity, showing that a low forward activation barrier alone does not determine the steady-state direction of a reaction. Methanol provides an additional competing sink for oxygenated C₁ carbon. Within the present Rh(211) reaction network, higher-alcohol formation therefore depends not only on forming C–C bonds but also on preventing newly formed C₂ intermediates from returning to C₁ species before they are converted to ethanol.

papers.title: A single reference-energy outlier nearly eliminates Co–O chemistry from a generative model's training distribution
papers.abstract: An element-resolved audit of 44,688 oxide structures generated by MatterGen under chemical-system conditioning revealed that the aggregate composition compliance (73.27% exact match) concealed a severe chemistry-specific failure. Cobalt was omitted from 71.27% of the structures requesting it, against 8.12 ± 3.28% for the other 19 requested elements, and 98.17% of the cobalt omissions removed cobalt alone. Cell size, cation substitutability, stability gain and a general training-frequency effect did not account for the anomaly. Tracing the failure upstream showed that only one of the 8,924 cobalt oxides in the public Alex-MP-20 reference set passed the stability filter. The deficit was traced to a single anomalous reference-energy entry distorting the Co–O convex hull; excluding it raises the number of training-eligible cobalt oxides from 1 to 2,499. Four independent DFT calculations and the current Materials Project value agree within 0.024 eV atom-1, whereas the value implied by the released file deviates from them by 6.26 eV atom-1. A pre-registered intervention experiment showed that neither removal of the stability condition nor stronger diffusion guidance normalised the blind spot. These results show how a single high-leverage reference-energy anomaly can be amplified through stability filtering into a training deficit at the scale of a chemical family. Two audits that detect this class of failure without retraining are presented, namely an element-resolved condition-fidelity audit and a reference-hull vertex audit.

papers.title: Layered Double Hydroxides with Interlayer Electrons Activate Strong Chemical Bonds
papers.abstract: Layered electrides are an unusual class of materials in which excess electrons occupy interlayer regions and serve as anionic, charge-balancing species. Many prototypical layered electrides are based on subnitrides and subcarbides, motivating the search for new types of host structures. Here, we use density functional theory (DFT) to characterize a class of layered electrides derived from layered double hydroxides (LDHs). Through an anion–electron exchange process, we predict that several LDH compositions can stabilize an electride state wherein significant charge is confined in the interlayer galleries. We evaluate the thermodynamic and finite-temperature stability of the LDH electrides, demonstrating that the balance between stability and interlayer charge can be controlled through partial anion exchange. DFT calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that the interlayer electrons impart unique chemical reactivity by facilitating the activation of strong chemical bonds, such as the spontaneous dissociation of Br 2 and the reduction of CO 2 to formate.

papers.title: Open Sesame! Simulation of the Adsorption Induced Phase Transformation Mechanism of MOF Nanocrystallites
papers.abstract: One of the most compelling features of certain MOFs is their ability to undergo stimuli-induced phase transformations with large changes in the accessible pore volume, leading to phenomena like “gate opening”. Theoretical simulations are an indispensable tool in order to understand such processes on a molecular level. However, adsorption phenomena are usually investigated within the approximation of periodic boundary conditions (PBC) and using Grand Canonical methods. This ignores the interface to the gas reservoir and any transport effects, which prevents the investigation of transformation kinetics. Previously, we developed methods to simulate explicit MOF nanocrystallites beyond PBC with the aim to understand size effects. In this work, the results of the natural next step, namely an in silico adsorption experiment for DUT-8 (Cu) nanocrystallites (about 10 nm edge length) in a reservoir of carbon dioxide are presented: Unbiased molecular dynamics simulations reveal a surprisingly rapid gate opening within a few nanoseconds. The first-order phase transition is initiated by a characteristic pore opening at an edge of the crystallite. The anisotropy of the pillared-layer MOF, with its channels along the crystallographic c-axis, leads to a rapid transport along these channels when the pore opening of the MOF proceeds. The simulations allow for an unprecedented view on the molecular mechanism, including the structural transformation of the MOF and the connected transport of the guest molecules into the MOF pores. Already this first attempt of a realistic adsorption simulation beyond PBC revealed the widening of a single channel at the obtuse angle edge of the NC as the secret “Open Sesame!” to open the gate. This confirms that for an in–depth view into the kinetics of adsorption induced phase transformations, an explicit interface between MOF and gas reservoir is pivotal and serves as a basis for further investigations with even larger systems and more realistic surface terminations to be performed in the future.

papers.title: Tuning covalence for phosphorus-mediated C-C coupling in carbon monoxide electroreduction to multicarbon oxygenates
papers.abstract: Electrochemical carbon monoxide reduction (COR) is a promising route for sustainable production of multicarbon chemicals from CO2, as it bypasses the large carbon losses of direct CO2 electroreduction. In most electrocatalysts currently explored to tune COR selectivity towards highadded value multicarbon oxygenated molecules, like acetate and ethanol, copper is the catalytic site of C-C bond formation. Herein, we show that by designing nanoparticles of a strongly covalent copper compound, CuSi2P3, we retain isolated copper atoms during COR and trigger the intervention of phosphorus atoms as C-C coupling sites, without directly involving copper atoms. This profound change in COR mechanism results in a high selectivity towards C2 molecules (80 % Faradaic efficiency), especially oxygenates (73%), at a current density of -150 mA cm-2. This work reveals the importance of tailoring, via the crystal structure, the local environment of metal atoms, to achieve original selectivity in COR with new families of electrocatalysts.

papers.title: Head-to-tail cyclization of a peptide using a tethered homopolymer as a docking station for ring-closing and its extension to peptide cyclization and synthesis in the low bulk with mm-long tethers
papers.abstract: A physical extension to chemical procedures for head-to-tail cyclization of peptides at the single molecule level that uses a charged homopolymer (such as polyglutamate E m with m residues) as a tethered docking station to close a linear peptide at its N- and C-ends is proposed. The homopolymer may be anchored in three ways: 1) tethering one end to a nanopore in an electrolytic cell (e-cell); 2) immobilizing one end on a fixed glass slide similar to a flow cell surface in fluorosequencing and microarrays; 3) attaching it to and stretching it between two moveable platforms in an e-cell’s cis and trans chambers, this is similar to a recent proposal for general peptide modification (doi: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15006068/v1). Multiple molecules of the target peptide containing one internal Lysine (K) residue with unprotected side chain and the N- and C-ends capped are added to trans or the flow cell. Aided by a catalyst the K residue can form a lactam bond with any of the residues of E m in trans ; this docks the target onto E m . The target’s N- and C-ends are then uncapped to enable ring closing with the aid of a catalyst. Lactamization and ring closing can be detected optically, and the cyclized target cleaved from the host orthogonally. Convergence of reactants was computationally simulated at a coarse-grained level; convergence occurs in a few milliseconds. Parallel cyclization can be done with an array of E m anchors; with adequate separation, docking and ring closing can occur without cross-talk. Tethering obviates solubility issues, the purification required is minimal. The molar ratio of catalyst to target peptide in a reaction space 10 nm × 10 nm × (0.1-1.0) mm is 10 4 -10 6 ; even though this is high virtually all of the excess products can be recovered and recycled. With small m (~30) and a 2 cm × 2 cm chip with 20 nm pore separation the maximum yield is ~1.6 femtomoles or 2.5 picograms of 1.5 kDa peptides. Scale-up can be achieved with the third anchoring method by using one platform and mm-long stretched tethers that behave like rods holding coat-hangers; long homopolymers can be assembled recursively with Native Chemical Ligation in trans followed by docking/ring-closing of peptides in cis to obtain outputs at the mg level or possibly higher. The method’s relative simplicity and low process complexity suggest its suitability for rapid construction of macrocyclic peptide libraries. With a few modifications, the method can be extended to peptide synthesis at the low bulk level. If peptide copies are situated with adequate physical separation along the tether, aggregation- and oligomerization-free synthesis of arbitrary sequences may be possible in the microgram to milligram range with only minor restrictions and without major solubility or purification issues.

papers.title: Bead-Spring Model Analysis of Linear Viscoelasticity for Unentangled Multi-Cyclic Polystyrene Melts
papers.abstract: Multi-cyclic (MC) polymers, in which multiple ring units are connected within a single molecule, are expected to exhibit properties distinct from those of linear and trivial ring polymers. Here, we performed graph-theory-based bead-spring model calculations for a series of unentangled MC polystyrene (MC-PS) melts with different chain connectivities and compared the results with previously reported experimental linear viscoelastic data. This calculation allows for the comparison of linear viscoelasticity among different MC molecules using a single, architecture-independent time-scale. The distribution and multiplicity of the eigenvalues λ p at mode number p , which determine the relaxation times through τ p ∝ 1/ λ p , of the MC molecules depends strongly on the architecture and its overall symmetry. In addition, the model reasonably captured the experimental linear rheological behavior of the MC-PS melts, including the complex modulus G * ( ω ) and the zero-shear viscosity η 0 , although the experimental data have modest differences. Furthermore, we found that the architecture dependence of η 0 can be semi-quantitatively organized using the squared radius of gyration calculated from the bead-spring model, R g,BS 2 , rather than relying only on the number of constrained segments, n cs , which has been used as an empirical architectural parameter in previous studies. This descriptor also distinguishes MC architectures with the same n cs but different rheological responses, demonstrating that chain connectivity provides a physically grounded basis for describing the linear viscoelasticity of unentangled MC polymer melts.

papers.title: AI-driven design of a novel synthetic route to malaria drug ganaplacide
papers.abstract: Malaria is a deadly infectious disease that disproportionately affects low- and middle-income countries. Ganaplacide is a drug candidate that is highly effective against malaria, and the ability to produce it at low cost is essential. Here we show how we used a combination of AI-driven design and expert chemistry knowledge to develop a novel synthetic route to ganaplacide. The AI retrosynthesis algorithm suggested a non-evident two-steps synthesis of the imidazolopiperazine core of the molecule from benzyl-protected dimethylpiperazinone through a strategic thioimidate intermediate. We also present the Synthetic Confidence Score, which assesses the level of risk associated with a given retrosynthetic disconnection and allows balancing creativity and reliability. The synergy between AI creativity, metrics such as the Synthetic Confidence Score and expert chemist knowledge has the potential to unlock non-evident efficient routes for important molecules, when expert chemists alone have explored mainstream chemistry unsuccessfully.

papers.title: FAIRaman: making clinical Raman spectroscopy data FAIR through biobanking and NeXus standards
papers.abstract: Raman spectroscopy is increasingly applied in biomedical and diagnostic research, generating spectral datasets that could support the development of robust artificial intelligence (AI) models for disease diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment guidance. However, most clinical Raman datasets remain difficult to reuse across laboratories because spectra are often stored separately from structured metadata describing the samples, their clinical context, experimental conditions, and data governance. This limits reproducibility, external validation, multicentre integration, and the development of transferable models. Here, we introduce FAIRaman, a FAIR-by-design framework and open-source software tool for the structured organisation of clinical Raman spectroscopy data. FAIRaman combines the hierarchical logic of the Investigation–Study–Assay (ISA) model with biobanking-derived descriptors for sample, donor, and processing-event annotation, and with NeXus/NXraman-inspired metadata for Raman acquisition parameters and spectral data. The resulting structure implemented in the open HDF5 file format. The software, developed in Python, converts native Renishaw WDF files and vendor-neutral text-based spectral files into FAIRaman-compliant HDF5 files through a graphical user interface (GUI), allowing users to combine batch-level metadata with sample-specific clinical data. We demonstrate the framework using a real Raman map of breast cancer tissue, and a Raman spectrum acquired from plasma-derived extracellular vesicles. These examples show that spectral data, acquisition metadata, and clinical sample descriptors can be stored within a single structured file and that the stored information can be easily retrieved using independent, freely available software tools.

papers.title: Inverse theoretical spectroscopy via Monte Carlo sampling: From spectra to ensembles of molecular conformations
papers.abstract: A molecule’s structure determines its spectroscopic properties, and vice versa, molecular spectra are indispensable for elucidating its three-dimensional structure. Here, we present a Monte Carlo sampling scheme for generating an ensemble of molecular structures that is compatible with an ensemble of spectra around a given reference spectrum. By analyzing this spectrally-constrained ensemble, we can determine which structural changes are compatible with the given reference spectrum. By constraining the spectrum only in selected windows, a more fine-grained analysis of selected spectral features becomes possible. We explore our spectral Monte Carlo sampling method for the dye molecule DFHBI, considering its electronic excitation spectrum. We find that the conformational space of molecular structures with similar spectra is vast, and we identify high-energy distorted structures whose spectra closely match that of the ground-state structure. Our method provides a novel, ensemble-based perspective on the inverse mapping from spectra to molecular structures.

papers.title: GVIM 2.0: A Multi-Agent Research System for Chemistry and Materials Science
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as natural-language interfaces for chemistry and materials research, but their utility in scientific workflows depends on their ability to connect user requests with executable tools, structured data handling, and verifiable outputs. Here, we present GVIM 2.0, a multi-agent research system designed to support computational and informatics workflows in chemistry and materials science. GVIM 2.0 integrates language-model-based task planning with domain-specific Skills, packagebacked computational tools, sandboxed execution, and artifact generation. On a 400-question public benchmark suite spanning ChemBench, MaScQA, and ChemLLMBench, the complete GVIM 2.0 workflow answered 325/400 questions correctly, achieving an accuracy of 81.25%, compared with 285/400 questions and 71.25% accuracy for a same-base API-only baseline. We further evaluated GVIM 2.0 on task-native workflows covering molecular solubility prediction, steel yield-strength prediction, reaction-table extraction, MS/MS spectral retrieval, chemical entity extraction, retrospective BACE inhibitor prioritization, Matbench experimental band-gap modelling, and temporal external validation of BACE1 activity prediction. These workflows generated inspectable outputs, including prediction files, metrics, figures, and reports. The results show that GVIM 2.0 can organize reproducible data-to-result workflows for selected chemistry and materials informatics tasks, providing a practical framework for tool-augmented scientific research assistance.

papers.title: Mapping Hierarchical Motifs in disorder-order transitions: learning structural motifs in supercooled liquids and crystals
papers.abstract: Disorder-order transitions pass through structurally rich intermediates that conventional order parameters cannot fully resolve. Here, we introduce a hierarchical motif framework to characterize structural motifs from nucleation of supercooled water. Inspired by language modeling, our framework learns a discrete vocabulary and a grammar of how motifs interact in space and time. By applying vector quantization (VQ) to the learned embeddings of a variational autoencoder (VAE) trained on the structural descriptors, we establish a vocabulary of motifs comprising discrete labels of liquid, transient, and ice motifs. Moreover, the VAE quantifies local disorder that decreases from liquid to ice motifs. Analysis of the motif grammar, including motif-motif transitions, spatial co-occurrences, and ring occupancies, unifies mechanistic descriptions of the spatiotemporal dynamics of ice nucleation. The transient motifs resolve two structural roles: locally-ordered low-density (LD) environments that constitute precursors during supercooling, and non-consolidating interfacial regions. These LD precursors organize into a continuum of ring networks, revealing two processes during nucleation: trimers/tetramers continuously re-organize into closed pentamers/hexamers in ring scaffolds, while atomwise motifs relabel in bursts along an energy ladder. Next, we extend the motif framework to characterize metastable motifs formed by hypothetical polymorphs in heterogeneous nucleation simulations, which elucidates how structural motifs at the ice/liquid interface control ice nucleation. Beyond disorder-order transitions in supercooled water, we further demonstrate the generality of our framework in characterizing transitions in the nucleation of silicon and liquid-liquid transition of water.

papers.title: Quantifying the Synergistic and Antagonistic Effects of Metal–Organic Complexation on Particulate Matter Oxidative Potential via Redox Kinetics
papers.abstract: Oxidative potential (OP) reflects the ability of redox-active particulate matter (PM) species to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) in lung lining fluid. Previous studies reported non-additive (synergistic/antagonistic) OP effects in metal–organic mixtures and attributed them to complexation-induced changes in redox potential and kinetics; however, the quantitative validity of this hypothesis remains unclear. We evaluated this hypothesis using a chemical equilibrium–kinetic dithiothreitol (DTT) assay model for the Fe–oxalate system. The model reproduced the observed non-additive interactions, indicating that the proposed redox-potential-driven kinetic mechanism can quantitatively explain these effects under the examined conditions. At atmospherically relevant oxalate-to-Fe ratios, Fe–oxalate complexation enhanced Fe(II)-driven oxidant reduction kinetics but did not produce strong synergy. Accelerated Fe(II) oxidation shifted the Fe redox balance toward Fe(III), decreasing Fe(II) concentrations and offsetting much of the kinetic enhancement. At higher oxalate-to-Fe ratios, strong antagonism arose from suppression of Fe(III)-driven DTT oxidation by weakly reactive Fe(III)–oxalate species. These results revealed that non-additive OP effects cannot be inferred from complexation-induced changes in rate constants alone, but are determined by the combined effects of reaction kinetics, chemical speciation, and metal redox balance. This framework provides a basis for incorporating metal–organic interactions into atmospheric PM OP prediction.

papers.title: Conformational and Tautomeric Effects on the excited-states of Sulfonated Azo Dyes
papers.abstract: In this work, we present a systematic investigation of the ground- and excited-states of six anionic sulfonated azo dyes with broad applications in the textile industry: Allura Red, Amaranth, Carmoisine, Ponceau, Red 2G, and Sunset Yellow. Ground-state properties were evaluated using density functional theory (DFT) at the $\omega$B97X-D4/ma-def2-SVP level of theory. To identify the most suitable functional for excited-state calculations and to assess vertical excitation energies to low-lying excited-states, we tested a series of hybrid, meta-hybrid, and range-separated hybrid functionals from Jacob's ladder using the Tamm-Dancoff approximation (TDA) and the ma-def2-SVP basis set and compared to results from RI-CC2 and STEOM-DLPNO-CCSD approaches. excited-state properties were then further examined using TDA at the CAM-B3LYP//$\omega$B97X-D4/ma-def2-SVP level of theory. Additionally, the quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM) was applied to explore density-related properties in both ground and excited-states. We found, perhaps not surprisingly, that excitation weakens the \ce{N=N} bond in both the enol and keto forms of the dyes, but with variations depending on the molecule, conformer, and electronic state.

papers.title: Stimulated geological CO 2 reduction
papers.abstract: Converting captured CO 2 into products typically requires externally supplied electricity or H 2 . Although abiotic carbon reduction has been observed in water–rock systems, productive and verifiable conversion of newly supplied inorganic carbon has not been established. Here we establish stimulated geological CO 2 reduction (Geo-CO 2 R), in which reducing equivalents released during oxidation of Fe(II)-bearing minerals drive productive conversion of supplied inorganic carbon. Natural olivine-rich rock converts supplied 13 C-bicarbonate to isotope-verified 13 C-formate within six hours, reaching a mass- and time-normalized productivity more than five orders of magnitude above the strongest prior olivine system. Experiments and calculations identify two mechanistic design rules: bicarbonate minimizes stoichiometric acid–base drift and sustains a productive interfacial pH window, while K + supports greater water dissociation and a more labile interfacial hydration environment than Na + , consistent with enhanced proton-coupled bicarbonate reduction. Mineral transformation links Fe(II) oxidation to reducing-power supply, and mechanism-guided control further enhances formate production. Translating the measured natural-rock productivity using a stimulated-rock framework indicates that laboratory-scale rates could support significant, potentially commercially relevant in-situ production even when only a small fraction of the accessible formation sustains the measured activity. Upper-bound estimates further indicate a lattice-electron inventory capable of reducing millions of gigatons of CO 2 , equivalent to tens of thousands of years of current annual global CO 2 emissions. Together, these results establish Geo-CO 2 R as a productive, verifiable and controllable pathway for coupling carbon conversion to geological reducing power and subsurface reaction environments.

papers.title: Engineering cyanobacterial carbonic anhydrase surface mutations for fast CO2 hydration and capture
papers.abstract: Equilibration between CO 2 and the other forms of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is slow under ambient conditions, bottlenecked by the hydration of dissolved CO 2 to form bicarbonate and a proton. This step is often rate-limiting for aqueous CO 2 capture processes under ambient temperature and pressure, and is precisely the chemistry catalyzed by the family of carbonic anhydrase enzymes. As a result, incorporation of carbonic anhydrases (CAs) into various CO 2 capture schemes may be used to accelerate CO 2 hydration, increasing the rates of downstream processes coupled to this DIC equilibrium. While this potential use for CA has been long-studied, extending these basic chemical principles to real applications have been hampered by practical questions of how to economically source carbonic anhydrase enzymes at mass scale. This work explores the use of modified cyanobacterial expression hosts as a potential resolution to that problem. Successful engineering of carbonic anhydrase surface display in fast-growing, marine cyanobacteria would yield a self-sustaining CO 2 hydration catalyst that requires only sunlight, CO 2 itself, and nutrients freely available in seawater, as inputs for passively generating carbonic anhydrases on the cell envelope during cell growth.

papers.title: A Nickel–Capped Calcium Hydride: Implications for Diene Hydrometallation
papers.abstract: We report here the synthesis and comprehensive characterization of a molecular nickel complex featuring a σ–[Ca–H–Ni] interaction. Although numerous σ–[E–H–M] species have been characterized, analogous complexes featuring heavier alkaline–earth hydrides remain exceptionally rare owing to their highly ionic and reactive nature. Reaction of [Ni(t,t,t–cdt)] (t,t,t–cdt = t,t,t–cyclododeca–1,5,9–triene) with the calcium hydride, [{(DippBDI)Ca(THF)}(μ–H)]2 affords [{(DippBDI)Ca(THF)(μ–H){Ni(t,t,t–cdt)}], representing the first well–defined Ca–H–M complex (where M = transition metal) characterized in both the solution– and solid–state. Multinuclear NMR spectroscopy, single–crystal X–ray diffraction, and computational studies collectively establish the presence and electronic structure of a σ–[Ca–H–Ni] unit, revealing a polarized interaction in which the hydride is primarily associated with nickel, while retaining a significant interaction with calcium. The isolation of this σ–[Ca–H–Ni] adduct provides a molecular framework for understanding cooperative reactivity between calcium hydrides and nickel. We show that this and related σ–[Ca–H–Ni] species are likely intermediates in the nickel–promoted hydrometallation of non–activated dienes.

papers.title: Flexible force field-based screening and machine learning predictions for CO2 sorption and diffusion in MOFs
papers.abstract: Machine learning offers an efficient route for screening metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), but most existing models rely on rigid-framework simulations that neglect framework flexibility. In this work, DFT-derived flexible force fields were used to calculate CO2 sorption and self-diffusion for 5,418 MOFs, providing the training data for machine-learning models capable of rapidly predicting these properties. We investigated different ML algorithms, featurization methods, and the role of physical descriptors in predicting CO2 sorption and self-diffusion in MOFs. For CO2 sorption, a categorical boosting classifier coupled with Stoichiometric-45 featurization method used with scalar descriptors provided predictive accuracy of 76.1%. For CO2 self-diffusion, we tuned a categorical boosting regressor on revised autocorrelation functions coupled with scalar descriptors and achieved moderate predictive accuracy (R2 = 0.69). These results demonstrate that machine learning trained on properties generated from flexible force field simulations can substantially accelerate computational screening while incorporating key effects of framework flexibility, providing an efficient strategy for discovering MOFs for low-pressure CO2 capture. Summary Computational screening of 5,418 metal–organic frameworks using flexible DFT-based force fields captures framework motion effects on CO2 sorption and self-diffusion. Machine learning models were evaluated across descriptors and algorithms. A CatBoost classifier achieved 76.1% sorption accuracy, while an autocorrelation-based regressor predicted self-diffusion (R2 = 0.69), demonstrating the value of flexibility-aware modeling.

papers.title: Analytic Derivative Couplings for MRSF-TDDFT: Applications to Nonadiabatic Molecular Dynamics and Conical Intersections
papers.abstract: We present an analytic formulation of derivative couplings for mixed-reference spin-flip time-dependent density functional theory (MRSF-TDDFT). Cross terms between the two states' excitation amplitudes and the orbital-rotation derivative of their wave-function overlap enter the interstate Lagrangian. Together they define the source of a state-pair Z-vector equation with the reference orbital Hessian, yielding the analytic derivative coupling vector. The analytic vectors enable conical-intersection searches using both branching directions. At twelve reference conical-intersection geometries, the median branching-plane projector overlap between MRSF-TDDFT and multireference configuration interaction with singles and doubles (MRCISD) is 0.991. As a further application, nonadiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD) simulations of uracil photorelaxation reproduce the previously predicted rapid formation of a twisted intermediate while using the analytic derivative-coupling direction for nuclear-momentum adjustment at surface hops. We also identify four major numerical causes of premature trajectory termination and develop corresponding treatments to improve trajectory stability and reduce trajectory loss in NAMD ensembles.

papers.title: Crystalline core micelles
papers.abstract: A micelle is defined as a loosely bound aggregation of several tens to hundreds of surfactant molecules, forming a colloidal particle. Micelles possess well-defined core and shell regions, both of which exist in a liquid-like state. This liquid-like character allows micelles to be dynamic structures, with surfactant molecules continuously exchanging within the micelle and between the micelle and bulk solution. In contrast to this classical model, we report rod-like reverse micelles with a well-defined three-dimensional crystalline core. The core is held together by hydrogen bonds and exhibits the morphology of a four-faceted, elongated crystal. Alkyl chains surround the core and sterically hinder it, confining crystal growth to a single direction.

papers.title: CO on Small Metal Clusters: Site-Resolved Vibrational Shifts and DMRG and VQE Benchmarks of Electron Correlation
papers.abstract: Strong electron correlation in transition-metal chemistry motivates both advanced classical solvers, such as the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG), and quantum algorithms, but a claim of quantum utility requires a converged classical baseline. This baseline is established for a concrete problem, the C–O stretching signature of CO on small Mn clusters (M = Cu, Ag, Au, Pd, Pt; n = 2–5). Shifts and adsorption energies of 35 complexes from PBE0/def2-TZVPP full numerical Hessians, corrected with CCSD(T) and tested against six further functionals, are organized by site coordination: top-site CO shifts by +6 to −108 cm −1 , bridgesite CO by −202 to −387 cm −1 , and hollow-site CO by −339 to −508 cm −1 , separated by at least 94 cm −1 , more than the estimated uncertainty of 15–20 cm −1 . Multireference diagnostics test the classical hierarchy. CASSCF with 8 and 12 active orbitals gives linear minima for CuCO and AuCO, which contradicts the bent minima of PBE0. DMRG for eight cluster complexes with up to 36 active orbitals and 61 electrons changes by 0.5 m E h or less between bond dimensions 500 and 1000 and takes 0.3–2.8 h per complex. Seven complexes are weakly entangled (largest single-orbital entropy 0.21–0.26), whereas top-site Pt5CO is moderately multiconfigurational (0.62). A noiseless UCCSD variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) reproduces CASSCF in 16-qubit active spaces only to within 2.0–4.3 m E h , above chemical accuracy. For these systems classical methods suffice, and entanglement screening with DMRG is proposed as the test that a candidate system must pass before quantum advantage is sought.

papers.title: Unveiling the Molecular Basis of Silver(I) Sequestration by Glutathione: Stoichiometry, Stability and Structure at Neutral pH
papers.abstract: The complexation of Ag(I) ions by reduced glutathione (GSH) at neutral pH was studied by UV-vis, CD and NMR spectroscopies and mass spectrometry, aided by DFT calculations. A tetrameric Ag 4 (GSH) 4 complex was found to be the sole species at these conditions, containing the octagonal Ag 4 S 4 ring with digonal S-Ag-S coordination mode. The pH-independent stability constant of this complex was determined by competitive titrations with excess of thiosulfate ions as KAg4(GSH)4 = 1.6 × 10 67 M -7 . Equilibrium calculations using this constant indicate that physiological millimolar GSH concentrations can sequester all substoichiometric Ag(I) ions, presumably preventing their toxicity towards cellular proteins. However, the ring structure of the complex is not compatible with the standard cellular heavy metal detoxication mechanism. These results provide a molecular basis for deciphering the role of glutathione in cellular silver toxicity and detoxication.

papers.title: CuPd Dilute Alloys Enhance Stability During CO2 Electroreduction in Zero-Gap Electrolyzers
papers.abstract: Copper is uniquely capable of driving CO2 electroreduction toward multicarbon products, yet its performance deteriorates under industrially relevant conditions due to surface restructuring and increased hydrogen evolution. In this work, we systematically evaluate dilute CuPd alloy nanoparticles with controlled Pd content (2-6 at.%) and well-defined size distribution in a zerogap electrolyzer across current densities ranging from 100 to 300 mA cm-2. We demonstrate that dilute alloying improves the stability of the nanoparticles. At high current densities (200-300 mA cm-2), monometallic Cu undergoes significant degradation, while CuPd dilute alloys exhibit improved multicarbon selectivity and reduced hydrogen evolution. This behavior is attributed to stabilization of active sites against Cu oxidation and restructuring under high-rate while retaining the good selectivity of Cu, which is supported by in situ x-ray absorption spectroscopy and first principles calculations. An optimal Pd content (ca. 4.5 at.%) is identified to offer the best balance between stability, performance and Pd atom efficiency. These findings demonstrate that dilute Pd

papers.title: Thermodynamics and Kinetics of Ga Surface Segregation in Cu–Ga Nanoparticles across Composition and Particle Size
papers.abstract: Cu–Ga nanoparticles are promising catalysts for thermochemical and electrochemical CO2 conversion, with their catalytic behavior determined by their surface composition. Here, we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations with machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to determine how Ga distributes within Cu–Ga nanoparticles depending on composition, size, and temperature. DFT results show that Ga forms a homogeneous solid solution within the bulk Cu lattice, whereas Ga-rich terminations are favored for surfaces. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations at the nanosecond scale for particles (within 2 nm to 4.5 nm) and Ga contents up to 24 % reveal progressive Ga migration toward the surface. The extent and rate of this redistribution increase with temperature and Ga content, accompanied by increasing sphericity and structural disorder, until Ga surface enrichment saturates. The surface Ga fraction remains similar across particle sizes, whereas the fraction of total Ga at the surface decreases as particle size increases. A mean-field model captures this surface-to-interior partitioning, reproducing the surface compositions for the MD simulations at high temperatures. At lower temperatures and for larger nanoparticles, Ga redistribution is kinetically limited within the timescale of the simulations. Calculated apparent diffusion barriers for Cu and Ga obtained at high temperatures support this interpretation.

papers.title: Atomistic Origin of Transition-Metal Dissolution in Ni-Rich Cathodes: The Role of Oxygen Loss
papers.abstract: High-voltage operation of Ni-rich cathodes accelerates degradation through surface reconstruction and transition-metal dissolution. Although these processes occur concurrently, their mechanistic relationship remains unresolved. Here, we identify oxygen loss as the unifying mechanism coupling cathode surface reconstruction and transition-metal release in LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2||graphite cells, consistent with the increased Ni deposition observed at the graphite anode. Surface-sensitive Ni L-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy reveals that crossing the oxygen-loss threshold not only induces cathode surface reconstruction, but also progressively thins the reconstructed surface layer, evidenced by the evolution of signal attenuation. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations corroborate this interpretation by showing that reconstructed-layer thinning originates from energetically favorable surface-layer detachment following oxygen-loss-driven destabilization of the near-surface lattice. Together, these findings establish oxygen loss as the mechanistic origin of coupled cathode degradation and transition-metal deposition, and identify stabilization of lattice oxygen as a key materials-engineering strategy to mitigate degradation and extend the cycling performance of next-generation Ni-rich Li-based energy storage devices.

papers.title: Benchmarking Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Plus One Double (TDDFT-1D) for Potential Energy Surfaces
papers.abstract: Time-dependent density functional theory plus one double (TDDFT-1D) improves on conventional TDDFT by including one specially chosen doubly excited electronic configuration. In this study, we evaluate the ability of that method to describe the ground-and excited-state potential energy surfaces (PESs) of selected model compounds relevant to photochemistry. We find that its accuracy is highly dependent on the given test case. For some systems with relatively little multiconfigurational character, the calculated PESs coincide very closely with benchmark data derived from high-level wavefunction-based calculations. In the most favorable cases–methylene and azomethane–and with specific choices of adjustable simulation parameters, TDDFT-1D PESs follow the benchmark data to around 0.2 eV. For some others, the calculated PESs are distorted to a varying degree. In order to pave the way for future studies employing TDDFT-1D, we identify some specific situations where it may potentially fail, and which should be therefore avoided.

papers.title: A substrate-versatile operando electrochemical cell for X-ray absorption spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Operando characterization techniques allow the understanding of electrochemical energy materials under operating conditions, which is essential to design high-performance electrocatalysts. Here, we present a novel operando electrochemical cell designed for X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), enabling the simultaneous acquisition of electrochemical data, real-time oxygen detection, and XAS spectra on X-ray opaque electrodes. The incident X-ray beam reaches the sample through the electrolyte rather than through the substrate in contrast to the majority of other cells. This configuration removes constraints related to substrate transparency and thickness, thereby broadening the range of compatible electrode materials and samples that can be analyzed. The cell was commissioned using a well-characterized CoOx catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction in alkaline media. Reversible shifts in the Co K-edge position were observed under applied potential steps, directly correlating electronic structure changes with electrochemical activity and oxygen production.
