The neutral polar and charged terminal groups exhibit similar total thermal resistances (4.2–4.7 K m2 GW−1), whereas the hydrophobic CH3 termination produces a marked increase to ∼ 7 K m2 GW−1, primarily because of the PEG–water interfacial resistance. The thermal transport trends are consistent with differences in interfacial hydration and polymer–water organization, whereas vibrational spectral overlap alone does not provide a sufficient descriptor across the complete terminal group series. Increasing the PEG chain length raises the resistance of the PEG layer, whereas the coverage dependence of the effective Au interfacial resistance is described by a parallel thermal circuit model that combines Au–water and Au–PEG heat transfer contributions. These results identify terminal group chemistry, PEG chain length, and surface coverage as molecular design variables for tuning the thermal resistance of polymer-coated solid–liquid interfaces.

papers.title: Advances on doping strategies and emerging applications of organic (semi)conducting polymers
papers.abstract: Conducting polymers have evolved from intrinsically conductive macromolecules into versatile organic (semi)conductors that combine electronic transport with ionic, optical, mechanical, and spin functionalities. A central challenge in this evolution is to generate and stabilize charge carriers while retaining control over molecular organization, processability, and operational stability. This Review examines how molecular design and doping chemistry have progressively addressed this challenge, from early polyacetylene- and polyaniline-based systems to processable polythiophene derivatives and contemporary donor–acceptor conjugated polymers. Across p-type, ntype, and self-doped systems, we consider how advances in molecular architecture and doping chemistry have expanded the means of generating, stabilizing, and transporting charge carriers. Emerging approaches—including side-chain-enabled doping, protoncoupled electron transfer, catalytic and photoinduced doping, and intrinsically open-shell self-doping—are considered in the context of their potential to overcome limitations in doping efficiency, stability, and morphological control. These advances have expanded conducting polymers beyond conventional charge-transport materials toward multifunctional platforms for energy storage, 3D printing, organic electrochemical transistors, neuromorphic computing, and spintronics. We further identify the need to establish more precise relationships among molecular structure, doping state, solid-state organization, and device-level performance. Continuing progress along these directions will be essential for translating the tunable optical, electronic, electrochemical and mechanical properties of these organic conducting polymers into stable, scalable, and multifunctional technologies beyond the reach of classical inorganic (semi)conductors such as silicon and metals.

papers.title: Semiempirical Quantum Chemistry in the Age of ab initio Data and Differentiable Programming: II. Parameter Optimization
papers.abstract: Semiempirical quantum chemistry (SQC) represents an invaluable asset in the toolbox of molecular and materials modeling. Thanks to their explicit quantum-mechanical treatment of electrons, they allow to capture an array of local and non-local interaction mechanisms and offers access to electronic structure properties, which can be of crucial importance in order to better understand and design molecular systems and materials. In a previous publication, we presented our recent advances within the PySEQM package, enabling rapid gradient evaluations for SQC parameters and thus developing an efficient and reliable back-end for SQC parametrizations. In this work, we detail our implementation of this parametrization procedure, SQCFit, and its features. Offering a high degree of automation, SQCFit implements a suite of tailor-made tools for the optimization of SQC parameters. Specifically, we present local versus global parametrization schemes, the use of train-validation splits and early stopping to avoid overfitting, and advanced scoring/loss functions including appropriately standardized quantitative error measures as well as more qualitative measures such as the performance in ranking candidate systems according to a given molecular property. Based on a set of test applications, we highlight how SQCFit allows to obtain performant parametrizations tailor-made for the modern use cases of SQC.

papers.title: Engineered Phenylalanine Ammonia Lyases Enable Biocatalytic Synthesis of a Non-Canonical Phenylalanine Derivative at Scale.
papers.abstract: Phenylalanine ammonia lyases (PALs) are an enzyme class of high synthetic utility as they catalyze the synthesis of chiral non-canonical phenylalanine amino acids from readily available cinnamic acids using simple ammonia as the amine donor. However, the applications of PAL in chemical manufacturing have been rare due to the challenges in identifying PALs active under industrially relevant conditions. Herein, we report our efforts towards engineering a PAL enzyme from Planctomyces brasiliensis (PbPAL) for the synthesis of L-3-cyanophenylalanine as an intermediate in the synthesis of Enlicitide, the clinically approved macrocyclic peptide to lower cholesterol levels. Protein engineering identified several key mutations that resulted in an evolved PbPAL variant with >100-fold improved activity and enhanced recombinant expression in E. coli. The computational studies suggest the final variant has increased substrate accessibility to the active site, which enabled high conversion (up to 97%) to L-3-cyanophenylalanine with excellent enantioselectivity at low enzyme loading (3 w/w%), demonstrated at up to 250-gram scale. In addition, the final variant represents a broad substrate scope against a variety of heterocyclic cinnamic acids with high enantioselectivity. This work showcases how protein engineering can enable the biocatalytic synthesis of non-canonical amino acids at scale.

papers.title: Multivalent Avidity in C-type Lectins: How Glycan Surface Density and Presentation Define Superselective Recognition by DC-SIGN
papers.abstract: Multivalent lectin–glycan interactions (MLGIs) are fundamental to many biological processes. While individual carbohydrate recognition domains (CRDs) determine glycan specificity, their clustering enhances binding affinity and selectivity through multivalency. However, the number of CRDs engaged during binding can vary, and individual CRDs may exhibit weak, non‑specific interactions with off‑target glycans. How these factors collectively shape MLGI behaviour remains unclear. Here, we address this question using a vitally important tetravalent, mannose‑specific C-type lectin DC‑SIGN (4M) and its engineered variants – a heterotetramer containing two mannose‑specific and two galactose‑specific CRDs (2M2G), and a fully galactose‑specific tetramer (4G) – and model surfaces presenting mannose at tuneable densities and defined organisation. We find that DC-SIGN 4M binding increases superlinearly with the increasing mannose density, although such ‘superselective’ recognition is attenuated at high mannose densities (≥50%). Interestingly, DC-SIGN 4M binds more strongly to mannose surfaces diluted by a low-affinity, non-specific galactose over a non-binding hydroxyl-terminated spacer. Whilst both 4M and 4G show weak cross‑binding to surfaces presenting non‑cognate glycans, 4M displays only ~2.7‑fold stronger binding to 100% mannose surface than 2M2G despite its higher mannose-specific valency. Confronting the experimental data with a mathematical model, we quantify the gradually decreasing contributions of the first, second, third and fourth CRD binding to the overall binding avidity, and how these are shaped by the balance of intrinsic CRD-glycan affinity, steric constraints imposed by the glycan surface and conformational constraints imposed by DC-SIGN 4M’s molecular organisation. Together, these results demonstrate that by modulating CRD number and glycan engagement, multivalent lectins can fine‑tune their binding avidity and selectivity for glycan surfaces of varying density and heterogeneity, thus affording them diverse functions and the ability to discriminate heterogeneous glycan environments on cell and pathogen surfaces.

papers.title: Stimulus-Responsive AIE-Active Magnetic Fluorescent Composite Enables High-Quality Visualization of Latent Fingerprints on Complex Substrates
papers.abstract: Latent fingerprint visualization on complex substrates remains challenging because conventional fluorescent developing materials generally possess fixed emission states after deposition, limiting their adaptability toward diverse background environments. In this work, a novel AIE-active fluorescent material (B-N) was synthesized via a two-step Suzuk-Miyaura coupling and Knoevenagel condensation strategy, in which pyridine groups were introduced to impart stimulus-responsive properties for reversible fluorescence switching under external acid/base stimulation, enabling dynamic modulation of fingerprint color after development. By further integrating the AIE-active molecule B-N into a magnetic fluorescent composite system (with non-fluorescent Fe3O4 as the magnetic component), high-resolution latent fingerprint imaging was successfully achieved on eight representative substrates with different textures and background colors. More importantly, acid fumigation enabled fluorescence color regulation and improved fingerprint contrast on challenging surfaces, particularly those with strong background interference. Gray value profile analysis further confirmed clear ridge selectivity, uniform material adhesion, and stable imaging quality during the stimulus-responsive processes. Overall, this work demonstrates an adaptive strategy for latent fingerprint visualization. The findings highlight the potential of stimulus-responsive AIE materials in forensic applications.

papers.title: Photocatalytic Divergent Skeletal Remodeling through Strain Release: Modular Access to Carbocycles and Heterocycles
papers.abstract: Deconstructive skeletal remodeling of three-dimensional architectures offered a unique strategy to access structurally distinct carbocyclic and heterocyclic frameworks. A common, highly strained central σ-bond enabled two divergent skeletal-reorganization pathways, providing direct access to 1,3-disubstituted naphthalenes and pyrroles. A subtle change in reaction environment dictates divergent product formation during this photocatalytic double-strain-release skeletal-remodeling process. Under rigorously anhydrous conditions, skeletal reorganization furnishes carbocycles, whereas the addition of water redirects the reaction pathway toward heterocycle formation. The method accommodates a wide range of functional groups and substitution patterns. Mechanistic studies show that both pathways proceed through a common electron-transfer manifold and shared reactive intermediate. A delicate change in reaction conditions then leads to distinct aza-diene intermediates, driving divergent, regioselective outcomes.

papers.title: Structure-Independent Genetic Algorithm-Based Molecular Optimization Using Pocket-Aware Molecular Representations
papers.abstract: De novo molecular design typically depends on target structures or ligand poses, limiting its applicability when structural information is unavailable. Here, we introduce the pocket-aware molecular representation-guided genetic algorithm (PAMR-GA), a target-structure-independent molecular optimization framework that learns pocket-aware representations from structure–activity relationship (SAR) data using only molecular structures represented as SMILES strings and experimental pIC50 values. By encoding latent spatial constraints inferred from SAR without requiring target structures, the learned representations guide genetic algorithm-based molecular optimization through a Gaussian process surrogate model. Benchmarking on BACE-1 demonstrated that PAMR-GA achieved comparable predictive performance, docking scores, and drug-likeness profiles to existing optimization approaches while generating molecules with substantially greater structural novelty and higher Murcko scaffold diversity. Evaluation on four additional targets, including a kinase, serine proteases, and an NADbinding enzyme, further showed consistent improvements in molecular novelty. These results highlight PAMR-GA as a complementary approach for incorporating SAR-derived spatial constraints into de novo molecular design without requiring target structures. 1 Scientific Contribution PAMR-GA enables structure-independent molecular design by learning binding constraints implicitly from 2D structure–activity relationship data, without requiring protein structures or ligand poses. By introducing a pocket-aware molecular representation that integrates solvent-accessible surface area and partial-charge features, PAMR-GA bridges molecular topology with 3D binding compatibility. Our results demonstrate that constrained generation, rather than improved activity prediction alone, drives structural novelty. Evaluation across five diverse targets from four protein classes highlights the generalizability of PAMR-GA as a broadly applicable framework for target-aware molecular design.

papers.title: Leveraging Microenvironment Effects to Enhance Bifunctional Metal–Organic Framework-Catalyzed Aldol Reactions
papers.abstract: Solvent effects are known to shift the position of chemical equilibria, alter reaction rates, and dictate the outcome of chemical transformations. Here, we show that tuning the pore surface chemistry of metal–organic framework (MOF) catalysts can mimic desirable solvent effects, more than doubling catalytic activity. First, we demonstrate that templated MOFs featuring bifunctional secondary amine–carboxylic acid pairs are effective catalysts for aldol reactions but exhibit high sensitivity to solvent polarity. Catalytic activity decreases dramatically upon increasing solvent polarity, likely due to the stabilization of off-cycle charged iminium intermediates. We show that high activity can be partially recovered by incorporating nonpolar n-hexyl chains into the framework backbone that destabilize charged species. Overall, this work highlights how precise control over the local pore environment can be a powerful tool for improving catalyst performance.

papers.title: Lewis-acid mediated borodegermylation grants access to donorand acceptor-substituted azaboraspirobifluorenes
papers.abstract: Boron-centered spiro compounds represent a prominent platform for the design of optoelectronic materials. The orthogonally arranged π-conjugated systems around boron enhance stability toward air and moisture, facilitate processing, and allow electronic tuning through donor and acceptor substitution. Synthetic methods reported to date for the preparation of these compounds suffer from low efficiency and poor functional group tolerance, limiting the diversity of accessible electronic materials with tailored properties. Herein, we present a synthetic method leveraging the “Goldilocks” reactivity of germoles among Group 14 analogues to achieve a highly efficient and versatile AlCl3-catalyzed borodegermylation reaction, granting access to donor- and acceptor-functionalized azaboraspirobifluorenes. Furtheremore, the reaction efficiency can be enhanced by employing the sublimed catalyst and the use of an additive. Owing to their high stability, comparatively low toxicity and non-pyrophoric nature, the use of organogermanium compounds provides a more robust and safer alternative to methods that rely on other organometallic reagents.

papers.title: Directing Generation of Polynuclear Plutonium Species with Reduction and Protonation
A Cellular Sheaf Model for Aromaticity in Discrete Molecular Systems
papers.abstract: Aromaticity underpins molecular stability in fields ranging from pharmaceuticals to organic semiconductors, yet existing prediction methods are either too computationally costly for large-scale screening or too empirically restricted for broad applicability. This work introduces the molecular sheaf, a cellular sheaf model free of empirical parameters for chemical bonding that generalizes standard molecular graph theory. From this the frontier eigengap Δ_F is derived as a spectral approximation of the HOMO-LUMO gap requiring only molecular topology and electron count. Δ_F correctly classifies the aromaticity and antiaromaticity of the full annulene series, including benzene and cyclobutadiene, exactly recovering Hückel theory for regular hydrocarbon systems. At scale, it accounts for 62.5% of the variance in DFT HOMO-LUMO gaps across 17,523 structurally diverse polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and 21.7% across 52,000 heteroaromatic systems, with the reduction reflecting the deliberate cost of parameter freedom. This confirms that aromatic character can be approximated from molecular connectivity and electron count alone, suggesting that cellular sheaves offer a largely unexplored mathematical framework for the modeling of chemical bonding and structure. All calculations run at under 1 ms per molecule, over seven orders of magnitude faster than corresponding DFT calculations. The molecular sheaf thus also enables rapid, parameter-free pre-screening of aromatic character from structural data alone.

papers.title: Comprehensive multi-technique study of the electrochemical lithiation of Fe <sub>3</sub> O <sub>4</sub> with different particle sizes under operando conditions
papers.abstract: Fe3O4 is a conversion-type anode material with high storage capacity that suffers from limited cycling performance. Nanosizing Fe3O4 is one promising strategy to enhance its cycling stability and overall electrochemical performance; however, the details of particle size dependent reaction kinetics remain poorly understood. We investigate the conversion reactions of bulk- and 50 nm-sized cubic Fe3O4 particles as active material using a multi-technique approach, by combining operando XRD, SAXS and magnetometry techniques. The results from the operando XRD and SAXS indicate that during initial lithiation reaction, the bulk electrode undergoes phase reduction with amorphization and formation of metallic iron nanograins, whereas the nanoparticle Fe3O4 retains its ccp oxygen anion framework throughout the lithiation process, hindering structural breakdown and amorphization and delaying the the growth of metallic iron nano grains. Operando vibrating sample magnetometry isused to cross-check the transformation and presence of metallic iron nanodomains owing to its unique sensitivity to local structural details hidden in conventional XRD. The reaction products were found to differ when time-resolved investigations are compared to ex-situ prepared specimens. These results highlight the critical importance of integrating complementary operando techniques to ex situ methods, to capture particle size–dependent lithiation pathways and relaxation mechanisms in conversion-type electrodes.

papers.title: Acetylene as a C2 bridge for modular 1,4-dicarbonyl synthesis
papers.abstract: Acetylene is among the cheapest and most abundant C2 feedstocks, yet catalytic methods that exploit both of its π-bonds remain scarce, and its use in fine-chemical synthesis is 15 confined largely to mono-functionalization. Here we report the traceless bridging of aldehydes and formamides with a single acetylene molecule through a catalytic double hydroacylation, in which direct hydrogen-atom transfer generates acyl and carbamoyl radicals without decarbonylation or any sacrificial group. Coupling of two identical radicals assembles 1,4-diketones and 1,4-diamides in a single operation, whereas the sequential 20 delivery of two different radicals provides unsymmetrical 1,4-dicarbonyl products with good cross-selectivity. The transformation accommodates aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes and diverse formamides, proceeds under mild conditions with 100% atom economy, and requires

papers.title: A Decade of Progress: Quantifying Air Pollution Reductions in West Oakland, CA with Hyperlocal Monitoring
papers.abstract: West Oakland is a disadvantaged community in California that has historically experienced a high and disproportionate exposure to diesel air pollution due to its proximity to major transportation infrastructure, including the Port of Oakland and several interstate freeways. However, years of community activism, statewide regulation and targeted local emissions mitigation have altered these conditions. In 2025/26, we replicated a 2015/16 mobile monitoring campaign that characterized hyperlocal spatial gradients in diesel air pollution by repeatedly sampling every road within the community. By comparing how concentrations changed in both magnitude and location, we study the impact of the different mitigation strategies across the last decade. Community wide, weekday daytime black carbon (BC) and NO x concentrations fell by 59.5% [54.2-64.6] (-0.51 μg m -3 ) and 60.0% [54.0-65.7] (-22.0 ppb) respectively, with near uniform fractional declines across seven community identified high impact residential zones (57-62% for BC, 52-64% NO x ). This reduction is consistent with California’s aggressive statewide diesel truck regulations, a phased transition completed in 2023, under which every truck operating within the state must use diesel particulate filter and selective catalytic reduction exhaust treatment technologies. Concentration reductions on individual roads scaled linearly with measured truck traffic (R 2 ~ 0.9), while roads in and around the Port show BC reductions beyond those expected from truck traffic alone, consistent with local investment in cleaner off road equipment. Overall, the decade’s changes avoided an estimated excess lifetime cancer risk from diesel particulate matter of 269 [209-328] per million for those who grow up in the community, and cut absolute disparity in exposure between the most and least polluted zones by 70% for BC and 58% for NOx. These results demonstrate the measurable air quality benefits associated with sustained emissions control and provide quantitative evidence of progress towards goals identified through decades of community-led monitoring and advocacy.

papers.title: Editing-site selection for constrained QED improvement through frozen GenMol remasking
papers.abstract: Shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph-attention models were trained on a remaskingsite selection task utilizing the GenMol generator and a subset of bioactive molecules (30,000 training and 5,000 validation) from the ChEMBL 37 dataset. Models learned to optimize fragment selection policies by maximizing the fraction of successful remasked candidates, with success contingent on an increase in the RDKit quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED) under several chemical constraints. All three models show a marked increase in generation of at least one successful derivative out of 16 remasking runs on a held-out test set comprising 5,000 bioactive molecules: 66.0%–66.9%, 67.0%–67.4% and 66.3%–66.7% for the shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph models, compared to 54.8%–55.6% for a fixed policy selecting the largest fragment (one-sided bootstrap 𝑝 < 10−4 for all models). A trivial baseline, selecting fragments randomly, displays 47.3% success. The fraction of valid candidates produced by all policies is about 99%. Analysis of learned policies showed consistent trends among the three models. Selection is biased toward larger pendants. Additionally, pendant selection shows several trends conditioned on the pendant-side, but not core-side, attachment atom. Larger carbon-and oxygen-attached fragments are selected more often (two-sided binomial 𝑝 < 10−10 in every model); a reversed tendency, albeit not statistically significant (𝑝 ≈ 0.02–0.30), is observed for nitrogen attachments. Controlling for fragment size, learned policies show preference for pendant-side nitrogen over oxygen and carbon, and for both chlorine and bromine over fluorine and carbon. Only LightGBM displays a statistically significant (two-sided exact binomial 𝑝 < 0.01) preference for sp2 over sp3 hybridization of pendant-side carbon atoms. At equal size, carbonyl-attached pendants are preferred to hydrocarbons.

papers.title: Cu-Catalyzed Enantioconvergent Synthesis of N-Alkyl Amides from Racemic Alcohols
papers.abstract: Enantioconvergent amidation of racemic alcohols offers a powerful retrosynthetic disconnection to convert abundant, readily accessible alcohol feedstocks into chiral N-alkyl amides, while streamlining access to valuable enantioenriched primary amines. However, a mechanistic framework that can integrate efficient C(sp3)–O bond cleavage with enantioselective amidation has remained understudied. Herein, we report the enantioconvergent deoxygenative amidation of racemic alcohols through a Cu-catalyzed radical relay. β-Scission of oxidant-derived electrophilic alkoxy radicals was leveraged as a radical-umpolung event, producing nucleophilic methyl radicals that effectively activate alcohol substrate-derived xanthates. Computation-guided optimization revealed that increasing xanthate electrophilicity facilitates methyl-radical addition and improves reaction efficiency. The transformation accommodates a variety of alcohols and amides with high enantioselectivity, and the reaction conditions are compatible with medicinally relevant functional groups, heterocycles, and pharmaceutical frameworks. Synthetic applications of this protocol streamline access to enantioenriched β-amino alcohols and biologically active primary amines, circumventing the need for enantioenriched alcohol precursors. Mechanistic studies revealed that polarity matching favors the capture of electron-deficient carbon-centered radicals by electron-rich CuII–amidates. Under catalytic conditions, however, the greater acidity of electron-deficient amides facilitates transmetalation, accelerating the formation of CuII–amidate and enhancing coupling efficiency.

papers.title: Cross-flow microfluidic photocatalysis with metal-organic framework thin films
papers.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) offer tunable reaction space, and using them as porous photocatalysts also allows the catalyst to be recovered and reused. In practice, though, performance is often constrained by how quickly reactants diffuse through the porous material and how well light reaches the active sites. In this work, we present an approach that pairs a MOF thin-film photocatalyst with a cross-flow microfluidic reactor. The thin film sets a well-defined diffusion length, the transparent thin film let light reach the active layer, and crossflow microfluidics allow diffusion control. Together, these features give control over reactant transport and improve illumination of the photocatalyst. To build the photocatalyst, we noncovalently load Ru(bpy)3(PF6)2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) into mesopores created by defects in a hierarchically porous Zr-based UiO-66 thin film. The well-established aerobic oxidation of ethyl 2-bromo-2-phenylacetate to ethyl 2-oxo-2-phenylacetate serves as a benchmark reaction; it is a test case rather than the main finding of the study. Under cross-flow conditions, the photocatalyst reaches a turnover frequency about ten times that of the equivalent MOF powder system, and it also outperforms the homogeneous benchmark. These findings highlight cross-flow microfluidics as a promising strategy for managing both mass transport and light delivery in MOF-based photocatalysis.

papers.title: Generic aspects of neutral polymer brush bilayers immersed in an implicit solvent under steady-state shear
papers.abstract: Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with a Langevin thermostat, I study polymer brush bilayers immersed in an implicit solvent under steady-state shear. I use high-precision MD simulations, with 5×104 sampling steps, to measure the stress tensor, viscosity, kinetic friction coefficient, and chain extension as functions of the shear rate. The results show that the shear stress scales linearly with the Weissenberg number, Wi, over the entire range studied. The normal stress decreases without following a universal power law. The lateral chain extension decreases up to a critical value of Wi and then increases. The normal chain extension scales as Wi−0.3. The viscosity remains constant, whereas the kinetic friction coefficient increases without following a universal power law.

papers.title: A dipole-forbidden conduction-band transition and the mid-infrared absorption of n-type Mg2Si, Mg2Ge and Mg2Sn: all-electron quasiparticle self-consistent GW calculations
The Mechanical Bond Reveals Hidden Interrupted Click Reactions
papers.abstract: The Cu I -triazolide intermediate of the Cu-mediated alkyne-azide cycloaddition (CuAAC) typically undergoes rapid proto-demetallation but can be intercepted by suitable coupling partners to give 5-substituted triazole products. However, the scope of such “interrupted click” reactions is restricted because some partners react too slowly to outcompete proto-demetallation or even actively promote the decomposition of the Cu I -triazolide in preference to the desired coupling. Here we show that mechanical stabilisation of a Cu I -triazolide within a [2]rotaxane can allow otherwise unproductive “hidden” interrupted click reactions to proceed; the triazolide intermediate of the active template CuAAC reaction couples with cyanide and primary amines under oxidative conditions to install these groups at the triazole 5-position in up to 99% yield. In contrast, the interlocked triazolide reacts slowly with some typical interrupted electrophiles that intercept non-interlocked Cu I -triazolides. Based on these reactivity trends, we propose that the mechanical bond prevents direct attack of electrophiles on the Cu-C bond, instead enforcing inner-sphere reactivity at the Cu I centre with a Cu I /Cu III /Cu I redox cycle. The C-5 substituent leads to a new source of mechanical positional isomerism and a suitably designed macrocycle can be removed after the coupling, allowing the interlocked architecture to serve as an auxiliary for products of otherwise inaccessible interrupted click reactions.

papers.title: Fully Automated System for Exploring Molecular Dynamics Trajectories
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) studies often require separate tools for system preparation, simulation, enhanced sampling, analysis, and reporting, creating opportunities for inconsistent settings and undocumented decisions. We present FastMDXplora, an open-source Python framework built on OpenMM that integrates setup, simulation, analysis, and report phases through a single declarative configuration. A shared schema supports command-line and browser-based graphical interfaces. An optional artificial intelligence (AI) agent generates study configurations from natural-language descriptions, subject to the same validation as user-defined configurations. Each phase records its resolved settings, software versions, and execution environment. When a requested result lacks sufficient support, the software withholds it and reports the reason through a registry of 111 typed refusal codes. Fifteen estimator tests recover analytical benchmarks, including statistical inefficiencies within 2 % of reference values and WHAM reconstruction of analytical free-energy profiles from synthetic umbrella-sampling data with root-mean-square errors below 0.1 kJ mol−1. A labeled corpus of 25 defective and 26 clean studies produces the expected outcomes in all 51 cases. Calibration against ten replicas shows that singlerun standard errors at 20 ns can be up to tenfold smaller than replica-based estimates, even when the estimated correlation time is resolved. The software withholds standard errors when its correlation diagnostics fail, but passing these diagnostics does not establish calibrated uncertainty. In a trypsin–benzamidine case study, interaction analysis reveals differences in the engagement of Asp189 between two ligand charge states that are not distinguished by total contact counts. FastMDXplora provides an integrated framework for reproducible MD studies, combining workflow automation with explicit validation and provenance while preserving the need for independent assessment of sampling and uncertainty. The source code is available at https://github.com/aai-research-lab/FastMDXplora.

papers.title: Thermo-photo catalytic partial oxidation of methane on hematite nanosheets functionalized with silver nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Converting reactions driven by thermocatalysis to thermo-photo catalysis can offer several advantages, such as allowing the reaction to proceed under less harsh conditions to improve stability and tune reaction selectivity. Here, we report on using a dilute loading of silver nanoparticles on high surface area hematite nanosheets, an earth-abundant material, to transform our demonstrated thermocatalytic conversion of methane to a thermo-photo conversion of methane with lowered onset temperatures and a shift in reaction mechanism. With a dilute loading of spherical silver nanoparticles, reaction onset temperatures were lowered to 150 °C from 300 °C. Additionally, reaction products were shifted to CO, decreasing the selectivity toward CO 2 and suggesting novel mechanistic pathways. The catalysts demonstrate great stability, with only a corresponding 4.9% and 11.3% decrease in activity over the bare and decorated catalyst over 15 hours. The fundamental relationships between reaction conversion and temperature, light intensity, and light wavelength studied in this work are important for providing a guideline for tuning other reactions with thermo-photo catalysis to improve catalyst conversion, selectivity, and stability.

papers.title: Substituent Effects on the Photochemistry of Aqueous Phenolate-Based Anions Revealed by Extreme Ultraviolet Time-Resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Phenolate (PhO-) is a prototypical chromophore and a recurring motif in photoactive biomolecular systems. Here, we use extreme-ultraviolet time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (XUV-TRPES) to probe how para-substitution redirects the photophysics of aqueous 4-nitrophenolate (4NP-) and 4-chlorophenolate (4CP-) anions. In 4NP-, following 400 nm excitation, internal charge reorganization accompanied by nitrogroup torsion forms a stabilized twisted intramolecular charge-transfer (TICT) configuration in 74 fs, efficiently funneling the population through a conical intersection to the ground state within 200 fs. Similar dynamics are seen upon excitation at 240 nm, although the initially excited state is even shorter-lived (40 fs). No hydrated electron production is seen at either wavelength. In 4CP-, following 240 nm excitation of the S2 state, internal conversion to S1 occurs within 120 fs. Chlorine substitution introduces a competing 1πσ* dissociative channel whose potential energy surface intersects S1, but the higher S1/1πσ* crossing barrier relative to 4BP- allows the S1 population to survive long enough (25 ps) for solvent-assisted electron ejection and internal conversion. The dynamics thus resemble those of PhO- rather than the sub-picosecond dissociative relaxation of 4BP-. Taken together with our previous PhO- and 4-bromophenolate (4BP-) measurements, these results reveal how para-substitution across this prototypical series drives the accessibility of competing excited-state dynamical processes, leading to very different photostability and photochemistry.

papers.title: Two extrapolation axes for many-body systems: interaction without an interaction module, chemical mixtures as the main example
papers.abstract: We separate the extrapolation problem in many-body systems into two axes: toward combinations with more components, and toward components unseen. The prevailing pipeline—encode then interact—performs poorly when extrapolating in composition count. We propose a route that expresses interaction without an interaction module: a per-component encoder shaped by the task compresses interaction behaviour into each component’s encoding, and the encodings are combined and read out by a simple MLP. Where component identities are bounded while their combinations are not, this route performs better along the composition axis—a difference that follows from the underlying function form rather than from the data. Chemical mixtures are the main example, synthetic tasks isolate the two axes, and the same structure recurs in other fields.

papers.title: Certifying the Kinetics of Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials from Single-Point Energies
papers.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials are validated by force errors on equilibrium configurations, yet activated rates depend on transition regions that equilibrium sampling rarely visits. In a onedimensional metastable double well, the worst-case rate sensitivity to force error grows as eβB/2 with barrier height B; a path-space bound valid at any friction shows that force error certifies rare-event frequencies only to within a factor that grows at the same rate. The leverage density weights energy errors by their influence on reactive transport: it is the normalised dissipation density of the reactive current. For reversible overdamped dynamics, the Dirichlet and Thomson principles give two-sided capacity bounds, converted to metastable rate bounds by basin population corrections. A path representation evaluates their averages from reactive trajectories, committor values and single-point energies. Sampling uses reference paths to assess sampled transitions and model paths to expose additional or overpopulated pathways. In alanine dipeptide, closely matched force errors produce rate changes from 0.49 to 3.5, consistent with estimated intervals. In Li3OCl, mechanism-resolved upper endpoints track six models’ vacancy-hop rates with a systematic underestimation of about 7%. Labels selected from both ensembles improve kinetics even as force errors rise. We propose reporting the energy-error contrast M between the leverage density and the basins, and the spread σν under the leverage density, alongside force error; both are independent of the energy zero.

papers.title: Regioisomeric Engineering for Triplet Harvesting through Triplet–Triplet Annihilation
papers.abstract: Three regioisomeric donor–acceptor–donor luminophores, 1DBF, 2DBF, and 3DBF, based on phenanthrene-9,10-dicarbonitrile (PHCN) acceptor and dibenzofuran (DBF) units, are designed to investigate regioisomer-dependent triplet exciton harvesting. The three emitters exhibit strong blue fluorescence in solution, with photoluminescence quantum yields of 63–87%, and show delayed fluorescence (DF) in both solution and solid states. Low temperature time-gated measurements, large singlet–triplet energy gaps, and concentration-dependent studies collectively support DF from triplet–triplet annihilation (TTA) mechanism rather than thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF). Notably, the substitution pattern strongly influences the excited state dynamics and triplet harvesting efficiency. Among the three regioisomers, 2DBF exhibits the most efficient TTA-derived DF, owing to favorable donoracceptor electronic coupling and a balanced contribution of 3 LE and 3 CT states, whereas the weaker coupling in 1DBF favors predominantly 3 LE character, resulting in stronger phosphorescence and less efficient triplet harvesting through TTA. These results demonstrate that regioisomeric engineering can effectively modulate donor–acceptor electronic coupling and triplet state character, providing a useful molecular strategy for tuning the balance between DF and phosphorescence in organic emitters.

papers.title: Supramolecular Preorganisation Enables Reversible Solid-state Photopolymerisation
authors: Bart W. L. van den Bersselaar
papers.abstract: Supramolecular preorganisation enables reversible solid-state photopolymerisation in an oligo(phenylenevinylene)-siloxane material. Photopolymerisation proceeds quantitatively in the ordered state but reaches only ~7% conversion in the disordered melt. Polymerisation disrupts columnar order and alters optical and local-current responses, while thermal depolymerisation largely restores the initial molecular and supramolecular state.

papers.title: Light-Programmed Persistent and Rewritable Anisotropy in Photoresponsive Mesogenic Microdroplets
authors: Bart W. L. van den Bersselaar
papers.abstract: Photo-responsive liquid-crystalline systems can translate molecular photoisomerization into mesoscale reorganization, but retaining light-written anisotropy in fluid mesophases remains challenging because the programmed order readily relaxes. Here, we show that photo-responsive RM-AzoSi3 microdroplets enable polarized-light writing, rewriting, and quantitative readout of mesophase anisotropy at single-droplet resolution. Microdroplet arrays prepared by µ-contact printing on PDMS exhibit a hyperbolic hedgehog internal organization that can be reoriented by polarized irradiation into directional anisotropic states perpendicular to the incident polarization. Polarized imaging enables the monitoring of internal organization and shows that repeated irradiation progressively suppresses relaxation, yielding long-lived anisotropy while preserving rewritability. Under inert atmosphere, photopolymerization further tunes the balance between structural fixation and preservation of mesoscopic order, with strong sensitivity to irradiation power, exposure time, and pulse frequency. Together, these results establish light-programmed persistent anisotropy as an accessible design principle in fluid soft matter and position photo-responsive microdroplets as a versatile platform for directional optical programming in soft-photonic materials.

papers.title: Assessing the Limits of He Isotope Separation Under Confinement in Nanoporous Materials
papers.abstract: Separation of helium isotopes is of interest owing to the critical importance and limited supply of helium-3 ( 3 He). Nanoporous materials offer a viable route for gas-phase isotope separation through either selective adsorption or quantum sieving. Here, to maximize the isotope selectivity of quantum sieving we propose coupling a strongly attracting open-metal site for He adsorption to a surrounding nanopore acting as a confining potential. We demonstrate that upon tightening the pore, the zero-point energy (ZPE) elevates up to a point where 3 He detaches while 4 He remains bound. Our model shows that 100% isotope-selective adsorption of 4He is achieved when pores of diameter 4.8-5.3 Å are coupled to metal sites with He binding energies of 2-20 kJ/mol. At 20 K, operating pressures between 0.3-30 bar are estimated, which increase to 2-6 kbar at 77 K. Even if the exact pore size for 100% isotope-selective adsorption cannot be realized, our results provide a rational design strategy for materials with unprecedentedly large He isotope separation factors at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: The helium ground-state energy to 60 significant figures on a laptop
papers.abstract: We report a variational upper bound on the nonrelativistic, infinite-nuclear-mass ground-state energy of helium whose first 60 significant figures are converged, E0 = −2.903 724 377 034 119 598 311 159 245 194 404 446 696 925 311 117 290 339 042 34 Eh, 16 more than the best previous record. The calculation runs on a laptop and the method, which we call FLAKE (Fock-log anisotropic Kronecker eigensolver), combines four ingredients. (i) A change of variables making Schwartz’s Hylleraas-type basis with logarithms an exact tensor product, so the Hamiltonian is a sum of 27 Kronecker products of small matrices. (ii) Exact, arbitrary-precision orthonormalisation of the small radial and angular Gram factors removes all cancellation from the large computation. (iii) Fixed-point products at about 280 bits are split without error into ordinary double-precision matrix multiplications. (iv) The variational space is anisotropic: it carries extra radial degree and a tower of (ln s)p functions only at low angular order, as dictated by channelresolved convergence rates. Every energy quoted is certified by an independent arbitrary-precision evaluation of the Rayleigh quotient of the explicit trial function. The remaining error is estimated from geometric convergence laws that predicted subsequent energy increments to within 2%.

papers.title: Atomic memory in complex molecular decay patterns after deep inner-shell ionisation.
papers.abstract: A single low-keV X-ray photon can strip a molecule of more than ten electrons. Deep inner-shell ionization of heavy atoms, including those incorporated into radiosensitizers in emerging cancer therapies, initiates an Auger cascade that rapidly builds up high charge and can drive extensive fragmentation. How this charge accumulates, not the total energy deposited alone, governs the molecular response to irradiation. Yet cascade-driven charge buildup is neglected in current radiation-damage and dosimetry models because complex Auger cascades remain poorly understood, and tracing how this initially local atomic process develops into an extended molecular response remains challenging. We demonstrate that the total charge produced by an Auger cascade is already encoded in the first Auger decay step, which can be described using existing atomic data. State-selective Auger-electron–ion coincidence measurements on atomic xenon resolve this earliest branching and reveal markedly different final charge distributions, with mean charges ranging from +4 to +11 depending on the first Auger decay channel. In molecules, the later cascade is strongly modified by the surrounding valence-electron environment. Measurements on molecular iodine show substantially enhanced charge buildup, which is captured by an “ideal electron-reservoir model” representing how sustained access to valence electrons increases both the final charge and electron emission. Together, these results connect the intrinsically atomic first Auger decay step to the final molecular charge buildup and provide a route to include cascade-driven charging in predictive descriptions of X-ray damage, from structural biology to emerging Auger therapies.

papers.title: Per-Stage Controls and Failure Modes in a Co-Folding Virtual Screening Cascade for the Keap1–Nrf2 Interaction
papers.abstract: Virtual-screening cascades combine learned affinity prediction, co-folding, physics-based rescoring and molecular dynamics, but each score requires an independent control. We audited these stages for the Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1)–nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) interaction using a 130,793-compound make-on-demand library. Two affinity models showed molecular-weight coupling and ordered activity-cliff pairs above chance (about 68%), but neither showed a detectable association between predicted and measured potency gaps or above-chance enantiomer ordering. Co-folding confidence weakly discriminated valid from invalid poses, whereas training-free guidance raised the share of poses with preserved stereochemistry from 28% to 95–97%. For five co-crystal references, the best of five top-ranked poses lay within 2 Å; three structures were released after the model’s training cutoff. A seeded gate separated eleven seed compounds from model-selected decoys with a stratified area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.98. In a size-stratified, anion-restricted test of 101 actives and 124 assay-defined inactives, molecular mechanics generalised Born surface area (MM-GBSA) rescoring reached an AUROC of 0.68 (95% confidence interval 0.60–0.76), was not resolved from the strongest descriptor baseline (0.64), and fell below both affinity models (0.82–0.86). Ensemble molecular dynamics of five candidates did not reproduce the single-structure ordering, and two solvation models disagreed on candidate separability. The results bound the supported use of each stage on this test system. The controls and their data are released as a reusable audit suite.

papers.title: Leveraging Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Fast and Accurate AMBER-Compatible Force Field Parameterization
Argon Coordination to the 3d Transition-Metal Monohalides: A Systematic Study of σ-Acceptor Accessibility in Ar–MX (M = Sc–Cu; X = F, Cl, Br)
papers.abstract: Argon is generally regarded as chemically inert, yet direct Ar–metal coordination has been established for several late transition-metal complexes. Here, we systematically investigate Ar coordination across the 3d transition-metal monofluorides, MF (M = Sc–Cu), and subsequently extend the analysis to the corresponding chlorides and bromides. Density functional theory, population analysis, energy decomposition, and multireference calculations reveal a pronounced and nonmonotonic variation in Ar-binding propensity across the MF series. Ar binding is characterized by Ar 3pσ donation into a metal-centered σ-acceptor manifold of mixed 4s and 3dz2 character. In predominantly single-reference systems, the metal 4s population of bare MF provides a simple descriptor of the accessibility of this manifold: low 4s occupation is generally associated with Ar coordination, whereas high 4s occupation is associated with dissociation. Consistent with this picture, single-reference calculations give shortrange Ar-bound minima for MnF and FeF on lower-spin DFT surfaces with reduced 4s occupation, although these solutions are SCF-unstable and require multireference confirmation. The same metaldependent trend is largely retained for the chlorides and bromides, with additional modulation by the M–X framework. Sc halides mark the multireference limit of the simple 4s-based description.

papers.title: Computationally Guided Discovery of Cannabinoid Derivatives for Antiviral and Anticancer Applications: From Chemical Space to Experimental Validation
papers.abstract: Cannabinoids represent a chemically diverse and structurally tunable class of natural and synthetic compounds that have attracted growing interest as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic discovery. However, their extensive chemical diversity, polypharmacology, conformational flexibility, and complex pharmacokinetic properties make the systematic identification and optimisation of therapeutically useful derivatives challenging. Recent advances in computer-aided drug discovery (CADD), molecular simulation, quantum chemistry, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modelling, and artificial intelligence (AI) provide opportunities to interrogate the chemical space of cannabinoids in a systematic and mechanistically informed manner. This review examines computational strategies for the discovery and optimisation of cannabinoid derivatives with potential antiviral and anticancer applications, emphasising the integration of complementary computational approaches rather than reliance on isolated in silico predictions. A hierarchical computational workflow is described, progressing from cannabinoid chemical-space generation and ligand preparation to disease-relevant target identification, virtual screening, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, binding free-energy estimation, quantum-chemical analysis, and ADMET/drug-likeness prediction. For antiviral discovery, computational investigations of SARS-CoV-2 targets, including the main protease (Mpro/3CLpro), papain-like protease (PLpro), spike protein, and spike–ACE2 interface, are discussed alongside emerging host-directed targets. For anticancer applications, computational studies involving EGFR, HER2, VEGFR, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, apoptosis, autophagy, oxidative stress, and cell-cycle regulation are evaluated. Particular emphasis is placed on the complementary roles of docking and MD simulations in characterising binding modes, interaction persistence, conformational stability, and molecular recognition, while MM-PBSA/MM-GBSA and related approaches provide additional energetic criteria for candidate prioritisation. QSAR and AI/ML-assisted approaches are further considered as complementary tools for expanding chemical-space exploration, predicting biological activity and ADMET properties, and enabling multi-parameter candidate prioritisation. Importantly, computational affinity scores are not treated as sufficient evidence of target inhibition or therapeutic efficacy. Instead, the review emphasises a progressive validation framework in which computationally prioritised candidates are evaluated through biochemical target-engagement studies, cellular assays, and, where appropriate, in vivo models. Experimental observations can subsequently inform structure–activity relationship analysis, lead optimisation, and iterative computational rescreening, establishing a closed-loop strategy for integrating molecular recognition, dynamic behaviour, binding energetics, pharmacokinetic properties, toxicity, and biological activity during cannabinoid lead development. The review critically examines key limitations of current computational approaches, including incomplete treatment of ligand flexibility, scoring-function limitations, protein conformational heterogeneity, limited experimental validation, dataset bias in AI/ML models, and translational challenges associated with cannabinoid solubility, bioavailability, metabolism, receptor promiscuity, psychoactive liabilities, and off-target effects. Collectively, current evidence indicates that computationally guided cannabinoid discovery is a promising but predominantly preclinical strategy. Further progress will depend on integrating CADD, molecular simulation, AI-assisted molecular design, uncertainty-aware prediction, and experimental validation into iterative multi-objective optimisation frameworks that jointly address potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics, toxicity, and translational relevance.

papers.title: Electrostatic preactivation, a missing step in dioxygen activation
papers.abstract: Dioxygen is the oxidant of aerobic life, yet most closed-shell molecules are stable in its presence. 1–4 Conventional accounts of dioxygen activation begin with electron transfer to O 2 , typically from a redox-active metal centre or cofactor. 5–9 Here we show that preparing dioxygen to receive that electron is a separate function, discharged by the electrostatic environment alone, and that the two can be tuned independently. At the equilibrium geometry of neutral O 2 the anion that must receive the electron is unbound; 10,11 a Lewis-acidic field removes this obstacle before any charge moves, a stage we term preactivation . Point charges alone split the O 2 π* manifold and bind the anion at the neutral geometry. Reaction-path calculations show that inner-sphere electron transfer from the Zn–C bond, which generates a superoxide/alkyl-radical pair without metal-centred redox chemistry, is rate-determining. Calibrated on dialkylzincs alone, the in-plane anisotropy of the field gradient, with one term in the charge and distance of the metal resolved within the same series, predicts the π* splitting to within 7% in four enzyme active sites containing iron, copper, nickel or no metal. The electrostatic contribution of an enzyme active site to preactivation can thus be quantified on a scale calibrated with redox-silent organozinc compounds.

papers.title: Atomic Layer Deposition of Ferroelectric HfxZr(1-x)O2 from Metal-β-diketonate Precursors with Fine Cation Tunability.
papers.abstract: HfxZr1-xO2 (HZO) is a promising ferroelectric material for next-generation neuromorphic devices, where precise compositional control and complementary metal-oxidesemiconductor (CMOS) compatible processing are critical. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is particularly attractive for HZO integration due to its excellent conformality for future three-dimensional device architectures and possibility to control the composition. However, many widely used Hf and Zr precursors suffer from limited volatility and thermal stability. In this work, we exploit the robustness and favourable growth rates of the β-diketonate precursors Hf(thd)4 and Zr(thd)4 (thd = 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-3,5heptanedionate) - with ozone co-reactant – to demonstrate the ALD growth of binary HfO2, ZrO2, and ferroelectric HZO thin films with finely controlled Hf/Zr cation ratios enabling the Hf/Zr composition required for ferroelectric thin films. Optimized binary ALD processes yield low growth-per-cycle (GPC) values of 0.085 Å/cycle for HfO2 and 0.12 Å/cycle for ZrO2, these low GPCs enable fine and reproducible control of the Hf:Zr

papers.title: AutoSolvate 2.0: Automated Preparation of Chemically Diverse Explicit-Solvent Systems for Multiscale Molecular Simulation
papers.abstract: Advanced quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM), machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), and hybrid methods provide powerful engines for modeling solution-phase chemistry. Yet before production begins, chemically diverse explicit-solvent systems must be parameterized, assembled at the desired composition, relaxed, equilibrated, and sampled. This preparatory “first mile” remains labor-intensive, requiring multiple software packages and manual customization, particularly for transition-metal complexes, solvent mixtures, and multicomponent electrolytes. Here, we present AutoSolvate 2.0, a modular, open-source framework that converts molecular structures and solution compositions into equilibrated, simulation-ready explicit-solvent ensembles. The new AutoMCPB module automates Metal Center Parameter Builder (MCPB.py)-based parameterization of transition-metal complexes (TMCs), while generalized system representations support multiple solutes and solvents at arbitrary molar, weight, or volume ratios. Standardized wrappers integrate force-field generation, box construction, minimization, heating, equilibration, classical sampling, and microsolvated-cluster extraction. Native classical molecular dynamics (MD) and TeraChem-based QM/MM workflows execute directly; equilibrated coordinates, velocities, trajectories, and clusters provide starting points for external quantum mechanical (QM), other QM/MM, MLIP training, and hybrid machine learning (ML)/classical workflows. JSON, guided command-line, and Model Context Protocol interfaces support high-throughput and agent-assisted use. We demonstrate these capabilities by reproducing the solvent-dependent absorption spectrum of an aqueous transition-metal photosensitizer, the composition-dependent microsolvation of water–acetonitrile mixtures, and characteristic ion-pairing features of a published multicomponent electrolyte simulation. Together, these applications establish AutoSolvate 2.0 as a preparation and initial-sampling layer connecting chemical system specification to classical, quantum, and machine-learning simulations. Rather than competing with higher-accuracy methods, AutoSolvate provides the on-ramp needed to apply them efficiently to complex explicit-solvent systems.

papers.title: Heat transport and time-resolved in situ thermography in mechanochemical reaction vessels
papers.abstract: Heat is intrinsic to mechanochemistry, and temperature is known to play a key role in the kinetics of many reactions. Here, we introduce a technique to accurately quantify temperatures within mechanochemical processes. Treating these processes as a thermodynamic system, we reveal the highly sensitive effects that reaction vessel, internal conditions, and environmental parameters can have on heat flow and temperature within the reaction space. We show how this also determines space-and time-resolved metrology limits when measuring temperature changes using single-point or full-field infrared thermography approaches. After identifying these fundamental limits, we present an accessible in situ thermography approach to directly obtain batch temperature accurately, nonintrusively, and in real-time.

papers.title: The CO₂ Concentration Inversion Effect: *CO Generation Rate and *CO C–C Coupling Efficiency as Dual Kinetic Descriptors for Catalyst-Dependent C₂ Selectivity in Dilute CO₂ Electroreduction¹
papers.abstract: The electrochemical reduction of dilute CO₂ (5–33% v/v) to multicarbon (C₂₊) products offers a route to utilize industrial exhaust directly, bypassing energy-intensive CO₂ capture and purification. Our systematic investigations from 2023 to 2026 reveal a counter-intuitive paradigm: under dilute CO₂ feed, the C₂ selectivity of copper-based catalysts can surpass the pure-CO₂ baseline. Here we define the CO₂ concentration inversion effect as a kinetic regime where C₂ selectivity under dilute CO₂ exceeds the pure-CO₂ baseline—first in the FE(C₂)/FE(C₁) ratio and, for an increasing number of catalyst families, in the absolute C₂ Faradaic efficiency at matched potentials. This non-monotonic selectivity shows that C₂ formation is governed by a catalyst-tunable balance between *CO supply and coupling kinetics. We introduce two quantitative kinetic descriptors—the *CO production rate r (in mol cm⁻² s⁻¹) and the *CO C–C coupling efficiency η ∈ [0,1]—that jointly resolve the fate of *CO intermediates. In-situ FT–IR spectroscopy confirms that coupling efficiency is primarily governed by CO₂ concentration; we resolve a decoupling between microscopic η and the macroscopic FE(C₂₊)/FE(C₁) ratio. This framework, validated across B-doped Cu, Ag@Cu₂O and Cu₂(OH)₂CO 3 -derived Cu, challenges the implicit assumption that high-purity CO₂ is a prerequisite for efficient C₂₊ electrosynthesis.

papers.title: Text-mined dataset of sol-gel synthesis protocols with phase purity outcomes using large language models
papers.abstract: Sol-gel synthesis is a versatile method for producing inorganic materials that offers advantages such as atomic-level mixing and lower processing temperatures over traditional solid-state methods. Despite these benefits, achieving phase purity remains a challenge due to the process's sensitivity to synthesis parameters such as precursor choice, solvent selection, and heating conditions. Negative results, such as phase-impure outcomes, are essential for understanding sol-gel reaction pathways, but are largely absent from existing curated datasets. This work leverages Gemini 3.0 Flash to construct a text-mined inorganic sol-gel database with phase purity information. The dataset contains ~148,000 synthesis records, including ~28,000 phase-impure entries. All extracted entities achieved F1 scores greater than 0.89. At the record level, 68% of extracted records match human annotation on all evaluated fields. Furthermore, to validate the scientific utility of our dataset, we demonstrate that the aggregated data reproduces previously reported phase-purity trends for BiFeO 3 thin films.

papers.title: Unraveling the Temperature-Dependent Redox Cycle of Chromium Species in Molten Chloride Salt via In-Situ X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Molten chloride salt is a widely studied high-temperature electrolyte, with established use in pyrochemical reprocessing and electrorefining, and frequent use as a model system for concentrated solar power and molten salt reactor applications. Chromium (Cr) is a key element in high-temperature structural alloys. However, the temperature-dependent evolution and stability of Cr species in this environment remain insufficiently understood. Cr-redox chemistry in molten chloride salts governs the dissolution, oxidation and transformation of Cr-containing species, with direct implications for corrosion and dealloying of structural alloys as well as broader molten-salt processing applications. In the present study, the chemical stability of CrCl 2 , CrCl 3 , and Cr 2 O 3 in LiCl-KCl eutectic molten salt during heating and cooling was systematically investigated using in-situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy. The results revealed that CrCl 3 and Cr 2 O 3 remained chemically stable under the tested conditions, whereas CrCl 2 underwent oxidation by impurities to form Cr 2 O 3 at 500 °C, but partially converted back to Cr 2+ species upon cooling to room temperature. Additional gas chromatography measurements detected H 2 evolution during heating of CrCl 2 in LiCl–KCl, supporting the involvement of residual moisture in the oxidation process. Additionally, the interaction between chromium and NiCl 2 in molten salt was examined, indicating that chromium likely reduced Ni 2+ to metallic Ni 0 , while being oxidized to Cr 2+ , which subsequently underwent a similar chemical evolution as CrCl 2 in the molten salt. These findings unravel a temperature-dependent, impurity-mediated redox cycle of Cr species between the initial room-temperature, molten, and post-cooling states in molten chloride salt, providing a foundation for understanding and controlling Cr the dissolution, oxidation and transformation, and for developing effective corrosion-mitigation strategies to enhance the stability of high-temperature structural alloys in molten-salt systems.

papers.title: Efficient Long-Wavelength Through-Space Charge Transfer Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence in Conformationally Adaptive Emitters without Conformational Locking
papers.abstract: Through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TSCT-TADF) emitters often employ conformationally constrained donor–acceptor architectures to control through-space electronic coupling, particularly for long-wavelength emission. Here, we report conformationally adaptive orange-to-red TSCT-TADF emitters based on an S-shaped donor–π–acceptor–π–donor framework composed of phenoxazine donors, xanthene linkers, and a dibenzo[ a,j ]phenazine acceptor. Structural and NMR analyses reveal substantial conformational mobility, while systematic conformational searches and excited-state calculations identify thermally accessible conformers with distinct donor-acceptor geometries and excited-state characteristics. Comparative studies with reference compounds and fragment-resolved transition-density analysis show that the xanthene linker primarily acts as a conformational regulator and that the low-energy CT states have predominant TSCT character with only minor linker involvement. Temperature-dependent early-time photoluminescence measurements reveal continuous spectral relaxation in fluid toluene that slows upon cooling and is absent in rigid Zeonex and mCBP hosts, providing strong evidence for structural relaxation following photoexcitation within a pre-existing conformational ensemble. The emitters exhibit orange-to-red TADF with reverse intersystem crossing rates on the order of 10 5 –10 6 s −1 . Organic light-emitting diodes employing these emitters show electroluminescence at 598–624 nm, external quantum efficiencies up to 14.9%, and limited efficiency roll-off over a broad luminance range. These results demonstrate that efficient long-wavelength TSCT-TADF can be realized without permanent conformational locking and establish a framework for understanding the interplay between ground-state conformational heterogeneity and excited-state structural relaxation.

papers.title: De Novo Design of Enantioselective Artificial Metalloenzyme Photocatalysts Containing Metal Polypyridine Cofactors
papers.abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins. In this study, we show that generative protein design can be harnessed to create de novo scaffolds that selectively accommodate one enantiomer of a metal polypyridine photocatalyst as a cofactor. The resulting ArMs enable efficient, enantioselective photocatalysis, highlighting a broadly applicable route for programming stereocontrol into metalloenzyme catalysts. High total turnover numbers are achieved, the ArMs can be recycled by simply extracting reaction products and reusing the aqueous ArM solution for subsequent reactions, and even commercially available racemic cofactor can be used for ArM formation. Transient Absorption characterization revealed that improvements to catalysis result from the increased quantum yield and excited state lifetime of the cofactor upon binding and substrate binding proximal to the cofactor within the ArM active site, which controls reaction stereoselectivity and the mechanism of energy transfer involved in photocatalysis. The simplicity of this approach could help transition ArM research out of a small group of specialist labs to any capable of expressing synthetic genes and working with commercially available metal complexes.

papers.title: A Statistical Mechanics Perspective on Memory and Forgetting in Nonequilibrated Polymer Films
papers.abstract: Polymer systems prepared far from equilibrium often retain long-lived memory of their processing history, manifested experimentally as molecular recoiling stresses and their anomalous relaxation behavior. Relaxation may therefore be viewed as the gradual erasure of stored nonequilibrium memory (forgetting). Experiments on spin-coated polymer thin films reveal relaxation behavior that lies beyond the scope of conventional equilibrium polymer dynamics and continuum viscoelastic descriptions, which only partially explain it. Yet a unifying statistical-mechanical framework for these observations has remained elusive. In this Perspective, I argue that such phenomena can be understood as the non-Markovian regression of constrained conformational entropy. Pivoting from Onsager’s regression hypothesis, the theory of dynamics of nonequilibrium variables, and the Mori–Zwanzig projection-operator formalism, molecular recoiling stress is identified as a slow nonequilibrium variable governing relaxation in nonequilibrated polymer systems. Projecting the microscopic dynamics onto this variable leads naturally to a stress-projected generalized Langevin equation with a history-dependent memory kernel. This minimal coarse-grained description accounts for stretched-exponential stress relaxation, Arrhenius temperature dependence, and the experimentally observed scaling of relaxation times with polymer chain length. The aim is not to introduce new microscopic models, but to provide a simple and general statistical-mechanics framework that rationalizes history-dependent stress relaxation in polymers and clarifies how polymers gradually forget their preparation history far from equilibrium. More broadly, this framework suggests that polymer memory and slow relaxation arise from the regression of constrained conformational entropy stored during nonequilibrium preparation, with topological constraints acting on nonequilibrium polymer ensembles to generate persistent, history-dependent mechanical responses.

papers.title: Metasurface information processor based on 4D bionic hardware and software for ultralow energy consumption computing
papers.abstract: As AI technology faces an energy crisis, one promising solution is bionic ultra-low energy computing hardware, which can operate at a power level as low as sub-20-watt based on the 4D model of Ca 2+ channels recently verified in brain information processing. Inspired by this model, here we design and fabricate a 4D bionic computing system based on information metasurface array with the powerful capability of electromagnetic controls. Paired with specific algorithms, each metasurface cell functions as a multifunctional unit, capable of storing, regulating, transmitting, and computing information simultaneously. The metasurface array also has high energy efficiency and precision required for high-performance bionic computing. Integrated with the DNA computing, this system is expected to achieve a variety of functions including DNA replication, DNA logical computation, and DNA produce/readout. We aim to pave the way for a new paradigm in advanced computational materials that meet the evolving demands of AI and robotics.

papers.title: Simulating Catalytic Resonance with Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Static heterogeneous catalysts are constrained by the Sabatier principle, where their overall turnover is limited by balancing the kinetics of reactant binding, surface reaction, and product unbinding. Modulating the surface binding energies between a strong binding state and a weak binding state can overcome this limit. For such a dynamic catalyst, a maximum turnover is achieved at a catalytic resonance modulating frequency. Here we demonstrate that classical molecular simulation approaches can be used to study this phenomena. Our method introduces a generic classical model for a surface reaction with time-dependent surface binding energy. Using a non-equilibrium molecular simulation in which reactants tend to be added to the system and products tend to be removed, we can simulate many catalyst cycles. Our approach reproduces catalytic resonance, with the dynamic catalyst providing up to a three-order-of-magnitude boost in turnover compared to the static catalyst. We further demonstrate the presence of a second resonant frequency in the gas phase, associated with resonance of the reacting bond. The general approach outlined here can be extended to more detailed models and used to study the molecular-scale effects of surface modulation and to computationally test input frequency, amplitude, and waveform for programmable catalysts.

papers.title: FRACTAL: A Ratiometric-based Fingerprinting Framework for Robust Spectral Classification and Ratio-based Spectroscopic Marker Discovery
papers.abstract: Spectral classification is conventionally performed on band intensities, yet ratios between bands have long served as diagnostic indices in vibrational spectroscopy, from lipid-to-protein markers of membrane composition to amide ratios reporting protein secondary structure. Their use, however, has remained confined to a handful of expert-selected pairs, leaving most of the ratio information contained in a spectrum unexamined. Here I present FRACTAL (Full Ratio Combinatorial Analysis for Classification and Analytical Interpretation), which computes every pairwise log-intensity ratio among detected peaks to form a complete ratiometric fingerprint, grounded in compositional data analysis. Each component is a contrast between two assigned bands and is invariant to the multiplicative factors that scale spectral intensities. Applied to serum Raman spectra from a total of 103 donors (53 with COVID-19, 50 healthy controls), FRACTAL screened all 105 ratios among 15 reproducible peaks and identified 38 discriminant contrasts; a ten-ratio fingerprint then matched full-spectrum performance across six classifier architectures spanning linear, kernel-based and ensemble methods (mean internal AUC 0.89–0.93) and generalized to a withheld 20-donor cohort, where every classifier exceeded an AUC of 0.92 and all six converged on the same donor-level prediction accuracy at the median-AUC seed. The retained ratios map onto aromatic amino acid, acute-phase protein and protein–lipid contrasts independently reported in COVID-19. FRACTAL establishes exhaustive ratiometric fingerprinting as a compact, robust and interpretable representation for spectral classification and spectroscopic marker discovery.

papers.title: Molecular Property Prediction with Well-Calibrated Uncertainties via Graph Neural Networks and Conformal Quantile Regression
papers.abstract: Accurate predictive uncertainty quantification (pUQ) is critical for assessing chemical property predictions. Incorrect quantification could lead to costly synthesis and characterization of drug candidates destined to fail, or result in misguided environmental regulations. This work integrates Conformal Quantile Regression (CQR) with graph neural networks to achieve accurate molecular property prediction and well-calibrated predictive uncertainty quantification. By combining conformal prediction with quantile regression, CQR provides model-agnostic, distribution-free prediction intervals with valid coverage for finite samples. We benchmark it against established pUQ approaches, including ensembling, Monte Carlo dropout sampling, mean-variance estimation, and evidential regression. Our experiments on datasets spanning quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, and pharmacokinetics show that CQR generally provides strong calibration while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy and uncertainty-ranking performance. It also effectively captures heteroskedastic noise across the data, which is a key requirement for robust pUQ. Furthermore, we demonstrate its efficacy with an uncertainty-guided retrospective virtual screening experiment for antibiotic discovery, achieving hit rates above 90%. These results establish CQR as a promising, scalable tool for pUQ in molecular property prediction, supporting informed decision-making in applications such as active learning and compound screening for drug discovery and materials design.

papers.title: Coacervate-engineered keratin bioelastomers with tunable mechanics
papers.abstract: Nature employs bottom-up strategies to create elastic materials from protein assemblies, yet transforming structural proteins from abundant agricultural byproducts into customizable bioelastomers remains challenging. Here, we develop a strategy to fabricate bioelastomers with tunable mechanics by co-assembling keratins from wool and feathers through acid-induced coacervation. Time-pH superposition rheology reveals that wool and feather protein coacervates share similar viscoelastic signatures regulated by pH, with relaxation timescales spanning several orders of magnitude. By adjusting the wool-to-feather ratio, the mechanical properties of the resulting materials can be tuned from soft compliance to high stiffness. Strain-resolved Raman spectroscopy and steered molecular dynamics simulations reveal that extensibility and shape recovery originate from reversible microstructural transitions, in which coiled α-helices unfold and reorganize into metastable β-sheet structures under strain. Finally, we demonstrate the compatibility of these coacervate precursors with top-down manufacturing techniques, including wet spinning, blade coating, and extrusion-based 3D printing, enabling the fabrication of moisture-responsive biomaterials with in vitro biocompatibility. This work establishes a scalable platform for upcycling agricultural protein residues into functional bioelastomers for soft devices and biomedical applications.

papers.title: DolphinQCT: The Light-Weighted, Python Based Quasi-Classical Trajectory Setup Tool for ORCA
papers.abstract: ORCA provides an ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) module, but quasi-classical trajectory (QCT) simulations require external preparation of initial coordinates and velocities. We present DolphinQCT, a lightweight, open-source Python tool that samples initial conditions from ORCA frequency calculations and exports them as molecular dynamics restart files. The workflow combines Boltzmann sampling of vibrational energy levels, random-phase normal-mode sampling, and screening based on deviations between electronic and harmonic potential energies.
