The measurements show asymmetric, time-dependent charging in pure water, with mobile counterions responding more rapidly than polymer-bound charge. Added electrolytes suppress this charging-rate imbalance; reversing the ionomer charge sign also reverses the asymmetry of the charging response, and a custom-synthesized more-flexible polymer backbone reduces the rate dependence of the apparent capacitance. The work here shows how the ionomer is an active part of the electrochemical interface, in addition to an ion conductor in the bulk. The platform and fundamental principles developed here are relevant to water electrolyzers, fuel cells, and other membrane-based electrochemical devices.

papers.title: An Ultrathin Embedded SnO2 Interface for Water Dissociation in Bipolar Membranes and pseudo-PEM Electrolyzers
papers.abstract: Water dissociation (WD) at bipolar membrane (BPM) junctions is a key reaction in a number of electrochemical energy conversion and separation technologies. While metal oxide catalysts like SnO 2 accelerate WD, conventional particle-based deposition methods typically yield thick and morphologically heterogeneous junction layers. We report a simple aqueous precursor-treatment route that reconstructs the near-surface region of Nafion into an ultrathin SnO 2 -bearing interface. In contrast to conventional spin-coated SnO 2 , which forms a discrete particulate overlayer, the embedded interface is smooth, spatially confined, and closely integrated with the membrane. Despite this major structural difference, BPMs fabricated from SnO 2 -eb-Nafion exhibit WD performance comparable to benchmark spin-coated SnO 2 junctions. When normalized by SnO 2 loading, the embedded junction delivers a ~21-fold higher current density in an electrolyzer test cell at a total cell voltage of 2 V, highlighting improved catalyst utilization. Structural and electrochemical controls show that the high activity arises from interfacially localized SnO 2 rather than bulk SnO 2 incorporation or altered proton conductivity. The embedded route improves precursor efficiency, increases membrane junction adhesion force by 7×, and maintains stable operation under continuous elec-trolyzer testing. A preliminary pseudo-PEM water-electrolysis demonstration further shows that the embedded SnO 2 interface remains beneficial in an AEI–PEM heterojunction architecture coupled to a PGM-free Co 3 O 4 anode. These results establish precursor-based interfacial self-reconstruction as a practical route to thin, active, and mechanically integrated catalyst–membrane junctions. Keywords: Bipolar membranes; Water dissociation; Tin oxide (SnO 2 ); Ionomer interfaces; Water electrolysis

papers.title: Sorting Commodity Plastics by MOF-based Molecular Sieving
papers.abstract: Efficient sorting of waste plastics according to their chemical structure is desirable for plastics recycling. Here, we present a novel methodology based on a molecular sieving mechanism to realize molecular-level sorting of polymer chains. Using nanopores in metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) as the sieve, polymer chains are differentiated by their thickness and branching structure through selective infiltration into the nanopores in the molten state. The infiltration process is evaluated in situ and semi-quantitatively via continuous monitoring of relative diffraction intensity from the MOF using variable-temperature X-ray diffraction. Three MOFs with varying effective pore window diameters are identified as promising candidates that enable sequential sorting of four highly important commodity plastics: low-density polyethylene, polystyrene, polypropylene, and high-density polyethylene. This work would open up a new paradigm in the field by providing a versatile method capable of sorting the waste plastics mixture with molecular-level precision.

papers.title: Interpretable QSPR Modeling of Surfactant Characteristic Curvature
papers.abstract: Characteristic curvature (Cc) quantifies the intrinsic interfacial curvature tendency of surfactants under defined reference conditions and is a key input to the hydrophilic–lipophilic deviation (HLD) framework for predicting microemulsion phase behavior; however, experimental determination remains laborious, and interpretable molecular structure–Cc relationships across diverse surfactant chemistries are comparatively underdeveloped. Here, we developed a quantitative structure–property relationship (QSPR) framework using a curated literature-derived dataset of 63 anionic and nonionic surfactants, with molecular structures verified against the original sources and experimental values curated to improve consistency of the Cc endpoint, and benchmarked multiple tree-based regression algorithms using two-dimensional RDKit descriptors, fold-contained preprocessing, Yeo–Johnson target transformation, SHAP-based feature selection, and nested cross-validation. XGBoost achieved the strongest performance on 13-surfactants test set, with R 2 = 0.85, RMSE = 0.53, and MAE = 0.44 Cc units, with all metrics calculated on the inverse-transformed scale; the observed error was of the same order of magnitude as reported experimental uncertainty, supporting preliminary prediction within the represented chemical domain rather than replacing experimental Cc determination. SHAP and partial-dependence analyses identified electrotopological, topological, hydrophobicity-related, and other physicochemical descriptors associated with the model response, revealing nonlinear and threshold-like patterns that support chemically interpretable structure–property hypotheses without establishing causal mechanisms or experimentally validated design rules; the framework therefore offers a reproducible basis for prioritizing structurally related surfactants for subsequent experimental evaluation and provides a methodological reference for future Cc modeling with broader chemical coverage and prospective validation.

papers.title: Liquid State 31P NMR as a Tool to Leverage the Understanding of Reconstituted Milk Systems
papers.abstract: The objective of this work was to establish the peak assignment in liquid state 31P NMR of milk systems and investigate the method as a tool to identify di!erences in casein micelles as consequence of di!erent processing history. Suspensions of milk protein concentrate with removal of casein micelles by EDTA addition and ultra-centrifugation were analyzed by liquid state 31P NMR and compared with the original suspensions. Moreover, 1H-31P total correlation spectroscopy NMR was applied to di!erentiate between peaks from phosphoserines and inorganic phosphate in dairy systems. The results provide direct evidence that the signals observed in liquid-state 31P NMR of milk systems originate from phosphoserine residues in soluble caseins and inorganic phosphate in the serum phase, thereby resolving conflicting assignments reported in previous studies. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that liquid state 31P NMR is able to quantitatively di!erentiate the native amount of inorganic phosphate in the serum phase in suspensions of milk protein concentrate and skim milk. In light of the crucial importance of the calcium phosphate equilibrium between milk serum and casein micelles for understanding the casein micelle structure and its changes, liquid state 31P NMR shows potential as a suitable technique to get a better understanding of how processing a!ect the mineral equilibrium in casein micelles.

papers.title: Diabat 2.0: A Comprehensive Diabatization Toolkit for Multichromophoric Systems
papers.abstract: The construction of physically meaningful quasi-diabatic states and the evaluation of their electronic couplings are essential for describing nonadiabatic processes in molecular aggregates and other multichromophoric systems. Existing software implementations, however, are often restricted to dimers, two-state models, or particular types of quasi-diabatic states. Here, we present Diabat 2.0, a comprehensive toolkit for multistate diabatization in multichromophoric systems. It constructs the adiabatic-to-diabatic (ATD) transformation based on the adiabatic-state wave functions and energies obtained from external quantum chemistry calculations, yielding quasi-diabatic states and their electronic couplings in a nearly black-box manner. Diabat 2.0 implements several advanced ATD methods, including a general approach that can reliably construct quasi-diabatic states with diverse charge and excitation distributions without prescribing state types. This enables Diabat 2.0 to support diabatization in a broad range of scenarios that involve not only conventional charge-transfer, locally excited, and correlated triplet pair states, but also a variety of exotic states, such as mixed radical-triplet states, trion states, radical-coupled triplet-pair states, and charge-localized dicationic states. These capabilities are demonstrated in applications to several multichromophoric systems that pose substantial challenges to existing software.

papers.title: Revealing Solvent-free Solid-fed Aerosol Flame Technique to Synthesize Copper Oxide Deposited on Ceria Catalyst for Efficient CO Oxidation Applications
papers.abstract: Developing efficient technologies for CO oxidation is an urgent priority in environmental catalysis. Copper oxide deposited on cerium oxide (CuO/CeO 2 ) has attracted considerable attention as a promising non-precious-metal catalyst for low-temperature CO oxidation. Furthermore, aerosol process emerged as a scalable route to engineer CuO/CeO 2 with tailored structures and interfacial properties, however, popular vapor-fed and liquid-fed aerosol flame approaches remain constrained by precursor requirements (vapor-fed: sufficient vapor pressure; liquid-fed: precursor solubility or dispersibility in carrier solvents). Here, for the first time, we introduce solid-fed aerosol flame synthesis (SAFS) as a single-step, solvent-free route to synthesize heterostructured CuO/CeO 2 catalysts. Through selective vaporization of Cu 2 O followed by heterogeneous nucleation onto solid CeO 2 particles, SAFS produces a well-defined architecture of CuO nanoparticles intimately deposited on CeO 2 supports. By varying the flame conditions and Cu loading, we systematically investigate their effects on particle formation, interfacial properties, and catalytic performance. The highest performance catalyst, synthesized at 2 L/min-CH 4 flame with 2 wt.% Cu 2 O, exhibits the highest CO oxidation activity, achieving a CO oxidation rate of 13.73 mLCO/min·gcat and a turnover frequency of 0.026 s -1 at 120 ºC. This enhanced performance, compared to other as-prepared CuO/CeO 2 samples, arises from an optimal balance between oxygen vacancy generation and metal-support interaction achieved during the SAFS process. Here, oxygen vacancy generation is favored under fuel-rich conditions, whereas metal-support interaction decreases with CeO 2 sublimation and CuO nanoparticle sintering under elevated combustion enthalpy. These findings advance the fundamental understanding of flame-based synthesis and provide a scalable route toward high-performance, cost-effective catalysts for environmental remediation.

papers.title: Novel Quinoxaline-Based Cyanocarbonimidodithioate Derivatives as Non-Hydroxamate Selective HDAC8 Inhibitors: Design, Synthesis, Biological Evaluation and Mechanistic Studies
papers.abstract: Histone deacetylase 8 (HDAC8) has emerged as a promising anticancer target; however, most clinically approved hydroxamate-based HDAC inhibitors possess several limitations. A novel series of quinoxaline-based HDAC inhibitors containing a sulfur-based cyanocarbonimidodithioate non-hydroxamate zinc-binding group was designed and synthesized to overcome the selectivity and toxicity limitations of conventional hydroxamate HDAC inhibitors. A total of twenty-three quinoxaline-cyanocarbonimidodithioate derivatives (QZ 1-23) were synthesized and evaluated for HDAC8 inhibitory activity. The compounds demonstrated preferential inhibition of HDAC8 over HDAC4. Among the series, QZ-11 (IC50 = 0.3 μM) and QZ-4 (IC50 = 0.57 μM) emerged as the most promising inhibitors exhibiting favourable selectivity profiles against other tested HDAC isoforms. Both compounds demonstrated moderate to good antiproliferative activity against the IMR-32, SH-SY5Y, and FaDu cell lines. Biological studies revealed that QZ-4 and QZ-11 significantly suppressed colony formation, induced apoptosis, activated caspase-3/7, and induced G2/M phase cell-cycle arrest in IMR-32 cells, and increased acetylation of the HDAC8 substrate SMC3 without altering total SMC3 expression. Molecular docking studies suggested key interactions with HDAC8 selectivity-determining residues His142, Tyr306, and Phe152, while molecular dynamics simulations revealed stable occupancy of the catalytic pocket and persistent Zn-associated interactions throughout 100 ns trajectories. Collectively, these findings identify quinoxaline-cyanocarbonimidodithioates as a promising class of non-hydroxamate HDAC8- inhibitors and support further optimization of sulfur-based zinc-binding pharmacophores for the development of next-generation epigenetic anticancer agents.

papers.title: Orthonym: verified IUPAC names for chemical structures in the wild
papers.abstract: Chemical structures can be named systematically, and the 2013 IUPAC recommendations define one preferred name for each. For most of history, only a specially trained chemist or dedicated closed software tools could generate a correct, systematic molecule name from a chemical structure. Published neural structure-to-name translators can produce a fluent name for the wrong molecule. Here we present Orthonym: a generator of verified IUPAC names for chemical structures. This open, deterministic, rule-based generator emits a name only after verifying that it correctly describes the input structure. OPSIN reads back each candidate name, and the InChIKey of the parsed structure must equal that of the input; otherwise, the engine declines to name. On 2.2 million selected molecules from ChEBI, QM9, PubChem and ZINC22, it named 97.37% correctly and emitted no name for the wrong molecule. Orthonym is available under the MIT licence as a Python package and a web application.

papers.title: Helium Compression Chamber: an ab initio molecular dynamics approach to chemical reactions under pressure
papers.abstract: Understanding how pressure affects chemical reactivity requires methods capable of describing both the structural response of molecules and the thermodynamics of reactions under compression. We present the Helium Compression Chamber (HeCC), a computational approach in which molecules are compressed within an explicit helium environment and their reaction free energy profiles are determined from finite-temperature molecular dynamics simulations. An on-the-fly machine-learning force field is employed to make extensive sampling feasible while retaining ab initio accuracy for the underlying potential-energy evaluations. The pressure response of four representative reactions is investigated, including bond cleavage, electrocyclization, cycloaddition, and hydrogen transfer. The calculated free-energy profiles show that compression systematically favors reactions associated with a decrease in molecular volume, while the opposite trend is observed for cyclobutene ring opening. In particular, the Diels–Alder reaction becomes barrierless at sufficiently high pressure, whereas the barriers for hexatriene cyclization and the 1,5-hydrogen shift decrease progressively with compression. The structural changes along the reaction coordinates and the pressure dependence of the corresponding activation and reaction volumes are compared with predictions from the extreme pressure-polarizable continuum model (XP-PCM) method. The comparison illustrates both the consistency and the differences between explicit-and continuum-pressure descriptions. HeCC therefore offers a route toward finite-temperature simulations of chemical reactions under pressure and provides a foundation for extending such calculations to more realistic solvation environments.

papers.title: ToSCA: Total Scattering Conditioned Variational Autoencoder for Atomic Structure Prediction from Pair Distribution Function Data
papers.abstract: Designing new materials is often slow and experimentally intensive, with structural characterization representing a particular bottleneck. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) aim to accelerate this process by predicting plausible atomic structures describing a material directly from experimental data. Here we present the total scattering conditioned variational autoencoder (ToSCA), a generative ML model for predicting plausible atomic structures of metal oxide nanomaterials from total scattering and pair distribution function (PDF) data. ToSCA learns a chemically meaningful latent representation and predicts unit cells within tolerances suitable for subsequent real-space refinement. The model also shows behavior consistent with learning structural relationships between related crystal types, and can correctly place the new CHILI-Interpolation dataset in the latent space. Finally, we demonstrate that ToSCA is able to retain useful performance in a realistic use-case by testing it on 11 experimental PDFs from 3 crystal types, including test cases outside of the training distribution.

papers.title: Neural Kinetics: LEARNING KINETICS AS TRANSPORT IN COMPOSITIONAL SPACE
papers.abstract: Complex bio-derived and fossil mixtures contain thousands of molecules whose individual structures and reaction pathways cannot be fully resolved, making conventional mechanism-based kinetic modelling impractical. A reaction network detailed enough to describe every formula-level transformation would contain far more reactions and parameters than the available data can constrain. We propose to overcome this limitation by representing mixtures directly as abundance fields on a compositional grid indexed by molecular descriptors, specifically carbon number (#C) and double-bond equivalent (DBE), and by learning a time-conditioned, chemistry-informed operator that maps the initial composition to predict a later state. The evolution rates of the chemical space are learned by a two-dimensional Fourier neural operator (FNO) acting jointly on a set of heteroatom classes, with normalized time and compositional coordinates appended as input channels. Because experimental data are limited, we enlarge the training set with synthetic trajectories generated from the measured samples, pre-train on this ensemble, and then calibrate a small subset of parameters on the measured distributions. We tested the framework on a case of oxidation of a complex hydrocarbon mixture that is tracked by FTICR-MS over sixty seconds of reaction. On an independent sample the framework, that we named NeuralKinetics, reproduced the measured endpoint class composition within a mean absolute error of approximately one percent and arranged the heteroatom classes correctly on the compositional grid. The second test was an entirely different system: litter decomposition in a peatland warming experiment, also followed by FTICR-MS but over two years. The developed operator accurately predicted the endpoint class composition of the held-out sample proving that the framework is flexible enough to adapt to diverse reactive systems.

papers.title: PtSe2/Graphene Interfacial Coupling Enhances the Intrinsic Electrocatalytic Activity of PtSe2 Edge Sites
papers.abstract: Platinum-based chalcogenides (PtX2) can be efficiently activated as electrocatalysts for water splitting through the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Edges in layered PtSe2 are effective in HER; however, the effect of edge interaction with conductive electrodes like graphene remains unclear. This study investigates the mechanism by which PtX2 (X = S, Se, Te) edges interact with graphene to uncover the origin of chalcogen-dependent differences in electrocatalysis through interfacial electronic coupling. Graphene flakes decorated with PtX2 nanosheets have reduced overpotential and enhanced kinetics in the HER. Interestingly, PtSe2/graphene exhibits the lowest overpotential among all samples, even though it also has the lowest electrochemically accessible surface area. First-principles calculations confirm the interfacial coupling between PtSe2 edges and graphene with pronounced charge accumulation in platinum-selenium edges. Gibbs free energy calculations show different activities for different chalcogens of PtX2/graphene, consistent with experimental results. Our findings indicate that graphene acts as an electronic regulator for PtSe2/graphene, which enhances the intrinsic catalytic activity of the platinum-selenium edge sites, making them more effective for the HER despite their lower density. This interfacial electronic coupling through conductive electrodes provides a powerful strategy for the rational design of next-generation electrocatalysts, enabling enhanced activity and selectivity in advanced electrochemical systems.

papers.title: An Algorithm for computing Three- and Four-Body Density Matrices from CASCI Wavefunction and AI-Assisted Code Optimization
papers.abstract: Three- and four-body reduced density matrices in the active space are required for second-order n-electron valence perturbation theory (NEVPT2) following complete active-space configuration interaction (CASCI) calculations. We developed an algorithm to generate these computationally demanding quantities by extending the pi-CASCI program, which is based on the graphical symmetric group approach (GSGA). A manually written prototype was subsequently optimized through AI-assisted code optimization, resulting in substantially improved performance.

papers.title: An Algorithm for computing Three- and Four-Body Density Matrices from CASCI Wavefunction and AI-Assisted Code Optimization
papers.abstract: Three- and four-body reduced density matrices in the active space are required for second-order n-electron valence perturbation theory (NEVPT2) following complete active-space configuration interaction (CASCI) calculations. We developed an algorithm to generate these computationally demanding quantities by extending the pi-CASCI program, which is based on the graphical symmetric group approach (GSGA). A manually written prototype was subsequently optimized through AI-assisted code optimization, resulting in substantially improved performance.

papers.title: Closing the Loop Between Synthetic and Living Cells
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells are moving beyond compartmentalised microreactors to become integrated components of biological networks that physically and chemically merge with their hosts. Existing reviews classify this field by mode of emission, by chemistry, or by architecture, and so describe the construct rather than its effect. This review takes the receiver's side, treating the functional adaptation of the living host as the readout of bio-hybrid function: how living cells probe their synthetic partners mechanically and adapt to them metabolically. We consider the bio-hybrid interface by how far the feedback loop (sensing-actuation) is closed and set out the evidence that would place a study in each of four tiers: open-loop, half-loop, partial feedback, and closed-loop. Read against these criteria, sixteen of the eighteen studies surveyed here are half-loop, two reach partial feedback, and none is closed-loop. Both partial-feedback systems work the same way, by metabolic interception, which the existing taxonomies have no category for. The one construct that comes closest to closed-loop operation contains no living cell at all. We then trace how single-cell coupling is scaling into hybrid prototissues that act as discovery platforms for pathological microenvironments, and we outline the translational barriers these constructs must survive to reach the clinic.

papers.title: Assessing the state of the art in ADMET prediction: Lessons from the OpenADMET-ExpansionRx community blind challenge
papers.abstract: Computational blind challenges are essential for advancing drug discovery, especially in research areas with limited public data, such as absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity (ADMET) prediction. In this paper, we present the results of our latest community blind challenge, organized in collaboration with Expansion Therapeutics (ExpansionRx). Participants were tasked with predicting nine distinct ADMET endpoints routinely evaluated during lead optimization of compounds in drug discovery programs. Following unprecedented engagement from the global community, this challenge provided valuable insights into the state of the art in machine learning for ADMET modeling. Evaluating submissions against a realistic, challenging dataset from active ExpansionRx drug discovery programs revealed that message-passing neural networks and chemical foundation models dominated among the top performers. Furthermore, the results highlighted the power of proprietary industry datasets and a critical need to optimize predictive workflows for different endpoints independently via multitasking and task-affinity grouping. We also demonstrate how hosting our open-source blind challenge infrastructure on a flexible platform like Hugging Face was pivotal for driving community engagement and visibility. Ultimately, blind challenges supported by robust infrastructure, widespread dissemination, and rigorous post-challenge analysis are fundamental to maximizing the utility of public data releases. We anticipate that these community benchmarks will continue to drive the advancement of ADMET models, enabling their deployment in both early- and late-stage drug discovery.

papers.title: Dynamic Parameter Screening for Accelerated Mechanistic Analysis
papers.abstract: Mechanistic studies are essential for the continued advancement of the chemical sciences however; classical approaches remain laborious and material intensive. Graphical reaction analysis techniques such as RPKA and VTNA have substantially reduced this burden, yet the time and resources required to comprehensively study increasingly complex reactions remain high. Medium- and high-throughput batch and flow kinetic methods have been developed to further streamline data acquisition, but their widespread adoption is limited by the need for specialized equipment or expertise. Here we introduce dynamic parameter screening (DPS), in which a single batch reaction is monitored continuously while sequential reagent and catalyst additions are used to probe kinetic impacts of multiple species within one experimental setup. Using the palladium-catalyzed Kumada–Tamao–Corriu cross-coupling as a model system, we compared DPS with traditional one-factor-at-a-time approach across three catalytic systems (PdCl 2 (dppf)·CH 2 Cl 2 , PEPPSI-iPr, and XPhos Pd G2). DPS afforded essentially identical qualitative and quantitative (kinetic modeling) conclusions except for the case of XPhos Pd G2. This latter system exhibited multiple kinetic regimes where the traditional approach revealed the global impact of reagent concentrations, whereas DPS provided complementary, higher-resolution insight into reagent effects within a specific kinetic regime. The insights obtained from DPS guided a simple slow-dosing strategy that markedly improved reaction rates even at reduced catalyst loadings. DPS therefore provides a practical, low-barrier route to high-resolution kinetic information that is fully compatible with conventional modeling, broadening access to mechanistic understanding in resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Azobenzene-Mediated Reversible Conformational Switching in 9,9′-Bifluorenylidene-Based Molecular Machines
papers.abstract: Intrinsically dynamic molecules offer attractive building blocks for molecular machines, yet controlling their conformational motion with external stimuli remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we report Azo–BF–Azo, a photoresponsive molecular machine in which an intrinsically dynamic 9,9′-bifluorenylidene (BF) core is coupled to two visible-light-responsive tetra-orthofluorinated azobenzene (Azo) units that act as molecular actuators. Irradiation at 525 nm induces trans-to-cis photoisomerization of the Azo units, accompanied by a shift of the BF framework from the closed toward the open conformation, whereas irradiation at 456 nm reverses Azo isomerization and restores the BF-closed state over time. DFT calculations reveal that the extended trans-Azo units favor intramolecular π–π interactions that stabilize the closed BF conformation, while their conversion to the folded cis state disrupts these interactions and alters the steric environment surrounding the BF core. Variable-temperature NMR spectroscopy provides experimental support for the role of these intramolecular interactions in regulating the BF conformational equilibrium. The photoinduced state additionally undergoes spontaneous thermal relaxation, recovering approximately 65% of the initial state. Together, these results demonstrate that local photoisomerization of peripheral Azo actuators can reshape the conformational landscape of an intrinsically dynamic BF core through the cooperative modulation of steric and intramolecular π–π interactions. This work provides a strategy for converting intrinsic molecular dynamics into externally programmable motion and establishes a design principle for constructing integrated molecular machines in which one type of molecular motion regulates another.

papers.title: Agentic Paper: From Tacit Expertise to AI-Ready Scientific Data and Knowledge Corpora
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for domain science demands large, well-structured training corpora that integrate experimental data with not only explicit knowledge but also tacit expertise underlying scientific decisions. However, the tacit knowledge regarding practical reasoning, assumptions, failed attempts, parameter choices, and interpretive judgment is often held by authors and unpublished, hindering its use for AI development. Here, we propose Agentic Paper, a large language model (LLM)-enabled, author-curated scientific publishing framework that organizes these resources into a structured Agentic Paper package accessible through LLM-based interfaces, enabling the integration of connected, AI-ready data, explicit knowledge, and tacit expertise. Within Agentic Paper, the LLM serves as an interactive reasoning and orchestration layer that connects knowledge content with raw and processed data, figures, methodological details, metadata, code, and author-provided interpretation. Case studies in materials synthesis and characterization demonstrate how the LLM-enabled framework supports questioning, data visualization and inspection, numerical verification, and preparation of AI-ready datasets. By combining author-based organization of scientific data and knowledge, Agentic Paper provides a scalable pathway toward provenance-rich training corpora and more reliable AI-enabled scientific workflows.

papers.title: Tissues As a Synthetic Target – A Framework For the Multiscale Molecular Design Of Thermogelling Polymers
papers.abstract: Tissues are living, water-swollen composite polymer networks whose dynamic biochemical composition, hierarchical architecture, and mechanics collectively regulate cell behavior and physiological function. Recreating these properties across biological and biomedical contexts ( e.g. , 2D and 3D cell culture, tissue engineering, organoid culture, and regenerative medicine) remains a critical challenge as existing synthetic matrices cannot fully recapitulate the multiscale organization and dynamic properties of native extracellular matrices. Most hydrogel platforms rely on “drag-n-drop” combinations of polymers, crosslinkers, fabrication methods, and bioactive motifs to approximate the biophysical and biochemical properties of an individual tissue or biomedical context. In this Review, we seek to motivate the pursuit of thermogel-based “plug-n-play” approaches by framing tissues as synthetic targets and examining the potential of polymers that undergo thermally-triggered assembly to serve as modular building blocks for next-generation synthetic ECMs. The ultimate goal is a universal framework for programming composition, structure, mechanics, and biofunction from a common multiscale molecular design language. We first closely examine the composition, assembly, and properties of ECMs to clearly establish targets of interest and processes that may serve as inspiration. Finally, we connect the thermodynamic principles of lower critical solution temperature behavior with macromolecular topology, phase separation, and hierarchical assembly to establish design opportunities for creating thermogeling polymers that more closely mimic the fibrous, hydrated, mechanically adaptive, and cell-instructive nature of native ECMs. We propose that future progress will require the integration of precise polymer synthesis, topology-dictated assembly, macromolecular crowding, high-throughput formulation, and multiscale characterization to establish predictive structure–assembly–property relationships. This framework is intended to facilitate the transition of thermogeling polymers from injectable or temperature-responsive materials to a latent scalable synthetic platform for writing bespoke tissue-like microenvironments from molecularly programmed building blocks.

papers.title: Symmetry Numbers: A Flexible Approach for Molecules and Transition States
papers.abstract: Symmetry numbers are essential corrections in thermochemistry and chemical kinetics, but their reliable assignment remains difficult in automated workflows, especially for stereochemical, fluxional, cyclic, and transition-state structures. We present a stereochemistry-aware automorphism (SAA) approach for computing symmetry numbers using the StereoMolGraph (SMG) framework. In this representation, local stereodescriptors encode rigid local geometries directly in the molecular graph, so the symmetry number is obtained as the order of the automorphism group that preserves both connectivity and encoded stereochemistry. This avoids the need for a post hoc “label stereocenter” correction and provides a direct graph-theoretical analogue of permutation-based symmetry number definitions. Model dependence is handled explicitly by choosing which molecular features are treated as fixed or fluxional, enabling consistent treatment of rigidity, free rotation, umbrella inversion, and pseudorotation assumptions. Beyond overall molecular and transition-state symmetry numbers, the same framework yields external and internal symmetry numbers for hindered-rotor treatments, including an effective external symmetry number for cases where the overall symmetry number is non-separable. Benchmark calculations reproduce the expected symmetry numbers for all supported benchmark molecules and resolve cases where existing rule-based or corrected-connectivity approaches fail, including stereochemically distinct structures with identical connectivity. The SAA approach is highly robust, making it suitable for automated thermochemical and kinetic modeling of molecules and reactions.

papers.title: Spins Afar - Long-Range Pulse Dipolar EPR Spectroscopy Uncovers Curvature in TRIM25’s Coiled Coil
papers.abstract: Pulse Dipolar Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (PDS) is a powerful method for determining nanometer distances in biomolecular systems. This methodology has been successfully used to validate structure hypotheses and to identify disorder. However, inherent distance limitations are under-explored. Many challenging biomolecular applications require long distance information, driving the need for a benchmarking study. We demonstrate distances up to 10.5 nm in TRIM25 reliably extracted from data obtained under standard sample conditions. By protein perdeuteration accurate distance measurements up to 17.3 nm were enabled. Enhancing sensitivity through optimization of the measurement and sample preparation conditions the achievable dipolar evolution time was extended to 150 µs. Thus, distances close to 20 nm should become experimentally accessible, highlighting the potential of advanced PDS methodologies for probing previously inaccessible long-range structural information in complex systems.

papers.title: Wireless Bipolar Electrochemistry for Organic Electrosynthesis: Principles, Mechanistic Insights, and Emerging Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: Wireless bipolar electrochemistry (BPE) has emerged as a powerful platform for organic electrosynthesis, enabling redox transformations on electrically floating conductors without direct electrical wiring. Through electric-field-induced polarization, bipolar electrodes simultaneously promote spatially separated oxidation and reduction reactions, offering unique opportunities for reaction design, miniaturized reactor architectures, parallel processing, and sustainable chemical synthesis. Recent years have witnessed significant advances in both exogenous and endogenous bipolar electrochemical systems, expanding the scope of wireless electrosynthesis to asymmetric transformations, flow chemistry, low-electrolyte conditions, autonomous microreactors, and self-propelled electrochemical systems. This review critically examines the fundamental principles governing bipolar electrochemistry, recent developments in organic synthesis, and emerging diagnostic methodologies, including split bipolar electrodes and electrochemiluminescence-based imaging, which have substantially improved mechanistic understanding of charge transport, polarization phenomena, and reaction control. The advantages and limitations of wireless bipolar systems are evaluated in comparison with conventional electrolysis, highlighting challenges associated with reaction selectivity, scalability, energy efficiency, and quantitative electrochemical characterization. Finally, future opportunities involving advanced materials, operando analytical techniques, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization, and continuous-flow processing are discussed. Collectively, these developments position wireless bipolar electrochemistry as a promising enabling technology for next-generation sustainable electrosynthesis and autonomous electrochemical manufacturing.

papers.title: Polyethyleneimine (PEI) molecular weight alters the photophysical and FRET properties of water dispersible NaYF4:Yb,Er upconversion nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) are optically active materials with near-infrared excitation and tuneable anti-Stokes emission, typically resulting in visible emission. A route to routine and reliable synthesis of water-dispersible UCNPs for biomedical imaging applications is the polyethyleneimine (PEI)- assisted solvothermal autoclave synthesis; however, the properties of the resulting UCNPs remain understudied. Herein, we report how PEI molecular weight alters properties of core-only, red-emitting, water-dispersible PEI-UCNPs. In terms of brightness, 1.2 kDa PEI-UCNPs exhibited 5 times more intense upconversion luminescence (UCL) than 25 kDa PEI-UCNPs and a 29% longer UCL lifetime (LT) for the red emission band (~640-690 nm, 4 F 9/2 → 4 I 15/2 Er 3+ transition) in DI H 2 O. Dispersal in D 2 O increased emission across wavebands, with green emission ( 2 H 11/2 , 4 S 3/2 → 4 I 15/2 Er 3+ transition) increasing by 248 - 365% whereas red emission only increased between 38-64%. From our results, we infer that PEI may quench the UCL via high-energy NH vibrations. We also examined Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) between PEI-UCNPs and an electrostatically adsorbed fluorescent model dye, AlexaFluor647® (AF647). 25 kDa PEI-UCNPs achieved highest LT-estimated FRET efficiencies of ~11% in H 2 O and 16% in D 2 O, respectively. These findings highlight that polymer MW should be considered when optimising UCNP synthesis.

papers.title: Excited-State Intramolecular Proton Transfer Dynamics with Neural Network Potentials and Nuclear Quantum Effects
papers.abstract: Excited-state intramolecular proton transfer is a prototypical ultrafast process that forms the foundation for many chemical and biological phenomena and is highly sensitive to changes in the underlying potential energy landscape. Here, we develop neural network potentials for 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline that describe ground- and excited-state dynamics with near ab initio accuracy. These neural network potentials enable efficient sampling of the proton transfer coordinate and incorporation of nuclear quantum effects through path-integral molecular dynamics. The free energy profiles show that excited-state intramolecular proton transfer proceeds on a largely barrierless excited-state surface, with nuclear quantum effects reducing and smoothing the residual barrier. Non-equilibrium simulations yield an average proton transfer time of ~11.5 fs for quantum hydrogen, consistent with experiment, and reveal a clear isotope effect, with slower dynamics for deuterium and classical nuclei. Mechanistic analysis identifies transient proton donor–acceptor contraction as the key enabling coordinate, while the proton crosses the midpoint prior to reaching the minimum of this coordinate, indicating a dynamically driven transfer. Subtle changes in the conjugated backbone precede proton transfer, reflecting early electronic reorganization and coherent coupling between proton motion and backbone vibrations. Bond-length alternation and vibrational coherence analysis reveal isotope-dependent coherence loss, with deuteration producing stronger damping and more localized proton/backbone dynamics relative to hydrogen. These results establish neural network potential-based approaches as an effective framework for simulating excited-state proton transfer with explicit nuclear quantum effects.

papers.title: Spatially-Resolved Viscoelastic Response with AFM-IR
papers.abstract: The viscoelastic response of phase-separated polymers systems may deviate from bulk values at the nanoscale. However, current measurement techniques lack the resolution to unmask local variations. We previously demonstrated the advantages of using a focused, pulsed infrared (IR) laser to photothermally heat a sample locally during nanomechanical measurements with an atomic force microscope (AFM), with heating controlled by varying the laser repetition rate. Herein, we demonstrate this IR heating coupled with nano-Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (nDMA). First, we measured the storage and loss modulus of a homogenous copolymer at varying IR repetition rates (i.e., at varying sample temperature), demonstrating a viscoelastic modulus response that is typical near the glass transition temperature. Further, we varied the IR laser repetition rate while modulating the AFM probe between 5 Hz and 100 Hz. With time-temperature superposition, modulus master curves were constructed through the Williams-Landel-Ferry relation, and the shift factors of IR heating-coupled nDMA curves were used to estimate the relation between IR repetition rate and surface temperatures. Lastly, this technique was applied to a phase-separated polymer blend to demonstrate the utility of the technique to decouple the viscoelastic behavior of different phases by leveraging the high spatial resolution of AFM.

papers.title: Cyclic Block Copolymers via Ring Expansion Metathesis Polymerization
papers.abstract: Cyclic block copolymers are a captivating class of macromolecules with the potential for advanced materials applications due to their distinctive self-assembly behavior. Ring expansion metathesis polymerization (REMP) is a promising method towards such high molar mass cyclic polymers, but uncontrolled intermolecular ring-transfer processes have precluded its extension to cyclic block copolymers synthesis. As a result, the synthesis of cyclic block copolymers remains exceedingly rare. In this work, we utilize newfound living characteristics of REMP with cyclic Ru-benzylidene initiator Pyr-CB6 to develop novel block copolymerization methodology. Using an operationally simple sequential monomer-addition strategy followed by thermally triggered intramolecular backbiting, we produce cyclic multiblock copolymers of low dispersity (<1.2) and high yields (up to 97%). Mechanistic analyses elucidate the delicate role that pyridine plays in the polymerization process. As a metathesis inhibitor, pyridine makes intermolecular ring-transfer prohibitively slow, but permits intramolecular backbiting when triggered. Overall, this study demonstrates the power of REMP with Pyr-CB6 as a vehicle towards a diverse future of cyclic block copolymer materials and applications.

papers.title: Self-Assembled 3,4,9,10-Perylenetetracarboxylic Dianhydride is a Molecular Graphite
papers.abstract: Viable organic charge storage materials must display rapid cation insertion. Typically, these materials are composed of monomers that undergo slow outer-sphere electron transfer coupled to significant bond rearrangement. Here we show that 3,4,9,10-perylenetetracarboxylic dianhydride (PTCDA) self-assembles into an organic material that undergoes graphite-like cation insertion-coupled electron transfer rather than forming a radical anion or an enolate, as previously thought. This charge storage pathway is enabled by a semiconducting band structure, coincident with cation insertion between self-assembled PTCDA molecules. Based on these results, we propose that self-assembled PTCDA is best thought of as a synthetically tunable “molecular graphite” that combines the best features of molecules with the rapid insertion pathways of traditional intercalation solids.

papers.title: When aggregation becomes the norm: interpreting experiments beyond their molecules
papers.abstract: Chemical theory and the interpretation of experiments are typically articulated in terms of individual molecules. In the condensed phase, this approach is less generally applicable than commonly believed: phases, aggregates and clusters abound. But without an indication if and when to look for them, they tend to escape the chemist’s eye and consideration. Nonetheless, assemblies of even a handful of molecules show behaviour that resembles that of bulk phases rather than of individual molecules. We review illustrative examples and revisit general scientific laws for assemblies. We then illustrate how they apply to surprisingly common experimental situations, and outline some methodology and general cues for detecting phase behaviour that could otherwise remain hidden. We conclude that analysis in terms of phases enables straightforward interpretation of behaviour that can otherwise be quite perplexing.

papers.title: Surface functionalization of soft photocathodes with an azido-phosphonic acid monolayer for robust and efficient solar-to-H2 conversion
papers.abstract: Organic semiconductors are promising candidates for light-assisted electrocatalysis but interfacial design remains a key challenge for improving performance and durability. Design guidelines include: i) appropriate matching of the catalyst Fermi level to the transport level of charges in the organic semiconductor under operando; ii) controlling surface hydrophilicity for rapid bubble-release in the hydrogen evolution reaction; and iii) retained operation in acidic and alkaline media. Herein we demonstrate a surface-modification approach on five different soft photocathodes to create terminating phosphonic acid surfaces, yielding high-surface energy interfaces across pH ranges from 1 to 13. In acidic conditions, using Pt nanoparticle catalysts, photoelectrochemical devices exhibit photocurrent densities of ~9 mA cm−2 and onset potential of ~0.82 V, surpassing non-surface modified controls by approximately 35–95% and 10–30%, respectively. Improvements are attributed to efficient gas bubble desorption kinetics and increased photovoltages. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy is then used to monitor the Stark shift of a vibrational probe molecule on a metal nanoparticle, enabling the quantification of the quasi-Fermi level of the catalytic site and photovoltage on the unmodified and modified polymer surfaces under operation (i.e., applied bias). The phosphonic acidterminated surfaces yield dramatically increased photovoltages relative to unmodified surfaces. Finally, to demonstrate the broader application of the modifier, we show the approach is readily amenable to increasing the pH~6 for Pt and the binding stability RuOx catalysts. Collectively, our observations suggest a scalable, robust, and efficient route to organic photoelectrochemical devices as well as energy conversion and storage and sensing platforms.

papers.title: Heavy Metal-Binding Peptide Phytochelatin Drives Membraneless Compartmentalization and Biomineral-Like Structures via Nanoparticle Formation within Condensates
papers.abstract: Phytochelatin is a heavy metal-binding biogenic peptide found across different organisms that helps cells mitigate cytotoxicity by chelating metal ions. Yeasts produce phytochelatin to chelate intracellular cadmium and sequester it as cadmium metal sulfide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles were proposed to be stored within cytoplasmic microcompartments, although it remains unclear whether they are stored within membrane-bound or membraneless compartments. Here, we focused on the structure of phytochelatin and hypothesized that it can form membraneless compartments with positively charged biomolecules, which are capable of internal cadmium sulfide sequestration. Indeed, mixing phytochelatin with natural polysaccharide chitosan led to the instant formation of membraneless condensates. Moreover, Cd and S were preferentially accumulated within the condensates relative to other elements and CdS nanoparticles formed inside them. These nanoparticles exhibited crystalline features, with sizes of 2–3 nm and structures comparable to those of the CdS particles observed in cells, which predominantly correspond to the hawleyite structure. This study demonstrated that heavy metal-binding peptides can participate in the formation of membraneless compartments and internal sequestration of nanoparticles. Our findings further indicate a potential role of phytochelatin-based membraneless compartments in spatially controlled intracellular biomineralization and heavy metal sequestration for cellular detoxification, which remains to be explored in vivo.

papers.title: QMzyme: A Python Package for Automated and Systematic QM-based Enzyme Modeling
papers.abstract: We introduce QMzyme, a Python package to automate the generation of Quantum mechanics (QM)-based enzyme models. QM calculations on enzymes are computationally challenging because full enzyme systems typically contain thousands of atoms, placing accurate QM treatments beyond practical computational limits.Therefore, QM-based enzyme studies rely on identifying a subset of atoms that captures the essential chemistry of the reaction environment, enabling tractable yet chemically meaningful calculations. However, constructing these reduced models requires numerous user-defined decisions, including selection of the starting structure, identification of atoms to include in the QM region, and definition of truncation strategies for QM-only models, all of which can substantially influence the resulting calculations. QMzyme aims to provide the community with a flexible and extensible framework for automated, systematic generation of QM-based enzyme models, enabling researchers to more rigorously evaluate how model construction decisions influence computational outcomes while improving reproducibility and transparency across workflows. By facilitating high-throughput generation and analysis of QM enzyme models, QMzyme supports largescale, data-driven investigations of enzyme structure, function, and reactivity. This effort is especially crucial for the creation of large, chemically consistent datasets that can support emergent artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches for accelerated digital discovery in enzymology and biocatalysis.

papers.title: An Algorithm for computing Three- and Four-Body Density Matrices from CASCI Wavefunction and AI-Assisted Code Optimization
papers.abstract: Three- and four-body reduced density matrices in the active space are required for second-order n-electron valence perturbation theory (NEVPT2) following complete active-space configuration interaction (CASCI) calculations. We developed an algorithm to generate these computationally demanding quantities by extending the pi-CASCI program, which is based on the graphical symmetric group approach (GSGA). A manually written prototype was subsequently optimized through AI-assisted code optimization, resulting in substantially improved performance.

papers.title: Evaluation of alternative polymerases for biocatalytic synthesis of modified oligonucleotides
papers.abstract: Enzymatic synthesis of modified nucleic acids is gaining a lot of traction. Most approaches involve the combination of modified nucleoside triphosphates and engineered polymerases capable of accepting such altered substrates. Such enzymes are obtained through engineering campaigns based on directed evolution, positional saturation mutagenesis, and rational design approaches potentially guided by in silico methods. However, most polymerase evolution/design approaches rely on a restricted diversity of enzyme chassis. Here, we have performed a biochemical characterization of two polymerases, the human DNA HsPolθ and the heterodimeric archaeal DNA primase PriSL from Pyrococcus abyssi, capable of synthesizing oligonucleotides under both template-dependent and -independent reaction conditions. We have assessed their capacity at accepting nucleotides with modifications at any position of the scaffold as well as reversible terminators. We have also evaluated the possibility of using high salt conditions to force polymerases to incorporate single nucleotides. Overall, our study reveals that both polymerases are tolerant to modifications and could be amenable to engineering campaigns to identify variants capable of producing hypermodified XNAs for de novo nucleic acid synthesis approaches.

papers.title: Twenty Years of COF-1: The Spark That Launched a Field and Its Mysteries That Remain
papers.abstract: COF-1, reported in 2005, was the first covalent organic framework (COF) and marked the birth of the field. Since then, COFs have quickly attracted attention by demonstrating how supramolecular chemistry and reticular design can be used to construct crystalline and porous organic frameworks with predictable molecularly defined pore sizes. More than two decades after its discovery, COF-1 remains one of the most studied COFs and has served as the gold standard for developing new methodologies and advances in COF crystallization. Yet, despite this extensive work, its precise crystal structure and the relationship between synthetic conditions and framework crystallinity remain debated and elusive. In this minireview, we revisit the story of COF-1, its evolution, and the open questions surrounding its structure, synthesis, stability and function.

papers.title: Extracting Latent Sequence-Function Information from Directed Evolution to Design Improved C-H Azidases
papers.abstract: Directed evolution is a powerful approach for enzyme engineering, but conventional workflows use only a fraction of the information generated during experimental screening. Typically, only top-performing variants are sequenced and propagated, while sequence-function information from the remainder of the library is discarded. Here, we develop a data-efficient strategy to recover and leverage this latent information for enzyme design. Screened variants are grouped into activity-defined bins, pooled, and subjected to long-read sequencing, enabling efficient acquisition of sequence-function relationships while preserving relative activity information. Ordinal machine learning models trained on these binned data are then used to predict beneficial mutations. We applied this strategy to SadX, an engineered Fe(II)- and α-ketoglutarate-dependent azidase previously evolved for site-selective C-H azidation. Using only data from a previous directed evolution campaign, the models identified mutations that significantly improved catalytic performance. Experimental validation showed that several predicted single mutations enhanced azidation activity by up to 3-fold relative to the parent enzyme. These results demonstrate that substantial gains in enzyme activity can be achieved by extracting additional information from existing directed evolution datasets, providing a general strategy for converting routinely generated screening data into actionable sequence-function information for enzyme design.

papers.title: Pore-Engineering Enhances Low-Temperature Mixed Ionic-Electronic Conduction in Two-Dimensional Polymer Lithium Ion-Battery Electrodes
papers.abstract: Understanding the fundamental relationships between ionic and electronic charge transport in polymer systems is essential for the systematic development of bioelectronic, optoelectronic, and energy-storage devices that leverage these materials. A classic strategy to improve ionic conductivity in mixed conducting materials involves attaching ionophilic oligoethylene glycol (OEG) groups to charge-carrying polymers. However, installation of oxygen heteroatoms into the framework of mixed ionic-electronic conductors also induces unintended structural changes in both the native and operational states, thereby adding complexity to structure-property relationships. Two-dimensional polymers (2DPs) are crystalline, planar macromolecules with well-defined one-dimensional channels that can be functionalized without significantly disrupting the crystalline scaffold. We designed topologically equivalent 2DPs with either ionophobic or ionophilic pore structures and studied these materials as lithium-ion battery cathodes. We observed that OEG pore-functionalized 2DP electrodes exhibit higher redox potentials, lower charge-transfer resistances, and higher overall achievable capacities than ionophobic-functionalized 2DP electrodes. Additionally, we found that pore-functionalized 2DP electrodes have higher capacity retention at Arctic temperatures (-30 °C) than commercially available inorganic cathode materials. Our findings demonstrate that pore functionalization is a viable strategy for enhancing the performance of 2DP mixed ionic-electronic conductors and engineering them for extreme environment deployment.

papers.title: ADMET-Informed Machine Learning Prioritization of Hydrogel-Associated Compounds for Nanocarrier Evaluation
papers.abstract: Experimental screening of large hydrogel-associated chemical collections is slow and resource-intensive. We developed an ADMET-informed machine-learning workflow for 2060 HydrogelDB-linked compounds, using the median of a separately reported admetSAR3.0 biodegradability-related output to define higher- and lower-score classes and the remaining 115 predicted ADMET properties as model inputs; preprocessing, feature selection, hyperparameter optimization, probability calibration, and threshold selection were confined to the training partitions of nested cross-validation. The calibrated linear SVM achieved a mean held-out MCC of 0.9116 ± 0.0222, an F2-score of 0.9662 ± 0.0112, and a ROC–AUC of 0.9904 ± 0.0048; performance remained high after proxy-feature removal and feature-family ablation, whereas structure-focused models showed a weaker but detectable signal. Strict eligibility criteria retained 19 candidates. Six-component ranking under changes in model outputs and weights identified D-Alanyl-D-Alanine, Prolyl-Glutamate, and Pro-Asp as the most stable leading candidates. N-Glycylalanine showed lower ranking stability, with Isoleucylglycine as the main alternative. All shortlisted compounds require experimental validation of biodegradability, hydrogel formation, and nanocarrier performance.

papers.title: Localized Sequential Backflow Ansatz for Scalable Neural Quantum States
papers.abstract: Neural Quantum State Architectures have been shown to have high accuracy on a variety of molecular and lattice systems, often outperforming traditional methods. This work replaces the all-to-all paradigm of current neural quantum states with a localized recurrent sequential backflow mechanism. Results have empirically exhibited approximately quadratic wall-clock scaling over the system sizes tested, namely the hydrogen chain with atom with length of H 10 to H 400 , suggesting a viable path towards a scalable Neural Quantum State.

papers.title: Bulk Post-Polymerization Modification of a Single-Crystalline 2D Polymer via the Katritzky Reaction: A Modular Platform for Functional 2D Materials
papers.abstract: Synthesizing two-dimensional polymers (2DPs) via single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) topochemical polymerization presents a dual challenge: preorganizing multifunctional monomers into two-dimensional crystal lattices and ensuring their polymerizable groups remain in close proximity to enable topochemical reaction in 2D. Consequently, topochemical 2DPs remain rare, and strategies for their post-polymerization modification, a standard tool in 1D polymer chemistry, are even more limited. Existing pyrylium-functionalized 2DPs suffer from severe steric hindrance caused by 2,6-di-tert-butyl substituents on pyrylium, restricting their post-synthetic Katritzky transformations solely to small nucleophiles like ammonia. To overcome this limitation, we synthesized a 2,6-di(isopropyl)styrylpyrylium triolefin monomer featuring 2,6-di-isopropyl substituents on pyrylium instead of 2,6di-tert-butyl. This subtle steric modification preserves topochemical polymerizability, while dramatically enhancing the reactivity of the resulting 2DP, enabling facile pore-wall functionalization with nucleophiles such as methylamine or ethylenediamine, to form Nmethyl- and N-(2-aminoethyl)pyridinium sites, respectively. Spectroscopic measurements show no detectable residual pyrylium in either derivative, while the ion-exchange capacity of the N-methyl derivative agrees with its theoretical capacity. These results establish solid-state pyrylium-to-pyridinium conversion as a strategy for post-polymerization modification of a topochemical 2DP precursor and represent a solid foundation for accessing a wide variety of topochemical 2DPs with engineered pore functionality.

papers.title: IRexp: A database of experimental infrared band lists from open literature
papers.abstract: IRexp is a collection of experimental infrared band lists (cm⁻¹ peak positions) mined from open chemistry literature, with author-reported ¹H/¹³C NMR strings and resolved structures where available. The research corpus holds 121,233 records from the PMC Open Access Subset and the Chemotion repository, including 57,646 structure-linked entries and 39,118 IR + ¹H + ¹³C + structure quadruples. The public dataset of record contains 88,519 CC-BY/CC0 records released under CC-BY-4.0, with ShareAlike and non-commercial records distributed separately under their source licences. Every record carries a source identifier and a per-record licence stamp. Technical validation covers automated transcription, recall-proxy, and consistency audits. IRexp targets multimodal training, retrieval, and structure-elucidation tools that need structured, attributable experimental peak lists.

papers.title: Acyl-1,4-Dihydropyridines as Efficient Dual-Mode Photoinitiators for Radical Polymerisation under Blue and Green Light
Ultramild conversion of nitrobenzene to aniline mediated by metal organic alloy NiGraf in green solvent
papers.abstract: The conversion of nitrobenzene to aniline can be carried out under ultramild conditions (35 °C under N2 at ambient pressure) with a 40% molar excess of hydrazine as reducing agent mediated by metal-organic alloy NiGraf in aqueous tetrahydrofuran, a green solvent. Conversion of nitrobenzene to aniline will optimally employ the stable and recyclable form of the NiGraf, consisting of reduced graphene oxide entrapped in jamborite nanoparticles, in renewable solvent system H2O/THF.

papers.title: Iterative Multimutant Design Creates a Family-Like Enzyme Ensemble
papers.abstract: Natural enzyme families achieve functional breadth by diversifying a common scaffold into specialized enzymes. Engineering comparable family-like diversity for synthetic chemistry is challenging because directed evolution workflows frequently optimize one enzyme for one substrate at a time. Here we show that an iterative process of designing and screening energetically compatible multimutant variants can explore sequence space broadly and efficiently. Starting from weak azole N-methylation by human nicotinamide N-methyltransferase, screening only 1,600 clones over three rounds yielded an enzyme ensemble with broad scope. The generated catalysts carried up to 11 active-site substitutions and displayed mean initial-rate gains equivalent to approximately 11-fold per round, with overall gains exceeding 3,000-fold for individual enzyme-substrate pairs. Regioselectivity exceeded 99:1, preparative methylation afforded 87% isolated yield, and all thermally characterized variants were more thermostable than the wild type. Broad activity across diverse azoles emerged collectively from sequence-diverse specialist enzymes. Mapping all mutational routes between two high-activity variants showed that each passed through a lessactive intermediate, revealing why stepwise local optimization can miss high-performing variants. Thus, iteratively testing energetically compatible multimutant designs transformed one promiscuous enzyme into a family-like ensemble of complementary catalysts.

papers.title: Piezoelectricity-Induced Mechanical Bond Formation in Solid-state Using Mechanochemistry
papers.abstract: Mechanochemistry, long promoted as a sustainable route to chemical synthesis, remains difficult to apply predictably to complex reactions due to a limited atomic-level understanding of how mechanical energy drives reactivity. Here, we demonstrated how piezoelectric polarization in tetragonal BaTiO3 directs solid-state mechanoredox chemistry, enabling electrode-free, reductant-free and solvent-free synthesis, for forming complex mechanically interlocked molecules for the first time. During ball milling, mechanically activated tetragonal BaTiO3 nanoparticles generate spatially separated redox sites that reduce viologen building blocks, promoting radical-pairing-driven pseudorotaxane formation and subsequent formation of stable [2] rotaxanes. First-principles calculations on BaTiO3 identify shear deformation as the dominant mechanical stimulus, where strain-induced polarization field produces an energetically favorable surface potential for the coupled redox reactions. These findings for the first time establish a direct mechanistic link between mechanical deformation, piezoelectric polarization, and mechanical bond formation, providing a predictive framework for sustainably constructing complex mechanically interlocked molecular architectures through piezoelectricity-mediated mechanochemistry.

papers.title: Nucleotide-mediated catalytic peptide synthesis from aminonitriles
papers.abstract: Aminonitriles are accessible from simple feedstock compounds and their hydrolysis offers an abiotic route to life’s amino acids on the early earth. However, controlled aqueous polymerisation of amino acids into peptides remains challenging. Here we show that peptides can be directly generated and elongated by aminonitriles when the latter are coupled to nucleotides as a phosphoramidate. Upon thiol catalysis and pH shifts, a series of selective reactivities drives iterative peptide bond formation in water. The high energy nitrile bond of aminonitriles circumvents amino acids’ need for concurrent activation chemistry in peptide elongation. Coupling the building blocks of life’s central biopolymers in this manner provides a pathway for early integration of peptides into biology.

papers.title: The Critical Role of Water in Safe, Scalable Diboron-Mediated Nitro Reductions .
papers.abstract: The use of diboron compounds for nitro group reduction, an essential transformation in the synthesis of a wide range of nitrogen-containing functional groups, offers an attractive alternative to traditional methods like hydrogenation and dissolving metal reduction. This method has seen limited uptake in the literature despite avoiding transition metals and specialized equipment. Using a combination of reaction calorimetry and kinetic analysis, careful selection of the reaction solvent, diboron source, and inclusion of water enabled the identification of safe and simple conditions for reduction of nitro groups. The scope of the reaction is broad under mild conditions where water plays a critical role in driving reactivity while maintaining wide safety margins.

papers.title: Enhanced Catalysis via Multiscale Force Propagation in All-Enzyme Glucose Oxidase Hydrogels
papers.abstract: Enzyme-based biomaterials are sustainable catalytic platforms with applications in biosensing, pharmaceutical synthesis, and environmental remediation. A key challenge is developing universal immobilisation strategies that preserve activity without requiring enzyme-specific optimisation. One promising approach is the photochemical cross-linking of native tyrosine residues to form self-supporting all-enzyme hydrogels, where the enzyme serves as both the catalytic and structural component. However, rational design of these materials requires understanding how gelation-induced forces propagate through the network and influence enzyme function. Here, we combine experiments and simulations to establish a multiscale framework linking hydrogel assembly, force propagation, and catalysis in glucose oxidase hydrogels. By varying the lamp intensity used during photochemical cross-linking, we control gelation kinetics and examine their consequences across molecular and network length scales. Slower gelation reduces enzyme unfolding and produces more loosely packed hydrogel networks with enhanced dynamic correlations and increased free volume around enzyme active sites. Integrating experimental measurements with modelling reveals that these structural changes enhance catalytic performance through altered force transmission across the network. Our findings demonstrate that enzyme activity is regulated not only by local active-site processes but also by collective mechanical interactions spanning multiple length scales, establishing network mechanics as a new design principle for functional biocatalytic materials.

papers.title: Hyperfine dynamics as an internal control of reactive-oxygen-species output in a triplet-born flavin–superoxide radical pair
papers.abstract: When reduced flavin is activated by molecular oxygen it forms a spin-correlated radical pair—a flavin semiquinone and superoxide (O₂•⁻)—born in the triplet manifold, because ground-state O₂ is a triplet. Its singlet/triplet recombination gates the branching of reactive oxygen species, and the pair is realised in the electron-transfer flavoprotein, whose output is field-dependent. Radical-pair theory almost always treats the hyperfine tensor as fixed and the field as the variable. We invert that: with the field held fixed, what upper bound does a time-dependent active-site hyperfine coupling place on the singlet yield? We pose a coefficient inverse problem with the principal-axis components Aₖ,ₐ(t) as the control and solve it for the genuine triplet-born flavin pair (two ¹⁴N at I = 1, three protons; dimension 288) at a 200 ns lifetime. A time-dependent coupling raises the yield to ΦS = 0.290 at 50 µT, against 0.241 for the best constant coupling in the same admissible set (1.20×) and 0.203 for the molecule’s own couplings (1.43×); the reduced models give larger gains, so they overestimate the effect. The optimum places 76% of its modulation in the first 0.5 µs and is smooth and numerically near-singular, unlike the bang–bang optimum of the external-field problem. These are coherent yields obtained over a control set far larger than conformational motion can access—an upper bound on an upper bound—with spin relaxation, the dipolar coupling and the superoxide g-anisotropy left unmodelled. The falsifiable quantity is the dynamic-over-static gain, not the absolute yield.

papers.title: Mechanochemical conglomerate formation by ball milling - or not?
papers.abstract: Inspired by a study reporting on the zinc oxide-induced mechanochemical conglomerate formation of racemic amino acids, we investigated the reaction behavior of the analogous 19F-labeled DL-valine. Solid-state NMR spectroscopy under magic-angle spinning (MAS) conditions was employed as the central analytical technique to analyze the reaction products. In contrast to our expectation, no conglomerate formation occurred, and in the presence of ZnO and methanol a polymeric complex with one zinc and two fluorinated valine molecules was formed in a vibrational ball mill. Repeating these experiments with non-fluorinated valine led to a rather unusual and unique tetranuclear species with an overall composition of Zn4(D-Val)4(L-Val)4 as determined by single-crystal analysis and solid-state NMR. The latter complex was also formed when an equimolar ratio of the two enantiopure valine phases was combined in the ball mill with ZnO and methanol. The use of Resonant Acoustic Mixing (RAM) led to the same complex, but the efficiency of its formation varied significantly depending on the reaction conditions.

papers.title: Probing Oxygen Transport in β-Cyclodextrin–Cyclohexane Crystalline Nanochannels by Luminescence Quenching from Nanoseconds to Seconds
papers.abstract: Molecular transport in supramolecular crystals under nanoscale confinement may exhibit different regimes across widely separated timescales, making their experimental characterization particularly challenging. Here, oxygen quenching of aromatic luminophores incorporated into a β -cyclodextrin–cyclohexane crystalline matrix in aqueous suspensions is investigated using steadystate and time-resolved luminescence spectroscopy. The probes provide emission lifetimes ranging from tens of nanoseconds to approximately 15 s. Effective bimolecular quenching rate constants referenced to the concentration of dissolved oxygen in the surrounding aqueous phase decrease from approximately 10 9 to 5×10 4 L mol -1 s -1 across the probe series. The decreasing branch approximately follows a power-law dependence on the unquenched emission lifetime, k q ∝ τ 0 -0.8 , whereas probes with lifetimes longer than approximately 10 ms exhibit a nearly constant quenching rate. A diffusion–reaction model relates the measured constants to temporal averages of the oxygen encounter flux and accounts for the finite excitation duration. Under the assumptions of comparable probe accessibility and diffusion-controlled quenching, the observed scaling is consistent with subdiffusive transport with an effective anomalous exponent of approximately 0.4. A finite range of local transition rates within a quenched random-barrier model provides a possible explanation for the crossover to the long-time plateau. These results show that lifetime-dependent luminescence quenching provides a means of probing oxygen transport over widely separated timescales and testing transport models in nanoscale-confined molecular systems.

papers.title: Majority-Rule of Enantiomeric Excess in Chiral Halide Perovskites for continuous tuning of chiroptical properties
papers.abstract: Chiral halide perovskites have emerged as promising platform for spin-optoelectronic applications, yet the role of chiral precursor composition in governing their chiroptical properties remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how enantiomeric excess (ee) controls the chiroptical response of the prototypical two-dimensional (2D) chiral halide perovskite (R/S-MBA)2PbI4 (MBA = methylbenzylammonium) across a compositional series spanning ee = -100% to +100% corresponding to R-MBA mole fractions ranging from 0% to 100%. By combining experimental spectroscopy with first-principles simulations, an approach we demonstrate to be transferable to tin-based analogues as well, we establish a quantitative structure-chiroptical property relationship across the full ee range. Circular dichroism (CD) spectra and absorption dissymmetry factors (gabs) exhibit a progressive, nonlinear evolution with increasing ee, consistent with cooperative majority-rule behavior governing chirality transfer from the organic cation to the inorganic framework. This effect is most pronounced in the 400-450 nm spectral region, where the CD signal tracks enantiomeric composition with high fidelity. Ab initio molecular dynamics coupled with time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) quantitatively reproduces both the experimental CD spectra and gabs values across the entire compositional series, revealing that the macroscopic chiroptical response originates from the collective arrangement of chiral ligands, acting as a continuous dial for simultaneously modulating optical activity. This positions the ee as a general, accessible design parameter for chiroptical engineering across the family of halide perovskites.

papers.title: Analysis of fine-tuned foundation interatomic potentials and their knowledge distillation into a cluster expansion for Ni–Pt ordering thermodynamics
papers.abstract: Predicting alloy ordering thermodynamics requires the energies of thousands of atomic arrangements at fixed composition, far more than density functional theory (DFT) can routinely provide. Fine-tuned foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are a promising alternative, but whether they resolve the small energy differences between arrangements has not been established. Here, we examine this for fcc Ni–Pt in three steps. First, six foundation MLIPs fine-tuned on the same DFT data are evaluated on a 64-structure DFT benchmark. All six reach low global errors (2-20 meV/atom), but these errors are dominated by a composition-dependent offset that cancels between arrangements of one composition. We therefore evaluate the configurational energy Econf, the energy of a structure relative to the other structures of the same composition. After relaxation only four models reproduce DFT Econf (R2conf = 0.93-0.94), whereas fine-tuned eqV2 and CHGNet do not (0.48 and 0.37). Second, we locate the source of this failure. Linear probes on the frozen embeddings of all six models recover EconfDFT (R2 = 0.87 to 0.98), showing that the learned representations are intact. The accuracy is lost during relaxation: through the cell response of eqV2 and through inaccurate forces near the energy minimum in CHGNet. Third, we use the most accurate model, fine-tuned eqV3, as a teacher for knowledge distillation into a cluster expansion. Trained on 6,434 MLIP energies instead of 64 DFT energies, the distilled cluster expansion reduces the held-out DFT error from 4.43 to 2.79 meV/atom and reproduces the DFT-based transition temperatures within 167 K, comparable to the 120 K statistical uncertainty of the DFT-trained expansion itself. These results establish when fine-tuned foundation MLIPs can be trusted for alloy ordering and provide a route for transferring their accuracy to thermodynamic simulations.
