papers.title: Multigram Copper-Catalyzed Azidodeboronation of Alkenyl Boronates
papers.abstract: A multigram synthetic approach to alkenyl azides based on copper-catalyzed azidodeboronation of alkenyl pinacol boronates was described. The optimized protocol relied on the use of Cu(OAc) 2 as the reaction promoter, which provided higher, reproducible yields and did not cause uncontrolled decomposition of the reaction mixture, unlike the CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O-based protocol reported previously. The method was applicable to β-, β,β-, and α,β-substituted substrates, including those bearing electron-withdrawing groups and saturated O -, N -, and S -heterocyclic motifs. Some alkenyl azides were prepared on up to 21 g scale, and their thermal behavior was evaluated by thermogravimetric analysis. The synthetic utility of the products was demonstrated through the preparation of a substituted pyrrole and 1-alkenyl-1,2,3-triazoles. Furthermore, a one-pot azidation – click reaction protocol enabled the direct conversion of alkenyl boronates into the corresponding triazoles without isolation of unstable or highly volatile alkenyl azide intermediates, thereby broadening the accessible substrate scope.

papers.title: Redox-Paired Activation of Sulfur Hexafluoride Enables Nucleophilic C(sp3)–F Bond Formation
papers.abstract: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is a potent greenhouse gas whose direct use as a fluorine source in organic synthesis remains underdeveloped. Here, we disclose complementary photoredox and electrochemical strategies for nucleophilic fluorinations with SF6, merging oxidative formation of carbocation intermediated from alkoxamines, carboxylic acids, or thiols with SF6 reduction, the latter providing fluoride for C(sp3)–F bond formation. The photochemical protocol efficiently converts electronrich substrates and tolerates a broad range of functional groups, whereas paired electrolysis extends the reaction to electronically deactivated substrates. Together, the two methods enable fluorination of diverse benzylic and aliphatic substrates, including late-stage fluorination of structurally complex derivatives of pharmaceuticals, natural products, and agrochemicals.

papers.title: Distinguishing Pharmaceutical Salts and Cocrystals by Fluorescence Lifetime Mapping and Quantum Crystallography
papers.abstract: Distinguishing between salt and cocrystal forms of a drug remains challenging in multicomponent systems with ambiguous proton transfer, particularly during bulk production in the pharmaceutical industry. Here, we address this challenge by combining fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) for rapid bulk-phase discrimination with Hirshfeld atom refinement (HAR) for single-crystal-level validation. This integrated FLIM–HAR approach was applied to 11 multicomponent solids derived from the pharmaceutical drugs niflumic acid, mefenamic acid, and sulfamethazine. Owing to its sensitivity to the local electronic environment and crystal-field effects, FLIM provided spatially resolved lifetime signatures that clearly distinguished salts from cocrystals, with salts consistently exhibiting longer fluorescence lifetimes. HAR unambiguously located the transferred protons, as evidenced by difference Fourier maps, thereby validating the salt–cocrystal assignments. Analysis of intermolecular interactions using the HAR models further revealed stronger interactions and tighter crystal packing in the salts, primarily arising from charge-assisted hydrogen bonding, consistent with the observed lifetime differences. The correlation between fluorescence lifetime and HAR-determined protonation state demonstrates that lifetime provides a sensitive probe of proton transfer in pharmaceutical solids. The integrated FLIM–HAR methodology therefore provides a rapid and reliable strategy for distinguishing pharmaceutical salts and cocrystals, with particular potential for bulk-phase characterization.

papers.title: Insights into Electrolyte Effects on Interfacial Kinetics and Transport in Porous Redox Flow Battery Electrodes: A Multiparadigm Modelling Study
papers.abstract: Redox flow batteries (RFBs) have emerged as promising candidates for large-scale energy storage owing to their decoupled energy and power densities. Electrolyte formulation plays a key role in determining the electrochemical performance of RFBs, influencing interfacial kinetics and transport within porous electrodes. Herein, we develop a multiscale modelling framework to investigate the coupled effects of the electrolyte concentration (Methyl Viologen (MV) and NaCl) and the fibrous 3D microstructure on the porous transport and electrochemical kinetics in organic RFBs using a kinetic Monte Carlo model. We link this interfacial kinetics to the advection-diffusion transport in stochastically generated carbon felt electrode microstructures through Lattice Boltzmann Method simulations via an interpolation-based coupling. We use two performance descriptors, the fibre-averaged rate of potential loss and convective area fraction, to quantify the kinetics and transport effects, along with their interplay. While increasing MV concentration enhances the interfacial kinetics, it limits the transport within the electrode microstructure. The interfacial kinetics shows to be nontrivially governed by the supporting electrolyte. A surface area-permeability trade-off appears across microstructures with different electrolyte concentrations. This multiparadigm modelling workflow provides mechanistic insights between porous transport and interfacial electrochemical kinetics, enabling the coupled optimization of microstructures and electrolytes in RFBs.

papers.title: Two barriers to benchmarking structure-based virtual screening against the AcrB efflux pump: a sample-size ceiling and an identifiability failure
papers.abstract: Background. The AcrAB-TolC system is the principal constitutive efflux pump of Escherichia coli and an attractive adjuvant target. Virtual screening campaigns against its distal binding pocket have been published without the retrospective validation standard elsewhere in the field. This study asked whether such a benchmark can be built from the published literature. Methods. Compounds reported as AcrB inhibitors were filtered against an independent reproducibility screen and assigned to a binding site by the strongest structural or mutational evidence available. Property-matched decoys, a library-representative background and a class of reported-but-non-reproducing inhibitors served as negatives. A pilot docking screen against the hydrophobic trap of 5ENQ was re-analysed under the curated labels, with areas under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve reported with analytic and bootstrap confidence intervals. Two controls were pre-specified: a wrong-site control, and a ligand-only ablation deleting the receptor entirely. Results. Of 49 compounds reported as AcrB inhibitors, 38 have been independently retested and 17 reproduced; 13 maps to the distal pocket and 5 have a co-crystal there. Two barriers follow. With 5 actives the 95% interval cannot be narrower than ±0.26; reaching a conventional ±0.06 would require 94 actives, while raising the decoy ratio from 40:1 to 500:1 narrows the interval by 0.8%. More seriously, the ligand-only ablation reached 1.000 against a docking area of 0.707: deleting the receptor improved performance. 4 of the 5 co-crystal actives are analogues spanning 2 scaffolds, with a median pairwise ECFP4 similarity of 0.574 against 0.077 to the negatives; every active–active pair lies above the decoy-exclusion threshold of 0.35 and every active–negative pair below it. Conclusions. A retrospective docking benchmark for the AcrB distal pocket cannot currently be built. The first barrier is quantitative and yields to more confirmed inhibitors of any kind; the second is qualitative and yields only to inhibitors that are chemically unlike one another. Screening against this pocket therefore proceeds unvalidated and cannot be validated until structurally diverse confirmed inhibitors exist, which is a medicinal-chemistry result rather than a computational one. The curated compound table, the metrics implementation with its unit tests and the analysis notebook are released.

papers.title: Project ⟨χ|χ⟩: Extending Dragonball towards Quantum Vibrational Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Semiclassical dynamics is able to add nuclear quantum effects to classical trajectories, in an approximate yet effective manner. However, moving from classical to semiclassical dynamics requires the careful consideration and implementation of many tools, especially in the case of ab initio semiclassical dynamics. In this paper, we present Project ⟨χ|χ⟩, a set of tools designed to extend the capability of the recently released Dragonball beyond quasi-classical trajectories. First, we improve Dragonball accessibility by providing a set of PySCF scripts to substitute ab initio software. Second, we expand Dragonball infrastructure by adding Adiabatic Switching and Hessian Database to make it semiclassical-ready, and CandyBeam to safely store the data. Finally, we showcase these tools by computing the semiclassical spectra of H2, H2O, CO2 and H2 ·C60 using Frieza, a code to compute Gaussian Wavepacket autocorrelation spectra, fully compatible with Dragonball.

papers.title: On the enzymatic synthesis of ketone-containing oligomers and their processing into sustainable crosslinked materials
papers.abstract: In this work, two ketone-containing pre-polyesters based on dimethyl 2-oxoglutarate (pDMOG) and dimethyl 1,3-acetonedicarboxylate (pDADC), were obtained via a solventless polymerization reaction in presence of Lipase B from Candida antarctica as the biocatalyst. 1 H-NMR indicated diol conversions over 90% for both monomers, while GPC analysis revealed differences between the two systems, with pDMOG reaching a M n of ≈ 8 kDa ( M w ≈ 30kDa) while pDADC reached a M n of ≈1.5 kDa ( M w ≈ 2.5 kDa). Molecular docking studies were performed to investigate the productive accommodation of the substrates and corresponding oligomeric products within the CaLB active site. Priamine TM 1071 (PR) was then used to crosslink these polymers using a solvent-free and catalyst-free reaction, showing that the network formation was directly governed by the molecular structure of the ketone-containing pre-polyester precursor. The thermal stability of the obtained materials showed an improvement at higher temperatures when compared with the neat pre-polyesters. DSC analyses showed that pDMOG and pDADC are semicrystalline materials, while the crosslinked materials led to fully amorphous systems. The rheological behaviour was also analysed, confirming that the crosslinked materials have temperature-dependent viscoelastic properties. These results can provide new perspectives for the design of processable crosslinked polymer systems obtained from bio-derived precursors by using chemo-enzymatic methods.

papers.title: Direct Asymmetric Hydroalkoxylation of Styrenes Through Flavin Brønsted Acid Biocatalysis
papers.abstract: Direct addition of free alcohols across alkenes would provide a concise route to chiral ethers, but controlling alkene activation, nucleophile capture, and stereochemistry remains difficult. We evolved an oleate hydratase, an enzyme that naturally adds water across alkenes, to favor alcohol addition instead. The resulting enzyme catalyzes intermolecular hydroalkoxylation of electron-rich styrenes in aqueous solution, reaching up to 80% yield and >99% enantiomeric excess. Evolution reshaped an alcohol-binding pocket around a conserved flavin-centered core, allowing alcohol to compete with water. Mechanistic studies support a redox-neutral cycle in which protein-bound neutral FADH 2 acts as a Brønsted acid to protonate the alkene. By placing direct asymmetric hydroalkoxylation within an engineerable enzyme scaffold, this work opens a route to expand both alkene and nucleophile scope through protein engineering.

papers.title: Asymmetric selectivity at the glycoprotein hormone receptor allosteric site
papers.abstract: Position 7.42 of the glycoprotein hormone receptors has been proposed as the determinant of mutual selectivity between LHCGR and FSHR, but has not been tested reciprocally. We compared the allosteric pockets of LHCGR with Org 43553 (PDB 7FIH) and FSHR with Cpd-21f (PDB 8I2G), and mapped each ligand into the other receptor by transmembrane superposition. Seven of 27 aligned contact positions diverge, a rate not distinguishable from the transmembrane background, and the mapping is markedly asymmetric. Cpd-21f placed in LHCGR makes a 2.31 Å contact with Tyr612, against 3.69 Å for the native His615 contact, and this is the single worst contact in the molecule. Org 43553 placed in FSHR meets no comparable barrier: 21 of 23 native contacts are preserved, burial increases, and the only sequence-driven loss is a hydroxyl-to-methyl van der Waals contact. Position 7.42 therefore excludes FSHR-selective ligands from LHCGR but does not explain why Org 43553 is weaker at FSHR. We further show that the morpholine tail of Org 43553 is buried rather than solvent-exposed and contacts only residues shared between the two receptors, accounting for published structure–activity data in which extensive variation of that tail failed to shift the LH:FSH ratio. A survey of ten orthologs identifies Phe515, the closest divergent contact and the only contact-shell position where LHCGR differs from a residue both paralogs share, as primate-specific; every non-primate examined, including all standard preclinical species, carries the paralog leucine. Finally, this pocket defeats several widely used scoring functions, which rank a reciprocal head-to-tail decoy above the crystallographic pose.

papers.title: Evolutionary Design for Anion-Derived Interphase Stability
papers.abstract: High-concentration electrolytes (HCEs) improve lithium-ion battery cycling by shifting interphase formation from the solvent to the anion, producing a more stable inorganic-rich interphase at the anode. However, the anions for HCEs has been mainly studied on FSI− and TFSI−, and the anion itself has received little systematic exploration relative to the solvent and the salt concentration. Here, anion chemical space is searched using evolutionary framework that couples genetic algorithm with quantum-chemical descriptors of reducibility, solvent coordination, and charge delocalization. Substructure analysis of the evolved populations identifies a sulfinimide (N−=S) core as the recurring motif in place of the sulfonyl chemistry of the reference anions, and a combinatorial scaffold-branch library built from these motifs exhibits distinction between the electronic and intermolecular contributions to anion performance. Charge localization is governed by the scaffold while solvent binding is set neither by scaffold nor by branch alone but by their specific pairing and by whether the two arms are chemically distinct. Higher-level solvation show that the leading candidates from the selected anion set exceed both baseline anions in bulk solvation, and transport calculations exhibit that every candidate carries a smaller Li+ first shell and diffuses faster than both baselines at concentrated salt content. Replacing a single sulfonyl oxygen with an imide nitrogen reorganizes the anion around a delocalized, asymmetrically substituted core and opens a salt chemistry for HCEs distinct from the sulfonyl imides in use today.

papers.title: Oxidative strong metal-support interaction determines selectivity in supported Rh catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation
papers.abstract: The restructuring of a catalyst’s interface with its support can be tailored via strong metal-support interactions (SMSI) in order to achieve desired product selectivity. SMSI is usually associated with reductive conditions, where a reduced oxide support covers a supported metal phase and alters catalytic activity. Here, pretreatment-dependent SMSI of rhodium nanoparticles supported on rutile titania is shown to control the selectivity profile for CO 2 hydrogenation reactions between methanation and the reverse water-gas shift reaction at 500 °C. Oxidative pretreatments at 400 °C were found to promote methanation with an initial rate of 5.1 mol/mol Rh /s for an O 2 pretreated sample and 5.8 mol/mol Rh /s for an O 2 followed by H 2 pretreated sample, whereas a H 2 pretreatment at 400 °C suppressed the methanation reaction to an initial rate of 0.25 mol/mol Rh /s. Instead of following classical methods of catalyst restructuring, such as sintering and reductive SMSI, the catalyst forms an SMSI overlayer under oxidative conditions, which restructures its active sites to selectively promote the methanation reaction. The effects of the restructuring are long-lived and dominated the catalyst selectivity even after more than 100 hours under reaction conditions. We demonstrate that this oxidative SMSI overlayer grows via a rhodium titanate intermediate and is necessary for creating active sites for methanation, shifting the catalyst’s selectivity away from the RWGS reaction. Theoretical calculations further demonstrate the thermodynamic favorability of TiO 2 overlayer growth under experimentally-relevant oxidative conditions. These results demonstrate that catalyst pretreatment conditions are a facile and effective tool for tuning the catalyst-support interface by allowing for the construction of an oxidative strong metal-support interaction that determines the product selectivity of supported rhodium catalysts.

papers.title: Design Rules for Mixed Rutile PGM Oxides
papers.abstract: Oxide solid solutions have important industrial applications including catal-ysis that require high stability under operating conditions. The stability of solid solutions is usually predicted using structural similarity, with low lattice mismatch resulting in stable solid solutions and high lattice mismatch resulting in unstable solid solutions. While this works for most solid solutions, some such as yttria-stabilised zirconia break the rules and remain stable due to other factors. Here we use density functional theory to study the substitutional solid solutions of the rutile platinum group metal (PGM) oxides IrO 2 and RuO 2 . These PGM oxides are commonly used as oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts in proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysers and both suffer from degradation in the harsh acidic conditions. In an effort to stabilise the PGM oxides and determine what factors affect the mixing thermodynamics, we mix the PGM oxides with each other and four other rutile oxides with different properties. Our results for the nine unique systems, including both PGM-only and PGM/non-PGM solid solutions, show that the mixing thermodynamics can be predicted using two new mixing rules. Firstly, rutile oxide solid solutions have negative mixing enthalpies when both solutes are metallic and positive mixing enthalpies otherwise. This is independent of all other factors. Secondly, increasing the electronegativity difference between solute metals decreases the mixing enthalpies as long as the first rule remains unbroken. This was shown by NbO 2 having the most favourable mixing with the PGM oxides despite its larger lattice. We hope these new mixing rules can be used to design new stable solid solutions of rutile oxides such as IrO 2 and RuO 2 .

papers.title: Parameter Recovery and Noise Sensitivity of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Michaelis–Menten Kinetics: A Benchmark Against Classical Nonlinear Least Squares
papers.abstract: This study evaluates a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for estimating Michaelis–Menten kinetic parameters from sparse and noisy concentration–time observations. The investigated system follows the ordinary differential equation , with a true maximum reaction rate of , Michaelis constant , initial substrate concentration , and a simulation duration of 10 time units. Synthetic observations were generated using numerical integration and additive Gaussian noise at 1% and 5% levels. The PINN consisted of a fully connected neural network with three hidden layers, 32 hidden units, and hyperbolic tangent activation functions. Its trainable kinetic parameters were constrained to positive values using the softplus transformation. Training minimized a weighted combination of data error, initial-condition error, and differential-equation residual error. To address optimization instability, the study used an increased training budget of up to 8000 epochs, early stopping, multiple initialization seeds, and cross-validation for selecting the physics-loss weight. A classical nonlinear least-squares estimator was used as a comparison method. In a diagnostic example, the corrected PINN produced errors of 1.04% for and 5.10% for , compared with 2.99% and 19.32% for the classical method. However, across the small benchmark of 18 replicates, the classical method generally achieved lower median errors and lower prediction RMSE, especially under 5% noise. The results show that the PINN can recover kinetic parameters accurately in favorable conditions, but its performance remains sensitive to data quantity, noise, optimization, and experimental design.

papers.title: Probing Nanoscale Carrier Dynamics in P3HT Blended with a Non-Fullerene Acceptor: Impact of Mixing on Device-Relevant Carrier Generation
papers.abstract: High-performing organic photovoltaics (OPVs) rely not only on the appropriate energetics and interfaces for separating excitons into charges, but on distinct areas of donor-rich and acceptor-rich domains to transport those charges to electrodes once separated. In this work, we study a bulk heterojunction (BHJ) of well-studied poly(3-hexylthiophene-2,5-diyl) (P3HT) and a non-fullerene acceptor with an A1-D-A2-D-A1 motif, octyl rhodanine-thiophene-benzothiadiazole-thiophene-octyl rhodanine (ORTBT). Using device characterization and time-resolved spectroscopic techniques, we show that despite promising picosecond photophysical properties P3HT:ORTBT blends do not lead to long-lived charges due to overly-imbalanced mixing between the ORTBT acceptor and P3HT donor on length scales that are either too small or too large. We compare results with a prototypical BHJ, P3HT and PC61BM fullerene to understand the photophysical differences in the exciton dissociation dynamics. The significant mixing in P3HT:ORTBT disrupts the crystalline regions of the P3HT that are necessary for effective hole transport. This work demonstrates the need to consider both the chemical and physical properties of non-fullerene acceptors to achieve an optimal balance of donor-acceptor mixing that facilitates high exciton dissociation efficiency and long-lived carrier transport pathways in the bulk.

papers.title: A numerically verified analytical framework for immobilised-enzyme packed-bed reactor design in the kinetically controlled regime applied to dihydroxyacetone production
papers.abstract: Continuous-flow biocatalysis can decouple enzymatic productivity from the cellular growth constraints inherent to fermentation, but exploiting this advantage requires a reactor design framework that links enzyme kinetics, immobilisation penalties, and catalyst deactivation to industrially relevant performance metrics. We develop an analytical quasi-steady-state (QSS) plug-flow reactor model for immobilised-enzyme packed-bed reactors (PBRs) operating under first-order catalyst deactivation, and verify its transport assumptions against a two-dimensional axisymmetric COMSOL™ finiteelement model. The close agreement between the analytical and numerical solutions confirms that reactor performance is kinetically controlled across the investigated operating window, and yields a closed-form expression for the time-averaged space–time yield (𝑆𝑇𝑌 ) that factorises into five independently controllable design levers. We apply this framework to a feasibility study on the continuous enzymatic conversion of formaldehyde to dihydroxyacetone (dha) using immobilised formolase (FLS), a reaction of interest for C1 biomanufacturing. Parametric mapping across substrate concentration, enzyme loading, and immobilisation-induced activity penalties, combined with sensitivity analysis incorporating enzyme deactivation, identifies substrate concentration, enzyme loading, substrate affinity (𝐾M), and catalyst stability as the principal parameters governing productivity, and shows that continuous immobilised FLS operation can sustain greater than 8-fold higher timeaveraged productivity than fermentation across the full range of product yields and operating scenarios considered. Beyond the specific case study, the verified QSS framework and its design-lever decomposition are directly transferable to other immobilised-enzyme PBR systems, offering a general route from laboratory kinetic data to quantitative reactor and catalyst design targets for continuous biomanufacturing.

papers.title: In situ Activation of Ni(II) with Boronic Acids and Application of a Phosphasilinane Ligand enable the Suzuki-Miyaura Cross-Coupling of Deactivated (Hetero)Aryl Chlorides
papers.abstract: The important substitution of costly palladium catalysts with earth-abundant nickel alternatives in Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reactions is still problematic for challenging substrates, such as heteroaryls and (hetero)aryl chlorides. In this context, we report the application of low Vbur and electron-rich biaryl-based phosphasilinane ligands in nickel-catalyzed Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reaction of electron-rich (hetero)aryl-chlorides with aryl boronic acid substrates, at catalyst loadings as low as 0.5 mol-% on gram-scale synthesis. To overcome the use of unstable Ni(0)-sources, the activation of cheap and bench-stable L2NiCl2 precatalysts with boronic acids was investigated and successfully applied, e.g., in the synthesis of intermediates for agrochemical and pharmaceutical products. Furthermore, this method enabled the synthesis of bench- and base-stable L2Ni(3-furyl)Cl complex, which was directly applied in cross-coupling reactions.

papers.title: Rate-independent limits on a sulphating, self-renewing oxide catalyst: exact master-equation results with lattice kinetic Monte Carlo checks
papers.abstract: Copper oxide takes up sulphur dioxide as a sorbent because sulphation converts it to inactive copper sulphate. Whether a copper oxide surface that sulphates in service and renews itself by exposing fresh copper can instead act as a catalyst for SO 2 oxidation is a question about site statistics as much as chemistry. We study it with a lattice model whose elementary rates are unknown, and we therefore restrict the main claims to statements that hold for every strictly positive assignment of rate constants. Three such results are established. First, under a dual-site mechanism in which O 2 adsorbs dissociatively onto a vacant nearest-neighbour pair and SO 2 onto a single site, an isolated patch of one or two active sites has a stationary product rate of exactly zero, and every connected patch of three or more sites has a strictly positive rate. This is proved and checked exhaustively on all 996 connected graphs of up to seven sites. Second, on a randomly deactivated lattice the share of surviving sites that can never turn over follows the closed form 𝐷 (𝑝) = (1 − 𝑝) 𝑧 + 𝑧𝑝(1 − 𝑝) 𝑡2 , which is 86.9% on a square lattice at 90% deactivation. Combined with exact stationary rates of every component shape, the classical cluster expansion gives the rate of a randomly deactivated surface without sampling. It shows that an earlier kinetic Monte Carlo run reporting a dead surface was a fluctuation in too short a window, on a surface that was never dead. Third, when sulphated sites are recovered only by discarding the oxide layer, the product obtained per copper atom consumed is exactly (𝑘 𝑑 /𝑘 𝑠 ) 𝑓 sulphate , bounded by the branching ratio between product release and sulphation. This quantity is the inverse cumulative site-loss selectivity of Foley, Johnson and Bhan, and a chemical regeneration channel is the only route past the bound. All stationary solutions use the Grassmann, Taksar and Heyman reduction, which we show is required. A least-squares solve used earlier was wrong by up to twelve orders of magnitude on small rates.

papers.title: Biomimetic remodelling of lipid membranes using DNA nanostructures
papers.abstract: The remodelling of biological membranes underpins a diverse range of sophisticated cellular processes, from cell crawling to mitosis to pathogen infection cycles. A refined understanding of the biophysical principles governing lipid bilayer remodelling is necessary to engineer ever-more advanced behaviours in microrobots, like synthetic cells, with disruptive applications in both fundamental biology and advanced biotechnology. Owing to its ability to afford control over structural and functional properties at the nano-scale, DNA nanotechnology has emerged as a prime toolkit to engineer, program, and host biomimetic responses within lipid bilayer membranes. This Perspective review surveys advances on biomimetic membrane remodelling pathways coordinated by DNA nanostructures. I discuss strategies to prescribe the interactions of DNA nanostructures with lipid bilayers, and summarise progress to drive membrane remodelling events including lateral patterning, out-of-plane restructuring, fusion, and scission. Finally, I discuss current challenges alongside the yet untapped potential of nucleic acid nanostructures in membrane bioengineering to coordinate sophisticated behaviours in synthetic cells.

papers.title: Mapping under-represented chalcone chemical space with an open-source Virtual Chalcone Library (VCL)
papers.abstract: Chalcones are highly versatile privileged scaffolds, yet substantial regions of their synthetically accessible chemical space remain under-explored. Herein, we report an open-source Virtual Chalcone Library (VCL) comprising 489,475 unique structures generated from commercially available aromatic ketones and aldehydes using the freely available DataWarrior platform. Comparison of the VCL with a curated dataset of 8,886 literature chalcones revealed structural bias towards a small number of pharmacophore motifs, while highlighting under-represented regions of chemical space. Benzofuran-containing chalcones emerged as a prominent example and were selected as a case study for prospective exploration. Physicochemical filtering for favourable medicinal chemistry properties reduced this region to 1,181 candidates, from which diversity analysis identified 30 representative structures. Six novel chalcones were selected and successfully prepared, establishing two “synthetic outposts” in under-represented chemical space. A series of “deep-space” virtual chalcones (DS1-DS9) were identified with DS6 synthesised from commercially available starting materials. These syntheses provide experimental validation of the data-driven, VCL-guided workflow. The VCL is openly available as a community resource, accompanied by tutorials for its implementation and analysis in DataWarrior. This study establishes a framework for identifying, prioritising and experimentally accessing under-represented regions of chalcone chemical space.

papers.title: Compositional flexibility and structure dynamics of Strätlingite
papers.abstract: Strätlingite, Ca 2 Al(AlSi)O 2 (OH) 10 ·2.25H 2 O a phyllosilicate found in nature and in ancient Roman concrete, was investigated for its synthesis conditions, phase stability, and thermal and chemical degradation mechanisms. Contrary to previous reports, phase formation was observed to be complete after ~3 days of setting, using hand-ground precursors, while the applied water:solid ratio has only minimal effect on purity of the resulting strätlingite. The chemical stability field is rather narrow, and off-stoichiometry in the initial Ca:Si:Al ratio of the starting materials promotes the formation of poorly crystalline C-(A-)S-H side phases, which are difficult to detect by XRPD and may compromise complementary data interpretation. Thermogravimetry, variable humidity in situ XRPD and water sorption measurements reveal a reversible hydration below 100 °C, that is reflected in gradual changes of the lattice parameters and unit cell volume up to 2%. Above 100 °C irreversible changes to the crystal structure occur, resulting in the loss of the long-range order, which is complete at 200 °C and further. Strätlingite remains chemically stable during setting LC 3 cement formulations, making it a potential cement additive, provided the temperatures remain below 100 °C.

papers.title: Donor–Acceptor Integration Modulates Reverse Intersystem Crossing in Multi-Resonant TADF Emitters
papers.abstract: Multi-resonant thermally activated delayed fluorescent (MR-TADF) compounds are attractive as emitters in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) owing to their high photoluminescence quantum yields and narrowband emission. However, these emitters generally have moderate reverse intersystem crossing rate constants (kRISC), which causes triplet exciton accumulation and leads to, amongst other excitonic processes, triplet-triplet annihilation. This process results in significant efficiency roll-off in OLEDs at high luminance. Here, we report the photophysical properties of a 2 boron–nitrogen doped MR-TADF emitter, tCzBN, and two of its derivatives, SpAc-tCzBN and TRZ-SpAc-DBN, using time-resolved absorption and emission spectroscopy. Kinetic modelling of their photophysical behavior reveals that combining a donor–acceptor core with the MR-TADF moiety in TRZ-SpAc-DBN results in a higher kRISC than tCzBN and its donor-appended analog, SpAc-tCzBN, while preserving the narrowband emission of the MR-TADF unit. We attribute this enhancement to the lower effective adiabatic singlet–triplet energy gap (∆EST) and stronger spinorbit coupling in this molecular design.

papers.title: Low-Cost, Home Synthesis of Vaterite: A Factorial Study of Calcium Source, Temperature, Citric Acid Modification, and Mixing Intensity
papers.abstract: This paper presents a low cost, home-accessible method for synthesizing vaterite-type calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) using consumer-available materials and simple household tools. Vaterite is a metastable CaCO₃ polymorph of interest for biomedical, filler, and coating applications, but existing synthesis protocols typically require laboratory-grade reagents and equipment, limiting accessibility for independent researchers. The two required precursors, sodium carbonate (from baking soda) and calcium acetate (from eggshells and vinegar), were prepared in house. A 16-factor design then tested how calcium source, solution temperature, citric acid addition, and mixing intensity affect morphology. Optical microscopy (400×) of the first successfully produced sample (condition 3-D: cooled calcium chloride, citric acid added, strongly mixed) showed small, circular clusters with a flour-like texture consistent with vaterite morphology. Qualitative comparison of the remaining conditions suggests that citric acid addition is associated with finer textures more than mixing intensity, though this remains unconfirmed under magnification for most samples. This is presented as an interim record of an ongoing study. Crystallographic confirmation (XRD/FTIR) and microscopy of the remaining samples are planned as direct follow-up work. The primary contribution at this stage is a documented, reproducible, low-cost synthesis protocol together with one positive proof-of-concept result.

papers.title: Scoring close linker analogues in PROTAC ternary complexes: A matched-pose study of VHL-recruiting SHP2 degraders
papers.abstract: Linker optimisation in targeted protein degradation remains largely empirical, and a computational method able to rank close analogues before synthesis would be valuable. Whether current methods can do so has not been tested against the smallest chemical difference that changes potency. Here two VHL-recruiting SHP2 degraders that differ by exactly one methylene, P9 and P10, were compared across 27 ternary complex arrangements generated for both compounds, so that in every comparison the protein–protein geometry was held fixed and only the degrader varied. RxDock interaction scores did not distinguish them (p = 0.66). Prime MM-GBSA favored P9 by 8.1 kcal mol−1, agreeing in direction with the reported potency order (p = 0.040), but the preference was overturned by removing any of twelve individual poses and arose entirely from the generalized-Born solvation term; the nonpolar contribution was zero (−0.01 kcal mol−1, p = 0.97). Interface geometry computed from coordinates alone was indistinguishable between the two ensembles, with buried surface areas differing by 0.23%, and the computed energies were uncorrelated with interface size across a 2.9-fold range (r2 ≤ 0.10). Two further observations emerged: rigid-body docking score did not predict ternary competence, since none of the highest-scoring 1% of arrangements accommodated either degrader, and the longer linker reached ten more arrangements while closing no better within those both could bridge. End-point scoring of single minimized ternary complexes therefore does not resolve a one-methylene linker difference, even when it recovers the correct direction, and conformational averaging rather than a different energy function is the most likely route to improvement. The ternary complex models reported here are the first for this series.

papers.title: All-Optical Spin Coherence in a Photosynthetic Electron-Transfer Metalloprotein
papers.abstract: Optically addressable, biocompatible spin qubits represent promising platforms for quantum sensing. However, current efforts have focused on genetic encodability and microwave-based approaches thus far limited to organic radicals. Utilizing time-resolved Faraday rotation, we measured electron spin coherence in plastocyanin, a protein in the photosynthetic electron transport chain. Persisting hundreds of picoseconds, this is the first measurement of spin coherence in a metalloprotein under ambient conditions. We show how the protein’s active-site geometric and electronic structure responsible for biological function also enabled a spin–photon interface. A related blue copper protein—azurin—also demonstrated all-optical spin coherence. The ability to measure bioinorganic spin coherence under functional conditions foreshadows metalloproteins as native quantum sensors and opens questions about the potential role of spin coherences in electron transfer.

papers.title: LipidOracle: Ambiguity-aware lipid annotation across fragmentation methods
papers.abstract: Tandem mass spectra (MS²) rarely determine a complete lipid structure, yet annotation software reports a best-scoring name and leaves users to judge whether the spectrum distinguishes it from other isomers. LipidOracle enumerates every isomer compatible with a precursor, converts the scores into probabilities with a softmax calibrated on standards, and reports the structural detail on which the credible candidates agree. An independent audit tests whether any observed fragment separates the reported structure from its closest rival. Annotation depth, from sum composition to double-bond position, is thus set by the evidence in each spectrum. The same inference handled collision-, electron- and ultraviolet photodissociation spectra, with only the fragment model exchanged. On standards, it located double bonds among thousands of candidate isomers with small credible sets, and in human plasma and mouse liver it named chains and double-bond positions only where the spectra supported them. The approach extends to any activation method whose fragments can be predicted.

papers.title: Thermal pathway reconstruction exposes a reliability gap for AI-guided materials design
papers.abstract: AI-guided materials design increasingly connects candidate generation with processing and experimental planning, yet recognizing a material’s final thermal endpoint is not the same as reconstructing how it gets there. We benchmarked closed-book reconstruction of source-qualified differential scanning calorimetry event maps for 30 molecular materials using GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5.5. In the primary API experiment, models recovered terminal melting in 194/216 opportunities (89.8%) but other thermal transitions and pathways in only 105/318 (33.0%). Additional frontier-model configurations reproduced this endpoint-pathway gap. Providing source-reported preparation and scan conditions did not improve pathway reconstruction: recall changed by −6.5 percentage points (95% CI, −14.5 to +0.9) for Sol and −4.9 points (−13.6 to +4.5) for Opus. Frontier models can therefore recognize where a material’s thermal trajectory ends while failing to reconstruct the state changes determining how it gets there.

papers.title: Reductive insertion of a trivalent metal leading to the isolation of Prussian blue-type EuIIIFe3[Fe(CN)6]3
papers.abstract: Reductive insertion reactions selectively modify three-dimensionally bonded solid-state structures through the addition of an elemental metal by electronation of the host structure and insertion of the metal cation into the host cavities for charge balance. However, with rare exceptions, this class of reactions has been largely restricted to insertions of monovalent metals. The reductive insertion of divalent and trivalent metal ions is intrinsically limited by their very slow diffusion through a host lattice at low temperatures and instability of a host lattice in the presence of these metals at high temperatures. These limitations originate from strong coordination of multivalent guest species to anions within the host lattice. By using coordinatively saturated anions such as cyanide in Prussian blue analogues, only relatively weak coordination modes to guest cations are available within the host structures, suggesting these host structures may participate in multivalent metalations. Herein, we report reductive insertion of europium into Berlin green Fe[Fe(CN) 6 ] under relatively mild conditions by reaction with EuI 2 at 150 °C in N-methyl-2-pyrolidone. The formation of the half-ferrous product, Eu III Fe 3 [Fe(CN) 6 ] 3 , is an exceptionally rare reductive insertion of a trivalent metal, and the first example of a phase pure Prussian blue (A n+ 1/n Fe[Fe(CN) 6 ]; A = metal cation) isolated with either a lanthanide or multivalent A-site metal. The resulting compound exhibits a distribution of iron oxidation and spin states not observed in previously reported Prussian blue phases of the form M I Fe[Fe(CN) 6 ]. The valence of Eu 3+ was confirmed by a combination of X-ray absorption, 57 Fe Mössbauer, and magnetic susceptibility measurements, which informed a possible reaction mechanism invoking redox exchange between the ferrous host, Eu 3+ guest ions, and excess Eu 2+ in solution.

papers.title: DrugForge-ADMET v0.3.0: An auditable BRICS-based workflow
papers.abstract: Early hit discovery normally begins with a physical or virtual collection of small molecules. Public resources such as PubChem, ChEMBL and ZINC have broadened access to chemical space, but using them effectively still requires retrieval, standardization, filtering, deduplication, three-dimensional preparation and provenance management; many laboratories also lack an in-house screening collection. We present DrugForge-ADMET v0.3.0, an open-source RDKit workflow intended to provide a compact, auditable starting set when a prepared library is unavailable. The software decomposes 30 inspectable, sp3-enriched seed templates into BRICS fragments, recombines them, sanitizes the products, and applies deterministic physicochemical rules, structural-alert catalogues and explicitly labelled descriptor-based risk proxies. Seed/reference similarity is assessed with radius-2, 2048-bit Morgan fingerprints and Tanimoto similarity; score-first diversity selection limits redundancy. Selected structures are exported as CSV and as SDF records with ETKDGv3 conformers followed, where parameterized, by MMFF or UFF optimization. In three fixed-seed technical validation runs, each capped at 10,000 enumerated products, 61, 157 and 194 candidates were selected. Across 412 outputs, 411 canonical SMILES were unique, all 412 SDF records were readable and all contained three-dimensional conformers. The pooled median values were molecular weight 355.50, cLogP 1.55, TPSA 79.25 Å2, fraction sp3 0.706, three rotatable bonds, one aromatic ring and QED 0.845. These results establish software execution and property-window compliance, not bioactivity, synthesizability, patent novelty or experimentally validated ADMET performance. DrugForge-ADMET is therefore positioned as a transparent candidate-generation and triage layer before target-specific modelling, retrosynthesis and experimental testing.

papers.title: Models building models for discovery of graphene metamaterial design principles in the context of failure
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence assists scientific discovery, but most agents operate previously developed instruments. Whether an agent can build an instrument, translating physical theory into reliable measurements and testable predictions, then use it for open-ended research remains open. Here, from a single prompt, an AI agent built and validated an atomistic simulator and conducted 96 simulations across ten graphene architecture families. At matched mass, load paths governed strength, and tilted slits revealed distinct failure mechanisms. Human–AI collaboration examined larger strains and hierarchical architectures. Sliding slit edges exhibited sequential geometric reconnection; hierarchical veins redistributed load, compartmentalized damage and deflected cracks. Selected larger hierarchical designs were about 25% stronger, with at least one-third greater work to failure, than equal-mass, equal-size controls. These results demonstrate a workflow where AI agents build scientific models and use reflective reasoning to falsify, validate and refine physical understanding, while human–AI collaboration drives mechanistic discovery and engineering of complex materials.

papers.title: In-column Synthesis and Atomic-resolution Electron Microscopic Analysis of Metastable Reactive Nitrides
papers.abstract: Metastable and air-sensitive compounds are challenging to synthesize and characterize because their formation often requires harsh conditions and their structures can rapidly evolve upon exposure to the environment. Here, we demonstrate that a high-vacuum environment inside a transmission electron microscope (TEM) column can serve simultaneously as a reaction platform and an atomic-scale analytical tool for generating and interrogating such materials. Electron-beam irradiation on sodium azide (NaN3) produces crystalline sodium nitride (Na3N) at room temperature, despite the conventional decomposition of NaN3 into sodium and nitrogen. The formation of Na3N is supported by high-resolution TEM, electron diffraction, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, which reveal correlated structural and compositional changes through irradiation. The resulting Na3N subsequently undergoes oxidation through an amorphous intermediate to form polycrystalline Na2O. The high-vacuum environment sufficiently suppresses this reaction to resolve its otherwise unachievable microscopic mechanisms. Extending this approach to potassium azide (KN3), we observe a transient crystalline phase that is most consistently indexed as K3N, a nitride known to be thermally unstable even under room temperature. Its transient appearance and decay indicate a dynamic balance between electron-beam-induced formation and degradation. These results establish in-column electron-beam chemistry as a route to metastable nitride formation while enabling multimodal characterization of highly reactive products. More broadly, this strategy offers a means of exploring nonequilibrium metastable compounds that are difficult to access using conventional synthesis and characterization workflows.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Nickel-Plated Steel Wool and Nickel Strip Electrodes for Hydrogen Production from Non-Potable Water Sources
papers.abstract: Traditional water electrolysis imposes a significant freshwater demand. This study evaluates alternative non-potable feedstocks to reduce this dependency. We present a comparative performance analysis of user-fabricated, three-dimensional (3D) porous nickel-plated steel wool scaffolds versus conventional flat nickel control strips. Testing was conducted across tap water, rainwater, and greywater utilizing a near-neutral sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) electrolyte. Operational performance was quantified via volumetric hydrogen (H2) yield, Faradaic efficiency, and cost-normalized output (mL/$). The porous electrode significantly outperformed the flat strip, increasing Faradaic efficiency by 7% in tap water and 5% in rainwater. Furthermore, the 3D scaffold achieved up to an 8.7× greater hydrogen yield per dollar. These results demonstrate the bench-scale feasibility of low-cost, structured electrodes for reducing freshwater dependence in water electrolysis.

papers.title: Persistent Alkyne-Bridged Bis-Trityl Diradicaloids with an Open-Shell Ground State
papers.abstract: Organic singlet diradicaloids are of interest for spintronics, singlet fission, and quantum information science because of their electronic and magnetic properties. However, the synthesis of persistent diradicaloids with high diradical character remains a challenge. Herein, we report the synthesis of three novel alkyne-bridged diradicaloids based on a tetrathiaarylmethyl (trityl) radical. Electron Paramagnetic Resonance spectroscopy and magnetic susceptibility measurements were used to determine the spin-spin exchange interaction J in all three compounds, revealing narrow singlet-triplet gaps of -1 kcal/mol, -0.4 kcal/mol, and -0.05 kcal/mol for 1 •• , 2 •• , and 3 •• , respectively. DFT calculations support the singlet open-shell nature of the ground state in all three diradicaloids and yield a diradical character y 0 of 0.47, 0.53, and 0.76 for 1 •• , 2 •• , and 3 •• , respectively. Furthermore, low-energy absorption bands at 780 nm for 1 •• and 2 •• and at 500 nm for 3 •• show the transition between the open-shell ground state and a closed-shell cumulenic state. In addition, the reactivity of all three compounds towards oxygen is rationalized based on the spin-spin interaction. Lastly, since the molecules share similar geometries, J is found to be in inverse correlation to y 0 .This study thereby provides extensive insight into the structural relations between polyynic and cumulenic states, and the stability of tritylbased diradicaloids.

papers.title: CuBr-Catalyzed Enantioselective Synthesis of Decahydroquinoxaline-Based Bis(propargylamines): Application to the Synthesis of an Axially Chiral Allene
papers.abstract: A CuBr-catalyzed one-pot protocol provides access to decahydroquinoxaline-based bis(propargylamines) from readily available terminal alkynes, aromatic aldehydes, and a C2symmetric chiral diamine. The three-component coupling proceeds at 120 °C within 12 h, affording the products in 58–93% yields with diastereomeric ratios of up to 99:1. The synthetic utility of the protocol is illustrated by the ZnI2-mediated conversion of a representative bis(propargylamine) (7a) into the corresponding axially chiral allene (8a) with 90% ee. This approach enables the stereoselective construction of bis(propargylamines) and demonstrates their application as precursors to axially chiral allenes.

papers.title: ProtMutMap: Predicting Protein Binding Free Energy Changes Using Multiple-Mutation Networks
papers.abstract: Predicting changes in binding free energy ΔΔ G caused by multiple mutations at protein−protein interfaces requires accounting for nonadditive interactions between mutations, which an additive approximation based on single mutations cannot capture, and for the dependence on the computational pathway in stepwise approaches that introduce mutations sequentially. Here, we propose ProtMutMap, a method that integrates information from multiple pathways in a network whose nodes represent target variants and variants containing subsets of their mutations, and whose edges represent free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations for residue substitutions. ProtMutMap simultaneously estimates the binding ΔΔ G of each variant from all edge values using Huber loss. We compared ProtMutMap with the additive approximation and the stepwise method at 30 evaluation points, including intermediate variants, using a multiple-mutation dataset comprising 7 protein complex systems derived from SKEMPI2. ProtMutMap achieved a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 1.13 kcal/mol, lower than that of either comparison method. ProtMutMap also yielded lower prediction errors than Rosetta flex ddG. These comparisons with experimental values demonstrate that integrating multiple pathways through variants containing subsets of the target mutations improves binding ΔΔ G predictions for protein variants with multiple mutations.

papers.title: GPCR–G protein structural endpoints carry evolutionarily localinformation about the captured G protein class
papers.abstract: Structures of GPCR–G protein complexes are widely used to infer coupling selectivity, yet receptor coordinates in a mature complex may carry information associated with the transducer that was captured. This study analysed 1,360 experimental class A GPCR structures to ask how captured G protein class information is represented in receptor coordinates, how far it transfers across receptor families, and how receptor-only coordinate models relate to the experimental specimens they derive from. Across 207 receptor–transducer units from 169 receptors, receptor sequence and endpoint geometry both predicted the captured class (Gs, Gi/o or Gq/11) under receptor-grouped validation, but transfer declined with evolutionary separation: geometry outperformed sequence at 50% sequence identity (macro ROC AUC 0.731 versus 0.638), and both were near chance at 30%. Among 34 receptors resolved with more than one transducer family, held-out receptor geometry retained a small captured-class signal that sequence cannot provide. By contrast, a compact four-feature receptor geometry recovered the annotated active/inactive state almost completely (ROC AUC 0.996), including when close homologues were separated. Functional coupling annotation showed that more than half of the mapped units come from receptors supported for at least two G protein families, and a specimen-level audit showed that most receptor-only coordinate models derive from transducer-containing cryo-EM specimens. Receptor coordinates in mature class A GPCR complexes therefore carry distributed, evolutionarily local information about the captured G protein class. A captured structural class should not be read as an intrinsic or exclusive coupling preference, and receptor-only coordinate models should not be equated with experimentally partner-free receptors

papers.title: Structure-Based Prioritization and Electronic Tuning of Cinnamate-Bearing Natural Products at Falcipain-2 and Falcipain-3
papers.abstract: Electronic descriptors can prioritize substituents on model electrophiles, but whether those choices persist in intact natural products across receptor states remains uncertain. We tested cinnamate-bearing natural products at falcipain-2 (FP-2) and falcipain-3 (FP-3). Screening 1,012 South African Natural Compounds Database records yielded 185 motif-bearing parents, 174 with paired profiles. Receptor-normalized Glide XP ranking placed acteoside and aloeresin C alone on the dual-target Pareto front; six composites agreed at Spearman ρ ≥ 0.93. A protocol-matched FP-2 benchmark showed limited but statistically resolvable enrichment (ROC-AUC 0.548, 95% CI 0.505–0.590; 0.641, 0.586–0.698 for covalent actives). In a para-substituted methyl-cinnamate series, OH→NO₂ increased global electrophilicity from 2.22 to 3.69 eV while decreasing the β-carbon Fukui response from 0.166 to 0.026 as 61% of the added-electron response shifted to the nitro fragment; fragment-level trends persisted across ESP and Mulliken partitions, whereas atom-condensed indices did not. In the intact glycoside, para-chlorination improved the FP-3 Docking Score by 0.77 units (more negative) at pH 7.0 but redistributed the cinnamoyl core across the pose ensemble (median displacement, 8.7 Å) without conventional halogen-bond geometry, so the score gain did not reflect simple pose conservation. Moving one proton within the FP-2 catalytic dyad shifted the matched-pair contrast by 3.89 units and altered one-third of the library by more than the substituent effect; at pH 5.5, the FP-3 contrast reversed to +0.62. Thus, substituent effects that survive score-selection and sampling checks can remain conditional on protonation-state treatment, placing ligand tuning and receptor-state uncertainty on the same quantitative scale.

papers.title: Dynamic Reactant Forcing Circumvents CO Poisoning in Catalytic CO Oxidation
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous catalysts are usually optimized under static feed conditions, forcing a compromise between reactant adsorption, surface reaction, and site regeneration. For CO oxidation on Pt, this compromise is especially severe because CO binds strongly and suppresses O2 activation. Here we show that externally imposed square-wave modulation of the CO pressure can break this static limitation on Pt(111). Using synchronized infrared reflection absorption spectroscopy and mass spectrometry under constant O2 background, we directly resolve the coupled evolution of CO∗ coverage and CO2 production during each forcing cycle. CO introduction produces an initial CO2 burst followed by CO poisoning, whereas CO removal generates a second CO2 burst as vacant sites reopen O2 dissociation pathways. A Langmuir–Hinshelwood microkinetic model reproduces these transients and identifies the optimum forcing window as a balance between CO replenishment, CO desorption, and O2 activation on regenerated sites. Model-guided experimentation indicates the most favorable regimes of forcing frequency and duty cycle. At 475 K and PO2 = 5 × 10−5 mbar, the strongest tested protocol (approximately 0.3 s CO-on and 0.7 s CO-off) gives an approximately threefold larger time-averaged normalized m/z = 44 signal than continuous CO exposure at the same temperature, O2 pressure, and peak CO pressure. These results provide direct experimental evidence that reactant forcing can access productive non-steady-state surface coverages unavailable under static operation, establishing a mechanistic framework for programmable catalytic rate enhancement.

papers.title: Less is more in mixture modeling: every molecular vector is a map, yet the mixture is the territory
papers.abstract: Predicting mixture properties is a key challenge across domains, yet current deep-learning designs approach it blindly: they largely reuse the single-molecule recipe, compressing each molecule into a vector and predicting the mixture’s property from these vectors. We find that mixtures, as components multiply, depend increasingly on precise topological information. We therefore advocate a new design: model the mixture directly as a unified atomic system with complete and precise molecular topology. A simple instantiation of this design reaches or approaches the best published baselines across diverse domains, and indicates that the failures of existing vector-based models on some tasks stem from the same thing: every molecular vector is a map, yet the mixture is the territory.

papers.title: Where the vibronic coupling lies: promoting-mode frequencies and second-order rate theory for reverse intersystem crossing in multiresonance TADF emitters
papers.abstract: Rate models for reverse intersystem crossing in multiresonance delayed-fluorescence emitters usually place the vibrational spectrum on one promoting mode near 75 meV and treat the triplet–triplet vibronic coupling at second order. Neither approximation has been tested at scale. This work computes nonadiabatic couplings and signed spin–orbit vectors (PBE0/def2-SVP, Tamm–Dancoff) for all 121 emitters of the Hagai et al. compilation, and full vibrational spectra for 17 of them. The coupling-weighted promoting quantum has a median of 173 meV, in the aromatic ring-stretch region, with about 25 modes carrying 90% of the squared coupling. Collapsing the spectrum onto a 75 meV oscillator inflates the coupling by a factor of 1.5, and second-order theory then fails: over 120 emitters its rate departs from exact diagonalisation of the vibronic problem by a median of 0.49 orders of magnitude and lies further from experiment. At the computed 173 meV the median departure is 0.10 orders, although 21 emitters still differ by more than an order. On a multimode model that preserves the residual coupling matrix it falls to 0.02 orders for the 17 emitters with spectra, against 0.61 and 0.23 orders for the single-mode model on the same molecules. Both multimode treatments overestimate the measured rate for 15 of the 17 emitters, by a median of 1.2 orders, so the remaining error lies in inputs they share. For these emitters the breakdown of second-order theory comes from the single-mode reduction; the near-resonant regime remains to be tested with full spectra.

papers.title: Bio-based furan- and bifuran-containing dilinoleic dimethacrylates: synthesis, photocuring, and network properties
Optimal sparging and mixing for enhanced mass transfer in U-loop bioreactors across scales
papers.abstract: Scaling up the utilization of CO 2 for fuel and protein production requires designing large-scale reactors that can enhance gas-liquid mass transfer rates. Here, the gas sparging and phase mixing strategies are optimized in the case of a 608 m 3 U-loop reactor using computational fluid dynamics (CFD). The optimization is made possible by constructing a surrogate model that maps the design variables to the quantity of interest that captures the mass transferred per unit of energy expended. It is found that the optimal design consists of distributing as many spargers as possible. A separate analysis investigates how optimization can be conducted across scales, operating conditions and model assumptions. It is shown that optimal designs are primarily affected by the reactor scale if the reactor volume ratio between the industrial scale and the lab-scale is greater than 100.

papers.title: When Do Quantum-Chemical Descriptors Improve Aqueous Solubility Prediction? A Residual-Rescue Benchmark under Chemical Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: Quantum-chemical descriptors are increasingly appended to molecular machine-learning representations, yet their computational cost is difficult to justify when the average accuracy gain is small. We asked a stricter question for aqueous solubility: do low-cost quantum descriptors contain information that is genuinely nonredundant with conventional two-dimensional chemistry, and under which chemical regimes is that information useful? A frozen 2,996-molecule internal cohort derived from AqSolDB was evaluated with random, Bemis-Murcko scaffold-disjoint, and Butina-cluster-disjoint splits, and an independent 820-molecule OChemUnseen cohort was reserved for external validation. GFN2-xTB/ALPB-water descriptors produced small but reproducible direct improvements when added to RDKit descriptors (mean internal RMSE reductions 0.009-0.018 logS across model/split combinations; all 10 seeds improved). More importantly, a strict out-of-fold residual-rescue architecture, in which a quantum-only model learned errors left by the 2D model, improved RMSE by 0.028, 0.047, and 0.028 logS under random, scaffold, and cluster splits, respectively (10/10 seeds; paired Wilcoxon p = 0.001953 for each). On the external set, quantum augmentation reduced the 95th-percentile absolute error by 0.055 logS. Frontier-orbital descriptors accounted for most of the external gain, and significant benefits after false-discovery-rate correction were concentrated in nitro, amine, amide, and alcohol/phenol subsets. A learned low-cost gate did not reliably predict which molecules would benefit, providing a useful negative result. These results show that inexpensive quantum descriptors add modest average accuracy but measurable orthogonal information, with the clearest value under chemical distribution shift and in difficult or electronically distinctive cases.

papers.title: Hybrid quantum dynamics based on the augmented correlated Gaussian wavepacket
papers.abstract: The nuclear quantum effects, including tunneling, zero-point energy and wavefunction delocalization, are increasingly recognized as relevant to reactivity, charge and energy transfer, and other properties of large molecular systems, including those in nano-scale and biological environments. In the presence of active dynamic quantum modes, however, application of the numerically exact quantum methods becomes unfeasible beyond a handful of atoms, while classical and semiclassical description can be very inaccurate, and the error is hard to quantify. Thus, theoretical approaches capable of accurately describing the quantum system on one side, and efficiently accounting for the environment on the other, remain an active area of method development. In this work, we present a hybrid approach combining basis representation of the active quantum modes correlated at the functional level with a “mean-field” version of the variational Gaussian wavepacket referred to as Augmented Correlated Gaussian (ACG) dynamics. This allows one to include the effects of the environmental modes on the system within quadratic scaling of the wavefunction with the system size. The method is demonstrated on a double well system coupled to a chain of harmonic oscillators capturing the tunneling dynamics. The ACG scalability is demonstrated by simulating the quantum vibrational densities of states of a five-dimensional molecular model of a hydrogen atom adsorbed on a graphene flake, incorporating anharmonicitiy into the CH stretch.

papers.title: Decoding Rotavirus Cell Entry through the Lens of Vesicle Budding-and-Collapse
papers.abstract: How nonenveloped viruses cross host membranes without causing cell lysis remains a central biophysical paradox. A recent cryogenic electron tomography study by de Sautu et al. proposed that rhesus rotavirus double-layered particles (DLPs) escape endocytic vesicles through a large, VP7-stabilized membrane pore. However, a static pore model is difficult to reconcile with live-cell single-particle tracking data showing multi-minute lags between VP7 dissociation and DLP release. Here, I show that these structural snapshots map onto the vesicle budding-and-collapse (VBC) framework, a recently discovered mechanism shared by a growing number of biological and synthetic membrane-translocation systems. Re-interpreting rotavirus entry through VBC resolves kinetic discrepancies in the literature and provides a unified physical paradigm for viral entry and drug delivery.

papers.title: Chemistry, Generative AI, and English: implications for chemistry researchers from diverse language backgrounds
papers.abstract: Background, context, purpose: English is essential in global science but poses challenges for researchers who speak it as an additional language (Eng+). We investigated how chemistry researchers’ language backgrounds shape their experiences and the impact(s) of digital tools, including generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). We administered a questionnaire to chemistry researchers having English-as-a-first (Eng1st) or English-as-an-additional (Eng+) language. Results, main findings: Both groups indicated that English proficiency is crucial for productivity, though Eng+ participants reported more difficulties. Eng+ participants viewed digital tools as more helpful, including GenAI, and primarily used for writing support. However, concerns about GenAI’s accuracy, ethics, and plagiarism risks were common. Some Eng+ researchers avoided over-relying on GenAI, preferring to improve their English skills. Few used GenAI beyond summaries and rephrasing/translation. Conclusions: This work is the first to identify how emerging technologies like GenAI are perceived and used by researchers from different language backgrounds, highlighting the potential to enhance equity and productivity for Eng+ scientists.

papers.title: Separating hydration propensity from hydrogen bond donation in trifluoromethyl ketone warheads
papers.abstract: Trifluoromethyl ketones populate carbonyl and gem-diol states, but the amount of hydrate present need not report how strongly that hydrate donates a hydrogen bond. We benchmarked 14 trifluoromethyl ketones against a recent colorimetric donor-strength dataset using 198 intended Q-Chem calculations, 181 of which completed normally. In the nine-member aryl subset, experimental hydrate abundance correlated weakly with hydrate-adjusted ln K (r = 0.276), whereas ωB97X-D/def2-TZVPD/SMD parent-relative electronic hydration energies correlated strongly (r = -0.896; ρ = -0.917). Four SMD density-functional profiles were nearly superposable (pairwise r = 0.988-0.999), and local mean C-O distance independently tracked donor strength (r = -0.904). Standardized hydrate-sensor interactions at 1.80 A tracked adjusted ln K (r = -0.683) but not hydrate abundance (r = -0.033). Intramolecular hydrogen bonding stabilized closed hydrate conformers yet weakened external donor interactions. These results separate hydrate population, intrinsic donor strength, and donor accessibility as distinct design variables.

papers.title: Persistent Ti–Cl Bonds Direct Self-Organization in Titanium–Ligand Artificial Photosynthesis Systems
papers.abstract: Hydrolyzed TiCl4–ligand systems capable of capturing atmospheric CO2 and converting it into reduced carbon products under ambient moisture and visible light exhibit an unexpected recurring feature: one or more Ti–Cl bonds persist after prolonged atmospheric exposure. Residual chloride is conventionally interpreted as incomplete hydrolysis preceding conversion to condensed Ti–O–Ti networks. The underlying Ti–OH/Ti–O photochemistry connects these systems to established TiO2 photocatalysis, but persistent Ti–Cl bonds and coordinated ligands prevent their simple description as incompletely formed TiO2. Here we propose a broader interpretation in which partial chloride retention is a structural control variable in the active material. By kinetically limiting extensive hydrolysis and condensation, retained chloride may preserve molecular or oligomeric titanium oxychloride–hydroxo species, maintain Lewis-acidic and exchangeable coordination sites, regulate the density and lifetime of Ti–OH groups, and support coexistence of multiple structural and redox generations. The nitrogen-containing ligands may be integral to this persistence: coordination to titanium can moderate hydrolysis and condensation, while ligand protonation can retain hydrolysis-generated acidity as local ligand–H+/Cl- ion pairs. Proton and chloride equivalents may therefore remain distributed among coordinated chloride, protonated ligands, Ti–OH···Cl environments, and more strongly hydrogen-bonded HCl-containing motifs. Such retention could establish a local proton–chloride reservoir and make individual hydrolysis and ligand-exchange steps dynamically reversible without implying global equilibrium. Related persistence of Zr–Cl bonds in zirconium–ligand CO2-capture systems suggests that chloride retention may be a broader feature of evolving Group 4 metal ensembles. The proposal distinguishes direct observations from mechanistic inference: persistent chloride-containing families support incomplete hydrolysis, whereas their roles in redox stabilization, proton-coupled electron transfer, self-repair, and catalytic turnover remain testable hypotheses. If confirmed, controlled partial chloride retention would constitute a design principle rather than a synthetic imperfection in this form of artificial photosynthesis.

papers.title: Lactic Acid Related Molecule Reaction Outcome Prediction via AI Chatbots
papers.abstract: Lactic acid (LA) and its related molecules like its polymer (Polylactic acid) have large importance in organic chemistry reactions. The objective of this experimental study was to determine the effectiveness of using AI chatbots to predict the outcomes and key findings of chemical reactions associated with the lactic acid chemical, along with understanding which chatbots are more effective to use in order to investigate a more efficient method to form hypotheses about these reactions. Reaction conditions of chosen reactions were put into specific models of ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot, and Gemini to test whether the outcomes they predicted matched with the key findings in the research papers the reactions were sourced from. Using statistical analysis by Cochran’s Q Test (p = 0.247237), a statistically significant difference between types of chatbot used for product prediction was not found. However, a Wilson Score Interval of the Perplexity Pro default model with 90% confidence yielded an interval of (0.6010, 0.8847). The findings essentially suggest a relatively high accuracy interval for the proportion of the types of LA related reactions in this study that the Perplexity Pro default model can predict correctly. The implications of this emphasize the importance of further examining what reactions can and cannot be used in AI chatbots to predict the outcomes.

papers.title: YOLOX-based detection of C60 molecules in time-resolved TEM
papers.abstract: Low contrast and heterogeneous backgrounds hinder automated molecular detection in time-resolved transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We prepared C60-loaded carbon nanohorns by solvent-free mechanochemistry and compared four preprocessing pipelines using YOLOX detectors trained on expert-annotated frames. Wiener filtering combined with contrastlimited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE) yielded the highest F1 score of 0.713 at an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.30 on temporally held-out frames from the same sequence. Applied to later frames, the model detected partially overlapping C60 candidates and yielded declining detection counts. Some projected intermolecular separations decreased to 0.90 nm, with a cumulative electron dose on the order of 108 e– nm–2 over approximately 15 s. These observations were consistent with, but not diagnostic of, [2+2] cycloaddition. The model also detected some fused structures as C60, indicating that counts reflect C60-like image features rather than true monomer populations. The workflow provides frame-wise localization and counting of molecular candidates. Multiclass detection of monomers, and fused structures, combined with tracking that accounts for detection errors and independent validation, could support quantitative kinetic analysis observed by atomic-resolution TEM.

papers.title: Nanodiamond as highly reductive catalyst: photohydrodeoxygenation of aryl ketones under mild conditions
papers.abstract: Recent developments in diamond materials have focused on their potential for photocatalytic applications. This is mainly driven by diamond’s unique band structure, which distinguishes it from typically used semiconductors and allows access to potentials as reductive as -3.6 V (vs NHE). Additionally, diamond presents itself as a sustainable alternative, being carbon-based, nontoxic and reusable. However, its use in applied organic chemistry remains scarcely reported. Here, we present for the first time the use of hydrogen-terminated detonation nanodiamond (H-DND) for the deoxygenation of aryl ketones. The deoxygenation of organic compounds is key to produce fine and commodity chemicals e.g. from biomass. Traditional deoxygenation methods involve harsh conditions and the use of toxic reagents due to the high dissociation energy of the C-O bond. We demonstrate the deoxygenation of aryl ketones using H-DND under 395 nm LEDs irradiation and mild conditions. The applicability relevance of the method is also supported by scalability and recyclability studies, highlighting the application of H-DND as efficient highly reductive photocatalysts.

papers.title: Selective Olefin Production from Complex Hydrocarbons via Pulsed Joule Heating
papers.abstract: Keywords: Joule heating; Complex hydrocarbon mixtures; Light olefins; Spatiotemporal reactor; Reaction-separation mechanism Introduction Light olefins are essential building blocks for the chemical industry, and expanding their production from diverse hydrocarbon mixtures is important for improving resource utilization and securing olefin supply. Complex carbonaceous resources, including waste plastics, petroleum, and coal liquefaction products, represent abundant feedstocks for light olefin production. Industrially, light olefins are produced mainly through steam cracking and catalytic pyrolysis.1, 2, 3 These processes rely heavily on fossil fuel combustion for heat supply, resulting in high energy consumption and carbon emissions.4 It poses a major challenge to the low-carbon transition of olefin production technology. Thus, developing low-carbon heat supply strategies while maintaining high olefin selectivity is critical for next-generation olefin production technologies.

papers.title: Synthesis of Semisaturated Polycycles via a Microwave-Promoted Iminyl Radical Cascade Cyclization
papers.abstract: A microwave-promoted iminyl radical cascade cyclization that furnishes semisaturated polycycles is reported. Competitive reduction was suppressed by lowering the reaction concentration. The protocol is simple and tolerates a wide range of O -aryloxime substrates, with those bearing an electron-withdrawing group on the participating aryl ring performing the best. The modular substrate synthesis renders the process useful for constructing compound libraries.

papers.title: Out-of-equilibrium Pd(II)-based cage populations with chiral memory
papers.abstract: Metallosupramolecular assembly has considerably progressed the rational creation of complex nano structures. Yet, their use has remained largely constrained to operating under thermodynamic control, far from reaching the functional sophistication seen in out-of-equilibrium biological systems. Here, we show that populations of heteroleptic Pd2L4-type coordination cages can be transiently and repeatedly driven out of equilibrium using a chiral cage-based chemical fuel and C 60 fullerene as an anti-fuel. This fueling cycle allows a temporary assembly to be formed through competition between ligand exchange and guest encapsulation reactions, operating at different timescales. The system behaves as an energy ratchet and can be refueled. At the center of the assembly, a chiral figure-of-eight motif formed by red diketopyrrolopyrrole ligands partially retains its handedness during ligand exchange, leading to a chiral memory effect. This work establishes chemically fueled coordination cage populations as a versatile basis for encoding transient structural and stereochemical information within complex dynamic systems.

papers.title: Synthesis of metastable t-ZrO2 via solid-state thermolysis of ZrOCl2·8H2O/NaHCO3: thermodynamics, oxygen vacancies, grain growth and phase stability
