papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive multiscale theoretical framework for the topotactic solid-state thermolysis of ZrOCl2·8H2O and NaHCO3 (1:2 molar ratio) to metastable tetragonal zirconia (t-ZrO2). Six quantitatively coupled sub-models are developed and validated against experimental data [1]: (i) a thermodynamic Hess-cycle analysis yielding ΔG°topo = −287 ± 18 kJ mol-1 per Zr at 400 °C, which is 56 ± 28 kJ mol-1 more negative than the sol–gel benchmark; (ii) a surface-energy crystallite stability model predicting a critical size Dcr = 13.5 ± 2.0 nm at 400 °C, consistent with the experimentally observed coherent scattering region (CSR) of 11.3 nm; (iii) an oxygen-vacancy thermodynamic model with ΔGvacancy = −3.7 to −36.8 kJ mol-1 for O/Zr = 1.63–1.98, rationalising the uniquely reductive micro-atmosphere of the solid-state route; (iv) a gas-wedge fragmentation model with ℱ = 2.07–4.17, confirming primary particle breakdown to 40–80 nm prior to t-ZrO2 crystallisation; (v) a JMAK kinetic analysis of the t → m transformation giving Ea = 81 ± 6 kJ mol-1 and Avrami exponent n = 0.27–0.31, consistent with defect-driven surface nucleation; and (vi) a grain-growth model with Q = 185 ± 15 kJ mol-1 in the presence of NaCl, representing a 25–40 kJ mol-1 reduction compared to NaCl-free systems. A (D, x)-phase stability map predicts a re-entrant t → amorphous boundary at O/Zr < 1.60 for D < 5 nm — a novel, falsifiable prediction — and quantitatively reproduces all experimental phase fields from ref. [1]. The by-product NaCl acts as a dual-role flux, stabilising t-ZrO2 nanoparticles below 500 °C via grain-boundary pinning but accelerating grain coarsening and the t → m transition above 600 °C. Optimal synthesis conditions are established: 1:2 molar ratio, heating rate β = 8–12 °C min-1, calcination at 350–450 °C, and post-synthesis drying at 55–65% relative humidity.

papers.title: Repurposing drugs for multi-target treatment of cytokine storm using machine learning
papers.abstract: Background: Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) is a major driver of acute organ failure in critical care settings, affecting approximately 49 million people and killing approximately 11 million people annually. Targeting multiple dysregulated feedback loops via single-molecule polypharmacology offers a promising strategy to blunt excessive immune activation and treat CRS-induced medical conditions such as sepsis. Methods: We used a computational workflow that combined machine-learning classification and molecular docking to identify multi-target modulators of NLRP3, IKBKB, JAK1, CCR5, and SIGMAR1. To eliminate data leakage, feature selection was strictly embedded within a 10-fold cross-validation loop. Candidates were structurally evaluated for binding affinity and active-site contact residues. Results: The model achieved an accuracy of 95.0% to 99.6% and an area under the receiver-operating curve (AUROC) of 0.995 to 1.000 across all five proteins, demonstrating robust generalization. Multiple compounds with average model-predicted scores above 0.50 across all five proteins were discovered. Docking analyses confirmed that the top candidates had favorable binding energetics, displaying stronger binding affinity than known protein inhibitors. Namely, Simeprevir had an average docking score of -10.3 kcal/mol. Shared key contact residues across drug candidates further support the validity of these docking scores and promise interesting in vitro work. Conclusion: Single-drug, multi-target inhibition effectively modulates interconnected inflammatory loops that drive the sepsis-related cytokine storm. This approach provides an alternative to multi-drug combination therapy in intensive care medicine.

papers.title: Small-Molecule Data Splitting for Machine Learning in Drug Design
papers.abstract: Data splitting is a critical determinant of machine-learning performance in small-molecule drug design. Different strategies impose distinct assumptions about structural similarity, temporal order, data provenance and chemical-space coverage, thereby affecting both evaluation realism and the interpretation of model performance. This perspective critically examines major splitting approaches, discusses their advantages, applicability and limitations, and offers evidence-based considerations for designing partitions aligned with intended prediction scenarios.

papers.title: Linker-Encoded Enzymatic Topology Control Enables Automated Peptide Stapling with Reusable Immobilized mTGase
papers.abstract: Microbial transglutaminase (mTGase) readily forms intermolecular isopeptide bonds, but this native bias promotes peptide oligomerization at synthetically useful concentrations. Here we encode reaction topology in a minimal diamine linker to redirect mTGase toward intramolecular stapling of unprotected glutamine-containing peptides. Direct comparison with a linker-free Lys–Gln substrate shows that the linker-encoded architecture maintains macrocyclization as the dominant pathway from 0.25 to 2.0 mM, whereas the native substrate undergoes exclusively intermolecular ligation. Linker and peptide studies establish geometric, electronic, and sequence requirements, and molecular simulations are consistent with the organization of the acyl–enzyme intermediate. The resulting staples serve as versatile synthetic handles for orthogonal bicyclization, late-stage functionalization, and reductive ring opening. The covalent immobilization of mTGase enables catalyst recycling and seamless integration into a continuous, automated peptide-stapling platform capable of processing diverse substrates. This linker-encoded strategy provides a route to control enzymatic reaction topology for programmable constrained-peptide synthesis.

papers.title: Antimicrobial-Peptide-Inspired Mixed-Charge Polyurethane Copolymer Hydrogels: Charge-Ratio Design and Screening for Infected Wound Repair
Self-Transforming Antibiofilm Polyurethane Copolymers with Arginine-Mimetic Cationic Activity for Infection-Resistant Implants
Computational Analysis of Competing Reduction Pathways in the Asymmetric Transfer Hydrogenation of 2-Alkenylquinolines
papers.abstract: Two competing reduction pathways can deliver a single stereochemical outcome. This computational study reveals that asymmetric transfer hydrogenation of 2-alkenylquinolines can begin through nearly isoenergetic 1,4-hydride transfer to either the quinoline ring or the alkenyl side chain. The resulting sequences converge on a common prochiral iminium intermediate, after which a final chiral phosphoric acid-controlled 1,2-hydride transfer establishes the experimentally observed enantioselectivity, providing a rational explanation of how competing reduction sequences ultimately afford the same product and stereochemical outcome.

papers.title: Regulation of Fused in Sarcoma Condensate Formation and Dissolution Using Butterfly-Shaped Gold Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: A Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), play a crucial role in organizing various cellular functions. Materials that can regulate condensate dynamics without genetic modification could provide new tools for controlling biomolecular organization. In this study, we explored butterfly-shaped gold nanoparticles (GNBs) as regulators of the phase behavior of maltose-binding protein-tagged fused in sarcoma (MBP–FUS), a model protein containing both folded and intrinsically disordered regions. We established a phase diagram to identify the conditions near the boundary between homogeneous and phase-separated states. Under these conditions, GNBs were found to promote the formation of spherical MBP–FUS condensates, while spherical gold nanoparticles and gold nanorods did not have a similar effect. Additionally, irradiation at 660 nm reduced both the size and abundance of the GNB-associated condensates, consistent with a photothermal response. These findings show that GNBs can influence MBP–FUS condensation near a phase boundary and suggest that nanoparticle geometry plays a significant role in this behavior. This study lays the groundwork for developing externally controlled, gene-modification-free methods for regulating biomolecular condensates.

papers.title: When Reactions Cross Back: Dynamical Effects in Manganese–Oxo Epoxidation
papers.abstract: The oxidation of alkenes into valuable functional products such as alcohols, carbonyls, and epoxides remains a cornerstone transformation in synthetic chemistry, yet achieving precise control over reaction pathways and selectivity continues to pose challenges. Although prior work has emphasized the influence of axial ligand identity—often comparing ligands with substantial electronic or steric divergence—this study delves into how subtle variations between structurally similar ligands, namely pyridine (Py) and 4-tert-butylpyridine (Ty), modulate the reactivity and stereoselectivity of manganese porphyrin-catalysed epoxidation. First-principles DFT calculations show that the activation of the manganese oxo species, a key step that initiates the catalytic cycle, proceeds with similar kinetic and thermodynamic profiles for both Py and Ty. The catalytic process involves initial olefin attack by the Mn-oxo to form a cis-oriented radical intermediate. This can either cyclize directly to give cis-epoxide, undergo internal rotation to yield a trans-radical species (eventually forming trans-epoxide), or proceed through a stepwise path that leads to carbonyl products via carbocation intermediates and hydride shifts. Notably, the substitution of Py with Ty selectively increases the barrier for transradical ring closure, attributed to differential stabilization of the radical and transition state, suggesting that small axial ligand changes primarily influence the later stages of the reaction coordinate. To uncover phenomena beyond static energy landscapes, quasi-classical trajectory (QCT) simulations were employed. These revealed that dynamic effects—such as momentum flow and intermediate lifetimes—govern the actual reaction outcomes. Despite DFT predicting comparable energetic profiles, QCT simulations captured ligand-dependent differences in mechanism: Ty-ligated systems predominantly followed rapid, ballistic pathways with minimal non-reactive trajectories, while Py-ligated analogs exhibited a greater variety of mechanisms, including more frequent non-reactive trajectories and unrelaxed intermediates. Reaction onset, as indicated by Mn–O bond elongation, occurred earlier with Ty, reflecting a sharper reaction impulse. These dynamic features correlate well with experimental observations of enhanced reactivity and diastereoselectivity for the Ty system. Collectively, these findings underscore that traditional static models may overlook critical aspects of reactivity. The presence of intermediates on potential energy surfaces does not inherently imply mechanistic relevance unless validated by real-time trajectory analysis. This study emphasizes the necessity of integrating dynamical simulations to gain a more accurate and mechanistically rich understanding of transition metal-catalysed oxidation reactions.

papers.title: From prediction to process control: a critical review of machine learning in reactive dyeing of cotton
papers.abstract: Reactive exhaust dyeing of cotton uses large amounts of water, salt, alkali and heat, partly because the recipe and programme are fixed when a batch starts. This review asks whether learned models, acting on the machine during a batch, have been shown to reduce that consumption. An OpenAlex search (2003 to September 2026, 862 records) and web searching identified 27 primary studies of learned, rule-based, model-based or search-based methods, or inline monitoring, in reactive dyeing of cotton. Each was coded by setting and by how far its output reached the process. Twenty-two stop at offline prediction, three only measure the bath, one advises an operator and one acts automatically; 24 are laboratory studies. No included study documents a learned model automatically changing an outcome-level decision (dye, salt or alkali quantity or timing, temperature programme, or rinse endpoint) during a batch. The one automatic controller, a fixed rule timing alkali injection at pilot scale, is not learned. A check on 135 studies of all fibres agreed. Reported fixation spans 40 to 70%, and no study has measured how much of the shortfall control could recover. Two priorities follow: measuring that share, and a matched-batch trial of learned, rule-based and operator control.

papers.title: Language-model-derived training data for polymer glass transition prediction: a controlled benchmark
papers.abstract: Experimental glass transition temperatures (Tg) are known for only a few thousand polymers, and each new one costs a synthesis and a measurement. Large language models (LLMs) have read much of the polymer literature and answer questions about polymers for a fraction of a cent. We tested whether such answers can replace or supplement measurements for Tg prediction by two routes: asking Claude Sonnet 5 to write polymers together with their Tg, and asking it to assign a Tg to existing hypothetical polymers. Both datasets were used to train a chemical language model, which was compared on held-out measurements with the same model trained on a growing number of real measurements, alone or after a first stage on the synthetic data. Controls with shuffled Tg values and with the model’s own pseudo-labels separated the value of the LLM’s labels from that of merely seeing more structures. Models trained only on LLM data were about as accurate as the LLM itself and clearly worse than models trained on real data. The LLM data helped only when a few hundred measurements were available, and the benefit disappeared when the Tg values were shuffled. Many “generated” polymers were recalled copies of known polymers, and the LLM’s Tg values were coarse and biased low. LLM-produced data are thus an inexpensive supplement when measurements are scarce, not a substitute for them.

papers.title: Beyond Swelling: Electrochemical Doping Tunes the Balance between Ion Compensation and Exchange in a Hydrated Organic Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductor
papers.abstract: Organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs) couple electronic doping to ion compensation and water reorganization. As doping increasing, molecular reorganization within the polymer–ion–water environment is thought to underlie the often nonmonotonic response of OMIEC devices, yet this process is essential for the understanding of structure-function relationship in related OMIEC devices but remains unclear. Although advanced operando measurements can resolve charge-state-dependent counterion localization within ordered OMIEC domains, jointly tracking electronic charging, explicit ion compensation, hydration, and molecular exchange across doping remains challenging; conventional simulations likewise do not allow these coupled variables to evolve together under constant electrochemical potential. To address these limitations under experimentally relevant electrochemical conditions, we develop an ion-regulated quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) grand-canonical molecular dynamics framework that operates at constant electrochemical potential and samples OMIECs across experimentally relevant doping levels. Experimental ²³Na and ³⁵Cl nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and layer-resolved computational sum-frequency-generation (SFG) spectra validate the polymer microstructure and polymer–electrolyte interfacial model. The simulations reveal a doping-dependent reorganization mechanism and identify a distinct compensation–exchange balance at the charging level associated with the experimental carrier-mobility maximum. With increasing doping, water–side-chain hydrogen bonding weakens and the glycol-rich environment crosses over from Na⁺ organization to Cl⁻-dominated compensation. Near the mobility maximum, persistent Na⁺ environments and a long-lived Na⁺–Cl⁻ motif coexist with a more rapidly exchanging Cl⁻ population. Further charging disrupts this balance, producing either kinetically trapped Cl⁻ or a more highly hydrated, rapidly exchanging environment. These findings establish distinct ion-compensation and exchange regimes across doping and provide a general framework for resolving polymer–ion–water structure–function relationships in OMIECs.

papers.title: Multiscale Insights into CO2 Chemisorption and Proton Transfer in Choline-Imidazolate based Deep Eutectic solvents: Exploring the Effect of Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Alkanolamine on Reaction Pathways and Product Distribution
papers.abstract: Understanding how solvent composition governs competitive CO2 chemisorption within solvents is essential for the rational design of solvents for CO2 capture. In this work, we combine density functional theory (DFT), classical molecular dynamics (cMD), and microkinetic modeling to investigate CO2 chemisorption in choline-imidazolate based systems containing different alkanolamine hydrogen bond donors (HBDs): monoethanolamine (MEA), diethanolamine (DEA), and methyldiethanolamine (MDEA). By systematically characterizing the thermodynamics, kinetics and liquid structure influence, our results show that within these systems, choline is the preferred CO2-binding site unless a HBD is present. Accordingly, the MEA system shifts almost entirely to amine-centered carbamate formation, the DEA system retains carbamate dominance but with stronger competition from choline-centered capture, and the MDEA system which additionally includes water shifts back toward choline-centered carbonate together with a competitive water-assisted bicarbonate pathway. The findings illustrate how CO2 chemisorption in multicomponent liquids is controlled by a combination of intrinsic reaction thermodynamics, liquid-structure, and CO2 concentration. More broadly, this work provides insights that will facilitate molecular-level design of solvents for CO2 uptake and regeneration.

papers.title: Empirical Evidence that Dirac–Fock Relativistic and Quantum Corrections are Z-indexing Artifacts
Hydrophobic Interaction as the Resolution of Interfacial Frustration
papers.abstract: The hydrophobic effect is one of the central organizing principles of molecular biology, underpinning protein folding, molecular recognition, membrane self-assembly and many forms of biomolecular recognition. Contemporary statistical-mechanical frameworks explain much of its thermodynamics, including the dependence of hydration on solute size, density fluctuations and interfacial formation. The remaining conceptual challenge is not the absence of successful theories, but the lack of a common spatial language to describe how heterogeneous non-polar interfaces perturb the collective state of water. In this paper, I propose interfacial frustration as such a descriptor, presenting it as a spatially distributed measure of the mismatch between the preferred state of hydrogen bonded water and the geometric constraints imposed by a non-polar interface. I propose that hydrophobic association can be viewed as a solvent-mediated reduction of this mismatch, while retaining the established thermodynamic description in terms of free energy (G), enthalpy (H), entropy (S) and density fluctuations. Hence, the proposed framework is intended as a complementary representation, and not a replacement of existing theories like Lum-Chandler-Weeks (LCW) theory. The spatial pattern, overlap, and non-additivity of interfacial frustration can provide a common descriptor for geometry dependent association and the crossover from localized hydration to collective interfacial drying. I also develop a more tentative extension to protein dynamics, in which hydration coupled fluctuations at and around hydrophobic cores may modulate distal conformational ensembles. The proposed framework generates explicit operational definitions, comparative predictions and falsification criteria that distinguish it from explanations based solely on surface area, local density or generic conformational entropy

papers.title: ROSE: a Foundation Model for Reusable One-dimensional Spectrum Embeddings in 1H NMR
papers.abstract: Most deep learning models for 1H NMR are trained for a single endpoint and do not provide representations that can be reused across analytical tasks. We introduce ROSE (Reusable One-dimensional Spectrum Embeddings), a 7.8-million-parameter spectrum-side foundation model pretrained on 3.2 million experimental and simulated spectra using an InChIKey-14 identity holdout that excludes all molecules appearing in the external benchmark test sets. Its shared spectral encoder supports denoising, peak detection, classification, cross-field alignment, molecular retrieval and structure-tospectrum prediction. Beyond internal evaluation on identity-disjoint holdouts, ROSE was assessed on external benchmarks excluded from pretraining, matching the published QIB PLS-DA result for 60-MHz edible-oil classification (98.8% balanced accuracy vs 98.9% accuracy), reducing NMRNet structure-to-spectrum Chamfer loss by 39% over Morgan+Ridge (0.79 vs 1.29), achieving 69% peak-detection F1 on NMRformer, and, after short domain adaptation, reaching 37.1% Top-1 and 67.7% Top-10 retrieval on NMR-Solver. ROSE represents a first step toward a general-purpose NMR foundation model for scalable industrial analytical applications.

papers.title: Simultaneous CEA and CDH-17 Detection from Cancer Extracellular Vesicles Via Machine Learning Enabled Bio Silent Azide-Infrared Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) provide a rich, minimally invasive source of cancer biomarkers, yet EV surface glycoproteins remain comparatively underexploited compared with EV internal cargo. Here, we report a bio silent, azide-based Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopic platform for simultaneous, label-minimal detection of two colorectal cancer (CRC) EV surface biomarkers, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and cadherin-17 (CDH-17), directly from intact vesicles. EVs from five CRC cell lines and a non-cancerous control line were first distinguished by their intrinsic biochemical fingerprints across the lipid, protein, carbohydrate, and nucleic acid spectral regions, achieving up to 97% classification accuracy by multivariate (PCA/SIMCA) and machine-learning (PLS-DA) analysis. Selective azide labeling of CEA and CDH-17 via biotinylated antibodies and streptavidin–azide generated a specific vibrational signal in the 2000–2300 cm⁻¹ bio-silent window without perturbing native EV spectra; peak authenticity was confirmed by Gaussian deconvolution, quantitative signal-to-noise analysis (SNR = 315 ± 99), and buffer/serum-artifact controls. Density-of-states overlap, cosine correlation, and constrained non-negative least-squares regression enabled simultaneous deconvolution and quantification of both biomarkers from mixed-antibody spectra, resolving cell line–specific expression patterns and enabling EV subtyping. Critically, the platform was validated on plasma-derived EVs from CRC patients and a healthy donor, where diagnostic performance exceeded that of the cell-line panel (AUC = 1.0 for metastatic CRC vs. healthy across all six spectral ratios; AUC = 0.58–1.0 for early-stage CRC vs. healthy). These results establish azide-FTIR spectroscopy as a rapid, label-efficient, and artifact-controlled platform for multiplexed EV biomarker detection, with direct evidence of its translatability to clinical liquid biopsy specimens rather than relying on cell-line data alone.

papers.title: AutoSolveX: automated batch structure solution, initial refinement and guest screening from diffraction data
papers.abstract: Modern three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) workflows can collect and process many datasets in a single session, whereas downstream structure solution, refinement and model interpretation often remain manual. Here we present AutoSolveX, a cross-platform Python pipeline with a graphical user interface for automated batch structure solution and initial refinement from processed diffraction data. AutoSolveX integrates SHELXT, SHELXS and SHELXL, applies electron scattering factors to 3D ED data, and extends automation to guest identification by screening candidate molecules against experimental Q-peak clusters and generating guest-containing models for subsequent refinement. We demonstrate AutoSolveX using five deposited electron-diffraction structures from different chemical classes, seven 3D ED datasets of Co-MOF-74, and ten 3D ED datasets of guest-containing structures of Bi-MOF SU-100 and 18 single-crystal X-ray diffraction datasets of Al-MOF-520. For the five deposited structures, AutoSolveX recovered the reported space groups and produced initial models with coordinate root-mean-square deviations of 0.015–0.052 Å from the deposited models. Automated batch solution and refinement of the Co-MOF-74 datasets generated comparable structural models across crystals and identified a dataset with poorer refinement results, demonstrating the value of systematic multi-dataset analysis. Guest screening retained the expected guest among the top three candidates for 9 of 10 SU-100 datasets and among the top five for 12 of 18 MOF-520 datasets. Complete molecular geometries were generated for all but the largest guests. AutoSolveX therefore provides a unified workflow from diffraction data to structural models and guest interpretation, reducing repetitive crystallographic work and facilitating analysis of large numbers of datasets.

papers.title: Scale degeneracy: the physical basis of calibration and absolute quantitation in molecular binding
papers.abstract: Quantitative biology, from clinical diagnostics to drug discovery, relies on molecular binding assays. Except digital PCR, these assays require calibration curves and cannot be compared across platforms. All binding assays obey one physical law: an exact finite-site equation of state from statistical mechanics, with two dimensionless variables, the relative target concentration and a regime parameter κ. κ maps assay platforms from the Langmuir limit (κ > 10) to near-complete capture (κ < 0.1). Invariance under joint rescaling of molecule number, capture capacity, and affinity (scale degeneracy) precludes their determination from one equilibrium measurement, explaining calibration. We identify three criteria for calibration-free absolute quantification, met today only by digital PCR, and prove analog assays intrinsically calibration-bound, increasingly so with precision. Validated on six decades of data, from the 1960 radioimmunoassay to single-molecule arrays and clinical samples, it unifies sensitivity standards, explains digital-assay error budgets, and turns calibration into a design parameter.

papers.title: Many-body machine-learned potential for the hydrated proton at CCSD(T) accuracy with fast analytical gradient
papers.abstract: The hydrated proton plays a central role in aqueous chemistry, biological proton transport, and electrochemical energy conversion. Reliable simulations of hydratedproton properties require an accurate reactive potential with low computational cost. Here, we report HP-AQUA, a high-level many-body machine-learned potential for the hydrated proton with fast analytical gradients. HP-AQUA combines the CCSD(T) quality q-AQUA-pol water potential and an accurate H3O + monomer potential with new permutationally invariant polynomial representations of the hydronium-water two-, three-, and four-body interactions. HP-AQUA demonstrates CCSD(T)-level accuracy across a series of gas-phase protonated water clusters for binding energies, harmonic frequencies, proton-transfer profiles, and configurations sampled along molecular dynamics trajectories. Analytical gradients implemented through reverse differentiation reduce the computational cost by more than an order of magnitude relative to our previous

papers.title: The Oxidation of Drug Molecules Using the Peroxygenase Activity of a Bacterial Family of Cytochrome P450 Enzymes
papers.abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes with peroxygenase activity can use H2O2 as the sole oxidant which is beneficial for biocatalytic applications. We investigated the peroxygenase activity of CYP105D18 from Streptomyces laurentii. The modification of the acid-alcohol pair in the I-helix through protein engineering reduced the peroxygenase activity for papaverine oxidation by 6-fold compared to the wild-type (WT) enzyme. We identified the oxidation metabolites as papaverine N-oxide, and two newly identified metabolites that arise from O-demethylation. The major O-demethylation metabolite was characterized as 6-O-desmethyl papaverine. Given the higher peroxygenase activity of the unmodified CYP105D18 enzyme we explored if another enzyme from the same CYP subfamily had similar activity. We produced and purified CYP105D41 from Streptomyces thermoviolaceus and found that this enzyme also has significant peroxygenase activity. CYP105D41 could catalyze the oxidation of papaverine and diclofenac. For this enzyme the oxidation of diclofenac was the more efficient reaction and generated 4′-hydroxydiclofenac, 5-hydroxydiclofenac and a doubly hydroxylated metabolite. Overall, we demonstrate that two CYP105 enzymes are effective natural peroxygenase biocatalysts and could efficiently oxidize drug molecules to generate human drug metabolites. These drug molecules are also emerging contaminants, and their oxidation would facilitate their removal from or breakdown in the environment.

papers.title: Enantioselective Strain-Release Formal (3 + 3) Cycloaddition of 1-Azabicyclo[1.1.0]butanes to Chiral 1,4-Diazabicyclo[3.1.1]heptanes via Relay Dy/Ir Catalysis
papers.abstract: *Email: nowmiracle@zjnu.edu.cn; dengwp827@zjnu.edu.cn ABSTRACT: Pyrazines and piperazines are privileged 1,4-diaza motifs, yet neither combines conformational rigidity with a stereochemically defined three-dimensional shape. Here we report the first catalytic enantioselective formal (3 + 3) cycloaddition of 1-azabicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (ABBs), providing direct access to enantioenriched 1,4diazabicyclo[3.1.1]heptanes—rigid, C(sp3)-rich scaffolds that serve as chiral three-dimensional complements to these classical motifs. Relay Dy/Ir catalysis merges Dy(OTf)3-promoted ABB strain release with iridium-catalyzed asymmetric allylic amination of allylamine-derived N,C,C synthons, extending ABB chemistry beyond conventional strain-release functionalization and previously reported racemic cycloadditions. The method furnishes 50 examples in up to 93% yield and 99% ee, with broad functional-group tolerance and compatibility with drug- and natural-product-derived substrates. Control experiments, 1H NMR studies, and DFT calculations support a staged mechanism involving carbonyl-assisted N,O-bidentate activation of the ABB by Dy(OTf)3. Preparative-scale synthesis, orthogonal product diversification, and access to pyrazineand piperazine-related drug analogues demonstrate the synthetic versatility and scaffold-hopping potential of this platform.

papers.title: Product Accelerated Photodegradation of Nitro-Spirothiopyrans
papers.abstract: The long term stability of conjugated fluorescent and photochromic compounds is essential for their application in materials and devices, but is often highly sensitive to changes in molecular structure. This aspect is particularly prominent in the 6'-nitro-spiropyran and 6'-nitro-spirothiopyran photochromes, which differ only in a O/S atom at the spiro center but show remarkably different stability under UV irradiation. Here, we show, using femtosecond and nanosecond transient absorption and NIR emission spectroscopy supported by quantum chemical calculations, that from a photo-physical and -chemical perspective the two compounds are remarkably similar. Time-resolved NIR emission of 1 O 2 , gas chromatography and NMR spectroscopy, reveal that the difference in observed photostability is due to the greater quantum yield for 1 O 2 generation of the photodegradation products in the case of NSTP .

papers.title: From prediction to process control: a critical review of machine learning in reactive dyeing of cotton
papers.abstract: Abstract Reactive exhaust dyeing of cotton uses large amounts of water, salt, alkali and heat, partly because the recipe and programme are fixed when a batch starts. This review asks whether learned models, acting on the machine during a batch, have been shown to reduce that consumption. An OpenAlex search (2003 to September 2026, 862 records) and web searching identified 27 primary studies of learned, rule-based, model-based or search-based methods, or inline monitoring, in reactive dyeing of cotton. Each was coded by setting and by how far its output reached the process. Twenty-two stop at offline prediction, three only measure the bath, one advises an operator and one acts automatically; 24 are laboratory studies. No included study documents a learned model automatically changing an outcome-level decision (dye, salt or alkali quantity or timing, temperature programme, or rinse endpoint) during a batch. The one automatic controller, a fixed rule timing alkali injection at pilot scale, is not learned. A check on 135 studies of all fibres agreed. Reported fixation spans 40 to 70%, and no study has measured how much of the shortfall control could recover. Two priorities follow: measuring that share, and a matched-batch trial of learned, rule-based and operator control.

papers.title: Ring-Conformer Ensembles Improve AutoDock Vina Docking; an Ant Colony Makes Them Affordable
papers.abstract: In standard preparation, AutoDock Vina holds five-and six-membered non-aromatic rings at their input pucker, and our failure analysis of 4 509 runs against searchreachable native poses shows what that costs: with the accurate preset, the search itself fails in only 6.5% of runs, while ring conformations, ranking and the scoring function account for most of the rest. Docking up to four ring conformers per ligand and keeping the best-scoring pose repairs part of that gap for every search we tested, raising top-1 success by 5.5 to 7.4 percentage points for Vina’s Monte Carlo at exhaustiveness 1 and 8 alike and for the two presets we tested it with in the continuous ant colony optimization (ACOR) search we built into Vina; a cost-matched control that docks the input conformer K times shows that most of this gain is ring geometry rather than repeated sampling (+8.9 against +2.9 points with the accurate preset). Because the ensemble multiplies the cost of docking, its price is what limits its use, and this is where the ant colony earns its place: it reaches the pose accuracy of Vina at exhaustiveness 1 with about nine times fewer scoring evaluations, so an ensemble of up to four conformers with the accurate preset costs 8.5 s per ligand on one core and reaches 52.7% top-1 success, against 50.4% for Vina at exhaustiveness 8 (37.9 s) and 46.1% for the same ensemble driven by exhaustiveness 1. Ring ensembles with Vina’s own Monte Carlo at exhaustiveness 8 are the most accurate arm we measured (56.2%), at thirteen times that cost, so the choice between them is one of budget rather than of search.

papers.title: Establishing Optical-Spin Interfaces in Luminescent Organic Diradicals using Spin-selective Symmetry-breaking Charge Transfer
papers.abstract: Luminescent organic diradicals based on tris(2,4,6-trichlorophenyl)methyl (TTM) radicals have shown promise as optical-spin interfaces important for quantum sensing. The optically driven spin polarization mechanisms of existing TTM diradicals remain limited by non-selective singlet-triplet intersystem crossing (ISC) pathways, which restrict optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast. Two TTM-based diradicals were prepared in which the two TTM subunits are linked at the para positions of one of their phenyls. Fully substituting the resulting biphenyl linkage between the radical centers with chlorines gives diradical 1, in which the two phenyls constituting the linkage are nearly orthogonal to one another. Subsequent replacement of the remaining four para positions of the TTM phenyls with p-tolyl groups gives diradical 2. Following photoexcitation of these diradicals to their triplet excited states, they undergo symmetry-breaking charge transfer to form a diamagnetic ion pair followed by charge recombination to form a spinpolarized triplet state. Diradical 2 shows spin-selective intersystem crossing from the triplet excited state resulting in an ODMR spectrum, while diradical 1 does not. These results show that spin-selective decay channels from the triplet excited state are a necessary requirement for establishing a spin-optical interface in TTM-based diradicals.

papers.title: Impact of Structural Water on Ionic Conductivity in Hydridoborates Solid Electrolytes
papers.abstract: Sodium closo-hydridoborates have emerged as promising solid-state electrolytes for Na-ion batteries because of their high ionic conductivity and electrochemical stability. However, their sensitivity to water makes them challenging to scale-up. In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of controlled hydration on the structure, ion transport, and interfacial stability of an anion-mixed hydridoborate, Na4(B10H10)0.5(B12H12)0.5. By exposing the hydridoborate to varying degrees of relative humidity (RH) of 30-70%, we find that hydration at 30% enables retention of its moderate Na-ion conductivity (∼0.7 mS/cm) while higher hydration levels lead to the separation of the two anions ([B10H10] 2− and [B12H12] 2−), resulting in significant disruption in the Na ion conduction pathways. X-ray diffraction (XRD) and solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements indicate that hydration leads to the formation of distinct crystalline phases and alters the local ion coordination environments. The hydrated phase at 30% RH reversibly returns the original structure, restoring its ionic conductivity and compatibility with Na metal anodes. These findings provide insights into the role of structural water in Na-ion transport and a practical strategy for the use of moisturesensitive closo-hydridoborates solid state electrolytes.

papers.title: Non-Covalent Interactions Directed Azobenzene Crystals: Photoisomerization-Induced Melting and Melt-Mediated Polymorphism
papers.abstract: Azobenzene molecular crystals have emerged as a compelling class of stimuli-responsive materials, yet the structural factors that determine whether a given crystal bends, melts, or remains entirely inert under UV irradiation are far from understood. Here, we investigate a series of eight structurally homologous 2,2′-dihydroxyazobenzene derivatives (Azo-0 to Azo-7) in which terminal functional groups (‒OH vs. ‒OMe) and pendant alkyl spacer length are independently varied, allowing the contributions of intramolecular conformation, intermolecular packing topology, and lattice compliance to be disentangled. Single-crystal Xray diffraction (SCXRD), UV-vis spectroscopy, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), together with thermal-stage polarized optical microscopy, reveal two mechanistically distinct melting pathways. The central finding is that an intramolecular O-H···N hydrogen bond, present in four derivatives (Azo-0, Azo-1, Azo-3, Azo-5), forms a pseudo-six-membered chelate ring that locks the azobenzene core in its planar trans conformation, fully suppressing photoisomerization in both solution and solid state. Removal of this intramolecular constraint through ‒OMe substitution liberates the azobenzene core in Azo-2, Azo-4, Azo-6, and Azo-7, enabling efficient and fully reversible cis-trans photoisomerization with visible-light-driven recovery. Critically, irradiation of these unlocked crystals below their equilibrium melting points (Ts < Tm) triggers rapid, cooperative crystal-to-liquid transitions that are absent in the dark and under 456 nm light irradiation, establishing photoisomerization-induced lattice strain—not photothermal heating—as the operative mechanism. The sole outlier, Azo-5, melts under intense UV irradiation through a purely photothermal pathway, consistent with its locked conformation and strong 370 nm light absorption. Additionally, Azo-7 undergoes a thermally driven solid, liquid, solid polymorphic transformation: melt-recrystallization converts the high-melting polymorph Azo-7α (Tm ≈ 59 °C) into a structurally distinct, lower-melting polymorph Azo-7β (Tm ≈ 42 °C), demonstrating that thermal history is itself an independent handle for programming crystal packing. These findings translate directly into three molecular design principles for photomechanical organic crystals: phenolic OH gates the photoisomerization switch via intramolecular hydrogen bonding; alkyl chain length tunes lattice compliance and packing dimensionality; and melt-mediated crystals provide access to structurally and thermally distinct polymorphic forms.

papers.title: RealBind: a leakage-controlled benchmark for experimental PXRD and Raman structure retrieval
papers.abstract: We present RealBind, a benchmark for retrieving crystal structures from experimental powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) and Raman spectra. It contains 3,288 curated candidate structures, of which 1,468 have linked measured PXRD patterns, and 16,005 experimental Raman spectra, of which 10,547 are linked to structures. We provide quality-control records, prototype-held-out and composition-held-out splits, and evaluation protocols that state candidate-library size and the chemical information available at retrieval time. On a 492-candidate prototype-held-out library, a contrastive model trained on simulated PXRD reaches 78.5% Recall@10 on simulated queries but 5.3% on measured queries; physics-inspired corruption raises measured-query Recall@10 to 34.4%. A model-free correlation against simulated candidate patterns, with no preprocessing beyond the common Q-grid resampling and the measuredwindow mask, achieves 82.8% Recall@10 on the same test library. In a separate split comparison, 44% of random-split test structures have a structure-matched training counterpart; measured-query Recall@10 is 59.1% on that split versus 20.7% on the prototype-held-out split, although test populations and libraries also differ. Holding the trained model and 420 queries fixed, restricting the candidate library and pre-screening candidates by the ground-truth element set of the query’s structure, used as an oracle chemistry-conditioned diagnostic, raises Recall@10 from 27.1% to 99.1%; 37.6% of filtered queries have a single candidate. A Raman-to-structure baseline reaches 34.7% Recall@10 on heldout mineral spectra against 979 candidates in the pooled evaluation and 45.7% on the 485-candidate test-only library, which includes no validation structures. RealBind provides an experimental test bed for comparing learned methods with simple simulation-based matching under explicit, leakage-aware protocols.

papers.title: Tautomeric Diversity in the Baicalein Radical Cation: EPR Fingerprints of a Traditional Chinese Medicine Antioxidant
papers.abstract: The radical cation of baicalein, the principal bioactive flavonoid of the Traditional Chinese Medicine herb Scutellaria baicalensis, has been predicted to undergo an intramolecular proton transfer from the 5-hydroxyl to the 4carbonyl oxygen. This tautomerization produces two distinct electronic configurations, denoted C1 (canonical) and C2 (proton-transferred), whose relative populations and reactivities may determine the antioxidant behavior of the molecule within the single-electron-transfer–proton-transfer (SET-PT) pathway. The two tautomers have not, however, been distinguished experimentally; their UV-Vis signatures differ only subtly. Here we report the first EPR hyperfine fingerprints of the two tautomers, computed at the DFT/UM06-2X/EPR-III level across fourteen media. Three qualitatively distinct signatures separate C1 from C2 (values in water): a near-doubling of the isotropic coupling at the 5-hydroxyl oxygen O5 (from −5.88 to −11.77 G), a sign reversal at the aromatic carbon C5 (from +4.83 to −5.77 G), and the disappearance of the mobile proton’s coupling (from −3.49 to +0.30 G). All three qualitative signatures are preserved across dielectric constants from 1 to 78, making them robust diagnostics of the tautomeric state in a wide range of environments. Because EPR hyperfine couplings report directly on spin density rather than on electronic transitions, they provide an unambiguous experimental handle for detecting the tautomeric diversity of the baicalein radical cation.

papers.title: Substituent Effects Govern the Fidelity of Responsive Persulfide Donors
papers.abstract: Persulfides (RSSH) are important intermediates in sulfur transfer and trafficking in redox biology, yet the intrinsic chemistry of these molecules complicates the design of small molecule donors that deliver persulfides on demand. Here, we investigate how specific parameters of both the persulfide payload and disulfide structure in selfimmolative donors influence persulfide release, H2S formation, and the susceptibility to degradation by biological thiols. Notably, we demonstrate that many common structures used for persulfide delivery likely do not produce the intended payloads due to a combination of unexpected thiol-disulfide exchange reactions prior to donor activation or subsequent instability of the released persulfide. Using a family of esterase-activated donor constructs, we show that geminal dimethyl substitution at the benzylic position accelerates self-immolative payload release and decreases unwanted thiol-disulfide exchange prior to donor activation. We also establish that steric protection of the release persulfide strongly influences its downstream fate, with unhindered cysteinederived persulfides generating substantially more H2S than sterically protected penicillamine-derived systems. Importantly, thiol exchange studies reveal that insufficiently protected caged disulfides can be consumed rapidly by GSH before trigger activation, thereby diminishing donor integrity. Together, these results establish that the functionality of persulfide donors is governed by steric protection, which influences the competing pathways of donor activation, thiol exchange, persulfide persistence, and H2S formation. More broadly, this work establishes design principles for high-fidelity persulfide delivery and provides a framework for interpreting biological studies in which persulfide donors may participate in competing sulfur transfer and sulfur release pathways.

papers.title: Acoustic-assisted HDX-MS for Intact Virion Analysis
papers.abstract: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) enables solution-phase characterization of protein interactions and conformational dynamics, but analysis of intact enveloped virions remains challenging because limited proteolytic accessibility restricts peptide recovery. Here, we developed an acoustic-assisted HDX-MS workflow integrating chemical denaturation with bath sonication during quenching and applied it to dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV2) strain D2Y98P. The workflow achieved sequence coverages of 96.0 ± 0.7%, 89.8 ± 0.8% and 87.1 ± 1.0% for the capsid (C), envelope (E) and membrane (M) proteins, respectively. Model peptide measurements showed comparable back-exchange between sonication and incubation at matched durations, although longer treatment increased deuterium loss. Improved E protein coverage enabled characterization of changes in deuterium uptake associated with binding of the neutralizing antibody 2D22. Protected regions overlapped spatially with the cryo-EM-defined quaternary interface, while additional protection occurred in regions remote from direct antibody contact. These findings are consistent with antibody-associated conformational stabilization extending beyond the binding interface. Acoustic-assisted HDX-MS therefore improves structural protein coverage and complements cryo-EM by revealing peptide-level changes in antibodyassociated protein dynamics in the intact virion context.

papers.title: A transcriptional reporting system for sensing interactions of small molecules with proteins
papers.abstract: Characterizing binding interactions of small molecules with proteins is important in many areas of chemistry and biology. We show here that a transcriptional activation sequence from Escherichia Coli (E. Coli) can be exploited to create a binding sensor for small molecule/protein interactions. The system requires two key components: small molecules connected to a DNA bearing a transcriptional activation sequence (TAS) and proteins of interest (POIs) expressed as fusions with the transcriptional activation domain (TAD) from the phage shock protein F (PspF). If the DNA bound small molecule binds to the POI, the induced proximity of the TAD to the TAS initiates transcription, with the number of copies of RNA produced proportional to the binding affinity. Although numerous direct binding measurement techniques are known, very few of these amplify binding signals, or convert the binding signal to a different molecular form which is then easy to handle and quantify. We demonstrate several use cases where the technique will prove valuable, such as in characterizing binders, identifying molecular glues, or as a reporter in DNA encoded library (DEL) selections.

papers.title: TKitOC PRO v8+: An Interactive Cloud-Based Platform Integrating Target Discovery and Chemoinformatics Workflows
papers.abstract: The transition from biological target identification to structure-based molecular analysis commonly requires researchers to combine multiple software environments, file formats, and external web services. This fragmentation can increase preprocessing effort and create practical barriers for computational biology education and early-stage in silico research. Here, we present TKitOC PRO v8+, an interactive cloud-based platform designed to integrate sequence analysis, molecular diagnostics, structural data preparation, and chemoinformatics workflows within a unified graphical interface deployed through Google Colab. The platform unifies the in silico workflow by distributing functionalities across 13 modular tabs organized into two core pipelines. The Target Discovery and Molecular Diagnostics pipeline provides nucleotide and protein sequence processing, open reading frame analysis across six frames, codonpreference back-translation, automated primer design through Primer3, in silico primer specificity assessment using NCBI BLASTn, and protein functional annotation via InterPro coupled with an immediate local motif-based Fast-Track algorithm. The Structure and Chemoinformatics pipeline integrates molecular descriptor calculation through RDKit, structural visualization with py3Dmol, ligand extraction and format preparation, and automated assembly of receptor–ligand complexes via DockPrime from externally generated docking outputs. As a proof-of-concept case study, we applied the platform to the KPC-2 carbapenemase—a critical antimicrobial resistance determinant from the ESKAPE group—using the crystallographic structure PDB 2OV5. The workflow started from the deposited protein sequence, verified taxonomic identity via BLASTn identified the Class Aβ-lactamase target, generated a corresponding nucleotide representation through back-translation, assessed sequence correspondence through BLASTn, generated candidate primer pairs targeting the blaKPC gene, and connected the resulting target characterization with functional annotation and structural analysis. The resulting workflow demonstrates how TKitOC PRO v8+ can reduce manual transitions between heterogeneous computational tools and provide an accessible environment for bioinformatics and chemoinformatics training and preliminary research workflows.

papers.title: Overriding Intrinsic Regioselectivity in Propargylic Substitution via Cu/Pd Synergistic Catalysis for Enantioselective Dienylation
papers.abstract: Propargylic substitution is a fundamental strategy in asymmetric catalysis for constructing enantioenriched unsaturated molecules, yet the dienylation pathway via nucleophilic attack at the central carbon of propargyl/allenyl-metal intermediates has remained elusive. Here we report that Cu/Pd synergistic catalysis enables the first catalytic asymmetric dienylation with broad carbon nucleophiles, delivering enantioenriched 1,3‑dienes with exceptional levels of regioselectivity (>20:1), enantioselectivity (up to 99% ee), and E/Z selectivity (>20:1). Mechanistic and DFT studies establish distinct roles for the two metals: palladium governs regiocontrol, while the chiral copper complex is responsible for enantioselectivity, enabling complementary dienylation with high regio- and enantioselectivity. Stronger palladium–terminal-carbon interactions make terminal attack energetically costly and direct the regioselective reaction to the central carbon of the π-propargyl-Pd complex, thereby overriding the inherent preference for propargylation and allenylation. The synthetic utility is demonstrated by diverse transformations of the enantioenriched diene products, thereby enabling the rapid assembly of complex molecular architectures. Beyond providing a general strategy for reprogramming the innate regioselectivity of π‑propargyl chemistry, this work highlights the potential of bimetallic synergistic catalysis as a practical platform for tackling long‑standing selectivity challenges in asymmetric synthesis.

papers.title: From Publications to Physical Knowledge Models: Transferable physical understanding for AI-native experimental science
papers.abstract: Scientific communication has repeatedly accelerated when the objects used to preserve and exchange knowledge became easier to validate, search, and reuse. The scientific paper remains a human-readable compression of a richer scientific state: quantitative physical and observational models, their uncertainty and validity, and the evidence that supports or challenges them. We propose Physical Knowledge Models (PKMs) as explicit, versioned, composable, and transferable representations of this state. The intellectual object per se is not fundamentally new: expert mental models, comprehensive textbooks, and domain model repositories already integrate equations, mechanisms, observations, and validity judgments. The proposed advance is to make that integrated understanding machine-readable and directly connected to experimentation. Broad PKMs can be projected into reduced experiment-specific models; local evidence produces versioned knowledge proposals rather than silently overwriting community knowledge; and a Knowledge Integration Layer aligns partially overlapping models, evaluates evidence and beliefs, preserves competing branches, and exposes contradictions requiring further tests. Because the ontology itself can change, PKMs retain persistent links to original measurements, sample histories, and instrument and decision traces so that prior evidence can be reinterpreted under revised concepts and models. Coupled to experimental planning, this creates a structured route from shared knowledge to local experiment and back. Data, code, digital twins, and agents remain essential, but they become mechanisms for populating, interrogating, testing, and updating durable physical knowledge rather than substitutes for it.

papers.title: Accelerating the Discovery of Marine Natural Products with Antimicrobial activity via Bioactivity-Driven Molecular Networking
papers.abstract: The growing threat of antimicrobial resistance underscores an urgent need to investigate underexplored natural sources to provide new chemical scaffolds for drug development. Marine environments, particularly those along the South African coastline, represent reservoirs of novel chemical diversity with the potential to provide new classes of antibiotics. This study reports the development of an efficient biodiscovery pipeline for the assembly and systematic screening of marine natural products extract libraries to identify novel antimicrobial leads. The workflow integrates microbial genomics and biological screening with non-targeted high resolution tandem mass spectrometry and molecular networking. Chemical extracts of 174 sponges and tunicates collected from the South African coast were evaluated for antibacterial, cytotoxic, and in vitro enzyme inhibitory activity. Guided by molecular networkbased feature prioritization, eleven known secondary metabolites spanning four major 2 structural classes (bifunctional sphingolipids, variabilin furanosesterterpenes, topsentin bisindole and pyrrolo iminoquinone -alkaloids) were isolated. The bioactivity of the isolated compounds was consistent with their corresponding crude extracts. Computational mass spectrometry analysis of extracts with antimicrobial activity revealed additional enriched metabolite families warranting further investigation. Finally, we profiled the taxonomic diversity of sponge associated bacterial communities to assess their utility in facilitating dereplication and prioritization of species of interest for further study.

papers.title: Detection of Molecular Oxidation States in Dye Sensitized Solar Cells-Relevant Organic Dyes Eosin Y Through Optical UV/Vis Absorption Spectrum Changes
papers.abstract: This study investigates oxidative degradation mechanisms of the non-metallic organic dye Eosin Y in order to examine precisely how they influence the light-harvesting efficiency (LHE) of Dye-Sensitized Solar Cells (DSSCs). Density Functional Theory (DFT) and Time-Dependent DFT (TD-DFT) computations with ABINIT are used to construct the molecular geometry and electronic configuration of the dye in its neutral form, oxidized adduct state , and oxidized state with excited electron. From the basic Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital (HOMO) to its Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital (LUMO) energy gaps and Ultraviolet-Visible (UV/Vis) absorbance spectra obtained from the computations, it is evident that both photo-oxidation and oxygen addition render the molecule inactive, resulting in up to 90% reduction in extinction coefficient and near disappearance of the visible absorption spectrum. In summary, this project provides a molecular-level interpretation of the efficiency reduction experienced in organic DSSCs due to oxidative degradation.

papers.title: A Novel Mononuclear Nickel Complex as a Precatalyst for Ionomer-Dependent Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity
papers.abstract: In electrocatalytic water splitting, ionomer-catalyst interactions can significantly influence electrochemical performance. Molecular metal–organic complexes offer a tractable platform to investigate such interactions. Here we report a novel nickel–2methylimidazole complex, [Ni(2-MeIm)4(NO3)]NO3, with Ni@N4O2 coordination environment. The structure of this new material is established by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and supported by vibrational spectroscopy and thermal analysis. We evaluate the complex as an oxygen evolution reaction precatalyst in 1.0mol L−1 KOH and show that its apparent activity depends strongly on the ionomer used in the catalyst ink. With Aemion+, an anion-exchange ionomer the catalyst reaches 10mAcm−2 current density at an overpotential of 0.331V, whereas the same catalyst formulated with Nafion exhibits a markedly reduced activity with an overpotential of 0.403V. The impedance spectra recorded at 1.6V vs RHE show considerable differences in charge-transfer resistances between the two formulations, consistent with differences in interfacial charge-transfer kinetics. We propose that specific catalyst–ionomer interactions may modulate active-site accessibility and the in situ transformation of the molecular precursor into catalytically competent NiOOH.

papers.title: An Epidemic of Misbranding: Marketplace Surveillance of MGM-15 and Kratom Alkaloids in Commercially Available Tablets by QuEChERS -LCMS/MS
papers.abstract: The commercial kratom market increasingly includes concentrated and semi-synthetic products, including 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and dihydro-7-hydroxymitragynine (MGM-15), whose prevalence and concentration across the marketplace remain largely uncharacterized. Kratom alkaloids, namely mitragynine (MIT) and its diastereomers, share the same molecular formula and connectivity. The product ions commonly monitored are not structurally specific, further exacerbated by the semi-synthetic derivates. Reliable identification and quantitation of the alkaloid class require chromatographic resolution in addition to mass spectrometric detection. Here, we present a validated QuEChERS extraction protocol and LC-MS/MS method for the simultaneous determination of ten kratom alkaloids in 42 commercially available pressed tablets. The method was linear from 0.05 to 2.0 μg/mL (mean R2 0.992), with limits of detection ranging from 0.0005-0.044 μg/mL, recoveries of 80-120% for seven of ten analytes, and interday precision below 12.5% for nine of ten analytes. MGM-15 was detected in 31 tablets (73.8%) at a median concentration of 6.62 mg/g. Twenty-two of 26 quantitative label claims were not met; in three products, the claimed alkaloids were nearly absent despite total alkaloid content exceeding the stated claim by more than sevenfold. Two products marketed without kratom claims contained eight and nine of the ten target alkaloids, respectively. Combining MGM-15 detection with the 7-OH:MIT ratio identified 34 of 42 products (81%) as semi-synthetically modified. These findings emphasize the need for reliable, robust, and label-independent analytical surveillance of this evolving product class.

papers.title: Advances in Multiscale Computational Modeling of 2D Nanomaterials for Solar Cells: From Interface Design to Fabrication and Stability
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) nanomaterials provide a versatile platform for next-generation solar cells because their electronic structure, optical response, carrier transport, and interfacial chemistry can be engineered across multiple scales. However, photovoltaic performance and operational stability are governed not only by intrinsic material properties but also by coupled processes involving charge redistribution, interfacial recombination, ion migration, thermal transport, degradation, and fabrication-dependent microstructure. This review presents a closed-loop multiscale computational framework for the design, fabrication, and optimization of 2D-material-enabled solar cells. Density functional theory (DFT) and related quantum-mechanical methods are discussed for predicting band structure, band alignment, charge transfer, defect states, and optical properties, while molecular dynamics (MD) simulations address structural stability, ion migration, thermal effects, interfacial dynamics, and degradation. Finite element method (FEM)/COMSOL and device-scale models connect material-level descriptors to charge transport, recombination, thermal behavior, and photovoltaic metrics. Machine learning (ML) further enables high-throughput screening, property prediction, processing optimization, and inverse design. Particular emphasis is placed on bridging the simulation-to-fabrication gap by linking processing variables, including concentration, flake dimensions, functionalization, deposition, annealing, and interface formation, to realized structure and device performance. Experimental characterization and feedback are incorporated to refine computational models and guide subsequent design decisions. Overall, integrating quantum, atomistic, device-scale, data-driven, and fabrication-aware approaches provides a pathway toward efficient, stable, reproducible, and scalable 2D-material-based photovoltaic technologies.

papers.title: Confinement-Driven Transient Coordination Complexes: H2 Dissociation and Quantum Channel Modification in Single-Atom Contacts
papers.abstract: Understanding chemical reactivity at cryogenic temperatures is essential for advancing both fundamental quantum science and next-generation catalytic technologies. At the single-atom limit, geometric confinement can promote ground-state electronic effects that drive novel chemical events without thermal activation. Using the H2 interaction with transition-metal nanocontacts as a benchmark, we report the barrierless formation of a transient tip complex characterized by a diborane-like 4-electron, 3-center bond (Pt–H ~0.17 and 0.18 nm). This 2 ground-state dissociation acts as a selective quantum channel modifier: while the intact, physisorbed molecule yields a conductance of ~0.2 G0, the dissociated transient complex results in a quantized conductance of 1 G0. This mechanism is correctly captured by mean-field orbital models when proper non-local exchange corrections are effectively considered. Furthermore, while bulk palladium is renowned for its high hydrogen affinity, our mean-field models and quantum calculations demonstrate the opposite: Pd nanocontacts merely physisorb H2 (H–H ~0.08 nm), behaving as a noble metal at this quantum limit. These findings illustrate how geometric confinement can drive novel chemical events, opening new avenues for zerotemperature catalysis at the single-atom limit.

papers.title: Mean First-Passage-Time-Directed Bias Optimization with Gaussian-Kernel Markov Models
papers.abstract: Rare transitions limit the direct simulation of molecular kinetics and complicate the design of enhanced-sampling biases that accelerate specific events without obscuring their mechanism. We develop a data-driven framework in which biased trajectory data are combined using dynamic histogram analysis and represented by either conventional grids or normalized kernel-anchor memberships to construct finite row-stochastic kinetic models. These models are used to adapt a bounded bias by directly minimizing an absorbing mean first-passage time (MFPT) objective, while reactive-current diagnostics independently assess whether accelerated trajectories preserve the reference transition mechanism. We first test the kernel-induced representation in equilibrium free-energy reconstruction and then apply the kinetic optimization framework to progressively more challenging rareevent problems, including membrane permeation, multidimensional barrier crossing, and a metastable molecular rearrangement. The benchmark calculations show that MFPT-directed biasing can efficiently promote target arrival and that soft kernel states provide a flexible alternative to rigid spatial discretization. At the same time, pathway analysis shows that faster arrival does not imply preservation of the underlying transition mechanism. A confounded high-dimensional stress test further exposes the limitations of projected kinetic models when the relevant dynamical coordinates are unresolved.

papers.title: Microstate-Aware Excited-State Descriptors Improve Scaffold-Robust Prediction of Drug Phototoxicity
papers.abstract: Drug phototoxicity depends on electronically excited states whose energies and intensities can change with protonation, tautomerism, and conformation, yet most predictive models represent a single parent structure. We evaluated a molecular-state-aware workflow on a curated 450-compound in vitro photoirritation (PIV) benchmark expanded to 1,088 microstates. Across 10 repeated 5-fold scaffold-held-out cross-validations, mean ROC-AUC increased from 0.745 for structure alone to 0.792 after adding parent xTB+sTDA descriptors, 0.807 with microstate summaries, and 0.808 with conformer aggregation; PR-AUC increased from 0.669 to 0.727. Compound-paired bootstrap analysis gave a full-model ROC-AUC gain of +0.0569 (95% CI 0.0234-0.0908) and PR-AUC gain of +0.0533 (0.0133-0.0933). Higher-level Q-Chem calculations preserved screening excited-state ordering (S1 Pearson r = 0.946; T1 r = 0.931), and an additional preselected state panel completed 22/24 TDA jobs with all four parent-alternate microstate pairs available. These pairs showed substantial state-dependent changes, including a 240.4 to 259.0 nm bright-state shift for trinexapac-ethyl. Clinical PIH endpoint transfer was modest (n = 155; ROC-AUC 0.609), consistent with endpoint and chemical-space shift. The results support molecular-state-aware excited-state featurization as a mechanistically grounded strategy for computational photosafety.

papers.title: Health risk assessment of carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic heavy metal exposure from commercial instant noodles in Bangladesh: a deterministic and probabilistic evaluation for adults and children
papers.abstract: The contribution of the instant noodle cake itself to dietary heavy metal exposure in Bangladesh has not been quantified. Nine metals (Pb, Cd, Cr, Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, Ni and Co) were determined by flame atomic absorption spectrometry in eight leading brands (102 packets) from Dhaka, Rajshahi and Khulna, seasoning sachet excluded. The hazard index (HI) and total cancer risk (TCR) were estimated for adults and children at national-average (0.36 g day -1 ) and high-consumption (25.6 g day -1 ) ingestion rates, with uncertainty propagated by bootstrap Monte Carlo simulation. Mean concentrations ranged from 17.7 mg kg -1 (Fe) to 0.030 mg kg -1 (Cd), and all brands complied with the Codex and Bangladeshi limits for Pb, Cd and Ni. No THQ exceeded 1; HI was 0.003 (adults) and 0.010 (children) at average intake and 0.19 and 0.71 at high intake, with Co contributing half of the HI. TCR was tolerable (10 -6 to 10 -4 ) at average intake but reached 9.8 × 10 -5 for high consuming adults and 3.7 × 10 -4 for high-consuming children, exceeding 10 -4 in 34% and 83% of simulations; Ni and Cr accounted for 95% of the cancer risk. Regulatory compliance therefore does not ensure negligible risk for frequent child consumers, and the risk-driving metals are those without a maximum level. Comparison with studies of noodles analyzed with their sachets indicates that the sachet, not the cake, is the main Pb source. Risk-based surveillance of Cr, Ni and Co, harmonization of the national standard with Codex, and control of sachet ingredients are recommended.

papers.title: Hydrogen-Bond-Induced Dual Structural Response in Amide-Functionalized Self-Assembled Monolayers
papers.abstract: Internal functionalization can reorganize intermolecular interactions across a self-assembled monolayer (SAM), yet its depth-dependent consequences remain poorly understood. Here, molecular dynamics simulations and vibrational sum-frequency generation (VSFG) spectroscopy reveal a dual structural response in N-(2-mercaptoethyl)heptanamide SAMs on Au(111). A persistent intermolecular hydrogen-bond network suppresses conformational fluctuations between the Au-S interface and the amide plane. Above this plane, however, the larger volume of the amide increases alkyl-chain separation and weakens van der Waals coupling and enhances conformational flexibility with temperature. Thus, a hydrogen-bond-stabilized, solid-like lower region coexists with a weakly coupled, liquid-like upper region. Simulated VSFG spectra reproduce the observed terminal CH3 stretching-mode intensities, including the enhanced asymmetric response. This response occurs without a correspondingly large average methyl tilt angle because inequivalent molecular environments produce broad, heterogeneous orientation distributions. Consequently, the conventional assignment of a single methyl tilt angle from VSFG intensity ratio breaks down for internally functionalized SAMs.

papers.title: Coupled Field-Gated Nucleation and Autocatalytic Growth in Ferroelectric Switching
papers.abstract: Polarization switching in fluorite (HfO2, Hf0.5Zr0.5O2) and wurtzite (AlScN) ferroelectrics is dispersive: nominally identical devices and domains switch over a spread of time rather than at a single threshold. The nucleation-limited-switching (NLS) model treats this phenomenon as a Lorentzian-in-log-time distribution of nucleation waiting times; Kolmogorov–Avrami–Ishibashi (KAI) theory instead treats switching as deterministic nucleation-and-growth. Recent AlScN transport studies report devices moving between these regimes in terms of defect density, thickness, or cycling, motivating a model in which nucleation and growth are explicit, coupled, field-dependent processes.

papers.title: Excited-State Photophysics Improves Scaffold-Robust Phototoxicity Prediction and Reveals Compound-Specific State Effects
papers.abstract: Phototoxicity is controlled by light absorption and access to reactive excited states, but predictive models usually encode only a single ground-state structure. Here, a physically staged representation was evaluated on 450 compounds (192 positive, 258 negative) with 10 repeated five-fold scaffold-grouped cross-validations. Structure alone gave ROC-AUC 0.745 ± 0.018 and PR-AUC 0.668 ± 0.027. Adding parent-state xTB/sTDA photophysics increased these metrics to 0.792 ± 0.012 and 0.716 ± 0.020; microstate aggregation reached 0.807 ± 0.012 and 0.726 ± 0.017, while conformer expansion plateaued at 0.808 ± 0.010 and 0.729 ± 0.017. In 10,000 paired compound bootstraps, the largest robust ranking increment was the structure-to-parent-photophysics step (ΔROC-AUC +0.0457, 95% CI +0.0274 to +0.0643). Microstates produced a smaller rank-based increment but reduced Brier error by 0.0080 (95% CI 0.0024–0.0134). Higher-level Q-Chem calculations preserved S1/T1 ordering (r = 0.946/0.931). Matched-state calculations showed large photophysical changes for avobenzone and 2-ethylanthraquinone but weak changes for pradofloxacin and ketoprofen. The results identify excited-state information as the dominant reproducible addition beyond structure and show that molecular-state effects are chemically meaningful but heterogeneous rather than universally accuracy-enhancing.

papers.title: Thermodynamics and Accurate Solubilities of Lithium and Sodium Salts in Imidazolium-Based Ionic Liquids
papers.abstract: Determining the solubility of metal salts in ionic liquids is challenging using visual methods or Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC). The slow crystallization kinetics of the metal salts impede accurate Solid-Liquid Equilibrium (SLE) measurements, resulting in significant discrepancies in the limited available literature. We propose Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) as an alternative technique to measure the solubility of metal salts in ionic liquids at different temperatures. Some new solubility data of lithium and sodium salts in imidazolium ionic liquid were determined. We show how the ITC experiments not only provide accurate solubility data at the studied temperatures but also reveal key thermodynamic properties of dissolution, including the enthalpy of dissolution; the mixing enthalpy and the partial molar excess enthalpy of both components at saturation.

papers.title: Precision of Gaussian, Lorentzian, and pseudo-Voigt peak fitting under Gaussian noise
papers.abstract: Discriminating subtle differences in measured signals is essential to scientific discovery. Knowledge of the attainable precision limits of fitted peak parameters and the physical and statistical factors that determine them provides a rational basis for improving this capability. However, without a common framework for comparing peak shapes and noise statistics, universal features of peak-parameter precision remain difficult to distinguish from those specific to a profile or noise regime, thereby hindering the development of general guidance for peak fitting and measurement design. Here we analyze Gaussian, Lorentzian, and pseudo-Voigt profiles in the Gaussian-noise (GN) limit using the same information-theoretic parameterization established for the Poisson-noise (PN) limit, enabling direct comparisons across peak shapes and noise regimes. Using the Fisher information matrix and the Cramér–Rao inequality, we derive analytical lower bounds on the standard deviations of peak intensity (I), center (ωc), full width at half maximum (Γ), area (A), and mixing parameter (η) and validate them against numerical calculations and Monte Carlo simulations. This unified framework addresses a long-standing question in peak analysis: whether intensity ratios or area ratios can be estimated more precisely. Whereas PN-limit theory predicts greater precision for area ratios across all three profiles, our GN-limit analysis shows that this advantage disappears for Gaussian and Lorentzian profiles and reverses for a pseudo-Voigt model with free η. Thus, neither I- nor A-based quantification is intrinsically more precise; their relative precision is governed by peak shape, parameter covariance, and noise statistics. This helps explain why experimental comparisons have not yielded a unique answer and provides a principled basis for selecting the more precise quantity. Fisher-information densities further show that information on I is concentrated in the peak core, information on ωc is concentrated on the flanks, and information on Γ and η extends into the wings. This indicates that precise estimation of Γ and η requires the fitting range to extend sufficiently into the peak wings. Finally, using Raman spectroscopy as an example, we combine the theory with detector-noise models to predict attainable precision before data acquisition and quantify how measurement conditions and instrument performance affect precision. The framework supports quantitative optimization of measurement conditions and instrument design to improve analytical precision across diverse signal-analysis applications.

papers.title: Capturing the Effect of Exact Exchange in Thio-Michael Additions with a Machine-Learned Functional at Meta-GGA Cost
papers.abstract: Semilocal density-functional approximations fail to describe the formation of anionic enolates in thio-Michael additions, the bond-forming step of covalent-inhibitor warheads; range-separated hybrids, which reintroduce long-range exact exchange, are required. Across the published CCSD(T)validated reaction pathways of eight warheads, we show that Skala—a deep-learned semilocal functional containing no exact exchange—matches the range-separated hybrid reference for the activation barriers, enolate geometries and relaxed reactant structures, outperforming the global hybrid B3LYP at meta-GGA cost. The one signature it does not reproduce is the orbital one: its Koopmans ionization potential stays at the semilocal scale, because the ionization-potential theorem constrains the exchange potential, not the energy. Skala thus captures the effect of exact exchange in the total energy, from training data alone.

papers.title: Access to Broad Organosulfur Chemical Space by Iron MHAT Sulfinamidation of Olefins
papers.abstract: Organosulfur groups, particularly in the S(VI) oxidation state, have seen increased adoption within the medicinal chemistry community in recent years. Although certain groups such as sulfones and sulfonamides have been utilized since the advent of modern drug development, others like sulfonimidamides or sulfoximines have only recently seen utilization. These desirable functionalities provide access to new chemical space and intellectual property while enabling the optimization of key ADME properties. Herein, we disclose a new method for the construction of these key organosulfur motifs via the hydrosulfinamidation of olefins.
