To maximize stiffness, oxides must be strategically introduced to enhance both network connectivity and volumetric packing density; hence, Y 2 O 3 , ZnO, and CeO 2 are investigated here due to their high single-bond dissociation energies and strong cationic field strengths. Magnesium aluminosilicate glasses (MAS) modified with Y 2 O 3 , ZnO, and CeO 2 were systematically investigated to establish composition–structure–property relationships. A constrained ternary mixture design (Y 2 O 3 –ZnO–CeO 2 = 14 wt.%) was used to span the compositional space efficiently. The measured Young’s modulus ranged from 97.5 to 113.8 GPa, while the specific modulus varied between 36.6 and 41.7 ×10 6 N·m/kg. The highest values were obtained for compositions adding Y 2 O 3 alone or Y 2 O 3 –ZnO. Raman spectroscopy revealed systematic changes in the Si–O stretching band, including shifts in band position and variations in band width depending on composition. These changes indicate structural reorganization of the glass network. A moderate correlation between Raman peak position and Young’s modulus confirms that structural connectivity effects contribute to stiffness, although additional factors such as packing density and cation field strength are also relevant. The results demonstrate that Y 2 O 3 is the most effective oxide for increasing stiffness, ZnO exhibits composition-dependent behaviour, and CeO 2 reduces the specific modulus. The combined analysis provides an experimental and structural basis to designing high-modulus glass systems.

papers.title: An Affinity-Based Model for Competitive Surfactant Adsorption in Microemulsions
papers.abstract: Mixtures of different surfactants are widely employed in microemulsions to tune aggregate stability, selectivity for solute incorporation (as part of separations), and phase behavior. Yet predicting how competing surfactants partition between the aggregate surface and the bulk medium remains an unsolved challenge. We introduce the affinity , a size-independent measure of polar-core coverage that is well-defined across polydisperse aggregates, and derive an affinity-based competitive Langmuir model from the grand canonical partition function. For TODGA/TBP in n-dodecane the model yields ΔΔGads. = -0.84 ± 0.04 kcal/mol favoring TBP and partitions it into an energetic term of -1.10 ± 0.04 kcal/mol and an entropic term of -0.84 ± 0.13 cal/mol K, the latter obtained from single-component simulations alone.

papers.title: Development of a Multivalent Macrocyclic Peptide that Protects Against SARS-CoV-2 Infection Following Intranasal Administration
papers.abstract: The risk of zoonotic spillover of coronaviruses poses a constant threat to humanity, as recently exemplified by SARS‑CoV-2. During the pandemic, the rapid emergence of immune escape mutations led to a loss of efficacy of both therapeutic and humoral anti‑spike antibodies, emphasizing the need for therapeutics that engage binding sites within the spike protein that are both conserved among related viruses and not under selective pressure from immune surveillance. Here, we report the development of a first-in-class fusion inhibitor cyclic peptide that targets such a site. Guided by a deep mutational scan of our earlier mRNA display hit we arrived at an analogue with 5 mutations that retains broad activity within the subgenus sarbecovirus, including against SARS-CoV-1, but shows up to 50-fold improved potency and approximately 25-fold improved solubility. Multimerization further improved IC50 by one order of magnitude to give a tetrameric construct (H4v1Az)4 that inhibits Omicron BA.2.86 replication with an IC50 of approximately 10 nM in cellular assays, including human airway epithelial cell primary cultures. Moreover, (H4v1Az)4 demonstrated significant antiviral efficacy in vivo in a Syrian golden hamster model following combined pre- and post-exposure prophylactic intranasal administration. This multimeric peptide represents a promising broadly active candidate suitable both for treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infection and for preparedness against future emerging sarbecoviruses.

papers.title: Multi-Step Oxygen Redox Mechanism in the Polyanionic Lithium-Rich Cathode Li2FeSiO4
papers.abstract: Lithium-rich cathode materials offer significantly higher energy densities than conventional cathode materials, due to their ability to store charge beyond the formal transition-metal redox limit, via so-called "oxygen redox". In lithium-rich oxides, oxygen redox is accompanied by molecular O 2 formation and transition-metal migration, associated with irreversible structural change and poor cycling stability. Lithium-rich silicates provide an alternative lithium-rich chemistry, and have been proposed to be resilient to O 2 formation at the top of charge, due to their covalently bonded [SiO 4 ]4- framework. We report a computational study of the top-of-charge behaviour of the prototypical silicate cathode Li 2 FeSiO 4 . Using density functional theory, we predict that fully delithiated FeSiO 4 is thermodynamically unstable with respect to oxidation of oxide ions to form molecular O 2 within the bulk material. Ab initio molecular dynamics shows this decomposition occurs spontaneously, via a multi-step mechanism involving Fe(IV) migration and disproportionation to Fe(III) and Fe(V), and subsequent Fe(V) reduction alongside molecular O 2 formation. Our findings demonstrate that polyanionic frameworks do not inherently prevent O 2 formation in lithium-rich cathodes, and illustrate how different previously proposed oxygen redox mechanisms can function as steps within a compound process.

papers.title: τ8: an Angle-Based Geometry Index for 8-Coordinate Complexes
papers.abstract: An angle-based geometry index for the direct comparison of 8-coordinate molecular complexes is presented herein. The method was designed as a readily accessible tool to evaluate experimental coordination complexes via the degree of distortion between the three most common interconvertible 8-vertex polyhedra for molecular compounds: square antiprism, biaugmented triangular prism, and dodecahedron. Analogous to the well-established geometric analysis methods for 4- and 5-coordinate compounds (τ4 and τ5, respectively), τ8 assesses the geometry of an 8-coordinate compound based on the angles around the metal center formed through ligand coordination contrasting with other methods utilizing the angles between polyhedral faces. This is an alternative and complementary approach to evaluating the central metal geometries of 8-coordinate compounds, designed to bolster the growing field of high-coordinate metal complex chemistry and provide a readily implemented framework for comparative analysis.

papers.title: An ‘empty’ [Fe16] cage and its transformation into [Fe17] and [Fe30]
papers.abstract: Polymetallic clusters of FeIII constructed without organic bridging ligands are an emerging class of molecules with structures akin to iron oxide minerals, possessing large spin ground states and/or displaying spin frustration effects. All previous examples, [Fe8], [Fe17], [Fe30] and [Fe34], have been isolated from pyridine or analogous heterocyclic amine solvents. Here, we report the isolation of an [Fe16] cluster from dmf. The complex is ‘isostructural’ with the previously reported [Fe17] molecular metal oxide, but with the central, tetrahedral FeIII ion absent. Antiferromagnetic exchange interactions between the tetrahedral and octahedral FeIII ions in [Fe16] lead to a spin ground state of S = 20, the highest yet for this family of materials, consistent with the S = 35/2 found for [Fe17] containing an additional (antiferromagnetically coupled) s = 5/2 ion. Dissolution of [Fe16] in pyridine regenerates [Fe17] or the larger [Fe30], depending on reaction conditions, demonstrating for the first time that these species can be interconverted.

papers.title: Catalytic-Defect Passivation on Amyloid-β Fibrils Using Atomically Precise Gold Nanoclusters
papers.abstract: Most pharmacological strategies targeting amyloid-β (Aβ) in Alzheimer’s disease have focused on reducing Aβ production, preventing aggregation, or removing deposited amyloid from the brain. Within the Aβ aggregation pathway, secondary nucleation is a critical amplification step in which pre-existing fibrils catalyze the formation of new aggregates on their surfaces. Some of these aggregates detach and grow into additional fibrils, sustaining an autocatalytic cycle that makes secondary nucleation an attractive target for pharmacological intervention. Biophysical studies indicate that rare defects formed during fibril growth act as hotspots for secondary nucleation, and that fibrils with fewer such defects show markedly lower secondarynucleation activity. Therefore, these findings raise the possibility that defect passivation could reduce the catalytic activity of Aβ fibrils without requiring their removal. This topical review proposes atomically precise, ligand-protected gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) as a tunable platform for selectively targeting and blocking these catalytic defects. Taking advantage of their welldefined metal cores and customizable ligand layers, we outline how AuNCs can be engineered for selective recognition of fibril surfaces and catalytic inhibition. We introduce an inversedesign strategy that integrates molecular modeling with machine learning-guided screening to identify optimal AuNC candidates before validating them through aggregation kinetics and neuronal assays. Defect-selective passivation would offer a distinct anti-amyloid approach by suppressing the critical autocatalytic amplification step of Aβ aggregation rather than removing deposited amyloid.

papers.title: Rotamer-Dependent Amino Acid Descriptors as Protein and Peptide Representation for Reactivity and Property Prediction
papers.abstract: We present RotADeL, a Rotamer-dependent Amino acid Descriptors Library designed to facilitate the use of chemically interpretable representations in machine learning models for peptide and protein reactivity. RotADeL contains precomputed steric and electronic descriptors for the rotamer ensembles of the canonical amino acids, accounting for their different protonation states. These descriptors can be queried either from a known protein structure, by selecting the closest library rotamer, or directly from an amino acid sequence, by averaging over the rotamer ensemble according to backbone and side-chain conformational probabilities. The latter approach avoids the need for computationally demanding protein geometry generation. We evaluated the resulting features in two case studies: first, the comparison of RotADeL descriptors to commonly used peptide representations for antimicrobial activity and toxicity classification; secondly, the application of RotADeL descriptors to predict the enantioselectivity of cyclisation reactions catalysed by GluER-T36A. Together, these results show that RotADeL provides a transferable and interpretable amino acid representation for machine learning predictions of peptide property and enzyme reactivity.

papers.title: Deciphering Chemical Cues of Pinus halepensis Infestation by the Pine Processionary Moth: Phytochemical Analysis and Computational Insights into Essential Oil Component Interactions with Insect Odorant Binding Protein
papers.abstract: Background The pine processionary moth, Thaumetopoea pityocampa, is a major defoliator of pine forests in the Mediterranean, notably affecting coniferous forests in Algeria. Insect odorant binding proteins (OBPs) play a crucial role in detecting pheromones and identifying host plants and oviposition sites. This study aimed to analyze the essential oils from both infested and healthy needles of Pinus halepensis and to investigate the role of GOBP2 in detecting plant volatiles through computational methods. Material and Methods Essential oils from infested and healthy Pinus halepensis needles were analyzed using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The interaction between these volatiles and GOBP2 was explored through molecular docking using SwissDock, and the stability of the top-scoring docked complexes was evaluated with molecular dynamics simulations via the iMODS server. Results The analysis indicated an increase in monoterpenes and a decrease in sesquiterpenes and diterpenes in infested trees. Among the 44 volatiles with increased production, 16 compounds, including Methyl 7,13,15-abietatrienoate, Abietadiene, Palustral γ-Eudesmol, β-Copaene, Phenethyl 2-furoate, trans-Cadina-1(6),4-diene, α-Eudesmol, Phenyl ethyl 3-methyl-butanoate, Phenethyl 2-methylbutanoate, Lavandulyl acetate, β-Elemene, Linalool acetate, Cyclosativene, cis-Linalool oxide, and Linalool, showed favorable interactions with the hydrophobic cavity of BmorGOBP2. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the complexes with Abietadiene and trans-Cadina-1(6),4-diene exhibited the highest stability. Conclusion The findings of this study provide valuable insights that could inform the development of pest management strategies targeting Thaumetopoea pityocampa.

papers.title: A Critical Review of Theoretical Approaches to Compute Ionic Conductivity in Solid-State Electrolytes: The Case Study of Li3YCl6 and Li3YBr6
papers.abstract: The development of next-generation batteries strongly depends on the design of electrolytes that ensure efficient ionic transport. In this context, computational in silico approaches have become increasingly important. Among them, molecular dynamics simulations are particularly powerful for investigating constitutive elements of batteries and providing a deeper understanding of structure-property relationships in solid-state electrolytes. Yet, for these systems, obtaining accurate ionic conductivity and activation energy is not straightforward as finding a force field to accurately describe the system and a robust workflow is challenging. In this work, a classical force field (CFF), based on the SoftBV bond-valence approach, and a machine learning potential (MLP) trained on density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces using the MACE neural network architecture, were optimized and compared to investigate the two solid electrolytes, Li3YCl6 (LYC) and Li3YBr6 (LYB). Our study proposes an integrated workflow (structure generation, property analysis with relevant statistical sampling) using standard methodologies based on the Einstein equations and a new method called STACIE[Toraman et al., J. Chem. Inf. Model., 65, 19, 2025, DOI:10.1021/acs.jcim.5c01475] (STable AutoCorrelation Integral Estimator) deriving these properties through the analysis of power spectral densities for transport property evaluation. Based on the evaluation and analysis of the contribution of the crosscorrelations between mobile ions, we provide clear rules to validate the use of Nernst-Einstein’s approximation to estimate the ionic conductivity. Results show trends in agreement with the literature. Notably the correct order of the conductivity activation energies Ea(LYC) > Ea(LYB), observed experimentally, is maintained. Overall, while CFF can provide an adequate representation when guided by experimental data, the strength of the MACE potential lies in its predictive capability. Using configurations generated by DFT calculations, the MLP generates trajectories with accurate crystallographic features from which realistic transport properties are extracted. Compared to their CFF counterparts, MLP results also show better mechanical stability at higher temperature for LYB, a softer system based on the analysis of solid-phase mechanical properties.

papers.title: Variable Rate Hydroxylamine Derivatization to Determine of Formaldehyde’s Role and Kinetics in CO2 Reduction to Methanol on Cobalt Phthalocyanine
papers.abstract: Heterogenized cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) catalyzes electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2R) to methanol. While it is clear that CO is a reaction intermediate, the role of formaldehyde, a sometimes-observed trace product, is less well-understood. Here, we gain insight into the methanol formation mechanism by selectively trapping formaldehyde. Using a simple preparation of CoPc heterogenized on multiwalled carbon nanotubes as the electrocatalyst, we employed three hydroxylamines which react with formaldehyde in the electrolyte to form stable, unreactive oximes at different rates: pentafluorobenzylhydroxylamine [PFBHA] (slowest), ethylhydroxylamine [EHA], and hydroxylamine [HA] (fastest). PFBHA has only a small effect on the methanol/formaldehyde selectivity, while EHA and HA (and higher concentrations of EHA) both reduce methanol molar selectivity by 25%, with a corresponding carbon-balanced increase in formaldehyde selectivity. Unbound formaldehyde thus is a relatively (compared to CO) short-lived intermediate responsible for only a quarter of the observed methanol. Extended CO2R in PFBHA-containing electrolyte scrubs the solution of CH2O without impacting MeOH selectivity, and we saw no noticeable difference in the rate of MeOH selectivity decline compared to control. This suggests that CH­2O is not a poison. 2D reaction-diffusion-convection simulations performed in a simplified geometry are consistent with the observed trends in methanol/formaldehyde selectivity, although derivatization rate constants larger than our experimental estimates need to be employed. We predict that hydroxylamine derivatization could be used for mechanistic analysis in other electrocatalytic networks with aldehyde intermediates.

papers.title: AI-Generated Peptide Vectors: Advancing Fluorescent Detection of Bacteria
papers.abstract: Molecular probes derived from antimicrobial peptides are powerful tools for diagnosing bacterial infectious diseases and guiding antibiotic therapy. However, existing probes rely on a limited repertoire of natural antimicrobial peptides, leaving the vast sequence space of linear peptides largely unexplored. Here, we used explainable artificial intelligence to design AIGP-3, a de novo peptide vector for fluorescent probes. Conjugated to Nile Red, NR-AIGP-3 exhibits high selectivity for Gram-positive bacteria, combining the environmental sensitivity of the fluorophore with the strong membrane binding of the vector and favorable MIC values for live-cell imaging. NR-AIGP-3 outperforms a ubiquicidin-derived probe in both flow cytometry and confocal microscopy, demonstrating its high potential for developing molecular probes for the diagnosis of bacterial infections.

papers.title: Directional Electric Fields at Designed MOF Sites: Implications for Electrostatic Preorganization and Catalysis
papers.abstract: Enzymes achieve their enormous catalytic power in part through electrostatic preorganization: non-covalent interactions arrange an electric field that is preorganized to stabilize the change in dipole moment between a reaction's ground and transition states. Thus, the catalytic relevance of an electric field depends not only on its magnitude but also on its orientation. Here we use the enforced rigidity of a metal–organic framework (MOF), PCN-521, to demonstrate this orientation dependence directly. We introduce an aldehyde carbonyl vibrational Stark probe in situ, first as a protected ketal, then deprotect it to reveal a carbonyl at the same node-capping site as a previously reported nitrile probe, extending field measurements to a field reporter of greater relevance to enzymatic catalysis. Electric field- vibrational frequency calibrated probes using the vibrational Stark effect report a trifluoroacetate field donor that projects nearly its full destabilizing field onto the collinear nitrile (sp, C≡N) but only a fraction onto the off-axis aldehyde (sp2, C=O) — a geometric effect. Because the framework's non-covalent contacts, unlike an enzyme active site's, cannot reorganize, this controlled, single-site comparison isolates alignment from magnitude. While electric fields are often invoked to explain observations near electrodes or droplet interfaces, these results show the importance of alignment which is often neglected.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Nickel-Plated Steel Wool and Nickel Strip Electrodes for Hydrogen Production from Non-Potable Water Sources
papers.abstract: Traditional water electrolysis imposes a significant freshwater demand. This study evaluates alternative non-potable feedstocks to reduce this dependency. We present a comparative performance analysis of user-fabricated, three-dimensional (3D) porous nickel-plated steel wool scaffolds versus conventional flat nickel control strips. Testing was conducted across tap water, rainwater, and greywater utilizing a near-neutral sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) electrolyte. Operational performance was quantified via volumetric hydrogen (H2) yield, Faradaic efficiency, and cost-normalized output (mL/$). The porous electrode significantly outperformed the flat strip, increasing Faradaic efficiency by 7% in tap water and 5% in rainwater. Furthermore, the 3D scaffold achieved up to an 8.7× greater hydrogen yield per dollar. These results demonstrate the bench-scale feasibility of low-cost, structured electrodes for reducing freshwater dependence in water electrolysis.

papers.title: Persistent Alkyne-Bridged Bis-Trityl Diradicaloids with an Open-Shell Ground State
papers.abstract: Organic singlet diradicaloids are of interest for spintronics, singlet fission, and quantum information science because of their electronic and magnetic properties. However, the synthesis of persistent diradicaloids with high diradical character remains a challenge. Herein, we report the synthesis of three novel alkyne-bridged diradicaloids based on a tetrathiaarylmethyl (trityl) radical. Electron Paramagnetic Resonance spectroscopy and magnetic susceptibility measurements were used to determine the spin-spin exchange interaction J in all three compounds, revealing narrow singlet-triplet gaps of -1 kcal/mol, -0.4 kcal/mol, and -0.05 kcal/mol for 1 •• , 2 •• , and 3 •• , respectively. DFT calculations support the singlet open-shell nature of the ground state in all three diradicaloids and yield a diradical character y 0 of 0.47, 0.53, and 0.76 for 1 •• , 2 •• , and 3 •• , respectively. Furthermore, low-energy absorption bands at 780 nm for 1 •• and 2 •• and at 500 nm for 3 •• show the transition between the open-shell ground state and a closed-shell cumulenic state. In addition, the reactivity of all three compounds towards oxygen is rationalized based on the spin-spin interaction. Lastly, since the molecules share similar geometries, J is found to be in inverse correlation to y 0 .This study thereby provides extensive insight into the structural relations between polyynic and cumulenic states, and the stability of tritylbased diradicaloids.

papers.title: Aggregation-Induced Emission Probes for Migrasome Imaging and Visualization
papers.abstract: Migrasomes are highly dynamic, migration-associated membrane organelles involved in intercellular communication, cargo transfer, mitochondrial quality control, and cellular homeostasis. Their continuous formation, growth, maturation, and detachment impose unique demands on fluorescence imaging, particularly for stable and long-term visualization in living systems. Conventional imaging approaches, including protein-based markers and lipophilic membrane dyes, often suffer from genetic manipulation requirements, cellular internalization, membrane redistribution, photobleaching, or insufficient retention. Aggregation-induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) provide a promising platform to address these limitations because their fluorescence can be activated by restricted molecular motion and their structures can be readily engineered for membrane interaction and functional sensing. In this review, we discuss the molecular design principles of AIEgens for migrasome imaging, with particular emphasis on membrane targeting, durable membrane retention, probe–lipid interactions, photophysical performance, and environmental responsiveness. Representative probes, including TTCPy, OT2SQ, and CDPP-2PF6, illustrate the evolution from phospholipid-targeted structural imaging to mechanosensitive sensing and long-term, lipid-dependent visualization. We further highlight emerging opportunities to improve migrasome selectivity, extend imaging in complex biological systems, and integrate functional readouts of membrane mechanics, lipid remodeling, and cargo dynamics. Together, these advances suggest that rational molecular engineering, rather than AIE activity alone, is central to the development of next-generation probes for selective, longitudinal, and functional migrasome imaging.

papers.title: Aromatic ring overlap affects excited-state properties of stacked nucleobases
papers.abstract: Photochemistry of nucleic acids has gained considerable attention because of their ability to undergo efficient charge transfer (CT) after absorption of UV light and its importance for DNA damage and repair. Recent computational and experimental studies demonstrated that CT rates and yields of DNA and RNA oligomers are strongly dependent on their secondary structure and relative arrangements of the chromophores. However, molecular and electronic origins of these differences still remain largely obscure. Here, we explored how stacking interactions and aromatic ring overlap affect the energetics of different locally excited (LE) and charge transfer (CT) states, as well as electronic couplings between them. For this purpose, we developed a novel approach and metric to quantify the stacking overlap between neighbouring aromatic rings. Based on quantum chemical calculations performed for a stacked adenine-guanine dimer, we show how the minima of different electronically excited states correlate with the degree of aromatic ring overlap and our stacking score metric. In particular, we demonstrate that electronic coupling values between the LE and CT states are maximised, whenever the aromatic subunits of stacked nucleobases are in perfect horizontal overlap. These correlations are preserved for more realistic nucleic acid fragments, such as different conformers of the AG RNA dinucleotide. Since the magnitude of electronic coupling has a strong effect on electron transfer rate, our results rationalize varying CT rates and yields observed across different DNA and RNA secondary structures, adopting different relative arrangements of the chromophores. Finally, our stacking score approach can be applied to the interpretation of excited-state and ground state properties of any chemical systems containing stacked aromatic rings.

papers.title: Anharmonic Vibrational Structure and Bound States of the He-CO2 van der Waals Complex
papers.abstract: We present a new flexible-monomer two-body ab initio potential energy surface for the He–CO2 van der Waals complex, extending our studies of the Ne–CO2, Ar–CO2, and Kr–CO2 complexes to the least polarizable and most weakly bound member of the series. The shallow, anisotropic interaction makes the intermolecular motion strongly anharmonic and delocalized, such that local-mode excitation energies cannot necessarily be identified with physically bound vibrational levels. Curvilinear vibrational self-consistent field (VSCF) and vibrational configuration interaction (VCI) calculations are therefore used primarily to characterize intramolecular anharmonicity and mode coupling, while the floppy intermolecular states are treated quantitatively using coupled-channel BOUND calculations on vibrationally averaged effective potentials. The bound-state calculations yield a dissociation energy of D0 = 16.106 cm−1 and four excited J = 0 levels between 7.699 and 15.001 cm−1 relative to the ground state. In contrast, the VCI-derived local-mode stretching fundamental and the reported overtone and combination features lie above the dissociation threshold and should not be interpreted as ordinary bound levels. The intramolecular spectrum remains largely monomer-like: the VCI ν3 band origin is in close agreement with experiment, the characteristic CO2 Fermi-resonance structure is retained, and the intramolecular bending degeneracy is predicted to be lifted by only ∼0.03 cm−1 . Both the direct and bound state treatments predict the experimentally observed positive sign of the complexation induced ν3 shift, although its magnitude remains sensitive to the vibrational treatment. These results ultimately show that the low-energy spectrum of He–CO2 is governed by large-amplitude motion near dissociation, thereby outlining the limits of local-mode descriptions for weakly bound complexes.

papers.title: Response to Comment “Rethinking the Evidence for a Liquid–Liquid Transition in Water: What Decompression Experiments Reveal"
papers.abstract: Ultrafast decompression experiments on deeply supercooled water have been interpreted as showing long-lived coexistence of high- and low-density liquid. We reassess this interpretation by separating the timescales of pressure release, structural relaxation, crystallization, and heat exchange. The experimental trajectories are adiabatic, and under these conditions the two fitted WAXS components cannot represent equilibrium HDL and LDL persisting along a common thermodynamic path. We show instead that the spectra are consistent with a responsive liquid fraction evolving during decompression together with a structurally lagged, HDA-like fraction produced by heterogeneous heating. This framework also rationalizes the fluence dependence and clarifies the distinct information contained in the SAXS response. The analysis identifies which observables can provide decisive evidence for a first-order liquid–liquid transition and constrain the location of its critical point.

papers.title: Molecular Design and Interface Engineering of Self-Assembled Monolayers for Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells: A Data-Driven Review of Efficiency, Stability and Scalability
papers.abstract: Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) have become indispensable hole-transport layers in inverted perovskite solar cells which enables power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) above 27% in single-junction devices and above 32% in tandems where the tandem devices benefit disproportionately from SAM engineering with certified efficiencies exceeding 31%. In the review eight hypotheses have been proposed including the prediction that bisphosphonic acid SAMs will outperform monophosphonic acid SAMs in thermal stability, glycol ether side chains will improve both PCE and stability and machine learning can identify new SAMs with >27% PCE and >90% retention at 1000 h , the studied researches shows that carbazole-based SAMs with phosphonic acid anchoring groups dominate the field with Me-4PACz and MeO-2PACz . Co-SAM strategies that have hydrogen-bonding additives consistently improve PCE by (1–3)% absolute over single-component SAMs and that bisphosphonic acid anchoring groups are emerging as a way to improve thermal and damp heat stability. Operational stability under maximum power point tracking now exceeds 1000 h for optimized SAM systems though ISOS protocol adoption remains inconsistent.

papers.title: Eugenol Sustained Release from a Non-Innocent Zn-MOF for Antimicrobial Fruit Preservation
papers.abstract: Active packaging is an effective strategy to extend food shelf life and reduce waste. In this work, a Zn-based Metal-Organic Framework (ZnBDP) was loaded with the natural antimicrobial eugenol using a vapour-phase impregnation, achieving complete encapsulation within the MOF pores (21 wt%), enabling sustained release in water over 3.5 months. Considering the bioactivity of Zn2+ and eugenol, the combined bactericidal and fungicidal effect of eugenol@ZnBDP_V was enhanced. Eugenol@ZnBDP_V demonstrated a superior activity against the bacteria Escherichia coli compared to free eugenol or pristine ZnBDP. 3 Further, important antifungal activity was observed against 5 plant pathogenic fungi, matching or exceeding the performance of free eugenol. Its practical potential was confirmed in strawberry preservation tests under extreme storage conditions, where fruit quality was maintained for up to 7.2 days. These findings highlight bioactive Zn-MOFs as promising platforms for the controlled delivery of natural antimicrobial agents in fruit packaging.

papers.title: (N-Hydroxy)amide-Mediated Ligation of Peptides in Chemical Protein Synthesis
papers.abstract: Chemical protein synthesis enables the production of synthetic proteins with precisely controlled structures. Some chemoselective methods for ligation of peptides in water have been developed thus far, and a variety of target proteins were successfully prepared, in which some specific amino acids such as N-terminal Cys, Ser/Thr or surrogates containing different auxiliaries are usually required at the ligation sites. Therefore, it is highly desirable to develop a chemoselective peptide ligation that is not limited by the specific amino acids at the ligation sites for chemical protein synthesis. In this paper, we have developed an efficient chemoselective ligation between C-terminal peptidyl (N-methoxy)aminoacyl hydrazides and N-terminal aminoacyl (N-hydroxy)peptides in water. In this protocol, nitrite oxidation of our prepared C-terminal peptidyl (N-methoxy)aminoacyl hydrazides at pH 3.0 at-15 oC afforded the corresponding peptidyl (N-methoxy)aminoacyl azides, intermolecular N,O-exchange of the in-situ formed peptide (N-methoxy)aminoacyl azides with N-terminal aminoacyl (N-hydroxy)peptides at pH 8.0 at room temperature afforded O-acyl peptides, and intramolecular O,N-acyl transfer of the O-acyl peptides across a six-membered ring gave the corresponding ligated N-methoxy (N'-hydoxy)peptides. Reduction of the N-methoxy (N'-hydoxy)peptides with zinc in water (pH 3.0) at 37 oC produced the ligated long peptides with native amide bonds. This peptide ligation strategy was successfully used in the total synthesis of a long peptide and a protein with biological activities. Interestingly, introduction of the N-methoxy group in C-terminal peptidyl (N-methoxy)aminoacyl hydrazides inhibited epimerization of the (N-methoxy)amino acid residues during the ligation of peptides. The present peptide ligation shows some advantages including no requirement for specific amino acid residues at the ligation sites, rapid ligation (completion within 60 minutes) even at the sterically hindered junctions, almost no epimerization, high yields and avoiding use of thiophenols that are prone to oxidation and have a foul smell in the native chemical ligation. Therefore, this (N-hydroxy)amide-mediated ligation of peptides provides a novel, efficient and versatile strategy for chemical protein synthesis.

papers.title: Revealing the Deactivation Mechanism of Aconitase at the Atomistic Level by Multiscale Simulations
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial aconitase is a key enzyme of the citric acid cycle that converts citrate to isocitrate at its [4 Fe−4 S] cluster cofactor. It is widely conserved across vertebrates and also found in numerous other organisms. Oxidation of the [4 Fe−4 S] cluster by reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS) leads to the release of one Fe center, denoted as Fe α . The remaining [3 Fe−4 S] cluster is catalytically inactive, meaning aconitase oxidation leads to enzyme deactivation. Aconitase deactivation regulates the citric acid cycle and mitochondrial respiration, which leads to decreased ROS and RNS formation. Thus, aconitase serves as a redox sensor that prevents high ROS and RNS concentrations. The deactivation process is well characterized on the macroscopic scale, meaning that the deactivation kinetics and the thermodynamics of oxidation are known.

papers.title: Topologically-constrained toehold-mediated strand displacement
papers.abstract: Toehold-mediated strand displacement (TMSD) is regarded as the simplest mechanism through which synthetic nucleicacid nanosystems can be dynamically actuated and is central to applications in biosensing, molecular computing, data storage and retrieval, and synthetic biology. In these implementations, TMSD often occurs in topologically-confined configurations, with the toehold domain being linked to other elements that restrict its conformational freedom. However, the effect of topological confinement on the biophysics of TMSD remains largely unexplored. Here, we study TMSD in a simple, physiologically-encountered configuration in which the toehold domain is located in a DNA ‘bubble’, a region where the two strands of an otherwise continuous DNA duplex are dehybridised. We show that this topological confinement reduces the rate of TMSD by ∼1–3 orders of magnitude as a result of alterations to the TMSD free-energy landscape. We further demonstrate that hybridisation of a short DNA strand to the target complex–away from the toehold domain–speeds up TMSD, hence providing a route for allosteric modulation of the reaction rate. Our results highlight the substantial effect of topological confinement on TMSD. These effects must be considered in the optimal design of dynamic nanostructures and molecular reaction networks while offering convenient strategies for the fine-tuning and modulation of reaction rates.

papers.title: Tweaking the Water Rigidity at Noble Metal Interfaces for Enhanced Alkaline Hydrogen Production via myo-Inositol Coating - A Bioinspired Approach
papers.abstract: Can an insulating sugar molecule help in water electrolysis? A unique cyclic polyhydroxy sugar myo-Inositol (MI) is used here to modify the oxide-free noble metal surfaces leading to enhanced electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) efficacy in alkaline medium. This non-permanent surface coating approach makes the HER activity of platinum in alkaline medium on par with that in acidic medium. This HER enhancement effect of MI is also demonstrated on another metal electrode, gold. A monolayer adsorption of MI on Au and Pt is verified with quartz crystal microbalance assisted studies. The presence of MI at the metal surface introduces weakly hydrogen bonded water molecules at the electrode-electrolyte interface by disrupting the hydrogen bonding network, as proven by the operando surface enhanced infrared spectroscopy studies. This approach highlights the unique role of MI in HER and effectively mitigates the kinetic limitations of alkaline water electrolysis.

papers.title: Collective vibrational strong coupling triggers dissociation reaction by overcoming energy threshold
papers.abstract: Ground-state reactions under vibrational strong coupling (VSC) have emerged as one of the central topics in polariton chemistry, yet how the energy redistribution under collective VSC translates into chemical reactivity remains an open question. Here we investigate vibrational predissociation in dilute ensembles of water trimers coupled to an optical cavity using full-dimensional cavity quasi-classical trajectory (cav-QCT) simulations with ab initio-quality potential-energy and dipole-moment surfaces. We demonstrate that collective VSC directly induces an otherwise energetically forbidden dissociation of the water trimer through cavity-mediated intermolecular VET. Remarkably, the enhancement of reactivity remains observable with increasing ensemble size despite reduced effective single-molecule light–matter coupling strength. Trajectory analyses identify collective energy transfer as the microscopic mechanism and reveal largely consistent quantum-state distributions of the reaction products. These findings establish a microscopic link between collective polaritonic energy transport and chemical reactivity, and suggest collective VSC as a route toward simultaneously manipulating reactivity and preserving product-state selectivity.

papers.title: A Congener-Substitution Strategy for Docking Heavy Metal Protein-Ligand Complexes with AutoDock Vina
papers.abstract: Molecular docking is widely used to predict ligand-protein interactions, but its application to transition metal complexes, particularly those containing second- and third-row elements, remains limited by the lack of explicit metal parameterization in commonly used programs such as AutoDock Vina. Here, we present a simple, practical strategy for docking heavy transition metal complexes without reparameterization: substituting the metal center with its first-row congener (e.g. Ru → Fe; Ir → Co) prior to docking. We applied this approach to a dataset of approximately 60 crystallographically characterized protein-ligand complexes containing Re, Ru, Os, Rh, Ir, Pt and Pd, and then focused on a streptavidin/avidin-biotin validation set of 18 crystallographically characterized protein-ligand complexes (4 Ru, 14 Ir) retrieved from the Protein Data Bank. The experimentally observed binding pose on the full set (rigid docking) was reproduced in 66% of cases, while for the streptavidin/avidin-biotin systems (flexible docking) the crystallography pose was fully or partially reproduced in 60% of cases (3/4 for the Ru systems and 8/14 for the Ir systems). Despite this outcome heterogeneity, the coordination geometry of the metal center and the broader protein-ligand interaction fingerprint were well preserved across the docked complexes, with a smaller perturbation observed for the Ru/Fe pair than for the Ir/Co pair, consistent with the higher pose-recovery rate obtained for the Ru systems. Overall, these results indicate that congener substitution offers a rapid, accessible route to docking second- and third-row transition metal complexes with unmodified AutoDock Vina, particularly in rigid docking, while revealing possible metal- and system-dependent limitations that should be considered when extending the strategy to other systems.

papers.title: A Unified Theory for Generalized Step-Growth Polymerization: From Flory’s Equal‑Reactivity to Kinetic Symmetry‑Breaking
papers.abstract: For nearly nine decades, Flory’s equal-reactivity hypothesis has universally underpinned the statistics of step-growth polymerization. However, modern monomers featuring rigid fused-ring architectures or catalytic bond-forming mechanisms routinely violate this core assumption. Consequently, the resulting molecular-weight anomalies have long been erroneously misattributed to side reactions or impurities, obscuring the underlying kinetic reality. Here, we resolve this theoretical blind spot by generalizing the AA + BB polycondensation into a strict analytical framework encompassing a kinetic enhancement parameter (𝛼). By exactly solving the infinitely coupled kinetic network, we derive closed-form expressions for the entire parameter space of stoichiometry (𝑟) and kinetics (𝛼), unveiling three macroscopic laws. First, a Terminal Dichotomy: on the A-deficient side (𝑟 < 1), the reaction undergoes "kinetic freezing," permanently archiving the kinetic 𝛼 -fingerprint within the end-cap inventory; conversely, on the A-excess side (𝑟 > 1 ), the system exhibits "𝛼 -amnesia," where terminal states are dictated solely by stoichiometry. Second, at the equimolar critical point (𝑟 = 1), the dispersity exhibits a profound singularity with non-commuting limits. Third, a Moving-Target Mechanism: while chain length grows monotonically with the feed ratio at fixed conversion, the optimal stoichiometry at a fixed reaction time migrates dynamically with 𝛼, allowing fast-asymmetric systems to achieve molecular weights nearly an order of magnitude higher than classical equimolar yields. Ultimately, this framework identifies a falsifiable end-group signature to reverse-engineer 𝛼 , transforming long-standing polycondensation anomalies into predictable, mathematically rigorously controllable levers for macromolecular design.

papers.title: Bridging the Training–Application Gap in Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian Learning through Dual-Space Supervision
papers.abstract: Predicting the Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian in density functional theory (DFT) via machine learning offers a promising pathway toward efficient electronic structure modeling. Existing models are typically trained by directly minimizing element-wise Hamiltonian matrix errors, yet a significant trainingapplication gap has been observed between Hamiltonian-space loss and errors in derived electronic properties, limiting their utility in practical applications. Noting that these properties are functions on the state space obtained by solving the Hamiltonian eigenvalue problem, this gap can be traced to a misalignment of the error metrics on the Hamiltonian space and its induced state space. The operator-tostate mapping is highly anisotropic, such that Hamiltonian errors of comparable numerical magnitude can induce markedly different downstream property errors. Motivated by the Hamiltonian–state variational duality rooted in Lieb’s convex formulation of DFT, we introduce Dual-Space Loss (DSLoss) to bridge this training–application gap. By leveraging error metrics in both spaces, DSLoss allows Hamiltonian optimization to account for errors in both the predicted operator and its induced state. Across molecular benchmarks, DSLoss consistently improves a broad range of derived properties over conventional element-wise supervision. On the challenging ∇2DFT benchmark, electron density and total energy errors are reduced by factors of 40 and 500, respectively, relative to the strongest competing method. The resulting model also extrapolates robustly to molecules containing up to twice as many heavy atoms as those encountered during training, achieving more than an order-of-magnitude lower errors for multiple properties and substantially outperforming direct density prediction models and endto-end property predictors. Moreover, the model enables stable molecular dynamics simulations with accurate energetics, forces, and vibrational dynamics. These results show that DSLoss addresses an unrecognized bottleneck limiting operator-prediction models across diverse downstream tasks, thereby advancing scalable and reliable electronic structure modeling.

papers.title: Influence of exchange–correlation functional on machine-learnt interatomic potentials accuracy: a systematic study in borosilicate glasses
papers.abstract: Machine-learnt interatomic potential (MLIP) has emerged as a strategy to accelerate molecular simulations, offering the promise of quantum chemical accuracy at a cost close to that of classical force fields. They are commonly trained on reference data obtained at the DFT level, which is itself a sufficiently affordable method to generate thousands of configurations and associated energies and atomic forces. However, this approach suffers from an elephant in the room, which is rarely addressed: the choice of exchange–correlation functional. Although it is understood to have a crucial impact on the accuracy of the description of interactions and therefore on the results of the molecular simulations, it has not been systematically evaluated in the past. To go beyond simple benchmarks on selected configurations, we set out to understand the influence of exchange–correlation (XC) functional on the training of MLIPs, and more importantly on the physical properties of the resulting condensed matter systems. As a complex chemical system to test this, we selected borosilicate glasses of a wide variety of compositions. We produced reference data sets of borosilicate glasses with nine different chemical compositions, with five different XC functionals at the GGA, meta-GGA and hybrid levels. We then trained MLIPs for all of them, produced glasses by melt-quenching, and compared their physical and structural properties with available experimental data. We show that there are significant differences between the different functionals. While the influence on bulk properties such as glass densities is minor, fine structural properties are more sensitive to the choice of functional, in particular when it comes to the coordination of boron atoms. Our results show how MLIPs can help us better understand the strengths and weaknesses of DFT functionals, where investigation through direct ab initio molecular dynamics was too expensive in the past. It also highlights that MLIPs depend on the ground truth on which they are trained, a fact often overlooked in practice, and this influence may be drastic on specific physical properties.

papers.title: CRISPR-Enabled Transition to Adsorption-Coupled Redox Transport: Toward the Use of Conventional Voltammetry in Electrochemical Biosensors
papers.abstract: Electrochemical aptamer-based (E-AB) biosensors and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) systems have independently advanced molecular diagnostics; however, their integration is less explored. Here, we present a CRISPR-enabled electrochemical sensing platform that directly links CRISPR Cas12a-mediated cleavage of non-specific aptamers to a change of charge transfer at the electrode interface. Methylene blue (MB)-labeled aptamers are immobilized on a gold electrode, forming an electrochemically surface-confined system. Upon target-activated CRISPR cleavage, MB-labeled aptamers are released into the medium, transforming the system into a diffusion-controlled regime. This transition is directly captured through real-time electrochemical monitoring, where alternating current voltammetry reveals a progressive decrease in surface-bound redox reporters, while cyclic voltammetry simultaneously shows an increase in faradaic current due to the accumulation of freely diffusing MB species. Scan rate-dependent analysis confirms a shift from non-ideal surface-limited behavior to diffusion-controlled kinetics, consistent with the Randles–Ševčík relationship. We propose an adsorption-coupled transport model, which supports this interpretation by showing that the plausible post-cleavage voltammetric response is best described by near-surface confinement of released MB-tagged fragments rather than by pure bulk diffusion alone. Dose-response analysis shows that cyclic voltammetry achieves a improved limit of detection (LOD) of approximately , outperforming square wave voltammetry ( across a broader – range), underscoring CV as the more sensitive readout for quantitative biosensing with this platform. By leveraging the exceptional molecular specificity of CRISPR alongside the high sensitivity of E-AB sensors, this work establishes a new sensing paradigm in which conventional steady-state voltammetry can be used for analytical detection.

papers.title: Universal Model for Atoms (UMA) in Computational Asymmetric Catalysis: Comparing Enantioselectivity Predictions
papers.abstract: Universal model for atoms (UMA) was evaluated for predicting enantioselectivity through direct modeling of diastereomeric transition states via conformational ensemble averaging. Across two organocatalytic and two metal-catalyzed transformations, UMA produced experimental selectivity trend with accuracy within 1-2 kcal/mol identifying key structural features governing stereoinduction. Findings discussed here highlight the promise of UMA foundation models as efficient alternatives for expensive quantum chemical methods in mechanistic modeling while also revealing current scope and limitations.

papers.title: Multivalent SO4-3-Galactose Glycopolymers Define a Structural Threshold for CD206 Endocytic Inhibition
papers.abstract: The Mannose Receptor (CD206) is a critical endocytic receptor involved in immune regulation and various pathologies, yet it remains largely unexplored as a therapeutic target due to the lack of specific modulators. We recently reported that multivalent SO 4 -3-Galactose (SO 4 -3-Gal) glycopolymers inhibit CD206 by blocking its recycling to the cell surface, but the role of ligand valency in this process was undefined. Here, using a monovalent SO4-3-Gal ligand together with a library of SO 4 -3-Gal glycopolymers spanning valencies from 6.5 to 211 – the latter synthesised via a new, scalable, metal-free aqueous RAFT route amenable to multigram production – we establish for the first time a quantitative, biphasic relationship between valency and CD206 inhibitory potency, with a steep increase up to a valency of ~28 SO 4 -3-Gal units followed by a shallower plateau, which may suggest a threshold-dependent, ligandinduced receptor clustering mechanism. Critically, these glycopolymers are non-cytotoxic, leave LPS-induced macrophage cytokine production (IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α) unaltered, and – as shown by bulk RNA sequencing of human macrophages – induce no detectable changes to the macrophage transcriptome, at baseline or upon LPS stimulation, demonstrating that CD206 blockade occurs without detectable perturbation of macrophage inflammatory responses or transcriptional profiles under the conditions tested.

papers.title: Battery models as controlled laboratory methods: simulated results across the operating envelope, code verification and a physics-informed surrogate
papers.abstract: Laboratories increasingly base formulation, protocol and safety decisions on battery models, yet models rarely receive the controls that laboratory methods do: versions, validation on unseen data, reproducible records and verification of the numerical solution. We report a suite of 9 registered models that run inside a laboratory platform (a cell simulator with equivalent-circuit, single-particle, electrolyte-corrected and transient-electrolyte rungs, electrode balancing, pulse and impedance predictors, a plating-limited charging optimiser, a receding-horizon charge controller, an unscented Kalman filter with a stability review, and a mechanistic ageing model), together with the results they produce for a published cell parameterisation and the evidence for trusting those results. Half-way through a 1C discharge, solid diffusion, electrolyte transport and contact resistance cost 85, 49 and 50 mV; the electrolyte-corrected and transient-electrolyte rungs agree within 25 mV at 1C but diverge by 1,051 mV at 3C, where the latter depletes its electrolyte. A plating-limited current staircase reaches 80% state of charge in 22.9 min at 25 ◦C and 83 min at 0 ◦C, and the closed-loop controller needs 21.5 min without a constraint violation, against 28.0 min for the fastest constant current that respects the constraints. Verification against analytic solutions finds the particle solver second-order accurate in its concentration profile but first-order in the surface value that sets the voltage, a reported state of charge that exceeds the charge balance by up to 19.8 points because shells are averaged without volume weights, and a reversed sign in a kinetic term that is numerically negligible. Varying 9 shipped parameters together by a factor of 1.5 gives a 90% voltage band of ±50 mV at 1C, dominated by the positive particle radius and larger than both the discretisation error and the difference between the two electrolyte rungs; at 3C the choice of electrolyte closure outweighs every other source. That budget assumes its parameters reach the decisions a laboratory makes, and they do not: moving the solid diffusivity over two decades changes the delivered capacity at 3C by 34.8 points while leaving the plating limit, the staircase time, the controlled charge time and the least anode potential unchanged in every digit reported, because the charging model reads 2 cell parameters and the controller 2. Where the discharge rung does respond its capacity collapses onto the diffusion time R2/D to within 0.7 points, and because the particle equation is stepped explicitly, the regime of small particles and fast solid diffusion is the most expensive one to simulate. A grid convergence index shows the simulated voltage converging at first order, leaving the default particle grid 30.7 mV from the extrapolated voltage at 3C; polynomial chaos confirms the linear apportioning of variance, and Gaussian-process emulators predict the voltage to 0.8 mV from 100 runs, with no gain from choosing runs by predictive spread. Drawing the same design from a Sobol sequence rather than a Latin hypercube cuts the largest index error at 256 runs from 0.082 to 0.00022, and a reduced two-parameter problem mapped in full on 625 runs puts the sampled estimator within 0.004 of indices computed exactly. Gaussian splatting of simulated fields, implemented for this study, did not compress regular two-dimensional grids better than proper orthogonal decomposition but fitted scattered samples with an error of 9.97 mV against 14.55 mV for triangulation; in three dimensions, across rate and temperature, it beat both decomposition and interpolation. An adaptation of a recent densification strategy from rendering failed at the largest budget; splitting along the axis of largest field change and band-limiting the primitives to the sample spacing made it stable, with a median held-out error over 10 fits of 13.2 mV against 14.4 mV for residual-driven control. Extended to the vehicle, battery power determines only 5 of 6 longitudinal parameters: a physics-informed network fitted it from 8 starting points with the identifiable combinations within 1.9% of the truth, while the masses it returned ranged from 0.79 to 0.98 times the true value. Re-executing the 10 recorded runs from their stored inputs reproduced 9 bit for bit; the exception showed that a run’s code reference names a month, not a version. A physics-informed extreme learning machine, fitted for this study, solves the particle-diffusion problem to a surface-stoichiometry error of 1.2× 10−4 and passes an admission tolerance that the platform’s 14-shell solver fails; a gradient-trained network of the same form improves 21-fold on least squares with the same few fixed features but still fails that tolerance. Toward a digital twin, the suite’s estimator tolerates the drift of an ageing cell, but calibrating the particle diffusivity through the default grid misses it by −17.4%, against −0.5% through the verified surrogate. Governance made each finding checkable; verification made them visible.

papers.title: A Roadmap for Supercrystallography: From Single-Supercrystal Diffraction to the Atomic Structure of Colloidal Nanocrystals
papers.abstract: Colloidal nanocrystals are complex objects, comprising a solid inorganic core and a soft shell of organic ligands, both of which contribute to defining their properties. Obtaining an atomically precise description of both components remains an open challenge. Yet, these hybrid building blocks can self-assemble into supercrystals sufficiently large to be isolated and analyzed individually. It may therefore come as a surprise that single-supercrystal X-ray diffraction is not routinely used to investigate the structure of their constituent nanocrystals. Here, we propose a roadmap for establishing supercrystallography as the science of obtaining structural information about colloidal building blocks through diffraction experiments performed on their supercrystals. We review existing examples of single-supercrystal X-ray diffraction, examine the opportunities that may emerge from extending crystallographic methods to colloidal supercrystals, and discuss the main challenges that must be overcome to realize this vision. Drawing inspiration from the crystallography of nanoclusters and proteins, systems that share deep similarities with colloidal nanocrystals, we outline a possible path connecting state-of-the-art experiments to complete atomistic models through innovative data-analysis strategies. Finally, we consider how supercrystallography could complement existing characterization techniques, and develop into an accessible framework for investigating the structure of colloidal nanocrystals and their surface chemistry.

papers.title: Economics-inspired molecular reactivity descriptors from atom-resolved reactivity inequality
papers.abstract: Reactivity descriptors in conceptual density functional theory (DFT) usually belong to one of two broad families. Global descriptors give one value per molecule, which is easy to compare between molecules but says nothing about which parts of the molecule are more reactive. Local descriptors show how reactivity varies within a molecule and point to its most reactive atoms, but their dimension changes from one molecule to the next, which makes them hard to compare. Mapping global reactivity onto atoms is well established; the reverse, compressing a local reactivity map into a few informative numbers, is not. Economics has long faced the equivalent problem of summarising how wealth is shared across a population. Here we borrow its solution, the Gini coefficient, and apply it to the atom-condensed dual descriptor. The positive and negative parts of the dual descriptor give two Gini reactivity descriptors, Gp and Gn, that measure how unevenly the response to nucleophilic and to electrophilic attack is spread across a molecule. Tested on three controlled series of substituted carbonyls, conjugated ketones and conjugated amines, Gp and Gn behave as chemically sensible measures. They separate inductive from conjugative perturbations, respond differently to electronwithdrawing and electron-donating groups, and trace a shift from localised to delocalised response as conjugation grows. The two descriptors carry distinct mechanistic information and are promising compact features for data-driven chemistry. More broadly, this work shows that tools developed to measure inequality in societies can quantify how reactivity is shared within a molecule, and that crossing disciplinary boundaries can open new ways of reading electronic structure.

papers.title: Photoactivated Hydrocarbon Oxidation Coupled with Ozone Decomposition with MnO2 Catalyst
papers.abstract: Treatment of hydrocarbon emissions such as methane and formaldehyde require effective conversion alongside control of energy consumption and secondary pollutant formation. A continuous-flow methane and formaldehyde treatment system combining ultraviolet-C (UVC) irradiation, manganese dioxide (MnO2), and water addition was investigated in this study. Optical, thermal, and structural characterisation established the experimental platform, while irradiation on-off measurements, gas chromatography (GC), and infrared (IR) spectroscopy assessed reaction conversion, reactor response, and any residual ozone formation. Humid condition with MnO2 catalyst provides the highest methane conversion and the presence of the MnO2 suppressed ozone of the exit stream. Methane-free control experiments showed that oxygen concentration and MnO2 loading influenced the levels of ozone of the exit stream. Under humid conditions, 1.5 g of MnO2 achieved complete methane conversion across inlet concentrations of 200-10,000 ppm at an incident irradiance of 42 mW cm-2. Mixed feed experiments further demonstrated simultaneous conversion of methane, methanol, and formaldehyde with conversions at 100%, 87% and 86%, respectively under an incident irradiance of 85 mW cm-2. These results established the lab-scale potential of UV-MnO2 treatment for methane and volatile organic compounds.

papers.title: Defect-Rich Fe3+-Substituted RuO2: A Novel Rutile Phase Setting a New Benchmark in Alkaline Water Oxidation
papers.abstract: We report a new material exhibiting outstanding oxygen evolution reaction (OER) performance in alkaline media, delivering an ultralow overpotential of 86 mV at 100 mA cm -2 , sustained operation above 200 mA·cm -2 , and exceptional long-term stability over 1000 hours without noticeable degradation. A low-temperature (200 °C) single-source precursor (SSP) strategy enabled the synthesis of a previously unreported Fe 3+ -substituted rutile phase, Ru 0.63 Fe 0.37 O 2-x , characterized by atomic-scale cation mixing, abundant oxygen vacancies, and ultrasmall particle sizes (2–5 nm). Structural analysis confirms uniform Fe 3+ incorporation into the rutile lattice, yielding defect-rich, porous oxide framework that is inaccessible through conventional synthetic routes. The resulting ternary oxide is chemically robust, remaining insoluble in both alkaline solutions and aqua regia, and exhibits enhanced porosity with a high BET surface area of 153 m 2 ∙g -1 and an electrochemically active surface area of 205.75 cm 2 , more than three times that of pristine RuO 2 , indicating substantially improved active-site accessibility. These results demonstrate how precise lattice substitution, low-temperature SSP synthesis, and targeted surface modulation synergistically optimize Ru-based OER catalysts, establishing a clear link between controlled structural design and high-rate electrochemical performance.

papers.title: Size-Dependent Conductivity of MOF Nanoparticles with Variable-Pressure Impedance Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Variable-pressure conductivity has attracted growing interest in recent years due to the importance of activation volumes for ion transport in energy storage systems like solid state batteries, solid oxide fuel cells and solid oxide electrolyzers. Most variable-pressure conductivity studies have overlooked the effect of particle size and size distributions even though they impact key determinants of charge transport: particle packing, interatomic distances, and lattice strain. Here, we utilize chromium(1,2,3-triazolate)2 nanoparticles as a model system to elucidate particle size effects on variable pressure conductivity. These materials lack deliberate surface capping ligands that would otherwise complicate analysis. Using impedance spectroscopy, we find significant size dependence in the variable pressure conductivity. A combination of strain analysis, density functional theory calculations, and particle packing simulations suggests the major cause of the size dependence is greater surface reactivity in smaller particles, which leads to a greater degree of particle fusion at lower pressures. These results hold practical importance for pressedpellet conductivity measurements of all powder materials in general.

papers.title: Micro-computed-tomography-guided multiphysics simulation: insights into enclosed microelectrochemical flow cells
papers.abstract: Quantitative interpretation of hydrodynamic electrochemical measurements commonly relies on analytical models that assume idealized device geometries. However, verifying the internal geometry of fully enclosed, single-step-3D-printed electrochemical flow cells is challenging because the devices cannot be taken apart without being destroyed. Herein, X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) is used to non-destructively characterize 3D channel architectures with sub-10 µm voxel resolution. The 3D-printed channels deviate substantially from the as-designed rectangular geometry, showing corrugated sloping sidewalls and a sagging, undulating ceiling. Yet, employing true (micro-CT-generated) geometries in three-dimensional multiphysics models of fluid flow and mass transport yielded currents in agreement with the channel flow electrode limiting current equation (based on flux equations formalized by Levich) for rectangular channels! This agreement and analysis of transport demonstrate that sidewall corrugation/slope and ceiling sag/undulation do not account for experimental deviations from ideal hydrodynamic behavior. Yet both the simulated and theory results deviate by 30-40% from experimental voltammetry, indicating a discrepancy that geometric non-idealities do not explain. Together, this suggests the disagreement between theory and experiment arises from incomplete consumption of the redox probe at the electrode surface, a condition consistent with the 3D-printed composite electrodes being partially blocked. More broadly, the work establishes the combination of micro-CT, multiphysics simulation, and experiment as a general, non-destructive framework for characterizing complex hydrodynamic electrochemical systems.

papers.title: Conductive Polymer Binder for Long-Term Stability of GaN Anode at Elevated Temperatures
papers.abstract: Temperature is a major factor influencing battery cycle life, with elevated temperatures generally accelerating capacity degradation. Here, we employed poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS), a conductive polymer, as a binder to stabilize GaN anodes for long-term cycling at 55°C. The GaN anode with the PEDOT:PSS binder (GaN/PE) exhibits over a 40× increase in its electrical conductivity compared to the GaN anode with a conventional polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder (GaN/PVDF). The GaN/PE anode achieves a specific capacity of up to 855.3 mAh/g at 0.1 A/g, approaching the theoretical capacity of GaN (960 mAh/g) and approximately tripling the maximum capacity of the GaN/PVDF anode under the same operating conditions. In addition, the GaN/PE anode demonstrates long-term stability, retaining about 600 mAh/g after 500 cycles at 55 °C, while the GaN/PVDF anode achieves only half of that value after 500 cycles. Notably, previous reports on Si-based anodes operated within 45-70°C show a dramatic decrease in their capacity, remaining about 600 mAh/g after only 100 cycles. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations explain the long-term stability of the GaN/PE anodes through improved thermomechanical stability of PEDOT:PSS, with a thermal expansion coefficient less than half that of PVDF, suggesting the reduction of thermal expansion mismatch within the GaN/PE anode during high-temperature operation. Operando X-ray diffraction exhibits crystalline stability in the GaN/PE anode, with less crystalline degradation than the GaN/PVDF anode. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) further demonstrates the stability of the GaN/PE anode, showing a 10-ohm decrease in charge-transfer resistance (Rct) after 500 cycles, whereas the GaN/PVDF anode shows an over 10× increase in Rct. . Together, our study proposes a binder technology approach that stabilizes GaN anodes by mitigating thermal degradation, enabling long-term cycling stability in LIBs for high-temperature applications.

papers.title: Aminomutase-Inspired Methylene Insertion for α-to-β Homologative Transposition of Amino Acids
papers.abstract: A versatile method for the preparation of synthetically valuable β2-homologated amino acid esters from simple α-amino acid esters is described. Inspired by pyridoxal 5′-phosphate-dependent aminomutase enzymes, the described strategy exploits a straightforward protocol for substrate activation, alkylation, and migration leveraging a bio-inspired 3-exo-trig radical cascade. This approach enables a novel homologative strategy towards β-amino acids via methylene insertion into the Cα–N bond of α-amino acids. A broad substrate scope is demonstrated, and key activator electronic factors are elucidated through experimental and computational mechanistic studies. By engaging α-amino acids directly, the method provides unique access to β2-homologated amino acids.

papers.title: Proton Solvation Thermochemistry: A Temperature-Resolved Calibration from Ammonium Acids
papers.abstract: Chemical reactions involving protonation are ubiquitous in nature, yet their accurate description using static quantum-chemical methods remains challenging. Here, we derive a temperature-resolved aqueous free energy of H+ (G◦,aq H+ ) by combining experimental pKa data for 12 ammonium acids over 293–333 K with a high-level composite quantum-chemical protocol based on LNO-CCSD(T)/CBS energies, CPCM solvation, and conformational thermochemistry. Thermodynamic analysis gives G◦,aq H+ = −270.0 kcal/mol at 298 K, within 0.3 kcal/mol of the canonical literature value (Tissandier et al., 1998). The fitted parameters are robust under cross-validation, and validation on an independent set of 18 acids yields a mean absolute error of 0.70 pKa units.

papers.title: ARMS: an Automated Robotized human-Mimicking Solid sampling system
papers.abstract: Chemists sample solid materials such as powders, highly viscous fluids, and semi-solids with a spatula in labs every day. Yet, this action remains the key bottleneck in the development of fully automated chemistry laboratories. While a handful of specialist tools have been developed to autonomously manipulate solids, these approaches target a limited range of material properties. In this work, we approach the problem from the other perspective by studying the capabilities of chemists to gain insights into the design of a generalist solid sampling approach with the aim of spanning the entire range of possible material properties. We observed and demonstrated that the key capabilities are characterizing, identifying the material descriptors that map material properties to actions; scooping, adding material to the spatula; depositing, removing material from the spatula; weighing, measuring the mass transferred; and auxiliary actions such as cleaning the spatula. We demonstrate how each of these actions can be combined in a bimanual robot platform and sample seven of nine materials chosen to span the range of possible materials. In order to achieve this performance, we leverage low-data learning from demonstration techniques such that demonstration collection takes less than an hour and training lasts less than a minute, exploit geometric structure, and transfer to novel materials within a descriptor class. Notably, we were able to move not only simpler granular free-flowing materials such as NaCl but also sticky materials such as honey, reaching standard deviations of 1.5–3.3 mg and 2.8–10.1 mg with scoop depth predicting delivered mass at 0.70 < R2 < 0.93 and 0.28 < R2 < 0.66, respectively.

papers.title: Judgment by agents, numbers by code: auditable automated speciation analysis towards a chemistry world model
papers.abstract: Chemical speciation governs the reactivity, solubility, and toxicity of a solution, yet assembling speciation calculations from evaluated thermodynamic data remains a manual expert task whose reasoning is discarded once the figure is drawn. To mirror real-world research, automation belongs within a chemistry world model (CWM) where language agents curate and analyze data. As a first module, our agentic framework converts plain-language questions into deterministic equilibrium calculations grounded in NIST Standard Reference Database 46 (SRD-46). Agents resolve intent, curate records, adjudicate duplicates, design calculations, and estimate values beyond database coverage through induction-deduction-validation loops, while deterministic code validates every agentic commitment before it reaches the solver and compacts diagram topology into text readable without a vision stage. Across four case studies of escalating difficulty, quoted constants, patched records, and boundary coordinates reproduced their sources essentially exactly, whereas the same model without the framework missed phases or failed to build a solver. Residual errors surfaced only as auditable narration flaws, from misread topology to a sign-flipped hydrogen-evolution argument. The framework serves as a human-in-the-loop instrument delivering consensus-grade starting points, turning evaluated databases into active discovery instruments, mapping where language-model chemical reasoning still fails, and providing a general agentic template for finetuning.

papers.title: Examining roles of varying synthesis and assembly conditions on the incorporation of complex multi-lipid extracts into membrane scaffold protein nanodiscs
papers.abstract: Nanodiscs are tunable and widely used membrane mimetics that can allow for the in vitro study of membrane proteins in a native-like lipid bilayer environment. The lipids incorporated into nanodiscs can be modulated to represent specific biophysical environments, but many nanodisc applications rely on simplified lipid compositions that inadequately represent native membrane complexity. Natural lipid extracts offer more physiological relevance; however, recent work has shown that (1) lipid composition of a nanodisc does not stoichiometrically reflect the initial mixture and that (2) assembly conditions such as temperature and belt size may influence lipid incorporation. Here, we add to this body of work by implementing an untargeted LC-MS/MS lipidomics workflow to profile the incorporation of multiple, combined natural lipid extracts into membrane scaffold protein nanodiscs, examining not only assembly temperature and belt size, but also the effects of detergent and synthetic lipid additives on lipid incorporation. Species level lipidomic analysis, including trends in acyl chain length and degree of unsaturation were evaluated. We observe that assembly temperatures have minimal impact on lipid incorporation, whereas belt size effects vary across extracts, as smaller scaffolds likely enrich lipids that promote a more tightly packed membrane. Furthermore, we found that lipid solubilization and incorporation into nanodiscs is broadly preserved regardless of detergent identity. Conversely, synthetic lipid additives influence incorporated lipid class composition more strongly than detergent, temperature, or MSP belt size, with unsaturated additives favoring glycerolipid enrichment. Taken together, this data demonstrates the interplay of nanodisc assembly conditions in shaping the incorporated lipid environment.

papers.title: Beyond the Kd Gate: Establishing Signal Causality in Electrochemical Aptasensors
papers.abstract: Electrochemical aptasensors combine aptamer-based molecular recognition with electrochemical transduction, but a signal correlated with nominal target concentration alone does not establish aptamer–target binding. Target addition or matrix exposure may alter solution composition, reporter or mediator chemistry, nucleic acid behavior, surface organization, electron-transfer kinetics, interfacial integrity, or surface fouling without aptamer–target complex formation. The Kd gate addresses this upstream problem by requiring auditable, construct-matched verification of aptamertarget binding in homogeneous, non-denaturing solution under sensing-relevant conditions. Passing the gate, however, does not show that an immobilized construct retains recognition or that recognition causes the electrochemical response. We propose a sequential framework in which the Kd gate qualifies the recognition reagent, controlled surface measurements establish retained recognition, transduction measurements determine whether retained recognition generates a measurable response, and signalcausality controls establish whether that response depends on recognition. It distinguishes solutionphase Kd,sol, surface-associated apparent Kd,app, and device-response midpoint C50. It links controls to alternative response pathways and separates claim classes: target-correlated, recognition-linked, mechanistic or thermodynamic, and intended-use. Aminoglycoside and doxorubicin lineages illustrate why sequence conversion, truncation, reporter conjugation, and immobilization require reassessment of recognition and signal attribution. The framework should guide electrochemical aptasensor development with independently supported recognition and intended-use performance claims.

papers.title: Integrative metabolomics, molecular networking and in silico analysis reveal bioactive antiplasmodial fractions from Aloe rigens
papers.abstract: Aloe rigens Reynolds & Bally (Asphodelaceae) is widely used in traditional medicine against malaria and demonstrated potent biological activity in our previous study. Despite its traditional use, its specific chemical and biological properties have not yet been comprehensively investigated.
