This study aimed to identify the phytochemical constituents responsible for the antiplasmodial activity of this plant through an integrated bioguided fractionation, untargeted metabolomics, and computational approach. Bioguided fractionation of Aloe rigens leaf extracts was conducted against Plasmodium falciparum (FcB-1 strain) using the SYBR Green fluorescence assay. The bioactive dichloromethane (RD) and ethyl acetate (RE) sub-extracts were profiled by LC-HRMS/MS and GC-MS. Untargeted metabolomic analysis, combining molecular networking (GNPS) with multivariate statistical analyses (PCA and hierarchical cluster analysis, HCA), was applied to characterize the fractions and identify discriminant features associated with antiplasmodial activity. Cytotoxicity was evaluated on AB943 human fibroblast cells using a resazurin-based assay. Additionally, an in silico molecular docking study was performed to assess the binding affinity of the highlighted compounds within the receptor pocket of Plasmodium falciparum Apical Membrane Antigen 1 (PfAMA1) in complex with the invasion-inhibitory peptide R1 (PDB ID: 3SRJ). 2 Bioguided fractionation of the RE sub-extract yielded fraction F2 as the most potent antiplasmodial fraction, with an IC50 of 1.38 ± 0.48 µg/mL and a selectivity index greater than 36.2. Metabolomic profiling and multivariate statistical analyses discriminated F2 from less active fractions and highlighted its distinctive chemical signature. Three major compounds preidentified in F2 namely genistein-like (C8), 7-hydroxy-3,5 dimethylisochromen-1-one-like (C3), and eupatorin-like (C5), exhibited promising in silico binding affinities within the PfAMA1 receptor pocket, with favorable interaction profiles compared to the reference inhibitory peptide R1. This study demonstrates that integrating bioguided fractionation, untargeted metabolomics, and computational approaches is a robust strategy for accelerated identification of bioactive scaffolds from medicinal plants. The findings validate the ethnopharmacological use of Aloe rigens against malaria and highlight genistein-like, 7-hydroxy-3,5-dimethylisochromen-1-onelike, and eupatorin derivatives as promising candidates for further antimalarial drug development.

papers.title: Uncovering Chemical Degradation Pathways in Amide-Functional Sulfur Polymers for Room-Temperature Na-S Batteries
papers.abstract: Sulfur-containing polymers are widely explored as cathode active materials for room-temperature sodium sulfur batteries because covalent sulfur confinement is generally considered to suppress polysulfide dissolution. However, their chemical stability under cycling remains insufficiently understood. Inverse vulcanization provides an attractive route to sulfur-rich cathode active materials by directly coupling elemental sulfur with unsaturated organic comonomers, thereby combining high sulfur content with tunable chemical functionality. In this study, an amide-rich sulfur material ( P1 ) was synthesized by the inverse vulcanization of elemental sulfur with N,N′ -ethylenebisacrylamide (EBA) and systematically evaluated as the positive electrode in sodium metal cells using an ether-based electrolyte (1 M NaCF 3 SO 3 in TEGDME) to elucidate its degradation pathways. The bifunctional acrylamide co-monomer provides two reactive C=C sites for sulfur incorporation while retaining polar amide environments within the resulting sulfur-rich network. Although P1 initially exhibits sulfur redox activity (initial discharge capacity is approximately 90 mAh g -1 at 500 mAh g -1 ), the electrochemical performance rapidly declines, resulting in rapid capacity decay and low coulombic efficiency. Post-mortem XPS analysis reveals pronounced changes in the S-S and C-S bonding environments, formation of oxidized sulfur species, and substantial irreversible reconstruction of both the carbon-sulfur framework and nitrogen coordination environments. We propose that this degradation is associated with chemical interactions between nucleophilic polysulfide intermediates and reactive amide-containing environments, promoting irreversible sulfur-carbon/nitrogen bond rearrangements. The observed XPS evolution is consistent with the formation of thioamide-like and C-S/N-S environments, although these assignments are treated as part of a proposed degradation pathway rather than a uniquely established reaction mechanism. While these reactions chemically immobilize sulfur, they render it electrochemically inactive. Thus, polysulfide interactions that are initially intended to provide chemical confinement may evolve into irreversible chemical trapping during cycling. These findings identify a critical chemical instability pathway in functional inverse-vulcanized sulfurrich materials in Na-S systems and highlight the need to control balance polysulfide affinity with the chemical stability of co-monomer-derived functionalities for stable sulfur-polymer cathodes.

papers.title: Rare Earth Elements Recovery with Membranes, Additive Manufacturing, and AI/ML Workflows
papers.abstract: Rare earth element (REE) extraction and separation from secondary sources are entering a critical stage as the demand for REE-enabled materials accelerates while conventional supply chains face technical, economic, and environmental pressure. Although significant progress has been made in REE separations from primary resources, inherent variability of secondary sources introduces substantial chemical and processing challenges, rendering REEs an ever-moving target for extraction and production. In this review, we discuss conventional and novel methods in separations, additive manufacturing–enabled separations, role of AI in separations, data driven approaches, AI/ML implementation, self-driving labs, and AI/ML workflows.

papers.title: The Transition Seam Ansatz of Kinetic Theory
papers.abstract: The Eyring formulation of transition-state theory fixes a single activated-complex population by equilibrium with the reactant state, so that a population in equilibrium with one state has no net flux from that state. This paper keeps the three assumptions of that theory and takes the barrier as the seam at which the electronic-structure manifolds of reactant and product have equal energetic chemical potential. One transition state then has two populations, one on each manifold, with separate amounts and configurational chemical potentials and with a shared energetic chemical potential and configurational excess. The flux on each manifold is a shared attempt frequency times its seam population, and De Donder referencing of the two fluxes is the isothermal rate law. Each seam population is in equilibrium with its own state, so transitivity of equilibrium places no condition on the two states. Recrossing, tunnelling, and non-adiabatic passage are contained in the attempt frequency rather than distributed across the rate expression. The transition-state population is an explicit quantity of the law. An ideal catalyst binds its intermediates neither so weakly that there is nothing to form a transition state from, nor so strongly that there is nowhere to form it. Mass action, Langmuir, and Butler–Volmer are decisions on the two excesses, the classical two-rate-constant law collects the energetic pieces into forward and reverse rate constants that share the attempt frequency, and a directional law is the limit in which the running amount of one intermediate is negligible against its equilibrium amount. The reversibility of a step is the ratio of the two seam populations, which occupy the same nuclear configuration and differ in electronic structure.

papers.title: Hybrid Grain-Core/Grain Boundary Proton Conductivity in Nanocrystalline La2Ce2O7 Thin Films at 298 - 453K
papers.abstract: La3+ doping of ceria promotes hydration at the site of oxygen vacancy defects and, consequently, also protonic conductivity, thereby positioning fluorite-structured La2Ce2O7 (LCO50) as a promising low temperature (LT, i.e., < 473 K) solid state proton-conducting electrolyte . With mean grain size for polycrystalline LCO50 thin films of ~5 nm by sputter-deposition at 293 K, room temperature total conductivity is measured by impedance spectroscopy to be ~7.5×10-9 S/cm. This is approximately two orders of magnitude higher than that previously measured for highly textured, LCO50 thin films, sputter-deposited at 733 K. Here, experimental evidence is provided that the dominant LT conduction mechanism in nanocrystalline LCO50 thin films is protonic, given the measured total activation energy of 0.396±0.007eV between 373K and 453 K. At these temperatures, the conductivity of the nanocrystalline LCO50 films is approximately independent of the atmospheric relative humidity while change is minimal even under high vacuum. We interpret these properties in terms of a hybrid grain-core/grain-boundary protonic conduction mechanism, in which the grain core acts as a proton reservoir and the grain boundary, as a rapid conduction path. Such a micro-fabrication compatible, solid state protonic conductor offers versatile applications including fuel cells, sensors and battery-run devices.

papers.title: Quantum Subspace Expansion for Molecular Excited States: Representability, Stability, and Practical Considerations
papers.abstract: Accurate treatment of excited states remains challenging for classical electronic-structure methods, motivating quantum algorithms that may provide more favorable resource scaling. We systematically assess the practical performance of Quantum Subspace Expansion (QSE) for low-lying electronic states across 28 organic molecules from the Thiel benchmark set. Statevector simulations reveal that QSE representability depends strongly on the target state, active space, and molecular electronic structure, with multiconfigurational character emerging as an important factor. In several cases, the one-body QSE subspace cannot adequately represent the target states, while explicit double-excitation operators improve representability at the cost of a larger operator space. Analysis of the QSE overlap matrix shows that although eigenmodes with small eigenvalues drive numerical instability, they cannot be discarded indiscriminately without compromising spectral accuracy. Under finite-shot sampling, energy errors exhibit an empirical scaling of approximately n2 orb/ √ Nshots, which, combined with the growth in measurement groups, yields a total measurement cost of approximately O(n11 orb) for constant accuracy under our direct-estimation protocol. These results expose a central tension between representability, numerical stability, and measurement cost. Encouragingly, we find that the projected matrices exhibit recurring structural patterns, while the finite-shot perturbations in the Hamiltonian and overlap matrices show nontrivial covariance, suggesting opportunities for more efficient structure-aware measurement and reconstruction strategies. Overall, our results provide an assessment of QSE across chemically-relevant organic molecules, identifying present limitations while highlighting potential routes toward more practical future implementations.

papers.title: A unique technology for creating thin gold layers inside medieval glass tesserae.
papers.abstract: A unique technology, based on a chemical process that creates a thin layer of gold inside medieval glass tesserae, has been identified analysing physicochemical test results, within a project conducted by the Anna Langer Memorial Foundation. The samples studied are part of a collection of glass tesserae, discovered in the remains of the palatium of Duke Mieszko I in Poznań, by archaeologists from Adam Mickiewicz University, working under the direction of Prof. Hanna M. Kóčka

papers.title: From sequences and structures to fitness, folding and function: challenges in the age of AI
papers.abstract: Deep-learning models have transformed our ability to predict the phenotypic effects of sequence perturbations. Protein language models (pLMs) score the evolutionary propensity of any amino-acid substitution, emerging as fast and accurate predictors of fitness changes. Inverse-folding (IF) models add structural information and are powerful alternatives for estimating folding-stability changes. But these likelihoods are imperfect and sometimes biased predictors of the biological quantities they are used to measure. Scaling pLMs has shown that bigger models do not always outperform smaller ones. IF models sometimes read sequence conservation as a stability constraint, which leads to biases when this signal is used to isolate functional contributions beyond folding. We review here the strategies emerging to mitigate, and where possible overcome, these limitations. Highlights:- Scaling protein language models does not close the likelihood–fitness gap - Inverse-folding models can read functional conservation as lost stability - Disentangling function from stability inherits both biases - Emerging strategies are attempting to address these issues

papers.title: Electronic Structure of Cobalamins Defined by High Energy Resolution Fluorescence Detected X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy: Insights into Photochemical Axial Bond Cleavage in the CarH Photoreceptor
papers.abstract: Nature utilizes cobalamin photochemistry within photoreceptor proteins to regulate vital biological functions. Rationalization of structure-function relationships that selectively activate/deactivate cobalamin photochemistry is essential for understanding how organisms leverage this photosensitivity. In this work, we systematically investigated the electronic structure and photochemistry of four cobalamin variants—both free in solution and bound to the CarH photoreceptor protein—using Cobalt Kα1 high-energy-resolution fluorescence-detected X-ray absorption near-edge structure (HERFD-XANES) spectroscopy and (time-dependent) density functional theory ((TD-)DFT) calculations. Stark differences in HERFD-XANES spectra between alkyl- and non-alkyl cobalamins are observed, with the former exhibiting more intense pre-edge features. TD-DFT simulations reproduce the observed pre-edge intensity trends and show that increased intensity correlates with enhanced cobalt 3dz 2/4pz mixing arising from greater axialligand σ-donor covalency. The higher resolution afforded by HERFD also enables identification of 1s → corrin π* pre-edge satellites that are obscured in lower-resolution measurements. Analysis of these features indicates that their intensity provides evidence for the presence of cobalt 4pz/3dz 2 orbital character in molecular corrin π* orbitals. This finding supports a mechanism for alkylcobalamin photochemistry and Co–C bond cleavage in which photoexcitation into a corrin π* orbital is followed by donation into the cobalt 3dz 2 orbital. Interestingly, HERFD-XANES profiles between free and CarH-bound cobalamins are similar, demonstrating that the cofactor’s groundstate electronic structure is largely preserved when protein-bound. This indicates that CarH tunes AdoCbl photochemistry in the photoexcited state. Finally, we demonstrate that a truncated CarH variant that permits higher Co concentrations yields high-quality HERFD-XANES with strong sensitivity to geometric and electronic structure, suggesting that applying this technique in future time-resolved pump-probe investigations could lead to breakthroughs in elucidating the transient intermediates that drive CarH photoactivity.

papers.title: Optimization of Bimetallic Catalysts for the Hydrogenation of Liquid Organic Hydrogen Carriers using Contaminated Hydrogen Gas
papers.abstract: Liquid organic hydrogen carriers enable safe storage of H2 at high densities, but scalable application is impeded by the tolerance towards impurities common in industrial H2 streams, notably CO that poisons noble metals. In this work, we investigated synergistic effects in Pd-, Ru-, and Ni-based catalysts on Al2O3 for benzyltoluene hydrogenation under pure H2 and COcontaminated feeds representative of realistic operation. By enforcing identical metal loadings, dispersion, and mesoporosity across a series of mono- and bimetallic samples, intrinsic metalmetal effects were isolated. XPS reveals a more electron-rich Ni surface phase in the bimetallics, with Ru exerting a stronger influence on the electronic state of Ni than Pd. Catalytic activity of the samples in the presence of CO follows Pd–Ni >> Ni ≳ Ru–Ni >> Pd ≈ Ru. Ni is essential to retain activity under CO, while monometallic Pd and Ru are strongly poisoned. This is due to Nidriven CO methanation which initiates near 525 K on bimetallics. In case of the best-performing Pd–Ni/Al2O3 catalyst, operando DRIFTS identifies isolated Pd sites embedded in Ni that reversibly segregate/redisperse under CO/H2, forming transient Pd2/Pd3 ensembles. Overall, this work shows that selective incorporation of low noble metal contents into Ni is a viable strategy to produce robust, CO-tolerant, and economically attractive catalyst for benzyltoluene hydrogenation under impure hydrogen.

papers.title: Phase-field modeling of porosity formation and evolution during hydrogen-based iron oxide reduction
papers.abstract: Hydrogen-based direct reduction of iron oxides (HyDRI) offers a low-emission route to solid-state ironmaking by replacing carbon-based reductants with hydrogen. The mass loss associated with oxygen removal generates porosity. The evolving pore network influences reduction kinetics through changes in transport pathways and internal reaction surfaces. Here, we develop a phase-field framework that couples solid-state oxygen transport, the wüstite–ferrite transformation, and pore evolution during the rate-controlling step of HyDRI. Pore generation follows the local transformation rate at the advancing reaction front, whereas surface diffusion redistributes existing porosity. The newly formed solid–pore interfaces provide additional oxygen-removal sites, coupling pore evolution back to front propagation. The simulations show that increasing reduction-generated porosity drives a transition from isolated pores to connected channels, raising the fraction of pore space connected to the external surface from approximately 7% to 97%. Additional internal reaction surfaces shorten the time to 90% reduction by approximately 15%, demonstrating how pore formation accelerates further reduction. Faster front propagation preserves fine, tortuous pores, whereas faster surface diffusion promotes smoothing and coarsening. The resulting structures differ by more than a factor of two in the solid–pore interfacial length available for oxygen removal, even at the same reduction-generated porosity. Pore connectivity and the internal surface available for reaction therefore depend on reduction history and cannot be inferred from porosity alone. These findings provide a physical basis for linking local pore evolution to gas access and overall reduction kinetics at larger scales.

papers.title: Direct generation of a prototypical n-pentyl peroxy radical reveals how mixedfate chemical regimes shape product distributions
papers.abstract: Organic peroxy radicals (RO2) are key branch points in atmospheric oxidation with competing fates in the troposphere: reaction with NO, reaction with HO2, self-/cross-reaction with another RO2, and isomerization. RO2 often react in mixed-fate regimes, yielding product distributions with a complex dependence on reactivity conditions. In traditional environmental chamber experiments, not all RO2 fates are equally accessible, and chemical regimes favoring RO2 self-/cross-reactions and isomerizations are poorly characterized. Here, we access these conditions in an environmental chamber via 1-iodopentane photolysis, monitoring product distributions with NH4 + chemical ionization mass spectrometry. We tune the relative importance of these reaction pathways by varying the initial conditions, spanning bimolecular lifetimes from ~100-2000 s. Across conditions, the major observed C5 product, C5H10O3 (~40-60% yield), requires at least one RO2 isomerization to form, demonstrating the importance of downstream RO2 unimolecular reactions even if they are not the major fate of upstream RO2. Model mechanisms partially reproduce observed product distributions but cannot quantitatively capture variations with changing RO2 fate. Discrepancies suggest poorly-understood RO2 cross-reactions substantially influence product distributions. Conditions favoring RO2 isomerization unintuitively enhance both fragmentation and accretion via downstream functionalized alkoxy and peroxy radical chemistry. Results illuminate important gaps in existing atmospheric reaction mechanisms when predicting product distributions in mixed-fate chemical regimes.

papers.title: Operational insights from the front lines of OpenADMET: lessons from our blind challenges
papers.abstract: The gap between reported machine learning (ML) model performance in drug discovery and the experience of using these models in live discovery projects remains a major hurdle for the field, because the retrospective nature of most benchmarks makes it difficult to objectively assess progress. To address this gap, OpenADMET has hosted a series of blind challenges to benchmark and advance predictive modeling in absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET). In this Perspective, we distill the operational, strategic, and community-level lessons from our first four blind challenges, providing a practical blueprint for designing and running collaborative machine learning competitions in the life sciences. In addition, we open-source our blind challenge infrastructure and data-validation tools to lower the barrier to entry for hosting rigorous, community-driven competitions and to foster a sustainable framework for collective learning in computer-aided drug discovery.

papers.title: Machine-learning force-field scoring rivals free-energy perturbation for congeneric ligand ranking across public benchmarks
papers.abstract: Relative binding free-energy (RBFE) methods such as free-energy perturbation (FEP) set the accuracy standard for ranking congeneric ligands in structure-based drug design, but their computational cost limits throughput. Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) now approach quantum-chemical accuracy at a small fraction of that cost, raising the question of whether they can recover much of RBFE’s ranking accuracy while remaining computationally efficient. We introduce a static-score methodology called taqo and benchmark 10 MLFF variants spanning 6 model families (UMA, MACE, Orb, eSEN, AIMNet2, AllScAIP), together with a classical molecular-mechanics force field, on a uniform static-pocket protocol, correlated against experiment across 22 benchmark systems. We find that the ten MLFFs cannot be resolved from one another at this sample size, while every one of them significantly outranks the classical force field reference, at a few seconds per ligand on a single GPU. Against published OpenFE and FEP+ results on the same systems and the same ligand sets, taqo is statistically indistinguishable from OpenFE and significantly below FEP+, at roughly three orders of magnitude lower cost. On the congeneric JACS subset taqo and FEP+ are statistically indistinguishable. On the same benchmark poses taqo outperforms classical docking scores and is statistically indistinguishable from deep-learning affinity models, without any affinity-specific training. Together these establish MLFF interaction-energy scoring as a practical high-throughput approach for lead optimization.

papers.title: Oxidative ArylSF4-tetrafluoroethylation to N-hydroxydicarboximides via in situ generated Silver intermediate from silver(I) fluoride.
papers.abstract: An efficient and streamlined protocol for the ArylSF4-tetrafluoroethylation of N-hydroxyimides has been developed utilizing an in situ generated silver- (1,2,2,2-tetrafluoro-1-(SF4Aryl)ethyl reagent. While traditional methods rely heavily on common fluoroalkylating agents, Aryl-SF4 containing polyfluoroalkylating reagents remain very rare. Herein, we generating a highly reactive silver-tetrafluoroethyl(SF4Aryl) species in situ, followed by its immediate oxidative radical reaction with a diverse range of N-hydroxyimides. Under optimized reaction conditions, using N-Bromosuccinimide as the terminal oxidant, the corresponding Aryl-SF4 containing tetrafluoroethylated products were obtained in moderate to good yields (up to 69 %). This transition-metal-promoted tandem process exhibits broad substrate scope, high functional group tolerance, and eliminates the need for the isolation of unstable organometallic intermediates. Given the high demand for fluorinated motifs in medicinal chemistry and materials science, this operational simplicity offers a powerful, robust strategy for late-stage SF4 containing polyfluoroalkylation.

papers.title: Charge Loss of Proteins in vacuo: Implications for Native Mass Spectrometry and Ion Mobility
papers.abstract: Native ion mobility–mass spectrometry (IM-MS) is a powerful biophysical technique for characterizing protein structure. Because individual charge states often exhibit distinct structural dynamics, accurate IM-MS measurements require charge states to be examined independently. Although anecdotal reports among mass spectrometrists suggest that protein ions can lose charges during native IM-MS experiments, a thorough investigation of this phenomenon has been lacking. Here, we demonstrate that protein ions undergo charge loss inside the mass spectrometer as a direct consequence of gas-phase collisions, potentially leading to altered charge state distributions and ion mobility data. This effect was consistently observed across two instrument platforms (Synapt G2-S and Q Exactive UHMR), both ion polarities (positive and negative mode) and for three proteins (bovine serum albumin, myoglobin, and immunoglobulin G). Systematic investigations of instrumental parameters revealed that collision gas pressure has the strongest impact on the magnitude of charge loss, and that higher charge states are more affected than lower charge states. We further show that this process is largely driven by the dissociation of salt adducts and can hence be minimized through desalting in solution or inside the mass spectrometer, prior to the first m/z -analyzer (usually a quadrupole). For collision-induced unfolding experiments, significant differences were found between fingerprints acquired with and without quadrupole selection, although it remains unclear whether this phenomenon is directly related to charge loss. Taken together, our study provides fundamental insights into collision-induced charge loss as a source of error in native IM-MS measurements and discusses the relevance of quadrupole m/z -selection for improving confidence in IM studies.

papers.title: Translation-rotation internal coordinates with splicing (TRICS): A new approach to molecular geometry interpolation
papers.abstract: We present TRICS (Translation-Rotation Internal Coordinates with Splicing), a novel internal-coordinate-based interpolation method for generating high-quality approximations to minimum energy pathways (MEPs). Non-redundant internal coordinate (IC) systems can be used to generate chemically reasonable interpolated pathways between reactant and product structures, but it may fail for regions of configuration space where the IC system becomes numerically ill-defined. TRICS overcomes this limitation using multiple IC systems to generate separate interpolated paths that are iteratively spliced together into one continuous trajectory. We benchmarked the new method on 679 chemically diverse reactions, demonstrating excellent performance in generating interpolated pathways close to optimized transition-state structures. We further demonstrate the utility of TRICS for generating smooth and barrier-free interpolated pathways between critical points on excited-state potential energy surfaces. TRICS is available from the open-source geomeTRIC package.

papers.title: Comparing Symmetry-Adapted Perturbation Theory to Intermolecular Energy Decomposition Analysis Based on Absolutely Localized Molecular Orbitals
Symmetric versus asymmetric electron transfer in symmetric molecules
papers.abstract: Photoinduced electron transfer (ET) in symmetric donor-acceptor-donor (D-A-D) or acceptor-donor-acceptor (A-D-A) molecules attracts attention due to applications in advanced materials. It is normally assumed that ET occurs asymmetrically, from one donor to acceptor, thus breaking molecular symmetry and resulting in a dipole moment in the excited state. However, the symmetry can be preserved with symmetric ET from both donors, leading to a nondipolar state with a high quadrupole moment. Here we report on symmetric ET in a D-A-D probe, 5,5'-di(9H-carbazol-9-yl)-2,2'-bipyridine. This probe is weakly solvatochromic in absorption, but highly solvatochromic in emission, revealing a nonlinear spectral shift and strong decay of the oscillator strength in solvents of increasing polarity. We develope a 3-excited-state model that fits the data quite well for symmetric ET, while no reasonable fit is possible for asymmetric ET. The model predicts the symmetric ET to be barrierless and ultrafast, in good agreement with observations.

papers.title: Resolving Active Sites in Cu/ZnO Methanol Synthesis via Coupled Modelling of Surface Reconstruction and Coverage-dependent Kinetics
papers.abstract: Identifying active sites in heterogeneous catalysis is central to fundamental understanding and designing catalysts, yet it becomes challenging when surface structures, adsorbate coverages and reaction kinetics co-evolve under operating conditions. This challenge is exemplified by the enduring controversy over the active site for methanol synthesis over ZnO/Cu catalysts. Here we combine global structure exploration, grand-canonical sampling, a reactive CuZnCHO machine-learning potential and coverage-consistent microkinetics to establish a condition-dependent picture of the active surface. We show that Zn-Cu alloys, ZnO-like overlayers and partially reduced Zn species are not mutually exclusive active-site models, but distinct states within the same dynamic structural landscape. Activity is maximized within an intermediate thermodynamic window, where a Cu-Zn/Cu-Cu bifunctional ensemble forms near a step rim. These findings reconcile seemingly conflicting active-site assignments and establish a general framework for understanding activity in complicated systems. More broadly, our approach provides a paradigm for identifying activity-structure relationships in catalytic systems.

papers.title: Interlayer Mismatch and Solvated Intermediates Control Spacer Mixing in 2D Perovskites
papers.abstract: Organic spacer mixing is a versatile strategy for tuning the structure and properties of two-dimensional layered halide perovskites (2DLHPs), yet the factors that govern the resulting mixing configuration remain poorly understood. Here we investigate mixtures of alkyl monoammonium Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) and alkyl diammonium Dion–Jacobson (DJ) 2DLHPs and identify three structural outcomes: alloying, phase separation, and superlattice formation. Across twenty spacer combinations, the interlayer-spacing mismatch between the parent perovskites largely determines the outcome, with small mismatch favoring alloys and large mismatch favoring phase separation. A superlattice phase with a period exceeding either parent, consistent with alternating RP and DJ layers, forms only at large mismatch and only for blends containing 1,4-butanediammonium (DC4). In situ absorption spectroscopy and single-crystal structure determination reveal that superlattice formation proceeds through a dimethylformamide (DMF)-containing intermediate in which DC4 and n-pentylammonium (C5) occupy distinct bridging and intercalated crystallographic sites, producing an ordered precursor that converts to the superlattice upon annealing. Structural mismatch and intermediate-phase chemistry together govern alloying, phase separation, and superlattice formation in mixed-spacer 2DLHPs.

papers.title: The Chemistry of the Golgi-Cox Stain
papers.abstract: Our review provides both a theoretical discussion and experimental investigation of the Golgi–Cox stain. While this procedure has been a mainstay in the histologist’s toolkit for centuries and is implemented quite straightforwardly, there is still significant uncertainty around the chemistry. As such, it remains unclear how the stain works and, therefore, how it can be improved to be safer, faster, more reliable and work for larger specimens. Here, we provide technical and chemical considerations supplemented with original experimental observation on tissue clearing methods. Our findings suggest that Golgi–Cox staining cannot be understood as a simple process of stain diffusion, but rather as the outcome of interactions between tissue structure, fixation, chromate-mediated redox chemistry, mercury binding, pH, and cellular composition. Membrane and lipid integrity influence impregnation, while chromate-dependent changes in pH and redox state create the chemical conditions necessary for subsequent mercury reactions whereby only a few neurons fit within this goldilocks zone and are thus successfully stained. Based on our review and our experimental investigations, we propose the first comprehensive mechanism of the Golgi–Cox stain. Our literature survey and experimental data have been synthesised into a resource for both new and experienced practitioners of histology.

papers.title: A Molecular View of Framework-Associated Zeolite Lewis Acid Sites: Linking Structure to Meerwein–Ponndorf–Verley Reactivity
papers.abstract: The Meerwein–Ponndorf–Verley (MPV) reaction has been used to probe the Lewis acidity and local environment of aluminum Lewis acid sites (LAS) in zeolites and how these properties evolve upon post-synthetic treatments such as calcination and steaming. However, directly linking catalytic activity to proposed framework-associated aluminum LAS remains challenging because the identity of the catalytically relevant species is often inferred indirectly from correlations between spectroscopic signatures and reactivity. Molecular mimics of heterogeneous active sites can test hypotheses related to structure and reactivity, yet there exists few scaffolds capable of faithfully recapitulating the primary coordination environments in zeolites under demanding catalytically relevant conditions. In this work, we report a molecular model of a framework-associated (SiO)3Al LAS supported by a rigid, tridentate tris(siloxide) ligand derived from truxenone. The model complex is a competent and robust catalyst for MPV transfer hydrogenation of benzaldehyde with iPrOH, and density functional theory calculations support a pathway initiated by protonation of a supporting siloxide ligand by iPrOH. In contrast, a structurally related anionic Al−OH complex was found to be inactive under the same conditions. These observations suggest that framework-associated (SiO)3Al LAS can mediate MPV reactivity and provide a molecular basis for metal–framework cooperativity occurring at Lewis acidic aluminum sites in zeolites.

papers.title: Dynamic Ni–Fe Interfaces Regulate Stimulated Geological Hydrogen Production
papers.abstract: Geological hydrogen (Geo-H2) generated by water-rock redox reactions could expand low-carbon hydrogen resources by tapping reducing equivalents stored in subsurface minerals. Stimulated Geo-H2 production remains difficult to engineer because the reaction sequence connecting rockhosted Fe2+ release to H2 evolution is incompletely constrained. Here, we support an interfacial sequence linking olivine Fe2+ release, an Fe(II)-bearing hydroxide intermediate state, Fe3O4bearing product growth, and Ni redistribution at evolving Fe-rich interfaces. Across olivine-rich rocks, basalt, and Fe(OH)2 model systems, trace dissolved Ni2+ enhanced H2 evolution over the examined temperatures, reaching rates more than two orders of magnitude above previously reported Geo-H2 systems at comparable temperatures, and dissolved Ni2+ outperformed solid Ni additives under matched additive-form comparisons. Fe-normalized controls show that dissolved Fe2+ alone produced far less H2 than Fe2+ converted to Fe(OH)2, supporting Fe(II)-hydroxide chemistry as a productive gateway to the magnetite-forming pathway. Electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and cross-sectional EDS connected olivine Fe redistribution with Fe-rich alteration products and Ni recruitment, whereas first-principles calculations indicated that adsorbed Ni-Fe sites stabilize dissociated H more strongly. The Ni response was finite, with excess loading suppressing H2 evolution through competing Ni2+ reduction and other high-Ni interfacial inhibitory pathways. These results connect Fe release, hydroxide-associated Fe(II) chemistry, magnetite-bearing product growth, and Ni loading and accessibility, providing an interfacial framework for promoting water reduction in stimulated Geo-H2 systems.

papers.title: Molecular Dynamics Studies of Model Ionizable Lipids in an mRNA Vaccine
papers.abstract: Effective COVID-19 mRNA vaccines encapsulate nucleoside-modified messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA), which encodes the prefusion-stabilized SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, inside lipid nanoparticles. Endosomal acidification motivates the study of ionizable-lipid protonation. Here, we isolate how protonation changes hydration, solvent preference, and structural organization of ALC-0315 in simplified model environments. Through molecular dynamics simulations, we identify clear protonationdependent differences in lipid orientation, hydration, and collective organization across three model systems. At a water/hexane interface, the protonated amine headgroup shows a stronger preference for the aqueous phase, reflecting enhanced interactions with water molecules. In 20-lipid assemblies, the protonated assembly remains more hydrated and aqueous-associated over the simulated trajectory, whereas the neutral assembly migrates toward and spreads along the water/hexane interface. In pure ALC-0315 bilayer simulations, protonation strengthens amine hydration and alters bilayerscale structural organization, with the observed morphology depending on the pressurecoupling protocol. Collectively, these findings demonstrate how protonation of ionizable amine headgroups can remodel ALC-0315 assemblies through strengthened lipid–water interactions. These simplified systems provide molecular-level insight into protonationdependent ALC-0315 behavior, while not directly modeling the full multicomponent LNP, the endosomal membrane, or mRNA release.

papers.title: Bidirectional Refractive-Index Programming via Three-Stage Sequential Thiol-Click Chemistry for High-Performance Holographic Recording
papers.abstract: Conventional holographic photopolymers (HPs) mainly rely on a polymerization–diffusion mechanism to record volume holographic gratings (VHGs), resulting in trade-offs among photosensitivity, refractive-index (RI) modulation (Δn), optical clarity, and VHG stability. To address these trade-offs, we propose a bidirectional refractive-index programming (BRIP) strategy based on three sequential thiol-click reactions. Stage I employs a base-catalyzed thiol–acrylate Michael addition to form a thiol-rich host matrix. Under holographic exposure, Stage II triggers photoinduced thiol–vinyl addition to incorporate a high-RI recording monomer into the bright regions, generating the initial VHG Δn while preserving residual thiol sites in the dark regions. After exposure, Stage III uses thermally activated thiol–epoxy addition to incorporate a low-RI enhancing monomer into these complementary dark regions, further increasing Δn. A representative BRIP HP formulation is developed to validate the strategy. Benefiting from the BRIP design, the material requires only 1.1–1.9 mJ/cm2 exposure dose to generate VHGs with initial Δn values of 0.0103–0.0232 after Stage II, which increase to 0.0193–0.0394 after Stage III, while maintaining >95% visible-light transmittance, <0.02% haze, and <4% Δn variation after ten thermal cycles between 200 and -197 °C. This work establishes a new molecular design paradigm for high-performance HPs.

papers.title: μ-Oxo-Bridged Iodine(III) Reagents Enable Catalyst- and Light-Free Fluoro(halo)methyl Radical Generation
papers.abstract: While conventional radical fluoroalkylation typically requires exogenous catalysts or photoactivation to overcome significant kinetic barriers, here we report bench-stable μ-oxo-bridged iodine(III) reagents that release fluoro(halo)methyl radicals upon heating without an external catalyst, additive, or light. The resulting radicals initiate cascade cyclizations of methacrylamides and methacrylohydrazides to afford fluorinated oxindoles, pyrazolones, and related heterocycles. Variation of the fluorinated carboxylate ligand within the iodine(III) reagent framework controls the identity of the transferred C1 fragment, thereby providing chlorofluoromethyl, bromofluoromethyl, difluoromethyl, and monofluoromethyl products from a common reagent architecture. The transformation is compatible with structurally diverse and natural-product-derived substrates and proceeds efficiently upon scale-up. By encoding the required bond lability directly into the iodine(III) framework, this strategy establishes a general platform for the catalyst-, additive-, and light-free generation and incorporation of fluorinated C1 radicals into complex molecular frameworks.

papers.title: DNA-Encoded Chemical Diversification of mRNA Display Libraries
papers.abstract: mRNA display can survey vast peptide populations, but the chemical diversity available to selection remains largely constrained by translation. DNA-encoded libraries possess the complementary advantage: synthetic diversity can be introduced through split-and-pool chemistry, although without the peptide scaffolds and evolutionary framework provided by translation. Here, we combine these approaches by performing DNA-encoded chemical diversification directly on mRNAdisplayed peptides. Successive DNA-barcoding steps were coupled to cysteine alkylation and lysine acylation, allowing each chemical operation to be recorded while preserving the linkage between peptide and encoding nucleic acid. Application of this workflow to a five-residue peptide library generated approximately 20 million nominal chemical structures. Selection against carbonic anhydrase IX preferentially enriched library members encoded for a carboxybenzene sulfonamide modification, including a lysine-containing peptide that was independently resynthesized and shown to bind CAIX with a Kd of 26 nM. These results establish a complete progression from encoded chemical diversification and selection to hit identification, resynthesis, and binding validation, providing a practical framework for the discovery of chemically modified peptide ligands.

papers.title: Acoustic Optimization and Standardized Fabrication of a Biomimetic Liver Phantom for Quantitative Multimodal Imaging
papers.abstract: We previously developed a structurally biomimetic liver phantom composed of alginate units that reproduce the scale and organization of hepatic lobules. Here, we optimized the non-steatotic baseline formulation and fabrication workflow to more closely reproduce normal liver properties across ultrasound, CT, and MRI. The updated formulation was evaluated using clinical imaging systems, followed by quantitative water-tank characterization of speed of sound (SoS) and attenuation coefficient (AC). Increasing alginate concentration and incorporating glycerol into both the alginate phase and calcium chloride crosslinking bath reduced the SoS mismatch while preserving the biomimetic architecture. Fabrication was further standardized using 3D-printed molds to precisely control phantom volume and component ratios across clinical-imaging and water-tank configurations. On clinical systems, the updated formulation achieved a SoS of ~ 1540 m/s and AC of ~ 0.4 dB/cm/MHz, together with CT attenuation of ~ 44 HU, MRI-PDFF of ~ 2.5 % and T2* ~ 41 ms. Quantitative immersion-based characterization independently confirmed liver-relevant acoustic properties with a SoS of ~ 1557 m/s and AC of ~ 0.34 dB/cm/MHz at 3.5 MHz). Together, these values were within or approached reported ranges for non-steatotic liver. The resulting platform provides a reproducible, standardized multimodal baseline for the subsequent incorporation of controlled steatotic microstructure and development of quantitative imaging biomarkers.

papers.title: Fractal Colonization of Prebiotic Niches: Mechanical Budding of Nano-vesicles and Kinetic Resource Depletion as an Oncological Atavism
papers.abstract: Periodic mechanical forcing of the early Earth, from lunar tides (period of about 10 h) and radiogenic geysers (about 15 min) to von Kármán vortex shedding (about 1 s), may have loaded fatty-acid protocell membranes on time scales comparable to their relaxation times. We present a minimal model in which the tension of a parent vesicle, relaxing with time constant τ under rectified periodic forcing, releases one nano-vesicle at each upward crossing of a budding threshold. The shed nano-vesicles deplete the free fatty-acid pool of the surrounding niche through a non-linear sink bounded by the critical micelle concentration (CMC). The depletion equation has an exact solution between shedding events, and numerical integration with illustrative parameters shows that the discrete, tension-gated release produces a staircase of quasi-steady monomer levels that the pool follows towards the CMC. We discuss a matching window fτ = O(1) as a possible paleophysical selection criterion and, as a hypothesis not tested here, an analogy with vesicle-mediated nutrient competition in tumour niches.

papers.title: Increasing high-temperature creep life via improved directional solidification: A novel Ni-based single crystal superalloy reinforced by in-situ MC carbide fibers
Ferrier Rearrangement Intermediates Featuring Aliphatic Acyl Protecting Groups
papers.abstract: The Ferrier rearrangement of 1,2-unsaturated monosaccharides (glycals) to 2,3-unsatured glycosides, is important for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals and natural products. Mechanistically, the nucleophilic substitution proceeds via a cationic intermediate, the “Ferrier cation”, whose structure is difficult to capture with conventional analytical techniques. Here, we characterize the Ferrier cations of glucal and galactal building blocks involving aliphatic acyl protecting groups (pivaloyl-, levulinoyl- and chloroacetyl esters) using cryogenic gas-phase infrared spectroscopy. Comparing experimental and computed spectra of candidate structures, we established that all intermediates are stabilized by interactions of the C4 acyl protecting group with the C3 carbon of the pyranose ring (neighboring participation), potentially steering the stereochemical outcome of the Ferrier rearrangement. The resulting C4-C3-dioxolenium ion structure appears to be general to aliphatic acyl protecting groups, contributing to our fundamental understanding of Ferrier rearrangement reactions.

papers.title: Controlled Buildup of Multiply Charged Anionic Clusters at Interfaces Using Anion-Anion Reactions
papers.abstract: Reactions between ions of identical polarity are usually prevented by a strong Coulomb barrier in the gas phase. Here, we systematically investigate the binding of gaseous reactive anions to anions at a vacuum layer interface and develop our findings into a method for the controlled build-up of highly charged molecular anions and nanoclusters. Following a previous observation of dimeric ions in trace amounts upon the mass-selective deposition of the reactive fragment anion [B 12 I 11 ] – , the procedure was optimized here to oligomerize such ions, resulting in highly charged anionic chains. The surface products were detected using electrospray mass spectrometry after their dissolution. Experimental and computational investigations show that the isolated multiply charged ions are metastable against charge-separating fragmentation. Sequential deposition of two distinct reactive anions enables the formation of mixed oligomers. The deposition sequence and ion-beam focus can control the interfacial reaction, thereby enabling the selective generation of constitutional isomers. To generate stable anions with high negative charge states, ions featuring a positive center for Coulomb stabilization and multiple interface-active organic groups for anion binding were deposited sequentially with reactive anions. Stable products with a negative charge state of –7 were detected as free gaseous anions, surpassing the known limits of negative charge states of similarly sized ions. Finally, we demonstrate that this concept of targeted anion-anion reactions at interfaces can be extended to other functional ions, paving the way for a broadly applicable approach to interface design with charged building blocks and, therefore, offering potential applications in charge-state-based multilevel memory nodes, electrode functionalization, and photonics. Furthermore, the generated products provide fundamental insights into excess charge stabilization in nanosized units and reactivity in highly charged environments.

papers.title: eZacros: Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations for Electrochemical Catalysis
papers.abstract: Free energy diagrams rank electrocatalysts thermodynamically but do not resolve which elementary step limits the rate under operating conditions, or how the surface coverage that governs that competition is established. Lattice kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) recovers both by treating elementary steps as stochastic events on an explicit lattice, but electrochemical kMC workflows remain far less standardized than the free-energy approaches common in computational electrocatalysis. Here we present eZacros, a framework that implements potential-dependent reaction energetics within the computational hydrogen electrode formalism, electrochemical Brønsted-Evans-Polanyi relations for activation barriers, and effective rate prefactors for charge-transfer steps. It is built on Zacros, a widely used kMC engine, and takes a compact Python input that specifies the lattice, the mechanism, and the energetics. We validate the implementation against an established microkinetic model of the oxygen reduction reaction on Pt(111), recovering its polarization curve and steady-state coverages. For hydrogen evolution, we sweep a single model definition over electrode potential and hydrogen adsorption free energy to generate activity, Tafel slope, and coverage maps. These resolve into a kinetic phase diagram in which no single rate-determining step characterizes the reaction across the full space: the boundaries between Volmer-, Heyrovsky-, and Tafel-controlled regimes are set by the steady-state coverage, which departs from equilibrium adsorption expectations under reaction conditions. eZacros makes potential-resolved kinetics accessible to anyone who can supply adsorption free energies and reference barriers, complementing free-energy screening in catalyst modeling and discovery.

papers.title: Life Cycle Assessment of Eight Ru-based catalytic hydrogenolysis configurations for the upcycling of waste polyolefins
papers.abstract: In recent years, plastics demand has exceeded 400 million tons annually worldwide. Due to their mechanical and chemical resistance and low cost, polyolefins, including polyethylene (PE), represent beyond 50% of global plastic production, contributing to the generation and accumulation of plastic waste. Traditional waste management technologies, including landfilling and incineration, result into greenhouse gases emissions and potential loss of valuable carbon sources, whereas mechanical recycling strategies generally imply materials degradation and loss of mechanical properties. Hence, chemical recycling technologies are emerging as low-impact strategies to valorize plastic waste. Assessing the potential impacts of chemical recycling alternatives is crucial to support developers in ensuring environmental competitiveness at higher scales. To this end, we propose a comparative Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of eight potential alternatives for ruthenium-based catalytic hydrogenolysis of PE into valuable lubricants and fuels. Assessed configurations adopt different driving forces to power the reaction: thermal energy, mechanical energy and thermally assisted mechanochemical configurations. Results outline how the highest energy consuming configurations entail the highest burdens, whereas thermally-assisted mechanochemical processes result into the lowest impacts. Overall, the assessment shows that energy-efficient thermos-mechanochemical technologies entail the lowest environmental profile, providing valuable information for developers towards selecting and optimizing the most competitive configurations.

papers.title: Microchemical Strategies and AI-Enabled Biosensing for Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy in Precision Oncology
papers.abstract: Traditional blood-based liquid biopsy platforms have established crucial paradigms in precision oncology by enabling the longitudinal tracking of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs). However, blood sampling remains minimally invasive, requires dedicated clinical infrastructure, and is restricted by physiological boundaries such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy (NILB) addresses these limitations by utilizing painlessly collected alternative biological matrices, including saliva, urine, breath, stool, sweat, sputum, tears, and cervical secretions. From a microchemical and analytical perspective, these biofluids present extreme analytical challenges: target biomarkers exist at attomolar-to-picomolar concentrations within dense, highly variable chemical matrices containing high background noise and interference. This review outlines the microchemical, physical, and bio-sensing strategies developed to overcome these pre-analytical and analytical barriers. We evaluate advanced microfluidic architectures, nanoscale deterministic lateral displacement, functionalized surface chemistry, isothermal signal amplification, and label-free optical spectroscopy. Furthermore, we evaluate how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and chemometric algorithms—such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and multivariate spectral extraction—decode low-abundance, fragmented multi-omic signatures from complex noise. Finally, we propose a standardized analytical framework to bridge point-of-care microchemical devices with routine clinical diagnostic pipelines.

papers.title: Engineering Gold Nanoparticles for Transmembrane Anion Transport
papers.abstract: Synthetic transmembrane ion transporters are traditionally classified as either ion channels or carriers. Here we introduce a new nanoparticle-based transporter architecture in which spherical gold nanoparticles densely decorated with flexible urea- and thiourea-based ion-binding arms efficiently mediate transmembrane anion transport, providing the first proof of principle for nanoparticle-based transmembrane anion transport. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal a dynamic relay mechanism in which chloride ions migrate across the membrane by successive hopping between flexible ion-binding arms, while thermal rotational motion of the nanoparticle further facilitates translocation by repeatedly dragging these arms between the aqueous phase and the membrane interior. These findings introduce a new design principle for the construction of synthetic ion transporters based on densely functionalized multivalent nanoparticles.

papers.title: A Convenient Crystalline Acyl Silane for the Colorimetric Titration of Diisobutylaluminum Hydride (DIBAL)
papers.abstract: Due to the intense color associated with acyl silanes and their fast reaction with DIBAL to generate colorless alcohols, these properties were utilized to develop a colorimetric titration of DIBAL. A convenient crystalline acyl silane was identified that can be prepared on gram scale without the need for chromatographic purification by direct crystallization of the reaction products. Use of this material for the colorimetric titration of DIBAL and n-BuLi was possible. A variety of other 2 hydride and organometallic reagents were also tested and showed unsatisfactory endpoints. This work was performed by an American Chemical Society Project SEED student during their summer fellowship under the direction of a senior graduate student. The work disclosed could be suitable for application to an advanced undergraduate level laboratory related to the titration of reactive hydride reagents including the significance of atom effects on the physical and chemical properties or organic compounds.

papers.title: One network to link them all: an untargeted multi-metabolomics-methods network
papers.abstract: Metabolomics aims to cover a large range of metabolites from polar metabolites to hydrophobic lipids. Therefore, multiple chromatographic methods – such as reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC) or hydrophilic interaction chromatography (HILIC) – are combined to provide a comprehensive overview. The resulting tables need to be combined afterward for data analysis, but several metabolites might be detected across multiple methods. Currently, it is only possible to deal with such multiple entries for identified metabolites. There is a strong requirement for data fusion strategies beyond the simple concatenation of individual peak tables. Networks have been shown to represent a powerful tool for metabolomics data analysis. Feature-based molecular networking, or ion identity networking, is a modern tool for reconstructing biochemical knowledge from metabolomics data. Here, we developed a molecular network across multiple acquisition methods to provide a more comprehensive combination of data and metabolite identification. MS/MS spectra between the different LC-method datasets were compared to merge features. Within single chromatographic methods, ion mode matching based on predefined adducts was used to identify metabolites. Within single-ionization modes, spectra were matched based on GNPS mass-shift cosine similarity. A large network of 4,862 nodes and 401,387 edges was generated based on the different connections. The network was tested on several blood-related matrices. Analyses were performed using RPLC-MS for mid- to non-polar metabolites and HILIC-MS for polar metabolites. Identification was performed using in-house and external spectral libraries, as well as prediction software such as Sirius. Well-known metabolites detected in all tested analytical methods, such as tryptophan, were successfully connected. Data were then mined for new metabolites and associations.

papers.title: CuBr-Catalyzed Enantioselective Synthesis of Decahydroquinoxaline-Based
papers.abstract: A CuBr-catalyzed one-pot protocol provides access to decahydroquinoxaline-based bis(propargylamines) from readily available terminal alkynes, aromatic aldehydes, and a C2symmetric chiral diamine. The three-component coupling proceeds at 120 °C within 12 h, affording the products in 58–93% yields with diastereomeric ratios of up to 99:1. The synthetic utility of the protocol is illustrated by the ZnI2-mediated conversion of a representative bis(propargylamine) (7a) into the corresponding axially chiral allene (8a) with 90% ee. This approach enables the stereoselective construction of bis(propargylamines) and demonstrates their application as precursors to axially chiral allenes.

papers.title: Predicting the Thermodynamic Stability of Ce/Ti Nanoclusters under Synthetic Conditions
papers.abstract: Predicting which molecular species will form under a given set of synthetic conditions requires determining their thermodynamic stability relative to precursors and competing products. For complex molecular systems in solution, this requires both accurate electronic-structure calculations and sufficient configurational sampling. Here, we investigate two hexanuclear Ce/Ti clusters that form under different synthetic conditions: a yellow Ce IV 4 Ti 2 cluster obtained under mild conditions and a red Ce III 2 Ti 4 cluster, presented here for the first time, that requires higher temperature, longer reaction times, and increased Ti precursor concentration. To determine whether the red cluster is thermodynamically less stable or instead kinetically hindered, we combine explicit-solvent configurational sampling using a fine-tuned foundation machine-learned interatomic potential with density functional theory calculations of the Gibbs free energies of formation. Simulated annealing identifies configurations approximately 1 eV lower in energy than those obtained by direct relaxation of the crystallographic structures. Despite requiring more forcing synthetic conditions, Ce III 2 Ti 4 is predicted to be 4.48 eV more stable than Ce IV 4 Ti 2 . Comparison with a hypothetical Ce IV 2 Ti 4 cluster separates this difference into a 2.86 eV stabilization associated with the Ce III oxidation state and a further 1.62 eV stabilization associated with the Ti-rich composition and corresponding cluster structure. The preference for CeIII is also found for the isolated solvated Ce ions, while the sampled Ce III 2 Ti 4 structures show reduced repulsion between capping ligands and a less distorted metal core. The calculations therefore identify Ce III 2 Ti 4 as the thermodynamic product, while its formation only under more forcing conditions is consistent with kinetic limitation. The results show that predicting the thermodynamic product in solution requires configurational sampling beyond direct optimization of experimentally determined structures.

papers.title: Determining Which Phonons Affect Dynamic Disorder and Charge Mobility in Molecular Crystals
papers.abstract: Organic semiconductors (OSCs), and especially molecular crystals, exhibit unique structural complexity and strong coupling between electronic and vibrational degrees of freedom. The strong electron-phonon coupling (EPC) localizes the charge carriers and limits the charge transport rate as a consequence of the dynamic disorder (σij). In principal, it should be possible to engineer new molecular crystals with reduced dynamic disorder, but determining which phonons contribute the most to dynamic disorder and what are the corresponding effects on charge transport has been elusive. Here, we propose the use of singular value decomposition (SVD) to study phonon modes within molecular crystals by transforming the original phonon modes (OMs) into a reduced set of ranked projected modes (PMs) that affect the EPC. The SVD phonon analysis reduces the number of modes to consider for phonon engineering while retaining the essential physical information which is validated with inelastic neutron scattering. This analysis shows that even the most significant PM for the selected molecules contribute at most 12-45% of the total dynamic disorder. That is, for none of the selected molecules is a single OM responsible for a large proportion of the dynamic disorder. Our results also identify the collective detrimental motions for charge transport by producing atomic displacement visualizations that reveal which atomic and molecular motions contribute to dynamic disorder. Finally, side-chain effects are probed by SVD phonon analysis; these are not usually considered in detail because the electronic coupling is carried exclusively by the conjugated backbone. Our results show that side-chain location and branching can alter the distribution of backbone vibrational states, harden high-energy backbone-involved motions, and couple side-chain motions to backbone dynamics, thereby indirectly affecting the extent of dynamic disorder. All of this supports the conclusion that SVD phonon analysis could be used as a robust phonon engineering tool to eliminate or generate specific features in a phonon spectrum, generating personalized design rules for next-generation OSCs.

papers.title: Computationally Accelerated Discovery of Efficient Dual Component White Light Emitters
papers.abstract: This work presents a computationally guided approach to formulating white light emission from a series of Hbonded iridium phosphors and a complementary H-bonding fluorophore. We computationally investigated thirty new Ir(III) complexes that all incorporate a previously studied H-bond rich biguanide functionalised ligand. The results of the computational screening, based on TD-DFT peak emission data and established lifetime and quantum efficiency data in the literature, identified seven Ir(III) candidates suitable for synthesis and further investigation. Of the seven Ir(III) complexes, four were chosen based on their synthetic feasibility and their suitability to further study based on the parameters of the screen. Photophysical investigations of these four candidates with our deep blue emitter showed how three of the four complexes could achieve near ideal white light in the appropriate ratio of the complementary H-bonding fluorophore, while all four hostguest-complements show promising white-light results in polymer (PMMA) films.

papers.title: A Pan-YTHDF Probe Enables Chemical Modulation and Dissection of RNA m6A Reader Programs
papers.abstract: Genetic perturbation has been central to defining the functions of RNA modification binding proteins (readers), but knockout approaches remove the entire protein and cannot readily distinguish modification-dependent reader activity from other protein-associated functions. Small molecules provide an orthogonal strategy by directly perturbing the reader protein–RNA recognition event while preserving the reader protein. Here we report DF142, a cell-active pan-YTHDF chemical probe developed through an m6A-anchored design strategy. Structure-guided optimization yielded a high-affinity ligand that engages endogenous YTHDF proteins, blocks YTHDF–m6A RNA recognition, and displays a favorable selectivity profile. In mouse B cells, DF142 closely recapitulated the transcriptional effects of genetic Ythdf1/2 loss but induced minimal effects in Ythdf1/2-deficient cells at the applied dose range, distinguishing m6A-dependent from putative m6A-independent programs. In AML cells, application of DF142 revealed a leukemia-relevant RNA program associated with YTHDF–m6A interactions. Its activity in cancer cells and mouse models further demonstrates the utility of DF142 for interrogating YTHDF function in disease-relevant settings. Together, these findings establish DF142 as a chemical probe for dissecting m6A-dependent YTHDF biology.

papers.title: Highly Luminescent Alkyl- and Alkoxy-Terminated Silicon Quantum Dots via Aging Following Single-Step Plasma Synthesis and Functionalization
papers.abstract: Nonthermal plasma synthesis enables the continuous production and immediate surface functionalization of silicon quantum dots (Si QDs) in a single, flow-through reactor. While this process occurs on a millisecond timescale, the resulting nanocrystals are often limited by low photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY) due to persistent surface defects. In this work, we demonstrate that a minimal post-treatment, aging the Si QDs in specific solvents, can enhance the PLQY to ~50%, approaching the performance of much more complex solution-phase methods. We find that the choice of the surface ligand and solvent is critical: hexanol-terminated Si QDs exhibit significantly higher initial and final PLQYs than decene-terminated particles, likely due to the faster reaction of alcohols with electrophilic surface sites in the gas phase. Among the solvents investigated, chloroform consistently yields the highest PLQY. Furthermore, we show that light irradiation at 400 nm and 633 nm drastically accelerates the Si QD aging process, reducing the aging time from hundreds of hours to under 20 hours. This practical “synthesize and forget” strategy offers an efficient pathway for optimizing high-PLQY Si QDs for applications in optoelectronics and bioimaging.

papers.title: Chiral Patterning Drives Peptide Coacervate Formation in Coarse-Grained SIRAH Simulations
papers.abstract: Peptide-based polyelectrolyte complexes (PECs) are a promising class of stimuli-responsive materials with applications in drug delivery. Yet, the molecular mechanism by which stereochemical patterning governs their phase behavior remains unresolved. Racemic chiral patterning is known to favor liquid coacervate formation over solid precipitation by disrupting the ordered β-sheet structure, but experimentally elucidating the molecular-level origin of the solution-phase selection remains challenging. Coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics simulations offer a practical route to accessing the time and length scales relevant to coacervate phase behavior but require force fields that capture sequence-dependent structural propensities. One of them is chirality, a capability that has not previously been validated for peptide-based PEC systems. Here, we expand the SIRAH CG force field for modeling chirally and hydrophobically patterned peptide-based PEC systems. By introducing D-chiral dihedral parameters, achieved by inverting the phase angles of the SIRAH backbone torsion potential, we simulate both racemic and homochiral variants of six model PEC systems and compare the results to microsecond atomistic C36m simulations and published FTIR secondary structure data. The racemic SIRAH model reproduces atomistic trends in peptide compaction, aggregate density, and interfacial structure, as assessed by radius of gyration distributions, radial density profiles, and hyperbolic-tangent fits to the droplet interface. Racemic systems exhibit higher backbone contact counts and greater peptide compaction than their homochiral counterparts, consistent with the formation of dense, disordered aggregates characteristic of the liquid coacervate phase, where chains maintain close contact without adopting long-range β-sheet order. These results provide molecular-level support for the macroscopic observation that racemic patterning favors coacervate over precipitate formation, and reveal that alternating chirality promotes compact, entangled chain conformations that satisfy backbone hydrogen bonding outside of canonical β-sheet structures rather than simply eliminating it, a mechanism beyond β-sheet disruption alone. Hydrophobicity-dependent trends in secondary structure and solvent exposure are well reproduced regardless of chiral patterning, establishing SIRAH as a viable framework for peptide-based coacervate simulations and identifying stereochemical patterning as an independent sequence-specific route for tuning coacervate density. Because the SIRAH protein and nucleic acid parameters were derived within a single, structurally consistent framework, the same approach extends naturally to peptide–nucleic acid complex coacervates, an assembly class of growing interest for delivery applications and one that few coarse-grained force fields can treat at backbone-level resolution.

papers.title: Photo-oxidation of Dilute Methane in Dairy Barn Air: Pilot Scale Optimization
papers.abstract: Low concentration (below 1000 ppm) methane emissions from point sources such as cattle barns remain a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions, and have proven hard to mitigate. Previously, a novel method for methane photo-oxidation using UV light to produce chlorine radicals from chlorine gas, which subsequently oxidize methane, was proposed. Here we present the first real-world experimental results from a pilot scale Methane Eradication Photochemical System (MEPS) deployed at a dairy farm in Denmark. Utilizing electrolysis generated chlorine and UV light, chlorine radicals were produced in a confined photoreactor to effectively oxidize methane. The system demonstrated methane oxidation with a specific energy of 0.32 kWh/gCH4 and 75 % methane removal efficiency at an inlet concentration of 89 ppm. To better understand the operational parameters, the reactor was operated at a variety of different methane concentrations, UV irradiance, airflow rates, and chlorine concentrations. Statistical evaluation indicated that increasing UV power and Cl2 concentration synergistically minimizes specific energy while maximizing removal efficiency. The ability to achieve low specific energy and high removal efficiency underscores the system’s viability. By addressing agricultural emissions, this technology offers a tangible pathway for mitigating atmospheric methane and limiting global temperature overshoot in the 21st century.

papers.title: Intramolecular N-Alkylation of O-Aryloximes Facilitates N–O Homolysis and Iminyl Radical Cyclization
papers.abstract: An attempt to improve a microwave-promoted iminyl radical cyclization cascade targeting the Securinega alkaloid virosinine A revealed that the process could be initiated at lower temperatures (66 °C versus 100 °C) under Finkelstein conditions. Mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations indicate that Finkelstein bromination or iodination facilitates intramolecular N-alkylation. This lowers the N–O BDE of the substrate and permits homolysis at lower temperatures than previously observed.

papers.title: Origin of Reagent-Dependent Diastereoselectivity in Grignard Additions to a TADDOL-Derived α-Ketiminophosphonate
papers.abstract: Grignard additions to a TADDOL-derived -ketiminophosphonate display pronounced reagent-dependent diastereoselectivity, with dr values of 94:6 for methylmagnesium bromide and 55:45 for 2-naphthylmagnesium bromide. In this study, we carried out DFT calculations showing that dimeric Grignard models coordinate to the phosphoryl and sulfonyl regions of the substrate, restricting C–P bond rotation and enabling facial differentiation. The nature of the Grignard reagent modulates the organisation of the reactive complex and the relative stability of the competing transition structures, providing a mechanistic rationale for the contrasting stereochemical

papers.title: BET Bromodomain Pan-D1-Biased Inhibitors with Improved Drug-Like Properties and hERG Profiles as Therapies for Inflammatory Liver Injury
papers.abstract: BET bromodomain inhibitors are efficacious as anti-inflammatory compounds, but clinical translation is hampered by dose-limiting toxicities from non-selective inhibition. We herein report compounds 16 and 26, based on previously reported 4-methyl-1,2,3-triazole-based inhibitor, DW34. 16 has a BRD4 BD1 Ki of 10 nM, and up to 13–38-fold selectivity for BRD4 BD1 over other BD2 domains, and an improved hERG affinity of 4.24 µM over DW34. 26, A biscyclopropyl analog of 16 showed further enhancement of BD1 selectivity over BD2 (26–203-fold), but exhibited more potent hERG inhibition. Compound 16 had improved liver and plasma clearance over DW34, with good biodistribution to the liver, and had an intracellular target-engagement affinity Ki of 92 nM, with reduction of Ccl2, Cxcl1, AST, and ALT in in vitro and in vivo mouse models of liver inflammation. 16 represents a useful lead for treating inflammatory liver diseases, with improved specificity, drug-like properties, and reduced hERG affinity.

papers.title: Cobalt(III)-Catalyzed Synthesis of Aminoisoquinolones and Amino-2-Pyridones via C–H Functionalization with Ynamides: A Combined Experimental and Computational Study
papers.abstract: Carbon–hydrogen (C–H) functionalization methodologies typically rely on electron-poor π-systems, whereas the engagement of electron-rich counterparts remains underdeveloped. Herein, we report the first cobalt-catalyzed, site- and regioselective C–H functionalization of O-phenyl hydroxamic acids with electron-rich ynamides to afford aminoisoquinolones and 2-pyridones. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies reveal a pathway governed by Curtin–Hammett kinetics, featuring reversible concerted metalation deprotonation, irreversible selectivitydetermining migratory insertion, and turnover-limiting C–N reductive elimination. The transformation proceeds via divergent pathways, wherein the major 4-aminoisoquinolone is generated through a Co(III) cycle and the minor 3aminoisoquinolone transits a Co(III)/Co(I) redox manifold. Furthermore, high-valent Co(V) nitrenoids, which are frequently invoked in related reactions, are ruled out as catalytic intermediates.

papers.title: Photophysics and Triplet Sensitization of the Molecular Lanthanide YbQ3
papers.abstract: The energy transfer mechanism between organic ligands and lanthanide-based near-infrared emitters, such as ytterbium ions (Yb3+), is of great photophysical interest. In recent years, lanthanides have attracted attention for their capacity for both up-and down-conversion for a range of applications. While lanthanides generally have extremely small absorption cross-sections, their light-matter interaction can be complemented by an appropriate choice of chromophore ligand. Here, we investigate intramolecular ligand-to-Yb3+ triplet energy transfer in ytterbium tris(8-hydroxyquinoline) (YbQ3) molecule as well as the intermolecular sensitization of Yb3+ by palladium(II) octaethylporphyrin (PdOEP). We find that the intramolecular sensitization leads to a Yb3+ photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of (9.7 ± 1.0)% and and that the local ligand environment results in a relatively short lanthanide emission lifetime of 12.1 ± 0.1 µs. As for the intermolecular energy transfer mechanism in the YbQ3/PdOEP mixture, this is governed by a dynamic quenching of the phosphorescence from PdOEP. Despite the relatively weak collisional probability of energy transfer, requiring ∼ 400 collision events in solution, the PLQY of Yb3+ emission in the mixture was (4.5 ± 0.7)% for selective PdOEP excitation. These results indicate that while triplets can be effective sensitizers for near-infrared lanthanide emission, careful design of the sensitization pathway is required.

papers.title: StateFlux: Physically Validated Quantum Metabolic State Networks Reveal Limited Incremental Value for Toxicity Prediction
papers.abstract: Mechanistic molecular representations are increasingly proposed as a route to improve toxicity prediction by supplementing parent structure with protonation, metabolism, and quantum-chemical reactivity. Whether those physically richer representations provide predictive information that is genuinely orthogonal to molecular structure remains uncertain. Here, StateFlux represents each drug as a network of chemical and predicted metabolic states with node-level GFN2-xTB properties and edge-resolved changes in ionization potential, electron affinity, electrophilicity, solvation, and local reactivity. On a locked DILIrank 2.0 development set (n = 376; 156 DILI-positive and 220 DILI-negative compounds), 10 × 5 scaffold validation gave AUROC/AUPRC values of 0.8249/0.7727 for ECFP, 0.8049/0.7430 for ECFP + FluxCore, and 0.8010/0.7261 for ECFP + StateFluxCore. The FluxCore AUROC decrement relative to ECFP was -0.0199 (95% paired-bootstrap CI, -0.0341 to -0.0072). Strict temporal and scaffold-novel tests likewise showed no consistent advantage, and an independent 5,367-compound genotoxicity benchmark reproduced the result (AUROC 0.7765 for ECFP versus 0.7732 for StateFluxCore).
