To distinguish limited predictive utility from inaccurate low-cost quantum chemistry, 24 parent-to-metabolite transformations were re-evaluated with 144 ωB97X-D/6-31+G*/SMD single-point calculations. GFN2-xTB closely tracked DFT changes in electrophilicity (Pearson r = 0.963; MAE = 0.408 eV; 79.2% sign agreement). Thus, transformation-induced quantum reactivity can be physically meaningful without providing reliable incremental information for broad toxicity classification. These results argue that mechanistic fidelity and predictive utility should be validated separately when increasingly elaborate molecular representations are introduced into chemical machine learning.

papers.title: A Catalyst Discovery Workflow Coupling MLIP with MOBO for Nitrite-to-Hydroxylamine Electroreduction
papers.abstract: The selectivity of electrocatalytic nitrite reduction to hydroxylamine is governed by multiple coupled steps within the multi-electron nitrogen–oxygen reduction network, which cannot be represented simultaneously by a volcano relation based on a single adsorption descriptor. To address this limitation, a catalyst discovery workflow coupling machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) is developed. A small set of physical descriptors maps discrete oxide–dopant candidates onto a low-dimensional continuous representation, while four thermodynamic objectives describe the competing steps in NH2OH formation. The MLIP provides unified, low-cost structural and energy evaluation for oxide candidates. A Gaussian process surrogate model together with expected hypervolume improvement sequentially selects candidates from the discrete pool and updates the Pareto front within a fixed evaluation budget. The workflow integrates chemical objectives, energy evaluation, and sequential decision-making for catalyst screening in oxide systems.

papers.title: Docking, Molecular Dynamics, QSAR, and Machine Learning in Alzheimer's Small-Molecule Drug Discovery: Current Utility, Key Limitations, and Reproducibility Challenges
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains one of the most challenging therapeutic areas for small-molecule drug discovery because of its multifactorial pathology, complex target biology, and demanding central nervous system drug-development requirements. In this context, computational methods have become increasingly important for compound prioritization, hypothesis generation, and structure–activity interpretation. Among these, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, and machine learning (ML) are widely used in AD-oriented medicinal chemistry, particularly in studies involving targets such as β-secretase 1 (BACE1) and tau. This review critically examines the practical roles of these four approaches in AD small-molecule discovery. Rather than presenting them as universally predictive solutions, the review evaluates their principal strengths, major limitations, and current challenges related to validation, interpretability, reproducibility, and experimental translation. Molecular docking remains useful for structure-based hypothesis generation and binding-pose analysis, especially for structurally characterized targets, but is frequently overinterpreted when numerical scores are treated as direct evidence of biological activity. MD simulations provide a complementary framework for examining protein–ligand stability, conformational flexibility, and interaction persistence, although simulation outcomes remain highly dependent on methodological choices and should not be regarded as definitive validation of binding or efficacy. QSAR continues to support ligand-based activity modeling and analogue prioritization, but its utility depends strongly on dataset quality, applicability domain, and validation strategy. ML offers greater flexibility for activity and property prediction, including multi-parameter prioritization and ADMET-related modeling, yet remains sensitive to dataset bias, overfitting, limited interpretability, and poor reproducibility. Across all four approaches, the review emphasizes that methodological rigor is at least as important as methodological sophistication. Particular attention is given to common problems including inadequate validation, overinterpretation of computational outputs, limited reproducibility, and weak integration with experimental medicinal chemistry. Overall, molecular docking, MD simulations, QSAR, and ML are best viewed as complementary support tools whose value depends on careful application, transparent reporting, and close integration with experimental evidence. A more critical, reproducible, and biologically informed use of these methods is likely to provide a stronger foundation for future AD small-molecule discovery. Keywords

papers.title: Language-model-derived training data for polymer glass transition prediction: a controlled benchmark
papers.abstract: Experimental polymer property data are scarce and costly, whereas large language models (LLMs) have absorbed much of the chemical literature and can be queried for a fraction of a cent per polymer. We ask whether LLM-produced data can replace or supplement experimental data for predicting the glass transition temperature (Tg). With Claude Sonnet 5 as the teacher we built two synthetic datasets for USD 10.28: a generated set of 7,912 polymers whose structures and Tg values were both written by the LLM, and a labeled set of 9,925 hypothetical PI1M polymers whose Tg the LLM predicted. Both were cleaned with RDKit, deduplicated with a cut-invariant polymer key, and purged of every polymer of a held-out test set (1,471 polymers) and validation set (589) drawn from a curated experimental collection. A fine-tuned MoLFormer student was trained along a learning curve of 250 to 5,297 real polymers, with and without a preceding stage on synthetic data, and compared with a fingerprint random forest, two controls (self-training pseudo-labels and shuffled labels) and the teacher’s own zero-shot predictions, over 5 seeds. Trained on synthetic data alone, the student reached a mean absolute error (MAE) of 36.8 ◦C (generated) and 38.5 ◦C (labeled), within about 1 ◦C of the teacher (37.3 ◦C) and far from a student trained on all real data (25.2 ◦C). Synthetic data helped only when real data were scarce: with 250 or 500 real polymers, a synthetic first stage reduced the MAE by 3 ◦C to 5 ◦C on average and on every seed, a gain that shuffled labels abolished and that free self-training pseudo-labels reproduced only in part; against a baseline trained with more patient early stopping it was 3 ◦C to 4 ◦C at 250 real polymers and about 2 ◦C at 500; with 5,297 real polymers the gain was below 1 ◦C and not distinguishable from zero. Of the unique generated polymers, 8.3 % were copies of real polymers, 56 % of the valid generated pairs were repeats, and the teacher’s labels were rounded to a few values and shifted to lower Tg. LLM-produced data are thus a cheap and, below a few hundred measurements, useful supplement, not a substitute for measurements.

papers.title: Differentiable mass transfer modeling enables wet lab validated inverse analysis of liquid chromatography
papers.abstract: Liquid chromatography (LC) is essential to organic synthesis and emerging selfdriving laboratories (SDLs), yet LC method development remains cost-intensive and dependent on expert intuition. Mechanistic chromatographic models offer a route to transferable and data-efficient method development, but their practical use is limited by the computational cost of inverse modeling and by the ill-posedness of parameter estimation from experimental chromatograms. Here we report a wet-lab-validated differentiable physics framework for LC inverse modeling. The framework integrates mechanistic column modeling with physics-informed machine learning (PIML) to enable efficient forward simulation and gradient-based inverse estimation of molecular transport and adsorption parameters from gradient-elution chromatograms. The primary PINN surrogate reproduces the mechanistic reference with a root-mean-square error of 10−3 in dimensionless concentration. To address the ill-posed nature of the inverse problem, we introduce an observability-guided experimental-design strategy that quantifies parameter identifiability and incorporates this information into the inverse objective to promote convergence toward the ground-truth parameters. Across 300 dry-lab simulation parameter combinations, the proposed strategy recovered the ground-truth parameters with relative errors ≤ 10% in 88.3% of cases using three gradient programs, compared with only 6.7% using a single gradient program. We further validate the framework against wet-lab LC 1 measurements, achieving an absolute retention-time error ≤ 10 s for 89.3% of samples and establishing a wet-lab database comprising 731 sets of transport and adsorption parameters extracted from 2,553 gradient-elution LC chromatograms. This work provides an observability-aware differentiable modeling foundation for autonomous LC method development and closed-loop analytical decision-making in AI-driven laboratories.

papers.title: Framework Connectivity Tunes the Nuclear Spin Bath and Extends Coherence in Cu(II) Metal–Organic Framework Qubit Lattices
papers.abstract: Designing solid-state spin-qubit arrays that retain long coherence at high spin density remains a central challenge in quantum information materials. In molecular qubits, this challenge arises because the same local coordination environment and lattice architecture that define the spin array also control the dominant decoherence channels, most notably nuclear-spin spectral diffusion and coupling to low-frequency phonons. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are therefore especially attractive because they combine dense, crystalline spin arrays with chemically programmable control over the coordination environment, framework connectivity, and supramolecular packing, yet a fundamental understanding of how specific structural changes translate into predictable relaxation behavior remains underdeveloped. Here we compare two closely related oxygen-coordinated Cu(II) frameworks, Cu-TPTC and Cu-TPTriC, that preserve the same first-sphere donor set while changing connectivity and supramolecular packing. Cu-TPTC comprises one-dimensional Cu–O chains assembled into hydrogen-bonded rods, whereas Cu-TPTriC forms coordination-connected Cu–O–Cu two-dimensional sheets that stack through interlayer aromatic contacts in the absence of hydrogen-bond stitching. Continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance (CW-EPR) spectroscopy shows that both lattices exhibit relatively narrow linewidths compared with a Cu–N porphyrinic benchmark, consistent with reduced ligand-derived superhyperfine broadening in an oxygenonly coordination sphere. Pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance measurements establish coherent spin control and reveal systematically longer spin–lattice relaxation times (T1) and phase-memory times (Tm) in Cu-TPTriC over 5–25 K, with Tm≈4.8 ± 0.011 μs at 5 K. This coherence gain persists despite substantially shorter Cu···Cu separations in Cu-TPTriC and is consistent with a reduced proton-bath density and modified lattice dynamics, as reflected in the weaker electron spin echo envelope modulation (ESEEM) observed for Cu-TPTriC. Together, these results suggest that within dense oxygen-coordinated Cu(II) framework lattices, the secondary-sphere nuclear-spin environment and lattice dynamics can play an important role in governing decoherence, potentially outweighing spin spacing alone.

papers.title: Closing the Loop Between Synthetic and Living Cells
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells are moving beyond compartmentalised microreactors to become integrated components of biological networks that physically and chemically merge with their hosts. Existing reviews classify this field by mode of emission, by chemistry, or by architecture, and so describe the construct rather than its effect. This review takes the receiver's side, treating the functional adaptation of the living host as the readout of bio-hybrid function: how living cells probe their synthetic partners mechanically and adapt to them metabolically. We consider the bio-hybrid interface by how far the feedback loop (sensing-actuation) is closed and set out the evidence that would place a study in each of four tiers: open-loop, half-loop, partial feedback, and closed-loop. Read against these criteria, fifteen of the eighteen studies surveyed here are half-loop, three reach partial feedback, and none is closed-loop. All three partial-feedback systems work the same way, by metabolic interception, which the existing taxonomies have no category for. The one construct that comes closest to closed-loop operation contains no living cell at all. We then trace how single-cell coupling is scaling into hybrid prototissues that act as discovery platforms for pathological microenvironments, and we outline the translational barriers these constructs must survive to reach the clinic.

papers.title: Selective and Modular Synthesis of N1 and C3 Dialkylated Indoles via Iridium-Catalyzed Hydrogen Borrowing
papers.abstract: An iridium-catalyzed strategy for the modular synthesis of N1,C3-dialkylated indoles from readily available alcohols and indolines is presented. The method enables the selective installation of two distinct substituents via N-alkylation, dehydrogenation, and C-alkylation. Mechanistic studies support a borrowing hydrogen pathway that overcomes the challenging C-alkylation of N-protected indoles.

papers.title: Optimizing Affinity and Pharmacokinetics of a Cysteine-sulfoxide Derivative as Potential Inhibitor of BACE-1 using Fragment Growing and Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Alliin (S-(2-propenyl)-L-cysteine sulfoxide) was initially identified as a potential inhibitor of BACE-1, with the ability to chelate the catalytic dyad, but with very poor pharmacokinetics. We aimed to optimize these pharmacokinetic parameters, with a possible gain in affinity by growing the ligand towards the sub-pocket of the active site under the flaps. We employed fragment growing, implemented in the ligand designer module of Schrodinger, to extend 2-propenyl-alliin (a derivative of alliin) from both ends, with the multiparameter optimization (MPO) score as a guide. Select hits were further validated using molecular dynamics simulations for 500ns in explicit water. Ligands C37, C47, and C57 showed MPO scores above 0.9 with great improvements in LogP ranging from 1.129 to 2.147 and MW from 358g/mol to 384g/mol compared to -0.421 and 225.35g/mol in 2-propenyl-alliin, respectively. All the derivatives maintained an iron-clad charged contacts with the aspartic dyad throughout the simulation; while C47 and C57 made π-π interactions with Phe112 under the flap, using their pyridine side chains. Global root mean square deviations (RMSD), ligand RMSD, and root mean square fluctuations showed very stable ligand-BACE-1 complexes. Binding free energies (BFE; kcal/mol), computed using the MMGBSA, were two-fold higher (in C47, -52.29 ± 5.56 kcal/mol and C57, -59.40 ± 4.66) than that of the verubecestat (-26.78± 3.91), or alliin (−33.82 ± 4.25) in the previously reported work. However, the ligand-bound BACE-1 maintained an open conformation (distance D0>13.0Å). We have utilized fragment growing and molecular dynamics to provide derivatives of cysteinyl sulfoxides with improved pharmacokinetics, hydrophobic contact with Phe112, and improved BFE, while maintaining interactions with the catalytic dyad of BACE-1.

papers.title: Exploration of Structure–Activity Relationships and Gut Restriction in Anti-Cryptosporidium Triazolopyridazine Series
papers.abstract: Cryptosporidiosis is a major cause of diarrheal disease worldwide, particularly in young children and immunocompromised individuals, yet effective therapeutic options remain limited. Previously, the triazolopyridazine derivative SLU-10482 was identified as a potent anti-Cryptosporidium lead, but it suffers from modest affinity for the hERG ion channel. In the present study, structure–activity relationships (SAR) were investigated through systematic modification of the 3-position of the aryl ring and by designing gutrestricted analogues intended to reduce systemic exposure while maintaining antiparasitic activity. A diverse library of analogues was synthesized using amide coupling, Sonogashira, Suzuki, and Buchwald–Hartwig cross-coupling reactions, followed by hydrogenation and late-stage functional group transformations to access alkynyl, alkyl, tertiary amine, quaternary ammonium, and substituted aryl derivatives. Compounds were evaluated for anti-Cryptosporidium parvum activity in infected HCT-8 cells. SAR studies revealed that smaller, less polar substituents at the 3-position were generally associated with improved potency, whereas increasing substituent size and polarity resulted in diminished activity, although several larger polar analogues retained measurable potency. To develop gut-restricted agents, molecular weight, polarity, and conformational flexibility were intentionally increased to reduce intestinal permeability and systemic exposure. While these modifications were expected to preserve local intestinal activity, the resulting analogues exhibited substantially reduced antiparasitic potency. Because the molecular target of this chemotype remains unknown, the observed loss of activity may arise from reduced target engagement, impaired penetration across the parasite membrane barriers, or a combination of both.

papers.title: GITT Evaluation with PyBaMM
papers.abstract: The accuracy of the galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) for determining solidstate lithium diffusion coefficients was systematically evaluated using synthetic data generated with Doyle–Fuller–Newman model in PyBaMM. GITT-derived diffusion coefficients were compared with the known values used to generate the data across a broad range of possible material properties. GITT systematically underestimated the diffusion coefficient, with absolute errors increasing at higher diffusivities. For an optimized cell, reliable determination was generally limited to D ≤ 10 -14 m2/s, while a non-optimized cell provided much worse performance. These results demonstrate that GITT-derived diffusivities should be used with caution for quantitative battery-model parametrization. Nevertheless, GITT remains useful for comparative materials evaluation when cell design and analysis conditions are kept consistent.

papers.title: Estimand Divergence Between Static Docking and Molecular Dynamics as a Triage Filter for Antimalarial Leads
Pt(II)-Flavin Complexes As Anticancer And Antibacterial Agents
papers.abstract: We report a new chelating pyridyl–imine ligand bearing a riboflavin-derived pendant group and its Pt(II) complexes 1 and 2, designed as cisplatin- and oxaliplatin-like derivatives. Both complexes reacted with DNA and a histone-derived peptide, with 1 showing markedly higher covalent reactivity. However, this trend was not reflected in biological activity. Complex 2 displayed micromolar antiproliferative effects and pronounced antibacterial activity, particularly against Bacillus subtilis, whereas 1 was inactive in the tested models. Cellular accumulation studies excluded enhanced Pt uptake as the origin of this difference. Fluorescence microscopy performed on Escherichia Coli and Bacillus subtilis indicated that 2 affects bacterial DNA and membrane potential, consistent with a dual antibacterial mechanism. Comparison with oxaliplatin and the free flavin ligands showed that both the Pt–oxalate fragment and the riboflavin-containing ligand are required for activity.

papers.title: Computer Vision for Predicting Electrochemical Reaction Performance from Electroanalytical Data
papers.abstract: Electrosynthesis has surfaced as a key approach in modern synthesis, enabling more sustainable chemical transformations with reduced chemical waste. The accurate prediction of electrosynthesis performance is crucial for accelerating the discovery and design of reactions. Despite indisputable advances, the descriptor-based predictions fall short in representing the full reaction regime due to the high‑dimensional parameter space of electrosynthesis. Cyclic voltammograms, which are typically employed for mechanistic analysis, inherently contain rich information about electrochemical processes. Herein, we applied computer vision techniques to collect a cyclic voltammogram image database and trained a neural network directly on these image data. The resulting models achieved reliable performance in predicting electrosynthesis outcomes, demonstrating the potential of image-based deep learning for electrochemical reaction evaluation and data-driven electrosynthesis studies.

papers.title: Assessing the state of the art in ADMET prediction: Lessons from the OpenADMET-ExpansionRx community blind challenge
papers.abstract: Computational blind challenges are essential for advancing drug discovery, especially in research areas with limited public data, such as absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity (ADMET) prediction. In this paper, we present the results of our latest community blind challenge, organized in collaboration with Expansion Therapeutics (ExpansionRx). Participants were tasked with predicting nine distinct ADMET endpoints routinely evaluated during lead optimization of compounds in drug discovery programs. Following unprecedented engagement from the global community, this challenge provided valuable insights into the state of the art in machine learning for ADMET modeling. Evaluating submissions against a realistic, challenging dataset from active ExpansionRx drug discovery programs revealed that message-passing neural networks and chemical foundation models dominated among the top performers. Furthermore, the results highlighted the power of proprietary industry datasets and a critical need to optimize predictive workflows for different endpoints independently via multitasking and task-affinity grouping. We also demonstrate how hosting our open-source blind challenge infrastructure on a flexible platform like Hugging Face was pivotal for driving community engagement and visibility. Ultimately, blind challenges supported by robust infrastructure, widespread dissemination, and rigorous post-challenge analysis are fundamental to maximizing the utility of public data releases. We anticipate that these community benchmarks will continue to drive the advancement of ADMET models, enabling their deployment in both early- and late-stage drug discovery.

papers.title: Reconfigurable Flow Reactors Assembled from 3DPrinted Self-Healing Hydrogel Modules
papers.abstract: Here, we introduce millimeter-scale fluidic reactors assembled from digital-light-processing (DLP)-printed self-healing hydrogel modules. A poly(acrylic acid-co-2-acrylamidophenylboronic acid)/poly(vinyl alcohol) formulation combines photoprintability with dynamic interfacial association. Printed modules contain straight, curved, branched, looping, and crossing channels, as well as mixing chambers. When brought into contact under ambient conditions, separate modules form liquid-tight interfaces that support continuous flow. Joined elements can subsequently be separated, rearranged, and rejoined to construct new fluidic circuits from the same building blocks. Finally, reactors containing active mixing chambers are used to perform a competitive thiol–maleimide reaction. Changing only the position at which two competing thiols enter the reactor shifts the apparent product ratio from 95:5 to 17:83 or 94:6. These results establish self-healing interfaces as reversible fluidic connections and provide a materials-based strategy for constructing reconfigurable flow reactors.

papers.title: Treatise on Present Practice and Perspectives of MDGC
papers.abstract: The state of affairs of multidimensional gas chromatography (MDGC) at present is no more than an implementation of a two-dimensional form (2D-GC) reducing the domain to the setup known as GCxGC. Introduced in 1991 with great expectation, however, GCxGC still happen to fall short of realizing the anticipated capabilities despite continuous efforts made over the elapsed 35 years. This got quantitative formulation in regard of separation performance as early as 2008, proving that it failed to be competitive with a well-governed 1D-GC. The present paper highlights further limitations of GCxGC: inadequate operation burdened with shortcomings are presented via examples taken from GCxGC literature; crowning the list with the inability to meet fundamental requirement that if a compound can be analyzed by 1D-GC it must remain analyzable by MDGC. The repertoire of the intertwining issues, each of which unavoidably rigs or even hamstrings the others, highlights that GCxGC has a built-in self-limiting feature. Attempts to overcome confinements via loosening the binding conditions turned GCxGC back to the form it emerged from decades ago, yet without getting rid of the hampering curbs. The unfavorable overall picture forces to consider viabilities of other concepts, with focus on avoiding errors and pitfalls of GCxGC while fulfilling basic requirements of MDGC. In our view, there are two alternatives. One is ZGC, principle of which was introduced in 1989, requirements and potential of which are presented here in more detail; the other is a concept called Quantum-GC, which is presented as an introductory approach.

papers.title: Steric Repulsion Driven Formation of a 3D Covalent Organic Framework Polymorph with Exceptionally High Surface Area
papers.abstract: Dimensional polymorphism, in which the same molecular building blocks form frameworks of different dimensionality, offers a direct route to distinct pore architectures in covalent organic frameworks (COFs). True 2D/3D polymorphism remains rare, since linkers capable of forming both 2D and 3D COFs tend to favor 2D structures. Accessing 3D polymorphs remains a challenge. We investigated the dimensional polymorphism in an imine-linked COF based on a terphenyl tetraaldehyde linker core, which is functionalized with two bulky methyl benzoate groups, and p-phenylenediamine. The tetraaldehyde linker can adopt planar or pseudo-tetrahedral conformations, while the methyl benzoate groups introduce steric crowding within the framework. Under a wide range of conditions, the system forms a 2D-kgm COF, whereas precise control over small amounts of water gives access to a second highly crystalline and highly porous 3D-dia COF. This phase is retained only after supercritical CO2 activation, while the 2D-kgm COF is retained with and without scCO2, highlighting the importance of activation in the search for 3D phases. The steric crowding appears to limit the degree of interpenetration, enabling the 3D-dia phase to reach a much higher BET surface area of up to 3883 m2 g-1 and a substantial high-pressure CO2 uptake of 31.9 mmol g-1 at 273 K and 19.5 bar compared with the 2D-kgm phase. These results show that steric interactions can shift the balance between competing dimensional polymorphs, while limiting the degree of interpenetration, leading to a compelling route towards materials with exceptionally high surface areas and high CO2 uptake.

papers.title: Localizing and quantifying the dynamic interfacial proton population in alkaline electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: In alkaline electrocatalysis, electrostatic theory predicts, and experiments confirm, interfacial acidity that deviates from bulk pHb. The location and magnitude of the proton population within the electric double layer (EDL) and its evolution with catalytic turnover have remained unresolved, leaving a critical gap for mechanistic interpretation across proton-coupled electrocatalysis. Here, using showcase alkaline (pHb 13) hydrogen evolution on Au, electrochemical fluorescence microscopy combined with electrostatic modelling demonstrates an apparent interfacial pH inversion of more than eight units within 1 nm of 1 the electrode, below the outer Helmholtz plane. This EDL proton population is dynamic. At hydrogen-evolution onset, the reaction can draw from it. As electrocatalytic turnover increases, H+ consumption outpaces its electrostatic replenishment, favouring a water-based reaction pathway. Localizing and quantifying this dynamic proton population closes a key gap in the mechanistic interpretation of alkaline hydrogen evolution with a proton-availability framework likely relevant to alkaline electrocatalysis and electrosynthesis at large.

papers.title: ProtMutMap: Predicting Protein Binding Free Energy Changes Using Multiple-Mutation Networks
papers.abstract: Predicting changes in binding free energy ΔΔ G caused by multiple mutations at protein−protein interfaces requires accounting for nonadditive interactions between mutations, which an additive approximation based on single mutations cannot capture, and for the dependence on the computational pathway in stepwise approaches that introduce mutations sequentially. Here, we propose ProtMutMap, a method that integrates information from multiple pathways in a network whose nodes represent target variants and variants containing subsets of their mutations, and whose edges represent free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations for residue substitutions. ProtMutMap simultaneously estimates the binding ΔΔ G of each variant from all edge values using Huber loss. We compared ProtMutMap with the additive approximation and the stepwise method at 30 evaluation points, including intermediate variants, using a multiple-mutation dataset comprising 7 protein complex systems derived from SKEMPI2. ProtMutMap achieved a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 1.13 kcal/mol, lower than that of either comparison method. ProtMutMap also yielded lower prediction errors than Rosetta flex ddG. These comparisons with experimental values demonstrate that integrating multiple pathways through variants containing subsets of the target mutations improves binding ΔΔ G predictions for protein variants with multiple mutations.

papers.title: Controlling polyethylene fibrillation in PFAS-free dry electrodes for processability and electrochemical performance
papers.abstract: Ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) is a more sustainable binder alternative to polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) for producing PFAS-free Li-ion battery electrodes using a solvent-free PE fibrillation process. We show that PE fibrillation is thermo-activated and can be controlled to produce an extensive network of nano-fibrils with a median size of 20-40 nm. PE-containing graphite electrode ultimate tensile strength (UTS), critical for roll-to-roll processing, improved more than 20-fold when the electrode calendering temperature increased from 100 to 160-200 °C, providing mechanical stability superior to equivalent PTFE-containing electrodes. PE-containing electrodes calendered at lower temperatures (120-140 °C) showed comparable charging rate performance but superior capacity retention of ∼90% after 100 cycles when compared with PTFE-containing electrodes. Removing PTFE by calcination to mimic direct recycling required temperatures > 600 °C and led to PFAS emissions. In contrast, PE removal was PFAS-free and achieved at 300-400 °C, aided by the catalytic effect of graphite on PE decomposition making PE-containing electrodes more suitable with direct recycling. Overall, integrating across fabrication, mechanical, electrochemical and end-of-life considerations, PE-containing electrodes offer significant potential for more sustainable solvent-free Li-ion batteries.

papers.title: Integrating Pathway Engineering and FoTO1-Mediated Oxidation for Taxadien-5α-ol Production
papers.abstract: Microbial reconstruction of paclitaxel biosynthesis is hindered by limited taxadiene (1) supply and poor selectivity in the first oxidative step. Here, we engineered Escherichia coli for the efficient de novo production of taxadien-5α-ol (2) by integrating enhanced taxadiene (1) biosynthesis with selective oxidation. Coordinated engineering of taxadiene synthase expression, precursor supply, pathway regulation, and geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase increased the titer of 1 7.5-fold, from 20.3 to 152.6 mg L−1. However, the CYP725A4–cytochrome P450 reductase fusion produced only 2.2 mg L−1 of 2, representing 7.4% of the detected oxygenated taxanes. Coexpression of facilitator of taxane oxidation 1 (FoTO1) markedly redirected the oxidation profile toward 2, increasing its proportion to 94.2% and its titer 20.8-fold to 45.5 mg L−1. Subsequent fermentation optimization increased the titer to 74.0 mg L−1, and addition of a 15% (v/v) n-dodecane overlay further increased production to 179.9 mg L−1. To our knowledge, this represents the highest reported titer of individually quantified taxadien-5α-ol (2) in a heterologous microbial host. These results highlight the importance of coupling precursor supply with control of oxidation selectivity and establish an efficient platform for further reconstruction of microbial paclitaxel biosynthesis.

papers.title: Polymer Informatics in the Era of Foundation Models: From Representation to Autonomous Design
papers.abstract: Foundation models, pretrained on broad datasets and adapted to multiple tasks, offer a way to reuse chemical knowledge across polymer property prediction and inverse design. Realizing this opportunity requires connecting learned representations to materials whose properties also depend on molecular populations, formulation, processing, and measurement conditions. Here, we review advances in polymer foundation models and the data, representations, and experimental workflows that support their use in materials design. We organize these developments around the polymer material state, a description linking chemical identity to molecular distributions, architecture, morphology, and preparation history relevant to a target property. This organization connects data resources and pretraining strategies to questions about what models learn, how that knowledge transfers, and which experimental choices it can support. We compare learning objectives and adaptation methods, examine representations of polymer chemistry and state, and follow inverse design from candidate generation through synthesis and processing to validation. Pretrained models now support prediction across multiple properties and generation for specified targets, with selected polymer candidates reaching synthesis and thermal characterization. Broader polymer design campaigns show how precursor accessibility, polymerization outcomes, and specimen preparation influence whether a predicted advantage becomes a measured material response. Building on this evidence, we discuss opportunities to combine chemical pretraining with richer sample information and to assess transfer across polymer families, preparation conditions, and experimental campaigns. The resulting synthesis connects model development to a practical objective for polymer informatics: reducing the new experimentation needed to obtain materials with reproducible, targeted performance.

papers.title: Data-Efficient Machine Learning Potentials for Organic Reactions through Active-Learning-Guided Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Transition states (TSs) are central to reaction barriers and mechanisms, yet their accurate localization remains computationally demanding. Reactive machine learning potentials can accelerate TS optimization by rapidly predicting potential energy surfaces, but achieving chemical transferability requires extensive sampling and quantum chemical (QC) labeling of reactive conformations. Here, we introduce an active-learning-guided fine-tuning strategy that couples pretrained chemical knowledge for broad generalization with adaptive labeling of informative reactive conformations for data efficiency. The resulting MACEPre-DeePEST-OS enables efficient TS optimization and barrier predictions across diverse organic reactions while requiring QC labeling for only ~2% of approximately 19 million candidate conformations. Across three in-distribution benchmarks, MACEPre-DeePEST-OS achieves an average root mean square deviation of 0.080 Å for TS geometries and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.938 kcal/mol for barriers. In cross-dataset evaluation on an external OrgReact subset, fine-tuning reduces the barrier MAE by 58% relative to the pretrained model. Out-of-distribution testing on a Ugi reaction network containing structures with more than 70 atoms yields a barrier MAE of 1.09 kcal/mol, indicating transfer to molecular sizes and reaction complexity beyond the fine-tuning data. These results establish a data-efficient route toward transferable reactive potentials for quantitative analysis of reaction mechanisms and competing pathways.

papers.title: A Dinucleating β-Thio-δ-Diiminate Ligand Enables Metal-Dependent CO2 Reactivity in Homo- and Heterobimetallic Zn and Cu Complexes
papers.abstract: Herein, we investigate the β-thio-δ-diimine (BTDDI) ligand, recently reported as a sulfur containing analogue of the established BODDI framework, as a platform for mono- and bimetallic Cu(I) and Zn(II) chemistry. Sequential metalation enables selective access to homo- and heterobimetallic complexes, including the first structurally characterised Cu/Zn derivative of this ligand class. Replacement of the central oxygen donor by sulfur expands the dinuclear framework, resulting in significantly increased metal–metal separations. The reactivity of these complexes towards CO 2 is strongly dependent on both metal identity and nuclearity: monometallic Cu(I) and Zn(II) complexes and the homobimetallic Cu(I) analogue are unreactive, whereas the Cu/Zn and di-Zn complexes undergo CO 2 activation. The di-Zn complex undergoes selective C–C bond formation at the γ-position of the ligand backbone to give a reversibly formed carboxylate-containing product featuring an unusual tripodal [N,S,O] donor motif. Isotopic labelling, spectroscopic and structural studies establish incorporation of CO 2 into the ligand framework, while DFT calculations reveal substantially lower barriers to γ-C insertion for the bimetallic complexes and identify Zn(II) as a key contributor to stabilisation of the resulting carboxylate through Zn–O interactions and subsequent dimerisation. These results establish a mode of CO 2 activation in which ligand-centred reactivity is coupled to metal-centred substrate stabilisation, with metal identity and nuclearity determining the outcome of the reaction.

papers.title: Residue-Conditioned In-Pocket Design for Paralogue Selectivity
papers.abstract: Structure based generative model explore chemical spaces inside the protein active site , typically prioritizing candidates through empirical scoring functions.Few evaluate wthether the results is selective for the intended protein over a close paralogue , and none of them combines that evaluation with residue level conditioning and covalent bounds placement . In this paper we describe a design loop in which each rounds installs one chemical group aimed at one named pocket residue that a pairwise alignment marks as divergent in a chosen anti target , subject while enforcing structural continuity by requiring each successive molecule to retain its predecessor as a substructure. The anti target pocket is built by mutating only the divergent position within the target's own structure , so the two differ at those residues and nowhere else . Across 17 design campaigns the selected scaffold was retained in every final lead . Comparison against 44 reference compounds from the literature that target 12 receptor pair demonstrated preservation of established recognition chemistry in 19 comparisons , against a 12.6% unrelated active decoy rate . generated candidates the structure relationships with established inhibitor , including 78% shared core with imatinib and a 59% with erlotinib while adding alternative chemical strategies . These included residue directed electrophile warhead such as a chloroacetamide targeting ABL1 Cys388, and the generation of a macrocyclic peptidomimetic architecture for KRAS G12C. Together, these results demonstrate an integrated computational framework capable of translating therapeutic objectives and structural evidence into traceable medicinal chemistry design decisions across multiple protein targets.

papers.title: Integrative Physics and Machine Learning-Based Optimal Binding Pose Generator for Protein-Ligand Complexes
papers.abstract: Accurately identifying the optimal protein–ligand binding pose is crucial for reliable binding affinity prediction, as molecular dynamics–based approaches are highly sensitive to the initial structure. However, there is currently no efficient way to predict such poses. Indeed, we assess the capabilities of three proposed AI-based software solutions (AlphaFold3, Boltz and RoseTTAFold All-Atom) and demonstrate their substantial shortcomings in this context. Here, we present a combined physics-and machine-learning-based method that predicts optimal protein-ligand poses in their relaxed states, enabling rapid and cost-effective downstream estimation of binding affinities. We apply our approach to two targets, tankyrase 2 (TNKS2) and the 3C-like protease (3CLPro), using datasets of 10,000 molecules for each system. Evaluation on an external validation set of approximately 3,000 molecules demonstrates the method’s ability to generalize to previously unseen datasets, aligning with the practical needs of high-throughput drug discovery pipelines that iteratively evaluate new molecules. Our method substantially reduces the need for costly calculations by efficiently filtering out poses unlikely to yield favorable binding affinities upon relaxation.

papers.title: Quantification of Levoglucosan in Biomass Burning Particulate Matter Using a Glucometer Test Strip
papers.abstract: Levoglucosan (LG) is highly abundant in biomass pyrolysate and is widely used as a tracer for biomass burning in environmental sciences. Current analytical standards rely on gas or liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC/LC-MS). Because these methods are expensive, there is a critical need for low-cost alternatives. This work explores using commercial glucometer strips to detect and quantify LG by first converting it into d-glucose with heat and acid. The hydrolysis condition was optimized to be at 150 °C, with 0.1 M H2SO4, for 60 min, while the sample was buffered at pH 7.3 for optimal detection. Following the optimization of the hydrolysis protocol, the glucometer strip signal exhibited a linear response, which was statistically indistinguishable from the response to d-glucose. However, when applied to authentic biomass burning filter samples, the glucometer method yielded concentrations approximately twice as high as GC–MS measurements. This discrepancy is likely due to interfering compounds in the sample matrix that also release d-glucose upon hydrolysis. Overall, this study establishes the proof-of-concept for using off-the-shelf glucometer testing strips for LG detection, while highlighting the distinct challenges of applying this method to complex environmental samples.

papers.title: Direct generation of a prototypical n-pentyl peroxy radical reveals how mixedfate chemical regimes shape product distributions
papers.abstract: Organic peroxy radicals (RO2) are key branch points in atmospheric oxidation with competing fates in the troposphere: reaction with NO, reaction with HO2, self-/cross-reaction with another RO2, and isomerization. RO2 often react in mixed-fate regimes, yielding product distributions with a complex dependence on reactivity conditions. In traditional environmental chamber experiments, not all RO2 fates are equally accessible, and chemical regimes favoring RO2 self-/cross-reactions and isomerizations are poorly characterized. Here, we access these conditions in an environmental chamber via 1-iodopentane photolysis, monitoring product distributions with NH4 + chemical ionization mass spectrometry. We tune the relative importance of these reaction pathways by varying the initial conditions, spanning bimolecular lifetimes from ~100-2000 s. Across conditions, the major observed C5 product, C5H10O3 (~40-60% yield), requires at least one RO2 isomerization to form, demonstrating the importance of downstream RO2 unimolecular reactions even if they are not the major fate of upstream RO2. Model mechanisms partially reproduce observed product distributions but cannot quantitatively capture variations with changing RO2 fate. Discrepancies suggest poorly-understood RO2 cross-reactions substantially influence product distributions. Conditions favoring RO2 isomerization unintuitively enhance both fragmentation and accretion via downstream functionalized alkoxy and peroxy radical chemistry. Results illuminate important gaps in existing atmospheric reaction mechanisms when predicting product distributions in mixed-fate chemical regimes.

papers.title: Accelerated Hygrothermal Aging of an Epoxy Barrier Coating: Correlating Laboratory Degradation with Performance
papers.abstract: This study investigates the hygrothermal aging behavior of an epoxy barrier coating. The coating was subjected to water immersion and dry-heat exposure at 20–80 °C for up to 14 months, and changes in water uptake, tensile properties, and thermal transitions were monitored by gravimetric measurements, tensile testing, dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). After two months, combined water and elevated-temperature exposure produced larger reductions in tensile modulus and strength than dry aging, while drying substantially restored the mechanical properties. This indicates that moisture-induced plasticization and swelling account for a major fraction of the early property loss. Longer exposure produced more severe mechanical deterioration, and at 60 °C the material continued to gain mass for up to eight months before subsequent weight loss, consistent with a transition from predominantly diffusioncontrolled water uptake toward degradation-associated behavior. In contrast, DMA and DSC glass-transition temperatures varied only modestly with aging temperature. The results show that mechanical measurements provide a more sensitive indicator of hygrothermal performance than Tg alone for this coating. The study provides material-level evidence relevant to the assessment of rubber-toughened epoxy barrier coatings under combined heat and moisture exposure.

papers.title: Experimental Data Analysis and Improved Cytochrome P450 Site-of-Metabolism Prediction for Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes mediate the oxidative metabolism of most marketed drugs, making early prediction of their sites of metabolism (SoMs) essential for addressing metabolic liabilities. In this work, we present a substantial update to our hybrid docking/quantum mechanics SoM prediction tool IMPACTS (J. Chem. Inf. Model., 2012, 52, 2471-2483). This update is evaluated on newly curated, fully annotated datasets containing over 2,400 datapoints and spanning nine human isoforms; these datasets are released to the community in MOL2 and JSON formats. Technical implementations presented in this work include 1) development of a three-dimensional solvent-accessible surface area correction to the precomputed activation energies, 2) design and integration of a highly efficient L-BFGS optimizer, and 3) elimination of a filter that had been historically used to remove unproductive binding modes. We follow these updates with extensive benchmarking and analysis on the newly curated datasets, where we show 1) achievement of a global Top-2 accuracy of ~75% across the nine isoforms and 2) the effective computational cost using the new optimizer was less than 1 minute per metabolite for eight of the nine isoforms. Finally, we present six real-world case studies comprised of approved drugs and discontinued clinical candidates. These case studies illustrate both the practical value and the remaining limitations of our approach.

papers.title: Hyperlocal PM2.5 Exposure and Health Burden Disparities Revealed by a Taxi-Based Mobile Monitoring Platform in Shenzhen
papers.abstract: Although fine particles (PM 2.5 ) concentrations in China have declined over the past decade, exposure disparities persist at hyperlocal scales. We conducted a six-month mobile monitoring campaign in Shenzhen, where four taxis with calibrated low-cost sensors gathered 24.6 million 1 Hz measurements (~3,700 hours) across 550 km² and 7.3 million residents. We developed a novel application of a multi-source XGBoost (MS-XGB) framework that integrates mobile and fixed-site station data to reconstruct a road-network PM 2.5 dataset at 30 m × 1 h resolution, filling 98% of missing observations. Validation demonstrates strong agreement with both mobile observations (R 2 = 0.97) and data from fixed regulatory monitoring stations (Pearson r = 0.82). We used the road-network dataset to generate a 100 m × 100 m population grid exposure map and benchmarked it against two conventional exposure assessment approaches that rely solely on fixed-site regulatory stations. Relative to MS-XGB, conventional methods systematically underestimated long-term PM 2.5 exposure, with grid-level differences of up to 15 μg/m³. Population-weighted mean exposure was higher in urban villages (16.51 µg/m³) than in other urban areas (14.41 µg/m³), with hotspots 52.5% more likely to occur in urban villages. In Longhua, high exposure was concentrated specifically in urban villages, indicating that district-level averages can mask substantial intra-district heterogeneity. In Nanshan, 40% of elderly residents live in high-exposure areas, compared with 34% of children aged 0–14 and 33% of adults aged 15–59, suggesting that older adults bear a disproportionate exposure burden and face elevated health risks. Our findings demonstrate that mobile-monitoring-based hyperlocal exposure assessment is essential for revealing true PM 2.5 exposure inequalities across population groups and spatial environments that are overlooked by conventional fixed-site approaches.

papers.title: Understanding Differential Chemical Activities of Eutectic Gallium Indium (eGaIn) Thin Films with Fluorinated Analytes using Raman Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Gallium oxide (Ga2O3) forms on the surface of eutectic gallium indium (eGaIn) alloy in air; In the presence of water, it transforms to gallium oxide monohydroxide, GaO(OH). During such transformation, it is challenging to differentiate the activities of the oxides while adsorbing solutes from the solvent. Herein, we address this challenge by investigating the temporal evolution of eGaIn thin films during adsorption of dilute organofluorines in water. We identify five hours as the stability threshold to obtain a water-modified thin film. Leveraging both fresh and five-hour-modified films in parallel, we distinguish water-specific changes and differentiate the signals uniquely caused by fluorinated analytes. The modified GaO(OH) interface demonstrates increased hydrophilicity for microdroplet studies and structural stability under high-energy (20 kV) electron beam irradiation. We leverage Frontier Molecular Orbital (FMO) theory to predict that the GaO(OH) surface is also a reactive catalytic interface. In the presence of the GaO(OH) surface and UVA irradiation, short-chain (HFBA) and long-chain (PFOA) fluorinated compounds exhibited altered interfacial activity. We leveraged Raman spectroscopy throughout our study to differentiate the in situ activities of Ga2O3 and GaO(OH). Our investigations will be useful for differentiating fresh and modified oxide dynamics during in situ interfacial studies or wet chemical measurements.

papers.title: A Solid-Phase Platform for Site-Specific Thiolation and Thioether Functionalization of DNA Oligonucleotides
papers.abstract: Thionucleobases provide distinctive hydrogen-bonding, electronic, and photochemical properties, but their site-specific incorporation into DNA often requires specialized sulfurcontaining phosphoramidites and multistep monomer synthesis. Here, we establish a unified protocol using sodium hydrosulfide (NaSH) and 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene (DBU) for direct on-support conversion of 8-bromo-2′-deoxyadenosine (Br 8 dA) to 8-thio-2′deoxyadenosine (s 8 dA), late-stage C8 thioether diversification, and concurrent conversion of Br 8 dA and 4-triazolylthymidine within a single DNA strand. Electrophilic precursor nucleosides were incorporated by standard solid-phase synthesis and subsequently converted while the oligonucleotide remained support-bound. Conversion of Br 8 dA to s 8 dA was first demonstrated using 2-(trimethylsilyl)ethanethiol and subsequently achieved directly with NaSH·xH2O, eliminating the need for a separate fluoride-mediated deprotection step. Substitution at the C8 was compatible with mixed sequences, multiple modifications, and a range of aliphatic and aromatic thiols, enabling late-stage installation of diverse sulfurcontaining functionalities. Application of the same support-bound protocol to 4-triazolylthymidine afforded DNA containing one or more 4-thiothymidine (s 4 T) residues, and both thionucleobases could be generated within the same strand. Products were characterized by strong-anion-exchange high-performance liquid chromatography and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. This workflow shifts sulfur installation from specialized monomer synthesis to a simple late-stage conversion and provides practical access to site-specifically thiolated and C8-thioether-functionalized DNA.

papers.title: Hydrophobic Interaction as the Result of Interfacial Frustration
papers.abstract: The hydrophobic effect is one of the most consequential organizing principles in molecular biology, laying the foundation for explanation of concepts like protein folding, molecular recognition, membrane self-assembly and allosteric communication. Its conceptual description remains dependent primarily on a framework established in the mid-twentieth century, as per which, hydrophobic association is driven primarily by the entropic release of water molecules ordered around non-polar surfaces. The framework, while thermodynamically correct, is incomplete in some ways that have become increasingly consequential as structural, dynamic and calorimetric data have been accumulated over the years. In this paper, I propose a reframing of the hydrophobic effect in terms of interfacial frustration- a continuous, geometry sensitive incompatibility between the hydrogen bond requirements of liquid water and non-polar surfaces it is forced to accommodate. This paper argues that hydrophobic association represents the resolution of this frustration, rather than the mere expulsion of constrained solvent. This reframing provides a unified mechanistic account of phenomena that the classical picture cannot explain alone, or treats as separate problems: the geometry dependence of hydrophobic association strength, the qualitative distinction between small-solute and extended-surface hydrophobicity, the thermodynamic crossover with temperature and the propagation of allosteric signals through hydrophobic protein cores. This paper also proposes that hydrophobic cores in proteins are not passive burial sites, but active and dynamic modulators of a distributed frustration landscape. Allosteric communication through these cores operates through cooperative frustration redistribution, a mechanism distinct from classical strain propagation, but consistent with the growing body of evidence that allostery frequently proceeds through changes in protein dynamics rather than average structure. This framework generates specific, experimentally testable predictions that distinguish it from both the classical entropic model and existing density functional theories of hydrophobicity

papers.title: How Fast Does a Glass Forget? LandscapeConnectivity, Not Barrier Height, Sets the Rateof Memory Erasure under Repeated ThermalCycling
Machine learning-enabled prediction of dynamic vertical triplet energies underscores the role of vibrational anharmonicity in energy transfer
papers.abstract: The concept of triplet energy has long served as the operative predictor of energy transfer reactivity in photochemistry, yet its reliable computational determination remains challenging for many organic systems. The recently introduced dynamic vertical triplet energy (DvTE) framework recasts triplet energy as a statistical ensemble of instantaneous vertical gaps sampled from molecular dynamics trajectories, achieving mean absolute errors of 1.7 kcal/mol against experimental data, but at a computational cost that limits its broader application. Here, DvTE-ML is introduced, which extends machine-learned interatomic potentials to dynamic, ensemble-based prediction of excited-state properties. Built by fine-tuning the MACE-OMOL foundation model, DvTE-ML incorporates path integral molecular dynamics to capture nuclear quantum effects explicitly, alongside an iterative filtering workflow that addresses a state-error contamination risk intrinsic to open-shell training data. Applied to a diverse set of 52 organic molecules, including biologically relevant systems previously intractable at the reference level of theory, DvTE-ML matches the accuracy of the original DvTE framework. Beyond this validation, higher-resolution sampling reveals that gap distributions can deviate from the normal form previously assumed, with vibrational anharmonicity producing skewed distributions, providing additional insights into the mechanisms of triplet energy transfer.

papers.title: An analytical potential energy surface and variational transition-state theory kinetics of the NH3 + Br → NH2 + HBr hydrogen-abstraction reaction
papers.abstract: We report the first full-dimensional analytical potential energy surface (PES) and a variational transitionstate theory (VTST) study of the endothermic gas-phase reaction NH3 + Br −−→ NH2 + HBr, completing the halogen series (NH3 + F, Cl, Br) of the group’s analytical surfaces. Stationary points and energetics were benchmarked at the CCSD(T)/CBS level with the bromine 3d shell frozen; a −3.51 kcal/mol spinorbit correction was added to the NH3 + Br asymptote for the Br(2P) splitting. The benchmark locates a genuine, product-like (Hammond) saddle 17.6 kcal/mol above reactants but submerged 2.1 kcal/mol below the NH2+HBr asymptote (zero-point-and spin–orbit-corrected). A valence-bond/molecular-mechanics PES was calibrated to reproduce these stationary points to better than 0.25 kcal/mol; it retains an exact analytical gradient and dedicated van der Waals wells for the entrance (NH3···Br) and exit (NH2···HBr) complexes. Canonical variational theory with multidimensional tunneling (µOMT) yields forward rate constants over 200 K to 2000 K. Because the adiabatic barrier lies below the product asymptote, the tunneling coefficient is unity and the reverse reaction NH2 +HBr −−→ NH3 +Br exhibits a negative apparent activation energy, as measured for the carbon analogue CH3 +HBr. Quasi-classical trajectories on the same surface, once product zero-point leakage is accounted for, reproduce the variational forward rate as an independent check of the barrier. In the absence of experimental data, the forward rate constants are presented as predictions anchored to the high-level energetics.

papers.title: Fully Atomistic Vibrational Free Energy of Molecular Crystals Using Distributed Multipole Moments
papers.abstract: Predicting the most stable crystal structure of a given molecule at given temperature and pressure remains challenging. While many crystal structure prediction (CSP) methods focus on identifying the structures with the lowest lattice energy at 0 K, there is growing recognition that accurate predictions require evaluating the vibrational free energy at the temperature(s) of interest. In current workflows, such evaluation is either carried out on a few putative structures using computationally demanding atomistic electronic structure calculations or on a larger number of structures using less expensive and less accurate force field approaches under the rigid-body approximation. There is thus a need for methods that offer a better compromise between accuracy and computational cost. We present, for the first time, lattice dynamics expressions that allow for a fully atomistic treatment of molecular flexibility with a force field commonly used in CSP, where electrostatic interactions are modelled with distributed multipole moments. We implement these expressions in the CrystalDynamics algorithm to calculate dispersion curves, phonon densities of states and vibrational free energies. We demonstrate the application of CrystalDynamics to molecular crystals of three compounds of increasing size and flexibility. The use of analytical derivations results in an efficient evaluation of the free energy of molecular crystals. Our work facilitates the study of relative stability as a function of temperature, enabling the evaluation of enantiotropic transitions between crystal forms. Thanks to its low computational cost, the approach can be integrated into CSP protocols to bridge the gap between static lattice energies at 0 K and temperature-dependent free energies.

papers.title: Mind the coverage gap: The crucial importance of the pH- and potential-dependent surface coverage in oxygen reduction electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: Understanding the origins of oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity and selectivity on gold electrodes remains a longstanding puzzle in electrocatalysis. In particular, it remains unclear why Au(100) in alkaline media is exceptionally active and selective toward the 4-electron ORR while acidic conditions and other gold surfaces catalyze exclusively 2-electron ORR. We address this question through extensive grand-canonical density functional theory calculations and investigate the pH- and potential-dependent surface coverage and its effect on ORR thermodynamics and kinetics on Au(111) and Au(100) electrodes. Our results reveal that ORR thermodynamics and kinetics are highly sensitive to pH- and potential-dependent surface coverage, an effect largely neglected in previous computational studies. The key steps governing ORR activity and selectivity – O 2 adsorption and O–O bond cleavage – are influenced even more strongly by surface coverage than by electrode potential. By integrating pH- and potential-dependent surface coverages with elementary reaction thermodynamics and kinetics, we propose a mechanism that consistently explains a broad range of voltammetric observations on ORR activity and selectivity trends on Au(100) and Au(111) across reaction conditions; neglecting coverage effects leads to qualitatively incorrect mechanistic predictions. Our findings demonstrate that ORR electrocatalysis on gold is not governed only by the intrinsic properties of pristine surfaces. Instead, ORR thermodynamics, kinetics, mechanisms, activity, and selectivity depend explicitly on the interplay between pH, electrode potential, surface coverage, and adsorbate–adsorbate interactions which together define the local reaction environment. More broadly, our work establishes the central importance of pH- and potential-dependent surface coverage in (computational) electrocatalysis.

papers.title: Chemically Neutral, Electrokinetically Charged: Ligand Shell Thickness Governs the Zeta Potential and In Vivo Fate of Ultrasmall HfO2 Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Nanoparticles are extensively explored in biological contexts, and while their core composition determines their specific functionality, surface chemistry governs their interactions with the biological environment. In this work, we used ultrasmall (d < 5 nm) hafnium oxide nanoparticles as a model system, given their biocompatibility and established use in contrast-enhanced X-ray computed tomography and external-beam radiotherapy. We systematically compared three surface ligands featuring the same high-affinity nitrocatechol anchoring group but different terminal moieties: a short ethylene glycol (EG) oligomer, a 2 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) polymer, and a short zwitterionic (ZW) chain. Despite the neutral character of all ligand tails, only the long PEG chains yielded nanoparticles with a near-neutral zeta potential. The short ligands produced nanoparticles with significantly negative zeta potentials (-30 mV), which was found to be an essential component of their colloidal stability. NPs stabilized with short EG or ZW ligands exhibited enhanced uptake by THP-1 macrophages in vitro and short circulation times in vivo in zebrafish larvae, despite suppressed protein corona formation on ZW nanoparticles. The ZW nanoparticles thus present antifouling but not stealth behavior. In contrast, nanoparticles stabilized with long PEG chains largely escaped detection by the phagocyte system. They exhibited prolonged circulation and extravasation in the zebrafish larva model. Zeta potential showed the strongest correlation with macrophage uptake and biodistribution. It reflects the combined effect of surface charge and steric screening. These results highlight the need for long ligand tails for the design of targeted nanomaterials for therapeutic of imaging applications, which require long circulation times.

papers.title: Fragment-Based Representation Learning for Polymers and Heterogeneous Formulations
Triplet Pruning and Spatial Decomposition in M3GNet: Accuracy and Memory Trade-offs in Scaling Graph Neural Network Potentials
Accelerating Lead Optimization away from Anti-Targets: Navigating the Structural Complexity of Promiscuous ADMET Proteins
papers.abstract: The development of a small-molecule suitable for clinical use involves optimization of ligand binding to an identified target protein but also frequently the reduction of binding to a variety of anti-target proteins known to pose translational risk. These anti-targets, often referred to as ADMET proteins, often contain large, highly flexible binding sites leading to promiscuous binding of small molecules. This property often frustrates efforts to execute structure-based design against these anti-targets. Here we demonstrate the application of a combination of induced fit docking and free energy perturbation to structurally enable several of the most common anti-targets: cytochrome P450 isoforms 3A4 and 2D6, the hERG ion channel, and PXR. Crucially, the enforcement of a consensus binding mode across a congeneric series allowed for the efficient exploration of a wide range of receptor conformation space. Results are presented for both public retrospective datasets and prospective application in active drug discovery programs.

papers.title: Gas-Phase Fragmentation in Mass Spectrometry Informs the Shape and Topology of Thiolated Metal Nanoclusters
papers.abstract: Thiolated metal nanoclusters (NCs), comprising a metal core protected by outer-layer staple motifs, have attracted widespread interest due to their promising applications in catalysis, biosensing, and biomedicine. While mass spectrometry (MS) is widely used to determine the chemical composition of metal NCs via intact mass measurement, its potential for in-depth structural analysis via gas-phase fragmentation in tandem MS (MS/MS) has been relatively underexplored and mostly focused on the collision induced dissociation (CID) technique involving gas collisions. Herein, we systematically compared the fragmentation pathways between CID and an alternative method, surface induced dissociation (SID), using model Au NCs featuring distinct symmetries and structural motifs. We show that gas-phase fragments in CID and SID overall shared the common fragmentation behavior of breaking the outer staples of Au NCs, but with different preferences in the location of bond cleavages. In addition, SID showed characteristic Au losses in ellipsoidal Au NCs with trimeric staples; and fragmentation efficiency in CID and SID varied differentially according to the shape of the NCs. Building on these findings, we applied the method to study non-crystallizable Au-Ag NCs with heterogeneous stoichiometry. The SID fragmentation data helped locate the Au and Ag atoms, providing valuable insights into the synthetic pathway of the NCs, which was otherwise inaccessible experimentally. Together, these results support SID as a complementary MS/MS tool for metal NCs, with particular promise for heterogeneous systems like the mixed NCs that cannot be easily crystallized.

papers.title: A Physically Grounded Discrete Causal Recording Formalism Based on Spatiotemporal Isolation for Surface Propagation Pattern Reconstruction
Embedded Morgan Fingerprints for more efficient molecular property predictions with machine learning
papers.abstract: High-dimensional molecular fingerprints have become a quiet bottleneck for chemical machine learning, where bit collisions in large, chemically diverse datasets and escalating computational costs constrain model discovery. This work introduces the embedded Morgan Fingerprint (eMFP), a post-processing scheme that compresses standard Morgan Fingerprints into continuously valued, lower-dimensional representations governed by a compression factor q. Applied to three molecular datasets of increasing size (RedDB, Non-Fullerene Acceptors and QM9), five regression models and four encoding configurations under scaffold-aware nested cross-validation, eMFP maintains the predictive power of full-length fingerprints for tree-based methods at moderate compression (q≤32), while exhibiting more model- and setting-dependent behaviour elsewhere. Its continuous outputs pair favourably with Fourier Feature Neural Networks, where they interact more naturally with sinusoidal feature mappings than the original binary fingerprints, and consistently shorten training times per trial. Together, these results position eMFP as a simple, drop-in route to more scalable molecular representations that retain accuracy while easing the computational burden of model development.

papers.title: Fundamental Investigations into the Activity and Stability of Iron-Based Bimetallic Catalysts for the Oxygen Evolution Reaction
papers.abstract: Engineering electrocatalyst resistance to degradation in alkaline media remains a major challenge for developing stable, earth-abundant oxygen evolution reaction (OER) anodes. Here, we combined acid–base titration and X-ray fluorescence to quantify Fe dissolution from a series of bimettalic FexMy (oxy)hydroxides deposited on Fe foils (My = Sn, Hf, Mn, Se) at 1.66–2.11 VRHE, showing that apparently stable current densities and cycle voltametery alone can mask significant electrode degradation. After initial restructuring (~2 h), end-of-life anodes showed steady-state dissolution rates of 0.15–0.67 mgFe cm⁻² h⁻¹ near OER onset (~1.75 VRHE). Across alloys, dissolution rates and OER overpotentials correlated with the Fe–My electronegativity difference. Dissolution rates were highest for those alloys where My was less electronegative than Fe, and XPS revealed a more reduced surface with higher concentrations of hydroxoligands. Spin-polarized DFT+U shows Sn reduces neighboring Fe atoms, shifting the potential-limiting OER step to Fe–O* formation, lowering its formation free energy (consistent with a reduced OER overpotential); but elongating Fe-O bonds (perhaps accelerating dissolution). Generalizing these results toward future work, we suggest that the dissolution resistance of FeOOH surfaces may be controlled by alloy-driven modulation of their protonation state (revealed by XPS) and Fe-O bond character (probed by DFT).

papers.title: Electronic Control of Composition in Multicomponent oDCPD Fragment Functionalization
papers.abstract: Deconstruction of poly(dicyclopentadiene)-co-cleavable comonomer (pDCPD-co-CC) thermosets generates oligomers with C=C bonds amenable to chemical functionalization; strategies for doing so remain limited. We report a one-step electrophilic multicomponent post-polymerization modification of deconstruction-relevant model hydroxyl-terminated poly(dicyclopentadiene) oligomers (oDCPD-OH), installing bromine, ether, and sulfonamide motifs. Sulfonamide substituent electronics influence apparent alkene conversion and sulfonamide functional group installation in the isolated oligomers, with electron-poor aryl sulfonamides yielding higher functionalization than electron-rich aryl sulfonamides (32 mol%, and 1 mol%, respectively). Mixed p-CF3/p-NO2 sulfonamide feeds (9:1–1:3) were examined, systematically varying oligomer composition. The incorporated fraction of p-NO2 ranges from 18 to 86%, consistently exceeding its feed fraction and indicating preferential incorporation under competitive conditions. Functionalized fragments show composition-dependent thermal decomposition, with thermal decomposition temperature (Td,5%) ranging from 126 to 176 °C. These results establish electronically guided multicomponent post-polymerization functionalization as a strategy for systematically modulating oDCPD fragment composition.

papers.title: Approaching Chemical Accuracy for Neutral and Ionic Water Clusters with the bn-r2SCAN Meta-GGA
papers.abstract: Gas-phase neutral and ion–water clusters are fundamental models for hydrogen bonding, many-body interactions, proton transfer, and ionic hydration in liquid water and aqueous environments, and they are stringent tests for density functional approximations: semilocal functionals without exact exchange or an explicit self-interaction correction have typically described their interaction and binding energies poorly. The non-self-consistent SCAN@HF approach was recently shown to describe water clusters and liquid water with high accuracy, but subsequent analysis demonstrated that this performance arises largely from cancellation between a substantial functional-driven error and an opposing error introduced by the overlocalized Hartree–Fock density. Here we assess a new self-consistent meta-generalized gradient approximation, bonded-norm r2SCAN (bn-r2SCAN), for neutral, protonated, and deprotonated water clusters and for alkali-and halide–water complexes. bn-r2SCAN approaches chemical accuracy across these diverse systems, with overall mean unsigned binding-energy errors of 0.33− 1.04 kcal/mol for the benchmark sets considered, and substantially improves upon r2SCAN. Error decomposition shows that this accuracy does not rest on the near-total cancellation of large opposing errors underlying SCAN@HF: for the BEGDB dataset, the mean functional-and density-driven errors of bn-r2SCAN are 0.34 and −0.89 kcal/mol, and even for the largest clusters both remain a small fraction of the total binding energy, whereas for SCAN@HF the functional-driven error of SCAN and the nonvariational density over-localization introduced by the Hartree–Fock density each exceed 5 kcal/mol and cancel to within a few tenths. Notably, bn-r2SCAN was parametrized using band gaps and lattice constants (not weak bonds) of simple solids, making its performance for aqueous clusters a demanding test of transferability and identifying it as a self-consistent and computationally efficient route to modeling water and aqueous systems.

papers.title: Water hydrogen bond network elongation below the lower critical solution temperature in aqueous triethylamine solution probed by soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy
papers.abstract: The lower critical solution temperature (LCST) mechanism of aqueous triethylamine (TEA) solution was investigated by the element-specific observation of molecular interactions using soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). The H 2 O‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds were probed by O K-edge XAS, and the hydrophobic interactions of TEA and TEA‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds were probed by C and N K-edge XAS. Molecular interactions in aqueous TEA solutions at temperatures below the LCST were analyzed using radial distribution functions obtained from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Temperature-dependent changes in the XAS spectra were evaluated by inner-shell calculations using snapshots from MD simulations. These studies revealed that the LCST mechanism of aqueous TEA solution is governed by the balance of H 2 O‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions of TEA, and TEA‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds. Aqueous TEA solution is miscible below the LCST, where the H 2 O‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds elongate owing to the TEA‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions of TEA. The H 2 O‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds near the LCST are closer to those of liquid water owing to the weakening of the TEA‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds. The hydrophobic interactions of TEA are also enhanced owing to the strong H 2 O‒H 2 O hydrogen bonds, resulting in liquid‒liquid phase separation above the LCST. These three factors provide a framework for interpreting the LCST mechanisms of amphiphilic molecules, polymers, and soft matter related to protein folding and DNA packing.

papers.title: Green synthesis of SnO2 nanoparticles using Brassica oleracea leaf extract for dual-functional photocatalytic degradation of Malachite Green and adsorptive removal of Pb(II) and Cr(VI)
papers.abstract: Green-synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles using Brassica oleracea leaf extract (BO-SnO2 NPs) were prepared and evaluated for photocatalytic dye degradation and heavy metal adsorption. The biosynthesized BO-SnO2 NPs were characterized by UV-Vis, FTIR (Sn-O-Sn at 583 cm-1), XRD, FESEM, and EDX analyses. XRD analysis revealed a tetragonal rutile crystalline structure with an average crystallite size of 5.32 nm. FESEM showed spherical particles with a mean size of ∼22.65 nm, indicating that the observed particles are agglomerates of several individual crystallites. In photocatalytic experiments, BO-SnO2 NPs achieved a maximum degradation of 95.00% for Malachite Green dye under UV irradiation within 120 min. Batch adsorption studies for Pb(II) and Cr(VI) showed maximum removal of 65.0% at pH 6.0 and 61.5% at pH 2.0 within 60 min, respectively. The equilibrium adsorption capacity increased from 2.60 to 15.60 mg/g for Pb(II) and from 2.46 to 14.70 mg/g for Cr(VI) as the initial concentration increased from 2 to 16 mg/L. The equilibrium data fitted well to both Langmuir and Freundlich isotherm models with R2 ≥ 0.99, with maximum adsorption capacities of 29.41 mg/g for Pb(II) and 28.65 mg/g for Cr(VI) (Langmuir). The RL values ranging from 0.317 to 0.804 and 1/n values of 0.723 and 0.740 confirmed favorable adsorption. The results suggest that BO-SnO2 NPs are a promising eco-friendly material for wastewater treatment.

papers.title: Self-recycling Fenton chemistry through the ordered hydration shells of Fe
papers.abstract: The century-old Fenton reaction has been constrained by the kinetic bottleneck of Fe3+/Fe2+ cycling, which demands excessive iron dosing and generates hazardous sludge. Here we report that Fe3+ ions intrinsically bypass this limitation through a remote through-space ligand effect that induces long-range ordering of water molecules beyond the first coordination shell. This ordered hydration network functions as a visible-to-red-light antenna via a collective water-network-to-metal charge transfer mechanism, continuously generating electrons that reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+ without exogenous photocatalysts or chemical reductants.
